name: Characteristic Organic Reactions
section: 13. An Introduction to AS Level Organic Chemistry

parts.problemMd: Which pair of homologous series does **not** have the same C:H ratio in their general formulae?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- A homologous series is a group with the same functional group and similar chemical properties.
- Alkanes and alkenes are different homologous series as they have different functional groups.
- Alkanes have single carbon-carbon bonds and the general formula C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n+2</sub>
- Alkenes have a double carbon-carbon bond and the general formula C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n</sub>

![Structural diagrams of an alkane (C–C single bond) and an alkene (C=C double bond) illustrating the different bonding in these two homologous series](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/13-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistry/13-2-characteristic-organic-reactions/assets/001-structural-diagrams-of-an-alkane-c-c-single-bond.jpg)

**A** is incorrect as aldehydes and ketones both have the general formula C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n</sub>O, giving a C:H ratio of 1:2.

**C** is incorrect as aldehydes (C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n</sub>O) and alkenes (C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n</sub>) both have a C:H ratio of 1:2.

**D** is incorrect as carboxylic acids and esters both have the general formula C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n</sub>O<sub>2</sub>, giving a C:H ratio of 1:2.

parts.problemMd:
The following mechanism shows hydrogen cyanide reacting with propanone.

![Two-step nucleophilic addition mechanism showing CN- attacking the carbonyl carbon of propanone to form a tetrahedral intermediate, followed by proton transfer from HCN to give 2-hydroxy-2-methylpropanenitrile and regenerate CN-](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/13-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistry/13-2-characteristic-organic-reactions/assets/005-two-step-nucleophilic-addition-mechanism-showing.jpg)

Which statement is **not** correct?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- The reaction between hydrogen cyanide and propanone is a nucleophilic addition reaction.
- A nucleophile is an electron-pair donor.
- An electrophile is an electron-pair acceptor.
- In this reaction, CN<sup>-</sup> is donating a pair of electrons (as shown by the arrow) and the carbon in propanone is accepting them.

**B** is incorrect as this is heterolytic bond breaking. Only one atom receives both electrons from the covalent bond, making this heterolytic.

**C** is incorrect as propanone is a ketone, so this statement is true.

**D** is incorrect as this is an example of a nucleophilic addition reaction.

choices.label: A
choices.textMd: The organic molecule acts as an electrophile and becomes less saturated.

choices.label: B
choices.textMd: The organic molecule acts as an electrophile and becomes more saturated.

choices.label: C
choices.textMd: The organic molecule acts as a nucleophile and becomes less saturated.

choices.label: D
choices.textMd: The organic molecule acts as a nucleophile and becomes more saturated.

parts.problemMd: Which statement describes an electrophilic addition reaction?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- If a reaction is electrophilic, the inorganic reagent is acting as an electrophile (electron-pair acceptor).
- Therefore, the organic reactant acts as a nucleophile (electron-pair donor). This is usually because the organic molecule is an alkene, and one of the electron pairs in the double bond is donated to the inorganic reagent, e.g. HBr.
- In an addition reaction, the organic molecule gains atoms.
- In an electrophilic addition reaction, an alkene is converted to a halogenoalkane and therefore becomes more saturated.

**A** is incorrect as the inorganic reagent (e.g. HBr) acts as the electrophile, not the organic molecule. In addition reactions the organic molecule gains atoms, becoming more saturated.

**B** is incorrect as the inorganic reagent acts as the electrophile, not the organic molecule. In electrophilic addition, the organic molecule acts as the nucleophile.

**C** is incorrect as addition reactions result in the organic molecule gaining atoms, making it more saturated, not less saturated.

parts.problemMd: Which species acts as a nucleophile?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- A nucleophile is an electron-pair donor; it is either a negative ion or has a lone pair of electrons capable of being donated.

- OH<sup>-</sup> has three lone pairs of electrons and a negative charge, making it a nucleophile.

**A** is incorrect as ethane has no lone pairs and will not act as a nucleophile.

**B** is incorrect as a free radical has an unpaired electron and reacts via homolytic (radical) mechanisms. It does not donate or accept electron pairs, so it is neither a nucleophile nor an electrophile.

**C** is incorrect as a hydrogen ion has no electrons. It accepts electron pairs and is therefore an electrophile, not a nucleophile.

parts.problemMd: What type of reaction occurs when 1-chloroethane reacts with aqueous sodium hydroxide?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- When a halogenoalkane reacts with aqueous sodium or potassium hydroxide, the OH<sup>-</sup> ion replaces the halogen, forming an alcohol.
- The hydroxide ion is a **nucleophile** (an electron-pair donor).
- The hydroxide ion takes the place of the halogen in the compound, so this is a **substitution** reaction.
- The overall mechanism is nucleophilic substitution.

  - The reaction can be summarised as:

![Nucleophilic substitution mechanism showing OH- attacking the delta-positive carbon of 1-chloroethane, displacing Cl- to give ethanol](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/13-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistry/13-2-characteristic-organic-reactions/assets/004-nucleophilic-substitution-mechanism-showing-oh-a.jpg)

**A** is incorrect as electrophilic addition involves an electrophile attacking a C=C double bond. 1-chloroethane has no double bond, and OH<sup>-</sup> is a nucleophile, not an electrophile.

**B** is incorrect as electrophilic substitution involves an electrophile. OH<sup>-</sup> is a nucleophile, not an electrophile.

**C** is incorrect as nucleophilic addition adds atoms across a double bond. 1-chloroethane has no C=C double bond. Instead, the halogen is replaced by OH<sup>-</sup> in a substitution reaction.

parts.problemMd:
Which row gives correct statements about a homologous series?

|   | **same general formula** | **similar chemical properties** | **gradual change in physical properties** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A** | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| **B** | ✓ | ⨯ | ✓ |
| **C** | ⨯ | ✓ | ✓ |
| **D** | ✓ | ✓ | ⨯ |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- A homologous series is a family of carbon compounds that all contain the same functional group.
- All members can be represented by the same general formula, e.g. C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n+2</sub> for alkanes.
- Since all members contain the same functional group, they have similar chemical properties and undergo the same types of reactions.
- As successive members increase in size by one –CH<sub>2</sub>– unit, their intermolecular forces increase.

  - This results in a gradual change in physical properties, such as increasing boiling points and densities.

**B** is incorrect as members of a homologous series do have similar chemical properties, because they all contain the same functional group and undergo the same types of reactions.

**C** is incorrect as all members of a homologous series share the same general formula by definition (e.g. C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n+2</sub> for alkanes).

**D** is incorrect as the gradual increase in chain length does produce a gradual change in physical properties, such as increasing boiling points and densities.

parts.problemMd: Which diagram correctly shows the heterolytic fission of the C–Cl bond in 1-chloropropane?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- Heterolytic fission involves the movement of a pair of electrons.
- This means that a double-headed arrow is required.
- To form a chloride ion, Cl<sup>-</sup>, the double-headed arrow should go from the centre of the bond to the chlorine atom.

**A** is incorrect as the electron pair (double-headed arrow) is going to the carbon atom, which would result in a CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub><sup>-</sup> ion and a Cl<sup>+</sup> ion.

**C** is incorrect as there are 2 double-headed arrows, which would suggest the movement of 4 electrons from a single covalent bond that contains only 2 electrons.

**D** is incorrect as this is the correct diagram for homolytic fission of the C–Cl bond, which forms a CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub><sup>•</sup> radical and a Cl<sup>•</sup> radical.

parts.problemMd:
The reaction sequence below shows a pair of reaction types.

CH<sub>3</sub>CH=CHCH<sub>3</sub> $\overset{\mathrm{HI} \mathrm{in} \mathrm{CH}_{3}\mathrm{COOH}}{\rightarrow}$ CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CHICH<sub>3</sub> $\xrightarrow{NaOH ( \text{aq} )}$ CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH(OH)CH<sub>3</sub>

Which row in the table identifies reaction 1 and reaction 2?

|   | **Reaction 1** | **Reaction 2** |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | Nucleophilic addition | Nucleophilic substitution |
| **B** | Electrophilic addition | Electrophilic substitution |
| **C** | Nucleophilic addition | Electrophilic substitution |
| **D** | Electrophilic addition | Nucleophilic substitution |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- The first reaction is electrophilic addition because:

  - HI is acting as an electrophile and is accepting a bonding pair of electrons from the alkene double bond; therefore the reaction is electrophilic.

  - The resulting organic molecule contains 2 more atoms than the initial organic molecule; therefore it is an addition reaction.

![Electrophilic addition mechanism of HI to but-2-ene, showing overall equation, polarisation of HI and attack on the double bond forming a carbocation intermediate, and nucleophilic capture by I- to give 2-iodobutane](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/13-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistry/13-2-characteristic-organic-reactions/assets/002-electrophilic-addition-mechanism-of-hi-to-but-2-.jpg)

- The second reaction is nucleophilic substitution because:

  - The OH<sup>-</sup> ion from NaOH is acting as a nucleophile and is donating a bonding pair of electrons to the organic molecule; therefore the reaction is nucleophilic.

  - In the resulting organic molecule, the hydroxyl (OH) group has replaced the iodine; therefore it is a substitution reaction.

![Nucleophilic substitution mechanism showing OH- attacking the delta-positive carbon of 2-iodobutane, displacing iodide ion to give 2-butanol](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/13-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistry/13-2-characteristic-organic-reactions/assets/003-nucleophilic-substitution-mechanism-showing-oh-a.jpg)

**A** is incorrect as the first reaction is not nucleophilic addition. HI acts as the electrophile by accepting electrons from the alkene double bond, making reaction 1 electrophilic addition.

**B** is incorrect as the second reaction is not electrophilic substitution. OH<sup>-</sup> is a nucleophile that replaces the iodine atom, making reaction 2 nucleophilic substitution.

**C** is incorrect as the first reaction is not nucleophilic addition. HI acts as the electrophile, not as a nucleophile, making reaction 1 electrophilic addition.

parts.problemMd:
The methyl group, CH<sub>3</sub>, can exist as an anion, a cation or a free radical. The CH<sub>3</sub> species can act as a nucleophile, an electrophile or a free radical depending on the number of outer shell electrons on the methyl carbon atom.

How many outer shell electrons must be present for CH<sub>3</sub> to act in these different ways?

|   | **nucleophile** | **electrophile** | **free radical** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A** | 6 | 8 | 7 |
| **B** | 8 | 6 | 7 |
| **C** | 6 | 7 | 8 |
| **D** | 8 | 7 | 6 |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- A nucleophile is a species that donates a pair of electrons.

  - The CH<sub>3</sub> species has a lone pair of electrons when it has 8 outer shell electrons.

- An electrophile is a species that accepts a pair of electrons.

  - An electron-deficient CH<sub>3</sub> species has 6 outer shell electrons.

- To act as a free radical, the CH<sub>3</sub> species must have an unpaired electron, giving 7 outer shell electrons.

**A** is incorrect as the nucleophile and electrophile values are swapped. The nucleophile (lone pair, electron donor) requires 8 outer shell electrons and the electrophile (electron-deficient) requires 6.

**C** is incorrect as the free radical requires 7 outer shell electrons (unpaired electron), not 8. The electrophile requires 6 outer shell electrons, not 7.

**D** is incorrect as the free radical requires 7 outer shell electrons (unpaired electron), not 6. The electrophile requires 6 outer shell electrons, not 7.

parts.problemMd:
Which row correctly describes a nucleophile and an electrophile?

|   | **nucleophile** | **electrophile** |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | Has a lone pair of electrons | Accepts a pair of electrons |
| **B** | Is a negative ion | Is a positive ion |
| **C** | Attacks double bonds | Is only involved in substitution reactions |
| **D** | Accepts a pair of electrons | Has a lone pair of electrons |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- Nucleophiles have a lone pair of electrons and are electron-pair donors.
- Electrophiles accept electron pairs and are electron-pair acceptors.

**B** is incorrect as both nucleophiles and electrophiles can be covalently bonded molecules or atoms. For example, the double bond in alkenes makes them nucleophiles, and the permanent dipole in HBr makes it an electrophile.

**C** is incorrect as nucleophiles react with many functional groups, not just molecules with double bonds. Electrophiles are involved in both addition reactions (e.g. electrophilic addition to alkenes) and substitution reactions (e.g. electrophilic substitution in benzene).

**D** is incorrect as nucleophiles are electron-pair donors and electrophiles are electron-pair acceptors.

name: Shapes of Organic Molecules; σ & π Bonds
section: 13. An Introduction to AS Level Organic Chemistry

parts.problemMd: How many π bonds are present in one molecule of ethene?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- π bonds are formed by the sideways overlap of adjacent p orbitals
- Ethene contains one carbon-carbon double bond (C=C)
- The C=C double bond consists of one σ bond, formed by head-on orbital overlap, and one π bond, formed by sideways overlap of p orbitals

**A** is incorrect as 0 would suggest ethene contains only single bonds with no π bonds present.

**C** is incorrect as 2 would suggest the C=C double bond consists of two π bonds. A double bond consists of one σ bond and one π bond only.

**D** is incorrect as 3 π bonds would require multiple double or triple bonds, which are not present in ethene.

parts.problemMd: Which type of bond is formed by the sideways overlap of p orbitals?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- A π bond is formed by the sideways overlap of adjacent p orbitals above and below the internuclear axis

**A** is incorrect as a dative covalent bond is formed when one atom donates both electrons to a shared pair. It is not formed by the sideways overlap of p orbitals.

**B** is incorrect as a hydrogen bond is an intermolecular force of attraction between an electron-deficient hydrogen atom (bonded to N, O, or F) and a lone pair on a neighbouring electronegative atom. It is not formed by orbital overlap.

**D** is incorrect as a σ bond is formed by the head-on (end-to-end) overlap of atomic orbitals along the internuclear axis, not by sideways overlap.

parts.problemMd:
How many σ bonds and π bonds are present in a double bond?

|   | **σ bonds** | **π bonds** |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | 0 | 2 |
| **B** | 1 | 1 |
| **C** | 1 | 2 |
| **D** | 2 | 0 |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- A double bond consists of one σ bond, formed by the head-on overlap of atomic orbitals, and one π bond, formed by the sideways overlap of p orbitals

**A** is incorrect as a combination of 0 σ bonds and 2 π bonds is not possible. The internuclear axis between two bonded atoms must always be occupied by a σ bond before any π bonds can form.

**C** is incorrect as a combination of 1 σ bond and 2 π bonds is the composition of a triple bond, not a double bond.

**D** is incorrect as a combination of 2 σ bonds and 0 π bonds would suggest a double bond consists of two σ bonds. A double bond always consists of one σ bond and one π bond.

parts.problemMd: What is the hybridisation of the carbon atom in methane?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- Methane contains four σ bonds between the central carbon atom and four hydrogen atoms
- To form four equivalent bonds, the carbon atom hybridises one s orbital and three p orbitals to give four identical sp<sup>3</sup> hybrid orbitals
- Four sp<sup>3</sup> hybrid orbitals arrange themselves tetrahedrally to minimise repulsion

**A** is incorrect as sp hybridisation involves mixing one s orbital and one p orbital, producing two hybrid orbitals. This is associated with triple bonds, such as in ethyne.

**B** is incorrect as sp<sup>2</sup> hybridisation involves mixing one s orbital and two p orbitals, producing three hybrid orbitals. This is associated with double bonds, such as in ethene.

**D** is incorrect as sp<sup>4</sup> hybridisation is not possible. The p subshell contains only three orbitals (p<sub>x</sub>, p<sub>y</sub>, p<sub>z</sub>), so a maximum of three p orbitals can participate in hybridisation with one s orbital.

parts.problemMd: Which molecule is a straight-chain hydrocarbon?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- A straight-chain hydrocarbon consists of a continuous series of carbon atoms without any branches or ring structures
- Propane (CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>) contains a continuous, unbranched chain of three carbon atoms

**A** is incorrect as 2-methylpropane is a branched aliphatic hydrocarbon. The longest continuous chain contains three carbon atoms with a methyl group branching off the central carbon atom.

**B** is incorrect as benzene is an aromatic hydrocarbon. It consists of a planar, cyclic ring of six carbon atoms, not an open chain.

**C** is incorrect as cyclopentane is an alicyclic hydrocarbon. The five carbon atoms form a closed ring rather than an open chain.

parts.problemMd:
Methyl isocyanate, CH<sub>3</sub>NCO, is a toxic liquid which is used in the production of adhesives.

The sequence of atoms in a methyl isocyanate molecule is H<sub>3</sub>C—N=C=O.

What is the approximate angle between the bonds formed by the N atom?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- From the sequence H<sub>3</sub>C—N=C=O, the nitrogen atom forms a single bond with the methyl group and a double bond with the isocyanate carbon
- Nitrogen has 5 valence electrons; after forming these bonds, one lone pair remains
- The nitrogen atom therefore has three regions of electron density: two bonding regions and one lone pair

![Dot-and-cross diagram of the nitrogen atom in methyl isocyanate showing three regions of electron density in a trigonal planar arrangement](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/13-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistry/13-3-shapes-of-organic-molecules--and--bonds/assets/006-dot-and-cross-diagram-of-the-nitrogen-atom-in-me.jpg)

- Three regions of electron density arrange in a trigonal planar geometry, giving an approximate bond angle of 120° (slightly less than 120° due to the greater repulsion from the lone pair)

**A** is incorrect as 107° is the bond angle in ammonia (NH<sub>3</sub>), where nitrogen has three bonding pairs and one lone pair giving a tetrahedral electron geometry. In methyl isocyanate, the nitrogen has three regions of electron density, not four.

**B** is incorrect as 109.5° is the bond angle for a perfect tetrahedral geometry with four bonding pairs and no lone pairs. The nitrogen in methyl isocyanate has three regions of electron density, giving a trigonal planar geometry.

**D** is incorrect as 180° is the bond angle for a linear geometry with only two regions of electron density. The carbon atom in the isocyanate group (—N=C=O) has a 180° bond angle, not the nitrogen atom.

parts.problemMd:
The diagram shows part of the structure of cysteine, an amino acid, with three bond angles labelled.

![Chemical structure of the amino acid cysteine, with bond angles labelled x, y and z ](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/13-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistry/13-3-shapes-of-organic-molecules--and--bonds/assets/005-chemical-structure-of-the-amino-acid-cysteine-wi.png)

What is the correct order of the bond angles *x*, *y* and *z*, from smallest to largest?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- Angle *y*:

  - The central carbon atom has four bond pairs and no lone pairs, giving a tetrahedral geometry with a bond angle of 109.5°
- Angle *x*:

  - The nitrogen atom in the amine group has three bond pairs and one lone pair, giving a trigonal pyramidal geometry with a bond angle of 107°
- Angle *z*:

  - The oxygen atom has two bond pairs and two lone pairs, giving a bent geometry with a bond angle of 104.5°
- The correct size order from smallest to largest is *z* (104.5°) < *x* (107°) < *y* (109.5°)
- All three central atoms have a base tetrahedral electron geometry. Lone pairs repel more strongly than bond pairs, compressing the bond angle by approximately 2.5° per lone pair.

**A** is incorrect as *x* < *y* < *z* would place the oxygen atom as having the largest bond angle. Oxygen has two lone pairs, which cause greater repulsion and produce a smaller bond angle than either carbon or nitrogen.

**B** is incorrect as *x* < *z* < *y* incorrectly assigns a smaller angle to oxygen than to nitrogen. Oxygen has two lone pairs (giving 104.5°), which produce a smaller bond angle than the single lone pair on nitrogen (107°).

**D** is incorrect as *z* < *y* < *x* would suggest the nitrogen atom has the largest bond angle. The tetrahedral carbon atom, with no lone pairs, has the largest bond angle of 109.5°.

parts.problemMd: What is the minimum number of carbon atoms required to form a chiral acyclic alkane?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- For a carbon atom to be a chiral centre, it must be bonded to four different groups
- In an acyclic alkane, the four substituents are limited to hydrogen atoms and alkyl chains
- The four smallest different substituents are: H (0 additional carbons), methyl (1 carbon), ethyl (2 carbons), and propyl (3 carbons)
- Minimum total: 1 (central chiral carbon) + 0 + 1 + 2 + 3 = 7 carbon atoms

![Structural formula of 3-methylhexane showing the chiral centre at carbon 3, bonded to four different groups: a hydrogen atom, a methyl group, an ethyl group, and a propyl group](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/13-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistry/13-3-shapes-of-organic-molecules--and--bonds/assets/004-structural-formula-of-3-methylhexane-showing-the.jpg)

**A** is incorrect as 6 carbon atoms is not sufficient. After the central chiral carbon, only 5 remain. The three smallest different alkyl groups (methyl, ethyl, propyl) require 1 + 2 + 3 = 6 carbons, but only 5 are available. Any valid distribution of 5 carbons among three groups requires two identical groups, which destroys the chiral centre.

**C** is incorrect as 9 carbon atoms, while sufficient, is not the minimum. The smallest chiral acyclic alkane (3-methylhexane) requires only 7 carbon atoms.

**D** is incorrect as 11 carbon atoms, while sufficient, is not the minimum required to form a chiral acyclic alkane.

parts.problemMd: What is the bond angle around an sp<sup>2</sup> hybridised carbon atom?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- An sp<sup>2</sup> hybridised carbon atom has three regions of electron density (three σ bonds and no lone pairs)
- Three regions of electron density arrange in a trigonal planar geometry to minimise repulsion
- A trigonal planar geometry gives bond angles of 120°

**A** is incorrect as 104.5° is the bond angle associated with a central atom having two bond pairs and two lone pairs, such as the oxygen atom in water (H<sub>2</sub>O). Carbon does not have two lone pairs in any stable organic molecule.

**B** is incorrect as 109.5° is the bond angle for a perfect tetrahedral geometry, corresponding to sp<sup>3</sup> hybridisation with four σ bonds and no lone pairs, such as in methane (CH<sub>4</sub>).

**D** is incorrect as 180° is the bond angle for a linear geometry, corresponding to sp hybridisation with only two regions of electron density, such as in ethyne.

parts.problemMd:
The structure of the amino acid cysteine is shown.

![Structural formula of cysteine showing three carbon atoms: the carboxyl carbon with a C=O double bond, the alpha-carbon bonded to four different groups, and the beta-carbon bonded to the thiol group](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/13-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistry/13-3-shapes-of-organic-molecules--and--bonds/assets/001-structural-formula-of-cysteine-showing-three-car.png)

How many carbon atoms in a molecule of cysteine are sp<sup>2</sup> hybridised?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- An atom is sp<sup>2</sup> hybridised when it is surrounded by three regions of electron density, as a double bond counts as one region
- In cysteine, only the carboxyl carbon (-COOH) is bonded to three groups: a hydroxyl (-OH) group, the adjacent carbon, and a C=O double bond
- The alpha-carbon and beta-carbon each form four σ bonds with no double bonds, so both are sp<sup>3</sup> hybridised

**A** is incorrect as there is one sp<sup>2</sup> hybridised carbon atom in cysteine (the carboxyl carbon). A value of 0 would suggest no carbon atom in the molecule contains a double bond.

**C** is incorrect as only one carbon atom (the carboxyl carbon) is sp<sup>2</sup> hybridised. The alpha-carbon has four different single-bond groups attached and is sp<sup>3</sup> hybridised.

**D** is incorrect as only one carbon atom is sp<sup>2</sup> hybridised. The alpha-carbon and beta-carbon each form four σ bonds with no double bonds and are therefore sp<sup>3</sup> hybridised.

parts.problemMd:
Limonene is found in the peel of citrus fruits.

![Skeletal formula of limonene showing a six-membered carbon ring with an isopropenyl substituent and one endocyclic double bond, giving two C=C double bonds in total](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/13-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistry/13-3-shapes-of-organic-molecules--and--bonds/assets/002-skeletal-formula-of-limonene-showing-a-six-membe.png)

How many σ and π bonds are present in this molecule?

|   | **σ** | **π** |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | 12 | 2 |
| **B** | 22 | 4 |
| **C** | 24 | 4 |
| **D** | 26 | 2 |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- Limonene has the molecular formula C<sub>10</sub>H<sub>16</sub>

![Displayed formula of limonene](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/13-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistry/13-3-shapes-of-organic-molecules--and--bonds/assets/003-displayed-formula-of-limonene.png)

- Every covalent bond contains one σ bond

  - The carbon skeleton contains 10 C-C σ bonds and 16 C-H σ bonds
  - This gives 26 σ bonds in total
- Each C=C double bond consists of one σ bond and one π bond:

  - Limonene contains two C=C double bonds
  - This gives 2 π bonds

**A** is incorrect as 12 σ bonds accounts only for the visible bonds in the carbon skeleton and does not include the C-H σ bonds to implicit hydrogen atoms. Each CH, CH<sub>2</sub>, or CH<sub>3</sub> group contains additional σ bonds that must be counted.

**B** is incorrect as 4 π bonds would suggest each double bond contains two π bonds. A C=C double bond consists of one σ bond and one π bond only, giving 2 π bonds for a molecule with two double bonds.

**C** is incorrect as 24 σ bonds and 4 π bonds reflects an undercount of σ bonds and an overcount of π bonds. Not all C-H σ bonds have been included in the total, and each double bond contributes only one π bond.

name: Isomerism: Structural Isomerism & Stereoisomerism
section: 13. An Introduction to AS Level Organic Chemistry

parts.problemMd: Which compound exhibits both optical and geometrical isomerism?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- Optical isomers are isomers that have the same atoms and bonds but different spatial arrangements of the atoms.

  - The isomers are mirror images of each other and cannot be superimposed over one another (they are enantiomers).

- These are formed when a molecule has a chiral centre.

  - A chiral centre is identified by a carbon atom with 4 different groups/atoms bonded to it.
- Two types of geometric isomers are possible due to the restriction surrounding the C=C double bond.

  - Cis isomers have the functional groups on the same side of the carbon chain.
  - Trans isomers have the functional groups on opposite sides of the carbon chain.

![Structural diagrams showing cis isomers with identical groups on the same side of the C=C double bond, and trans isomers with identical groups on opposite sides](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/13-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistry/13-4-isomerism-structural-isomerism-and-stereoisomerism/assets/011-structural-diagrams-showing-cis-isomers-with-ide.webp)

**A** is incorrect as this has cis-trans but no chiral carbons, therefore no optical isomerism.

**B** is incorrect as this has cis-trans but no chiral carbons and therefore no optical isomerism.

**D** is incorrect as this doesn't have cis-trans isomerism.

parts.problemMd:
Which labelled carbon atom is a chiral centre?

![Skeletal structure of an organic compound with four carbon atoms labelled A, B, C and D](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/13-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistry/13-4-isomerism-structural-isomerism-and-stereoisomerism/assets/014-skeletal-structure-of-an-organic-compound-with-f.png)
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- This carbon has four different atoms / groups of atoms:

  - A hydrogen atom.
  - A CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> group.
  - A chlorine atom.
  - A COCH<sub>2</sub>Cl group.

**A** is incorrect as this carbon has two hydrogen atoms attached.

**B** is incorrect as this carbon does not have four groups attached due to the C=O carbonyl group.

**D** is incorrect as this carbon has two hydrogen atoms attached.

parts.problemMd:
Pentane and 2,2-dimethylpropane are isomers.

Which type of isomerism exists between these two molecules?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- Chain isomers have the same molecular formula but a different length carbon chain due to branching.
- 2,2-dimethylpropane has the same molecular formula as pentane (C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub>), but the longest carbon chain is three carbons long in 2,2-dimethylpropane and five carbons long in pentane.

![Structural diagrams comparing pentane with a five-carbon chain and 2,2-dimethylpropane with a three-carbon longest chain, illustrating chain isomerism](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/13-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistry/13-4-isomerism-structural-isomerism-and-stereoisomerism/assets/001-structural-diagrams-comparing-pentane-with-a-fiv.jpg)

**B** is incorrect as there is not a different functional group in 2,2-dimethylpropane compared to pentane, so it cannot be a functional group isomer.

**C** is incorrect as position isomers have the same carbon skeleton with a substituent at a different position. The carbon chain length changes between pentane and 2,2-dimethylpropane, so they are chain isomers, not position isomers.

**D** is incorrect as 2,2-dimethylpropane does not show stereoisomerism. It has no chiral centre and no restricted double bond.

choices.label: A
choices.textMd: A compound that contains a different molecular formula and the atoms are arranged differently in space

choices.label: B
choices.textMd: A compound that contains the same molecular formula but the atoms are arranged differently in space

choices.label: C
choices.textMd: A compound with the same empirical formula but different structural formula

choices.label: D
choices.textMd: A compound with the same molecular formula but different structural formula

parts.problemMd: Which statement defines **structural isomers**?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- Structural isomers include chain isomers, positional isomers and functional group isomers.
- All of which have the same molecular formula but different structural formula.

**A** is incorrect as this is an incorrect definition. Isomers must have the same molecular formula, not a different one.

**B** is incorrect as this is the definition for stereoisomers, which have the same molecular and structural formula but atoms arranged differently in space.

**C** is incorrect as empirical formula is the smallest whole number ratio of atoms in a compound. Molecular formula is the actual number of atoms of elements in a compound.

parts.problemMd:
Gamma-linolenic acid is an active compound found in evening primrose oil.

CH<sub>3</sub>(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>4</sub>CH=CHCH<sub>2</sub>CH=CHCH<sub>2</sub>CH=CH(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>4</sub>COOH

What is the maximum number of stereoisomers of gamma-linolenic acid?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- Stereoisomers are compounds only different by the **spatial arrangement** of the atoms in the molecule.
- One type of stereoisomerism is **optical isomerism.**

  - These are non-superimposable mirror images of each other around a chiral carbon.
  - A chiral carbon is one with 4 different bonds attached.
  - No carbon atoms in this molecule are chiral.
- Another type of stereoisomerism is **geometric.**

  - This is shown below showing examples of ***cis-trans isomers*** of gamma-linolenic acid.
  - In **trans** isomers, the groups on either side of the double bond are on **different** sides of the double bond plane.
  - In **cis** isomers, the groups on either side of the double bond are on the **same** side of the double bond plane.

![Skeletal structures showing examples of cis and trans isomers at the three C=C double bonds in gamma-linolenic acid](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/13-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistry/13-4-isomerism-structural-isomerism-and-stereoisomerism/assets/008-skeletal-structures-showing-examples-of-cis-and-.jpg)

- The maximum number of stereoisomers of gamma-linolenic acid is 8, as the configuration at each double bond can be as follows:

  1. cis, cis, cis
  2. cis, cis, trans
  3. cis, trans, trans
  4. cis, trans, cis
  5. trans, cis, cis
  6. trans, cis, trans
  7. trans, trans, cis
  8. trans, trans, trans

**A** is incorrect as 3 is the number of C=C double bonds in gamma-linolenic acid, not the number of stereoisomers. Each double bond can independently adopt a cis or trans configuration, giving 2<sup>3</sup> = 8 stereoisomers in total.

**B** is incorrect as 4 would result from considering only 2 of the 3 double bonds as sources of geometric isomerism (2<sup>2</sup> = 4). All three double bonds in gamma-linolenic acid produce cis/trans isomers.

**C** is incorrect as 6 is not the correct count. The number of stereoisomers is 2<sup>n</sup>, where n is the number of double bonds giving geometric isomerism. With 3 such double bonds, there are 2<sup>3</sup> = 8 stereoisomers.

parts.problemMd: How many structural isomers have the molecular formula C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>5</sub>Br<sub>3</sub>?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- Structural isomers have the atoms arranged in a completely different order.
- These can be:

  - Chain isomers (branched chains)
  - Position isomers (groups moved on the carbon skeleton)
  - Functional group isomerism (different functional groups and a member of a different homologous series).
- The 5 structural isomers of C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>5</sub>Br<sub>3</sub> are shown below:

![Five structural isomers of C3H5Br3: 1,1,1-tribromopropane; 1,1,2-tribromopropane; 1,1,3-tribromopropane; 1,2,2-tribromopropane; and 1,2,3-tribromopropane](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/13-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistry/13-4-isomerism-structural-isomerism-and-stereoisomerism/assets/010-five-structural-isomers-of-c3h5br3-1-1-1-tribrom.jpg)

**A** is incorrect as there are more than 4 structural isomers of C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>5</sub>Br<sub>3</sub>. Systematically placing the three bromine atoms at all possible positions on the propane chain gives 5 unique structures.

**C** is incorrect as 6 would involve counting the same structure twice when numbered from opposite ends of the chain. For example, 1,2,2-tribromopropane and 2,2,3-tribromopropane are the same compound. There are only 5 unique structural isomers.

**D** is incorrect as 7 significantly overcounts the structural isomers of C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>5</sub>Br<sub>3</sub>. A systematic approach to placing three bromine atoms at all positions on the propane chain gives only 5 unique structures.

parts.problemMd: How many structural isomers with the molecular formula C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O<sub>2</sub> are esters?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- Structural isomers have the atoms arranged in a completely different order.

  - Isomeric esters are esters with a different location of the functional group or different carbon chain arrangement.
- The 9 possible ester structural isomers of C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O<sub>2</sub> are shown below:

![Nine structural isomers of C5H10O2 that are esters, including methyl butanoate, ethyl propanoate, propyl ethanoate, butyl methanoate, and their branched-chain equivalents](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/13-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistry/13-4-isomerism-structural-isomerism-and-stereoisomerism/assets/002-nine-structural-isomers-of-c5h10o2-that-are-este.jpg)

**A** is incorrect as 4 accounts for only the methanoate ester isomers of C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O<sub>2</sub>. The ethanoate, propanoate, and butanoate ester groups must also be considered, giving 9 structural isomers in total.

**B** is incorrect as 5 does not account for all structural isomers of C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O<sub>2</sub>. Both branched and unbranched carbon chains must be considered for each ester group, giving 9 structural isomers in total.

**C** is incorrect as 7 does not include all possible branched-chain arrangements. A systematic approach considering all combinations of ester group and alkyl group, including chain branching in both R and R' groups, gives 9 structural isomers.

parts.problemMd:
11-*cis* retinal, C<sub>20</sub>H<sub>28</sub>O, is found in the retina of animal eyes and is required for vision. The molecule contains an aldehyde group, a cyclohexene ring and an aliphatic side chain. Within the side chain, there is a double bond between carbons 11 and 12.

Which row shows the correct information for 11-*cis* retinal?

|   | **Arrangement of atoms around the adjacent carbons 11 and 12 ** | **Total number of carbon-carbon double bonds** |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | ![Structural diagram showing a trans arrangement of substituents around the C11=C12 double bond](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/13-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistry/13-4-isomerism-structural-isomerism-and-stereoisomerism/assets/003-structural-diagram-showing-a-trans-arrangement-o.jpg) | 5 |
| **B** | ![Structural diagram showing a trans arrangement of substituents around the C11=C12 double bond](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/13-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistry/13-4-isomerism-structural-isomerism-and-stereoisomerism/assets/004-structural-diagram-showing-a-trans-arrangement-o.jpg) | 6 |
| **C** | ![Structural diagram showing the cis arrangement of substituents around the C11=C12 double bond](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/13-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistry/13-4-isomerism-structural-isomerism-and-stereoisomerism/assets/005-structural-diagram-showing-the-cis-arrangement-o.jpg) | 5 |
| **D** | ![Structural diagram showing the cis arrangement of substituents around the C11=C12 double bond](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/13-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistry/13-4-isomerism-structural-isomerism-and-stereoisomerism/assets/006-structural-diagram-showing-the-cis-arrangement-o.jpg) | 6 |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- The question states that it is a *cis* isomer. In a *cis* isomer, the substituents are on the **same** side of the double bond, as shown below.

![Structural diagram showing the cis arrangement of substituents around the C=C double bond between C11 and C12, with both substituent groups on the same side of the double bond](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/13-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistry/13-4-isomerism-structural-isomerism-and-stereoisomerism/assets/007-structural-diagram-showing-the-cis-arrangement-o.jpg)

- The cyclohexene ring contains one C=C double bond. There are 4 further C=C double bonds on the aliphatic chain, giving 5 carbon-carbon double bonds in total.

**A** is incorrect as the image shows a *trans* arrangement of substituents around the C11=C12 double bond. 11-*cis* retinal has a *cis* arrangement at this position.

**B** is incorrect as the image shows a *trans* arrangement at C11=C12, and 6 incorrectly includes the C=O double bond of the aldehyde group. Only carbon-carbon double bonds are counted, giving 5.

**D** is incorrect as 6 includes the C=O double bond of the aldehyde group in the count. The question specifies carbon-carbon double bonds only, of which there are 5.

parts.problemMd: Which compound is both chiral and acidic?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- The question asks for a molecule that is both chiral and acidic.
- Molecule **D** is acidic due to the carboxylic acid group (COOH).
- Molecule **D** is chiral because the highlighted carbon is bonded to 4 different groups:

![Skeletal structure of molecule D with the chiral carbon highlighted, showing four different substituent groups](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/13-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistry/13-4-isomerism-structural-isomerism-and-stereoisomerism/assets/015-skeletal-structure-of-molecule-d-with-the-chiral.jpg)

**A** is incorrect as this is 1-methylcyclohexanol, an alcohol, and it is achiral (no carbon atoms with 4 different groups attached to it).

**B** is incorrect as it is acidic but not chiral due to the double bond.

**C** is incorrect as this is chiral but not acidic.

parts.problemMd:
Cholesterol is a biological molecule used in the production of steroid hormones.

![Skeletal structure of cholesterol (C27H46O) showing the fused four-ring steroid system with a hydroxyl group at C3 and an aliphatic side chain](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/13-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistry/13-4-isomerism-structural-isomerism-and-stereoisomerism/assets/012-skeletal-structure-of-cholesterol-c27h46o-showin.png)

How many chiral centres are there in one molecule of cholesterol?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- The following **8** carbons are chiral centres:

  - C3 (OH, C4, C2, H).
  - C8 (C9, C14, C7, H).
  - C9 (C10, C8, C11, H).
  - C10 (C5, C9, C1, C19).
  - C13 (C14, C17, C12, C18).
  - C14 (C13, C8, C15, H).
  - C17 (C13, C20, C16, H).
  - C20 (C17, C22, C21, H).

- The 4 different groups that each carbon is bonded to are shown in brackets.

![Skeletal structure of cholesterol with 8 chiral centres highlighted at C3, C8, C9, C10, C13, C14, C17, and C20](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/13-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistry/13-4-isomerism-structural-isomerism-and-stereoisomerism/assets/013-skeletal-structure-of-cholesterol-with-8-chiral-.jpg)

- A chiral centre is an atom that has four different groups bonded to it. Each chiral centre gives rise to 2 optical isomers.
- When trying to find chiral centres, remember the following:

  - Hydrogens are not shown in skeletal drawings, but hydrogens often determine if the carbon is chiral. If a carbon has more than one hydrogen attached, you can dismiss it as a potential chiral centre.
  - Carbons on double or triple bonds cannot be chiral centres because they can't have bonds to 4 **different** groups.
  - Within complex cyclic molecules, each carbon in a ring can be considered as a different group if the overall group it is attached to is different.

**A** is incorrect as there are more than 5 chiral centres in cholesterol. This answer arises from identifying only the most visually obvious stereocentres and missing the ring junction carbons.

**B** is incorrect as one of the tertiary ring junction carbons (C8, C9, or C14) has been missed. These carbons have an implicit hydrogen atom that is not drawn in the skeletal structure.

**D** is incorrect as this overcounts the chiral centres. Carbons in the C=C double bond are sp<sup>2</sup> hybridised and cannot be chiral, and C25 at the end of the tail is bonded to two identical methyl groups.

parts.problemMd: How many isomeric alkenes, including stereoisomers, are produced when 2-bromobutane is heated with ethanolic NaOH?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- When a halogenoalkane reacts with ethanolic NaOH (elimination conditions), dehydrohalogenation occurs.
- Secondary halogenoalkanes undergo both substitution and elimination; the ethanolic solvent favours elimination.
- The following elimination reactions can occur, producing 3 isomeric alkenes:

![Reaction scheme showing the elimination reactions of 2-bromobutane with ethanolic NaOH, producing but-1-ene, cis-but-2-ene, and trans-but-2-ene](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/13-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistry/13-4-isomerism-structural-isomerism-and-stereoisomerism/assets/009-reaction-scheme-showing-the-elimination-reaction.jpg)

**A** is incorrect as only one product (the major alkene) has been identified, without considering elimination in both directions.

**B** is incorrect as this identifies but-1-ene and but-2-ene as structural isomers but misses that but-2-ene exists as cis and trans stereoisomers.

**D** is incorrect as but-1-ene cannot show cis-trans isomerism. The terminal alkene carbon (=CH<sub>2</sub>) is bonded to two identical hydrogen atoms, so no geometric isomerism is possible.

parts.problemMd: How many isomers, including structural and stereoisomers, with the molecular formula C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub> contain a π bond?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- There are 6 different isomers of C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub> that contain a π bond (have a C=C double bond).

![Six isomers of C5H10 that contain a C=C double bond: pent-1-ene, cis-pent-2-ene, trans-pent-2-ene, 2-methylbut-1-ene, 2-methylbut-2-ene, and 3-methylbut-1-ene](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/13-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistry/13-4-isomerism-structural-isomerism-and-stereoisomerism/assets/016-six-isomers-of-c5h10-that-contain-a-c-c-double-b.jpg)

**A** is incorrect as there are more than 3 isomers of C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub> that contain a π bond. All 5 alkene structural isomers must be identified, and cis-pent-2-ene and trans-pent-2-ene must be counted as separate stereoisomers, giving a total of 6.

**B** is incorrect as 4 is an undercount of the structural isomers of C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub> that are alkenes. Five structural isomers exist; including cis- and trans-pent-2-ene as separate stereoisomers gives a total of 6.

**C** is incorrect as 5 represents only the number of structural isomers of C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub> that are alkenes. Cis-pent-2-ene and trans-pent-2-ene are two distinct stereoisomers, so the total is 6.

parts.problemMd: Which equation represents a valid propagation step in the free radical reaction between ethane and chlorine?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- A propagation step involves a free radical reacting with a stable molecule to produce a new radical and a new stable molecule, keeping the chain reaction going.
- **A** shows how a chlorine radical abstracts a hydrogen from chloroethane, producing a chloroethyl radical and HCl.

  - The number of free radicals is unchanged, so this is a valid propagation step.
- The standard propagation steps for the ethane and chlorine reaction are:

C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub> + Cl• → C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>• + HCl

C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>• + Cl<sub>2</sub> → C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>Cl + Cl•

- Further substitution of the product C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>Cl is also a valid propagation step.

**B** is incorrect as it shows two radicals combining to form one stable molecule, which is a termination step (net destruction of radicals).

**C** is incorrect as it produces an H• radical. Hydrogen radicals are not formed in this mechanism; Cl• abstracts H to form HCl, not H•.

**D** is incorrect as the equation is unbalanced. Chlorine appears in the product (HCl) but not in the reactants.

parts.problemMd:
One of the reactions taking place in a catalytic converter in a car exhaust system is between nitrogen oxide and octane (unburned petrol). The products of this reaction are non-toxic.

Which is the correct equation for the reaction?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>18</sub> is the correct formula for octane.
- Carbon dioxide (CO<sub>2</sub>), nitrogen gas (N<sub>2</sub>) and water (H<sub>2</sub>O) are all non-toxic products.

**A** and **B** are incorrect as octane is an alkane with formula C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>18</sub>, whereas **A** and **B** show C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>16</sub>, which is octene.

**C** is incorrect as CO is carbon monoxide, which is a toxic gas.

parts.problemMd:
The hydrocarbon C<sub>17</sub>H<sub>36</sub> can be cracked.

Which compound is the **least** likely to be produced in this reaction?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- Cracking is a reaction in which larger alkane molecules are broken down into smaller alkane and alkene molecules.
- For C<sub>16</sub>H<sub>34</sub> to be produced from C<sub>17</sub>H<sub>36</sub>, the remaining fragment would be CH<sub>2</sub>:

C<sub>17</sub>H<sub>36</sub> → C<sub>16</sub>H<sub>34</sub> + CH<sub>2</sub>

- CH<sub>2</sub> cannot exist as a stable molecule.
- The minimum stable alkene requires at least two carbon atoms to form a C=C double bond (ethene, C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>).
- Therefore, C<sub>16</sub>H<sub>34</sub> cannot be produced by cracking.

**A**, **B** and **C** are incorrect as these compounds can all be produced by valid cracking equations that leave a stable alkane or alkene as the other fragment:

C<sub>17</sub>H<sub>36</sub> → C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub> + C<sub>14</sub>H<sub>28</sub> (alkane + alkene)

C<sub>17</sub>H<sub>36</sub> → C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub> + C<sub>13</sub>H<sub>28</sub> (alkene + alkane)

C<sub>17</sub>H<sub>36</sub> → C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>16</sub> + C<sub>9</sub>H<sub>20</sub> (alkene + alkane)

parts.problemMd:
In the presence of ultraviolet light, ethane and chlorine react to give a mixture of products.

Which compound could be present in the mixture of products?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- Initiation = net formation of radicals
- In the initiation step, free radical Cl• atoms are formed:

Cl<sub>2</sub> → 2Cl•

- Propagation = no change in the number of free radicals
- These free radical Cl• atoms remove a hydrogen from the ethane making an ethyl free radical, C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>•:

C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub> + Cl• → C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>• + HCl

- Termination = net destruction of free radicals
- Two of these radicals can then pair up in a termination step to form butane, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> (C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub>):

C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>• + C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>• → C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub>

- Therefore, option **C** is the only compound that could be present in the mixture.

**A** is incorrect as CH<sub>3</sub>Cl cannot be formed from the reaction between ethane and chlorine. All carbon-containing products must retain the two-carbon skeleton of ethane; a one-carbon product such as chloromethane is not possible.

**B** is incorrect as CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Cl (1-chloropropane) contains three carbon atoms and cannot be formed from ethane and chlorine. No three-carbon products can arise from a two-carbon starting material.

**D** is incorrect as CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> (pentane) contains five carbon atoms. The termination step joining two ethyl radicals (C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>•) produces butane (four carbons), not pentane.

parts.problemMd:
The cracking of a single hydrocarbon molecule, C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n+2</sub>, produces two hydrocarbon molecules only. Each hydrocarbon product contains the same number of carbon atoms in one molecule.  Each hydrocarbon product has non-cyclic structural isomers.

What is the value of n?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- Cracking an alkane to produce exactly two molecules with the same number of carbon atoms yields one alkane and one alkene.

  - For n = 8, C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>18</sub> cracks to give C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub> (butane) and C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub> (butene).

- Both products must have non-cyclic structural isomers:

  - C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub> has two non-cyclic structural isomers: butane and methylpropane
  - C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub> has three non-cyclic structural isomers: but-1-ene, but-2-ene, and 2-methylpropene
  - Cis-but-2-ene and trans-but-2-ene are E/Z stereoisomers of but-2-ene, not separate structural isomers.
- Both products satisfy the condition, so n = 8.

**A** is incorrect as when n = 4, cracking gives ethane (C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub>) and ethene (C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>). Neither 2-carbon compound has any structural isomers.

**B** is incorrect as when n = 6, cracking gives propane (C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub>) and propene (C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>6</sub>). Propane has no structural isomers, and propene's only structural isomer is cyclopropane, which is cyclic. Neither product satisfies the condition.

**D** is incorrect as n = 9 is odd. It is not possible to split an odd number of carbon atoms into two products with the same number of carbons each.

parts.problemMd:
Which hydrocarbon would **not** be collected in the inverted tube by heating pentane, CH<sub>3</sub>(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>, in the apparatus shown?

![Diagram of cracking apparatus: a horizontal tube containing pentane on mineral fibre and aluminium oxide heated strongly, connected by a delivery tube to an inverted test tube submerged in water for gas collection](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/14-hydrocarbons/14-1-alkanes/assets/001-diagram-of-cracking-apparatus-a-horizontal-tube-.png)
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- Heating pentane over an aluminium oxide catalyst cracks the molecule.
- Cracking breaks down larger alkane molecules into smaller alkanes and alkenes.
- So, for pentane, the cracking process will produce alkanes and alkenes of five or fewer carbons.
- Therefore, CH<sub>3</sub>(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>8</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> would not be produced in this reaction as it contains 10 carbons, which is more than the original pentane (5 carbons).

**A** is incorrect as methane (CH<sub>4</sub>) is a gas at room temperature and pressure and could be produced by cracking pentane, for example:

C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub> → CH<sub>4</sub> + C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub>

Gases are collected in the inverted tube by displacement of water.

**B** is incorrect as ethane (CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>) is a gas at room temperature and pressure and could be produced by cracking pentane, for example:

C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub> → C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub> + C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>6</sub>

It would be collected in the inverted tube.

**C** is incorrect as but-1-ene (CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH=CH<sub>2</sub>) is a gas at room temperature and pressure and could be produced by cracking pentane, for example:

C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub> → C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub> + CH<sub>4</sub>

It would be collected in the inverted tube.

parts.problemMd:
0.200 mol of a hydrocarbon undergoes complete combustion to give 35.2 g of carbon dioxide and 14.4 g of water as the only products.

What is the molecular formula of the hydrocarbon?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- List the known values:

  - mass of CO<sub>2</sub> = 35.2 g, *M*<sub>r</sub>(CO<sub>2</sub>) = 44
  - mass of H<sub>2</sub>O = 14.4 g, *M*<sub>r</sub>(H<sub>2</sub>O) = 18
  - moles of hydrocarbon = 0.200 mol
- Calculate the moles of CO<sub>2</sub>:

moles = $\frac{m}{M_{r}}$

moles = 35.2 / 44

moles of CO<sub>2</sub> = 0.800 mol

- Calculate the moles of H<sub>2</sub>O:

moles = $\frac{m}{M_{r}}$

moles = 14.4 / 18

moles of H<sub>2</sub>O = 0.800 mol

- Scale to per mole of hydrocarbon to find the molecular formula:

C atoms per molecule = 0.800 / 0.200 = 4

H atoms per molecule = (2 x 0.800) / 0.200 = 8

- The molecular formula is C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub>.

**A** is incorrect as C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub> has the same empirical formula (CH<sub>2</sub>) as C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub>. This traps candidates who calculate only the simplest ratio without using the 0.200 mol value to scale to the molecular formula.

**B** is incorrect as C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub> would give a CO<sub>2</sub> to H<sub>2</sub>O mole ratio of 2:3, not 1:1.

**C** is incorrect as C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>4</sub> would give only 0.400 mol H<sub>2</sub>O from 0.200 mol of compound, not 0.800 mol.

choices.label: A
choices.textMd: Propagation steps involve the collision of two radicals to form a stable molecule

choices.label: B
choices.textMd: The final mixture will only contain chloroethane and hydrogen chloride

choices.label: C
choices.textMd: The initiation step involves heterolytic fission of a C–H bond

choices.label: D
choices.textMd: Ultraviolet light is required to provide the activation energy for the homolytic fission of Cl–Cl bonds

parts.problemMd: Which statement about the free-radical substitution of ethane with chlorine is correct?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- In free-radical substitution of ethane with chlorine, the reaction begins with an initiation step.
- Ultraviolet light provides the energy needed to break the Cl–Cl bond by homolytic fission.
- This produces chlorine radicals, which are required to start the chain reaction.

**A** is incorrect as the collision of two radicals to form a stable molecule occurs in the termination step, not propagation.

**B** is incorrect as the final mixture also contains unreacted ethane, unreacted chlorine, and further substituted products such as dichloroethane.

**C** is incorrect as the initiation step involves homolytic, not heterolytic, fission of the Cl–Cl bond, not the C–H bond.

parts.problemMd:
Samples of 10 cm<sup>3</sup> of each of the first four members of the alkane series are separately mixed with 70 cm<sup>3</sup> of oxygen. Each is then burned and the total volume, *V*, of residual gas measured again at room temperature and pressure.

Which graph represents the results that would be obtained?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- The first four members of the alkane series are methane (CH<sub>4</sub>), ethane (C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub>), propane (C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub>) and butane (C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub>).
- At room temperature, water produced by combustion condenses to liquid and contributes negligible volume to the residual gas.
- Methane:

CH<sub>4</sub> + 2O<sub>2</sub> → CO<sub>2</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O

O<sub>2</sub> consumed = 2 x 10 = 20 cm<sup>3</sup>; CO<sub>2</sub> produced = 10 cm<sup>3</sup>

Residual volume = (70 − 20) + 10 = 60 cm<sup>3</sup>

- Ethane:

C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub> + $\frac{7}{2}$O<sub>2</sub> → 2CO<sub>2</sub> + 3H<sub>2</sub>O

O<sub>2</sub> consumed = 3.5 x 10 = 35 cm<sup>3</sup>; CO<sub>2</sub> produced = 20 cm<sup>3</sup>

Residual volume = (70 − 35) + 20 = 55 cm<sup>3</sup>

- Propane:

C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub> + 5O<sub>2</sub> → 3CO<sub>2</sub> + 4H<sub>2</sub>O

O<sub>2</sub> consumed = 5 x 10 = 50 cm<sup>3</sup>; CO<sub>2</sub> produced = 30 cm<sup>3</sup>

Residual volume = (70 − 50) + 30 = 50 cm<sup>3</sup>

- Butane:

C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub> + $\frac{13}{2}$O<sub>2</sub> → 4CO<sub>2</sub> + 5H<sub>2</sub>O

O<sub>2</sub> consumed = 6.5 x 10 = 65 cm<sup>3</sup>; CO<sub>2</sub> produced = 40 cm<sup>3</sup>

Residual volume = (70 − 65) + 40 = 45 cm<sup>3</sup>

- The four values (60, 55, 50, 45 cm<sup>3</sup>) decrease linearly by 5 cm<sup>3</sup> per member, as shown in graph **B**.

parts.problemMd:
The petrol additive tetraethyl-lead (IV), Pb(C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>)<sub>4</sub>, is now banned in many countries. When it is completely burned in air, lead (II) oxide, CO<sub>2</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>O are formed.

How many moles of oxygen are required to burn one mole of Pb(C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>)<sub>4</sub>?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- Expand the formula Pb(C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>)<sub>4</sub>:

1 Pb, 4 x 2 = 8 C, 4 x 5 = 20 H

- The balanced equation for complete combustion is:

Pb(C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>)<sub>4</sub> + $\frac{27}{2}$O<sub>2</sub> → PbO + 8CO<sub>2</sub> + 10H<sub>2</sub>O

- Count the total oxygen atoms required on the right-hand side:

1 (in PbO) + 16 (in 8CO<sub>2</sub>) + 10 (in 10H<sub>2</sub>O) = 27 oxygen atoms

- Calculate the moles of O<sub>2</sub>:

moles of O<sub>2</sub> = 27 / 2

moles of O<sub>2</sub> = 13.5

**A** (9.5) is incorrect and results from failing to multiply the carbon count by 4 when expanding the bracket, giving only 4 CO<sub>2</sub> molecules instead of 8.

**B** (11) is incorrect and results from failing to multiply the hydrogen count by 4 when expanding the bracket, giving only 5 H<sub>2</sub>O molecules instead of 10.

**D** (27) is incorrect as 27 is the total number of oxygen atoms required, not the number of moles of O<sub>2</sub> molecules. Dividing by 2 is required since oxygen is diatomic.

parts.problemMd:
The cracking of eicosane, C<sub>20</sub>H<sub>42</sub>, produces a hydrocarbon that is in very high demand for transportation and also three consecutive members of the same homologous series of hydrocarbons.

What are the correct products of cracking for the given reaction?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- The highest demand hydrocarbon for transportation is octane (C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>18</sub>).
- Subtract octane from eicosane to find the remaining fragment:

C<sub>20</sub>H<sub>42</sub> - C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>18</sub> = C<sub>12</sub>H<sub>24</sub>

- C<sub>12</sub>H<sub>24</sub> has the general formula C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n</sub>, so the remaining three products are alkenes.
- Let the smallest alkene have n carbons.

  - Three consecutive alkenes total 12 carbons:

n + (n + 1) + (n + 2) = 12

3n + 3 = 12

n = 3

- The three consecutive alkenes are propene (C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>6</sub>), butene (C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub>) and pentene (C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub>).
- Overall cracking equation:
- C<sub>20</sub>H<sub>42</sub> → C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>18</sub> + C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>6</sub> + C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub> + C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub>

**A** is incorrect as the carbon count of the products (4 + 4 + 6 + 8 = 22) exceeds the 20 carbons in eicosane, so it is stoichiometrically impossible.

**C** is incorrect as ethane is not a hydrocarbon in high demand for transportation (it is a gas at room temperature, not a liquid fuel). The remaining alkenes in this option are also not consecutive members of the same homologous series.

**D** is incorrect as ethene is not a hydrocarbon in high demand for transportation, and the three alkenes (ethene, pentene, heptene) are not consecutive members of the same homologous series.

parts.problemMd:
Ethene reacts with steam in the presence of phosphoric acid.

C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O → CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH

What type of reaction is this?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- In an addition reaction, two compounds come together to form one larger compound.
- There are no other products produced.
- Therefore, the reaction between ethene and steam is an addition reaction.

**A** is incorrect as an acid-base reaction involves an acid and a base as reactants.

**C** is incorrect as in a hydrolysis reaction, chemical bonds are broken by the addition of water, however that is not the case here.

**D** is incorrect as in a substitution reaction, an atom or functional group is replaced by another similar species.

> **[exam-tip]**
> This reaction is also known as hydration, which is the addition of water across the C=C double bond. Do not confuse hydration with hydrolysis:
> 
> - Hydration forms a single product with no bonds broken by water
> - Hydrolysis uses water to break a bond in the substrate (e.g. ester → carboxylic acid + alcohol).

parts.problemMd: What is the mechanism for the reaction between propene and bromine in an organic solvent?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- In an addition reaction, two compounds come together to form one larger compound with no other products, as shown:

![Equation showing the addition of bromine to propene to form 1,2-dibromopropane](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/14-hydrocarbons/14-2-alkenes/assets/020-equation-showing-the-addition-of-bromine-to-prop.jpg)

- As Br<sub>2</sub> approaches the electron-rich C=C double bond in propene, the Br<sub>2</sub> molecule is polarised: the nearer Br atom develops a δ+ charge and acts as an electrophile.
- The π electrons from the C=C double bond attack the δ+ Br atom, and the Br–Br bond breaks heterolytically.
- A Br atom becomes attached to each carbon.
- Therefore, it is an electrophilic addition reaction.

![Curly arrow mechanism showing electrophilic addition of bromine to propene, forming 1,2-dibromopropane](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/14-hydrocarbons/14-2-alkenes/assets/021-curly-arrow-mechanism-showing-electrophilic-addi.jpg)

**B** is incorrect as electrophilic substitution involves an electrophile replacing an existing atom or group. No atoms are replaced here.

**C** is incorrect as nucleophilic addition involves a nucleophile attacking an electrophilic carbon. Br<sub>2</sub> acts as an electrophile, not a nucleophile.

**D** is incorrect as nucleophilic substitution involves a nucleophile replacing a leaving group. There is no leaving group in this reaction.

parts.problemMd:
A molecule of a polymer contained the sequence shown.

![Structural formula of a linear hydrocarbon chain with alternating hydrogen and chlorine atoms bonded to carbon atoms along the backbone](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/14-hydrocarbons/14-2-alkenes/assets/015-structural-formula-of-a-linear-hydrocarbon-chain.jpg)

Which monomer could produce this polymer by addition polymerisation?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

1. Identify the monomers in the displayed diagram

![Polymer chain with each repeating monomer unit highlighted to show the two-carbon, one-chlorine repeating structure](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/14-hydrocarbons/14-2-alkenes/assets/016-polymer-chain-with-each-repeating-monomer-unit-h.jpg)

2. Break the bond between these monomers

![Polymer chain with the single bond between adjacent repeating units broken to show individual monomer units](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/14-hydrocarbons/14-2-alkenes/assets/017-polymer-chain-with-the-single-bond-between-adjac.jpg)

3. Add in the double bond between the carbon atoms

![Monomer unit with C=C double bond re-introduced between the two backbone carbon atoms](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/14-hydrocarbons/14-2-alkenes/assets/018-monomer-unit-with-c-c-double-bond-re-introduced-.jpg)

4. Convert the structural formula to the condensed formula

![Condensed structural formula of chloroethene CH2=CHCl, the monomer for this polymer](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/14-hydrocarbons/14-2-alkenes/assets/019-condensed-structural-formula-of-chloroethene-ch2.jpg)

**B** is incorrect as CHCl=CHCl (1,2-dichloroethene) would produce a polymer in which every backbone carbon carries a Cl atom, giving two Cl atoms per repeating unit. This is inconsistent with the structure shown.

**C** is incorrect as CH<sub>3</sub>CCl=CH<sub>2</sub> is a three-carbon monomer. Polymerisation would give a three-carbon backbone repeating unit, not a two-carbon one.

**D** is incorrect as CH<sub>3</sub>CCl=CHCl is also a three-carbon monomer. Polymerisation would give a three-carbon backbone with two Cl atoms per repeating unit.

parts.problemMd: Which reaction would **not** give propene?
parts.solutionMd:

**A** is incorrect as adding excess hot concentrated sulfuric acid to propan-1-ol gives propene by a dehydration reaction:
