parts.problemMd:
Ethene reacts with aqueous bromine to give two products, CH<sub>2</sub>BrCH<sub>2</sub>Br and CH<sub>2</sub>BrCH<sub>2</sub>OH.

Which statement about these products is correct?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- Bromine is an electrophile (electron-accepting species) and reacts with ethene via electrophilic addition.

![Mechanism of electrophilic addition of bromine to ethene, showing formation of both 1,2-dibromoethane and 2-bromoethanol](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/14-hydrocarbons/14-2-alkenes/assets/030-mechanism-of-electrophilic-addition-of-bromine-t.jpg)

- Both products, CH<sub>2</sub>BrCH<sub>2</sub>Br (1,2-dibromoethane) and CH<sub>2</sub>BrCH<sub>2</sub>OH (2-bromoethanol), can be hydrolysed using hot aqueous NaOH to give the same organic compound, ethane-1,2-diol.

![Equations showing hydrolysis of 1,2-dibromoethane and 2-bromoethanol both giving ethane-1,2-diol](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/14-hydrocarbons/14-2-alkenes/assets/031-equations-showing-hydrolysis-of-1-2-dibromoethan.jpg)

**A** and **B** are incorrect as both products are formed by electrophilic addition, not electrophilic substitution or nucleophilic addition.

**D** is incorrect as 1,2-dibromoethane (CH<sub>2</sub>BrCH<sub>2</sub>Br) has no N–H, O–H, or F–H bonds, so it cannot form hydrogen bonds with water. Only 2-bromoethanol (CH<sub>2</sub>BrCH<sub>2</sub>OH) can form hydrogen bonds via its –OH group.

parts.problemMd:
Pent-2-ene, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH=CHCH<sub>3</sub>, reacts in a similar way to ethene.

Pent-2-ene is reacted with cold, dilute, acidified manganate (VII) ions.

What will be produced in the greatest amount?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- When ethene reacts with cold, dilute, acidified manganate(VII) ions, ethane-1,2-diol is produced.

![Equation showing ethene reacting with cold dilute acidified KMnO4 to form ethane-1,2-diol](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/14-hydrocarbons/14-2-alkenes/assets/008-equation-showing-ethene-reacting-with-cold-dilut.jpg)

- In a similar way, pent-2-ene reacts with cold, dilute, acidified manganate(VII) ions to form pentan-2,3-diol:

CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH=CHCH<sub>3</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O + [O] → CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH(OH)CH(OH)CH<sub>3</sub>

**B** is incorrect as CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COCOCH<sub>3</sub> (pentane-2,3-dione) cannot be synthesised from pent-2-ene by mild oxidation with cold, dilute manganate(VII) ions.

**C** is incorrect as CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH(OH)CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> (pentan-3-ol) and CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH(OH)CH<sub>3</sub> (pentan-2-ol) are the products of hydration of pent-2-ene, not mild oxidation with manganate(VII) ions.

**D** is incorrect as CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COOH (propanoic acid) and CH<sub>3</sub>COOH (ethanoic acid) are produced only by oxidative cleavage using hot, concentrated, acidified manganate(VII) ions.

parts.problemMd:
Isomers **X** and **Y** both react with HBr.

![Structural formulae of isomers X and Y, both containing C=C double bonds that react with HBr by electrophilic addition](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/14-hydrocarbons/14-2-alkenes/assets/022-structural-formulae-of-isomers-x-and-y-both-cont.jpg)

A mixture of **X** and **Y** is reacted with HBr.

Which three structures represent three **different** possible products of this reaction?

| **A** | (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CHCBr<sub>3</sub> | (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CBrCHBr<sub>2</sub> | CH<sub>3</sub>CHBrCHBrCH<sub>3</sub> |
|---|---|---|---|
| **B** | (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CHCBr<sub>3</sub> | (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CBrCHBr<sub>2</sub> | CH<sub>3</sub>CBr<sub>2</sub>CHBrCH<sub>3</sub> |
| **C** | (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CBrCBr<sub>3</sub> | (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CHCBr<sub>3</sub> | CH<sub>3</sub>CBr<sub>2</sub>CHBrCH<sub>3</sub> |
| **D** | (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CBrCHBr<sub>2</sub> | CHBr<sub>2</sub>CBr(CH<sub>3</sub>)CH<sub>3</sub> | CH<sub>3</sub>CHBrCBr<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- In the electrophilic addition of HBr to an alkene, the H end of HBr acts as the electrophile.

  - The δ+ H is attracted to the electron-rich C=C double bond.
- H adds to one carbon and Br adds to the other, breaking the C=C double bond.
- Drawing out the structural formula of each product from X and Y is the clearest approach:

![Structural formulae showing all possible products from electrophilic addition of HBr to isomers X and Y](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/14-hydrocarbons/14-2-alkenes/assets/023-structural-formulae-showing-all-possible-product.jpg)

- The three different products from the reaction of HBr with isomers **X** and **Y** are:

  1. (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CHCBr<sub>3</sub>
  2. (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CBrCHBr<sub>2</sub>
  3. CH<sub>3</sub>CBr<sub>2</sub>CHBrCH<sub>3</sub>

**A** is incorrect as the third product listed (CH<sub>3</sub>CHBrCHBrCH<sub>3</sub>) is not formed from this reaction. This product would arise from addition of Br<sub>2</sub>, not HBr.

**C** is incorrect as the first product listed ((CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CBrCBr<sub>3</sub>) is not formed; HBr addition to these isomers cannot produce a CBr<sub>3</sub> group at that position.

**D** is incorrect as none of the three products in that row correctly reflects the regiochemistry of HBr addition to isomers X and Y.

parts.problemMd:
What is the major product formed when compound Q is warmed with excess HBr?

![Structural formula of compound Q, an organic molecule containing a C=C double bond and one or more hydroxyl groups](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/14-hydrocarbons/14-2-alkenes/assets/028-structural-formula-of-compound-q-an-organic-mole.jpg)
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- Each –OH group in compound Q reacts with HBr to undergo nucleophilic substitution, replacing –OH with Br.
- The C=C double bond also reacts with HBr by electrophilic addition, adding H to one carbon and Br to the other.
- With excess HBr, both types of reaction proceed fully, giving the product shown in option **C**.

**A** is incorrect as it does not show complete substitution of all –OH groups or full addition across the C=C double bond.

**B** is incorrect as it shows an incorrect or incomplete transformation of compound Q with excess HBr.

**D** is incorrect as it shows incorrect regiochemistry or an incomplete reaction with excess HBr.

parts.problemMd:
The oxidative cleavage of an alkene using hot, concentrated, acidified potassium manganate(VII) results in the complete rupture of the carbon–carbon double bond.

Which row correctly identifies the final products formed from the specified structural groups?

|   | Structural group in alkene | Final products formed |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | R–CH=CH–R′ | Two different aldehydes |
| **B** | CH₂=C(R)₂ | Carbon dioxide and a ketone |
| **C** | R–CH=CH₂ | A carboxylic acid and methanoic acid |
| **D** | R–CH=C(R)₂ | A carboxylic acid and an alcohol |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- Hot, concentrated, acidified KMnO<sub>4</sub> causes oxidative cleavage, meaning the C=C bond breaks and each carbon is oxidised as far as possible.
- In CH<sub>2</sub>=C(R)<sub>2</sub>, the CH<sub>2</sub> end is terminal, so it is fully oxidised to CO<sub>2</sub> (and H<sub>2</sub>O).
- The other carbon is disubstituted (no H attached to that double-bond carbon), so it forms a ketone, which is not oxidised further under these conditions.
- Therefore, the final products are carbon dioxide and a ketone.

**A** is incorrect because R–CH=CH–R’ gives two monosubstituted alkene carbons. Each –CH= fragment is oxidised to a carboxylic acid, not an aldehyde as aldehydes are intermediate products that are further oxidised.

**C** is incorrect because the terminal =CH<sub>2</sub> end in R–CH=CH<sub>2</sub> is fully oxidised to CO<sub>2</sub> (and H<sub>2</sub>O), not methanoic acid.

**D** is incorrect because oxidative cleavage produces carbonyl compounds (carboxylic acids or ketones), not alcohols.

parts.problemMd:
A polymer has the repeating unit

![Chemical structure of polyisobutylene, showing a repeating unit with a methyl group branch on a carbon chain.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/14-hydrocarbons/14-2-alkenes/assets/001-chemical-structure-of-polyisobutylene-showing-a-.png)

Which monomer would produce this polymer by addition polymerisation?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- The repeating unit shows a two-carbon backbone, indicating addition polymerisation of an alkene.
- One backbone carbon has one H atom and one CH<sub>3</sub> group; the other has two H atoms.
- This corresponds to propene, CH<sub>2</sub>=CH–CH<sub>3</sub>, which gives the repeating unit –[–CH<sub>2</sub>–CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)–]–.

**A** is incorrect as ethene would produce a –[–CH<sub>2</sub>–CH<sub>2</sub>–]– backbone with no CH<sub>3</sub> side groups.

**C** is incorrect as butane is a saturated alkane and cannot undergo addition polymerisation.

**D** is incorrect as but-2-ene would give a repeating unit in which both backbone carbons carry a CH<sub>3</sub> group, not just one.

parts.problemMd:
Limonene is an oil formed in the peel of citrus fruits.

![Structural formula of limonene, a cyclic terpene containing a six-membered ring with one endocyclic C=C double bond and an isopropenyl side chain containing a second C=C double bond](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/14-hydrocarbons/14-2-alkenes/assets/002-structural-formula-of-limonene-a-cyclic-terpene-.png)

Which product is formed when an excess of bromine, Br<sub>2</sub> (l), reacts with limonene at room temperature in the dark?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- Limonene contains two C=C double bonds

  - One in the six-membered ring
  - One in the isopropenyl side chain.
- The reaction is carried out at room temperature in the dark.

  - In the dark, only electrophilic addition occurs.
  - UV light would initiate free-radical substitution instead.
- When reacted with excess Br<sub>2</sub>, electrophilic addition occurs across both double bonds.
- Each double bond reacts with one molecule of Br<sub>2</sub>, adding two Br atoms across each bond, giving four Br atoms in total.

![Structural diagram showing electrophilic addition of excess bromine to both double bonds in limonene, producing a tetrabromo product](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/14-hydrocarbons/14-2-alkenes/assets/003-structural-diagram-showing-electrophilic-additio.jpg)

**A** is incorrect as it shows bromine added across only one of the two double bonds. Excess Br<sub>2</sub> ensures both double bonds react fully.

**B** is incorrect as it shows an incomplete or incorrect bromination product of limonene.

**C** is incorrect as it shows addition to only one double bond or addition in the wrong positions.

parts.problemMd: Which isomer of C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>13</sub>OH gives the greatest number of different alkenes when it is dehydrated?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- Alcohols can be dehydrated to form alkenes by losing a water molecule across adjacent carbons to form a C=C double bond.
- CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH(OH)CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> (hexan-3-ol) can lose H from either C2 or C4, giving two constitutional isomers, each with E/Z stereoisomers:

  - hex-2-ene: (E)-hex-2-ene and (Z)-hex-2-ene
  - hex-3-ene: (E)-hex-3-ene and (Z)-hex-3-ene
- That gives 4 different alkenes in total (more than any other option).

![Structural formulae of the four alkenes formed by dehydration of hexan-3-ol, showing both constitutional isomers and their E/Z stereoisomers](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/14-hydrocarbons/14-2-alkenes/assets/032-structural-formulae-of-the-four-alkenes-formed-b.jpg)

**A** and **D** are incorrect as these are primary alcohols. Elimination can only occur in one direction, giving fewer alkene isomers than a secondary alcohol.

**C** is incorrect as CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>C(CH<sub>3</sub>)(OH)CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> (3-methylpentan-3-ol) gives 3 different alkenes on dehydration: (E)-3-methylpent-2-ene, (Z)-3-methylpent-2-ene and 2-ethylbut-1-ene, which is fewer than the 4 from option **B**.

parts.problemMd:
Acrylic acid is produced from propene, a gaseous product of oil refineries.

![Structural formula of acrylic acid (prop-2-enoic acid, CH2=CHCOOH), with bond angles x and y labelled at the sp2 carbon atoms](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/14-hydrocarbons/14-2-alkenes/assets/029-structural-formula-of-acrylic-acid-prop-2-enoic-.jpg)

Which statement about acrylic acid is **not** correct?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- 2,4-Dinitrophenylhydrazine (2,4-DNPH) reacts with the C=O bond in aldehydes and ketones to give an orange precipitate.
- Although acrylic acid contains a C=O bond (as part of the –COOH group), 2,4-DNPH does not react with carboxylic acids.
- Therefore, acrylic acid does not produce an orange precipitate with 2,4-DNPH.

**A** is incorrect as each sp<sup>2</sup> carbon in acrylic acid has 3 bonding groups and no lone pairs, giving bond angles x and y of approximately 120°.

**B** is incorrect as acrylic acid contains a C=C double bond, which undergoes electrophilic addition with aqueous bromine and decolourises it.

**D** is incorrect as acrylic acid is a carboxylic acid, which reacts with alcohols in an esterification reaction to form an ester.

parts.problemMd: Which compound has an *M*<sub>r</sub> of 84 and will react with HBr to give a product with an *M*<sub>r</sub> of 164.9?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- HBr undergoes electrophilic addition with alkenes only: H adds to one carbon and Br adds to the other across the C=C double bond. Only alkenes react with HBr, so only **B** and **D** are candidates.
- Check compound **D** (hex-3-ene, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>):
- Calculate the *M*<sub>r</sub> of hex-3-ene:

*M*<sub>r</sub> = (6 x 12) + (12 x 1)

*M*<sub>r</sub> = 72 + 12

*M*<sub>r</sub> = 84

- In electrophilic addition, HBr adds across the C=C bond. The *M*<sub>r</sub> of the product equals *M*<sub>r</sub>(alkene) + *M*<sub>r</sub>(HBr):

*M*<sub>r</sub>(product) = 84 + 80.9

*M*<sub>r</sub>(product) = 164.9

- Both conditions are satisfied, confirming compound **D**.

![Structural diagram confirming hex-3-ene reacting with HBr to form 3-bromohexane with the correct molecular masses](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/14-hydrocarbons/14-2-alkenes/assets/009-structural-diagram-confirming-hex-3-ene-reacting.jpg)

**A** and **C** are incorrect as these compounds are not alkenes and do not react with HBr by electrophilic addition.

**B** is incorrect as although it is an alkene with *M*<sub>r</sub> = 84, its product with HBr does not have *M*<sub>r</sub> = 164.9.

parts.problemMd:
Alkane **X** has molecular formula C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub>.

**X** reacts with Cl<sub>2</sub> (g) in the presence of ultraviolet light to produce only two different monochloroalkanes, C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>9</sub>Cl. Both of these monochloroalkanes produce the same alkene **Y**, and no other organic products, when they are treated with hot ethanolic KOH.

What is produced when **Y** is treated with hot concentrated acidified KMnO<sub>4</sub>?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- Alkane **X** (C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub>) must be branched for two different monochloroalkanes to both give the same alkene on dehydrohalogenation.

  - Alkane **X** is therefore 2-methylpropane, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>CH.
- Free radical substitution of 2-methylpropane with Cl<sub>2</sub> in sunlight gives 1-chloro-2-methylpropane and 2-chloro-2-methylpropane.
- Both undergo dehydrohalogenation with hot ethanolic KOH to give the same alkene, **Y** = 2-methylprop-1-ene (CH<sub>2</sub>=C(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>).

![Structural diagram showing pathways from 2-methylpropane through both monochloroalkanes to 2-methylprop-1-ene, then oxidative cleavage products](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/14-hydrocarbons/14-2-alkenes/assets/010-structural-diagram-showing-pathways-from-2-methy.jpg)

- Hot concentrated acidified KMnO<sub>4</sub> cleaves the C=C bond by vigorous oxidation:

  - The terminal =CH<sub>2</sub> end is fully oxidised to CO<sub>2</sub> (and H<sub>2</sub>O).
  - The C(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> end is disubstituted (no H on that carbon) and forms a ketone: CH<sub>3</sub>COCH<sub>3</sub> (propanone).

**A** is incorrect as propanoic acid (CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>H) would require a –CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> fragment on the double bond, which is not present in 2-methylprop-1-ene.

**C** is incorrect as methanoic acid (HCO<sub>2</sub>H) comes from a –CH= fragment. The terminal =CH<sub>2</sub> in 2-methylprop-1-ene is fully oxidised to CO<sub>2</sub>, not methanoic acid.

**D** is incorrect as ethanoic acid (CH<sub>3</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>H) alone would result from oxidative cleavage of a symmetric alkene such as but-2-ene, not 2-methylprop-1-ene.

choices.label: B
choices.textMd: Polymerise ethene followed by oxidation with cold acidified KMnO<sub>4</sub>.

choices.label: D
choices.textMd: Polymerise 1,2-dichloroethene followed by oxidation with cold acidified KMnO<sub>4</sub>.

parts.problemMd:
The following diagram represents the structure of a possible polymer.

![Structural diagram of a polymer repeating unit in which each backbone carbon atom carries a hydroxyl group](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/14-hydrocarbons/14-2-alkenes/assets/024-structural-diagram-of-a-polymer-repeating-unit-i.jpg)

Which sequence of reactions could be used to produce this polymer?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

1. Draw the monomer structural formula

**A** is incorrect as polymerising ethene gives a saturated poly(ethene) backbone with no substituents. Hydrating a saturated polymer does not introduce –OH groups along the chain.

**B** and **D** are incorrect as oxidation with cold acidified KMnO<sub>4</sub> converts C=C double bonds into diol groups. parts.problemMd:
Oxidation of an alkene **Y** gives a diol; further oxidation gives a diketone.

What could be **Y**?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- Mild oxidation with cold dilute KMnO<sub>4</sub> converts the C=C double bond into a diol, adding an –OH group to each alkene carbon.
- For the diol to undergo further oxidation to a diketone, both –OH groups must be secondary, i.e. each carbon bearing –OH must also carry at least one H atom.

  - A secondary alcohol oxidises to a ketone.
  - A tertiary alcohol (no H on that carbon) cannot be oxidised further.
- In option **C** (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CH=CHC<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>), each alkene carbon carries one H and one C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub> group. After diol formation, both –OH groups are secondary and are oxidised to C=O, giving a diketone.

![Structural diagram showing the oxidation of C6H5CH=CHC6H5 first to the diol then to the diketone product](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/14-hydrocarbons/14-2-alkenes/assets/011-structural-diagram-showing-the-oxidation-of-c6h5.jpg)

**A** is incorrect as CH<sub>3</sub>CH=C(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> gives a diol in which the right-hand C bears no H atoms (tertiary). This –OH group cannot be oxidised further, so a diketone cannot form.

![Structural diagram showing the diol from CH3CH=C(CH3)2, with the tertiary C-OH group that cannot be further oxidised](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/14-hydrocarbons/14-2-alkenes/assets/012-structural-diagram-showing-the-diol-from-ch3ch-c.jpg)

**B** is incorrect as (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CHCH=CH<sub>2</sub> gives a diol in which the terminal C has a primary –OH group. A primary alcohol oxidises to a carboxylic acid, not a ketone, so a diketone is not formed.

![Structural diagram showing the diol from (CH3)2CHCH=CH2, with the primary C-OH group highlighted](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/14-hydrocarbons/14-2-alkenes/assets/013-structural-diagram-showing-the-diol-from-ch3-2ch.jpg)

**D** is incorrect as (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>)<sub>2</sub>C=CHCH<sub>3</sub> gives a diol in which the left-hand C carries two C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub> groups and no H atoms (tertiary). This –OH group cannot be further oxidised.

![Structural diagram showing the diol from (C6H5)2C=CHCH3, with the tertiary C-OH group that cannot be further oxidised](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/14-hydrocarbons/14-2-alkenes/assets/014-structural-diagram-showing-the-diol-from-c6h5-2c.jpg)

parts.problemMd:
Ethene is prepared by adding ethanol dropwise to heated reagent **Y**. To purify the ethene, it is bubbled through solution **Z** and then collected.

Which row identifies reagent **Y** and solution **Z**?

|   | **Reagent Y** | **Solution Z** |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | Acidified K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> | Dilute NaOH |
| **B** | Concentrated H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> | Dilute H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> |
| **C** | Concentrated H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> | Dilute NaOH |
| **D** | Ethanolic NaOH | Concentrated H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- Ethanol undergoes dehydration to form ethene.

  - Concentrated H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (heated) is the correct reagent for this reaction, eliminating options **A** and **D**.
- The ethene produced contains acidic impurities, principally SO<sub>2</sub> formed by oxidation of ethanol by hot concentrated H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>.

  - These must be removed before the gas is collected.
- In option **C**, passing the gas through dilute NaOH neutralises the acidic SO<sub>2</sub> impurity, giving purified ethene.

**A** is incorrect as acidified K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> oxidises ethanol to ethanal rather than dehydrating it to ethene.

**B** is incorrect as passing the gas through dilute H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> adds more acid rather than removing it.

**D** is incorrect as ethanolic NaOH promotes elimination of HX from haloalkanes, not dehydration of alcohols.

parts.problemMd:
**X** and **Y** are the reagents required to convert 1-bromopropane into butanoic acid.

![Reaction scheme showing the two-step conversion of 1-bromopropane to butanoic acid via a nitrile intermediate, with reagent boxes X and Y to complete](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/15-halogen-compounds/15-1-halogenoalkanes/assets/013-reaction-scheme-showing-the-two-step-conversion-.png)

Which row correctly identifies **X** and **Y**?

|   | **X** | **Y** |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | NH<sub>3</sub> | HCl (aq) |
| **B** | KCN in C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH | NaOH (aq) |
| **C** | KCN in C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH | HCl (aq) |
| **D** | HCN | NaOH (aq) |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- If a halogenoalkane is heated under reflux with a solution of potassium cyanide in ethanol, the halogen is replaced by a -CN group and a nitrile is produced.

  - So, reagent X must be KCN in C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH.
- Next, to produce a carboxylic acid, the nitrile is heated under reflux with dilute hydrochloric acid.

  - So, reagent Y must be HCl.

**A** is incorrect as the reaction of a halogenoalkane with ammonia would produce a primary amine, not a carboxylic acid.

**B** and **D** are incorrect as reagent Y could not be NaOH, as this would produce the sodium salt –COONa rather than the carboxylic acid –COOH.

parts.problemMd: Which reaction occurs when ethane and chlorine are mixed in diffused sunlight?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- Ethane reacts with chlorine by free radical substitution in the presence of sunlight.
- In the presence of sunlight, Cl<sub>2</sub> breaks down to form two chlorine radicals:

Cl<sub>2</sub> → 2Cl•

- The generated chlorine radical can then react with ethane to give an ethane radical (C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>•) and HCl:

C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub> + Cl• → C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>• + HCl

- Therefore, the reaction is a free-radical substitution with hydrogen chloride produced.

**A** is incorrect as free radical substitution produces HCl, not H<sub>2</sub>.

**C** is incorrect as the reaction produces HCl gas; a gas is produced.

**D** is incorrect as the mechanism is free radical substitution, not nucleophilic substitution. Nucleophilic substitution requires a nucleophile attacking a carbon bonded to a leaving group, which does not apply here.

parts.problemMd:
Chlorofluoroalkanes, CFCs, can be used as refrigerants, aerosol propellants and fire extinguishers.

CFCs such as CCl<sub>3</sub>F and CCl<sub>2</sub>F<sub>2</sub> are more stable than chloroalkanes such as CCl<sub>4</sub>.

What is the reason for their greater stability?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- CFCs and chloroalkanes are similar as they both contain C–Cl bonds, but they differ in that CFCs contain C–F bonds.
- The bond energy of the C–F bond is larger than the C–Cl bond.
- So, it takes less energy to release Cl atoms than F atoms from CFCs.

  - This is why CFCs are more stable than chloroalkanes.

**A** and **B** are incorrect as the stability of a molecule comes from the strength of the bonds within the molecule, not the ionisation energy or stability of radicals.

**D** is incorrect as the polarity of a bond tells us how electronegative an atom is, which contributes to the strength of the bond, but is not the direct reason for the stability of the molecule overall.

parts.problemMd:
Light initiates the following reaction.

alkane + chlorine $\rightarrow$ chloroalkane + hydrogen chloride

What happens to the chlorine molecule during this photochemical reaction?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- Homolytic fission = splitting a bond to produce two particles which both have a single unpaired electron (both are free radicals).

- Heterolytic fission = producing two particles which are different because one is a positive ion and the other is a negative ion.

- In this photochemical reaction, energy from sunlight causes chlorine molecules to split into two chlorine atoms, each with one unpaired electron.

- Free radicals are formed when a bond splits evenly, with each atom getting one of the two electrons.

- Hence, chlorine undergoes homolytic fission to give free radicals.

**A** is incorrect as heterolytic fission produces ions, not free radicals, and would give an electrophile (Cl<sup>+</sup>), not a radical.

**B** is incorrect as heterolytic fission does not occur here; the process is homolytic, producing radicals not electrophiles.

**C** is incorrect as homolytic fission does occur, but it produces free radicals, not electrophiles.

parts.problemMd:
High-energy irradiation in the stratosphere produces radicals from halogenoalkanes.

Which radical could result from this irradiation of CHFClCF<sub>2</sub>Cl?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- In the given molecule above, there are:

C–H bonds, C–F bonds, C–Cl bonds and a C–C bond.

- In all the options the C–C bond remains intact.
- The order of bond strength of the remaining 3 bonds is:

C–F > C–H > C–Cl

- Therefore, a C–Cl bond will be broken since it requires the least energy – this only occurs in option **C**.

**A** is incorrect as the molecule loses an F atom, suggesting that a C–F bond is broken.

**B** is incorrect as the molecule loses a different F atom, yet still suggesting that a C–F bond is broken.

**D** is incorrect as the molecule loses an H atom, suggesting that a C–H bond is broken.

parts.problemMd: Which reaction is an example of nucleophilic substitution?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- A nucleophile is either a negatively charged species or a molecule with a lone pair of electrons, e.g. H<sub>2</sub>O.
- Nucleophilic substitution reactions involve substitution of a group or atom by a nucleophile.
- The only option which contains a nucleophile is water (H<sub>2</sub>O) in **C**, which acts via a lone pair on the oxygen atom.
- The mechanism for the reaction with bromopropane is as follows:

![Curly arrow mechanism for the SN2 nucleophilic substitution of 1-bromopropane with water, showing attack by the lone pair on oxygen and departure of bromide ion](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/15-halogen-compounds/15-1-halogenoalkanes/assets/024-curly-arrow-mechanism-for-the-sn2-nucleophilic-s.jpg)

**A** is incorrect as this is an elimination reaction; KOH in ethanolic solution removes HBr to form the alkene.

**B** is incorrect as this is an electrophilic addition reaction.

**D** is incorrect as this is a free radical substitution.

parts.problemMd:
Bromomethane, CH<sub>3</sub>Br, is used as a fumigant to destroy insect pests in grain that is to be stored. It can be made by reacting methanol with hydrogen bromide.

CH<sub>3</sub>OH  +  HBr  $\rightarrow$  CH<sub>3</sub>Br  + H<sub>2</sub>O

What type of reaction is this?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- A nucleophile is either a negatively charged species or a molecule with a lone pair of electrons.
- Nucleophilic substitution involves a nucleophile replacing a leaving group at a carbon atom.
- In this reaction, the Br<sup>–</sup> leaving group departs and is replaced by a nucleophile, as shown below:

![SN2 mechanism diagram for the reaction between methanol and hydrogen bromide to give bromomethane, showing curly arrows for bond breaking and forming](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/15-halogen-compounds/15-1-halogenoalkanes/assets/001-sn2-mechanism-diagram-for-the-reaction-between-m.jpg)

**A** is incorrect as condensation reactions involve the joining of two molecules with the loss of a small molecule (e.g. H<sub>2</sub>O); that does not occur here.

**B** is incorrect as electrophilic substitution requires an electrophile attacking an electron-rich centre (e.g. a benzene ring); OH<sup>–</sup> is a nucleophile, not an electrophile.

**C** is incorrect as free radical substitution involves homolytic fission and radical intermediates, initiated by UV light; no radicals are involved in this reaction.

parts.problemMd:
Dichlorodifluoromethane, CCl<sub>2</sub>F<sub>2</sub>, has been used in aerosol propellants and as a refrigerant.

Which statement helps to explain why dichlorodifluoromethane is chemically inert?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- In dichlorodifluoromethane, there are two C–F bonds and two C–Cl bonds.
- Both are strong bonds, and the C–F bond energy is the larger of the two.
- The C–F bond strength is the reason for the inertness of CCl<sub>2</sub>F<sub>2</sub> and CFCs in general.
- These bonds are so strong that they do not break under the energy of ordinary visible light.

  - UV light is required to break them.

**A** is incorrect as the non-flammability of fluorine compounds is a consequence of the inertness of CCl<sub>2</sub>F<sub>2</sub>, not a reason for it.

**B** is incorrect as the high electronegativity of fluorine contributes to the strength of the C–F bond, but electronegativity alone is not the direct reason for the inertness.

**D** is incorrect as the C–F bond is in fact highly polar; furthermore, bond polarity is not the direct reason for the inertness – bond energy is.

parts.problemMd:
The reaction of chlorine with methane is carried out in the presence of ultraviolet light.

What is the function of the ultraviolet light?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- This reaction is known as chlorination of methane and proceeds through the radical chain mechanism.
- The radical chain mechanism involves three steps: **initiation**, **propagation** and **termination**.
- Initiation requires an input of energy but after that the reaction is self-sustaining.
- This energy comes from the ultraviolet light source, which breaks the Cl–Cl bond homolytically to form two chlorine radicals.

**A** is incorrect as ultraviolet light does not break the C–H bonds in methane. It is the chlorine radical produced in initiation that abstracts a hydrogen atom in the propagation step.

**B** is incorrect as ultraviolet light causes homolytic fission of the Cl–Cl bond to give radicals, not ions.

**D** is incorrect as ultraviolet light provides the activation energy to form radicals, not heat for the mixture. The reaction proceeds at room temperature once initiated.

parts.problemMd:
Four drops of 1-chlorobutane, 1-bromobutane and 1-iodobutane were put separately into three test-tubes containing 1.0 cm<sup>3</sup> of aqueous silver nitrate at 60 °C.

A hydrolysis reaction occurred.

R represents the butane chain C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>9–</sub> and *X* the halogen atom.

H<sub>2</sub>O (l) + R–*X* (l) + Ag<sup>+</sup> (aq) $\rightarrow$ R–OH (aq) + Ag*X* (s) + H<sup>+</sup> (aq)

The rate of formation of cloudiness in the tubes was in the order RCl < RBr < RI

Which statement explains this order of reactivity?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- The rate of formation of cloudiness (the order of reactivity) is related to the strength of the R–*X* bond.
- The carbon-iodine bond is the weakest and the carbon-chlorine bond is the strongest: C–Cl > C–Br > C–I
- So 1-iodobutane would react the quickest, followed by 1-bromobutane and then 1-chlorobutane.
- In order for a halide ion to be produced, the carbon-halogen bond must break – the weaker the bond, the more easily it breaks.
- Therefore, **bond energy** is the main factor deciding the relative rates of reaction.

**B** is incorrect as the ionisation energy of the halogen is a property of the isolated atom. It does not determine how easily the C–*X* bond breaks in solution.

**C** is incorrect as bond polarity is not the main factor here; although polarity contributes to bond strength, the dominant factor is bond energy.

**D** is incorrect as the solubility of the silver halide precipitate does not control the rate of the initial hydrolysis reaction.

parts.problemMd: What is involved in the mechanism of the reaction between aqueous sodium hydroxide and 1-bromobutane?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- Haloalkanes undergo nucleophilic substitution because the greater electronegativity of the halogen creates a partial positive charge (C<sup>δ+</sup>) on the carbon bonded to it.
- The nucleophile attacks the C<sup>δ+</sup> carbon while the C–Br bond breaks simultaneously.

  - This is a concerted, one-step process with no carbocation intermediate.
- This is an S<sub>N</sub>2 reaction.

  - **S**ubstitution **N**ucleophilic **b**imolecular, a reaction in which a bond is broken and a new bond formed simultaneously in one step.

![Curly arrow mechanism for the SN2 reaction of 1-bromobutane with hydroxide ion, showing simultaneous attack by OH⁻ on the δ+ carbon and departure of Br⁻](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/15-halogen-compounds/15-1-halogenoalkanes/assets/016-curly-arrow-mechanism-for-the-sn2-reaction-of-1-.jpg)

**B** is incorrect as, although the C–Br bond does break by heterolytic fission, S<sub>N</sub>2 has no discrete carbocation intermediate as the bond breaks and the new bond forms in the same step.

**C** is incorrect as the hydroxide ion (OH<sup>–</sup>) is a nucleophile, not an electrophile.

**D** is incorrect as the reaction does not involve homolytic fission. Homolytic fission produces two free radicals and is characteristic of radical chain reactions. Nucleophilic substitution proceeds by heterolytic fission of the C–Br bond, not radical combination.

parts.problemMd:
A reaction between chlorine and propane in the presence of ultraviolet light produces two isomeric monochloropropanes, C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>7</sub>Cl.

Which row identifies the type of bond fission in the initiation step and the expected ratio of 1-chloropropane to 2-chloropropane produced?

|   | **Type of bond fission in initiation step** | **Expected ratio of 1-chloropropane to 2-chloropropane produced** |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | Heterolytic | 1:1 |
| **B** | Heterolytic | 3:1 |
| **C** | Homolytic | 1:1 |
| **D** | Homolytic | 3:1 |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- Homolytic fission = splitting a bond to produce two free radicals (that are the same).
- Heterolytic fission = splitting a bond to produce a positive ion and a negative ion (that are different).
- Propane reacts with chlorine by free radical substitution in the presence of UV light.
- In the presence of UV, Cl<sub>2</sub> breaks down to form two chlorine radicals.

Cl<sub>2</sub> → 2Cl•

- This is an example of homolytic fission, which eliminates options **A** and **B**.
- In the next step, propane reacts with a chlorine radical to form the two isomers of chloropropane.

C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub> + Cl• → C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>7</sub>Cl

- For 1-chloropropane to form, the chlorine radical has 6 hydrogens it can react with – probability $\frac{6}{8}$
- For 2-chloropropane to form, the chlorine radical has 2 hydrogens it can react with – probability $\frac{2}{8}$
- Therefore, the expected ratio of 1-chloropropane to 2-chloropropane = 6 : 2 = **3 : 1**.

![Structural diagram of propane showing the six primary hydrogen atoms at C1 and C3 and two secondary hydrogen atoms at C2 for the statistical ratio calculation](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/15-halogen-compounds/15-1-halogenoalkanes/assets/009-structural-diagram-of-propane-showing-the-six-pr.jpg)

parts.problemMd:
Bromine and propene undergo an addition reaction.

Which statement about the product is correct?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- When bromine and propene undergo an addition reaction, the double bond breaks, and a bromine atom becomes attached to each carbon.
- In this reaction with propene, 1,2-dibromopropane is formed.

![Displayed formula of 1,2-dibromopropane, product of electrophilic addition of Br₂ to propene, with bromine atoms on adjacent C1 and C2](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/15-halogen-compounds/15-1-halogenoalkanes/assets/017-displayed-formula-of-1-2-dibromopropane-product-.jpg)

- A chiral carbon atom is a carbon atom that is attached to four different types of atoms or groups of atoms.

![Structural formula of 1,2-dibromopropane with the chiral centre at C2 marked with an asterisk](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/15-halogen-compounds/15-1-halogenoalkanes/assets/018-structural-formula-of-1-2-dibromopropane-with-th.jpg)

- 1,2-dibromopropane possesses a chiral centre, so **C** is correct.

**A** is incorrect as haloalkanes don't contain a double bond, and hence don't exist as cis-trans isomers.

**B** is incorrect as 1,2-dibromopropane is less volatile than propene. Volatility depends on intermolecular forces, not covalent bond strength. 1,2-dibromopropane has a larger, more polarisable electron cloud, resulting in stronger London dispersion forces between molecules compared to propene.

**D** is incorrect as carbon-halogen bonds do not enable hydrogen bonding. Hydrogen bonding requires hydrogen to be directly bonded to a highly electronegative atom (N, O, or F).

parts.problemMd: Which compound undergoes an S<sub>N</sub>1 substitution reaction?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- S<sub>N</sub>1 reactions are nucleophilic substitutions, involving a nucleophile replacing a leaving group (just like in S<sub>N</sub>2).

  - However, S<sub>N</sub>1 reactions are unimolecular, so the rate of this reaction depends only on one species (the halogenoalkane).
- Tertiary halogenoalkanes tend to be the most reactive and tend to undergo nucleophilic substitution via the S<sub>N</sub>1 carbocation mechanism.
- Whereas, primary halogenoalkanes tend to be the least reactive and react via the S<sub>N</sub>2 mechanism.
- So, overall carbocation stability:

3º > 2º >> 1º

- Option **D**, 1-chloro-1-methylcyclohexane, is a tertiary halogenoalkane, hence it is the most likely option to undergo S<sub>N</sub>1 substitution.

**A** is incorrect as (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>CCH<sub>2</sub>I is a primary halogenoalkane (neopentyl iodide). Despite the bulky neopentyl group, the carbon bearing the iodine has no alkyl substituents, so this compound favours S<sub>N</sub>2.

**B** is incorrect as CH<sub>2</sub>=CHCl is a vinyl halide, where the halogen is directly attached to a C=C double bond, which delocalises electron density and makes nucleophilic substitution extremely unfavourable.

**C** is incorrect as CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Br is a primary halogenoalkane, which favours S<sub>N</sub>2 nucleophilic substitution rather than S<sub>N</sub>1.

parts.problemMd:
CCl<sub>2</sub>FCClF<sub>2</sub> is converted to a fluorocarbon by the following route:

CCl<sub>2</sub>FCClF<sub>2</sub> $\overset{\text{step 1}}{\rightarrow}$ CCl<sub>3</sub>CF<sub>3</sub> $\overset{\text{step 2}}{\rightarrow}$ CCl<sub>2</sub>FCF<sub>3</sub>

What type of reaction is **step 2**?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- In the reaction CCl<sub>3</sub>CF<sub>3</sub> → CCl<sub>2</sub>FCF<sub>3</sub>
- A Cl atom is replaced with an F atom.
- F<sup>–</sup> (fluoride ion) is the nucleophile; hence it undergoes nucleophilic substitution:

![SN2 mechanism showing F⁻ acting as nucleophile displacing Cl⁻ from CCl₃CF₃ to give CCl₂FCF₃](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/15-halogen-compounds/15-1-halogenoalkanes/assets/007-sn2-mechanism-showing-f-acting-as-nucleophile-di.jpg)

**A** is incorrect as electrophilic substitution requires an electrophile attacking an electron-rich centre; F<sup>–</sup> is a nucleophile, not an electrophile.

**B** is incorrect as free-radical substitution involves homolytic fission and radical intermediates initiated by UV light; no radicals are involved in this halogen exchange reaction.

**C** is incorrect as isomerisation involves rearrangement of atoms within the same molecular formula; here a Cl atom is replaced by F, changing the formula.

parts.problemMd:
The presence of a halogen in an organic compound may be detected by warming the organic compound with aqueous ethanolic silver nitrate.

Which compound would be the quickest to produce a precipitate?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- Heating the compounds causes the bonds to break, releasing the halide ions, which then react with the silver ions in AgNO<sub>3</sub> to form precipitates.
- The smaller the bond energy, the weaker the bond, the more quickly it breaks and the faster a precipitate is produced.
- Among F, Cl, Br and I, iodine has the largest atomic radius and the lowest electronegativity, so the C–I bond is the longest and least polar and therefore the weakest.
- Compound **C** is the only compound containing I, so it produces a precipitate most quickly.

**A** is incorrect as the compound shown contains Br. The C–Br bond is stronger than the C–I bond, so it reacts more slowly.

**B** is incorrect as the compound shown also contains Br. The same reasoning applies where C–Br breaks less easily than C–I.

**D** is incorrect as the compound shown contains Cl. The C–Cl bond has the highest bond energy of the three and is the slowest to break.

parts.problemMd:
In the hydrolysis of bromoethane by aqueous sodium hydroxide, which row correctly describes the attacking group and the leaving group?

|   | **Attacking group** | **Leaving group** |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | Electrophile | Electrophile |
| **B** | Electrophile | Nucleophile |
| **C** | Nucleophile | Electrophile |
| **D** | Nucleophile | Nucleophile |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- The reaction between bromoethane and sodium hydroxide is **nucleophilic substitution**.
- The OH<sup>–</sup> ion uses a lone pair to attack the δ<sup>+</sup> carbon bonded to Br – OH<sup>–</sup> is the attacking nucleophile.
- The Br<sup>–</sup> ion departs with both bonding electrons – Br<sup>–</sup> has lone pairs and is the leaving nucleophile.
- Therefore, both the attacking group and the leaving group are nucleophiles.

![SN2 mechanism for the hydrolysis of bromoethane showing OH⁻ attacking the δ⁺ carbon and Br⁻ departing as the leaving nucleophile](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/15-halogen-compounds/15-1-halogenoalkanes/assets/008-sn2-mechanism-for-the-hydrolysis-of-bromoethane-.jpg)

**A** is incorrect as OH<sup>–</sup> is a nucleophile, not an electrophile; electrophiles accept electron pairs, whereas OH<sup>–</sup> donates them.

**B** is incorrect as the attacking group (OH<sup>–</sup>) is a nucleophile, not an electrophile.

**C** is incorrect as the leaving group (Br<sup>–</sup>) has lone pairs of electrons and acts as a nucleophile, not an electrophile.

parts.problemMd: Which reaction will give the highest yield of 2-chloropropane as the only organic product?
parts.solutionMd:

- Propan-2-ol reacts with SOCl<sub>2</sub> to give 2-chloropropane as the only organic product.
- The by-products SO<sub>2</sub> and HCl are gases and are easily removed.
- This makes the reaction high yielding and selective for 2-chloropropane.

**A** is incorrect as no substitution reaction occurs between alcohols and dilute NaCl without a catalyst or halogenating agent.

**C** is incorrect as free radical substitution of propane with chlorine forms a mixture of chloropropanes and other substitution products, lowering the yield of 2-chloropropane.

**D** is incorrect as the electrophilic addition of HCl (g) to propene follows Markovnikov’s rule and gives mainly 2-chloropropane, but also forms some 1-chloropropane, so the yield is lower than with SOCl<sub>2</sub>.

parts.problemMd:
Aqueous sodium hydroxide reacts with 1-bromopropane to give propan-1-ol.

Which statement correctly describes the mechanism of this reaction?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- This reaction can be written as follows:

CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Br + OH<sup>–</sup> → CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH + Br<sup>–</sup>

- The OH<sup>–</sup> ion, acting as a nucleophile, uses its lone pair to attack the δ<sup>+</sup> carbon bonded to Br.
- This is shown by a curly arrow from the lone pair on OH<sup>–</sup> to the carbon atom.

**B** is incorrect as curly arrows always go from the nucleophile to the electrophile, not the other way around.

**C** is incorrect as the curly arrow should go from the C–Br bond to the Br atom to show bond breaking, not from the bond to the C atom.

**D** is incorrect as the C–Br bond breaks by heterolytic fission (both electrons go to Br<sup>–</sup>), not homolytic fission.

parts.problemMd:
The table shows the time taken for a silver halide precipitate to appear when halogenoalkanes react with aqueous ethanolic silver nitrate at 50 <sup>o</sup>C.

| halogenoalkane | time for precipitate / s |
|---|---|
| 1-chlorobutane | >300 |
| 1-bromobutane | 120 |
| 1-iodobutane | 15 |

Which statement explains the differences in the times taken for the precipitate to appear?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- The table shows the reaction is slowest for 1-chlorobutane and fastest for 1-iodobutane.
- In this test, the rate depends mainly on how easily the C–X bond breaks to form ions.

  - C–I has the lowest bond enthalpy, so it breaks most easily → fastest precipitate.
  - C–Cl has the highest bond enthalpy, so it breaks least easily → slowest precipitate.
- This trend explains the observed order of reaction times.

**A** is incorrect as the C–I bond is the weakest of the carbon-halogen bonds, not the strongest.

**C** is incorrect as the oxidising power of the halogen is not the factor controlling the rate of this hydrolysis reaction.

**D** is incorrect as bond polarity is not the main factor here; it is the overall bond enthalpy that determines how easily the bond breaks.

parts.problemMd:
Bromoethane reacts with ammonia to form ethylamine.

Which set of conditions is required to maximise the yield of ethylamine and minimise further substitution products?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- Bromoethane reacts with ammonia by nucleophilic substitution to form ethylamine.
- To maximise the yield of the primary amine, a large excess of ammonia is used.
- This reduces the chance of the ethylamine product acting as a nucleophile and undergoing further substitution to form secondary and tertiary amines.
- Ethanol is used as the solvent because it dissolves both the halogenoalkane and ammonia.
- A sealed tube is required to prevent volatile ammonia from escaping during heating.

**A** is incorrect as using excess bromoethane increases the likelihood of further substitution of the amine product, reducing the yield of ethylamine.

**B** is incorrect as, although heating bromoethane with excess ammonia in a sealed tube would form ethylamine, the solvent used is not ethanol. Without ethanol the halogenoalkane and ammonia are not in a suitable common solvent, reducing the yield of the primary amine.

**C** is incorrect as aqueous ammonia is a less effective solvent for the halogenoalkane and encourages competing reactions, reducing the yield of the primary amine.

parts.problemMd:
Consider the two-step synthesis:

ethane  $\overset{\mathrm{step}1}{\rightarrow}$ bromoethane $\overset{\mathrm{step}2}{\rightarrow}$ ethylamine

|   | step 1 reagents | step 2 reagents |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | Br<sub>2</sub>, UV light | NH<sub>3</sub>, ethanol, heat under pressure |
| **B** | HBr, room temperature | NH<sub>3</sub>, aqueous, reflux |
| **C** | Br<sub>2</sub>, UV light | KCN, ethanol, reflux |
| **D** | PBr<sub>3</sub>, reflux | HNO<sub>3</sub>, room temperature |

Which row shows the correct reagents and conditions?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

**Step 1: Ethane → bromoethane**

- Ethane is an alkane, so it reacts with bromine by free-radical substitution.
- This requires Br<sub>2</sub> and UV light to initiate homolytic fission of the Br–Br bond and form radicals.

**Step 2: Bromoethane → ethylamine**

- Bromoethane undergoes nucleophilic substitution with ammonia to form an amine.
- The conditions used are ethanolic ammonia, heat in a sealed tube, to prevent ammonia escaping and to increase the yield.

**B** is incorrect as HBr does not convert an alkane into a bromoalkane under these conditions.

**C** is incorrect as KCN would form a nitrile, not an amine.

**D** is incorrect as PBr<sub>3</sub> is used to convert alcohols to bromoalkanes, not alkanes, and HNO<sub>3</sub> is not used to make amines from halogenoalkanes.

parts.problemMd:
When an isomer **Y** of molecular formula C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>9</sub>Br undergoes hydrolysis in aqueous sodium hydroxide to form an alcohol C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>9</sub>OH, the rate of reaction is found to be independent of the concentration of OH<sup>–</sup> ions present.

Which is the most likely molecular structure of **Y**?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- The rate of reaction is independent of the concentration of OH<sup>–</sup>, which means the rate depends only on the concentration of the halogenoalkane, not the nucleophile.

  - This is characteristic of an S<sub>N</sub>1 reaction (**S**ubstitution **N**ucleophilic **u**nimolecular).
- In S<sub>N</sub>1, the C–Br bond breaks first (slow step) to form a carbocation intermediate, and then the nucleophile attacks (fast step).
- Tertiary carbocations are stabilised by the electron-donating inductive effect of three alkyl groups, making them more stable than secondary or primary carbocations.
- This stability lowers the activation energy of the first step and makes the S<sub>N</sub>1 pathway favourable.
- (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>CBr is a tertiary halogenoalkane, so it readily forms a stable tertiary carbocation and undergoes S<sub>N</sub>1 hydrolysis.

**A** is incorrect as (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CHCH<sub>2</sub>Br has Br on a primary carbon. Primary halogenoalkanes react by S<sub>N</sub>2, where the rate depends on the concentration of both the halogenoalkane and the nucleophile.

**B** is incorrect as CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Br is a primary halogenoalkane and reacts by S<sub>N</sub>2. Its rate would be affected by changes in [OH<sup>–</sup>].

**D** is incorrect as CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CHBrCH<sub>3</sub> is a secondary halogenoalkane. Secondary halogenoalkanes can undergo both S<sub>N</sub>1 and S<sub>N</sub>2, but the rate is not entirely independent of [OH<sup>–</sup>] as it would be for a tertiary compound.

parts.problemMd:
A tertiary bromoalkane, indicated here by      C–Br, reacts with aqueous NaOH. The mechanism has the reaction pathway below.

![Double-bump reaction pathway diagram for SN1 hydrolysis of a tertiary bromoalkane, with energy maxima as transition states and energy minimum as carbocation intermediate, points X and Y labelled](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/15-halogen-compounds/15-1-halogenoalkanes/assets/011-double-bump-reaction-pathway-diagram-for-sn1-hyd.png)

Which point in the diagram is correctly identified?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- A tertiary halogenoalkane reacts with a hydroxide ion by a two-step mechanism.
- This mechanism is known as an S<sub>N</sub>1 mechanism.

  - The '1' tells us that the rate of the reaction only depends on one reagent, in this case the concentration of the halogenoalkane, as shown in the first (slow) step of the mechanism.
- The first step in the mechanism is the breaking of the carbon-halogen bond – this forms a tertiary carbocation, as shown below:

![Two-step SN1 mechanism showing heterolytic C–Br bond breaking to form a tertiary carbocation intermediate, followed by OH⁻ attack](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/15-halogen-compounds/15-1-halogenoalkanes/assets/012-two-step-sn1-mechanism-showing-heterolytic-c-br-.jpg)

- Then, the tertiary carbocation is attacked immediately by the hydroxide ion.
- Reaction pathway diagrams display information about the energy changes during chemical reactions.
- The first bump corresponds to the slow step, as more energy is required here, and the second bump corresponds to the fast step, as less energy is required at this stage.
- Point X corresponds to the breaking of the C–Br bond (first transition state, energy maximum).
- Point Y corresponds to the intermediate step when the tertiary carbocation is formed (energy minimum between the two bumps).
- Therefore, option **C** is correct.

**A** is incorrect as it misidentifies point Y – in a two-step S<sub>N</sub>1 mechanism, Y is the energy minimum between the two transition states, corresponding to the tertiary carbocation intermediate, not a transition state.

**B** is incorrect as it misidentifies point X – X is at the first energy maximum (transition state for C–Br bond breaking), not at the carbocation intermediate.

**D** is incorrect as it misidentifies both points X and Y in the double-bump energy profile of the S<sub>N</sub>1 mechanism.

parts.problemMd: When a solution of potassium cyanide in ethanol is heated under reflux with 1-chloropropane, what is the organic product of the reaction?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- The cyanide ion CN<sup>–</sup> is a nucleophile and reacts with haloalkanes to produce a nitrile.
- This is a useful reaction for increasing the chain length by one carbon atom.

Potassium cyanide + 1-chloropropane → butanenitrile + potassium chloride

KCN + CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Cl → CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CN + KCl

- Mechanism:

  - **Step 1:** The cyanide ion attacks at the partially positive carbon of the C–Cl dipole, leading to a high energy transition state.
  - **Step 2:** The chlorine atom leaves with its bonding electrons as a chloride ion.
  - **Step 3:** The final product is butanenitrile, a 4-carbon nitrile.

![SN2 mechanism showing CN⁻ attacking the δ⁺ carbon of 1-chloropropane via a transition state to form butanenitrile and Cl⁻](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/15-halogen-compounds/15-1-halogenoalkanes/assets/010-sn2-mechanism-showing-cn-attacking-the-carbon-of.jpg)

**A** is incorrect as the CN<sup>–</sup> replaces Cl and extends the chain. No chlorine remains in the organic product, so 1-chloropropanenitrile cannot form.

**C** is incorrect as ethanenitrile contains only 2 carbons. The product must contain the original 3-carbon chain plus the CN carbon, giving 4 carbons in total.

**D** is incorrect as propanenitrile contains only 3 carbons. The CN group adds one carbon to the chain, giving a 4-carbon nitrile, not a 3-carbon one.

parts.problemMd:
The compound 2-ethyl-3-methylbutanoic acid is used as a flavouring in some food.

![Structural formula of 2-ethyl-3-methylbutanoic acid showing a branched carbon chain with ethyl and methyl substituents on adjacent alpha and beta carbons and a carboxylic acid group](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/15-halogen-compounds/15-1-halogenoalkanes/assets/004-structural-formula-of-2-ethyl-3-methylbutanoic-a.jpg)

Which compound produces 2-ethyl-3-methylbutanoic acid when heated under reflux with potassium cyanide in ethanol, followed by acid hydrolysis of the reaction product?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- When halogenoalkanes are heated under reflux with ethanolic potassium cyanide, the CN<sup>–</sup> ion replaces the halogen and adds one carbon atom to the chain.
- 2-ethyl-3-methylbutanoic acid has a total of 7 carbon atoms.
- Therefore, the starting halogenoalkane must contain 6 carbon atoms.
- Compound **B** is a 6-carbon halogenoalkane; when heated with KCN in ethanol, the Br is substituted by CN:

![CN substitution step showing the reaction of the 6-carbon branched bromoalkane with KCN in ethanol to give the corresponding nitrile](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/15-halogen-compounds/15-1-halogenoalkanes/assets/005-cn-substitution-step-showing-the-reaction-of-the.jpg)

- Acid hydrolysis of the nitrile then gives the carboxylic acid:

![Acid hydrolysis step showing conversion of the nitrile intermediate to 2-ethyl-3-methylbutanoic acid under reflux with dilute acid](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/15-halogen-compounds/15-1-halogenoalkanes/assets/006-acid-hydrolysis-step-showing-conversion-of-the-n.jpg)

**A** is incorrect as it contains a different number of carbons or a different connectivity. Substitution with CN would not give the required branching pattern to produce 2-ethyl-3-methylbutanoic acid.

**C** is incorrect as its carbon skeleton does not match the structure needed. Even after CN substitution and hydrolysis, the product would not be 2-ethyl-3-methylbutanoic acid.

**D** is incorrect for the same reason that the carbon framework does not give the correct branching pattern in the target molecule.

parts.problemMd:
When phenacyl chloride, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>COCH<sub>2</sub>Cl, is reacted with aqueous NaOH, the substitution reaction follows an S<sub>N</sub>2 mechanism.

Which structure represents the transition state for this reaction?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- The structure of phenacyl chloride is:

![Structural formula of phenacyl chloride showing a benzene ring attached to a carbonyl group with a CH₂Cl group](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/15-halogen-compounds/15-1-halogenoalkanes/assets/002-structural-formula-of-phenacyl-chloride-showing-.jpg)

- In an S<sub>N</sub>2 mechanism, OH<sup>–</sup> attacks the carbon bonded to Cl, while the C–Cl bond breaks simultaneously, forming a pentacoordinate transition state.
- When reacted with aqueous NaOH, the reaction proceeds as follows:

![SN2 mechanism for phenacyl chloride with NaOH showing the pentacoordinate transition state with OH⁻ attacking and Cl⁻ departing simultaneously](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/15-halogen-compounds/15-1-halogenoalkanes/assets/003-sn2-mechanism-for-phenacyl-chloride-with-naoh-sh.jpg)

- Option **C** correctly represents the transition state for this S<sub>N</sub>2 reaction.

**A** is incorrect as the structure shown does not represent the correct transition state for S<sub>N</sub>2 attack on phenacyl chloride.

**B** is incorrect as the structure shown does not correspond to the transition state for the S<sub>N</sub>2 mechanism of this reaction.

**D** is incorrect as the structure shown does not correspond to the transition state formed during the S<sub>N</sub>2 reaction of phenacyl chloride with NaOH.

parts.problemMd:
Coniine is the major constituent of the poison 'oil of hemlock'.

![Structure of coniine showing a six-membered piperidine ring with a nitrogen atom and a propyl substituent](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/15-halogen-compounds/15-1-halogenoalkanes/assets/019-structure-of-coniine-showing-a-six-membered-pipe.jpg)

Coniine can be synthesised by reacting ammonia with a dibromo compound, **X,**C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>16</sub>Br<sub>2</sub> .

NH<sub>3</sub> + **X**$\rightarrow$ coniine + 2HBr

What is the name of compound **X**?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- Coniine contains a six-membered ring with a nitrogen atom (a piperidine ring).
- To form a six-membered ring from NH<sub>3</sub> via two nucleophilic substitutions, the two Br atoms must be separated by four carbons (positions 1 and 5 of an octane chain).
- 1,5-dibromooctane has Br at C1 and C5, which allows NH<sub>3</sub> to displace both Br atoms and close into a six-membered ring.

![Structural formula of 1,5-dibromooctane showing bromine atoms at positions C1 and C5 of the octane chain with a propyl substituent at C5](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/15-halogen-compounds/15-1-halogenoalkanes/assets/020-structural-formula-of-1-5-dibromooctane-showing-.jpg)

![Step 1: NH₃ attacking the C1–Br bond of 1,5-dibromooctane by SN2 nucleophilic substitution to displace Br⁻](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/15-halogen-compounds/15-1-halogenoalkanes/assets/021-step-1-nh-attacking-the-c1-br-bond-of-1-5-dibrom.jpg)

- Ammonia attacks the C–Br bonds via nucleophilic substitution to form coniine.

![Step 2: intramolecular SN2 cyclisation forming the six-membered piperidine ring intermediate with a positive charge on nitrogen](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/15-halogen-compounds/15-1-halogenoalkanes/assets/022-step-2-intramolecular-sn2-cyclisation-forming-th.jpg)

![Step 3: deprotonation of the ammonium salt intermediate to give coniine, a piperidine ring with a propyl chain](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/15-halogen-compounds/15-1-halogenoalkanes/assets/023-step-3-deprotonation-of-the-ammonium-salt-interm.jpg)

**A** is incorrect as 1,1-dibromo-2-propylcyclopentane has both Br atoms on the same carbon (geminal dibromide). Two substitutions at the same carbon cannot form the required ring.

**B** is incorrect as 1,2-dibromo-2-propylcyclopentane has Br atoms on adjacent carbons. The two N–C bonds formed would be too close together to produce the six-membered ring of coniine.

**C** is incorrect as 1,4-dibromooctane has Br at C1 and C4, separated by only three carbons. Double substitution with NH<sub>3</sub> would give a five-membered ring, not the six-membered piperidine ring of coniine.

parts.problemMd:
A reaction pathway diagram is shown.

![Double-bump reaction pathway diagram with two transition state energy maxima and one intermediate energy minimum, characteristic of a two-step mechanism](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/15-halogen-compounds/15-1-halogenoalkanes/assets/014-double-bump-reaction-pathway-diagram-with-two-tr.jpg)

Which reaction does **not** have such a profile?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- Reaction pathway diagrams display information about the energy changes during chemical reactions.
- The reaction pathway diagram shown has two bumps, indicating a two-step mechanism with a stable intermediate between the two transition states.

  - This is characteristic of the S<sub>N</sub>1 mechanism.
- The halogenoalkane C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>Br in option **B** is a primary halogenoalkane, which undergoes the S<sub>N</sub>2 mechanism for nucleophilic substitution.
- S<sub>N</sub>2 is a concerted one-step mechanism with a single transition state, represented by a single-bump energy profile.

![Energy profile diagram of a nucleophilic substitution, showing reactants, high transition state, and products C–O–H and Br⁻ with partial charges and bonds](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/15-halogen-compounds/15-1-halogenoalkanes/assets/015-energy-profile-diagram-of-a-nucleophilic-substit.jpg)

- Therefore, **B** does not have the double-bump profile shown.

**A** is not the answer as (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>CBr is a tertiary halogenoalkane that reacts by the S<sub>N</sub>1 mechanism, giving the double-bump profile shown.

**C** is not the answer as the addition of HCN to CH<sub>3</sub>CHO proceeds by nucleophilic addition to the carbonyl group. Although this is not an S<sub>N</sub>1 reaction, it is a two-step mechanism: CN<sup>–</sup> attacks the carbonyl carbon to form a tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate, which is then protonated. This gives a double-bump energy profile.

**D** is not the answer as the addition of Br<sub>2</sub> to cyclohex-1-ene proceeds via a cyclic bromonium ion intermediate; this two-step mechanism also gives a double-bump energy profile.

parts.problemMd: Which molecule has **no** permanent dipole?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- C<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>4</sub> (tetrachloroethene) is a symmetrical molecule: both carbon atoms carry two Cl atoms each.
- The C–Cl bond dipoles are arranged symmetrically and cancel exactly, so there is no net permanent dipole.

**A** is incorrect as CCl<sub>2</sub>F<sub>2</sub> contains both C–Cl and C–F bonds. These bonds have different dipole magnitudes because F and Cl have different electronegativities, so the bond dipoles do not cancel – there is a net permanent dipole.

**B** is incorrect as CHCl<sub>3</sub> contains three C–Cl bonds and one C–H bond. The molecule is not symmetrical, so the dipoles do not cancel – there is a net permanent dipole.

**D** is incorrect as C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>Cl contains a C–Cl bond and the molecule is not symmetrical, giving a net permanent dipole.

parts.problemMd:
Compound **X** produces a carboxylic acid when heated under reflux with acidified potassium dichromate (VI). Compound **X** has no reaction with sodium metal.

What could be the identity of compound **X**?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- When an aldehyde is heated under reflux with acidified potassium dichromate(VI), a carboxylic acid is produced.

  - This is an oxidation reaction.
- Propanal is an aldehyde, so oxidation of this compound would produce a carboxylic acid.
- Propanal does not react with sodium metal.

**B** and **D** are incorrect as propanone is a ketone, and propan-2-ol is a secondary alcohol. Secondary alcohols are oxidised to ketones, and ketones do not oxidise further.

**C** is incorrect as propan-1-ol is a primary alcohol. Primary alcohols are oxidised to aldehydes and then to carboxylic acids. Alcohols react with sodium metal, so compound **X** cannot be propan-1-ol.

parts.problemMd: Which reagents could be used in the laboratory to convert propan-1-ol into 1-bromopropane?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- Instead of using hydrobromic acid, propan-1-ol can be treated with a mixture of sodium or potassium bromide and concentrated sulfuric acid.

H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> + 2KBr $\rightarrow$ K<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> + 2HBr

- The hydrogen bromide then reacts with the alcohol.
- The reaction mixture is then warmed to distil off the bromoalkane.

![Reaction scheme showing propan-1-ol reacting with HBr to produce 1-bromopropane and water](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/16-hydroxy-compounds/16-1-alcohols/assets/012-reaction-scheme-showing-propan-1-ol-reacting-wit.jpg)

parts.problemMd: Which skeletal formula represents 4-chloropentan-2-ol?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- The best approach to questions like this is to number the carbon chains.
- Generally, the lowest possible numbers want to be used, then groups are numbered in order of priority.
- The hydroxyl (OH) group is a higher priority group and therefore has a lower number, 2.
- Chlorine therefore takes the higher number, 4.

![Skeletal formula of 4-chloropentan-2-ol with carbons numbered showing OH on carbon 2 and Cl on carbon 4](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/16-hydroxy-compounds/16-1-alcohols/assets/017-skeletal-formula-of-4-chloropentan-2-ol-with-car.jpg)

- The compound is called 4-chloropentan-2-ol.

  - Pentane has 5 carbons, so draw and label this first.
  - Then, the -OH group will be on carbon 2, and the Cl will be on carbon 4.

**A** is incorrect as this compound has 6 carbons. It is 2-chlorohexan-4-ol.

**B** is incorrect as this compound is 2-chloropentan-3-ol.

**C** is incorrect as this compound is 3-chloropentan-2-ol.

parts.problemMd: Which alcohol has a chiral centre **and** can be oxidised to a ketone?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- First, draw each compound:

![Skeletal formulae of pentan-2-ol, pentan-3-ol, 3-methylhexan-1-ol and 3-methylhexan-3-ol](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/16-hydroxy-compounds/16-1-alcohols/assets/001-skeletal-formulae-of-pentan-2-ol-pentan-3-ol-3-m.jpg)

- A ketone is produced when a **secondary alcohol** is oxidised.

  - This eliminates options **C** (a primary alcohol) and **D** (a tertiary alcohol).
- A chiral centre is a carbon atom bonded to four different atoms or groups.
- The only compound with a chiral centre is pentan-2-ol:

![Skeletal formula of pentan-2-ol with the chiral centre highlighted](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/16-hydroxy-compounds/16-1-alcohols/assets/002-skeletal-formula-of-pentan-2-ol-with-the-chiral-.jpg)

- Therefore, **A** is correct.

**B** is incorrect as pentan-3-ol is a secondary alcohol, but it does not have a chiral centre.

**C** is incorrect as 3-methylhexan-1-ol is a primary alcohol.

**D** is incorrect as 3-methylhexan-3-ol is a tertiary alcohol.
