parts.problemMd: Which reaction does **not** produce propanoic acid?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- When propanenitrile is heated with aqueous sodium hydroxide under reflux, the products are sodium propanoate and ammonia.
- To produce the free carboxylic acid the products would need to be acidified.

**A**, **B** and **D** are incorrect as all of these reactions would produce propanoic acid.

parts.problemMd:
Propanenitrile, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>C$\equiv$N, is used to produce propanoic acid.

What are the conditions for this reaction?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- When propanenitrile is heated under reflux with dilute acid, an ammonium salt and propanoic acid are produced.

**B** is incorrect as acidified potassium dichromate(VI) is used to oxidise alcohols and aldehydes to carboxylic acids, not to hydrolyse nitriles.

**C** is incorrect as sodium borohydride is a mild reducing agent and will not reduce nitrile groups.

**D** is incorrect as while nitriles can be hydrolysed with alkali under reflux, the resulting solution would need to be acidified to produce the carboxylic acid.

parts.problemMd:
Sour milk contains a compound called lactic acid (2-hydroxypropanoic acid) which has the molecular formula CH<sub>3</sub>CH(OH)CO<sub>2</sub>H.

Which of the following reactions could lactic acid undergo?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- Lactic acid has a secondary alcohol group and a carboxylic acid group.
- Reacting lactic acid with **methanoic acid** (HCO<sub>2</sub>H) produces an **ester** from the secondary alcohol group, as shown in reaction B.
- This is a condensation reaction and produces water alongside the ester.

![Diagram showing the esterification of lactic acid with methanoic acid, forming a lactate ester and water](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/18-carboxylic-acids-and-derivatives/18-1-carboxylic-acids/assets/007-diagram-showing-the-esterification-of-lactic-aci.jpg)

**A** is incorrect as Cl<sub>2</sub> does not substitute the –OH group of a secondary alcohol under normal conditions. The byproduct would also be HOCl, not OCl.

**C** is incorrect as methanol (CH<sub>3</sub>OH) would react with the **carboxylic acid** group in lactic acid, not the alcohol group, producing the methyl ester CH<sub>3</sub>CH(OH)CO<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>.

**D** is incorrect as NaHCO<sub>3</sub> reacts with the **carboxylic acid** group, not the alcohol group. The product would be CH<sub>3</sub>CH(OH)CO<sub>2</sub>Na, not CH<sub>3</sub>CH(ONa)CO<sub>2</sub>H as shown.

parts.problemMd:
Apples contain a compound called malic acid.

![Structural formula of malic acid (2-hydroxybutanedioic acid), showing two carboxylic acid groups and one secondary alcohol group](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/18-carboxylic-acids-and-derivatives/18-1-carboxylic-acids/assets/008-structural-formula-of-malic-acid-2-hydroxybutane.jpg)

Which substance will react with only one hydroxyl group in malic acid under suitable conditions?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- A 'hydroxyl' group is an '–OH' group, which in malic acid appears in both carboxylic acid groups and the alcohol group.
- If the substance only reacts with one hydroxyl group, this must be the alcohol group.

  - So, we must identify what does not react with a carboxylic acid group.
- The dichromate ion (Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub><sup>2-</sup>), produced when K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> is dissolved in acidified aqueous solution, acts as an oxidising agent.
- Carboxylic acids are already at their highest oxidation state and therefore will not react with acidified dichromate ions.
- The secondary alcohol in malic acid is oxidised to a ketone, which is not oxidised further.

**B** is incorrect as sodium metal reacts with **both** the carboxylic acid groups and the alcohol group in redox reactions, producing a salt and hydrogen gas:

2RCOOH + 2Na $\rightarrow$ 2RCOONa + H<sub>2</sub>

2ROH + 2Na $\rightarrow$ 2RONa + H<sub>2</sub>

**C** is incorrect as sodium hydroxide reacts with **both** carboxylic acid groups in a neutralisation reaction:

RCOOH + NaOH $\rightarrow$ RCOONa + H<sub>2</sub>O

**D** is incorrect as PCl<sub>5</sub> reacts with **both** the carboxylic acid groups (producing an acyl chloride) and the alcohol group (producing a haloalkane):

RCOOH + PCl<sub>5</sub> $\rightarrow$ RCOCl + POCl<sub>3</sub> + HCl

ROH + PCl<sub>5</sub> $\rightarrow$ RCl + POCl<sub>3</sub> + HCl

parts.problemMd:
The natural bacterial fermentation of milk produces a compound called propanoic acid.

Propanoic acid is partly responsible for the flavour of Swiss cheese. Its structure is shown below:

![Structural formula of propanoic acid (CH3CH2COOH), showing the ethyl group attached to the carboxylic acid group](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/18-carboxylic-acids-and-derivatives/18-1-carboxylic-acids/assets/010-structural-formula-of-propanoic-acid-ch3ch2cooh-.png)

Which starting materials could be used to produce propanoic acid?

| ** ** | **CH**<sub>**3**</sub>**CH**<sub>**2**</sub>**CN** | **CH**<sub>**3**</sub>**CH**<sub>**2**</sub>**CHO** | **CH**<sub>**3**</sub>**CH**<sub>**2**</sub>**CH**<sub>**2**</sub>**OH** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A** | **✓** | **✓** | **✓** |
| **B** | **✓** | **✓** | **x** |
| **C** | **x** | **✓** | **✓** |
| **D** | **✓** | **x** | **x** |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- Compound 1, propanenitrile, can be hydrolysed to propanoic acid by heating with dilute hydrochloric acid.

- Compound 2, propanal, can be oxidised to propanoic acid by heating with acidified aqueous potassium dichromate(VI).

- Compound 3, propan-1-ol, can be oxidised to propanoic acid by heating under reflux with acidified aqueous potassium dichromate(VI).

**B**, **C** and **D** are incorrect as each is missing at least one valid reaction route to propanoic acid.

parts.problemMd:
*Sirolimus* is a drug used to treat patients after kidney transplants.

![Structural formula of sirolimus, a macrolide drug containing both ester and amide bonds](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/18-carboxylic-acids-and-derivatives/18-1-carboxylic-acids/assets/004-structural-formula-of-sirolimus-a-macrolide-drug.png)

*Sirolimus* produces an equimolar mixture of two organic products, on reaction with hot aqueous sodium hydroxide.

What is the structural formula of the product with the lower relative molecular mass?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- NaOH hydrolyses the ester and amide bonds in sirolimus.
- The carboxylic acid produced undergoes neutralisation with NaOH to produce a carboxylate salt (RCOO<sup>–</sup>Na<sup>+</sup>) and water.

![Diagram showing the two organic products of sirolimus hydrolysis with hot aqueous NaOH, with the lower Mr product highlighted](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/18-carboxylic-acids-and-derivatives/18-1-carboxylic-acids/assets/005-diagram-showing-the-two-organic-products-of-siro.jpg)

> **[exam-tip]**
> Amide bonds appear in Topic 28 of the syllabus and, like ester bonds, can be hydrolysed by hot aqueous sodium hydroxide. Being familiar with both bond types helps when analysing complex molecules such as sirolimus, which contains both.

parts.problemMd:
Compound **K**, C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O, is oxidised by acidified aqueous potassium dichromate(VI) to compound **L**.

Compound **L** reacts with butan-2-ol in the presence of a little concentrated sulfuric acid to give liquid **M**.

What could be the formula of liquid **M**?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O has zero degrees of unsaturation.

  - So, **K **must be a saturated compound.
  - It cannot be a ketone or aldehyde.
- Since **K **is oxidised to give a carboxylic acid, **K **must be a primary alcohol and **L **is a carboxylic acid.
- When a carboxylic acid reacts with an alcohol in the presence of a sulfuric acid catalyst, an ester is produced.
- The ester contains the butan-2-ol portion -OCH(CH<sub>3</sub>)CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>

  - This is seen in **C**: CH<sub>3</sub>(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>3</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>

![Diagram showing the esterification of compound L with butan-2-ol to produce ester M, with the butan-2-ol portion of the ester highlighted](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/18-carboxylic-acids-and-derivatives/18-1-carboxylic-acids/assets/006-diagram-showing-the-esterification-of-compound-l.jpg)

**A** is incorrect as this would be the product if compound **L** reacted with 2-methylpropan-2-ol.

**B** is incorrect as this would be the product if compound **L** reacted with butan-1-ol.

**D** is incorrect as this would be the product if compound **L** reacted with 2-methylpropan-1-ol.

parts.problemMd:
Compound **X** can be made from 2-hydroxybutanoic acid.

![Structural formula of compound X, a cyclic diester formed from two molecules of 2-hydroxybutanoic acid condensing together](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/18-carboxylic-acids-and-derivatives/18-1-carboxylic-acids/assets/003-structural-formula-of-compound-x-a-cyclic-dieste.jpg)

What should be heated with 2-hydroxybutanoic acid in order to make compound **X**?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- 2-hydroxybutanoic acid has both an alcohol and carboxylic acid group
- Therefore, 2 molecules can react together in a condensation reaction, forming a diester (a molecule with two ester groups).
- Concentrated sulfuric acid acts as a catalyst in condensation reactions that result in esters.

**A** is incorrect as reacting 2-hydroxybutanoic acid with acidified aqueous potassium manganate(VII) would cause the secondary alcohol group to oxidise to a ketone, resulting in 2-oxobutanoic acid (CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COCOOH).

**B** is incorrect as aluminium oxide (Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>) acts as a catalyst in the dehydration of alcohols to alkenes, therefore reacting 2-hydroxybutanoic acid with aluminium oxide would produce but-2-en-oic acid (CH<sub>3</sub>CH=CHCOOH).

**D** is incorrect as 2-hydroxybutanoic acid and sodium hydroxide would undergo a neutralisation reaction resulting in an organic salt CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH(OH)COONa and water.

parts.problemMd:
Oxaloacetic acid can be synthesised from fumaric acid in a two-step process involving intermediate **Z**.

HO<sub>2</sub>CCH=CHCO<sub>2</sub>H $\overset{\mathrm{step}1}{\rightarrow}$ **Z** $\overset{\mathrm{step}2}{\rightarrow}$ HO<sub>2</sub>CCOCH<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>H

Each step involved can be achieved in the laboratory by using a single reagent.

Which row identifies intermediate **Z** and the reagent for step 2?

|   | **Z** | Reagent for step 2 |
|---|---|---|
| A | HO<sub>2</sub>CCH(OH)CH<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>H | Fehling's solution |
| B | HO<sub>2</sub>CCH(OH)CH<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>H | Acidified aqueous potassium manganate(VII), heat |
| C | HO<sub>2</sub>CCHBrCH<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>H | Acidified aqueous potassium manganate(VII), heat |
| D | HO<sub>2</sub>CCHBrCH(OH)CO<sub>2</sub>H | Warm NaOH (aq) |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- Fumaric acid has an alkene functional group and oxaloacetic acid has a carbonyl functional group.
- Therefore, in step 1 the alkene group in fumaric acid is hydrated to produce an alcohol (**Z**) and in step 2 this alcohol group is oxidised to a ketone.
- The structure of **Z **is HO<sub>2</sub>CCH(OH)CH<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>H as there is an alcohol group on the 2nd carbon (which has the alkene group in fumaric acid).
- The reagent for step 2 is acidified aqueous potassium dichromate(VI), heated.

**A** is incorrect as Fehling's solution is an oxidising agent that converts aldehydes into carboxylic acids. Fehling's solution does not oxidise secondary alcohols as Cu<sup>2+</sup> is not a sufficiently strong oxidising agent.

**C** is incorrect as HO<sub>2</sub>CCHBrCH<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>H cannot be converted into oxaloacetic acid in a single step using acidified aqueous potassium manganate(VII).

**D** is incorrect as although the bromohydrin Z can be made in step 1 using Br<sub>2</sub> (aq), in step 2 NaOH would cause nucleophilic substitution of the C–Br bond and neutralise the carboxylic acid groups. It cannot produce the required ketone in a single step.

parts.problemMd:
Citric acid has the formula HO<sub>2</sub>CCH<sub>2</sub>C(OH)(CO<sub>2</sub>H)CH<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>H.

What is the volume of 0.2 mol dm<sup>–3</sup> aqueous sodium hydroxide required to neutralise a solution containing 0.008 mol of citric acid?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- Calculate moles of NaOH required:

- Citric acid contains 3 carboxylic acid groups, each neutralised by one NaOH molecule.
- Therefore, for every 1 mole of citric acid, 3 moles of NaOH are required.
- 0.008 moles of citric acid is used.

0.008 x 3 = 0.024 moles of NaOH are required.

- Calculate volume of NaOH required:

moles = concentration x volume

volume = $\frac{\mathrm{moles}}{\mathrm{concentration}}$

volume = $\frac{0.024}{0.2}$

volume = 0.12 dm<sup>3</sup>

- Convert from dm<sup>3</sup> to cm<sup>3</sup>:

volume = 0.12 × 1000 = 120 cm<sup>3</sup>

**A** is incorrect as it assumes a 1:1 molar ratio between citric acid and NaOH, giving 40 cm<sup>3</sup>. The word "acid" does not always mean one acidic group.

**B** is incorrect as it assumes a 1:2 molar ratio. This occurs when only two of the three carboxylic acid groups are identified, giving 80 cm<sup>3</sup>. The most common mistake is missing the one written as CO<sub>2</sub>H in the central bracket

**D** is incorrect as it assumes a 1:4 molar ratio by incorrectly treating the alcohol –OH group as acidic. The –OH group is an alcohol, not a phenol, and does not react with NaOH. Counting all four –OH-containing groups gives 160 cm<sup>3</sup>.

parts.problemMd:
The compound 2-ethyl-3-methylbutanoic acid has the following structure:

![Structural formula of 2-ethyl-3-methylbutanoic acid, showing a branched 4-carbon chain with an ethyl group at C2 and methyl group at C3](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/18-carboxylic-acids-and-derivatives/18-1-carboxylic-acids/assets/001-structural-formula-of-2-ethyl-3-methylbutanoic-a.jpg)

Which compound will produce 2-ethyl-3-methylbutanoic acid by heating under reflux with ethanolic sodium cyanide and subsequent acid hydrolysis of the reaction product?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- Ethanolic sodium cyanide (NaCN) reacts with the halogenoalkane in option A via nucleophilic substitution, extending the carbon chain by one carbon to form a nitrile.
- Acid hydrolysis of the nitrile produces the corresponding carboxylic acid: 2-ethyl-3-methylbutanoic acid.

![Reaction scheme showing the two-step synthesis: halogenoalkane A reacts with ethanolic NaCN to form a nitrile intermediate, which is then hydrolysed under acidic conditions to give 2-ethyl-3-methylbutanoic acid](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/18-carboxylic-acids-and-derivatives/18-1-carboxylic-acids/assets/002-reaction-scheme-showing-the-two-step-synthesis-h.jpg)

**B**, **C** and **D** are incorrect as these halogenoalkanes would produce different carboxylic acids on reaction with ethanolic NaCN followed by acid hydrolysis.

parts.problemMd: Which compound requires the largest amount of cold aqueous sodium hydroxide for the complete neutralisation of 1 mole?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- Malic acid has 2 carboxylic acid groups, so 1 mole of malic acid requires 2 moles of NaOH for complete neutralisation.
- Each of the compounds in **A**, **B **and **C **has only 1 carboxylic acid group, requiring only 1 mole of NaOH per mole of compound.

**A**, **B** and **C** are incorrect as lactic acid, gluconic acid and aspirin each have only 1 carboxylic acid group and therefore each require only 1 mole of NaOH per mole.

parts.problemMd: How many isomeric esters, including stereoisomers, can be synthesised from the reaction of methanoic acid with an alcohol of formula C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****C**

- Methanoic acid has the formula HCOOH
- When an ester is formed:

  - The acid contributes the group HCOO–
  - The rest of the ester comes from the C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>9</sub> alcohol
  - This gives an overall molecular formula of C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O<sub>2</sub>
- There are four different alcohols that can combine with methanoic acid to give four structural isomers of methanoate esters

  - One of these esters (butan-2-yl methanoate) contains a chiral centre, meaning it exists as two enantiomers
- This gives a total of 5 isomers (4 structural isomers, with 1 of them existing as a pair of optical isomers)

![Structural formula of butyl methanoate, showing carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen atoms with single and double bonds, labelled beneath.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/18-carboxylic-acids-and-derivatives/18-2-esters/assets/005-structural-formula-of-butyl-methanoate-showing-c.png)

![Chemical structure of 2-methylpropyl methanoate, showing carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen atoms. The formula depicts bonds and methyl group arrangement.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/18-carboxylic-acids-and-derivatives/18-2-esters/assets/006-chemical-structure-of-2-methylpropyl-methanoate-.png)

![Structural formula of 2-methylpropan-2-yl methanoate, depicting carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen atoms with bonds.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/18-carboxylic-acids-and-derivatives/18-2-esters/assets/007-structural-formula-of-2-methylpropan-2-yl-methan.png)

![Chemical structure of butan-2-yl methanoate, showing a carbon chain with an ester group. A chiral carbon is highlighted with a yellow circle.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/18-carboxylic-acids-and-derivatives/18-2-esters/assets/008-chemical-structure-of-butan-2-yl-methanoate-show.png)

parts.problemMd:
The structure of ester **E** is shown in the diagram below.

![Structural formula of 3-methylbutan-1-yl ethanoate (ester E)](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/18-carboxylic-acids-and-derivatives/18-2-esters/assets/009-structural-formula-of-3-methylbutan-1-yl-ethanoa.jpg)

**E** is hydrolysed in the presence of hydrochloric acid.

Which are the products of this hydrolysis?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- Ester E is **3-methylbutan-1-yl ethanoate**.
- Acid hydrolysis (using dilute HCl and heat) breaks the ester bond by adding water across it.
- The ethanoate group produces **ethanoic acid**: CH<sub>3</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>H.
- The 3-methylbutan-1-yl group produces **3-methylbutan-1-ol**: (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CHCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH.

![Diagram showing the acid-catalysed hydrolysis of 3-methylbutan-1-yl ethanoate with H2O and H+ catalyst, producing ethanoic acid (labelled carboxylic acid) and 3-methylbutan-1-ol (labelled alcohol), with the ester bond highlighted in yellow](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/18-carboxylic-acids-and-derivatives/18-2-esters/assets/010-diagram-showing-the-acid-catalysed-hydrolysis-of.jpg)

**A** is incorrect as the alcohol product is incorrectly written as an aldehyde with an extra carbon. Acid hydrolysis of an ester produces an alcohol, not an aldehyde, and 3-methylbutan-1-ol has 5 carbons, not 6.

**C** is incorrect as chloride ions are spectator ions in acid hydrolysis and do not substitute into the ester. The reaction is a hydrolysis (addition of water across the ester bond), not a nucleophilic substitution by Cl<sup>-</sup>.

**D** is incorrect as CH<sub>3</sub>CHO is an aldehyde, not a carboxylic acid. Hydrolysis of an ester always produces a carboxylic acid, in this case ethanoic acid (CH<sub>3</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>H), not an aldehyde.

parts.problemMd:
The ester shown is responsible for the odour of bananas.

![Structural formula of 3-methylbutan-1-yl ethanoate, the ester responsible for the odour of bananas](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/18-carboxylic-acids-and-derivatives/18-2-esters/assets/002-structural-formula-of-3-methylbutan-1-yl-ethanoa.jpg)

Which pair of compounds reacts to form this ester?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- The ester in the question is **3-methylbutan-1-yl ethanoate**.
- To identify the reactants, the ester bond is broken:

  - The –C(=O)O– linkage shows the acid contributes –C(=O)–
  - The alcohol contributes –O–.
- The acid part is **ethanoic acid** (CH<sub>3</sub>COOH) as it is a straight-chain 2-carbon carboxylic acid.
- The alcohol part is **3-methylbutan-1-ol** as it is a branched 5-carbon alcohol with the methyl group at C3.
- **C** shows ethanoic acid and 3-methylbutan-1-ol, which is the correct pair.

**A** is incorrect as option A shows a branched carboxylic acid paired with an unbranched alcohol. The branching belongs on the alcohol (3-methylbutan-1-ol), not the acid. The acid in this ester is the straight-chain ethanoic acid.

**B** is incorrect as option B makes the same error as A. A branched carboxylic acid is shown paired with an unbranched alcohol, but the correct combination requires the straight-chain ethanoic acid and the branched 3-methylbutan-1-ol.

**D** is incorrect as option D shows ethanoic acid paired with an alcohol in which the methyl branch is on the wrong carbon. The correct alcohol is 3-methylbutan-1-ol (methyl at C3), not 2-methylbutan-1-ol (methyl at C2).

parts.problemMd:
Cetyl palmitate is a waxy solid and has the molecular formula C<sub>15</sub>H<sub>31</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>C<sub>16</sub>H<sub>33</sub>.

Which products are formed when cetyl palmitate is heated under reflux with an excess of aqueous sodium hydroxide?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- Step 1: the **ester**, C<sub>15</sub>H<sub>31</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>C<sub>16</sub>H<sub>33</sub>, is hydrolysed by dilute alkali under heat:

C<sub>15</sub>H<sub>31</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>C<sub>16</sub>H<sub>33</sub> + NaOH → C<sub>15</sub>H<sub>31</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>H + C<sub>16</sub>H<sub>33</sub>OH

- Step 2: the carboxylic acid product, C<sub>15</sub>H<sub>31</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>H, reacts with excess sodium hydroxide in a neutralisation reaction to produce C<sub>15</sub>H<sub>31</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>Na and water:

C<sub>15</sub>H<sub>31</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>H + NaOH → C<sub>15</sub>H<sub>31</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>Na + H<sub>2</sub>O

- Therefore, the two organic products are C<sub>15</sub>H<sub>31</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>Na and C<sub>16</sub>H<sub>33</sub>OH.

**B** is incorrect as sodium does not replace hydrogen in alcohol groups, only in carboxylic acids.

**C** is incorrect as the structural formula C<sub>15</sub>H<sub>31</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>C<sub>16</sub>H<sub>33</sub> shows the carboxylic acid part of the ester before the ester bond and the alcohol part after. This option gets this the wrong way around.

**D** is incorrect as sodium does not replace hydrogen in alcohol groups, only in carboxylic acids. The structural formula also shows the carboxylic acid part before the ester bond and the alcohol part after, so this option reverses both.

parts.problemMd:
The diagram shows the structure of ethanedioic acid.

![Structural formula of ethanedioic acid: HOOC−COOH](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/18-carboxylic-acids-and-derivatives/18-2-esters/assets/003-structural-formula-of-ethanedioic-acid-hooc-cooh.jpg)

Ethanedioic acid reacts with ethanol in the presence of a few drops of concentrated sulfuric acid to form a diester. The molecular formula of the diester is C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O<sub>4</sub>.

What is the structural formula of the diester?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- Ethanedioic acid has two –COOH groups, each of which undergoes esterification with one ethanol molecule to form one ester linkage.
- After both –COOH groups react, the product is the diester **diethyl oxalate**: CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>-O-CO-CO-O-CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>.
- The two adjacent carbonyl groups (–CO–CO–) come from the ethanedioic acid backbone, and each is linked to an ethyl group (–O–CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>) from ethanol.

![Structural formula of diethyl oxalate (option B): CH3CH2-O-CO-CO-O-CH2CH3](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/18-carboxylic-acids-and-derivatives/18-2-esters/assets/004-structural-formula-of-diethyl-oxalate-option-b-c.jpg)

**A** is incorrect as this structural formula shows two ester linkages joined directly (–CO<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>–), which places four oxygens consecutively and is not the structure of diethyl oxalate.

**C** is incorrect as the ester linkage atoms are in the wrong order (–O<sub>2</sub>C– instead of –CO<sub>2</sub>–). In a valid ester the carbonyl carbon must come before the ester oxygen when reading from the acid side.

**D** is incorrect as this structural formula represents the diester of ethane-1,2-diol with ethanoic acid (CH<sub>3</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OCOCH<sub>3</sub>). This is a different combination of reactants, not the product of ethanedioic acid with ethanol.

choices.label: B
choices.textMd: Two molecules can react together in strong acid.

parts.problemMd:
Lactic acid is a naturally occurring molecule.

![Structural formula of lactic acid (2-hydroxypropanoic acid), showing a hydroxyl group and a carboxylic acid group](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/18-carboxylic-acids-and-derivatives/18-2-esters/assets/013-structural-formula-of-lactic-acid-2-hydroxypropa.jpg)

What is a property of lactic acid?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- Lactic acid (2-hydroxypropanoic acid) contains both an **alcohol** (–OH) and a **carboxylic acid** (–COOH) functional group in the same molecule.
- In the presence of concentrated sulfuric acid as a catalyst, the –OH group of one lactic acid molecule reacts with the –COOH group of another in a condensation reaction.
- An ester linkage (–CO–O–) forms and water is eliminated, producing a dimer ester.
- The product has the structure: HOOC–CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)–O–CO–CH(OH)–CH<sub>3</sub>.

![Structural formula of the ester product formed when two lactic acid molecules undergo self-esterification](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/18-carboxylic-acids-and-derivatives/18-2-esters/assets/014-structural-formula-of-the-ester-product-formed-w.jpg)

**A** is incorrect as aqueous bromine is decolourised by alkenes via electrophilic addition. Lactic acid contains no C=C double bond, so it does not react with bromine water.

**C** is incorrect as Fehling's solution is only reduced by aldehydes. Lactic acid does not contain an aldehyde group.

**D** is incorrect as lactic acid is soluble in water because the alcohol (–OH) and carboxylic acid (–COOH) groups both form hydrogen bonds with water molecules.

parts.problemMd: How many ester compounds have the molecular formula C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O<sub>2</sub>?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O<sub>2</sub> has one degree of unsaturation, consistent with the C=O group in an ester.
- By varying which part comes from the carboxylic acid and which from the alcohol, exactly 4 structural ester isomers are possible:

  - **Methyl propanoate**: CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> (propanoic acid + methanol)
  - **Ethyl ethanoate**: CH<sub>3</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> (ethanoic acid + ethanol)
  - **Propan-1-yl methanoate**: HCO<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> (methanoic acid + propan-1-ol)
  - **Propan-2-yl methanoate**: HCO<sub>2</sub>CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> (methanoic acid + propan-2-ol)

![Structural formulae of the four ester isomers of C4H8O2: propan-1-yl methanoate, propan-2-yl methanoate, ethyl ethanoate, and methyl propanoate](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/18-carboxylic-acids-and-derivatives/18-2-esters/assets/001-structural-formulae-of-the-four-ester-isomers-of.jpg)

**A** is incorrect as 2 is an undercount. There are more structural isomers possible by varying both the acid and alcohol components.

**B** is incorrect as 3 is also an undercount. A common error is to overlook propan-2-yl methanoate (the branched-chain methanoate ester).

**D** is incorrect as 5 is an overcount. C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O<sub>2</sub> has two other isomers with this molecular formula (butanoic acid and 2-methylpropanoic acid) but these are carboxylic acids, not esters. Counting these as esters gives 5.

parts.problemMd:
Compound **Q** has the formula CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>.

Which row correctly shows the name of compound **Q** and how its boiling point compares with that of butanoic acid?

|   | **Name of Q** | **Boiling point compared to butanoic acid** |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | Methyl propanoate | Lower |
| **B** | Propyl methanoate | Lower |
| **C** | Methyl propanoate | Higher |
| **D** | Propyl methanoate | Higher |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- Compound Q is an **ester** made from propanoic acid, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>H, and methanol, CH<sub>3</sub>OH.
- The name of an ester starts with the alkyl group from the alcohol (in this case **methyl**), followed by the name of the carboxylic acid (in this case **propanoate**).
- Therefore, the name is **methyl propanoate**.
- The boiling point of methyl propanoate is **lower** than that of butanoic acid because it has only **dipole-dipole attractions** between molecules, whereas butanoic acid has stronger **hydrogen bonds**.

**B** is incorrect as propyl methanoate is the ester formed from methanoic acid and propan-1-ol, not propanoic acid and methanol. The name must reflect which compound provides the alkyl group (methanol → methyl) and which provides the acyl group (propanoic acid → propanoate).

**C** is incorrect as the name methyl propanoate is correct, but the boiling point comparison is wrong. Methyl propanoate has a lower boiling point than butanoic acid, not higher.

**D** is incorrect as both the name and the boiling point comparison are wrong. The correct name is methyl propanoate (not propyl methanoate) and the boiling point is lower than butanoic acid (not higher).

parts.problemMd:
In the presence of an H<sup>+</sup> catalyst, compound X reacts with ethanoic acid to produce the compound below.

![Displayed structural formula of the ester product, showing CH3-C(=O)-CH2-CH2-O-C(=O)-CH3: a 3-oxobutyl chain linked to an ethanoyl group via an ester bond](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/18-carboxylic-acids-and-derivatives/18-2-esters/assets/011-displayed-structural-formula-of-the-ester-produc.jpg)

What is the molecular formula of compound X?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- The ester shown is produced when compound X reacts with ethanoic acid, CH<sub>3</sub>COOH, in an esterification reaction.
- The -O-C(=O)-CH<sub>3</sub> group in the ester is the ethanoate part, contributed by ethanoic acid.
- The remaining part of the ester, CH<sub>3</sub>-C(=O)-CH<sub>2</sub>-CH<sub>2</sub>-, must come from compound X minus its -OH group.
- Compound X is therefore 1-hydroxybutan-3-one: HO-CH<sub>2</sub>-CH<sub>2</sub>-C(=O)-CH<sub>3</sub>.
- Its molecular formula is C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O<sub>2</sub>.

![Diagram showing the acid-catalysed hydrolysis of the ester, with the ester bond highlighted in yellow. Products are labelled 1-hydroxybutan-3-one (C4H8O2) and ethanoic acid (C2H4O2)](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/18-carboxylic-acids-and-derivatives/18-2-esters/assets/012-diagram-showing-the-acid-catalysed-hydrolysis-of.jpg)

**A** is incorrect as C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O has only one oxygen atom. Compound X requires two oxygen atoms: one for the alcohol (-OH) group and one for the ketone (C=O) group.

**C** is incorrect as C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub>O<sub>2</sub> contains only two carbon atoms. The 3-oxobutyl chain in the ester requires compound X to have four carbon atoms.

**D** is incorrect as C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub>O<sub>3</sub> contains only two carbon atoms and three oxygen atoms, so neither the carbon count nor the oxygen count matches compound X.

parts.problemMd:
During a lesson, a teacher heated ethyl propanoate under reflux with aqueous sodium hydroxide. The mixture was then acidified, and the two organic products are then separated, purified and weighed.

Out of the total mass of products obtained, what is the percentage by mass of each product?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- Alkaline hydrolysis of ethyl propanoate produces ethanol and sodium propanoate.
- After acidification, the sodium propanoate is converted to propanoic acid.
- The two organic products weighed are therefore **ethanol** and **propanoic acid**.
- Known values:

  - *M*<sub>r</sub>(ethanol, C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH) = (2 x 12) + (6 x 1) + 16 = 46 g mol<sup>-1</sup>
  - *M*<sub>r</sub>(propanoic acid, C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>COOH) = (3 x 12) + (6 x 1) + (2 x 16) = 74 g mol<sup>-1</sup>
- The two products are formed in a 1:1 molar ratio, so total *M*<sub>r</sub> = 46 + 74 = 120 g mol<sup>-1</sup>
- Calculate the percentage by mass of propanoic acid:

% propanoic acid = $\frac{74}{120}$ x 100

% propanoic acid = 61.7%

- Calculate the percentage by mass of ethanol:

% ethanol = $\frac{46}{120}$ x 100

% ethanol = 38.3%

**A** is incorrect as the two products have different molecular masses, so their percentage by masses cannot be equal.

**B** is incorrect as 57.7% and 42.3% arise from using incorrect molecular masses.

**D** is incorrect as 67.6% and 32.4% are obtained when sodium propanoate (*M*<sub>r</sub> = 96) is used instead of propanoic acid (*M*<sub>r</sub> = 74). The mixture was acidified before weighing, so the carboxylate salt is converted to the carboxylic acid.

parts.problemMd:
30 g of an alcohol and 30 g of a carboxylic acid are heated under reflux together to produce 33.2 g of propyl butanoate.

What is the yield of the ester?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- 1 mole of alcohol reacts with 1 mole of carboxylic acid to produce 1 mole of ester.
- Propyl butanoate is produced from propanol (C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>7</sub>OH) and butanoic acid (C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>7</sub>COOH).
- Known values:

  - mass of propanol = 30 g
  - *M*<sub>r</sub>(propanol) = (3 x 12) + (8 x 1) + 16 = 60 g mol<sup>-1</sup>
  - mass of butanoic acid = 30 g
  - *M*<sub>r</sub>(butanoic acid) = (4 x 12) + (8 x 1) + (2 x 16) = 88 g mol<sup>-1</sup>
  - *M*<sub>r</sub>(propyl butanoate) = (7 x 12) + (14 x 1) + (2 x 16) = 130 g mol<sup>-1</sup>
  - mass of propyl butanoate produced = 33.2 g
- Calculate the moles of each reactant:

moles of propanol = $\frac{30}{60}$

moles of propanol = 0.50 mol

moles of butanoic acid = $\frac{30}{88}$

moles of butanoic acid = 0.34 mol

- Butanoic acid provides fewer moles and is therefore the limiting reactant.

- Calculate the theoretical yield of propyl butanoate:

theoretical yield = 0.34 x 130

theoretical yield = 44.2 g

- Calculate the percentage yield:

% yield = $\frac{33.2}{44.2}$ x 100

% yield = 75 %

**A** is incorrect as 25% is obtained by dividing the mass of ester produced (33.2 g) by its *M*<sub>r</sub> (130 g mol<sup>-1</sup>) and treating the result as a percentage, rather than calculating the theoretical yield from the limiting reactant.

**B** is incorrect as 38% arises from dividing the actual mass of ester (33.2 g) by the *M*<sub>r</sub> of butanoic acid (88 g mol<sup>-1</sup>) rather than the theoretical yield (44.2 g).

**C** is incorrect as 50% arises from using propanol as the limiting reactant. Propanol provides 0.50 mol whereas butanoic acid provides only 0.34 mol, so butanoic acid is the limiting reactant, giving a theoretical yield of 44.2 g.

parts.problemMd: Which statement correctly describes the hydrolysis of an ester?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- Acid hydrolysis of an ester (using dilute acid such as sulfuric acid) produces a carboxylic acid and an alcohol.
- This reaction is reversible, so an equilibrium mixture is formed.
- Rule of thumb:

  - Acid hydrolysis = reversible → carboxylic acid
  - Alkaline hydrolysis = irreversible → carboxylate salt

**A** is incorrect as sodium carboxylates are formed in alkaline, not acidic, hydrolysis.

**B** is incorrect as alkaline hydrolysis forms a carboxylate salt, not a carboxylic acid.

**D** is incorrect as alkaline hydrolysis is irreversible, not reversible.

parts.problemMd: What is the displayed formula of ethylamine?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- 'Ethyl' indicates a two-carbon chain.
- '-amine' indicates the -NH<sub>2</sub> group is at the end of the chain.
- Therefore, B shows ethylamine, a primary amine with a two-carbon chain terminating in -NH<sub>2</sub>.

**A** is incorrect as this is dimethylamine, a secondary amine with two methyl groups bonded to nitrogen.

**C** is incorrect as this is methylamine, a primary amine with only one carbon atom rather than two.

**D** is incorrect as this is trimethylamine, a tertiary amine with three methyl groups bonded to nitrogen.

parts.problemMd: Which type of reaction is used to synthesise ethylamine from bromoethane?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- Bromoethane reacts with excess ethanolic ammonia under pressure.
- Ammonia acts as a nucleophile, donating a lone pair to the electron-deficient carbon bonded to bromine.
- Bromine is displaced as a bromide ion, forming ethylamine via nucleophilic substitution.
- The reaction mechanism is:

![Four-step SN2 nucleophilic substitution mechanism showing ammonia attacking 1-bromoethane, formation of intermediate, deprotonation by second ammonia molecule, and production of ethylamine and ammonium bromide](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/19-nitrogen-compounds/19-1-primary-amines/assets/002-four-step-sn2-nucleophilic-substitution-mechanis.jpg)

**A** is incorrect as electrophilic substitution requires an electrophile as the attacking species. Ammonia is a nucleophile, not an electrophile.

**C** is incorrect as oxidation of bromoethane replaces the C-Br bond with a C-OH bond, forming ethanol (an alcohol), not an amine.

**D** is incorrect as reduction of bromoethane replaces the C-Br bond with a C-H bond, forming ethane (an alkane), not an amine.

parts.problemMd:
Bromoethane reacts with reagent **X**. Which row correctly identifies reagent **X** and the organic product formed?

|   | **X** | **Product** |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | Excess ethanolic ammonia | Primary amine |
| **B** | Methanol | Ether |
| **C** | Methylamine | Secondary amine |
| **D** | Water | Alcohol |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- Halogenoalkanes react with excess ethanolic ammonia under pressure via nucleophilic substitution to form a primary amine.
- Ammonia acts as the nucleophile, donating a lone pair to the electron-deficient carbon bonded to bromine, displacing bromide to form ethylamine.

![Four-step SN2 nucleophilic substitution mechanism showing ammonia attacking bromoethane to form ethylamine and ammonium bromide](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/19-nitrogen-compounds/19-1-primary-amines/assets/005-four-step-sn2-nucleophilic-substitution-mechanis.jpg)

**B** is incorrect as methanol reacts with bromoethane via nucleophilic substitution to form an ether (methoxyethane), not an ester.

**C** is incorrect as methylamine does react with bromoethane via nucleophilic substitution, but the product is a secondary amine (N-methylethanamine), not an amide.

**D** is incorrect as water reacts with bromoethane via hydrolysis (nucleophilic substitution) to form ethanol, which is an alcohol and not an acid.

choices.label: A
choices.textMd: A mixture of methylamine, dimethylamine and trimethylamine

parts.problemMd: Iodomethane is heated under pressure with ethanolic ammonia. The ammonia is not in excess. Which organic compounds are formed in the reaction mixture?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- When ammonia is not in excess, the primary amine formed (methylamine) can react further with iodomethane.
- Methylamine acts as a nucleophile and reacts with a second molecule of iodomethane to form dimethylamine (a secondary amine).
- Dimethylamine reacts with a third molecule of iodomethane to form trimethylamine (a tertiary amine).
- A mixture of all three amines is therefore produced.

![Reaction scheme showing iodomethane reacting with ammonia to give methylamine, then with further iodomethane to give dimethylamine and trimethylamine, labelled as primary, secondary, and tertiary amines respectively](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/19-nitrogen-compounds/19-1-primary-amines/assets/001-reaction-scheme-showing-iodomethane-reacting-wit.jpg)

**B** is incorrect as dimethylamine alone would only be produced if the reaction stopped after a single further substitution. In practice all three amines form when ammonia is not in excess.

**C** is incorrect as trimethylamine also forms when ammonia is not in excess. The cascade continues past dimethylamine.

**D** is incorrect as methylamine alone would only be the sole product if ammonia were in excess. Without excess ammonia the reaction cascade continues to give secondary and tertiary amines.

> **[exam-tip]**
> To produce only a primary amine, excess ethanolic ammonia under pressure should be used. The high concentration of ammonia suppresses further substitution, favouring formation of the primary amine only.

parts.problemMd:
1-chloropropane can be used to make propylamine.

Which row shows the correct reagent and type of reaction?

|   | **Reagent** | **Type of reaction** |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | Aqueous ammonia | Electrophilic addition |
| **B** | Aqueous ammonia | Nucleophilic substitution |
| **C** | Ethanolic ammonia | Electrophilic addition |
| **D** | Ethanolic ammonia | Nucleophilic substitution |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- 1-chloropropane reacts with excess ethanolic ammonia under pressure via nucleophilic substitution.
- Ammonia acts as the nucleophile, attacking the electron-deficient carbon bonded to chlorine; the chlorine is displaced as a chloride ion to form propylamine.
- The overall equation is:

CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Cl + 2NH<sub>3</sub> → CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> + NH<sub>4</sub>Cl

**A** is incorrect as electrophilic addition requires an electrophile as the attacking species and applies only to unsaturated molecules. 1-chloropropane is saturated and ammonia is a nucleophile, not an electrophile.

**B** is incorrect as aqueous ammonia hydrolyses 1-chloropropane via nucleophilic substitution to form propan-1-ol (an alcohol), not propylamine. Ethanolic ammonia is required to synthesise the amine.

**C** is incorrect as electrophilic addition applies only to unsaturated molecules. Even with ethanolic ammonia, the reaction type is nucleophilic substitution, not electrophilic addition.

parts.problemMd:
Chloroethane is heated under pressure with an excess of ethanolic ammonia.

Which compound is the main organic product?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- When a halogenoalkane is reacted with excess ethanolic ammonia under pressure, the main product is a primary amine.
- Ammonia acts as the nucleophile, displacing the chlorine atom from chloroethane via nucleophilic substitution to form ethylamine.
- Excess ammonia suppresses further substitution, so the primary amine is the main product.

**B** is incorrect as diethylamine is a secondary amine formed when ethylamine undergoes a further substitution with chloroethane. Excess ammonia suppresses this reaction.

**C** is incorrect as triethylamine is a tertiary amine that would form through a further cascade substitution. Again, excess ammonia prevents this from being the main product.

**D** is incorrect as tetraethylammonium chloride is a quaternary ammonium salt, not an amine, and would only form through extensive substitution in the absence of excess ammonia.

parts.problemMd:
Which row correctly identifies the reagents and conditions for the two reactions shown?

|   | **(CH**<sub>**3**</sub>**)**<sub>**2**</sub>**CO **$\rightarrow$** (CH**<sub>**3**</sub>**)**<sub>**2**</sub>**CHCN** | **CH**<sub>**3**</sub>**CHC*****l*****CH**<sub>**3**</sub>** **$\rightarrow$** CH**<sub>**3**</sub>**CH(NH**<sub>**2**</sub>**)CH**<sub>**3**</sub> |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | Ethanolic KCN, heat | Aqueous NH<sub>3</sub>, heat |
| **B** | Ethanolic KCN, heat | Excess ethanolic NH<sub>3</sub>, heat under pressure |
| **C** | KCN and dilute H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> | Aqueous NH<sub>3</sub>, heat |
| **D** | KCN and dilute H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> | Excess ethanolic NH<sub>3</sub>, heat under pressure |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- In the first reaction, propanone undergoes nucleophilic addition with acidified KCN (KCN and dilute H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>); CN<sup>-</sup> acts as the nucleophile, attacking the carbonyl carbon to form 2-hydroxy-2-methylpropanenitrile.
- Dilute H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> is required to generate HCN in situ and maintain the acidic conditions needed for nucleophilic addition.

  - Ethanolic KCN alone does not give the cyanohydrin product reliably.
- In the second reaction, 2-chloropropane undergoes nucleophilic substitution with excess ethanolic ammonia under pressure.

  - Ammonia acts as the nucleophile, displacing chlorine to form propan-2-amine.
- Propan-2-amine (CH<sub>3</sub>CH(NH<sub>2</sub>)CH<sub>3</sub>) is a primary amine because the nitrogen carries only one carbon substituent, regardless of the class of the carbon it is bonded to.
- Excess ammonia suppresses further substitution and ensures the primary amine is the main product.

**A** is incorrect as ethanolic KCN does not provide the acidic conditions required for nucleophilic addition in reaction 1, and aqueous ammonia hydrolyses 2-chloropropane to give propan-2-ol (an alcohol) rather than the amine in reaction 2.

**B** is incorrect as ethanolic KCN is the wrong reagent for reaction 1. Dilute H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> is required to generate HCN in situ and promote cyanohydrin formation.

**C** is incorrect as aqueous ammonia hydrolyses 2-chloropropane via nucleophilic substitution to give propan-2-ol (an alcohol), not an amine. Ethanolic ammonia under pressure is required for amine synthesis.

parts.problemMd: Which amine can **not** be produced by the reduction of a nitrile?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- Nitrile reduction always produces a primary amine with the -NH<sub>2</sub> group on a primary carbon.
- When a nitrile (-C≡N) is reduced, the nitrile carbon gains two hydrogen atoms and the nitrogen gains two more, giving a -CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> group.

  - The -NH<sub>2</sub> is always positioned on a primary carbon.
- Butan-2-amine has the -NH<sub>2</sub> group attached to C-2, a secondary carbon, which cannot arise from nitrile reduction.

**A** is incorrect as 2,2-dimethylpropan-1-amine can be produced by reducing 2,2-dimethylpropanenitrile. The -NH<sub>2</sub> group is on a primary carbon.

**B** is incorrect as 2-methylpropan-1-amine can be produced by reducing 2-methylpropanenitrile. The -NH<sub>2</sub> group is on a primary carbon.

**C** is incorrect as butan-1-amine can be produced by reducing butanenitrile. The -NH<sub>2</sub> group is on a primary carbon.

parts.problemMd:
What is the systematic name of the compound shown?

![Structural formula of a quaternary ammonium chloride salt showing nitrogen bonded to two methyl groups and two ethyl groups with a positive charge, paired with a chloride anion](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/19-nitrogen-compounds/19-1-primary-amines/assets/003-structural-formula-of-a-quaternary-ammonium-chlo.png)
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- The compound is a quaternary ammonium salt containing two ethyl groups and two methyl groups bonded to a positively charged nitrogen, with chloride as the counterion.
- Substituents are named in alphabetical order.

  - So, diethyl (e) comes before dimethyl (m).
- Each pair of identical groups requires the prefix 'di-'.
- The systematic name is therefore diethyldimethylammonium chloride.

![Annotated structural formula of diethyldimethylammonium chloride with labels identifying the two ethyl groups, two methyl groups, ammonium cation, and chloride anion](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/19-nitrogen-compounds/19-1-primary-amines/assets/004-annotated-structural-formula-of-diethyldimethyla.png)

**B** is incorrect as the compound contains two methyl groups; the 'di-' prefix is missing, giving 'diethylmethyl' instead of 'diethyldimethyl'.

**C** is incorrect as the groups are correct but placed in the wrong alphabetical order. Dimethyl appears before diethyl, whereas alphabetically diethyl (e) precedes dimethyl (m).

**D** is incorrect as both 'di-' prefixes are absent. The compound contains two ethyl and two methyl groups, requiring 'diethyldimethyl', not 'ethylmethyl'.

parts.problemMd: Hydrolysis of CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CN with dilute HCl produces which compound?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- **Hydrolysis** is the breakdown of a compound using water.
- When a nitrile is **refluxed** with dilute hydrochloric acid, **hydrolysis** occurs.
- The -CN group at the end of the hydrocarbon chain is converted into a -COOH group, forming a **carboxylic acid.**
- The ammonia in solution will act as a **base** and form an **ammonium salt** with Cl<sup>-</sup> (**NH**~**4**~**Cl**).
- The reaction equation for this **hydrolysis** is:

CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CN + 2H<sub>2</sub>O + HCl → CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COOH + NH<sub>4</sub>Cl

**A** is incorrect as this is a primary amine which would have been formed if the nitrile group in CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CN was **reduced** instead of **hydrolysed**.

**B** is incorrect as this is an aldehyde and would not form upon hydrolysis of the nitrile.

**D** is incorrect as though a carboxylic acid is formed, the carbon chain is one carbon too short.

parts.problemMd:
The equation shows a chemical reaction

CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CHClCH<sub>3</sub>  +  CN<sup>–</sup>  →  CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)CN  +  Cl<sup>–</sup>

What is the name for this type of reaction?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- A **nucleophilic substitution** reaction is one in which a **nucleophile** replaces another nucleophile.

  - A **nucleophile** is a species which can donate a pair of electrons.
- The cyanide ion (CN<sup>-</sup>) in this reaction is the **nucleophile** and replaces the **chlorine atom** in CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CHClCH<sub>3</sub>.
- 2-chlorobutane is a **secondary halogenoalkane** so the nucleophilic substitution of 2-chlorobutane by the cyanide ion can follow an S<sub>N</sub>2 or S<sub>N</sub>1 reaction mechanism.
- The reaction of the halogenoalkane with cyanide ions (CN<sup>-</sup>) will add an extra carbon atom to the carbon chain.
- The reaction mechanism for this reaction via S<sub>N</sub>2 is as follows:

![SN2 mechanism: CN^-^ attacks the electrophilic carbon bearing the Cl leaving group in 2-chlorobutane, forming 2-methylbutanenitrile (CH~3~CH~2~CH(CH~3~)CN) and Cl^-^](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/19-nitrogen-compounds/19-2-nitriles-and-hydroxynitriles/assets/002-sn2-mechanism-cn-attacks-the-electrophilic-carbo.jpg)

**A** is incorrect as CN<sup>-</sup> is not an **electrophile**, which is an electron pair acceptor.

**B** is incorrect as a free radical substitution reaction is the reaction in which **halogen atoms** (not CN<sup>-</sup>) replace **hydrogen atoms** in alkanes.

**C** is incorrect as the reaction is a substitution reaction, **not** an addition reaction.

parts.problemMd: What are the reagents needed in the reaction of 1-bromopropane to butanenitrile?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- A **nucleophilic substitution** reaction is one in which a **nucleophile** replaces another nucleophile.

  - A **nucleophile** is a species which can **donate** a pair of electrons.
- The reaction of halogenoalkanes with cyanide ions, CN<sup>-</sup>, is an example of a **nucleophilic substitution** reaction.
- The cyanide ion (CN<sup>-</sup>) in this reaction is the **nucleophile** and **replaces** the **bromine atom** in bromopropane to give butanenitrile.
- The reaction of the halogenoalkane with cyanide ions (CN<sup>-</sup>) will add an extra carbon atom to the carbon chain.

  - '-**propane**' changes into '**butane**-' as there are now four carbon atoms in the carbon chain instead of three.
- The reaction should be carried out with KCN (to provide the **nucleophile** which is the cyanide ion) in ethanol (also known as **ethanolic solution of potassium cyanide**) which is then **heated** under reflux with the 1-bromopropane.

**A** is incorrect as ethanol and heat alone do not provide the cyanide ion (CN<sup>-</sup>) needed for the nucleophilic substitution reaction.

**B** is incorrect as KCN alone does not provide the correct conditions. Ethanol (as solvent) and heat under reflux are also required.

**C** is incorrect as KCN and ethanol are necessary but heat under reflux is also required to drive the nucleophilic substitution reaction.

parts.problemMd: What are the products when ethanenitrile is heated under reflux with dilute hydrochloric acid?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- Hydrolysis is the breakdown of a compound using water.
- When a nitrile is refluxed with dilute hydrochloric acid, hydrolysis occurs.
- The -CN group at the end of the hydrocarbon chain is converted into a -COOH group, forming a carboxylic acid.
- The ammonia in solution will act as a base and form an ammonium salt with Cl<sup>-</sup> (NH<sub>4</sub>Cl).
- The reaction equation for this hydrolysis is:

CH<sub>3</sub>CN + 2H<sub>2</sub>O + HCl → CH<sub>3</sub>COOH + NH<sub>4</sub>Cl

**C** & **D** are incorrect as the number of carbons in the carbon chain remains unchanged. The carboxylic acid should therefore be ethanoic acid and not propanoic acid.

**A** is incorrect as the ammonia will react in solution to form an ammonium salt.

parts.problemMd: What are the products in the reaction of ethanenitrile and sodium hydroxide?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- Hydrolysis is the breakdown of a compound using water.
- When a nitrile is refluxed with sodium hydroxide solution, hydrolysis occurs.
- Instead of forming an ammonium salt (as seen in HCl reflux reactions), a sodium salt is formed, and ammonia gas is given off.
- The ammonia is formed from the reaction between ammonium (NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>) ions and hydroxide (OH<sup>-</sup>) ions.
- The reaction equation for this hydrolysis is:

CH<sub>3</sub>CN + H<sub>2</sub>O + NaOH → CH<sub>3</sub>COONa + NH<sub>3</sub>

- To form the free carboxylic acid the final solution has to be acidified with a strong acid such as dilute hydrochloric acid (HCl)

  - This means that the ethanoate ion in the sodium ethanoate salt will react with the hydrogen ions to form ethanoic acid.
  - Once reacted, ethanoic acid is a weak acid and holds onto the hydrogen rather than dissociating.

**C** & **D** are incorrect as the number of carbons in the carbon chain remain unchanged. The sodium salt should therefore be sodium ethanoate and not sodium propanoate.

**B** is incorrect as the ammonium salt is formed when a nitrile is refluxed with dilute hydrochloric acid, not sodium hydroxide.

parts.problemMd: Which one of the following reactants would **not** produce a nitrile in a one-step reaction?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- Alkanes are very unreactive compounds due to their non-polar C-H bonds.
- They are therefore not likely to undergo reactions with nucleophiles and electrophiles.

  - Nucleophiles are species that can donate a pair of electrons.
  - Electrophiles are species that can accept a pair of electrons.
- The conversion of alkanes to nitriles is therefore a multi-step process.

**A **is incorrect as aldehydes can undergo a 1-step addition reaction with HCN at room temperature to form nitriles:

CH<sub>3</sub>CHO + HCN → CH<sub>3</sub>CH(OH)(CN)

**C **is incorrect as amides can undergo a 1-step dehydration reaction to form nitriles.

**D **is incorrect as halogenoalkanes undergo a 1-step substitution reaction with KCN in ethanol and heat to form nitriles:

CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Br + CN<sup>-</sup> → CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CN + Br<sup>-</sup>

parts.problemMd: Which of the following reactions would produce 2-hydroxy-2-methylpropanenitrile?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- 2-hydroxy-2-methylpropanenitrile is a hydroxynitrile.
- Hydroxynitriles can be formed from the nucleophilic addition reaction of aldehydes and ketones with HCN at room temperature.
- A nucleophilic addition is when a nucleophile is added to an unsaturated bond to form a single product.

  - A nucleophile is a species that donates a pair of electrons.
- Propanone (which is a ketone) and hydrogen cyanide are the correct reagents required for the conversion of propanone to 2-hydroxy-2-methylpropanenitrile.
- The reaction mechanism is:

![Three-step nucleophilic addition mechanism: CN^-^ attacks the electrophilic carbonyl carbon of propanone, forming an alkoxide intermediate, which is protonated to give 2-hydroxy-2-methylpropanenitrile](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/19-nitrogen-compounds/19-2-nitriles-and-hydroxynitriles/assets/001-three-step-nucleophilic-addition-mechanism-cn-at.jpg)

**A, B** & **C** are incorrect as though these reactions contain the correct reactant (either an aldehyde or ketone), they do not contain the correct reagent (hydrogen cyanide, HCN).

|   | **Reactant** | **Reagent** |

| **A** | Halogenoalkane | Potassium cyanide and ethanol |

| **C** | Aldehyde | Hydrogen cyanide |
| **D** | Ketone | Ammonia |
parts.solutionMd:

**A, B** & **C** are incorrect as these are all correct combinations of reactants and reagents.

parts.problemMd: The following equations show reactions with nitrogen compounds. Which one correctly shows the hydrolysis of nitriles with dilute acid?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- Hydrolysis is the breakdown of a compound using water.
- Nitriles can be hydrolysed either by refluxing it with dilute hydrochloric acid or with sodium hydroxide solution.
- When hydrolysed with a dilute acid the -CN group at the end of the hydrocarbon chain is converted into a -COOH group, forming a carboxylic acid.
- Ammonia in solution will act as a base to form ammonium salt with Cl<sup>-</sup> (NH<sub>4</sub>Cl).

  - Option **B **is therefore the only correct option.
- When a nitrile is refluxed with sodium hydroxide solution, hydrolysis can also occur.

  - Instead of forming an ammonium salt, now a sodium salt is formed, and ammonia gas is given off.
  - The ammonia is formed from the reaction between ammonium (NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>) ions and hydroxide (OH<sup>-</sup>) ions.
- The reaction equation for this hydrolysis is:

CH<sub>3</sub>CN + H<sub>2</sub>O + NaOH → CH<sub>3</sub>COONa + NH<sub>3</sub>

- To form the free carboxylic acid the final solution has to be acidified with a strong acid such as dilute hydrochloric acid (HCl).

  - This means that the ethanoate ion in the sodium ethanoate salt will react with the hydrogen ions to form ethanoic acid.
  - Once reacted, ethanoic acid is a weak acid and holds onto the hydrogen rather than dissociating.

**A** is incorrect as ammonium chloride (NH<sub>4</sub>Cl) is formed, not ammonia chloride (NH<sub>3</sub>Cl).

**C** is incorrect as ammonium chloride (NH<sub>4</sub>Cl) is formed, **not** ammonia (NH<sub>3</sub>). Ammonia would have been formed if the nitrile was hydrolysed by a sodium hydroxide solution.

**D** is incorrect as the water molecules are not correctly balanced in this reaction. 2 moles of water are needed for the reaction to become balanced.

parts.problemMd: The following equations show reactions with nitrogen compounds. Which one correctly shows the hydrolysis of nitriles with dilute sodium hydroxide?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- **Hydrolysis** is the breakdown of a compound using water.
- **Nitriles** can be hydrolysed either by **refluxing** it with **dilute hydrochloric acid** or with **sodium hydroxide solution.**
- When hydrolysed with **sodium hydroxide solution**, instead of forming an **ammonium salt**, now a **sodium salt** is formed, and **ammonia gas** is given off.
- The ammonia is formed from the reaction between **ammonium** (NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>) ions and **hydroxide** (OH<sup>-</sup>) ions.

  - Option **C** is therefore the correct option.
- To form the free carboxylic acid the final solution has to be acidified with a strong acid such as dilute hydrochloric acid (HCl).

  - This means that the ethanoate ion in the sodium ethanoate salt will react with the hydrogen ions to form ethanoic acid.
  - Once reacted, ethanoic acid is a weak acid and holds onto the hydrogen rather than dissociating.

**A** is incorrect as the water molecules are not correctly balanced in this reaction. 1 mole of water is needed for the reaction to become balanced.

**B** is incorrect as the water molecules are not correctly balanced in this reaction. 1 mole of water is needed for the reaction to become balanced and ammonium is not formed in the hydrolysis of nitriles by dilute aqueous hydroxide.

**D** is incorrect as ammonia (NH<sub>3</sub>) is formed, not ammonium (NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>). An ammonium salt would have been formed if the nitrile was hydrolysed by dilute hydrochloric acid solution.

parts.problemMd:

| **B** | Heat with aqueous NaOH under reflux | Acidification with dilute HCl |

| **D** | Heat with dilute H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> under reflux | Distillation |
parts.solutionMd:

- Acidification converts the carboxylate salt into the carboxylic acid
- This sequence correctly converts butanenitrile into butanoic acid

**A** is incorrect as acid hydrolysis already forms the acid and does not require neutralisation.

parts.problemMd:
The reaction sequence shows the two-step synthesis for the production of 2-hydroxybutanenitrile from propan-1-ol.

CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH $\overset{\text{step 1}}{\rightarrow}$  **X**  $\overset{\text{step 2}}{\rightarrow}$ CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CHOHCN

|---|---|---|

| **B** | NaCl / H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> | NaCN / Ethanol |
| **C** | NaCN (aq) / H<sup>+</sup> (aq) | K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> / H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> under distillation |
| **D** | NaCN / Ethanol | NaCl / H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- 2-hydroxybutanenitrile is a hydroxynitrile.
- Hydroxynitriles can be formed from the nucleophilic addition reaction of aldehydes and ketones with HCN at room temperature.
- A nucleophilic addition is when a nucleophile is added to an unsaturated bond to form a single product — a nucleophile donates a pair of electrons.
- Since propan-1-ol is a primary alcohol it should be first oxidised to an aldehyde using acidified potassium dichromate under distillation to form propanal.

![Two-step synthesis: propan-1-ol is oxidised to propanal using acidified K~2~Cr~2~O~7~ under distillation; propanal then undergoes nucleophilic addition with NaCN (aq) / H^+^ (aq) to form 2-hydroxybutanenitrile](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/19-nitrogen-compounds/19-2-nitriles-and-hydroxynitriles/assets/003-two-step-synthesis-propan-1-ol-is-oxidised-to-pr.jpg)

parts.solutionMd:

parts.problemMd:
Poly(ethenol) is a polymer used to make dissolvable plastic bags. It can be made by addition polymerisation of CH<sub>2</sub>=CH(OH).

Which structure shows a polymer chain consisting of two monomer residues?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- In addition polymerisation, the C=C double bond in ethenol, CH<sub>2</sub>=CH(OH), opens to form the repeat unit −CH(OH)−CH<sub>2</sub>−:

![Diagram showing addition polymerisation of ethenol (CH₂=CH(OH)) to form poly(ethenol): ethenol monomer on the left with an arrow pointing to the bracketed repeat unit −CH(OH)−CH₂− with subscript n on the right](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/20-polymerisation/20-1-addition-polymerisation/assets/022-diagram-showing-addition-polymerisation-of-ethen.jpg)

- Structure A shows two of these repeat units joined together, which is the correct polymer chain section.

**B** is incorrect as while the first repeat unit is correctly drawn, the second is connected via a C−O ether linkage rather than a C−C bond. In addition polymerisation only carbon-carbon bonds join repeat units in the main chain.

**C** is incorrect as in **addition polymerisation** only C−C bonds connect repeat units in the main chain. Oxygen atoms within the backbone (as shown) are characteristic of condensation polymerisation, not addition polymerisation.

**D** is incorrect as in addition polymerisation the hydroxyl (−OH) group remains as a pendant side group throughout the chain. It does not react or appear as a terminal end group.

parts.problemMd:
Plastic waste can be incinerated to provide energy.

Which statement explains why poly(chloroethene), PVC, is removed from the waste before incineration?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- PVC, poly(chloroethene), is made by the addition polymerisation of chloroethene, H<sub>2</sub>C=CHCl:

![Diagram showing addition polymerisation of chloroethene (CH₂=CHCl) to form poly(chloroethene)/PVC: chloroethene monomer on the left with an arrow pointing to the bracketed repeat unit −CH₂−CHCl− with subscript n; below shows the expanded polymer chain −CH₂−CHCl−CH₂−CHCl−](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/20-polymerisation/20-1-addition-polymerisation/assets/008-diagram-showing-addition-polymerisation-of-chlor.jpg)

- When PVC is incinerated, **harmful gases** are produced, including **hydrogen chloride (HCl)**, **dioxins** and **carbon monoxide (CO)**, all of which are toxic to humans and animals.

**A** is incorrect as ozone layer destruction is caused by chlorine free radicals (Cl<sup>•</sup>) from CFC compounds, not by incinerating PVC. Burning PVC produces HCl gas, not chlorine radicals.

**B** is incorrect as while PVC has some flame-retardant properties due to its chlorine content, it can still be incinerated at high temperatures. The reason for its removal is the **toxic combustion products** (HCl, dioxins, CO), not difficulty in burning.

**C** is incorrect as PVC is **not** biodegradable. Synthetic polymers are not broken down by bacteria, so biodegradability is not relevant to the decision to remove it before incineration.

parts.problemMd:
The diagram below shows 2-methylpropene, C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub>, a monomer used in the production of synthetic rubber.

![Displayed formula of 2-methylpropene: CH₂=C(CH₃)₂ with a C=C double bond, two hydrogen atoms on C1, and two methyl groups on C2](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/20-polymerisation/20-1-addition-polymerisation/assets/016-displayed-formula-of-2-methylpropene-ch-c-ch-wit.jpg)

What is the compound formed by 2-methylpropene when it undergoes addition polymerisation?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- When 2-methylpropene undergoes addition polymerisation its C=C **double bond breaks** to leave a single bond between the carbons, allowing each carbon to form a bond with adjacent monomer units.
- The compound's name indicates that the double bond is between carbons 1 and 2, and the methyl substituent is on carbon 2.
- Therefore, in the repeat unit the second carbon has two methyl groups (one from C3 of the main chain and one from the 2-methyl substituent):

![Diagram showing addition polymerisation of 2-methylpropene to poly(2-methylpropene): 2-methylpropene monomer with C1=C2 double bond and methyl branch at C2 on the left, arrow pointing to the bracketed repeat unit −CH₂−C(CH₃)₂− with subscript n on the right](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/20-polymerisation/20-1-addition-polymerisation/assets/017-diagram-showing-addition-polymerisation-of-2-met.jpg)

**A** is incorrect as repeat units in addition polymers have a **2-carbon backbone**. The 3-carbon backbone shown would require a different monomer or polymerisation mechanism.

**B** is incorrect as this is the repeat unit of **poly(but-2-ene)**, not poly(2-methylpropene). In poly(but-2-ene) each carbon in the repeat unit carries one methyl group.

**D** is incorrect as during addition polymerisation one bond in the C=C double bond breaks. The repeat unit contains only C−C single bonds in the main chain, not a retained double bond.

parts.problemMd: What is the repeat unit of PVC, poly(chloroethene)?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- In addition polymerisation, the C=C double bond in chloroethene, H<sub>2</sub>C=CHCl, breaks to form a C−C single bond, giving the repeat unit −CH<sub>2</sub>−CHCl−.
- PVC (polyvinylchloride) is more correctly named poly(chloroethene), made from the addition polymerisation of chloroethene.

**B** is incorrect as this is the repeat unit for poly(1,2-dichloroethene), which has one chlorine atom on each of the two adjacent carbons in the repeat unit.

**C** is incorrect as repeat units in addition polymers do **not** contain a C=C double bond. All C=C bonds break during addition polymerisation.

**D** is incorrect as repeat units in addition polymers do **not** contain a C=C double bond, and the repeat unit of PVC has only **one** chlorine atom, not two.

parts.problemMd:
But-2-en-1-ol, CH<sub>3</sub>CH=CHCH<sub>2</sub>OH, is a monomer that undergoes addition polymerisation.

Which structure is the repeat unit in poly(but-2-en-1-ol)?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- In but-2-en-1-ol:

  - 'but' = 4 carbons
  - '2-en' = C=C double bond between C2 and C3
  - '1-ol' = OH group on C1.
- In addition polymerisation, the C=C double bond breaks, forming a 2-carbon backbone in the repeat unit.

  - All other groups remain as pendant substituents:

![Diagram showing addition polymerisation of but-2-en-1-ol to poly(but-2-en-1-ol): displayed formula of but-2-en-1-ol with numbered carbons (C4−C3=C2−C1−OH) on the left with an arrow pointing to the bracketed repeat unit with subscript n on the right; below shows the simplified repeat unit −CH(CH₃)−CH(CH₂OH)−](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/20-polymerisation/20-1-addition-polymerisation/assets/007-diagram-showing-addition-polymerisation-of-but-2.jpg)

- The repeat unit is −CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)−CH(CH<sub>2</sub>OH)−:

  - C3 (bearing the methyl group) and C2 (bearing the hydroxymethyl group) form the 2-carbon backbone.

**A** is incorrect as repeat units in addition polymers do **not** contain C=C double bonds; all C=C bonds break during polymerisation.

**B** is incorrect as in addition polymerisation only the **two carbons** of the original double bond form the backbone. C1 (CH<sub>2</sub>OH) and C4 (CH<sub>3</sub>) remain as pendant groups, giving a 2-carbon rather than 4-carbon backbone.

**C** is incorrect as in addition polymerisation only the **two carbons** of the original double bond form the backbone. The OH group remains as a pendant substituent, not a terminal end group.

choices.textMd: Combustion of PVC waste produces a highly acidic gas

choices.label: C

choices.label: D
