parts.problemMd: Which statement about PVC, poly(chloroethene), is **not** correct?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- PVC, poly(chloroethene), is made by the addition polymerisation of chloroethene, H<sub>2</sub>C=CHCl.
- In the repeat unit −CH<sub>2</sub>−CHCl−, there is **one** chlorine atom per repeat unit (not two).
- The repeat unit −CHCl−CHCl− would correspond to poly(1,2-dichloroethene), not PVC.

**A** is not the answer as the statement 'Combustion of PVC waste produces a highly acidic gas' is correct. PVC combustion produces hydrogen chloride (HCl), which is a highly acidic gas.

**B** is not the answer as the statement 'PVC molecules are saturated' is correct. All C=C double bonds break during addition polymerisation, leaving only C−C single bonds in the polymer chain.

**C** is not the answer as the statement 'The empirical formula of PVC is the same as the empirical formula of its monomer' is correct. This holds for all addition polymers because no atoms are gained or lost during polymerisation.

parts.problemMd:
PVC is produced by the addition polymerisation of chloroethene.

Which row correctly describes the carbon-carbon bond in chloroethene compared with the carbon-carbon bond in PVC?

|   | **Bond length** | **Bond strength** |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | Longer | Stronger |
| **B** | Longer | Weaker |
| **C** | Shorter | Stronger |
| **D** | Shorter | Weaker |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- Chloroethene contains a C=C **double bond**; PVC contains C−C **single bonds** in the polymer chain.
- **Double bonds** are **shorter** and **stronger** than single bonds, because more electrons are shared between the two carbons, pulling the atoms closer together.
- Therefore, the C=C bond in chloroethene is **shorter and stronger** than the C−C bond in PVC.

**A** is incorrect as the C=C double bond in chloroethene is **shorter** than the C−C single bond in PVC, not longer.

**B** is incorrect as the C=C double bond is both **shorter** (not longer) and **stronger** (not weaker) than the C−C single bond.

**D** is incorrect as the C=C double bond in chloroethene is **stronger** than the C−C single bond in PVC, not weaker.

choices.label: D
choices.textMd: Approximately half are 109.5° and half are 120°

parts.problemMd: What are the C−C−C bond angles along the polymeric chain in PVC?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- The C−C−C bonds referred to are those in the carbon backbone of poly(chloroethene) (PVC).
- PVC is **fully saturated**, meaning there are only single bonds in the molecule.
- Carbon forms **4 bonds** arranged in a **tetrahedral** geometry to maximise separation between bonding electron pairs.
- The C−C−C bond angles along the backbone are **approximately 109.5°** (slightly less than ideal due to the bulky Cl substituents).

![Diagram showing the tetrahedral geometry of three adjacent carbon atoms in a polymer chain backbone, with approximately 109.5° bond angles marked between C−C−C bonds and generic R groups as pendant substituents, labelled 'tetrahedral' and 'polymer chain'](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/20-polymerisation/20-1-addition-polymerisation/assets/005-diagram-showing-the-tetrahedral-geometry-of-thre.jpg)

**B** is incorrect as 120° corresponds to **trigonal planar** geometry, which is seen in **alkenes** such as chloroethene (the PVC monomer). Once polymerised, PVC has only C−C single bonds.

![Diagram showing trigonal planar geometry of chloroethene (CH₂=CHCl): C=C double bond with 120° bond angle marked, labelled 'trigonal planar' and 'alkene'](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/20-polymerisation/20-1-addition-polymerisation/assets/006-diagram-showing-trigonal-planar-geometry-of-chlo.jpg)

**C** is incorrect as 180° corresponds to **linear** geometry (e.g. CO<sub>2</sub>), not the tetrahedral geometry of the sp<sup>3</sup> carbons in PVC.

**D** is incorrect as PVC has only C−C single bonds throughout the polymer chain. The 120° angles associated with C=C double bonds (as in the chloroethene monomer) are not present in PVC.

parts.problemMd:
The absorbent material in disposable nappies is made from the addition polymer shown.

![Section of a poly(prop-2-enoic acid) chain showing alternating CH₂ and CH groups in the backbone with a CO₂H carboxylic acid pendant group on each CH carbon, with continuation bonds at both ends](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/20-polymerisation/20-1-addition-polymerisation/assets/009-section-of-a-poly-prop-2-enoic-acid-chain-showin.png)

Which monomer is used to make this polymer?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- Repeat units in addition polymers have a **2-carbon backbone**.

![Annotated polymer chain section showing the 2-carbon repeat unit boundaries: carbon atoms are numbered 1 (CH₂) and 2 (CH bearing the CO₂H pendant group), with highlighted markers showing where each repeat unit begins and ends](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/20-polymerisation/20-1-addition-polymerisation/assets/010-annotated-polymer-chain-section-showing-the-2-ca.jpg)

- One repeat unit:

![Single repeat unit of poly(prop-2-enoic acid): −CH₂−CH(CO₂H)−, with carbon 1 (CH₂) and carbon 2 (CH bearing the carboxylic acid group) labelled, shown with continuation bonds](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/20-polymerisation/20-1-addition-polymerisation/assets/011-single-repeat-unit-of-poly-prop-2-enoic-acid-ch-.jpg)

- The repeat unit is −CH₂−CH(CO₂H)−, giving the polymer name **poly(prop-2-enoic acid)**.

  - The corresponding monomer is prop-2-enoic acid with a C=C double bond.

![Identification diagram: displayed formula H₂C=CH(CO₂H) on the left labelled 'which is', arrow pointing to the condensed formula H₂C=CHCO₂H boxed with label D, identifying the correct monomer](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/20-polymerisation/20-1-addition-polymerisation/assets/012-identification-diagram-displayed-formula-h-c-ch-.jpg)

**B** is incorrect as this monomer has no C=C double bond; addition polymerisation requires a C=C double bond. The resulting polymer would also contain a hydroxyl group, which is not present in the polymer shown.

**C** is incorrect as this monomer has no C=C double bond and would not undergo addition polymerisation. The hydroxyl group would give an incorrect pendant group in the resulting polymer.

**D** is incorrect as, although this monomer contains a C=C double bond, addition polymerisation would give **poly(but-2-enedioic acid)**, in which every backbone carbon carries a CO₂H group; in the polymer shown, CO₂H appears on only alternate backbone carbons.

![Displayed formula of poly(but-2-enedioic acid): polymer chain section in which every backbone carbon carries a carboxylic acid (CO₂H) pendant group alternating above and below the chain](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/20-polymerisation/20-1-addition-polymerisation/assets/013-displayed-formula-of-poly-but-2-enedioic-acid-po.jpg)

parts.problemMd:
In the addition polymerisation of alkenes, which row identifies the types of bond breakage and bond formation that occur?

|   | **Bond breakage** | **Bond formation** |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | π only | σ and π |
| **B** | π only | σ only |
| **C** | σ and π | σ and π |
| **D** | σ and π | σ only |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- During addition polymerisation the C=C double bond on the alkene monomer breaks.
- The π bond is broken and the two electrons are used to form new C−C σ bonds with adjacent monomer units.

![Orbital diagram showing bond changes during addition polymerisation: on the left, an ethene monomer (CH₂=CH₂) with the π orbital (figure-8 shape, highlighted) indicating the C=C double bond; an arrow points to the right showing two carbons now joined by a σ bond only (circular orbital highlighted); labels explain that π orbitals form double bonds (overlap twice) and σ orbitals form single bonds (overlap once)](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/20-polymerisation/20-1-addition-polymerisation/assets/021-orbital-diagram-showing-bond-changes-during-addi.jpg)

- Therefore, **π bonds are broken** and **σ bonds are formed**.

**A** is incorrect as no π bonds are formed. New C−C σ bonds form, not double bonds.

**C** is incorrect as no σ bonds are broken. Only the π component of the C=C double bond breaks, and no π bonds are formed.

**D** is incorrect as no σ bonds are broken. Only the π bond in the C=C double bond breaks during addition polymerisation.

parts.problemMd:
1,1-Dichloroethene undergoes addition polymerisation to form a polymer used in cling film.

Which sequence appears in a short length of the polymer chain?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- 1,1-Dichloroethene (CCl<sub>2</sub>=CH<sub>2</sub>) has a C=C double bond, with **two** chlorine atoms on C1 and two hydrogen atoms on C2.
- In addition polymerisation, the π bond breaks and each carbon forms new C−C bonds with adjacent monomers.
- So, the repeat unit is −CCl<sub>2</sub>−CH<sub>2</sub>−:

![Diagram showing addition polymerisation of 1,1-dichloroethene (CCl₂=CH₂) to form a polymer chain: the monomer on the left with C=C double bond, arrow pointing to a chain section showing two joined units (−CCl₂−CH₂−CCl₂−CH₂−), with brackets labelling each monomer contribution and the label '2 monomers joined together'](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/20-polymerisation/20-1-addition-polymerisation/assets/001-diagram-showing-addition-polymerisation-of-1-1-d.jpg)

**A** is incorrect as −CCl<sub>2</sub>CCl<sub>2</sub>CCl<sub>2</sub>CCl<sub>2</sub>CCl<sub>2</sub>CCl<sub>2</sub>− has **two** chlorine atoms on **every** backbone carbon. This would correspond to a monomer of 1,1,2,2-tetrachloroethene, not 1,1-dichloroethene.

**C** is incorrect as −CH<sub>2</sub>CCl<sub>2</sub>CHClCHClCH<sub>2</sub>CCl<sub>2</sub>− contains CHCl units (one Cl per carbon) within the chain. In poly(1,1-dichloroethene) the two Cl atoms are always on the same carbon (CCl<sub>2</sub>), never distributed singly across two carbons.

**D** is incorrect as −CHClCHClCHClCHClCHClCHCl− has one chlorine per backbone carbon. This corresponds to poly(1,2-dichloroethene), not poly(1,1-dichloroethene).

parts.problemMd: Which polymer is **not** made when ethenol and propene undergo addition polymerisation?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- A copolymer is an addition polymer made from two different monomers.
- Each monomer contributes a **2-carbon** unit to the main chain.

  - All other groups (e.g. −OH, −CH<sub>3</sub>) must be pendant substituents, written **in brackets**.
  - Groups written without brackets are assumed to be part of the main chain.
- Hydrogen atoms may be written with their carbon.

![Diagram showing why a copolymer chain sequence is incorrect: top left shows ethenol monomer (CH₂=CH(OH)), top right shows propene monomer (CH₂=CH(CH₃)); bottom section shows a polymer chain with CH₃ groups circled in red and annotated 'these should be functional groups off the main chain' and 'repeating units should only be 2 carbons long'](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/20-polymerisation/20-1-addition-polymerisation/assets/020-diagram-showing-why-a-copolymer-chain-sequence-i.jpg)

**A** is incorrect as this accurately shows the copolymer of ethenol and propene with the pattern: propene, ethenol, ethenol, propene.

**C** is incorrect as this accurately shows the copolymer of ethenol and propene with the two monomers alternating: ethenol, propene, ethenol, propene.

**D** is incorrect as this accurately shows poly(ethenol), which could be produced from a reaction mixture with a large excess of ethenol and very little propene.

parts.problemMd:
The diagram shows a short length of an addition polymer chain.

![Short section of addition polymer chain showing six consecutive backbone carbons, each bearing one H atom above and one OH group below, with dashed bonds at both ends indicating the chain continues](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/20-polymerisation/20-1-addition-polymerisation/assets/004-short-section-of-addition-polymer-chain-showing-.png)

The polymer has a relative molecular mass of 9600.

Approximately how many monomer units are joined together in each polymer molecule?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- The repeat unit of the polymer contains 2 carbons, 2 oxygens and 4 hydrogens.
- Calculate the *M*<sub>r</sub> of the repeat unit:

*M*<sub>r</sub> = (2 x 12) + (2 x 16) + (4 x 1)

*M*<sub>r</sub> = 60 g mol<sup>-1</sup>

- Calculate the number of monomer units:

number of monomer units = $\frac{9600}{60}$

number of monomer units = **160**

**A** is incorrect as 80 monomer units gives a polymer *M*<sub>r</sub> of 4800, not 9600.

**C** is incorrect as 240 monomer units gives a polymer *M*<sub>r</sub> of 14 400, not 9600.

**D** is incorrect as 320 monomer units gives a polymer *M*<sub>r</sub> of 19 200, not 9600.

parts.problemMd:
A naturally occurring compound is formed by the addition polymerisation of four identical monomer molecules, as shown.

![Cyclic naturally occurring addition polymer formed from four identical monomer units, showing a ring structure with alternating C=C double bonds and four pendant CH3 methyl groups around the ring](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/20-polymerisation/20-1-addition-polymerisation/assets/014-cyclic-naturally-occurring-addition-polymer-form.png)

Which structural formula represents the monomer?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- The polymer molecule contains double bonds in its main chain, which means the monomer must have 2 sets of double bonds.

  - This narrows the answer down to **B** or **D**.

- The 2 double bonds open up during addition polymerisation, forming a new double bond in the middle of the repeat unit as well as single bonds to the adjacent monomers.

- To distinguish between **B** and **D**:

  - Option **B **has a methyl group (CH<sub>3</sub>) on carbon 2, which matches the methyl group visible coming off the polymer chain.

![Diagram showing monomer CH2=C(CH3)CH=CH2 with arrows illustrating how the two C=C double bonds open during polymerisation to form a new C=C bond between carbons 2 and 3, and how four monomer units join to form the cyclic polymer ring; CH3 methyl groups are highlighted in orange on the ring](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/20-polymerisation/20-1-addition-polymerisation/assets/015-diagram-showing-monomer-ch2-c-ch3-ch-ch2-with-ar.jpg)

**A** is incorrect as CH<sub>2</sub>=C(CH<sub>3</sub>)CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> has only one C=C double bond and cannot form a polymer with double bonds in the main chain.

**C** is incorrect as CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH=CH<sub>2</sub> has only one C=C double bond and cannot form a polymer with double bonds in the main chain.

**D** is incorrect as CH<sub>3</sub>CH=CHCH=CH<sub>2</sub> would place the methyl group on carbon 1, not carbon 2, which does not match the polymer structure.

parts.problemMd:
Which row correctly describes what happens when poly(propene), (C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>6</sub>)~*n*~, is burned in an excess of air?

|   | **Moles of O**<sub>**2**</sub> | **Products** |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | 3.0*n* | 3*n*CO + 3*n*H<sub>2</sub>O |
| **B** | 1.5*n* | 3*n*C + 3*n*H<sub>2</sub>O |
| **C** | 4.5*n* | 3*n*CO<sub>2</sub> + 3*n*H<sub>2</sub>O |
| **D** | 9.0*n* | 3*n*CO<sub>2</sub> + 3*n*H<sub>2</sub>O |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- In this question n is the number of propene repeat units in the polymer chain.
- Complete combustion occurs because the question states burning in an excess of air.
- The balanced equation for the complete combustion of one propene unit is:

C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>6</sub> + 4.5O<sub>2</sub> → 3CO<sub>2</sub> + 3H<sub>2</sub>O

- On each side:

  - 3 carbon
  - 6 hydrogen
  - 9 oxygen.
- Therefore, for n repeat units:

(C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>6</sub>)<sub>***n***</sub> + **(*****n***** x 4.5)**O<sub>2</sub> → **(*****n***** x 3)**CO<sub>2</sub> + **(*****n***** x 3)**H<sub>2</sub>O

**A **is incorrect as this shows incomplete combustion (CO formation). Burning in an excess of air gives complete combustion, so CO<sub>2</sub> is produced, not CO.

**B **is incorrect as burning in excess of air gives complete combustion. Carbon dioxide (CO<sub>2</sub>) is produced, not carbon.

**D **is incorrect as the stoichiometry for O<sub>2</sub> is incorrect. 9.0n moles of O<sub>2</sub> does not balance the equation for complete combustion of (C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>6</sub>)<sub>***n***</sub>.

parts.problemMd:
The structure of a polymer is shown.

![Displayed formula of a polymer chain section in which every backbone carbon carries a pendant hydroxyl group: −CH(OH)−CH(OH)−CH(OH)−CH(OH)−CH(OH)−CH(OH)−, shown with dashed continuation bonds at both ends](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/20-polymerisation/20-1-addition-polymerisation/assets/018-displayed-formula-of-a-polymer-chain-section-in-.jpg)

Which row identifies step 1 and step 2 to make this polymer?

|   | **Step 1** | **Step 2** |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | Polymerise 1,2-dichloroethene | Hydrolysis |
| **B** | Polymerise 1,2-dichloroethene | Oxidation with H<sup>+</sup> / KMnO<sub>4</sub> |
| **C** | Polymerise ethene | Hydration |
| **D** | Polymerise ethene | Oxidation with H<sup>+</sup> / KMnO<sub>4</sub> |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- **Step 1:**

  - 1,2-Dichloroethene (CHCl=CHCl) undergoes addition polymerisation to form poly(1,2-dichloroethene).
  - The repeat unit is −CHCl−CHCl−.
- **Step 2:**

  - Hydrolysis of the C−Cl bonds converts each −CHCl− group to −CH(OH)−.
  - This produces the poly-diol polymer shown in which every backbone carbon carries an −OH group.

![Two-step reaction diagram: Step 1 shows addition polymerisation of 1,2-dichloroethene (CHCl=CHCl) to form poly(1,2-dichloroethene) (−CHCl−CHCl−)n; Step 2 shows the hydrolysis mechanism — chlorine leaves as a secondary halogen, a carbocation transition state forms, water attacks as a nucleophile, and loss of H⁺ from the oxonium ion produces the pendant hydroxyl group (−CH(OH)−CHCl−)](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/20-polymerisation/20-1-addition-polymerisation/assets/019-two-step-reaction-diagram-step-1-shows-addition-.jpg)

**B** is incorrect as alcohol groups are **not** produced from chlorine substituents by oxidation with H<sup>+</sup> / KMnO<sub>4</sub>. **Hydrolysis** is the correct step to convert C−Cl bonds to C−OH.

**C** is incorrect as polymerising ethene produces repeat units with the structure −CH<sub>2</sub>−CH<sub>2</sub>− (an alkane backbone). Alkanes are unreactive and cannot be subsequently converted to an alcohol polymer by hydration.

**D** is incorrect as polymerising ethene gives an unreactive alkane backbone that cannot be converted to an alcohol polymer. Furthermore, oxidation with H<sup>+</sup> / KMnO<sub>4</sub> does not convert C−H bonds to alcohol groups.

parts.problemMd:
Some micro-organisms produce the naturally occurring polymer PHB (polyhydroxybutyric acid), shown below.

![Structural formula of the PHB (polyhydroxybutyric acid) repeat unit: −[O−CH(CH₃)−CH₂−C(=O)]n, showing an ester linkage within a 4-carbon backbone with a methyl side group, with subscript n](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/20-polymerisation/20-1-addition-polymerisation/assets/002-structural-formula-of-the-phb-polyhydroxybutyric.png)

Which type of reaction would break down PHB?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- PHB contains an **ester repeat unit**: the −O− and C=O groups within the chain form an ester linkage.

![Diagram showing hydrolysis of the PHB polyester: the ester bond (C(=O)−O linkage, highlighted) between two adjacent repeat units is broken by addition of water (+H₂O), producing a carboxylic acid end (−CH₂−C(=O)OH) on one fragment and an alcohol end (HO−CH(CH₃)−) on the other](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/20-polymerisation/20-1-addition-polymerisation/assets/003-diagram-showing-hydrolysis-of-the-phb-polyester-.jpg)

- The PHB monomer contains both a hydroxyl group and a carboxylic acid group.

  - These react by **condensation polymerisation** to form the polymer chain.

- Ester bonds are broken by **hydrolysis** reactions ('hydro' = water; 'lysis' = to break), which is why PHB is biodegradable.

**A** is incorrect as addition reactions involve adding small molecules (e.g. Br<sub>2</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>O) across a C=C double bond. PHB contains no C=C bonds.

**C** is incorrect as reduction involves the addition of hydrogen or removal of oxygen and does not break ester linkages.

**D** is incorrect as substitution involves replacing one atom or group with another. Breaking the ester bonds in PHB requires hydrolysis (reaction with water).

parts.problemMd:
Lactic acid occurs naturally, for example in sour milk.

![Displayed formula of lactic acid (CH₃CH(OH)COOH) showing the hydroxyl group on the central carbon and the carboxylic acid group](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/21-organic-synthesis/21-1-organic-synthesis/assets/021-displayed-formula-of-lactic-acid-ch-ch-oh-cooh-s.png)

Which property does lactic acid have?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- Lactic acid contains a **carboxylic acid** (-COOH) group.
- **Sodium carbonate** reacts with carboxylic acids to form a salt, carbon dioxide and water.

![Reaction scheme showing 2 moles of lactic acid reacting with sodium carbonate (Na₂CO₃) to form sodium lactate (carboxylate salt), carbon dioxide and water](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/21-organic-synthesis/21-1-organic-synthesis/assets/022-reaction-scheme-showing-2-moles-of-lactic-acid-r.jpg)

**A** is incorrect as bromine water is decolourised when shaken with an **alkene** which undergoes an **addition reaction** with the bromine. Lactic acid contains no C=C double bond.

**B** is incorrect as lactic acid contains two **polar** groups: -COOH (carboxylic acid) and -OH (hydroxyl) which can form H-bonds with water. Lactic acid is therefore readily soluble in water.

**D** is incorrect as only **aldehydes** react with Fehling's reagent by being oxidised to a **carboxylic acid**, reducing the Cu²⁺ ions. This causes the **clear blue** solution to become an **opaque red/orange** colour as lactic acid contains no aldehyde group.

choices.label: D
choices.textMd: Sulphur dichloride oxide (thionyl chloride, SOCl<sub>2</sub>) at 50 °C

parts.problemMd: Which reagent can be used to convert CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> into CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Cl?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- The **halogenation** of methyl propanoate (CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>) can be achieved by a **free-radical substitution** reaction.
- The hydrogen atom in the alkyl group (-CH<sub>3</sub>) is substituted for a halogen.
- The reaction is **initiated** by the formation of two **radicals** using UV light (which comes from the Sun).

  - Radicals are species with unpaired electrons.
- In the **propagation** step the formed radicals attack **reactant molecules** to generate more free radicals.
- In the **termination** step two radicals react together to form an unreactive molecule.
- **Initiation step**

Cl<sub>2</sub> $\overset{\mathrm{UV}}{\rightarrow}$ 2Cl<sup>•</sup>

- **Propagation steps:**

CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> + Cl<sup>•</sup> → CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub><sup>•</sup> + HCl

CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub><sup>•</sup> + Cl<sub>2</sub> → CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Cl + Cl<sup>•</sup>

- **Termination steps:**

2Cl<sup>•</sup> → Cl<sub>2</sub>

CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub><sup>•</sup> + Cl<sup>•</sup> → CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Cl

2CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub><sup>•</sup> → CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>

**B**, **C** & **D** are incorrect as these reagents are used in the **nucleophilic substitution** reaction of alcohols. CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> is not an alcohol but an ester.

parts.problemMd: Which reaction produces a coloured organic compound?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- **Aldehydes** and **ketones** react with 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine (2,4-DNPH) in a **condensation** reaction.
- Two molecules join together while eliminating a small molecule (water) to form a **deep orange** precipitate.
- CH<sub>3</sub>CHO (ethanal) is an **aldehyde** which undergoes condensation with 2,4-DNPH to form a deep orange precipitate.

**A** is incorrect as ethene undergoes **mild oxidation** with cold dilute acidified KMnO<sub>4</sub> to form a colourless diol (ethane-1,2-diol). The purple MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>-</sup> ions are reduced to colourless Mn<sup>2+</sup> ions.

**B** is incorrect as ethanol is **oxidised** by acidified K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub>, but the coloured product is Cr<sup>3+</sup> (green), which is an **inorganic** species, not a coloured organic compound. The organic product (ethanal or ethanoic acid) is colourless.

**D** is incorrect as **ketones** do not react with Fehling's solution. Only aldehydes reduce the Cu<sup>2+</sup> ions in Fehling's solution to form a brick red Cu<sub>2</sub>O precipitate, which is an inorganic product.

parts.problemMd:
A compound **X** has the following properties:

- liquid at room temperature
- soluble in water
- reacts with cold aqueous sodium hydroxide

Which of the following could be compound **X**?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- Propanoic acid is a **liquid** at room temperature.
- The carboxylic acid group (-COOH) is highly polar and forms H-bonds with water, causing propanoic acid to be readily soluble in water.
- Propanoic acid is an **acid** which reacts with cold aqueous sodium hydroxide in an acid-base reaction to form sodium propanoate and water.

**B** is incorrect as propanol does not react with cold sodium hydroxide. Propanol is a very weak acid and OH<sup>-</sup> is not strong enough to deprotonate the alcohol group.

**C** is incorrect as propene is a **gas** at room temperature. It is also insoluble in water as it is non-polar, and it does not react with sodium hydroxide.

**D** is incorrect as propyl propanoate does not react with cold aqueous sodium hydroxide. Saponification of an ester requires heating under reflux with concentrated alkali. Additionally, the large non-polar alkyl groups make propyl propanoate poorly soluble in water.

parts.problemMd:
Tartaric acid (HO<sub>2</sub>CCH(OH)CH(OH)CO<sub>2</sub>H) can occur naturally, for example in wine, and may be synthesised in the laboratory.

The laboratory synthesis occurs in 2 steps:

OHCCHO  $\overset{\mathrm{step}1}{\rightarrow}$  intermediate  $\overset{\mathrm{step}2}{\rightarrow}$  HO<sub>2</sub>CCH(OH)CH(OH)CO<sub>2</sub>H

Which reagents could be used for this synthesis?

|   | **Step 1** | **Step 2** |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | HCl (aq) | HCN (g) |
| **B** | H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (aq) | K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> / H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (aq) |
| **C** | KCN (aq/alcoholic) | K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> / H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (aq) |
| **D** | HCN, NaCN (aq/alcoholic) | H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (aq) |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- The first step involves **nucleophilic addition** of HCN (with trace NaCN to generate CN<sup>-</sup> ions) at **room temperature**.

  - The CN<sup>-</sup> nucleophile attacks the slightly positive carbonyl carbon of each aldehyde group in OHCCHO to form a **dihydroxynitrile**.

- In the second step, the nitrile groups are **hydrolysed** by refluxing with dilute aqueous sulfuric acid, forming a **carboxylic acid** and an ammonium salt.

![Two-step synthesis of tartaric acid: Step 1 shows nucleophilic addition of HCN with NaCN catalyst at room temperature to both aldehyde groups of glyoxal (OHCCHO), forming a dihydroxynitrile intermediate; Step 2 shows acid hydrolysis of the nitrile groups with dilute H₂SO₄ to give tartaric acid and ammonium sulfate](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/21-organic-synthesis/21-1-organic-synthesis/assets/017-two-step-synthesis-of-tartaric-acid-step-1-shows.jpg)

**A** is incorrect as HCl does not perform nucleophilic addition to an aldehyde group. Cl<sup>-</sup> is a weaker nucleophile than CN<sup>-</sup> and this combination of reagents does not produce a hydroxynitrile.

**B** is incorrect as H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (aq) alone cannot add across the C=O bond of an aldehyde, and K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub>/H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> is an oxidising agent used to oxidise alcohols and aldehydes, not to hydrolyse nitriles.

**C** is incorrect as KCN in aq/alcoholic solution can form the dihydroxynitrile (step 1 is plausible), but K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub>/H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (step 2) would oxidise the secondary alcohol groups in the intermediate to ketones, rather than hydrolysing the nitrile groups to carboxylic acids.

parts.problemMd:
This molecule is responsible for the flavour of spearmint chewing gum.

![Structural formula of carvone (spearmint flavour molecule) with arrow 1 pointing to the C=C alkene double bond in the cyclohexene ring and arrow 2 pointing to the C=O ketone carbonyl group](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/21-organic-synthesis/21-1-organic-synthesis/assets/018-structural-formula-of-carvone-spearmint-flavour-.png)

Which statement about functional groups **1** and **2** is correct?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- The oxygen is more electronegative and therefore has a stronger pull on the electrons in the C=O bond.
- This leaves the carbon slightly positively charged and the oxygen slightly negatively charged.
- The carbonyl carbon is attracted to **nucleophiles** and will undergo **nucleophilic addition**.
- A nucleophile attacks the carbon atom in the carbonyl group and addition across the C=O bond occurs.

**A** is incorrect as the C=C in group **1** cannot undergo electrophilic substitution because there are no groups on the double bond that can be replaced. Group **1** undergoes **electrophilic addition**.

**B** is incorrect as the C=C double bond in group **1** is rich in electrons and is therefore attracted to **electrophiles**. Group **1** undergoes **electrophilic addition**, not nucleophilic addition.

**C** is incorrect as the carbon in C=O is slightly positively charged because oxygen is more electronegative and draws electrons away from the carbon. The carbonyl carbon is attracted to **nucleophiles**, not electrophiles. Group **2** undergoes **nucleophilic addition**, not electrophilic substitution.

parts.problemMd:
Sorbic acid is a natural organic compound which is used as a food preservative because it kills fungi. Sorbic acid reacts with bromine in an organic solvent and hydrogen in the presence of a nickel catalyst.

![Displayed formula of sorbic acid showing H₃C group connected through two conjugated C=C double bonds to a carboxylic acid (COOH) group, with all hydrogen atoms shown](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/21-organic-synthesis/21-1-organic-synthesis/assets/004-displayed-formula-of-sorbic-acid-showing-h-c-gro.png)

How many moles of bromine (in an organic solvent) and of hydrogen (in the presence of a Pt / Ni catalyst) will be incorporated into one mole of sorbic acid by these reactions?

|   | **Moles of bromine** | **Moles of hydrogen** |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | 2 | 2 |
| **B** | 2 | 3 |
| **C** | $\frac{1}{2}$ | 2 |
| **D** | 2$\frac{1}{2}$ | 3 |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- Sorbic acid contains two C=C double bonds.
- Each C=C double bond undergoes **electrophilic addition** with one mole of bromine (Br<sub>2</sub>) in an organic solvent.

  - So, two moles of Br<sub>2</sub> are incorporated per mole of sorbic acid.
- Each C=C double bond also undergoes **addition** with one mole of hydrogen in a **hydrogenation** reaction in the presence of a Ni catalyst.

  - So, two moles of H<sub>2</sub> are incorporated per mole of sorbic acid.

![Reaction scheme showing two reactions of sorbic acid: (1) Sorbic Acid + 2Br₂ — electrophilic addition of bromine through a carbocation intermediate gives 2,3,4,5-tetrabromopentanoic acid; (2) Sorbic Acid + 2H₂ with nickel catalyst gives pentanoic acid](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/21-organic-synthesis/21-1-organic-synthesis/assets/005-reaction-scheme-showing-two-reactions-of-sorbic-.jpg)

**B** is incorrect as sorbic acid reacts with two moles of hydrogen, not three. There are two C=C double bonds in sorbic acid, each incorporating one mole of H<sub>2</sub> during hydrogenation.

**C** is incorrect as sorbic acid reacts with two moles of bromine, not half a mole. Each of the two C=C double bonds undergoes electrophilic addition with one mole of Br<sub>2</sub>.

**D** is incorrect as sorbic acid reacts with two moles of bromine (not 2½) and two moles of hydrogen (not three). Each C=C double bond reacts with one mole of each reagent.

parts.problemMd:
The naturally-occurring molecule civetone was one of the first known ingredients used in perfumery.

![Structural formula of civetone: a 17-membered cyclic ketone containing a C=O group and one C=C double bond (HC=CH), with the remaining ring positions occupied by CH₂ groups](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/21-organic-synthesis/21-1-organic-synthesis/assets/019-structural-formula-of-civetone-a-17-membered-cyc.png)

Which reagent will **not** react with civetone?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- Fehling's reagent tests for the presence of **aldehydes** by oxidising the aldehyde to a **carboxylic acid**.

  - The Cu<sup>2+</sup> ions are reduced to Cu<sup>+</sup> ions, changing the clear **blue** solution to an **opaque orange/red** due to the formation of copper(I) oxide.
- Civetone does not contain any aldehyde group, so it will **not** react with Fehling's reagent.

**A** is incorrect as the ketone group in civetone can undergo a **condensation reaction** with **2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine** to form a **deep-orange** precipitate and water.

**C** is incorrect as the C=C double bond in civetone can undergo **electrophilic addition** with HBr.

**D** is incorrect as the ketone group in civetone will be reduced by NaBH<sub>4</sub> to a secondary alcohol.

parts.problemMd:
An alkene is reacted with acidified manganate (VII) ions, MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>- </sup>. The organic product has a relative molecular mass greater than that of the alkene by 34.

Which of the following are the correct conditions for this reaction?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- A relative molecular mass increase of 34 corresponds to the addition of two hydrogen atoms and two oxygen atoms.

- This occurs when an alkene undergoes mild oxidation with cold, dilute acidified MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>-</sup> to form a **diol**.

  - A diol is an organic compound containing two -OH groups.

- The relative molecular mass of the two -OH groups added: 2 x (16 + 1) = 34

**A** is incorrect as cold, concentrated MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>-</sup> would be too strongly oxidising for selective diol formation. Dilute conditions are required for mild oxidation.

**C** is incorrect as hot, concentrated MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>-</sup> is a strong oxidant that fully cleaves the C=C bond, forming ketones, aldehydes, or carboxylic acids rather than a diol.

**D** is incorrect as hot conditions promote stronger oxidation that cleaves the C=C bond rather than forming a diol. Cold conditions are required to limit the extent of oxidation.

parts.problemMd:
Pentanoic acid can be produced from 1-bromobutane using reagents Y and Z as shown below.

1-bromobutane  $\overset{\mathrm{reagent}Y}{\rightarrow}$  compound X  $\overset{\mathrm{reagent}Z}{\rightarrow}$  pentanoic acid

Which of the following could be reagents Y and Z?

|   | **Y** | **Z** |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | KCN in ethanol | HCl (aq) |
| **B** | KCN in ethanol | NaOH (aq) |
| **C** | NaOH (aq) | HCl (aq) |
| **D** | NH<sub>3</sub> in ethanol | H<sup>+</sup>/Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub><sup>2-</sup> (aq) |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- 1-bromobutane undergoes **nucleophilic substitution** with KCN in ethanol, in which the CN<sup>-</sup> ion replaces the bromine atom to form pentanenitrile.
- Pentanenitrile then undergoes **hydrolysis** with dilute HCl under reflux to produce pentanoic acid and ammonium chloride.

![Reaction scheme for conversion of 1-bromobutane to pentanoic acid in two steps: Step 1 — nucleophilic substitution of 1-bromobutane with CN⁻ in ethanolic KCN under heat to give pentanenitrile and KBr; Step 2 — hydrolysis of pentanenitrile with HCl and 2H₂O to give pentanoic acid and NH₄Cl](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/21-organic-synthesis/21-1-organic-synthesis/assets/015-reaction-scheme-for-conversion-of-1-bromobutane-.jpg)

**B** is incorrect as KCN in ethanol does form a nitrile correctly, but NaOH (aq) hydrolyses the nitrile under alkaline conditions to give a carboxylate salt, not pentanoic acid.

**C** is incorrect as NaOH (aq) substitutes the bromine to give 1-butanol (an alcohol); treatment with HCl (aq) then substitutes the -OH with Cl, giving 1-chlorobutane, not pentanoic acid.

**D** is incorrect as NH<sub>3</sub> in ethanol substitutes the bromine to give a primary amine; primary amines cannot be oxidised by H<sup>+</sup>/Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub><sup>2-</sup> (aq) to produce a carboxylic acid.

parts.problemMd: In which reaction does a carbocation intermediate form?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- **Alkenes** will undergo an addition reaction when shaken with orange/yellow bromine water (Br<sub>2</sub>) to turn the solution colourless.
- The first step involves **electrophilic** attack of the slightly positively charged bromine atom on the C=C bond.
- This results in the formation of a primary carbocation, which then undergoes **nucleophilic** attack by the Br<sup>-</sup> to form 1,2-dibromoethane.

![Mechanism of electrophilic addition of bromine to ethene: induced dipole in Br₂ (δ⁻Br...Brδ+) attacks the C=C double bond to form a carbocation intermediate, which is then attacked by Br⁻ to give 1,2-dibromoethane](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/21-organic-synthesis/21-1-organic-synthesis/assets/003-mechanism-of-electrophilic-addition-of-bromine-t.jpg)

**B** is incorrect as this is **nucleophilic substitution** of the bromine by OH<sup>-</sup> in the primary halogenoalkane following an S<sub>N</sub>2 mechanism. This reaction does not involve a carbocation intermediate.

**C** is incorrect as this is a **free-radical substitution** reaction initiated by sunlight, which involves free radicals, not carbocation intermediates.

**D** is incorrect as this is **nucleophilic addition** of CN<sup>-</sup> to the carbonyl carbon to form a hydroxynitrile. This reaction does not involve a carbocation intermediate.

choices.label: A
choices.textMd: CH<sub>3</sub>(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>5</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> when hept-4-enal is reduced by H<sub>2</sub> / Ni

choices.label: B
choices.textMd: CH<sub>3</sub>(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>5</sub>CHO when hept-4-enal is reduced by NaBH<sub>4</sub>

choices.label: C

parts.problemMd:
Hept-4-enal, shown below, naturally occurs in cow's milk.

CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH=CHCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CHO

Which organic product is formed when hept-4-enal is reduced with **either** hydrogen with a nickel catalyst **or** sodium borohydride?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- The addition of H<sub>2</sub> to a double bond in the presence of a Ni catalyst is a **hydrogenation** reaction, which reduces the C=C but does not affect the aldehyde group.

  - When reacted with H<sub>2</sub> / Ni, the alkene group in hept-4-enal undergoes hydrogenation to give heptanal (aldehyde preserved).
- NaBH<sub>4</sub> is a reducing agent that reduces **ketones** and **aldehydes** to secondary and primary alcohols respectively.

  - When reacted with NaBH<sub>4</sub>, the aldehyde group in hept-4-enal is reduced to a primary alcohol, giving hept-4-en-1-ol (C=C preserved).

![Two reactions of hept-4-enal: (1) H₂/Ni with heat — hydrogenation of the C=C double bond gives heptanal (aldehyde group preserved); (2) NaBH₄ — reduction of the aldehyde group gives hept-4-enol (hept-4-en-1-ol; C=C double bond preserved)](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/21-organic-synthesis/21-1-organic-synthesis/assets/020-two-reactions-of-hept-4-enal-1-h-ni-with-heat-hy.jpg)

**A** is incorrect as the alkene group has been reduced but so has the aldehyde group, which is not possible using a single reagent from those given.

**B** is incorrect as NaBH<sub>4</sub> reduces **aldehydes**, not **alkenes**. The product shown is heptanal (saturated, CHO preserved), which is the H<sub>2</sub>/Ni product, not the NaBH<sub>4</sub> product.

**C** is incorrect as H<sub>2</sub>/Ni reduces **alkenes**, not **aldehydes**. The product shown has the C=C preserved and the aldehyde reduced, which is what NaBH<sub>4</sub> does, not H<sub>2</sub>/Ni.

parts.problemMd:
The diagram shows the structure of the naturally-occurring molecule cholesterol.

![Skeletal structure of cholesterol: a steroid with four fused rings, a hydroxyl (-OH) group on ring A, a C=C double bond in ring B, and an isooctyl side chain attached to ring D](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/21-organic-synthesis/21-1-organic-synthesis/assets/013-skeletal-structure-of-cholesterol-a-steroid-with.png)

Two separate test tubes of cholesterol are used in an experiment. One test tube of cholesterol is treated with cold, dilute acidified KMnO<sub>4</sub>, and the other is treated with hot, concentrated acidified KMnO<sub>4</sub>.

Which row correctly describes the change in the **number** of chiral carbon atoms in the molecule during each reaction and the structure of the product in each test tube?

|   | **Cold, dilute acidified KMnO**<sub>**4**</sub> | **Hot, concentrated acidified KMnO**<sub>**4**</sub> |   |   |
|---|---|---|---|---|
|   | Change in the number of chiral carbons | Number of hydroxy groups in product | Change in the number of chiral carbons | Number of 6-membered rings remaining in product |
| **A** | +1 | 1 | -1 | 3 |
| **B** | +1 | 1 | 0 | 2 |
| **C** | +2 | 3 | -1 | 2 |
| **D** | +2 | 3 | 0 | 3 |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- **Cold, dilute acidified MnO**<sub>**4**</sub><sup>**-**</sup> is a **mild** oxidising reagent which oxidises alkenes to a diol.
- The C=C in cholesterol becomes a **diol**.

  - The two carbon atoms are now bonded to four different groups, creating **two new chiral centres** (+2).
- Cold, dilute MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>-</sup> will not oxidise the -OH group already present in cholesterol.

  - Therefore, the **total number of hydroxy groups** in the product is **three** (1 original + 2 from diol).
- **Hot, concentrated acidified MnO**<sub>**4**</sub><sup>**-**</sup> is a **strong** oxidising reagent that completely breaks the C=C bond to form a ketone and an aldehyde.

  - The aldehyde is further oxidised to a carboxylic acid.
- The secondary alcohol group already present in cholesterol is also oxidised to a **ketone**, removing that chiral centre (**−1 chiral centre**).
- Only **two 6-membered rings** remain in the product.

![Two reactions of cholesterol: (top) cold, dilute acidified KMnO₄ oxidises only the alkene to a diol, adding 2 new chiral carbons and giving 3 OH groups total; (bottom) hot, concentrated acidified KMnO₄ oxidises both the C=C and the secondary alcohol to their furthest extent, leaving 2 six-membered rings and losing one chiral centre](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/21-organic-synthesis/21-1-organic-synthesis/assets/014-two-reactions-of-cholesterol-top-cold-dilute-aci.jpg)

**A** is incorrect as the cold, dilute KMnO<sub>4</sub> values are wrong: the diol formation adds **two** new chiral centres (+2, not +1) and gives **three** hydroxy groups in total (not one). The hot value of -1 chiral centre is correct, but **two** 6-membered rings remain (not three).

**B** is incorrect as the cold, dilute KMnO<sub>4</sub> values are wrong for the same reasons as A (+1 and 1 should be +2 and 3). The hot value of 2 rings is correct, but the chiral change is **-1** (not 0) as the secondary alcohol is oxidised to a ketone, removing that chiral centre.

**D** is incorrect as the cold, dilute KMnO<sub>4</sub> values (+2 and 3) are both correct. However, both hot, concentrated KMnO<sub>4</sub> values are wrong: the chiral change is **-1** (not 0), and **two** 6-membered rings remain (not three).

parts.problemMd:
The cyclic compound G is heated with dilute hydrochloric acid.

![Skeletal formula of compound G (morpholine-2,5-dione): a 6-membered ring containing an NH amide group, an ester linkage (C=O bonded to ring oxygen), and two CH₂ groups](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/21-organic-synthesis/21-1-organic-synthesis/assets/006-skeletal-formula-of-compound-g-morpholine-2-5-di.jpg)

Which of the following are the products of the reaction?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- Compound G contains an **amide** and an **ester** group which can both undergo **hydrolysis** when heated with dilute hydrochloric acid.

  - Hydrolysis of the **amide** produces an **amine** and a **carboxylic acid**.
- Under acidic conditions, the basic amine is protonated to give NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup>.

  - Hydrolysis of the **ester** produces an **alcohol** and a **carboxylic acid**.

![Hydrolysis of compound G with HCl: the ester linkage and amide linkage both hydrolyse; the amine formed is protonated by H⁺ under acidic conditions, giving HO₂CCH₂NH₃⁺ (glycinium) and HO₂CCH₂OH (glycolic acid)](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/21-organic-synthesis/21-1-organic-synthesis/assets/007-hydrolysis-of-compound-g-with-hcl-the-ester-link.jpg)

**A** is incorrect as neither product is the result of complete hydrolysis. H<sub>2</sub>NCOCH<sub>2</sub>OH retains the amide bond intact rather than breaking it to give separate amine and carboxylic acid groups. HOCH<sub>2</sub>CHO (glycolaldehyde) has an aldehyde group rather than a carboxylic acid, which is not the product of ester hydrolysis.

**C** is incorrect as HOCH<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>H (glycolic acid from ester hydrolysis) is correct, but H<sub>2</sub>NCH<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>H (glycine) is incorrect. Under acidic conditions (dilute HCl), the amine is protonated to NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup>, so the correct amide hydrolysis product is HO<sub>2</sub>CCH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup>, not the free amine.

**D** is incorrect as the amide bond in HOCH<sub>2</sub>CONH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup> has not been hydrolysed. The amide linkage is merely protonated, not broken. Acid hydrolysis of the amide produces separate NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup> and carboxylic acid groups. HOCH<sub>2</sub>CHO is also incorrect for the ester product (should be HOCH<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>H).

parts.problemMd:
Santonin is a drug that has been used to treat a worm infection.

![Skeletal formula of santonin: a bicyclic sesquiterpene lactone with a 6-membered ring containing a conjugated C=C–C=O enone system and two CH₃ groups, fused to a 5-membered γ-lactone ring containing a C=O ester group, ring oxygen, and CH₃](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/21-organic-synthesis/21-1-organic-synthesis/assets/023-skeletal-formula-of-santonin-a-bicyclic-sesquite.png)

When santonin is first treated with warm dilute H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>, product X is formed. If X is treated with cold acidified KMnO<sub>4</sub>, the final product Y is obtained.

How many atoms of hydrogen in each molecule of product Y could be displaced in a reaction with sodium metal?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- When a **lactone (cyclic ester)** is heated with dilute H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>, it undergoes **hydrolysis** to form a **carboxylic acid** and an **alcohol** (+2 active H atoms from these two -OH groups).
- Santonin contains **two alkene groups**, both of which undergo **mild oxidation** by cold, dilute acidified MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>-</sup> to form **diols** (+4 active H atoms from the four -OH groups).
- Cold, dilute MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>-</sup> is not a strong enough oxidising reagent to further oxidise the alcohol from ester hydrolysis.
- Total displaceable H atoms:

4 (from two diols) + 1 (carboxylic acid -OH) + 1 (alcohol -OH) = **6**.

- **Alcohols** and **carboxylic acids** both react with reactive metals such as Na to form a **salt** and **hydrogen gas (H**<sub>**2**</sub>**)**.

![Conversion of santonin to product Y: the lactone is hydrolysed by H₂SO₄ to give a carboxylic acid and an alcohol; the two alkene groups are mildly oxidised by KMnO₄ to give two diol groups; product Y has 6 acidic O–H hydrogens (numbered 1–6) that can be displaced by sodium](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/21-organic-synthesis/21-1-organic-synthesis/assets/024-conversion-of-santonin-to-product-y-the-lactone-.jpg)

**A** is incorrect as 2 accounts only for the carboxylic acid (1 H) and alcohol (1 H) produced by lactone hydrolysis. The four additional O–H groups from mild oxidation of the two C=C bonds to diols are not included.

**B** is incorrect as 4 would account for two diol OH groups (from one C=C) plus the carboxylic acid and alcohol (2 H). However, santonin contains two C=C double bonds, both oxidised to diols, giving four diol OH groups in total, not two.

**C** is incorrect as 5 omits one of the six displaceable hydrogen atoms. Both the carboxylic acid and the alcohol produced by lactone hydrolysis each contribute one active hydrogen, and the two diols from mild oxidation of the two alkenes contribute four more, giving six in total.

parts.problemMd:
Compound M is used in leather processing.

![Skeletal formula of compound M (glycolide/1,4-dioxane-2,5-dione): a 6-membered cyclic diester ring containing two C=O groups and two ring oxygen atoms, with two CH₂ groups completing the ring](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/21-organic-synthesis/21-1-organic-synthesis/assets/008-skeletal-formula-of-compound-m-glycolide-1-4-dio.png)

Compound M is synthesised in the presence of concentrated sulfuric acid and heat.

Which other starting materials are required to synthesise compound M?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- Two molecules of HOCH<sub>2</sub>COOH will react with each other to form **two ester groups** in a cyclic structure.
- Each ester group is formed by a **condensation** reaction between the **alcohol** (-OH) of one molecule and the **carboxylic acid** (-COOH) of the other, eliminating water.

![Formation of compound M: two molecules of HOCH₂COOH (glycolic acid) undergo double condensation reactions with hot concentrated H₂SO₄, eliminating 2H₂O to form the 6-membered cyclic diester (glycolide)](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/21-organic-synthesis/21-1-organic-synthesis/assets/009-formation-of-compound-m-two-molecules-of-hoch-co.jpg)

**A** & **C** are incorrect as neither molecule contains a free alcohol (-OH) group that can react with a carboxylic acid group of another molecule to form an ester linkage. Without a free -OH, self-esterification to give the cyclic diester cannot occur.

**B** is incorrect as mixing CH<sub>3</sub>COOH with HOCH<sub>2</sub>COOH would not produce compound M. The CH<sub>3</sub>COOH would react with the alcohol group of HOCH<sub>2</sub>COOH to give a single linear mixed ester, not a cyclic diester with two ester groups.

![Single condensation reaction between CH₃COOH and HOCH₂COOH with hot concentrated H₂SO₄, eliminating H₂O to give a linear ester product rather than the cyclic diester compound M](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/21-organic-synthesis/21-1-organic-synthesis/assets/010-single-condensation-reaction-between-ch-cooh-and.jpg)

parts.problemMd:
Mixture **F** is produced upon refluxing compound **G** with aqueous sodium hydroxide.

Upon distillation of mixture **F** with acidified potassium dichromate (VI), propanone is produced. Mixing compound **G** with aqueous silver nitrate and dilute nitric acid gives a cream precipitate.

Which of the following could be compound **G**?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- Since propanone is produced upon oxidation of mixture **F** with acidified potassium dichromate, **F** must contain a **secondary alcohol**.
- **Propan-2-ol** (**F**) forms when compound **G** reacts with aqueous NaOH via **nucleophilic substitution**, in which OH<sup>-</sup> replaces the halogen.
- Compound **G** is therefore a **secondary halogenoalkane** which reacts with silver nitrate to form a coloured precipitate of a **silver halide**.
- **Silver bromide** gives a **cream precipitate**, so the unknown halogen is **bromine**.

![Reaction scheme: 2-bromopropane (compound G, a secondary halogenoalkane) undergoes nucleophilic substitution with OH⁻ under heat to give propan-2-ol (compound F), which is then oxidised by acidified KMnO₄ to give propanone](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/21-organic-synthesis/21-1-organic-synthesis/assets/016-reaction-scheme-2-bromopropane-compound-g-a-seco.jpg)

**A** is incorrect as CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Br is a **primary** halogenoalkane. Reaction with NaOH gives propan-1-ol (a primary alcohol), which is oxidised to **propanal** (an aldehyde), not propanone.

**B** is incorrect as CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>I is a **primary** halogenoalkane, also giving propanal on oxidation rather than propanone. Additionally, silver iodide gives a **yellow** precipitate with silver nitrate, not a cream precipitate.

**D** is incorrect as CH<sub>3</sub>CHICH<sub>3</sub> is a secondary halogenoalkane and would give propan-2-ol and thus propanone on oxidation. However, silver iodide gives a **yellow** precipitate with silver nitrate, not a cream precipitate.

parts.problemMd:
Antipyrine is a drug used to reduce fever. The initial step of its synthesis is the reaction of phenylhydrazine with compound **X**.

![Reaction equation showing phenylhydrazine (C₆H₅-NHNH₂) reacting with compound X (ethyl acetoacetate: CH₃COCH₂CO₂CH₂CH₃, containing both a ketone and an ester group) to give product Y](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/21-organic-synthesis/21-1-organic-synthesis/assets/011-reaction-equation-showing-phenylhydrazine-c-h-nh.png)

Which of the following is product **Y**?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- Phenylhydrazine contains a terminal **hydrazine group** (-NHNH₂) which undergoes a **nucleophilic addition-elimination (condensation)** reaction with the **ketone group** (C=O) of compound **X**.

  - The ketone carbonyl carbon is electrophilic due to the electronegativity of the oxygen.
  - The nitrogen lone pair of the terminal NH<sub>2</sub> attacks this carbon.
- After proton transfers, a water molecule is eliminated to form a **C=N** (hydrazone) linkage, giving the phenylhydrazone product.
- The **ester group** in compound **X** is not attacked and is preserved in product **Y**.

![Mechanism of condensation reaction between phenylhydrazine and compound X: the terminal NH₂ nitrogen lone pair attacks the electrophilic ketone carbonyl carbon of compound X (ethyl acetoacetate); after proton transfers, H₂O is eliminated to give the phenylhydrazone product with a C=N-NHPh linkage](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/21-organic-synthesis/21-1-organic-synthesis/assets/012-mechanism-of-condensation-reaction-between-pheny.jpg)

**A** is incorrect as the ester group of compound **X** has been replaced by an amide linkage (-CONH-Ph), suggesting reaction at the ester rather than the ketone. In the condensation, phenylhydrazine reacts selectively with the more electrophilic ketone C=O; the ester group is preserved in the product.

**B** is incorrect as both the ketone group of compound **X** and the N–N bond of phenylhydrazine appear to have been lost. In the actual condensation, only the ketone oxygen is lost as water. The N–N bond is retained in the C=N–NHPh linkage of the phenylhydrazone.

**C** is incorrect as the NHNH<sub>2</sub> group remains unreacted and the acyl group has been transferred directly to the phenyl ring, which does not occur under these conditions. In the condensation, the terminal NH<sub>2</sub> attacks the ketone to form a hydrazone C=N linkage with elimination of water.

parts.problemMd:
Ibuprofen is an anti-inflammatory drug, the structure of which is shown below.

![Skeletal formula of ibuprofen: a para-substituted benzene ring with an isobutyl group at one position and a methylcarboxylic acid group (-CH(CH₃)CO₂H) at the para position](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/21-organic-synthesis/21-1-organic-synthesis/assets/001-skeletal-formula-of-ibuprofen-a-para-substituted.png)

Which reaction leads to the formation of ibuprofen?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- Warm acidified potassium dichromate (VI) **oxidises** aldehydes to **carboxylic acids**.
- The aldehyde group (-CHO) in the precursor shown in **A** is oxidised to give the carboxylic acid (-CO<sub>2</sub>H) group of ibuprofen.

![Oxidation of aldehyde precursor: (CH₃)₂CHCH₂-C₆H₄-CH(CH₃)CHO reacts with warm acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ (oxidising agent) to oxidise the CHO group to CO₂H, giving ibuprofen](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/21-organic-synthesis/21-1-organic-synthesis/assets/002-oxidation-of-aldehyde-precursor-ch-chch-c-h-ch-c.jpg)

**B** is incorrect as hot, concentrated KMnO<sub>4</sub> causes **oxidative cleavage** of the C=C double bond. The =CH<sub>2</sub> end is oxidised to CO<sub>2</sub> and the ring-attached carbon becomes a ketone, giving a methyl ketone and CO<sub>2</sub>.

**C** is incorrect as warm H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (aq) cannot oxidise a **ketone** to a carboxylic acid. Ketones are resistant to mild oxidation, and H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> is not an oxidising agent under these conditions.

**D** is incorrect as H<sub>2</sub>/Pt catalyst causes **hydrogenation**, reducing the C=C double bonds to C–C single bonds. This does not introduce a carboxylic acid group, so ibuprofen is not formed.

parts.problemMd: Which of the following statements about propanal, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CHO, and propanone, CH<sub>3</sub>COCH<sub>3</sub>, is **not** correct?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- The molecular ion peak (M<sup>+</sup>) is the peak with the highest *m/e* ratio, excluding any peaks due to heavier isotopes.

- Both propanal and propanone have the molecular formula C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>6</sub>O and so both have a molecular ion peak at *m/e* = 58.

- Propanal arises from the CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CHO<sup>+</sup> ion.
- Propanone arises from the CH<sub>3</sub>COCH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup> ion.

- Propanal mass spectrum.

![Mass spectrum of propanal (CH3CH2CHO) showing molecular ion peak at m/e = 58 and characteristic fragmentation pattern](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/22-analytical-techniques/22-1-infrared-spectroscopy/assets/002-mass-spectrum-of-propanal-ch3ch2cho-showing-mole.jpg)

- Propanone mass spectrum.

![Mass spectrum of propanone (CH3COCH3) showing molecular ion peak at m/e = 58 and characteristic fragmentation pattern](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/22-analytical-techniques/22-1-infrared-spectroscopy/assets/003-mass-spectrum-of-propanone-ch3coch3-showing-mole.jpg)

**A** is incorrect as propanal and propanone do have a different fingerprint region in the infrared spectrum.

**B** is incorrect as both compounds show absorption in the infrared spectrum due to the C=O bond.

**C** is incorrect as propanal and propanone do have different fragmentation patterns in the mass spectrum.

choices.textMd: The identity of a compound through comparison with other spectra

parts.problemMd: Which of the following **cannot** be obtained from an infrared spectrum?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- Infrared spectroscopy measures the absorption of infrared radiation by molecules, which is used to identify functional groups based on the bond strength and mass of the atoms involved.
- It is not used to determine the molecular mass.

  - A mass spectrometer is used for this.

**A** is incorrect as the identity of a compound can be determined by comparing its infrared spectrum with reference spectra.

**C** is incorrect as the presence of C=O bonds can be detected from the infrared spectrum.

**D** is incorrect as the presence of O-H bonds can be detected from the infrared spectrum.

parts.problemMd:
Which type of organic compound could have produced the infrared spectrum shown?

![IR spectrum showing a broad absorption from 2500 to 3000 cm-1 and a strong absorption at approximately 1700 cm-1](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/22-analytical-techniques/22-1-infrared-spectroscopy/assets/010-ir-spectrum-showing-a-broad-absorption-from-2500.png)
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- A carboxylic acid shows two key absorptions in the infrared spectrum:
- The C=O bond absorbs at 1670–1740 cm<sup>-1</sup>.
- The O-H bond in carboxylic acids produces a broad absorption at 2500–3000 cm<sup>-1</sup>.

**A** is incorrect as an alcohol would only show an O-H absorption at 3200–3600 cm<sup>-1</sup> and not the broad O-H absorption at 2500–3000 cm<sup>-1</sup> characteristic of a carboxylic acid.

**B** is incorrect as an aldehyde would only show a C=O absorption at 1670–1740 cm<sup>-1</sup> and not the broad O-H absorption at 2500–3000 cm<sup>-1</sup>.

**D** is incorrect as a ketone would only show a C=O absorption at 1670–1740 cm<sup>-1</sup> and not the broad O-H absorption at 2500–3000 cm<sup>-1</sup>.

parts.problemMd:
The infrared spectrum of a compound is shown below.

![IR spectrum showing a strong absorption at approximately 1700 cm-1 with no O-H absorption](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/22-analytical-techniques/22-1-infrared-spectroscopy/assets/011-ir-spectrum-showing-a-strong-absorption-at-appro.jpg)

Which compound is shown by the infrared spectrum?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- The infrared spectrum has a strong absorption at approximately 1700 cm<sup>-1</sup>.
- This matches the C=O absorption of propanone in the range 1670–1740 cm<sup>-1</sup>.
- Propanone contains a ketone C=O group, consistent with this absorption.

![Skeletal formula of propanone (CH3COCH3)](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/22-analytical-techniques/22-1-infrared-spectroscopy/assets/012-skeletal-formula-of-propanone-ch3coch3.jpg)

**A** is incorrect as propan-1-ol would not show an absorption at approximately 1700 cm<sup>-1</sup> but would show an O-H absorption at 3200–3600 cm<sup>-1</sup> due to the hydroxyl group.

![Skeletal formula of propan-1-ol](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/22-analytical-techniques/22-1-infrared-spectroscopy/assets/013-skeletal-formula-of-propan-1-ol.jpg)

**B** is incorrect as propan-2-ol would not show an absorption at approximately 1700 cm<sup>-1</sup> but would show an O-H absorption at 3200–3600 cm<sup>-1</sup> due to the hydroxyl group.

![Skeletal formula of propan-2-ol](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/22-analytical-techniques/22-1-infrared-spectroscopy/assets/014-skeletal-formula-of-propan-2-ol.jpg)

**C** is incorrect as propanal would show a C=O absorption at approximately 1700 cm<sup>-1</sup>, but also shows characteristic aldehyde C-H absorptions at 2700–2775 cm<sup>-1</sup> and 2820–2900 cm<sup>-1</sup>, which are absent in this spectrum.

![Skeletal formula of propanal (CH3CH2CHO)](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/22-analytical-techniques/22-1-infrared-spectroscopy/assets/015-skeletal-formula-of-propanal-ch3ch2cho.jpg)

parts.problemMd:
The infrared spectrum of a compound is shown below.

![IR spectrum showing a strong absorption at approximately 1720 cm-1 with no O-H absorption](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/22-analytical-techniques/22-1-infrared-spectroscopy/assets/009-ir-spectrum-showing-a-strong-absorption-at-appro.png)

Which compound is shown by the infrared spectrum?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- Butanal contains a C=O (carbonyl) group, which gives the characteristic absorption between 1670 and 1740 cm<sup>-1</sup>.

**A** is incorrect as there is no absorption at 1500–1680 cm<sup>-1</sup> due to C=C, therefore the compound cannot be but-1-ene.

**B** is incorrect as there is no absorption at 3200–3600 cm<sup>-1</sup> due to O-H (alcohol), therefore the compound cannot be butan-1-ol.

**D** is incorrect as there is no absorption at 2500–3000 cm<sup>-1</sup> due to O-H (acid), therefore the compound cannot be butanoic acid.

parts.problemMd: Which class of compound does **not** contain the functional group responsible for the strong absorption between 1670 cm<sup>-1</sup> and 1740 cm<sup>-1</sup>?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- The absorption between 1670 and 1740 cm<sup>-1</sup> is characteristic of the C=O (carbonyl) bond, found in aldehydes, ketones, and carboxylic acids.
- Alcohols do not contain a C=O bond; the characteristic absorption of an alcohol is the O-H bond at 3200–3550 cm<sup>-1</sup>.

**B** is incorrect as aldehydes contain a C=O bond, which produces the characteristic absorption between 1670 and 1740 cm<sup>-1</sup>.

**C** is incorrect as carboxylic acids contain a C=O bond as part of the carboxyl group, which absorbs between 1670 and 1740 cm<sup>-1</sup>.

**D** is incorrect as ketones contain a C=O bond, which produces the characteristic absorption between 1670 and 1740 cm<sup>-1</sup>.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The three key infrared absorptions to learn for CIE IAL Chemistry are:
> 
> - O-H (alcohol): 3230–3550 cm<sup>-1</sup>.
> - C=O (aldehyde, ketone, carboxylic acid): 1670–1740 cm<sup>-1</sup>.
> - O-H (carboxylic acid, broad): 2500–3000 cm<sup>-1</sup>.

parts.problemMd:
The infrared spectrum below shows an unknown compound.

![IR spectrum showing a sharp O-H absorption at 3200 to 3600 cm-1 and a strong C=O absorption at approximately 1700 to 1740 cm-1, with complex fingerprint region absorptions](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/22-analytical-techniques/22-1-infrared-spectroscopy/assets/001-ir-spectrum-showing-a-sharp-o-h-absorption-at-32.jpg)

Which compound could have produced the infrared spectrum?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- The spectrum shows an absorption at 3200–3600 cm<sup>-1</sup>, characteristic of the O-H bond in an alcohol.
- The spectrum also shows an absorption at approximately 1700–1740 cm<sup>-1</sup>, characteristic of a C=O (carbonyl) bond in a ketone or aldehyde.
- The compound contains both an alcohol O-H and a ketone C=O; the O-H of a carboxylic acid absorbs at 2500–3000 cm<sup>-1</sup>, which is not observed here.

**A** is incorrect as butanoic acid is a carboxylic acid whose O-H absorption appears at 2500–3000 cm<sup>-1</sup>, not at 3200–3600 cm<sup>-1</sup> as shown in the spectrum.

**C** is incorrect as pent-4-en-1-ol contains a C=C bond that would produce a characteristic absorption at 1500–1680 cm<sup>-1</sup>, which is absent in this spectrum.

**D** is incorrect as pent-4-en-2-one does not contain an O-H bond, but the spectrum shows an O-H absorption at 3200–3600 cm<sup>-1</sup>.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Note the position of the O-H absorption carefully:
> 
> - In alcohols it appears at 3200–3600 cm<sup>-1</sup>
> - In carboxylic acids it is a broader absorption at 2500–3000 cm<sup>-1</sup>.
> 
> A common error is to label the C-H absorption (2850–2950 cm<sup>-1</sup>) as O-H.

parts.problemMd:
The infrared spectrum below shows an unknown compound.

![IR spectrum showing C-H absorptions at 2700 to 2950 cm-1 including a characteristic aldehyde C-H doublet, and a strong C=O absorption at approximately 1720 cm-1 with no O-H absorption](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/22-analytical-techniques/22-1-infrared-spectroscopy/assets/004-ir-spectrum-showing-c-h-absorptions-at-2700-to-2.jpg)

Which compound would give this spectrum?

- C-H absorptions are visible at 2850–2950 cm<sup>-1</sup> (alkyl C-H) and at approximately 2700–2820 cm<sup>-1</sup> (the characteristic aldehyde C-H doublet).
- Butanal is an aldehyde and contains a C=O group consistent with the spectrum.

![Skeletal formula of butanal](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/22-analytical-techniques/22-1-infrared-spectroscopy/assets/005-skeletal-formula-of-butanal.jpg)

**B** is incorrect as butan-1-ol would show a strong O-H absorption at 3200–3600 cm<sup>-1</sup> due to the hydroxyl group, with no C=O absorption at approximately 1700 cm<sup>-1</sup>.

**D** is incorrect as butanoic acid would show a broad O-H absorption at 2500–3000 cm<sup>-1</sup> due to the carboxyl group, in addition to the C=O absorption.

![Skeletal formula of butanoic acid](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/22-analytical-techniques/22-1-infrared-spectroscopy/assets/008-skeletal-formula-of-butanoic-acid.jpg)

parts.problemMd: Which of the following infrared spectra could show a carboxylic acid?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- A carboxylic acid shows a broad O-H absorption from 2500 to 3000 cm<sup>-1</sup>, caused by hydrogen bonding of the carboxyl O-H group, in addition to a strong C=O absorption at approximately 1700 cm<sup>-1</sup>.

**B** is incorrect as this is the IR spectrum of an alcohol, identified by the sharp O-H absorption at 3200–3600 cm<sup>-1</sup> with no C=O absorption present.

**C** is incorrect as this is the IR spectrum of an ester, showing a strong C=O absorption between 1710 and 1750 cm<sup>-1</sup> with no O-H absorption.

**D** is incorrect as this is the IR spectrum of a ketone, identified by the strong C=O absorption at approximately 1710 cm<sup>-1</sup> with no O-H absorption.
