i) Calculate the lattice energy of lithium fluoride.

Show your working.

[2]

ii) Explain and justify how the lattice energy of LiBr compares with that of LiF.

You must refer to the size of the ions in your answer.

[3]
parts.solutionMd:
i) To calculate the lattice energy of LiF:

- Set up the Hess equation:

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>latt</sub>(LiF) = Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>f</sub>(LiF) – Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>at</sub>(Li) – IE<sub>1</sub>(Li) – ½D(F–F) – E<sub>ea</sub>(F)

- Substitute the values (note: ½ x 158 = 79 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>):

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>latt</sub>(LiF) = –594 – 216 – 520 – 79 + 348 **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the result:

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>latt</sub>(LiF) = **–1061 kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii) The lattice energy of LiBr compared to LiF:
> 
> - LiBr has a less negative / less exothermic lattice energy than LiF **[1 mark]**
> - Br<sup>-</sup> is larger than F<sup>-</sup>
> **OR**
> Br<sup>-</sup> has more electron shells than F<sup>-</sup> **[1 mark]**
> - Therefore the inter-ionic distance between Li<sup>+</sup> and Br<sup>-</sup> is greater, so the electrostatic attraction between them is weaker **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> When calculating lattice energy using a Born-Haber cycle, the easiest method is to rearrange the Hess equation so that lattice energy is the subject. Any enthalpy change going in the same direction as the lattice energy arrow is added; any going in the opposite direction is subtracted.
> 
> Remember to halve the F<sub>2</sub> bond dissociation energy, since only 1 mole of F atoms is needed to form LiF.
> 
> When comparing lattice energies, consider ionic charge and ionic radius. A larger ion means a greater inter-ionic distance, which reduces the electrostatic attraction between the ions and gives a less exothermic (less negative) lattice energy.

parts.problemMd:
This question is about enthalpy changes in solution.

i) Write the equation for the process showing the enthalpy of solution of potassium fluoride. Include state symbols in your answer.

[1]

ii) Use the data in Table 2.2 to calculate the standard enthalpy of solution of potassium fluoride.

Show your working.

[2]

**Table 2.2**

| **Name of enthalpy change in solution** | **Enthalpy change (kJ m**<sup>**-1**</sup>**)** |
|---|---|
| Enthalpy of lattice dissociation of potassium fluoride | +829 |
| Enthalpy of hydration of potassium ions | –340 |
| Enthalpy of hydration of fluoride ions | –504 |
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The equation for the enthalpy of solution of potassium fluoride:
> 
> - KF (s) → K<sup>+</sup>(aq) + F<sup>-</sup>(aq) **[1 mark]**
> 
> Allow H<sub>2</sub>O over the arrow or an equilibrium arrow.

ii) To calculate the standard enthalpy of solution of potassium fluoride:

- Apply the equation:

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>sol</sub> KF = Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>latt diss</sub> KF + Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>hyd</sub> K<sup>+</sup> + Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>hyd</sub> F<sup>-</sup>

- Substitute the values:

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>sol</sub> KF = 829 + (–340) + (–504) **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the result:

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>sol</sub> KF = **–15 kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> When writing equations for enthalpy of solution, you must include state symbols and charges on the ions.
> 
> Note the sign convention: lattice dissociation is endothermic (positive value), while lattice formation is exothermic (negative value). The values are equal in magnitude but opposite in sign. The table gives dissociation (+829), so use +829 directly.
> 
> A common error is using the wrong sign for the lattice enthalpy. Always check whether the table gives lattice formation or lattice dissociation.

parts.problemMd: Explain why the value for the enthalpy of hydration, Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>hyd</sub>, of Group 1 ions increases from lithium to caesium.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The enthalpy of hydration becomes less exothermic (increases in value) from Li<sup>+</sup> to Cs<sup>+</sup> because:
> 
> - Ionic radius increases down Group 1 (more electron shells) **[1 mark]**
> - Therefore the attraction between the ion and the δ<sup>-</sup> oxygen atoms in water molecules decreases, so less energy is released on hydration **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The enthalpy of hydration becomes less exothermic (less negative) going down Group 1. The approximate values are:
> 
> - Li<sup>+</sup>: –538 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>
> - Na<sup>+</sup>: –424 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>
> - K<sup>+</sup>: –340 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>
> - Rb<sup>+</sup>: –315 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>
> - Cs<sup>+</sup>: –291 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>
> 
> A smaller ion has a higher charge density, so it attracts the δ<sup>-</sup> oxygen of water molecules more strongly, releasing more energy on hydration. A larger ion has a lower charge density, so less energy is released.

parts.problemMd:
Calcium chloride, CaCl<sub>2</sub>, is an important industrial chemical used in refrigeration plants, for de-icing roads and for giving greater strength to concrete.

Construct an equation to show what is meant by the lattice energy of calcium chloride.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The lattice energy of calcium chloride is shown by the equation:
> 
> - Ca<sup>2+</sup> (g) + 2Cl<sup>-</sup> (g) → CaCl<sub>2</sub> (s) **[1 mark]**
> 
> State symbols must be correct to score the mark.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Lattice energy is the enthalpy change when 1 mole of ionic compound is formed from its gaseous ions under standard conditions. The equation must show 1 mole of CaCl<sub>2</sub> being formed.
> 
> Don't forget to balance the chloride ions as 2 Cl<sup>-</sup> are needed for 1 Ca<sup>2+</sup>.

parts.problemMd:
Explain how the lattice energies of the following salts compare in magnitude with that of calcium chloride.

- calcium fluoride
- calcium sulfide
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The lattice energies of calcium fluoride and calcium sulfide compared to calcium chloride:
> 
> - Both have larger lattice energies (more exothermic) than CaCl<sub>2</sub>
> **OR**
> Both lattice energies are more negative than that of CaCl<sub>2</sub> **[1 mark]**
> - F<sup>-</sup> is smaller than Cl<sup>-</sup>, so the Ca<sup>2+</sup>–F<sup>-</sup> distance is shorter and the electrostatic attraction is stronger (for CaF<sub>2</sub>) **[1 mark]**
> - S<sup>2-</sup> has a higher charge than Cl<sup>-</sup>, so the electrostatic attraction between Ca<sup>2+</sup> and S<sup>2-</sup> is greater (for CaS) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Two factors affect the magnitude of lattice energy:
> 
> Charge on the ions:
> 
> - Higher charge
> - → stronger electrostatic attraction
> - → more exothermic lattice energy
> 
> Size of the ions:
> 
> - Smaller ion
> - → shorter inter-ionic distance
> - → stronger attraction
> - → more exothermic lattice energy
> 
> For CaF<sub>2</sub> vs CaCl<sub>2</sub>: same charge, but F<sup>-</sup> is smaller than Cl<sup>-</sup>, so the Ca<sup>2+</sup>–F<sup>-</sup> distance is shorter and the lattice energy is more exothermic.
> 
> For CaS vs CaCl<sub>2</sub>: S<sup>2-</sup> has a 2- charge compared to 1- for Cl<sup>-</sup>, giving stronger electrostatic attraction and a more exothermic lattice energy.

parts.problemMd:
Use the data in Table 3.1 to calculate the lattice energy of CaCl<sub>2</sub>.

Show your working.

**Table 3.1**

| **Enthalpy change** | **Value / kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup> |
|---|---|
| Standard enthalpy change of formation of CaCl<sub>2</sub> (s) | –796 |
| Standard enthalpy change of atomisation of Ca (s) | +178 |
| Electron affinity per mole of Cl atoms | –349 |
| First ionisation energy of Ca | +590 |
| Second ionisation energy of Ca | +1150 |
| Standard enthalpy change of atomisation of Cl<sub>2</sub> (g) | +244 |
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the lattice energy of CaCl<sub>2</sub>:

- Identify the relevant values and apply correct multipliers (2 Cl atoms required, so 2 × E<sub>ea</sub>(Cl)):

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>at</sub>(Ca) = +178; IE<sub>1</sub>(Ca) = +590; IE<sub>2</sub>(Ca) = +1150; Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>at</sub>(Cl<sub>2</sub>) = +244; 2 x E<sub>ea</sub>(Cl) = 2 x (–349) = –698 **[1 mark]**

- Apply Hess's Law:

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>latt</sub>(CaCl<sub>2</sub>) = –796 – 178 – 590 – 1150 – 244 – (–698) **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the result:

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>latt</sub>(CaCl<sub>2</sub>) = **–2260 kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> To calculate lattice energy, rearrange the Hess equation: Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>latt</sub> = Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>f</sub> minus all other enthalpy changes in the cycle.
> 
> Be careful with the sign of the electron affinity. The electron affinity of Cl is –349 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> (exothermic). When you subtract E<sub>ea</sub> from the rearranged Hess equation, you get: –(–349) = +349 per mole of Cl. For 2 moles of Cl, this contributes +698 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>.
> 
> Lattice energy is always exothermic (negative), as forming ionic bonds releases energy. If your answer is positive, check the signs in your calculation.

parts.problemMd:
When a solution of CaCl<sub>2</sub> is added to a solution of the dicarboxylic acid, malonic acid, the salt calcium malonate is precipitated as a white solid.

The solid has the following composition by mass: Ca, 28.2%; C, 25.2%; H, 1.4%; O, 45.2%.

i) Calculate the empirical formula of calcium malonate.

[2]

ii) Suggest the structural formula of malonic acid.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
i) To find the empirical formula, divide each percentage by the relative atomic mass:

Ca: $\frac{28.2}{40.1}$ = 0.703

C: $\frac{25.2}{12.0}$ = 2.100

H: $\frac{1.4}{1.0}$ = 1.400

O: $\frac{45.2}{16.0}$ = 2.825

**[1 mark]**

- Divide all values by the smallest (0.703):

Ca : C : H : O = 1 : 2.99 : 1.99 : 4.02

Ca : C : H : O ≈ 1 : 3 : 2 : 4

- Empirical formula:

CaC<sub>3</sub>H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii) The structural formula of malonic acid:
> 
> - CH<sub>2</sub>(COOH)<sub>2</sub> / HOOC–CH<sub>2</sub>–COOH **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> To find an empirical formula: divide the percentage of each element by its relative atomic mass to get moles, then divide all values by the smallest to find the whole-number ratio.
> 
> For part ii): the empirical formula of the calcium salt (CaC<sub>3</sub>H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>) consists of Ca<sup>2+</sup> and the malonate ion C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub><sup>2-</sup>. Malonic acid is a dicarboxylic acid, so it contains two COOH groups, accounting for 2C and 4O. The remaining group is CH<sub>2</sub>. The malonate ion is CH<sub>2</sub>(COO)<sub>2</sub><sup>2-</sup>, so malonic acid is CH<sub>2</sub>(COOH)<sub>2</sub>.

parts.problemMd:
Magnesium reacts with fluorine to form magnesium fluoride.

Define the term first electron affinity.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The definition of first electron affinity:
> 
> - Enthalpy change when 1 mole of electrons is gained by 1 mole of gaseous atoms **[1 mark]**
> - To form 1 mole of gaseous ions with a single negative charge, under standard conditions **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Make sure you learn all the thermodynamic definitions for CIE IAL Chemistry. The exact wording matters for scoring marks on definition questions.

parts.problemMd:
i) Construct an equation for the second electron affinity of fluorine.

[1]

ii) Explain why the second electron affinity of fluorine is endothermic.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The equation for the second electron affinity of fluorine:
> 
> - F<sup>-</sup> (g) + e<sup>-</sup> → F<sup>2-</sup> (g) **[1 mark]**
> 
> State symbols must be included.
> 
> ii) The second electron affinity of fluorine is endothermic because:
> 
> - Energy is needed to overcome the repulsion between the incoming electron and the negatively charged F<sup>-</sup> ion **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The second electron affinity is the enthalpy change when 1 mole of electrons is added to 1 mole of gaseous 1– ions to form 1 mole of gaseous 2– ions under standard conditions. The equation must start with the fluoride ion F<sup>-</sup> (g), not the neutral atom.
> 
> The first electron affinity is always exothermic (energy is released when electrons are added to neutral atoms). The second electron affinity is always endothermic because the incoming electron must be forced onto an already-negative ion, requiring energy to overcome the repulsion.

parts.problemMd:
Calculate the electron affinity of a fluorine atom, Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>EA</sub>, using Table 5.1.

Show your working.

[3]

**Table 5.1**

| **Name of enthalpy change** | **Energy change (kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup>**)** |
|---|---|
| Enthalpy of atomisation of magnesium | +150 |
| First ionisation energy of magnesium | +738 |
| Second ionisation energy of magnesium | +1450 |
| Enthalpy of formation of magnesium fluoride | –642 |
| Enthalpy of atomisation of fluorine | +79.5 |
| Lattice energy of magnesium fluoride | –2493 |
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the electron affinity of fluorine:

- Apply Hess's Law and rearrange:

2 x E<sub>ea</sub>(F) = Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>f</sub>(MgF<sub>2</sub>) – Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>at</sub>(Mg) – IE<sub>1</sub>(Mg) – IE<sub>2</sub>(Mg) – 2Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>at</sub>(F) – Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>latt</sub>(MgF<sub>2</sub>) **[1 mark]**

- Substitute the values (note: 2 x Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>at</sub>(F) = 2 x 79.5 = 159 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>):

2 x E<sub>ea</sub>(F) = –642 – 150 – 738 – 1450 – 159 – (–2493) **[1 mark]**

2 x E<sub>ea</sub>(F) = –646

- Calculate the result:

E<sub>ea</sub>(F) = $\frac{-646}{2}$ = **–323 kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> To solve this type of calculation, sketch a simple Born-Haber cycle, then identify which enthalpy changes form the indirect route (all except the one being calculated). Apply Hess's Law to rearrange and solve.
> 
> Be careful to multiply the atomisation enthalpy of fluorine by 2 (since MgF<sub>2</sub> contains 2 moles of fluorine atoms), giving 2 x 79.5 = 159 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Define the term first electron affinity.

The definition of first electron affinity:
- Enthalpy change when 1 mole of electrons is gained by 1 mole of gaseous atoms
- To form 1 mole of gaseous ions with a single negative charge, under standard conditions

Explain why the first electron affinity of chlorine is less exothermic than that of fluorine.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The first electron affinity of chlorine is less exothermic than that of fluorine because:
> 
> - Cl has more electron shells than F, so the outer shell electrons are further from the nucleus **[1 mark]**
> - There is greater shielding by inner electron shells in Cl than in F **[1 mark]**
> - Therefore the attraction between the incoming electron and the nucleus is weaker in Cl, so less energy is released **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The three factors that affect electron affinity are the same as those for ionisation energy: nuclear charge, atomic radius, and shielding by inner electrons.
> 
> For comparisons within the same group (e.g. F vs Cl): nuclear charge increases but so does shielding and atomic radius. The increase in atomic radius and shielding outweighs the increased nuclear charge, so the electron affinity becomes less exothermic going down the group.
> 
> You should be able to explain trends in electron affinity both across a period and down Groups 16 and 17.

parts.problemMd: Define the term lattice energy.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The definition of lattice energy:
> 
> - The energy change (or enthalpy change) when one mole of an ionic compound is formed **[1 mark]**
> - From its constituent gaseous ions, under standard conditions **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Learn all thermodynamic definitions for CIE IAL Chemistry. Lattice energy is always exothermic (negative), as forming ionic bonds from gaseous ions releases energy.

parts.problemMd: Construct an equation, including state symbols, to represent the first electron affinity of chlorine.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The equation for the first electron affinity of chlorine is:
> 
> - Cl (g) + e<sup>-</sup> → Cl<sup>-</sup> (g) **[1 mark]**
> 
> State symbols must be included for the mark.

> **[exam-tip]**
> ½Cl<sub>2</sub> (g) + e<sup>-</sup> → Cl<sup>-</sup> (g) is not an acceptable answer because this represents both the enthalpy of atomisation and the electron affinity, not just the electron affinity.

parts.problemMd:
Some energy changes are shown in Table 1.1.

**Table 1.1**

| **Energy change** | **Value / kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup> |
|---|---|
| Standard enthalpy change of formation of MgCl<sub>2</sub> (s) | –641 |
| Standard enthalpy change of atomisation of magnesium | +148 |
| First ionisation energy of magnesium | +738 |
| Second ionisation energy of magnesium | +1450 |
| Standard enthalpy change of atomisation of chlorine | +121 |
| Lattice energy, Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>latt</sub>, of magnesium chloride, MgCl<sub>2</sub> (s) | –2526 |

Calculate the first electron affinity of chlorine. Use relevant data from Table 1.1 in your working.

Show your working.

It may be helpful to draw a labelled energy cycle.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the first electron affinity of chlorine:

![Born-Haber cycle for MgCl2 showing enthalpy changes with values in kJ mol^-1^](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/23-chemical-energetics/23-1-lattice-energy-and-born-haber-cycles/assets/001-born-haber-cycle-for-mgcl2-showing-enthalpy-chan.png)

- Use the Born-Haber relationship:

Δ*H*<sub>f</sub> = Δ*H*<sub>at</sub>(Mg) + IE<sub>1</sub>(Mg) + IE<sub>2</sub>(Mg) + 2Δ*H*<sub>at</sub>(Cl) + 2(EA<sub>Cl</sub>) + Δ*H*<sub>latt</sub>(MgCl<sub>2</sub>)

–641 = 148 + 738 + 1450 + 2(121) + 2(EA<sub>Cl</sub>) + (–2526) **[1 mark]**

- Simplify:

–641 = 52 + 2(EA<sub>Cl</sub>) **[1 mark]**

2(EA<sub>Cl</sub>) = –693 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>

- Calculate the result:

EA<sub>Cl</sub> = **–346.5 kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct Born-Haber equation with correct substitution
> **OR**
> 1 mark for a correctly drawn and labelled Born-Haber cycle
> 
> 1 mark for correct simplification: –641 = 52 + 2(EA<sub>Cl</sub>)
> **OR**
> 2(EA<sub>Cl</sub>) = –693 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for EA<sub>Cl</sub> = –346.5 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>

> **[exam-tip]**
> When calculating using a Born-Haber cycle, always check:
> 
> - Correct values from the data table
> - Lattice energy is negative (energy released on forming the solid)
> - Correct multipliers for the formula (MgCl<sub>2</sub> contains 2 Cl, so use 2 x EA<sub>Cl</sub> and 2 x Δ*H*<sub>at</sub>(Cl))
> 
> A very common error is forgetting the stoichiometry of the chlorine. Since the formula is MgCl<sub>2</sub>, two chloride ions are formed. Therefore both the enthalpy of atomisation of chlorine and the electron affinity must be multiplied by 2.

parts.problemMd: Explain, in terms of ionic radius, charge density and polarisation, why the thermal stability of Group 2 carbonates increases down the group.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The thermal stability of Group 2 carbonates increases down the group because:
> 
> - The ionic radius of the Group 2 cation (M<sup>2+</sup>) increases down the group **[1 mark]**
> - The charge density of M<sup>2+</sup> decreases as a result **[1 mark]**
> - There is less polarisation / less distortion of the CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2-</sup> ion by the cation **[1 mark]**
> - The C–O bonds are weakened less, so a higher temperature is needed to decompose the carbonate **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Students often lose marks on questions like this by mixing up cause and effect.
> 
> Make sure you clearly connect the chain:
> 
> - larger cation
> - → lower charge density
> - → less polarisation of CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2-</sup>
> - → C–O bonds less weakened
> - → harder to decompose
> - → greater thermal stability.
> 
> When explaining polarisation, focus on the carbonate anion and use the word "polarisation" or "distortion" explicitly. Restating that thermal stability increases does not explain the underlying reason.

parts.problemMd: Predict and explain the sign of the standard entropy change, Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>, for the decomposition of MgCO<sub>3</sub> (s).
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The sign of Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> for the decomposition of MgCO<sub>3</sub> (s) is:
> 
> - Positive
> **OR**
> Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> > 0 **[1 mark]**
> - A gas (CO<sub>2</sub>) is produced from solid reactants, increasing the number of gaseous particles and therefore increasing disorder/entropy **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> When explaining entropy changes, focus on what happens to the particles, not just the states of matter involved.
> 
> Many students lose marks by writing vague statements such as "a solid turns into a gas" without explaining that a gas is produced from solids, which increases disorder.
> 
> In entropy questions, always check whether the number of gaseous particles increases, as this is usually the dominant factor affecting Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>.

parts.problemMd:
Potassium sulfide is a reagent used in analytical chemistry and pharmaceutical preparations.

Draw a fully labelled Born-Haber cycle for the formation of potassium sulfide from its elements.

Include state symbols for all species involved.
parts.solutionMd:
The complete Born-Haber cycle for the formation of potassium sulfide is:

![Born-Haber cycle for the formation of potassium sulfide (K2S), showing enthalpy changes for formation, atomisation of sulfur and potassium, first and second ionisation energies of potassium, first and second electron affinities of sulfur, and lattice energy, with all species and state symbols labelled](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/23-chemical-energetics/23-1-lattice-energy-and-born-haber-cycles/assets/008-born-haber-cycle-for-the-formation-of-potassium-.jpeg)

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for enthalpy of formation (Δ*H*<sub>f</sub>) correctly labelled with 2K (s) + S (s) as starting species and K<sub>2</sub>S (s) as product
> 
> 1 mark for atomisation of sulfur (Δ*H*<sub>at</sub>(S)) and atomisation of potassium (2Δ*H*<sub>at</sub>(K)) both correctly labelled with correct species and state symbols
> 
> 1 mark for double first ionisation energy (2Δ*H*<sub>ie</sub>(K)) correctly labelled, giving 2K<sup>+</sup> (g) + S (g) + 2e<sup>-</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for first electron affinity (E<sub>ea1</sub>(S)), second electron affinity (E<sub>ea2</sub>(S)), and lattice energy (Δ*H*<sub>latt</sub>) all correctly labelled

> **[exam-tip]**
> You must be able to draw Born-Haber cycles from scratch.
> 
> Harder questions often include elements that form ions with a 2+ or 2– charge, so ensure your cycle reflects this with two ionisation energy steps and two electron affinity steps.
> 
> Arrows pointing upwards represent an endothermic process; arrows pointing downwards represent an exothermic process.

parts.problemMd:
Use the data in Table 1.1 to calculate the lattice energy of potassium sulfide, Δ*H*θ*latt*. Show your working. **Table 1.1** | **Enthalpy change** | **Enthalpy change**
**/ kJ mol**-1 | |---|---| | Formation of potassium sulfide | -381 | | 1st electron affinity of sulfur | -200 | | 2nd electron affinity of sulfur | +640 | | Atomisation of sulfur | +279 | | 1st ionisation energy of potassium | +419 | | Atomisation of potassium | +89 |
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the lattice energy of potassium sulfide:

- Write the Born-Haber equation relating lattice energy to the other enthalpy changes:

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>f</sub> = Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>at</sub>(S) + 2Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>at</sub>(K) + 2Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>ie</sub>(K) + E<sub>ea1</sub>(S) + E<sub>ea2</sub>(S) + Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>latt</sub> **[1 mark]**

- Rearrange and substitute values:

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>latt</sub> = –381 – (279 + 178 + 838 – 200 + 640) **[1 mark]**

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>latt</sub> = **–2116 kJ mol**<sup>**–1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The Born-Haber equation can be simplified to Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>f</sub> = Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>1</sub> + Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>latt</sub>, where Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>1</sub> includes all the steps that convert elements from their standard state into gaseous ions (atomisation, ionisation, and electron affinities).
> 
> Rearranging gives Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>latt</sub> = Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>f</sub> – Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>1</sub>, after which the values can be substituted in.
> 
> Remember to multiply the atomisation enthalpy and ionisation energy of potassium by 2, as two moles of potassium are needed to form one mole of K<sub>2</sub>S.
> 
> You can also use the Born-Haber cycle by starting at the lattice energy arrow and travelling around the cycle in the other direction, changing the sign of any step that points opposite to your direction of travel.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Table 1.1

| Enthalpy change | Enthalpy change / kJ mol^-1^ |
| :---: | :---: |
| Formation of potassium sulfide | -381 |
| 1st electron affinity of sulfur | -200 |
| 2nd electron affinity of sulfur | +640 |
| Atomisation of sulfur | +279 |
| 1st ionisation energy of potassium | +419 |
| Atomisation of potassium | +89 |

Explain the difference in values between the first and second electron affinities of sulfur.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explanation of the difference between the first and second electron affinities of sulfur:
> 
> - (The value for) the first electron affinity is exothermic
> **AND**
> the second electron affinity is endothermic **[1 mark]**
> - (Energy is required because of) repulsion between the negative ion S<sup>-</sup> (g) and the incoming negative electron **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The first electron affinity is the enthalpy change when one mole of gaseous atoms gains one electron to form gaseous ions with a single negative charge.
> 
> The second electron affinity is the enthalpy change when one mole of gaseous ions with a single negative charge gains one electron to form gaseous ions with a double negative charge.
> 
> The second electron affinity is always endothermic because energy is needed to overcome electrostatic repulsion between the negative ion and the incoming electron.
> 
> Exam questions frequently ask about the second electron affinity of oxygen or sulfur, so make sure you can explain the sign difference.

parts.problemMd:
Magnesium oxide is often used in optical applications due to its light-reflecting properties in crystal form.

Write an equation to represent the lattice energy of MgO.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> An equation to represent the lattice energy of MgO is:
> 
> - Mg<sup>2+</sup> (g) + O<sup>2-</sup> (g) → MgO (s) **[1 mark]**
> 
> State symbols and ionic charges are required

> **[exam-tip]**
> Lattice energy is the enthalpy change when one mole of an ionic compound is formed from its gaseous ions under standard conditions.
> 
> For magnesium oxide, the equation is Mg<sup>2+</sup> (g) + O<sup>2-</sup> (g) → MgO (s). Both state symbols and the correct ionic charges (2+ and 2–) must be shown.

parts.problemMd:
Use the data in Table 2.1 to calculate a value for the second ionisation energy of magnesium, Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>ie2</sub>. Show your working.

**Table 2.1**

| **Enthalpy change** | **Enthalpy change / kJ mol**<sup>-1</sup> |
|---|---|
| Lattice energy of MgO (s) | – 3791 |
| Enthalpy change of atomisation of Mg | + 148 |
| Enthalpy of atomisation of oxygen | + 248 |
| Electron affinity of the oxygen atom | – 141 |
| Electron affinity of the oxygen anion, O<sup>-</sup> | + 798 |
| First ionisation energy of Mg | + 736 |
| Enthalpy of formation of MgO | – 552 |
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the second ionisation energy of magnesium:

- Write the Born-Haber equation relating all enthalpy changes:

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>f</sub> = Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>at</sub>(Mg) + Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>ie1</sub>(Mg) + Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>ie2</sub>(Mg) + Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>at</sub>(O) + E<sub>ea1</sub>(O) + E<sub>ea2</sub>(O) + Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>latt</sub>(MgO) **[1 mark]**

- Rearrange and substitute values:

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>ie2</sub>(Mg) = –552 – 148 – 736 – 248 + 141 – 798 + 3791 **[1 mark]**

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>ie2</sub>(Mg) = **+1450 kJ mol**<sup>**–1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Rearrange the Born-Haber equation to make Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>ie2</sub>(Mg) the subject before substituting values. When a term moves to the other side of the equation, its sign changes.
> 
> The second ionisation energy must always be positive (endothermic), as energy is always required to remove an electron from an already positively charged ion.
> 
> Show your working clearly — if you make an arithmetic error you can still gain marks for a correct method.

parts.problemMd: Magnesium oxide is generally insoluble in water whereas calcium oxide is sparingly soluble. Explain why there is no enthalpy of solution data for calcium oxide.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> There is no enthalpy of solution data for calcium oxide because:
> 
> - Calcium oxide reacts with water to produce OH<sup>-</sup> ions in solution **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The reaction of calcium oxide with water is:
> 
> CaO (s) + H<sub>2</sub>O (l) → Ca(OH)<sub>2</sub> (aq)
> 
> This is a chemical reaction rather than a simple dissolution into ions, so the enthalpy of solution definition does not apply. The enthalpy of solution is the enthalpy change when one mole of an ionic compound dissolves in excess water to give its constituent ions at infinite dilution.

parts.problemMd:
The incomplete Born-Haber cycle for sodium selenide is shown below in Fig. 3.1.

Write the equations for processes 1, 2 and 3.

![Incomplete Born-Haber cycle diagram for sodium selenide (Na2Se), with three energy levels labelled as processes 1, 2, and 3, showing species at each stage with some equations left blank for completion](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/23-chemical-energetics/23-1-lattice-energy-and-born-haber-cycles/assets/011-incomplete-born-haber-cycle-diagram-for-sodium-s.jpeg)

**Fig. 3.1**
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The equations for processes 1, 2 and 3 are:
> 
> - 1: 2Na (s) + Se (s) **[1 mark]**
> - 2: 2Na (g) + Se (g) **[1 mark]**
> - 3: 2Na<sup>+</sup> (g) + Se<sup>-</sup> (g) + e<sup>-</sup> **[1 mark]**
> 
> State symbols and, where applicable, ionic charges and electrons are required

> **[exam-tip]**
> When labelling species in a Born-Haber cycle, always include state symbols. For charged species, include the correct charge; for ionisation steps, show the electrons released.

parts.problemMd: If sulfur is used as opposed to selenium in the lattice, suggest the change in value of the lattice energy, Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>*latt*</sub>. Explain your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> If sulfur replaces selenium, the change in lattice energy and the reasoning are:
> 
> - Lattice energy would become more negative / more exothermic **[1 mark]**
> - The S<sup>2-</sup> ion is smaller than the Se<sup>2-</sup> ion
> **OR**
> The S<sup>2-</sup> ion has fewer electron shells than the Se<sup>2-</sup> ion **[1 mark]**
> - Therefore there is a stronger electrostatic attraction between Na<sup>+</sup> and S<sup>2-</sup> ions **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Lattice energy is the enthalpy change when one mole of an ionic lattice forms from its gaseous ions. It is always exothermic (negative) because energy is released as the lattice forms.
> 
> Smaller ions have shorter interionic distances, which increases electrostatic attraction and makes the lattice energy more negative.
> 
> Both the size argument (S<sup>2-</sup> is smaller than Se<sup>2-</sup>) and the electron shell argument (S<sup>2-</sup> has fewer electron shells) are accepted as equivalent explanations.

parts.problemMd:
Use the data in Table 3.1 to calculate the lattice energy of aluminium oxide, Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>*latt*</sub>. Show your working.

**Table 3.1**

| **Enthalpy Change** | **Enthalpy Change / kJ mol**<sup>-1</sup> |
|---|---|
| Atomisation of aluminium | +326 |
| Atomisation of oxygen | +249 |
| First ionisation energy of aluminium | +578 |
| Second ionisation energy of aluminium | +1817 |
| Third ionisation energy of aluminium | +2745 |
| Electron affinity of O atom | –141 |
| Electron affinity of O<sup>-</sup> | +753 |
| Formation of aluminium oxide | –1670 |
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the lattice energy of aluminium oxide:

- Write the Born-Haber equation relating all enthalpy changes:

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>f</sub>(Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>) = 2Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>at</sub>(Al) + 3Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>at</sub>(O) + 2Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>ie1</sub>(Al) + 2Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>ie2</sub>(Al) + 2Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>ie3</sub>(Al) + 3E<sub>ea1</sub>(O) + 3E<sub>ea2</sub>(O<sup>-</sup>) + Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>latt</sub>(Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>) **[1 mark]**

- Rearrange and substitute values, multiplying each term by the stoichiometric coefficient:

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>latt</sub> = –1670 – (2 x 326) – (3 x 249) – (2 x 578) – (2 x 1817) – (2 x 2745) – (3 x –141) – (3 x 753)

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>latt</sub> = –1670 – 652 – 747 – 1156 – 3634 – 5490 + 423 – 2259 **[1 mark]**

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>latt</sub>(Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>) = **–15 185 kJ mol**<sup>**–1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The formula of aluminium oxide is Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>, so values for aluminium must be multiplied by 2 and values for oxygen by 3. The enthalpy of formation is not multiplied as it already refers to one mole of Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>.
> 
> Take care with the sign of E<sub>ea1</sub>(O): its value is –141, so 3 x (–141) = –423, which becomes +423 when moved to the other side of the equation.
> 
> Show your working clearly because  if you make an arithmetic error you can still gain marks for a correct method.

parts.problemMd: Define the term standard enthalpy change of hydration, Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>*hyd*</sub>.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The standard enthalpy change of hydration is the enthalpy change when:
> 
> - One mole of gaseous ions **[1 mark]**
> - Dissolves in excess water to form an infinitely dilute solution **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> CIE requires both elements of this definition: the quantity and state of the ions (one mole, gaseous) and the process (dissolving in excess water to form an infinitely dilute solution). Writing only "dissolves in water" without specifying excess water or infinite dilution will not score the second mark.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The standard enthalpy change of hydration is the enthalpy change when one mole of gaseous ions dissolves in excess water to form an infinitely dilute solution.

i) Construct an equation to represent the Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>*hyd*</sub> of the Mg<sup>2+</sup> ion.

[1]

ii) Suggest why the Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>*hyd*</sub> of the Mg<sup>2+</sup> ion is more exothermic than that of the Ca<sup>2+</sup> ion.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) An equation representing the Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>hyd</sub> of the Mg<sup>2+</sup> ion:
> 
> - Mg<sup>2+</sup> (g) → Mg<sup>2+</sup> (aq)
> **OR**
> Mg<sup>2+</sup> (g) + 6H<sub>2</sub>O (l) → [Mg(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> (aq) **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>hyd</sub> of Mg<sup>2+</sup> is more exothermic than that of Ca<sup>2+</sup> because:
> 
> - Mg<sup>2+</sup> has a smaller ionic radius / higher charge density than Ca<sup>2+</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For part i, both the simple ionic equation (Mg<sup>2+</sup> (g) → Mg<sup>2+</sup> (aq)) and the full coordination equation showing water molecules score the mark.
> 
> For part ii, Mg<sup>2+</sup> and Ca<sup>2+</sup> carry the same charge, so the smaller Mg<sup>2+</sup> ion has a greater charge density, forming stronger ion-dipole attractions with water molecules and releasing more energy on hydration.

parts.problemMd:
The standard enthalpy change of solution for MgCl<sub>2</sub> is represented by the following equation.

MgCl<sub>2</sub> (s) + aq → Mg<sup>2+</sup> (aq) + 2Cl<sup>–</sup> (aq)

Describe the apparatus used and the measurements taken to determine a value for the standard enthalpy change of solution of MgCl<sub>2</sub> in the laboratory.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The apparatus and measurements needed to determine Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>sol</sub> for MgCl<sub>2</sub>:
> 
> - Measure a known volume / mass of water into a polystyrene cup / calorimeter **[1 mark]**
> - Record the initial temperature of the water **[1 mark]**
> - Weigh out a known mass of MgCl<sub>2</sub> **[1 mark]**
> - Record the final / maximum temperature reached
> **OR**
> Record the temperature change **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> CIE rewards four distinct steps: setting up a calorimeter with a known volume of water, recording the starting temperature, measuring the mass of MgCl<sub>2</sub> added, and recording the temperature change. Once you have these measurements, calculate the energy change using *q* = *mc*Δ*T*, then convert to kJ mol<sup>–1</sup> using the molar mass of MgCl<sub>2</sub> (95.3 g mol<sup>–1</sup>).

parts.problemMd:
Use the data in Table 4.1 to calculate the standard enthalpy change of solution of magnesium chloride. Show your working.

**Table 4.1**

| Enthalpy change | Enthalpy change / kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> |
|---|---|
| Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>latt</sub> MgCl<sub>2</sub> (s) | –2526 kJ mol<sup>–1</sup> |
| Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>hyd</sub> (Mg<sup>2+</sup> (g)) | –1890 kJ mol<sup>–1</sup> |
| Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>hyd</sub> (Cl<sup>–</sup> (g)) | –398 kJ mol<sup>–1</sup> |
parts.solutionMd:
The standard enthalpy change of solution of MgCl<sub>2</sub> is calculated using Hess's law.

- State the relationship between Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>sol</sub>, Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>latt</sub> and Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>hyd</sub>:

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>sol</sub> = Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>hyd</sub>(Mg<sup>2+</sup>) + 2 x Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>hyd</sub>(Cl<sup>–</sup>) − Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>latt</sub> **[1 mark]**

- Substitute the values from Table 4.1 and calculate:

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>sol</sub> = (−1890) + 2 x (−398) − (−2526) **[1 mark]**

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>sol</sub> = **−160 kJ mol**<sup>**–1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct relationship: Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>hyd</sub>(Mg<sup>2+</sup>) + 2 x Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>hyd</sub>(Cl<sup>–</sup>) − Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>latt</sub>
> 
> 1 mark for correct substitution
> 
> 1 mark for −160 kJ mol<sup>–1</sup>; allow ECF from incorrect substitution if method is correct

> **[exam-tip]**
> The relationship Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>sol</sub> = ΣΔ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>hyd</sub> − Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>latt</sub> follows from Hess's law. The lattice energy in the table is for formation (exothermic, negative), so subtracting it effectively adds its magnitude back. Remember to multiply Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>hyd</sub>(Cl<sup>–</sup>) by two, as two chloride ions are released when one mole of MgCl<sub>2</sub> dissolves.

parts.problemMd:
i) Define the term standard enthalpy change of hydration in relation to the fluoride ion.

[2]

ii) State whether the standard enthalpy change of hydration of the fluoride ion is an exothermic or endothermic process. Explain your answer.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The standard enthalpy change of hydration of the fluoride ion is the enthalpy change when:
> 
> - One mole of F<sup>–</sup> (g) / one mole of gaseous fluoride ions **[1 mark]**
> - Dissolves in excess water to form an infinitely dilute solution / forms F<sup>–</sup> (aq) **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The standard enthalpy change of hydration of the fluoride ion is:
> 
> - Exothermic **[1 mark]**
> - The F<sup>–</sup> ion attracts the δ<sup>+</sup> hydrogen atoms in water molecules / ion-dipole bonds form between F<sup>–</sup> and water molecules / energy is released as bonds form between the ion and water **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For part i, both the quantity (one mole) and state (gaseous) of the fluoride ion must be stated, along with the product (infinitely dilute aqueous solution). A definition that omits "gaseous" or "excess water / infinite dilution" will lose a mark.
> 
> For part ii, state "exothermic" first. This earns the first mark independently. The explanation should focus on the ion-dipole attraction between the negative fluoride ion and the δ<sup>+</sup> hydrogen atoms on water molecules. Forming these bonds releases energy, making the process exothermic.

parts.problemMd:
The standard enthalpy changes of hydration of the fluoride and chloride ions are −524 kJ mol<sup>–</sup> and −364 kJ mol<sup>–</sup> respectively.

Explain why the standard enthalpy change of hydration of the fluoride ion is more exothermic than that of the chloride ion.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The fluoride ion's enthalpy change of hydration is more exothermic because:
> 
> - The fluoride ion has a smaller ionic radius than the chloride ion **[1 mark]**
> - The ion-dipole attraction between the fluoride ion and water molecules is stronger / the fluoride ion attracts the δ<sup>+</sup> hydrogen atoms in water more strongly **[1 mark]**
> 
> Hydrogen bonding is not accepted as the basis for the explanation.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Both ions carry the same charge (1−), so the difference in hydration enthalpy is determined by ionic radius. A smaller ion concentrates the same charge in a smaller space (higher charge density), forming stronger ion-dipole attractions with the δ<sup>+</sup> hydrogen atoms on water molecules and releasing more energy on hydration.

parts.problemMd:
Use the data in Table 2.1 to explain why the standard enthalpy change of hydration of the calcium ion is more exothermic than that of the sodium ion.

**Table 2.1**

| **name of enthalpy change** | **enthalpy change / kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup> |
|---|---|
| Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>hyd</sub> Cl<sup>–</sup> | −364 |
| Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>hyd</sub> Na<sup>+</sup> | −406 |
| Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>hyd</sub> Ca<sup>2+</sup> | −1579 |
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Ca<sup>2+</sup> has a more exothermic enthalpy change of hydration than Na<sup>+</sup> because:
> 
> - Ca<sup>2+</sup> has a higher charge (+2) than Na<sup>+</sup> (+1) / Ca<sup>2+</sup> has a higher charge density than Na<sup>+</sup> **[1 mark]**
> - Ca<sup>2+</sup> forms stronger ion-dipole attractions with water molecules / attracts water molecules more strongly **[1 mark]**
> 
> "Higher size to charge ratio" is not accepted; the correct comparison is charge density (charge relative to ionic radius).

> **[exam-tip]**
> The ionic radii of Ca<sup>2+</sup> and Na<sup>+</sup> are very similar (approximately 100 pm and 102 pm respectively), so the difference in hydration enthalpy is primarily due to the charge. Ca<sup>2+</sup> carries twice the charge of Na<sup>+</sup>. Higher charge means a stronger attraction to the partial charges on surrounding water molecules, releasing more energy on hydration.

parts.problemMd: Describe, in terms of electron transfer, the formation of solid calcium bromide, CaBr<sub>2</sub>, from its atoms.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The formation of CaBr<sub>2</sub> in terms of electron transfer:
> 
> - One calcium atom loses two electrons **[1 mark]**
> - Two bromine atoms each gain one electron **[1 mark]**
> - Forming one Ca<sup>2+</sup>
> **AND**
> Two Br<sup>–</sup> ions **[1 mark]**
> 
> Answers referring to "bromine ions" instead of "bromide ions" are not accepted in the third mark point.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The formula CaBr<sub>2</sub> tells you the ratio: one Ca to two Br. Calcium is in Group 2 and loses both outer electrons to form Ca<sup>2+</sup>. Each bromine atom individually gains one electron to form Br<sup>–</sup>, giving two bromide ions in total. Use "bromide" (not "bromine") when referring to the Br<sup>–</sup> ion.

parts.problemMd:
Table 3.1 gives thermodynamic data for calcium bromide, CaBr<sub>2</sub>.

i) Define the term lattice energy.

[2]

**Table 3.1**

| **enthalpy change** | **enthalpy change / kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup> |
|---|---|
| Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>hyd</sub> Br<sup>–</sup> | –348 |
| lattice energy of CaBr<sub>2</sub> | −2176 |
| Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>sol</sub> CaBr<sub>2</sub> | −99 |

ii) Using Table 3.1, calculate the standard enthalpy change of hydration of the calcium ion. Show your working.

enthalpy change of hydration of Ca<sup>2+</sup> = ........................ kJ mol<sup>–1</sup>

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) Lattice energy is the enthalpy change when:
> 
> - One mole of an ionic compound / ionic lattice is formed **[1 mark]**
> - From its constituent gaseous ions **[1 mark]**

ii) The enthalpy change of hydration of Ca<sup>2+</sup> is calculated from the energy cycle.

![Hess's law energy cycle for CaBr~2~: lattice energy from Ca^2+^ (g) and 2Br^–^ (g), with enthalpy of solution and enthalpies of hydration of Ca^2+^ and Br^–^ shown](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/23-chemical-energetics/23-2-enthalpies-of-solution-and-hydration/assets/001-hess-s-law-energy-cycle-for-cabr-2-lattice-energ.png)

- State the relationship from the energy cycle:

lattice energy + Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>sol</sub>(CaBr<sub>2</sub>) = Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>hyd</sub>(Ca<sup>2+</sup>) + 2 x Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>hyd</sub>(Br<sup>–</sup>)

- Rearrange and substitute values from Table 3.1:

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>hyd</sub>(Ca<sup>2+</sup>) = (−2176) + (−99) − 2 x (−348) **[1 mark]**

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>hyd</sub>(Ca<sup>2+</sup>) = **−1579 kJ mol**<sup>**–1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Allow error carried forward from incorrect sign convention if the method is otherwise correct.

> **[exam-tip]**
> For part i, CIE uses "lattice energy" exclusively, always defined as the formation of the ionic lattice from gaseous ions (always exothermic, negative). This differs from other exam boards, which use separate terms for formation and dissociation.
> 
> For part ii, the overall equation (lattice energy + Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>sol</sub> = ΣΔ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>hyd</sub>) is not awarded a mark, but writing it out avoids sign errors. Multiply Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>hyd</sub>(Br<sup>–</sup>) by two, as two bromide ions dissolve per mole of CaBr<sub>2</sub>.

parts.problemMd:
Use the data in Table 3.2 to calculate the standard enthalpy change of solution of potassium fluoride. Show your working.

**Table 3.2**

| **enthalpy change** | **enthalpy change / kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup> |
|---|---|
| lattice energy of KF | −830 |
| Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>hyd</sub> K<sup>+</sup> | −351 |
| Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>hyd</sub> F<sup>–</sup> | −504 |
parts.solutionMd:
The standard enthalpy change of solution of KF is calculated using Hess's law.

![Hess's law energy cycle for KF: lattice energy from K^+^ (g) and F^–^ (g), with enthalpy of solution and enthalpies of hydration of K^+^ and F^–^ shown](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/23-chemical-energetics/23-2-enthalpies-of-solution-and-hydration/assets/002-hess-s-law-energy-cycle-for-kf-lattice-energy-fr.png)

- State the relationship from the energy cycle:

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>sol</sub> = ΣΔ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>hyd</sub> − lattice energy **[1 mark]**

- Substitute the values from Table 3.2 and calculate:

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>sol</sub> = [(−351) + (−504)] − (−830) **[1 mark]**

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>sol</sub>(KF) = **−25 kJ mol**<sup>**–1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct relationship: ΣΔ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>hyd</sub> − lattice energy **OR** correctly constructed energy cycle
> 
> 1 mark for correct substitution
> 
> 1 mark for −25 kJ mol<sup>–1</sup>
> 
> Allow error carried forward from incorrect substitution if method is correct

> **[exam-tip]**
> The energy cycle gives:
> 
> lattice energy + Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>sol</sub> = ΣΔ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>hyd</sub>.
> 
> Rearranging:
> 
> Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>sol</sub> = ΣΔ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>hyd</sub> − lattice energy.
> 
> KF is a 1:1 ionic compound, so add both hydration enthalpies directly without multiplying either by a stoichiometric coefficient.

parts.problemMd:
A Group 1 metal, M, forms an ionic chloride compound.

The lattice energy of this compound is −773 kJ mol<sup>–</sup> and the standard enthalpy change of hydration of the chloride ion is −363 kJ mol<sup>–</sup>.

The standard enthalpy change of solution of the Group 1 chloride is +4 kJ mol<sup>–</sup>.

Using the information in Table 4.1, deduce the identity of the Group 1 ion, M<sup>+</sup>. Show your working.

**Table 4.1**

| **Group 1 ion** | Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>hyd</sub>** / kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup> |
|---|---|
| Li<sup>+</sup> | −519 |
| Na<sup>+</sup> | −406 |
| K<sup>+</sup> | −321 |
| Rb<sup>+</sup> | −296 |

Identity of M<sup>+</sup> = ...........................
parts.solutionMd:
The identity of M<sup>+</sup> is deduced by calculating Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>hyd</sub>(M<sup>+</sup>) from the energy cycle.

- State the relationship from the energy cycle:

lattice energy + Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>sol</sub> = Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>hyd</sub>(M<sup>+</sup>) + Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>hyd</sub>(Cl<sup>–</sup>) **[1 mark]**

- Rearrange and substitute the known values:

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>hyd</sub>(M<sup>+</sup>) = lattice energy + Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>sol</sub> − Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>hyd</sub>(Cl<sup>–</sup>)

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>hyd</sub>(M<sup>+</sup>) = (−773) + (+4) − (−363)

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>hyd</sub>(M<sup>+</sup>) = −406 kJ mol<sup>–1</sup> **[1 mark]**

- Compare with Table 4.1:

M<sup>+</sup> = **Na**<sup>**+**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct energy cycle relationship
> 
> 1 mark for Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>hyd</sub>(M<sup>+</sup>) = −406 kJ mol<sup>–</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for Na<sup>+</sup> **OR** correct identification of a Group 1 ion based on a numerical answer matching a value in Table 4.1
> 
> Allow error carried forward from incorrect rearrangement

> **[exam-tip]**
> Set up the energy cycle equation first:
> 
> lattice energy + Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>sol</sub> = ΣΔ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>hyd</sub>.
> 
> Rearranging to find Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>hyd</sub>(M<sup>+</sup>): subtract Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>hyd</sub>(Cl<sup>–</sup>) from both sides. The lattice energy given is negative. CIE defines lattice energy as the formation of the ionic lattice, so take care with signs when substituting.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A Group 1 metal, M, forms an ionic chloride compound.

The lattice energy of this compound is −773 kJ mol^–^.

Metal M forms an ionic compound with a different halide ion. The lattice energy of this new compound is −705 kJ mol<sup>–</sup>.

Deduce the formula of this compound. Explain your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> A possible formula for the new compound is:
> 
> - MBr (s) / MI (s) **[1 mark]**
> - The new halide ion has a larger ionic radius than Cl<sup>–</sup> / has more electron shells than Cl<sup>–</sup> **[1 mark]**
> - The attraction between M<sup>+</sup> and the new halide ion is weaker than between M<sup>+</sup> and Cl<sup>–</sup>, giving a less exothermic lattice energy **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The lattice energy of the new compound (−705 kJ mol<sup>–</sup>) is less exothermic than that of MCl (−773 kJ mol<sup>–</sup>). Since M<sup>+</sup> is unchanged, the difference must come from the halide ion. A less exothermic lattice energy means weaker ionic attractions, which occurs when the halide ion is larger. Both Br<sup>–</sup> and I<sup>–</sup> are larger than Cl<sup>–</sup>, so MBr and MI are both valid answers. MF would be incorrect as F<sup>–</sup> is smaller than Cl<sup>–</sup>, so MF would have a more exothermic lattice energy than MCl.

parts.problemMd:
i) Explain why the standard enthalpy change of hydration of Group 1 ions is an exothermic process.

[2]

ii) Explain why the standard enthalpy change of hydration becomes less exothermic down Group 1.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The standard enthalpy change of hydration of Group 1 ions is exothermic because:
> 
> - Group 1 ions / M<sup>+</sup> attract the δ<sup>–</sup> oxygen atoms in polar water molecules / ion-dipole attractions form between M<sup>+</sup> and water **[1 mark]**
> - Bonds form between the Group 1 ion and water molecules, releasing energy **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The standard enthalpy change of hydration becomes less exothermic down Group 1 because:
> 
> - The ionic radius of M<sup>+</sup> increases down the group **[1 mark]**
> - The ion-dipole attraction between M<sup>+</sup> and water molecules decreases / water molecules are attracted less strongly as charge density decreases **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For part i, connect two steps: the positive Group 1 ion is attracted to the δ<sup>–</sup> oxygen in water, and forming this attraction releases energy. Bond formation is always exothermic.
> 
> For part ii, all Group 1 ions carry the same charge (+1), so ionic radius is the only variable. A larger ion has a lower charge density, forms weaker ion-dipole attractions with water, and releases less energy on hydration.

parts.problemMd:
The following equation represents the melting of ice.

H<sub>2</sub>O (s) → H<sub>2</sub>O (l)            ∆*H*<sup>ϴ</sup> = +6.03 kJ mol<sup>–1</sup>    ∆*S*<sup>ϴ</sup> = +22.1 J K<sup>–1</sup> mol<sup>–1</sup>

State the meaning of the symbol <sup>ϴ</sup> in ∆*H*<sup>ϴ</sup>.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The meaning of the symbol <sup>⊖</sup> in Δ*H*<sup>⊖</sup> is:
> 
> - Standard conditions **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The <sup>⊖</sup> symbol indicates that the value was measured under standard conditions: a pressure of 101 kPa and a temperature of 298 K (25 °C).

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The following equation represents the melting of ice.

H~2~O (s) → H~2~O (l)            ∆*H*^ϴ^ = +6.03 kJ mol^–1^    ∆*S*^ϴ^ = +22.1 J K^–1^ mol^–1^

Explain why the standard entropy change for this process is positive.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The standard entropy change is positive because:
> 
> - A liquid is formed from a solid / ice melts to form liquid water **[1 mark]**
> - Liquid water is more disordered than solid ice / particles have greater freedom of movement in a liquid than in a solid **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Entropy is a measure of disorder in a system. The greater the disorder, the higher the entropy.
> 
> In this process, ice (a solid) changes to liquid water. Particles in a liquid have greater freedom of movement than those in a solid, so the system becomes more disordered and entropy increases, making Δ*S*<sup>⊖</sup> positive.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The following equation represents the melting of ice.

H₂O (s) → H₂O (l)            ∆H° = +6.03 kJ mol⁻¹    ∆S° = +22.1 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹

Calculate the temperature at which ∆*G*<sup>ϴ</sup> = 0 for this process.

Show your working.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the temperature at which Δ*G*<sup>⊖</sup> = 0:

- List the known values:

  - Δ*H*<sup>⊖</sup> = +6.03 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>
  - Δ*S*<sup>⊖</sup> = +22.1 J K<sup>−1</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup>
- Rearrange Δ*G*<sup>⊖</sup> = Δ*H*<sup>⊖</sup> − *T*Δ*S*<sup>⊖</sup> = 0 to find *T*:

*T* = `\frac{\Delta H^{\ominus}}{\Delta S^{\ominus}}` **[1 mark]**

- Convert Δ*H*<sup>⊖</sup> from kJ mol<sup>−1</sup> to J mol<sup>−1</sup> and substitute:

*T* = $\frac{6.03\times1000}{22.1}$ **[1 mark]**

*T* = **273 K** **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for the correct rearrangement: *T* = Δ*H*<sup>⊖</sup> ÷ Δ*S*<sup>⊖</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for correct substitution with consistent units (Δ*H*<sup>⊖</sup> converted to J mol<sup>−1</sup>, or Δ*S*<sup>⊖</sup> converted to kJ K<sup>−1</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup>)
> 
> 1 mark for the correct answer: 273 K

> **[exam-tip]**
> When using the Gibbs equation, Δ*H* and Δ*S* must be in the same units. Here, Δ*H*<sup>⊖</sup> is in kJ mol<sup>−1</sup> and Δ*S*<sup>⊖</sup> is in J K<sup>−1</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup>, so you must convert one to match the other before dividing.
> 
> The simplest approach is to multiply Δ*H*<sup>⊖</sup> by 1000 to convert to J mol<sup>−1</sup>: 6.03 x 1000 = 6030 J mol<sup>−1</sup>.
> 
> Alternatively, divide Δ*S*<sup>⊖</sup> by 1000 to convert to kJ K<sup>−1</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup>: 22.1 ÷ 1000 = 0.0221 kJ K<sup>−1</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup>. Both approaches give *T* = 273 K, which is 0 °C, the melting point of ice.

parts.problemMd:
Potassium nitrate is a soluble salt. When it dissolves in water the value of the enthalpy change Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> = +34.9 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup> and the value of the entropy change Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = +117 J K<sup>−1</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup>.

Construct an equation, including state symbols, for the process that occurs when potassium nitrate dissolves in water.
parts.solutionMd:

> KNO<sub>3</sub> (s) + aq → K<sup>+</sup> (aq) + NO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> (aq) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The standard enthalpy change of solution (Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>sol</sub>) is the enthalpy change when 1 mole of an ionic substance dissolves in sufficient water to form a very dilute solution.
> 
> The symbol (aq) indicates that the ions are dissolved in sufficient water to form a dilute aqueous solution.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Potassium nitrate is a soluble salt. When it dissolves in water the value of the enthalpy change Δ*H*^θ^ = +34.9 kJ mol^−1^ and the value of the entropy change Δ*S*^θ^ = +117 J K^−1^ mol^−1^.

Construct an equation, including state symbols, for the process that occurs when potassium nitrate dissolves in water.

KNO~3~ (s) → K^+^ (aq) + NO~3~^−^ (aq)

Explain why Δ*S*<sup>θ </sup>is positive for this process.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> is positive because:
> 
> - Disorder increases as the solid dissolves / solid changes to aqueous ions / particles have greater freedom of movement in solution **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> When KNO<sub>3</sub> dissolves, the ionic lattice breaks down:
> 
> KNO<sub>3</sub> (s) → K<sup>+</sup> (aq) + NO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> (aq)

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Potassium nitrate is a soluble salt. When it dissolves in water the value of the enthalpy change Δ*H*^θ^ = +34.9 kJ mol^−1^ and the value of the entropy change Δ*S*^θ^ = +117 J K^−1^ mol^−1^.

Calculate the temperature above which the dissolving of potassium nitrate becomes feasible. Show your working.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the temperature above which the dissolving of potassium nitrate becomes feasible:

- List the known values:

  - Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> = +34.9 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>
  - Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = +117 J K<sup>−1</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup>
- At the feasibility threshold, Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = 0. Rearrange Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> − *T*Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = 0 to find *T*:

*T* = $\frac{ΔH^{θ}}{ΔS^{θ}}$ **[1 mark]**

- Convert Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> from kJ mol<sup>−1</sup> to J mol<sup>−1</sup> and substitute:

*T* = $\frac{34.9\times1000}{117}$ **[1 mark]**

*T* = **298 K** **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for the correct rearrangement: *T* = Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> ÷ Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for correct substitution with consistent units
> 
> 1 mark for the correct answer: 298 K

> **[exam-tip]**
> The reaction becomes feasible when Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> ≤ 0. Setting Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = 0 gives the threshold temperature above which the reaction becomes feasible.
> 
> Remember to ensure Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> and Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> are in the same units before dividing. Here, multiply Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> by 1000 to convert from kJ mol<sup>−1</sup> to J mol<sup>−1</sup>: 34.9 x 1000 = 34 900 J mol<sup>−1</sup>. Then divide by Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = 117 J K<sup>−1</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup> to get *T* = 298 K.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Potassium nitrate is a soluble salt. When it dissolves in water the value of the enthalpy change ΔH^θ = +34.9 kJ mol^−1^ and the value of the entropy change ΔS^θ = +117 J K^−1^ mol^−1^.

Calculate the temperature above which the dissolving of potassium nitrate becomes feasible.

T = ΔH^θ ÷ ΔS^θ
T = (34.9 × 1000) ÷ 117
T = 298 K

i) State the sign of Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> for this process at a temperature lower than your answer to part (c).

[1]

ii) State what this value of Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> indicates about the dissolving of potassium nitrate at this lower temperature.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The sign of Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> at a temperature lower than 298 K:
> 
> - Positive / Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> > 0 **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) A positive Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> indicates that:
> 
> - The dissolving of potassium nitrate is not feasible / not spontaneous / does not occur at this temperature **[1 mark]**
> 
> Allow error carried forward from (d)(i): if negative, allow "feasible / spontaneous"

> **[exam-tip]**
> At the threshold temperature from part (c), Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = 0. Below this temperature, the *T*Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> term decreases in magnitude, so Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> − *T*Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> becomes more positive.
> 
> A positive Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> means the process is not feasible: potassium nitrate is less likely to dissolve at temperatures below 298 K.

parts.problemMd:
Ammonia, NH<sub>3</sub>, is produced by the Haber process and is an important chemical in the manufacture of fertilisers and cleaning products.

Ammonia gas can react with oxygen to produce nitrogen monoxide and steam, and is the first step in the Ostwald process which produces nitric acid.

i) Construct an equation for the reaction of ammonia with oxygen to produce nitrogen monoxide and steam.

[2]

ii) Standard entropies are shown in Table 2.1.

**Table 2.1**

| **substance** | **entropy values (J K**<sup>**-1**</sup>** mol**<sup>**-1**</sup>**)** |
|---|---|
| NH<sub>3</sub> (g) | 192.8 |
| O<sub>2</sub> (g) | 205.2 |
| H<sub>2</sub>O (g) | 188.8 |
| NO (g) | 210.8 |

Calculate Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> for this reaction at 298 K.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
i) The balanced equation for the reaction of ammonia with oxygen is:

4NH<sub>3</sub> (g) + 5O<sub>2</sub> (g) → 4NO (g) + 6H<sub>2</sub>O (g)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct reactants, products and balancing
> 
> 1 mark for all correct state symbols

ii) To calculate Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> for this reaction:

- Apply Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = ΣΔ*S*<sup>θ</sup>(products) − ΣΔ*S*<sup>θ</sup>(reactants):

Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = [(4 x Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>(NO (g))) + (6 x Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>(H<sub>2</sub>O (g)))] − [(4 x Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>(NH<sub>3</sub> (g))) + (5 x Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>(O<sub>2</sub> (g)))] **[1 mark]**

Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = [(4 x 210.8) + (6 x 188.8)] − [(4 x 192.8) + (5 x 205.2)]

Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = [843.2 + 1132.8] − [771.2 + 1026.0]

Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = 1976.0 − 1797.2

Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = **+178.8 J K**<sup>**−1**</sup>** mol**<sup>**−1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for the correct method: ΣΔ*S*<sup>θ</sup>(products) − ΣΔ*S*<sup>θ</sup>(reactants) with stoichiometric coefficients correctly applied
> 
> 1 mark for the correct answer: +178.8 J K<sup>−1</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup>

> **[exam-tip]**
> The equation to calculate entropy change is:
> 
> Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = ΣΔ*S*<sup>θ</sup>(products) − ΣΔ*S*<sup>θ</sup>(reactants)
> 
> Don't forget to multiply each standard entropy value by the stoichiometric coefficient of that species in the balanced equation. This balancing step must be carried through the entire calculation.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Ammonia gas can react with oxygen to produce nitrogen monoxide and steam, and is the first step in the Ostwald process which produces nitric acid.

i) Construct an equation for the reaction of ammonia with oxygen to produce nitrogen monoxide and steam.

The balanced equation for the reaction of ammonia with oxygen is:

4NH3 (g) + 5O2 (g) → 4NO (g) + 6H2O (g)

Explain why the standard entropy change for the reaction in **(a)** is positive.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The standard entropy change is positive because:
> 
> - There are 10 moles of gas in the products
> **AND**
> 9 moles of gas in the reactants
> **OR**
> There are more moles of gas in the products than in the reactants
> **OR**
> The system becomes more disordered **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Examiners noted that many candidates did not explicitly state the change in moles of gaseous species. For full credit, state both the number of moles of gas in the products and the number in the reactants: 10 moles of gas on the right and 9 moles of gas on the left means the system becomes more disordered, giving a positive Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Standard entropies are shown in Table 2.1.

**Table 2.1**

| **substance** | **entropy values (J K**^**-1**^** mol**^**-1**^**)** |
| :---: | :---: |
| NH~3~ (g) | 192.8 |
| O~2~ (g) | 205.2 |
| H~2~O (g) | 188.8 |
| NO (g) | 210.8 |

The second step in the Ostwald process produces nitrogen dioxide as shown in the equation

2NO (g) + O<sub>2</sub> (g) → 2NO<sub>2</sub> (g)             Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> = −112 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>

The standard entropy of NO<sub>2</sub> (g) is 240.0 J K<sup>−1</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup>.

i) Use Table 2.1 to calculate Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> for this reaction at 298 K.

[2]

ii) Use your answer to (c)(i) to calculate Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> for this reaction at 298 K. Show your working.

[3]
parts.solutionMd:
i) To calculate Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> for the reaction 2NO (g) + O<sub>2</sub> (g) → 2NO<sub>2</sub> (g):

- Apply Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = ΣΔ*S*<sup>θ</sup>(products) − ΣΔ*S*<sup>θ</sup>(reactants):

Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = [2 x Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>(NO<sub>2</sub> (g))] − [(2 x Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>(NO (g))) + Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>(O<sub>2</sub> (g))] **[1 mark]**

Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = (2 x 240.0) − [(2 x 210.8) + 205.2]

Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = 480.0 − [421.6 + 205.2]

Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = 480.0 − 626.8

Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = **−146.8 J K**<sup>**−1**</sup>** mol**<sup>**−1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> i)
> 
> 1 mark for the correct method: ΣΔ*S*<sup>θ</sup>(products) − ΣΔ*S*<sup>θ</sup>(reactants) with stoichiometric coefficients correctly applied
> 
> 1 mark for the correct answer: −146.8 J K<sup>−1</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup>

ii) To calculate Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> for this reaction at 298 K:

- List the known values:

  - Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> = −112 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>
  - Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = −146.8 J K<sup>−1</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup> (from (c)(i))
  - *T* = 298 K
- State the Gibbs equation:

Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> − *T*Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> **[1 mark]**

- Convert Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> to kJ K<sup>−1</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup> and substitute:

Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = −112 − (298 x −0.1468) **[1 mark]**

Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = −112 + 43.7

Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = **−68.3 kJ mol**<sup>**−1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii)
> 
> 1 mark for stating the Gibbs equation: Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> − *T*Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for correct substitution with consistent units
> 
> 1 mark for the correct answer: −68.3 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>
> 
> Allow error carried forward from an incorrect value of Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> in (c)(i)

> **[exam-tip]**
> For part (i), the entropy change is negative because the number of moles of gas decreases: 3 moles of gas on the left (2NO + O<sub>2</sub>) become 2 moles on the right (2NO<sub>2</sub>). Fewer moles of gas means less disorder, so Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> is negative.
> 
> For part (ii), remember to convert Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> from J K<sup>−1</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup> to kJ K<sup>−1</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup> before substituting into the Gibbs equation, since Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> is given in kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>. Divide Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> by 1000: −146.8 ÷ 1000 = −0.1468 kJ K<sup>−1</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup>.

parts.problemMd:
Fig. 3.1 shows how entropy changes with temperature.

**Fig. 3.1**

i) The entropy of water is zero when the temperature is zero Kelvin. Explain this in terms of the arrangement and motion of the water molecules.

[2]

ii) Explain why the entropy change, Δ*S*, is larger at temperature *T*<sub>2</sub> than at temperature *T*<sub>1</sub>.

[2]

iii) Label the boiling point, *T*<sub>b</sub>, on the appropriate axis.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
iii) The completed figure is:

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
