> Avoid discussing the change in disorder without clearly stating the change in state — for example, specify a change from liquid to gas, not just 'gas'.
> 
> The boiling point represents the largest change in entropy, as the state changes from liquid to gas. This is why *T*<sub>b</sub> is marked on the temperature axis, vertically below *T*<sub>2</sub> on Fig. 3.1.

parts.problemMd:
Standard entropies can be used to calculate the entropy change of a reaction, Δ*S*. For example, for the reaction between nitrogen monoxide and ozone.

NO (g) + O<sub>3</sub> (g) → NO<sub>2</sub> (g) + O<sub>2</sub> (g)

Standard entropy values are shown in Table 3.1

**Table 3.1**

| **Substance** | **Entropy value / J K**<sup>-1</sup>** mol**<sup>-1</sup> |
|---|---|
| NO (g) | 210.8 |
| O<sub>2</sub> (g) | 205.2 |
| NO<sub>2</sub> (g) | 240.0 |
| O<sub>3</sub> (g) | 238.9 |

Using Table 3.1, calculate Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> of the reaction between nitrogen monoxide and ozone at 298 K. Show your working.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> for the reaction:

- Apply the formula Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = Σ*S*<sup>θ</sup> (products) – Σ*S*<sup>θ</sup> (reactants):

Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = (240.0 + 205.2) – (210.8 + 238.9) **[1 mark]**

Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = 445.2 – 449.7

Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = **–4.5 J K**<sup>**–1**</sup>** mol**<sup>**–1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct formula and substitution: (240.0 + 205.2) – (210.8 + 238.9)
> 
> 1 mark for the correct final answer: –4.5 J K<sup>–1</sup> mol<sup>–1</sup>

> **[exam-tip]**
> When calculating the standard entropy change of a reaction, use the formula:
> 
> Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = Σ*S*<sup>θ</sup> (products) – Σ*S*<sup>θ</sup> (reactants)
> 
> Remember to account for the number of moles of each substance in the balanced equation when applying this formula.

parts.problemMd:
The contact process is a method used industrially to form sulfur trioxide, by reacting sulfur dioxide and oxygen together over a vanadium(V) oxide catalyst.

The equation for this reaction is shown below:

2SO<sub>2</sub> (g) + O<sub>2</sub> (g) ⇌ 2SO<sub>3</sub> (g)

Enthalpy of formation values are shown in Table 3.2

**Table 3.2**

| **Substance** | **Formation enthalpy values (kJ mol**<sup>-1</sup>**)** |
|---|---|
| SO<sub>2</sub> (g) | –297 |
| SO<sub>3</sub> (g) | –395 |

i) Using Table 3.2, calculate the standard enthalpy change of reaction, Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup>, using the data provided. Show your working.

[2]

ii) The standard entropy change of this reaction is –189 J K<sup>–1</sup> mol<sup>–1</sup>. Use this value and your enthalpy value from part (i) to calculate the standard Gibbs free energy change, Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup>, for this reaction at 298 K. Show your working.

[3]

iii) Use your answer to part (ii) to state whether the reaction is feasible at 298 K.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
i) To calculate the standard enthalpy change of reaction:

- Apply the formula:

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> = ΣΔ*H*<sub>f</sub><sup>θ</sup> (products) – ΣΔ*H*<sub>f</sub><sup>θ</sup> (reactants)

**OR**

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> = (2 x –395) – (2 x –297) **[1 mark]**

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> = –790 – (–594)

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> = **–196 kJ mol**<sup>**–1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> i)
> 
> 1 mark for the formula **AND** correct substitution: (2 × –395) – (2 × –297)
> 
> 1 mark for the correct final answer: –196 kJ mol<sup>–1</sup>

> **[exam-tip]**
> Writing out the formula at the start of a calculation can sometimes earn the first mark, and is good practice for structuring your working.

ii) To calculate the standard Gibbs free energy change at 298 K:

- Convert Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> from J K<sup>–1</sup> mol<sup>–1</sup> to kJ K<sup>–1</sup> mol<sup>–1</sup>:

Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = –189 ÷ 1000 = –0.189 kJ K<sup>–1</sup> mol<sup>–1</sup> **[1 mark]**

- Apply the formula:

Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> – *T*Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>

**OR**

Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = –196 – (298 x –0.189) **[1 mark]**

Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = **–140 kJ mol**<sup>**–1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii)
> 
> 1 mark for converting Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> to kJ K<sup>–1</sup> mol<sup>–1</sup>: –189 ÷ 1000 = –0.189 kJ K<sup>–1</sup> mol<sup>–1</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for the formula **AND** correct substitution into Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> – *T*Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>
> 
> Allow error carried forward from part (i) for the enthalpy value
> 
> 1 mark for the correct final answer: –140 kJ mol<sup>–1</sup>

> **[exam-tip]**
> For part (ii), convert Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> from J K<sup>–1</sup> mol<sup>–1</sup> to kJ K<sup>–1</sup> mol<sup>–1</sup> before substituting into the formula, as Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> is in kJ mol<sup>–1</sup>. Divide by 1000: –189 ÷ 1000 = –0.189 kJ K<sup>–1</sup> mol<sup>–1</sup>.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> iii) Whether the reaction is feasible at 298 K:
> 
> - (Yes,) the reaction is feasible because Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> is negative **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For part (iii), reference Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> being negative to justify feasibility at 298 K.

parts.problemMd: State the equation that links Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup>, Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup>, Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> and temperature *T*.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The equation that links Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup>, Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup>, Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> and temperature *T*:
> 
> - Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> − *T*Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> This equation must be learned. Other rearrangements are also accepted:
> 
> - Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> = Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> + *T*Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>
> - Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = (Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> − Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup>) / *T*
> - *T*Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> − Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup>

parts.problemMd: State the condition for a reaction to be feasible.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The condition for a reaction to be feasible:
> 
> - Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> is less than or equal to zero / Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> ≤ 0 **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> A reaction is feasible when Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> < 0 or when Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = 0. Both 'Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> is negative' and 'Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> ≤ 0' are accepted.

parts.problemMd:
Chlorine can be formed in the following reversible reaction:

4HCl (g) + O<sub>2</sub> (g) ⇌ 2Cl<sub>2</sub> (g) + 2H<sub>2</sub>O (g)

Use the information in Table 1.1 to calculate the standard entropy change, Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>, for this reaction. Show your working.

**Table 1.1**

|   | **HCl (g)** | **O**<sub>**2**</sub>** (g)** | **Cl**<sub>**2**</sub>** (g)** | **H**<sub>**2**</sub>**O (g)** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| *S*<sup>θ</sup> / J K<sup>–1</sup> mol<sup>–1</sup> | 187 | 205 | 223 | 189 |
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the standard entropy change, Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>, for this reaction:

- Apply Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = Σ*S*<sup>θ</sup>(products) − Σ*S*<sup>θ</sup>(reactants) and substitute values:

Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = [(2 x 223) + (2 x 189)] − [205 + (4 x 187)] **[1 mark]**

Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = 824 − 953 **[1 mark]**

Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = **−129 J K**<sup>**–1**</sup>** mol**<sup>**–1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct substitution including stoichiometric coefficients (2 x 223, 2 x 189, 4 x 187)
> 
> 1 mark for correct intermediate: 824 − 953
> 
> 1 mark for correct answer: −129 J K<sup>–1</sup> mol<sup>–1</sup>
> 
> An answer of +129 J K<sup>–1</sup> mol<sup>–1</sup> would score only 1 mark as the negative sign is required for full marks.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Multiply each *S*<sup>θ</sup> value by its stoichiometric coefficient before summing. Here, HCl has coefficient 4, Cl<sub>2</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>O each have coefficient 2, and O<sub>2</sub> has coefficient 1.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Chlorine can be formed in the following reversible reaction:

4HCl (g) + O~2~ (g) ⇌ 2Cl~2~ (g) + 2H~2~O (g)

Use the information in Table 1.1 to calculate the standard entropy change, Δ*S*^θ^, for this reaction. Show your working.

**Table 1.1**

|   | **HCl (g)** | **O**~**2**~** (g)** | **Cl**~**2**~** (g)** | **H**~**2**~**O (g)** |
| --- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| *S*^θ^ / J K^–1^ mol^–1^ | 187 | 205 | 223 | 189 |

Δ*S*^θ^ = −129 J K^–1^ mol^–1^

The standard enthalpy change for the reaction in (c) is −116 kJ mol<sup>–1</sup>.

Calculate the temperature above which this reaction is no longer feasible. Show your working.
parts.solutionMd:
To find the temperature above which this reaction is no longer feasible, set Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = 0:

- Rearrange Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> − *T*Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> to find *T*:

*T* = $\frac{ΔH^{θ}}{ΔS^{θ}}$

- Convert Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> to J mol<sup>–1</sup> and substitute:

*T* = $\frac{-116\times1000}{-129}$ **[1 mark]**

- Calculate *T*:

*T* = **899 K** **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct substitution *T* = Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> / Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> with Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> converted to J mol<sup>–1</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for correct answer: 899 K

> **[exam-tip]**
> At the feasibility boundary, Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = 0:
> 
> *T* = $\frac{ΔH^{θ}}{ΔS^{θ}}$
> 
> Since Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> is in kJ mol<sup>–1</sup> and Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> is in J K<sup>–1</sup> mol<sup>–1</sup>, convert Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> to J mol<sup>–1</sup> by multiplying by 1000 before dividing. When both values are negative, the negatives cancel to give a positive temperature.

parts.problemMd:
Ammonium chloride, NH<sub>4</sub>Cl, can dissociate to form ammonia, NH<sub>3</sub>, and hydrogen chloride, HCl.

NH<sub>4</sub>Cl (s) → NH<sub>3</sub> (g) + HCl (g)

Explain why the standard entropy change, Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>, for this reaction is positive.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The standard entropy change is positive because:
> 
> - A gas is formed from a solid **[1 mark]**
> - Gases have greater disorder / more ways to arrange energy than solids **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Entropy is a measure of the number of ways energy can be distributed among the particles in a system. The more arrangements possible, the higher the entropy.
> 
> When NH<sub>4</sub>Cl (s) dissociates, all products are gases. Gases have far more possible arrangements of particles than solids, so entropy increases significantly and Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> is positive.

parts.problemMd:
At 298 K, Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> = +176 kJ mol<sup>–1</sup> and Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = +285 J K<sup>–1</sup> mol<sup>–1</sup>.

Calculate Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> for this reaction at 298 K. Show your working.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> for this reaction at 298 K:

- Convert Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> from J K<sup>–1</sup> mol<sup>–1</sup> to kJ K<sup>–1</sup> mol<sup>–1</sup>:

Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = 285 ÷ 1000 = 0.285 kJ K<sup>–1</sup> mol<sup>–1</sup> **[1 mark]**

- Substitute into Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> − *T*Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>:

Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = (+176) − (298 x 0.285) **[1 mark]**

Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = **+91.1 kJ mol**<sup>**–1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for converting Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> to kJ K<sup>–1</sup> mol<sup>–1</sup> (0.285)
> 
> 1 mark for correct substitution into Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> − *T*Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for correct final answer: +91.1 kJ mol<sup>–1</sup> (allow +91.0 to +91.3)

> **[exam-tip]**
> The Gibbs free energy equation is:
> 
> Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> − *T*Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>
> 
> The most common mistake is forgetting to convert Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> from J K<sup>–1</sup> mol<sup>–1</sup> to kJ K<sup>–1</sup> mol<sup>–1</sup> before substituting. Divide by 1000 first.
> 
> Temperature must be in Kelvin. 298 K is already in the correct unit.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

At 298 K, Δ*H*^θ^ = +176 kJ mol^–1^ and Δ*S*^θ^ = +285 J K^–1^ mol^–1^.

Calculate Δ*G*^θ^ for this reaction at 298 K. Show your working.

Use your answer to (b) to state whether the reaction is feasible at 298 K.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> At 298 K, the reaction is:
> 
> - Not feasible / Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> is positive / greater than zero **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> A reaction is feasible when Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> < 0. When Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> > 0, the reaction is not feasible under those conditions.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

At 298 K, Δ*H*^θ^ = +176 kJ mol^–1^ and Δ*S*^θ^ = +285 J K^–1^ mol^–1^.

NH~4~Cl (s) → NH~3~ (g) + HCl (g)

State and explain how the feasibility of the reaction will change with increasing temperature.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> As temperature increases, the feasibility of this reaction:
> 
> - Increases / the reaction becomes more feasible **[1 mark]**
> - Because Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> becomes less positive / more negative as *T* increases **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> When both Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> and Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> are positive, the sign of Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> depends on temperature:
> 
> Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> − *T*Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>
> 
> At low temperatures, *T*Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> is small, so Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> is positive (not feasible). As temperature increases, *T*Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> grows until it exceeds Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup>, making Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> negative (feasible).

parts.problemMd:
State whether the standard entropy change, Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>, is positive or negative for each of the following processes. Explain your reasoning.

i) Steam condensing to water

[2]

ii) Zinc reacting with dilute nitric acid

[2]

iii) Solid sodium chloride dissolving in water

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) Steam condensing to water:
> 
> - Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> is negative / decreases **[1 mark]**
> - Because a gas condenses to a liquid / particles become less disordered / number of ways of arranging energy decreases **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) Zinc reacting with dilute nitric acid:
> 
> - Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> is positive / increases **[1 mark]**
> - Because a gas (H<sub>2</sub>) is formed from solid and aqueous reactants / disorder increases **[1 mark]**
> 
> iii) Solid sodium chloride dissolving in water:
> 
> - Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> is positive / increases **[1 mark]**
> - Because free-moving / mobile aqueous ions are formed from a solid / ions can move throughout the solution **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Entropy increases when a system becomes more disordered. Use state symbols to track how disorder changes:
> 
> - Gas → liquid: order increases, entropy decreases (Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> negative)
> - Solid + liquid → liquid + gas: disorder increases, entropy increases (Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> positive)
> - Solid → aqueous ions: ions free to move, entropy increases (Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> positive)
> 
> Writing out the balanced equation helps clarify the change in state of matter in each case.

parts.problemMd:
Calcium carbonate decomposes according to the following equation:

CaCO<sub>3</sub> (s) → CaO (s) + CO<sub>2</sub> (g)     Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> = +178 kJ mol<sup>–1</sup>

Table 1.1 shows the standard entropies, *S*<sup>θ</sup>, of the species.

**Table 1.1**

| **Substance** | *S*<sup>θ</sup> / J K<sup>–1</sup> mol<sup>–1</sup> |
|---|---|
| CaCO<sub>3</sub> (s) | 92.9 |
| CaO (s) | 39.8 |
| CO<sub>2</sub> (g) | 214.0 |

i) Calculate Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> for this reaction. Show your working.

[2]

ii) Calculate the standard Gibbs free energy change, Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup>, for this reaction at 298 K. Include a relevant sign in your answer. Show your working.

[3]

Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = .................. kJ mol<sup>–1</sup>
parts.solutionMd:
i) To calculate Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> for this reaction:

- Apply Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = Σ*S*<sup>θ</sup> (products) − Σ*S*<sup>θ</sup> (reactants):

Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = (39.8 + 214.0) − 92.9

Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = **+160.9 J K**<sup>**–1**</sup>** mol**<sup>**–1**</sup>

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct application of Σ*S*<sup>θ</sup> (products) − Σ*S*<sup>θ</sup> (reactants)
> 
> 1 mark for correct answer: +160.9 J K<sup>–1</sup> mol<sup>–1</sup>

ii) To calculate Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> at 298 K:

- Convert Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> from J K<sup>–1</sup> mol<sup>–1</sup> to kJ K<sup>–1</sup> mol<sup>–1</sup>:

Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = 160.9 ÷ 1000 = 0.1609 kJ K<sup>–1</sup> mol<sup>–1</sup> **[1 mark]**

- Substitute into Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> − *T*Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>:

Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = (+178) − (298 x 0.1609) **[1 mark]**

Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = **+130 kJ mol**<sup>**–1**</sup> (to 3 s.f.) **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for converting Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> to kJ K<sup>–1</sup> mol<sup>–1</sup> (0.1609)
> 
> 1 mark for correct substitution into Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> − *T*Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for correct answer to 3 significant figures: +130 kJ mol<sup>–1</sup> (allow ECF from part (i))

> **[exam-tip]**
> Make sure Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> and Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> are in the same units before substituting. Dividing Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> by 1000 converts J K<sup>–1</sup> mol<sup>–1</sup> to kJ K<sup>–1</sup> mol<sup>–1</sup>.
> 
> The question asks for the answer to three significant figures. 130 has 3 significant figures; don't round to 100 or leave as 130.05.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Calcium carbonate decomposes according to the following equation:

CaCO₃ (s) → CaO (s) + CO₂ (g)     ΔH° = +178 kJ mol⁻¹

Table 1.1 shows the standard entropies, S°, of the species.

**Table 1.1**

| **Substance** | S° / J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ |
| --- | :---: |
| CaCO₃ (s) | 92.9 |
| CaO (s) | 39.8 |
| CO₂ (g) | 214.0 |

Explain, with reference to Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup>, why this reaction becomes more feasible at higher temperatures.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> This reaction becomes more feasible at higher temperatures because:
> 
> - Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> is positive, so *T*Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> increases with temperature **[1 mark]**
> - *T*Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> eventually exceeds Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> **[1 mark]**
> - Therefore Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> becomes negative / decreases / becomes less positive **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Use the Gibbs equation to explain this step by step:
> 
> Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> − *T*Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>
> 
> For this reaction, Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> is positive (endothermic) and Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> is positive (gas formed). At low temperatures, *T*Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> is small so Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> remains positive (not feasible). As temperature rises, *T*Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> grows until it exceeds Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup>, making Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> negative (feasible).

parts.problemMd:
On heating, sodium hydrogencarbonate decomposes into sodium carbonate as shown.

2NaHCO<sub>3</sub> (s) → Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> (s) + CO<sub>2</sub> (g) + H<sub>2</sub>O (g)

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> = +130 kJ mol<sup>–1</sup>     Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = +316 J K<sup>–1</sup> mol<sup>–1</sup>

Calculate the temperature above which this reaction becomes feasible. Show your working.

Temperature = ............ K
parts.solutionMd:
To find the temperature above which this reaction becomes feasible, set Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = 0:

- Rearrange Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> − *T*Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> to find *T*:

*T* = $\frac{ΔH^{θ}}{ΔS^{θ}}$ **[1 mark]**

- Convert Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> to kJ K<sup>–1</sup> mol<sup>–1</sup> and substitute:

*T* = $\frac{130}{(316\div1000)}$ **[1 mark]**

*T* = **411 K** **[1 mark]**

Allow 410–412 K

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for setting Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = 0 and correctly rearranging to *T* = Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> / Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for correct substitution with Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> converted to kJ K<sup>–1</sup> mol<sup>–1</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for correct answer: 411 K (allow 410–412 K)

> **[exam-tip]**
> The temperature above which a reaction becomes feasible is found by setting Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = 0:
> 
> Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> − *T*Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = 0
> 
> *T* = $\frac{ΔH^{θ}}{ΔS^{θ}}$
> 
> Remember to convert Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> from J K<sup>–1</sup> mol<sup>–1</sup> to kJ K<sup>–1</sup> mol<sup>–1</sup> by dividing by 1000, so both quantities are in kJ.

parts.problemMd:
Potassium nitrate is a soluble salt. When it dissolves in water the standard enthalpy change Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> = +34.9 kJ mol<sup>–1</sup> and the standard entropy change Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = +117 J K<sup>–1</sup> mol<sup>–1</sup>.

Construct an equation, including state symbols, for the process that occurs when potassium nitrate dissolves in water.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The equation for potassium nitrate dissolving in water is:
> 
> - KNO<sub>3</sub> (s) → K<sup>+</sup> (aq) + NO<sub>3</sub><sup>–</sup> (aq)
> **OR**
> KNO<sub>3</sub> (s) + aq → K<sup>+</sup> (aq) + NO<sub>3</sub><sup>–</sup> (aq) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> When an ionic solid dissolves in water, it dissociates into its component ions. Include state symbols: (s) for the solid reactant and (aq) for the aqueous ions formed.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Potassium nitrate is a soluble salt. When it dissolves in water the standard enthalpy change ΔH^θ = +34.9 kJ mol^–1 and the standard entropy change ΔS^θ = +117 J K^–1 mol^–1.

Explain why Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> is positive for this process.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> is positive for this process because:
> 
> Any **one** from:
> 
> - The solid dissolves to form free-moving / mobile aqueous ions
> - Disorder increases
> - The number of ways of arranging energy increases
> 
> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> When KNO<sub>3</sub> dissolves:
> 
> KNO<sub>3</sub> (s) → K<sup>+</sup> (aq) + NO<sub>3</sub><sup>–</sup> (aq)
> 
> The ions are now free to move throughout the solution. This increased disorder means there are more ways to arrange energy among the particles, so Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> is positive.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Potassium nitrate is a soluble salt. When it dissolves in water the standard enthalpy change Δ*H*^θ^ = +34.9 kJ mol^–1^ and the standard entropy change Δ*S*^θ^ = +117 J K^–1^ mol^–1^.

Calculate the temperature above which the dissolving of potassium nitrate becomes feasible. Show your working.

*T* = .................. K
parts.solutionMd:
To find the temperature above which the dissolving becomes feasible, set Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = 0:

- Rearrange Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> − *T*Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> to find *T*:

*T* = $\frac{ΔH^{θ}}{ΔS^{θ}}$ **[1 mark]**

- Convert Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> to kJ K<sup>–1</sup> mol<sup>–1</sup> and substitute:

*T* = $\frac{34.9}{117\div1000}$ **[1 mark]**

*T* = **298 K** **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for setting Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = 0 and rearranging to *T* = Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> / Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for correct substitution with Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> converted to kJ K<sup>–1</sup> mol<sup>–1</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for correct answer: 298 K

> **[exam-tip]**
> The temperature above which a process becomes feasible is found by setting Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = 0 and rearranging:
> 
> *T* = $\frac{ΔH^{θ}}{ΔS^{θ}}$
> 
> Remember to convert Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> from J K<sup>–1</sup> mol<sup>–1</sup> to kJ K<sup>–1</sup> mol<sup>–1</sup> by dividing by 1000 before substituting.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Potassium nitrate is a soluble salt. When it dissolves in water the standard enthalpy change ΔH^θ = +34.9 kJ mol^–1^ and the standard entropy change ΔS^θ = +117 J K^–1^ mol^–1^.

Calculate the temperature above which the dissolving of potassium nitrate becomes feasible.
T = 298 K

i) State the sign of Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> for this process at a temperature lower than your answer to (c).

[1]

ii) State what this value of Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> indicates about the solubility of potassium nitrate at this lower temperature.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The sign of Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> at a temperature below 298 K:
> 
> - Positive / Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> > 0 **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) This value of Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> indicates that:
> 
> - The dissolving of potassium nitrate is not feasible / potassium nitrate does not dissolve / is less soluble **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> When both Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> and Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> are positive, the sign of Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> depends on temperature:
> 
> - Above the threshold temperature: *T*Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> > Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup>, so Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> < 0 (feasible)
> - Below the threshold temperature: *T*Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> < Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup>, so Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> > 0 (not feasible)
> 
> For KNO<sub>3</sub>, the threshold is 298 K, so below this temperature the dissolving process is thermodynamically unfavourable.

parts.problemMd:
Using Table 4.1, calculate the entropy change, Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>, for the combustion of ethanol at 298 K. Show your working.

**Table 4.1**

| **substance** | CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH (l) | O<sub>2</sub> (g) | CO<sub>2</sub> (g) | H<sub>2</sub>O (g) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ***S***<sup>**θ**</sup>** / J K**<sup>-1</sup>** mol**<sup>-1</sup> | +161 | +205.2 | +213.8 | +188.8 |

Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = ........................... (J K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>)
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the entropy change, Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>, for the combustion of ethanol at 298 K:

- Write the expression and substitute values:

Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = Σ*S*<sup>θ</sup>(products) − Σ*S*<sup>θ</sup>(reactants)

Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = [(2 x 213.8) + (3 x 188.8)] − [(1 x 161) + (3 x 205.2)] **[1 mark]**

- Calculate Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>:

Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = 994 − 776.6

Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = **+217.4 J K**<sup>**-1**</sup>** mol**<sup>**-1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Allow 217 to 218 J K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>
> 
> Allow error carried forward if the expression is set up correctly but arithmetic is incorrect

> **[exam-tip]**
> Multiply each *S*<sup>θ</sup> value by its stoichiometric coefficient before summing:
> 
> - 2 x *S*<sup>θ</sup> CO<sub>2</sub> (g)
> - 3 x *S*<sup>θ</sup> H<sub>2</sub>O (g)
> - 3 x *S*<sup>θ</sup> O<sub>2</sub> (g)
> 
> Forgetting to apply stoichiometric coefficients is a common error in this type of calculation.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Using Table 4.1, calculate the entropy change, Δ*S*^θ^, for the combustion of ethanol at 298 K. Show your working.

**Table 4.1**

| **substance** | CH~3~CH~2~OH (l) | O~2~ (g) | CO~2~ (g) | H~2~O (g) |
| --- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| ***S***^**θ**^** / J K**^-1^** mol**^-1^ | +161 | +205.2 | +213.8 | +188.8 |

Using the value of Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> given in part **(a)** and your answer to part **(a)**, calculate the standard Gibbs free energy change, Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup>, for the combustion of ethanol at 298 K. Show your working.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the standard Gibbs free energy change, Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup>, for the combustion of ethanol at 298 K:

- Write the expression:

Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> − *T*Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> **[1 mark]**

- Convert Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> to kJ K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup> and substitute values:

Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = 217.4 / 1000 = 0.2174 kJ K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>

Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = −1367 − (298 x 0.2174)

Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = −1367 − 64.8 **[1 mark]**

- Calculate Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup>:

Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = **−1432 kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct expression Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> − *T*Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for correct substitution with Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> converted to kJ K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for correct final answer
> 
> Allow −1431 to −1433 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>
> 
> Allow error carried forward from part (a)

> **[exam-tip]**
> Before substituting, convert Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> from J K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup> to kJ K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup> by dividing by 1000. This ensures the units match Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> (kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>):
> 
> 217.4 / 1000 = 0.2174 kJ K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>
> 
> Alternatively, convert Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> from kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> to J mol<sup>-1</sup> by multiplying by 1000. Either method is valid, but avoid mixing units in the same calculation.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Using Table 4.1, calculate the entropy change, Δ*S*^θ^, for the combustion of ethanol at 298 K.

Δ*S*^θ^ = +217.4 J K^-1^ mol^-1^

Δ*H*^θ^ = −1367 kJ mol^-1^

Explain whether changing the temperature for the combustion of ethanol will affect the feasibility of the reaction.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Whether changing the temperature affects the feasibility of the combustion of ethanol:
> 
> - Changing the temperature does not affect the feasibility of the reaction **[1 mark]**
> - Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> is always negative
> **AND**
> Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> is always positive **[1 mark]**
> - Therefore Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> is always negative at any temperature / the reaction is always feasible **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The feasibility of a reaction depends on the sign of Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> − *T*Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>:
> 
> | Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> | Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> | Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> | Feasible? |
> |---|---|---|---|
> | Negative (exothermic) | Positive (more disorder) | Always negative | At all temperatures |
> 
> When Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> < 0 and Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> > 0, Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> is negative at all temperatures, so the reaction is always feasible regardless of temperature.

parts.problemMd:
Carbon dioxide and hydrogen can react to form methanol.

CO<sub>2</sub> (g) + 3H<sub>2</sub> (g) ⇌ CH<sub>3</sub>OH (g) + H<sub>2</sub>O (g)

Data for standard enthalpy of formation and standard entropy is shown in Table 1.1.

**Table 1.1**

|   | CO<sub>2</sub> (g) | H<sub>2</sub> (g) | CH<sub>3</sub>OH (g) | H<sub>2</sub>O (g) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>f</sub> / kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> | -394 | 0 | -201 | -242 |
| *S*<sup>θ</sup> / J K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup> | 214 | 131 | 238 | 189 |

i) Calculate the standard enthalpy change, Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup>, for this reaction. Show your working.

[2]

ii) Calculate the standard entropy change, Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>, for this reaction. Show your working.

[2]

iii) Hence, calculate the standard Gibbs free energy change, Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup>, for this reaction at 790 K. Show your working.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the standard thermodynamic quantities for the reaction:

i) Standard enthalpy change, Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup>:

- Apply Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> = ΣΔ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>f</sub>(products) − ΣΔ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>f</sub>(reactants) and substitute values:

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> = [(−201) + (−242)] − [(−394) + (3 x 0)]

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> = −443 − (−394) **[1 mark]**

- Calculate Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup>:

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> = **−49 kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> i)
> 
> 1 mark for correct substitution into the Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> expression
> 
> 1 mark for Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> = −49 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>
> 
> Allow −48 to −50 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>

ii) Standard entropy change, Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>:

- Apply Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = Σ*S*<sup>θ</sup>(products) − Σ*S*<sup>θ</sup>(reactants) and substitute values:

Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = [(238) + (189)] − [(214) + (3 x 131)]

Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = 427 − 607 **[1 mark]**

- Calculate Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>:

Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = **−180 J K**<sup>**-1**</sup>** mol**<sup>**-1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii)
> 
> 1 mark for correct substitution with 3 x 131 for H<sub>2</sub> (g)
> 
> 1 mark for Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = −180 J K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>
> 
> Allow −179 to −181 J K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>

iii) Standard Gibbs free energy change, Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup>, at 790 K:

- Convert Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> to kJ K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup> and substitute into Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> − *T*Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>:

Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = −49 − (790 x (−0.180))

Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = −49 + 142.2 **[1 mark]**

- Calculate Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup>:

Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = **+93.2 kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> iii)
> 
> 1 mark for correct substitution with Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> converted to kJ K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = +93.2 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>; allow error carried forward from (i) and (ii)

> **[exam-tip]**
> In part (iii), before substituting into Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> − *T*Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>, convert Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> from J K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup> to kJ K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup> by dividing by 1000:
> 
> −180 / 1000 = −0.180 kJ K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>
> 
> In part (ii), remember to multiply *S*<sup>θ</sup>(H<sub>2</sub>, g) by 3 (its stoichiometric coefficient) before summing.

iii) Hence, calculate the standard Gibbs free energy change, Δ*G*^θ^, for this reaction at 790 K. Show your working.

Use your answer to part **(a)(iii)** to state whether this reaction is feasible at 790 K.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Carbon dioxide and hydrogen can react to form methanol.

CO₂ (g) + 3H₂ (g) ⇌ CH₃OH (g) + H₂O (g)

Data for standard enthalpy of formation and standard entropy is shown in Table 1.1.

**Table 1.1**

|   | CO₂ (g) | H₂ (g) | CH₃OH (g) | H₂O (g) |
| --- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| ΔH°f / kJ mol⁻¹ | -394 | 0 | -201 | -242 |
| S° / J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ | 214 | 131 | 238 | 189 |

i) Calculate the standard enthalpy change, ΔH°, for this reaction. Show your working.

ii) Calculate the standard entropy change, ΔS°, for this reaction. Show your working.

Using your answers to parts **(a)(i)** and **(a)(ii)**, calculate the temperature below which this reaction is feasible. Show your working.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the temperature below which the reaction is feasible:

- At the feasibility boundary, Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = 0, so *T* = Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> / Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>:

*T* = −49 / −0.180 **[1 mark]**

- Calculate *T*:

*T* = **272 K** **[1 mark]**

The reaction is feasible when *T* < 272 K

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct substitution *T* = Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> / Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> with Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> in kJ K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for *T* = 272 K; allow 270 to 275 K
> 
> Allow error carried forward from (a)(i) and (a)(ii)
> 
> The feasibility statement (*T* < 272 K) is not required for marks

> **[exam-tip]**
> At the feasibility boundary, Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = 0:
> 
> 0 = Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> − *T*Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>
> 
> *T* = Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> / Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>
> 
> Remember to convert Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> to kJ K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup> (−0.180) before dividing, to match the units of Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup>.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Carbon dioxide and hydrogen can react to form methanol.

CO₂ (g) + 3H₂ (g) ⇌ CH₃OH (g) + H₂O (g)

Explain why the reaction in part **(a)** has a negative entropy change.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Why the reaction in part (a) has a negative entropy change:
> 
> - Fewer moles / molecules of gas are produced than are consumed in the reaction **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> In the equation CO<sub>2</sub> (g) + 3H<sub>2</sub> (g) ⇌ CH<sub>3</sub>OH (g) + H<sub>2</sub>O (g), there are 4 moles of gas on the left and 2 moles of gas on the right. Fewer moles of gas means less disorder, so entropy decreases (Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> < 0).

parts.problemMd:
This question is about the feasibility of a reaction.

Calcium carbonate can be thermally decomposed to make calcium oxide.

CaCO<sub>3</sub> (s) → CaO (s) + CO<sub>2</sub> (g)    Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> = +178 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>

Table 2.1 shows the standard entropies of each substance.

**Table 2.1**

| **Substance** | CaCO<sub>3</sub> (s) | CaO (s) | CO<sub>2</sub> (g) |
|---|---|---|---|
| *S*<sup>θ</sup> / J K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup> | 89 | 40 | 214 |

i) Calculate the standard entropy change, Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>, for the decomposition of calcium carbonate. Show your working.

[2]

ii) Use the data given and your answer to (a)(i) to show that the decomposition of calcium carbonate is not feasible at 298 K. Show your working.

[2]

iii) Calculate the temperature above which the decomposition of calcium carbonate is feasible. Show your working.

[3]
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate thermodynamic quantities for the decomposition of calcium carbonate:

i) Standard entropy change, Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>:

- Apply Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = Σ*S*<sup>θ</sup>(products) − Σ*S*<sup>θ</sup>(reactants) and substitute values:

Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = (40 + 214) − 89

Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = 254 − 89 **[1 mark]**

- Calculate Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>:

Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = **+165 J K**<sup>**-1**</sup>** mol**<sup>**-1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> i)
> 
> 1 mark for correct substitution (40 + 214) − 89
> 
> 1 mark for Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = +165 J K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>
> 
> Allow 164 to 166 J K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>

ii) Show the decomposition is not feasible at 298 K:

- Convert Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> to kJ K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup> and substitute into Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> − *T*Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>:

Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = +178 − (298 x 0.165) **[1 mark]**

- Calculate Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup>:

Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = **+129 kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> > 0, so the decomposition is not feasible at 298 K

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii)
> 
> 1 mark for correctly substituting Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup>, *T* = 298 K, and Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> converted to kJ K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = +129 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>
> 
> Allow 128 to 130 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>
> 
> Allow error carried forward from (a)(i) throughout

iii) Temperature above which the decomposition is feasible:

- At the feasibility boundary, Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = 0; rearrange Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> − *T*Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> to find *T*:

*T* = Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> / Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> **[1 mark]**

- Substitute values with Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> in kJ K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>:

*T* = 178 / 0.165 **[1 mark]**

- Calculate *T*:

*T* = **1079 K** **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> iii)
> 
> 1 mark for *T* = Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> / Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for correct substitution with Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> in kJ K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for *T* = 1079 K; allow 1070 to 1090 K
> 
> Allow error carried forward from (a)(i) throughout

> **[exam-tip]**
> Before substituting into Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> − *T*Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>, convert Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> from J K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup> to kJ K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup> by dividing by 1000:
> 
> 165 / 1000 = 0.165 kJ K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>
> 
> Also convert temperature from °C to K:
> 
> 25 °C + 273 = 298 K.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

This question is about the feasibility of a reaction.

Calcium carbonate can be thermally decomposed to make calcium oxide.

CaCO₃ (s) → CaO (s) + CO₂ (g)    ΔH° = +178 kJ mol⁻¹

Table 2.1 shows the standard entropies of each substance.

Table 2.1

| Substance | CaCO₃ (s) | CaO (s) | CO₂ (g) |
| --- | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| S° / J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ | 89 | 40 | 214 |

Explain how the conditions can be changed for the reaction in **(a)** to make the reaction feasible.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> How conditions can be changed for the reaction in (a) to make it feasible:
> 
> - Increase the temperature **[1 mark]**
> - So that *T*Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> > Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> / Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> becomes negative **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Since Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> is positive (endothermic) and Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> is also positive, increasing *T* increases the *T*Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> term. Above 1079 K, *T*Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> > Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup>, making Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> negative and the reaction feasible.

parts.problemMd:
The evaporation of water is an endothermic reaction but also a **feasible** reaction.

Explain why.

Refer to the entropy change that occurs and the change in the arrangement of water molecules.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Why the endothermic evaporation of water is feasible:
> 
> - When water evaporates, molecules become more disordered / spread out; the entropy change is positive **[1 mark]**
> - At sufficiently high temperatures, *T*Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> > Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup>, so Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> < 0 and the reaction is feasible **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Even though evaporation is endothermic (Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> > 0), the large positive entropy change (liquid → gas, molecules become much more disordered) means the *T*Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> term can exceed Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> at high enough temperatures, giving Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> < 0 and a feasible process.

parts.problemMd:
The equation for the reaction between hydrogen and oxygen to form gaseous water is:

H<sub>2</sub> (g) + ½O<sub>2</sub> (g) → H<sub>2</sub>O (g)

Use the information in Table 2.2 to answer the following.

**Table 2.2**

|   | *S*<sup>θ</sup> / J K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup> | Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>f</sub> / kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> |
|---|---|---|
| H<sub>2</sub> (g) | 131 | 0 |
| O<sub>2</sub> (g) | 205 | 0 |
| H<sub>2</sub>O (g) | 189 | −242 |

i) Calculate the standard entropy change, Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>, for this reaction. Show your working.

[2]

ii) Calculate the temperature above which this reaction is not feasible. Show your working.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate thermodynamic quantities for the formation of gaseous water:

i) Standard entropy change, Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>:

- Apply Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = Σ*S*<sup>θ</sup>(products) − Σ*S*<sup>θ</sup>(reactants) and substitute values:

Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = 189 − [131 + (½ x 205)]

Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = 189 − 233.5 **[1 mark]**

- Calculate Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>:

Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = **−44.5 J K**<sup>**-1**</sup>** mol**<sup>**-1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> i)
> 
> 1 mark for correct substitution including ½ x 205 for O<sub>2</sub>
> 
> 1 mark for Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = −44.5 J K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>; allow −44 to −45 J K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>

ii) Temperature above which the reaction is not feasible:

- At the feasibility boundary, Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = 0; rearrange to find *T*:

*T* = Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> / Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>

- Convert Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> to J mol<sup>-1</sup> and substitute:

*T* = (−242 x 1000) / (−44.5) **[1 mark]**

- Calculate *T*:

*T* = **5438 K** **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii)
> 
> 1 mark for correct substitution using *T* = Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> / Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> with consistent units
> 
> 1 mark for *T* = 5438 K; allow 5400 to 5500 K
> 
> Allow error carried forward from (d)(i)

> **[exam-tip]**
> When calculating Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>, remember the stoichiometric coefficient for O<sub>2</sub> is ½ — multiply its *S*<sup>θ</sup> value by ½ before subtracting. This is a common source of error.
> 
> To calculate *T*, ensure units are consistent: either convert Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> from kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> to J mol<sup>-1</sup> (multiply by 1000) to match J K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>, or convert Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> to kJ K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup> (divide by 1000).

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The equation for the reaction between hydrogen and oxygen to form gaseous water is:

H~2~ (g) + ½O~2~ (g) → H~2~O (g)

Use the information in Table 2.2 to answer the following.

**Table 2.2**

|   | *S*^θ^ / J K^-1^ mol^-1^ | Δ*H*^θ^~f~ / kJ mol^-1^ |
| --- | :---: | :---: |
| H~2~ (g) | 131 | 0 |
| O~2~ (g) | 205 | 0 |
| H~2~O (g) | 189 | −242 |

ii) Calculate the temperature above which this reaction is not feasible.

Explain what would happen to the sample of gaseous water if it was heated to a higher temperature than that calculated in part **(d)(ii)**.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> What would happen to gaseous water heated above the temperature in (d)(ii):
> 
> - The water would decompose into hydrogen and oxygen / the reverse reaction becomes feasible **[1 mark]**
> - Because Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> for the decomposition of water is negative / less than 0 above this temperature **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Above 5438 K, the formation of gaseous water from H<sub>2</sub> and O<sub>2</sub> is no longer feasible (Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> > 0 for the forward reaction). The reverse reaction — decomposition of water into its elements — has Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> < 0 and so becomes feasible.

parts.problemMd:
Free energy changes can be used to predict the feasibility of chemical reactions and processes.

Table 3.1 shows the equations of five different chemical reactions or processes.

Complete the table to show the sign of Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> for each chemical reaction and process.

**Table 3.1**

| **chemical reaction or process** | **sign of Δ*****S***<sup>**θ**</sup> |
|---|---|
| MgCl<sub>2</sub> (s) + (aq) → MgCl<sub>2</sub> (aq) |   |
| Ca (s) + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (aq) → CaSO<sub>4</sub> (aq) + H<sub>2</sub> (g) |   |
| Na<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (s) + 10H<sub>2</sub>O (l) → Na<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>•10H<sub>2</sub>O (s) |   |
| 2CO (g) + O<sub>2</sub> (g) → 2CO<sub>2</sub> (g) |   |
| C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH (g) → C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH (l) |   |
parts.solutionMd:
The completed table is:

| **chemical reaction or process** | **sign of Δ*****S***<sup>**θ**</sup> |
|---|---|
| MgCl<sub>2</sub> (s) + (aq) → MgCl<sub>2</sub> (aq) | **Final answer:** **+** |
| Ca (s) + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (aq) → CaSO<sub>4</sub> (aq) + H<sub>2</sub> (g) | **Final answer:** **+** |
| Na<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (s) + 10H<sub>2</sub>O (l) → Na<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>•10H<sub>2</sub>O (s) | **Final answer:** **−** |
| 2CO (g) + O<sub>2</sub> (g) → 2CO<sub>2</sub> (g) | **Final answer:** **−** |
| C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH (g) → C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH (l) | **Final answer:** **−** |

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 2 marks for all 5 signs correct
> 
> 1 mark for 3 or 4 signs correct
> 
> 0 marks for 2 or fewer signs correct

> **[exam-tip]**
> Entropy increases (Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> positive) when the system becomes more disordered; it decreases (Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> negative) when the system becomes more ordered. Use state symbols as a guide:
> 
> - Solid or liquid → gas: entropy increases (+)
> - Gas → liquid or solid: entropy decreases (−)
> - Fewer moles of gas in products than reactants: entropy decreases (−)
> - More moles of gas in products: entropy increases (+)
> - Dissolving an ionic solid: entropy increases (+)
> 
> For the hydrated salt Na<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>•10H<sub>2</sub>O: a solid and a liquid combine to form a solid, so disorder decreases (−).

parts.problemMd:
The enthalpy and entropy changes of a reaction are both negative.

Explain how the feasibility of this reaction will change as the temperature decreases.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> How feasibility changes as temperature decreases when both Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> and Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> are negative:
> 
> - As temperature decreases, Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> decreases
> **AND**
> the reaction becomes more feasible **[1 mark]**
> - Because *T*Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> decreases in magnitude / becomes less negative **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> When Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> and Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> are both negative, the feasibility depends on temperature:
> 
> | Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> | Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> | Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> | Feasible? |
> |---|---|---|---|
> | Negative | Negative | Negative at low *T* | At low temperatures |
> 
> To see this numerically, substitute imaginary values. For example, with Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> = −100 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> and Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = −0.10 kJ K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>:
> 
> - At *T* = 100 K: Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = −100 − (100 x −0.10) = −90 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> (feasible)
> - At *T* = 1500 K: Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = −100 − (1500 x −0.10) = +50 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> (not feasible)
> 
> As *T* increases, −*T*Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> becomes more positive, pushing Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> positive. The reaction is feasible only at low temperatures.

parts.problemMd:
The equation for this reversible reaction is:

2SO<sub>2</sub> (g) + O<sub>2</sub> (g) ⇌ 2SO<sub>3</sub> (g)

Use the information in Table 3.2 to answer the following.

**Table 3.2**

|   | SO<sub>2</sub> | O<sub>2</sub> | SO<sub>3</sub> |
|---|---|---|---|
| Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>f</sub> / kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> | −296.8 | 0 | −395.7 |
| *S*<sup>θ</sup> / J K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup> | 248.2 | 205.1 | 256.8 |

i) Calculate the standard enthalpy change, Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup>, for the reaction. Show your working.

[2]

ii) Calculate the standard entropy change, Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>, for the reaction. Show your working.

[2]

iii) Calculate the temperature below which this reaction is feasible. Show your working.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate thermodynamic quantities for the reaction between SO<sub>2</sub> and O<sub>2</sub>:

i) Standard enthalpy change, Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup>:

- Apply Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> = ΣΔ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>f</sub>(products) − ΣΔ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>f</sub>(reactants) and substitute values:

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> = [2 x (−395.7)] − [2 x (−296.8) + 0]

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> = −791.4 − (−593.6) **[1 mark]**

- Calculate Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup>:

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> = **−197.8 kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> i)
> 
> 1 mark for correct substitution with 2 x (−395.7) and 2 x (−296.8)
> 
> 1 mark for Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> = −197.8 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>
> 
> Allow −197 to −198 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>

ii) Standard entropy change, Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>:

- Apply Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = Σ*S*<sup>θ</sup>(products) − Σ*S*<sup>θ</sup>(reactants) and substitute values:

Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = [2 x 256.8] − [2 x 248.2 + 205.1]

Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = 513.6 − 701.5 **[1 mark]**

- Calculate Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>:

Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = **−187.9 J K**<sup>**-1**</sup>** mol**<sup>**-1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii)
> 
> 1 mark for correct substitution with 2 x 256.8, 2 x 248.2, and 205.1
> 
> 1 mark for Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> = −187.9 J K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>
> 
> Allow −187 to −189 J K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>
> 
> Allow error carried forward from (c)(i)

iii) Temperature below which the reaction is feasible:

- At the feasibility boundary, Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = 0; convert Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> to kJ K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup> and find *T*:

*T* = Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> / Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>

*T* = −197.8 / −0.1879 **[1 mark]**

- Calculate *T*:

*T* = **1053 K** **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> iii) 1 mark for correct substitution *T* = Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> / Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> with Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> converted to kJ K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for *T* = 1053 K
> 
> Allow 1050 to 1060 K
> 
> Allow error carried forward from (c)(i) and (c)(ii)

> **[exam-tip]**
> Before calculating *T*, convert Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> from J K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup> to kJ K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup> by dividing by 1000:
> 
> −187.9 / 1000 = −0.1879 kJ K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>
> 
> Since both Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup> and Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> are negative, the two negatives cancel when dividing, giving a positive temperature value.
> 
> Note: Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>f</sub> of O<sub>2</sub> is 0 (element in standard state), but *S*<sup>θ</sup> of O<sub>2</sub> is not 0, which means that it must be included in the Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> calculation.

parts.problemMd: Define the term *electrolysis*.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The definition of electrolysis:
> 
> - Breaking down / decomposing a compound into its elements **[1 mark]**
> - Using an electric current
> **OR**
> Using electricity **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The word 'electrolysis' itself hints at the definition: 'electro' refers to electricity, while 'lysis' comes from the Greek meaning to loosen or separate.
> 
> This is a definition you should know from GCSE, so learn it precisely.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Remember PANIC: **P**ositive **A**node, **N**egative **I**s **C**athode. Anions and cations carry the matching charges to be attracted to their respective electrodes: anions (negative) to the positive anode; cations (positive) to the negative cathode.

parts.problemMd:
i) Define the terms *oxidation* and *reduction* in terms of electrons.

[2]

ii) Construct the half-equation for the reduction of copper(II) ions, Cu<sup>2+</sup>, to form copper metal.

[1]

iii) Construct the half-equation for the oxidation of chloride ions, Cl<sup>–</sup>, to form chlorine, Cl<sub>2</sub>.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The definitions of oxidation and reduction in terms of electrons:
> 
> - Oxidation = loss of electrons **[1 mark]**
> - Reduction = gain of electrons **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The half-equation for the reduction of copper(II) ions, Cu<sup>2+</sup>:
> 
> - Cu<sup>2+</sup> + 2e<sup>–</sup> → Cu **[1 mark]**
> 
> iii) The half-equation for the oxidation of chloride ions, Cl<sup>–</sup>:
> 
> - 2Cl<sup>–</sup> → Cl<sub>2</sub> + 2e<sup>–</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Remember OILRIG: Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain. This applies specifically to electrons in electrochemistry.
> 
> In half-equations, electrons appear on the right-hand side for oxidation (loss) and on the left-hand side for reduction (gain).

parts.problemMd:
Electrolysis is used to extract reactive metals from their metal ores, purify metals and produce non-metals such as fluorine.

Explain why ionic compounds need to be molten or aqueous for electrolysis to occur.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Ionic compounds need to be molten or aqueous for electrolysis to occur because:
> 
> - (When aqueous or molten) the ions are free to move / mobile
> **OR**
> (When solid) the ions are in fixed positions / cannot move **[1 mark]**
> 
> Answers that refer to electrons moving instead of ions are not accepted

> **[exam-tip]**
> For electrolysis to work, a current must flow through the compound. In ionic compounds, it is the ions that carry the charge. In the solid state, ions are held rigidly in a lattice and cannot move. Melting or dissolving the compound frees the ions so current can flow.
> 
> If you refer to electrons moving rather than ions, you will not gain this mark.

parts.problemMd:
i) Complete **Table 2.1** to show the electrolysis products of the molten ionic compounds.

**Table 2.1**

| **Ionic compound** | **Product at anode** | **Product at cathode** |
|---|---|---|
| NaH | Hydrogen | Sodium |
| CaCl<sub>2</sub> |   |   |
| Pb<sub>3</sub>O<sub>4</sub> |   |   |

[2]

ii) State why sodium forms at the negative cathode during the electrolysis of sodium hydride, NaH.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
i) The completed table is:

| **Ionic compound** | **Product at anode** | **Product at cathode** |
|---|---|---|
| NaH | Hydrogen | Sodium |
| CaCl<sub>2</sub> | **Final answer:** **Chlorine / Cl**<sub>**2**</sub> | **Final answer:** **Calcium / Ca** |
| Pb<sub>3</sub>O<sub>4</sub> | **Final answer:** **Oxygen / O**<sub>**2**</sub> | **Final answer:** **Lead / Pb** |

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for CaCl<sub>2</sub> row: anode = chlorine / Cl<sub>2</sub> AND cathode = calcium / Ca
> 
> 1 mark for Pb<sub>3</sub>O<sub>4</sub> row: anode = oxygen / O<sub>2</sub> AND cathode = lead / Pb
> 
> ii) Sodium forms at the cathode because:
> 
> - Sodium is a cation / positive ion attracted to the negative cathode
> **OR**
> Na<sup>+</sup> is attracted to the negative cathode **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> In molten electrolysis, the products are always the component elements. There are no competing ions from water, so the only ions present are those of the compound itself.
> 
> Sodium forms at the cathode because Na<sup>+</sup> is a positive ion. Opposite charges attract, so positive ions migrate to the negative cathode.

parts.problemMd:
Electrolysis of aqueous ionic solutions can give different products compared to the electrolysis of molten ionic compounds.

Give the formulae of **two** ions that can form the different products during the electrolysis of aqueous solutions.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The two ions that can form different products during the electrolysis of aqueous solutions are:
> 
> - H<sup>+</sup>
> **AND**
> OH<sup>–</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The key difference between aqueous and molten electrolysis is the water present in aqueous solutions. Water partially dissociates into H<sup>+</sup> and OH<sup>–</sup> ions. It is these ions that compete with the ions of the dissolved salt and can produce alternative products: hydrogen gas at the cathode and oxygen gas at the anode.

parts.problemMd:
Two factors that affect the actual ions discharged during the electrolysis of aqueous solutions are:

- The relative electrode potential of the ions
- The concentration of the ions

i) State the relationship between the relative electrode potential of the ions and the ions that are discharged during the electrolysis of an aqueous solution.

[1]

ii) Describe the relationship between the concentration of the ions and the ions that are discharged during the electrolysis of an aqueous solution.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The relationship between electrode potential and ions discharged:
> 
> - The ion / cation with the most positive electrode potential / *E*<sup>θ</sup> is discharged at the cathode
> **OR**
> The ion / anion with the most negative electrode potential / *E*<sup>θ</sup> is discharged at the anode **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The relationship between concentration and ions discharged:
> 
> - As the concentration of an ion increases, it is more likely to be discharged **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For part i), the rule follows standard electrode potential: the more positive the *E*<sup>θ</sup>, the more readily that species is reduced. At the cathode, reduction occurs, so the ion with the most positive *E*<sup>θ</sup> is preferentially discharged.
> 
> For part ii), a higher concentration means more ions are available at the electrode surface, increasing the likelihood of discharge. A classic example is the electrolysis of concentrated versus dilute NaCl(aq): concentrated solution gives Cl<sub>2</sub> at the anode; dilute solution gives O<sub>2</sub> instead because OH<sup>–</sup> ions are relatively more abundant.

parts.problemMd: State the equation linking charge, *Q*, current, *I*, and time, *t*. Give the units for each term.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The equation linking charge, current and time:
> 
> - *Q* = *I* x *t*
> **OR**
> *I* = *Q* / *t*
> **OR**
> *t* = *Q* / *I* **[1 mark]**
> 
> The units for each term:
> 
> - Charge = coulombs (C)
> **AND**
> Current = amps / amperes (A)
> **AND**
> Time = seconds (s) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Questions using Faraday's law are not very common at IAL level, but you should know the equations and be able to apply them.
> 
> The most useful form to learn is *Q* = *I* x *t*, since charge is usually what you calculate first in Faraday's law problems.

parts.problemMd:
The relationship between the Faraday constant, *F*, and Avogadro's constant, *L*, is shown in the equation.

*F* = *L* x e

State what one Faraday measures.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> One Faraday measures:
> 
> - The charge carried by 1 mole of electrons / 1 mole of singly charged ions **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The equation *F* = *L* x *e* shows this clearly: *L* is Avogadro's constant (one mole of particles) and *e* is the charge on a single electron. Multiplying gives the total charge on one mole of electrons.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The relationship between the Faraday constant, F, and Avogadro's constant, L, is shown in the equation.

F = L x e

One Faraday measures the charge carried by 1 mole of electrons / 1 mole of singly charged ions.

Complete Table 3.1 to show the number of moles of electrons and the amount of charge for each equation.

**Table 3.1**

| **Equation** | **Number of moles of electrons** | **Amount of charge / C** |
|---|---|---|
| K<sup>+</sup> + e<sup>–</sup> → K | 1 | 96 500 |
| Cr<sup>3+</sup> + 3e<sup>–</sup> → Cr |   |   |
| S<sup>2–</sup> → ..... + ...... |   |   |
parts.solutionMd:
The completed table is:

| **Equation** | **Number of moles of electrons** | **Amount of charge / C** |
|---|---|---|
| K<sup>+</sup> + e<sup>–</sup> → K | 1 | 96 500 |
| Cr<sup>3+</sup> + 3e<sup>–</sup> → Cr | **Final answer:** **3** | **Final answer:** **289 500** |
| **Final answer:** **S**<sup>**2–**</sup>** → S + 2e**<sup>**–**</sup> | **Final answer:** **2** | **Final answer:** **193 000** |

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for Cr<sup>3+</sup> row: 3 moles of electrons **AND **289 500 C of charge
> 
> 1 mark for S<sup>2–</sup> equation: S<sup>2–</sup> → S + 2e<sup>–</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for S<sup>2–</sup> values: 2 moles of electrons **AND **193 000 C of charge

> **[exam-tip]**
> The example row shows that K<sup>+</sup> requires 1 mole of electrons and 96 500 C of charge (one Faraday).
> 
> For Cr<sup>3+</sup> + 3e<sup>–</sup> → Cr:
> 
> - 3 moles of electrons are needed, so charge = 3 x 96 500 = 289 500 C.
> 
> For S<sup>2–</sup>:
> 
> - The ion carries a 2– charge, so it loses 2 moles of electrons to form neutral sulfur.
> - The half-equation is S<sup>2–</sup> → S + 2e<sup>–</sup>, and charge = 2 x 96 500 = 193 000 C.

parts.problemMd:
The chromium half-cell containing Cr / Cr<sup>3+</sup> is connected to a copper half-cell containing Cu / Cu<sup>2+</sup>.

The standard electrode potential for copper is shown as:

Cu<sup>2+</sup> + 2e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ Cu   *E*<sup>θ</sup> = +0.34 V

The standard cell potential of this combination was found to be +1.08 V, where the copper half-cell would undergo reduction.

Calculate the standard electrode potential of the Cr / Cr<sup>3+</sup> half-cell.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the standard electrode potential of the Cr / Cr<sup>3+</sup> half-cell:

- Write the cell potential equation:

*E*<sup>θ</sup><sub>cell</sub> = *E*<sup>θ</sup><sub>reduced</sub> − *E*<sup>θ</sup><sub>oxidised</sub>

- Rearrange the cell potential equation for *E*<sup>θ</sup><sub>oxidised</sub>:

*E*<sup>θ</sup><sub>oxidised</sub> = *E*<sup>θ</sup><sub>reduced</sub> − *E*<sup>θ</sup><sub>cell</sub>

- Substitute values and solve:

*E*<sup>θ</sup><sub>oxidised</sub> = +0.34 − 1.08

*E*<sup>θ</sup><sub>oxidised</sub> = **-0.74 V** **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The cell potential equation is *E*<sup>θ</sup><sub>cell</sub> = *E*<sup>θ</sup><sub>reduced</sub> − *E*<sup>θ</sup><sub>oxidised</sub>. Since the copper half-cell undergoes reduction, it provides *E*<sup>θ</sup><sub>reduced</sub>. Rearrange to find *E*<sup>θ</sup><sub>oxidised</sub> for the chromium half-cell.
> 
> Always identify which half-cell is reduced and which is oxidised before applying the equation. The question tells you copper is reduced, so chromium must be oxidised.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The chromium half-cell containing Cr / Cr^3+^ is connected to a copper half-cell containing Cu / Cu^2+^.

The standard electrode potential for copper is shown as:

Cu^2+^ + 2e^–^ ⇌ Cu   *E*^θ^ = +0.34 V

The standard cell potential of this combination was found to be +1.08 V, where the copper half-cell would undergo reduction.

Calculate the standard electrode potential of the Cr / Cr^3+^ half-cell.

*E*^θ^~oxidised~ = -0.74 V

Construct **two** half-equations to show what would occur if the chromium half-cell was attached to the standard hydrogen half-cell.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The two half-equations are:
> 
> - Cr (s) → Cr<sup>3+</sup> (aq) + 3e<sup>–</sup> **[1 mark]**
> - 2H<sup>+</sup> (aq) + 2e<sup>–</sup> → H<sub>2</sub> (g) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The standard electrode potential of Cr / Cr<sup>3+</sup> is negative (−0.74 V from the previous part), so chromium is more easily oxidised than hydrogen. This means chromium undergoes oxidation (loses electrons) and hydrogen undergoes reduction (gains electrons).

parts.problemMd:
Faraday's constant can be used to calculate the mass of a substance deposited at an electrode or the volume of gas liberated at an electrode during electrolysis.

A current of 1.65 A flows through molten lead(II) chloride for 10 minutes.

Construct the equation for the electrolysis of lead(II) chloride, PbCl<sub>2</sub>.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The equation for the electrolysis of lead(II) chloride:
> 
> - PbCl<sub>2</sub> → Pb + Cl<sub>2</sub> **[1 mark]**
> 
> State symbols are not required

> **[exam-tip]**
> The electrolysis of molten lead(II) chloride produces lead at the cathode (reduction) and chlorine at the anode (oxidation). The overall equation shows the decomposition of the ionic compound into its elements.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A current of 1.65 A flows through molten lead(II) chloride for 10 minutes.

i) Construct the half-equation for the reduction of the lead(II) ion, Pb<sup>2+</sup>.

[1]

ii) The equation to calculate the charge transferred is *Q* = *I* x *t*. The Faraday constant, *F* = 96 500 C mol<sup>-1</sup>.

Use the information in part (a) to calculate the number of coulombs required to deposit one mole of lead at the cathode, the charge transferred during the electrolysis of molten lead(II) chloride, and the mass of lead deposited at the cathode.

[5]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The half-equation for the reduction of the lead(II) ion, Pb<sup>2+</sup>:
> 
> - Pb<sup>2+</sup> + 2e<sup>–</sup> → Pb **[1 mark]**

ii) To calculate the mass of lead deposited at the cathode:

- Determine the number of coulombs required to deposit one mole of lead:

From Pb<sup>2+</sup> + 2e<sup>–</sup> → Pb, 2 moles of electrons are required per mole of lead

Coulombs per mole of Pb = 2 x 96 500

Coulombs per mole of Pb = **193 000 C** **[1 mark]**

- Convert time to seconds:

*t* = 10 x 60

*t *= **600 s** **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the charge transferred:

*Q* = *I* x *t*

*Q* = 1.65 x 600

*Q* = **990 C** **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the moles of lead deposited:

*n*(Pb) = $\frac{990}{193000}$

*n*(Pb) = **5.13 × 10**<sup>**-3**</sup>** mol** **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the mass of lead:

mass = n x *M*<sub>r</sub>

mass = 5.13 × 10<sup>-3</sup> x 207.2

mass = **1.06 g** **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Work through Faraday's law calculations step by step. The key is identifying the number of electrons from the half-equation.
> 
> For Pb<sup>2+</sup> + 2e<sup>–</sup> → Pb, two electrons are needed, so 2 x 96 500 = 193 000 C are required per mole of lead.
> 
> Always convert time to seconds before calculating charge.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A current of 1.65 A flows through molten lead(II) chloride for 10 minutes.

From part (b) calculations:
- Time converted: t = 10 x 60 = 600 s
- Charge transferred: Q = I x t = 1.65 x 600 = 990 C

i) Construct the half-equation for the oxidation of the chloride ion, Cl<sup>–</sup>, to form chlorine, Cl<sub>2</sub>.

[1]

ii) The equation to calculate the charge transferred is *Q* = *I* x *t*. The Faraday constant, *F* = 96 500 C mol<sup>-1</sup>.

Use the information in part (a) and your answers to part (b) to calculate the number of coulombs required to form one mole of chlorine at the anode and the volume of chlorine released at the anode.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The half-equation for the oxidation of the chloride ion, Cl<sup>–</sup>:
> 
> - 2Cl<sup>–</sup> → Cl<sub>2</sub> + 2e<sup>–</sup> **[1 mark]**

ii) To calculate the volume of chlorine released at the anode:

- Determine the number of coulombs required to form one mole of chlorine:

From 2Cl<sup>–</sup> → Cl<sub>2</sub> + 2e<sup>–</sup>, 2 moles of electrons are required per mole of Cl<sub>2</sub>

Coulombs per mole of Cl<sub>2</sub> = 2 x 96 500

Coulombs per mole of Cl<sub>2</sub> = **193 000 C** **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the moles of chlorine released:

*n*(Cl<sub>2</sub>) = $\frac{990}{193000}$

*n*(Cl<sub>2</sub>) = 5.1295 x 10<sup>-3</sup> mol

- Calculate the volume of chlorine released:

Volume = 5.1295 x 10<sup>-3</sup> x 24.0

Volume = **0.123 dm**<sup>**3**</sup>

**[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Since 2Cl<sup>–</sup> → Cl<sub>2</sub> + 2e<sup>–</sup> also involves 2 moles of electrons, the charge calculations are identical to part (b): 193 000 C per mole of Cl<sub>2</sub> and 990 C transferred.
> 
> At RTP, one mole of gas occupies 24.0 dm<sup>3</sup>. Convert moles to volume: 5.1295 x 10<sup>-3</sup> x 24.0 = 0.123 dm<sup>3</sup>.

A student decided to determine the value of the Faraday constant by an electrolysis experiment. Fig. 2.1 is an incomplete diagram showing the apparatus that was used.

List the measurements the student would need to make in order to use the results to calculate a value for the Faraday constant.

> 2. The moles of electrons that carried it

parts.problemMd: Using an equation, state the relationship between the Faraday constant, *F*, the Avogadro constant, *L*, and the charge on the electron, *e*.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The relationship between *F*, *L*, and *e*:
> 
> - *F* = *L* × *e*
> **OR**
> *L* = *F* / *e*
> **OR**
> *e* = *F* / *L* **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> One faraday is the charge carried by one mole of electrons. Each electron carries charge *e* coulombs, and there are *L* electrons per mole, so the total charge is *F* = *L* × *e*.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Using an equation, state the relationship between the Faraday constant, *F*, the Avogadro constant, *L*, and the charge on the electron, *e*.

The relationship between *F*, *L*, and *e*:

- *F* = *L* × *e*

OR

*L* = *F* / *e*

OR

*e* = *F* / *L*

The value the student obtained was: 1 faraday = 9.65 × 10<sup>4</sup> coulombs.

Use this value and your equation in part (c) to calculate the Avogadro constant. Take the charge on the electron to be 1.60 × 10<sup>–19</sup> coulombs.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the Avogadro constant using *L* = *F* / *e*:

*L* = $\frac{9.65\times10^{4}}{1.60\times10^{-19}}$

*L* = **6.03 x 10**<sup>**23**</sup>** mol**<sup>**-1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Allow 6.02 × 10<sup>23</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup> if the student uses a slightly different value of *F*

> **[exam-tip]**
> Rearrange *F* = *L* × *e* to *L* = *F* / *e*, then substitute.
> 
> The answer should be around 6 × 10<sup>23</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>.
> 
> If you get a small number or a negative exponent, recheck your entry into the calculator.

parts.problemMd:
The electrolytic purification of copper can be carried out in an apparatus similar to the one shown in **Fig. 5.1**.

![Electrolysis cell for copper purification showing impure copper anode and pure copper cathode in copper sulfate electrolyte](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/24-electrochemistry/24-1-electrolysis/assets/005-electrolysis-cell-for-copper-purification-showin.png)

**Fig. 5.1**

The impure copper anode contains small quantities of metallic nickel, zinc and silver, together with inert oxides and carbon resulting from the initial reduction of the copper ore with coke. The copper goes into solution at the anode, but the silver remains as the metal and falls to the bottom as part of the anode 'sludge'. The zinc also dissolves.

**Table 5.1** shows a list of standard electrode potentials at 298 K.

**Table 5.1**

| **Electrode reaction** | ***E***<sup>**θ**</sup>** / V** |
|---|---|
| Ag<sup>+</sup> + e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ Ag | +0.80 |
| Cu<sup>2+</sup> + 2e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ Cu | +0.34 |
| Fe<sup>2+</sup> + 2e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ Fe | −0.44 |
| Ni<sup>2+</sup> + 2e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ Ni | −0.25 |
| SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2–</sup> + 4H<sup>+</sup> + 2e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ SO<sub>2</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O | +0.17 |
| Zn<sup>2+</sup> + 2e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ Zn | −0.76 |

i) Construct a half-equation including state symbols for the reaction of copper at the anode.

[1]

ii) Use data from **Table 5.1** to explain why silver remains as the metal.

[2]

iii) Use data from **Table 5.1** to deduce what happens to the nickel at the anode.

[2]

iv) Construct a half-equation including state symbols for the main reaction at the cathode.

[1]

v) Use data from **Table 5.1** to explain why zinc is not deposited on the cathode.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The half-equation at the anode:
> 
> - Cu (s) → Cu<sup>2+</sup> (aq) + 2e<sup>–</sup> **[1 mark]**
> 
> State symbols required
> 
> ii) Silver remains as the metal because:
> 
> - *E*<sup>θ</sup> for Ag<sup>+</sup> / Ag (+0.80 V) is more positive than *E*<sup>θ</sup> for Cu<sup>2+</sup> / Cu (+0.34 V) **[1 mark]**
> - Silver is less easily oxidised than copper **[1 mark]**
> 
> iii) Nickel at the anode:
> 
> - *E*<sup>θ</sup> for Ni<sup>2+</sup> / Ni (−0.25 V) is more negative than *E*<sup>θ</sup> for Cu<sup>2+</sup> / Cu (+0.34 V) **[1 mark]**
> - Nickel is readily oxidised and dissolves as Ni<sup>2+</sup> (aq) **[1 mark]**
> 
> iv) The half-equation at the cathode:
> 
> - Cu<sup>2+</sup> (aq) + 2e<sup>–</sup> → Cu (s) **[1 mark]**
> 
> State symbols required
> 
> v) Zinc is not deposited at the cathode because:
> 
> - *E*<sup>θ</sup> for Zn<sup>2+</sup> / Zn is −0.76 V (more negative than Cu<sup>2+</sup> / Cu), so Zn<sup>2+</sup> is less easily reduced than Cu<sup>2+</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The key rule: the more positive the *E*<sup>θ</sup>, the more easily the left-hand species is reduced; the more negative the *E*<sup>θ</sup>, the more easily the right-hand species is oxidised.
> 
> Ag (+0.80 V) is more positive than Cu (+0.34 V), so Ag is harder to oxidise and stays as the metal.
> 
> Ni (−0.25 V) and Zn (−0.76 V) are more negative than Cu, so they dissolve from the anode. At the cathode, Cu<sup>2+</sup> (+0.34 V) is preferentially reduced over Zn<sup>2+</sup> (−0.76 V).

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The electrolytic purification of copper can be carried out in an apparatus similar to the one shown in **Fig. 5.1**.

The impure copper anode contains small quantities of metallic nickel, zinc and silver, together with inert oxides and carbon resulting from the initial reduction of the copper ore with coke. The copper goes into solution at the anode, but the silver remains as the metal and falls to the bottom as part of the anode 'sludge'. The zinc also dissolves.

**Table 5.1** shows a list of standard electrode potentials at 298 K.

| **Electrode reaction** | ***E***^**θ**^** / V** |
| --- | :---: |
| Ag^+^ + e^–^ ⇌ Ag | +0.80 |
| Cu^2+^ + 2e^–^ ⇌ Cu | +0.34 |
| Fe^2+^ + 2e^–^ ⇌ Fe | −0.44 |
| Ni^2+^ + 2e^–^ ⇌ Ni | −0.25 |
| SO~4~^2–^ + 4H^+^ + 2e^–^ ⇌ SO~2~ + 2H~2~O | +0.17 |
| Zn^2+^ + 2e^–^ ⇌ Zn | −0.76 |

As the electrolysis proceeds, the blue colour of the electrolyte slowly fades.

Explain why the blue colour fades.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The blue colour fades because:
> 
> - Cu<sup>2+</sup> ions are removed from solution at the cathode / the concentration of Cu<sup>2+</sup> decreases **[1 mark]**
> - Zn<sup>2+</sup> / Ni<sup>2+</sup> ions replace some Cu<sup>2+</sup> in solution
> **OR**
> the rate of Cu<sup>2+</sup> removal at the cathode exceeds the rate of Cu<sup>2+</sup> replacement from the anode **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The blue colour of copper sulfate solution comes from the Cu<sup>2+</sup> ion. As electrolysis proceeds, Cu<sup>2+</sup> is reduced to Cu at the cathode. Although the anode does release Cu<sup>2+</sup>, Zn and Ni impurities also dissolve as Zn<sup>2+</sup> and Ni<sup>2+</sup>, partially replacing the Cu<sup>2+</sup>. The net effect is a gradual decrease in Cu<sup>2+</sup> concentration, so the blue colour fades.

parts.problemMd:
Most of the current passed through the cell is used to dissolve the copper at the anode and precipitate pure copper onto the cathode. However, a small proportion of it is ‘wasted’ in dissolving the impurities at the anode which then remain in solution. When a current of 20.0 A was passed through the cell for 10.0 hours, it was found that 225 g of pure copper was deposited on the cathode.

[Faraday constant, *F* = 9.65 x 10<sup>4</sup> C mol<sup>-1</sup>]

i) Calculate the number of moles of copper produced at the cathode.

[1]

ii) Calculate the number of moles of electrons needed to produce this copper.

[1]

iii) Calculate the number of moles of electrons that passed through the cell.

[2]

iv) Hence calculate the percentage of the current through the cell that has been ‘wasted’ in dissolving the impurities at the anode.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the percentage of current wasted:

i) Calculate the moles of copper produced at the cathode:

n(Cu)  = $\frac{\mathrm{mass}}{A_{r}}$

n(Cu) = $\frac{225}{63.5}$

n(Cu) = **3.54 mol** **[1 mark]**

ii) Calculate the moles of electrons needed to produce this copper:

n(e<sup>–</sup>) needed = 2 × 3.54

n(e<sup>–</sup>) needed = **7.09 mol** **[1 mark]**

iii) Calculate the moles of electrons that passed through the cell:

- Convert time to seconds: *t* = 10.0 × 3600 = 36 000 s

*Q* = *I* × *t*

*Q* = 20.0 × 36 000

*Q* = **7.20 × 10**<sup>**5**</sup>** C** **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the moles of electrons:

n(e<sup>–</sup>) passed = $\frac{7.20\times10^{5}}{9.65\times10^{4}}$

n(e<sup>–</sup>) passed = **7.46 mol** **[1 mark]**

iv) Calculate the percentage wasted:

% wasted = $\frac{7.46-7.09}{7.46}$ × 100

% wasted = **5.0%** **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Accept 4.98% to 5.10% (variation due to rounding at intermediate steps)

> **[exam-tip]**
> Time must be in seconds for *Q* = *I* × *t*: 10.0 hours × 3600 = 36 000 s. Then moles of electrons passed = *Q* / *F*.
> 
> To find the percentage wasted: subtract the moles of electrons that actually deposited copper from the total moles that passed, then divide by the total and multiply by 100. For the best accuracy, carry unrounded intermediate values through your calculator.

Use data from **Table 5.1** to explain why nickel can be purified by a similar electrolysis technique to that used for copper, using an impure nickel anode, a pure nickel cathode, and nickel sulfate as the electrolyte.

parts.problemMd: State the relationship between the Faraday constant, *F*, the charge on an electron, *e*, and the Avogadro constant, *L*.

**[4 marks]**
