parts.problemMd:
The following are the results obtained from one such experiment.

| current passed through the cell | 0.375 A |
|---|---|
| time current was passed through cell | 40.0 min |
| initial mass of copper cathode | 49.637 g |
| final mass of copper cathode | 49.936 g |

Use the experimental results to calculate a value of the Avogadro constant, *L*, to 3 significant figures.

[electronic charge, *e* = 1.60 x 10<sup>-19</sup> C]
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the Avogadro constant, *L*:

- List the known values:

- current, *I* = 0.375 A
- time, *t* = 40.0 min = 40.0 x 60 = 2400 s
- mass of Cu deposited = 49.936 − 49.637 = 0.299 g

- Calculate the charge passed, *Q*:

*Q* = *It*

*Q* = 0.375 x 2400

*Q* = 900 C **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the moles of copper deposited, n(Cu):

n(Cu) = $\frac{0.299}{63.5}$

n(Cu) = 4.71 x 10<sup>-3</sup> mol **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the charge required to deposit 1 mol of Cu:

charge for 1 mol Cu = $\frac{900}{4.71\times10^{-3}}$

charge for 1 mol Cu = 191 083 C **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the charge carried by 1 mol of electrons (Cu<sup>2+</sup> + 2e<sup>–</sup> → Cu, so 1 mol Cu requires 2 mol e<sup>–</sup>):

charge on 1 mol e<sup>–</sup> = $\frac{191083}{2}$

charge on 1 mol e<sup>–</sup> = 95 541 C **[1 mark]**

- Calculate *L*:

*L* = $\frac{95541}{1.60\times10^{-19}}$

*L* = **5.97 x 10**<sup>**23**</sup>** mol**<sup>**-1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Allow Method 2: calculate n(Cu) → n(e<sup>–</sup>) = 2 x n(Cu) → Q = *It* → number of e<sup>–</sup> passed = Q / e → *L* = number of e<sup>–</sup> / n(e<sup>–</sup>), also giving *L* = 5.97 x 10<sup>23</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>.
> 
> Allow intermediate values rounded to 3 sf at each step, provided the final answer rounds correctly to 5.97 x 10<sup>23</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Each Cu<sup>2+</sup> ion requires 2 electrons to be reduced to Cu, so 1 mol Cu requires 2 mol of electrons. This is the key step that converts charge per mole of Cu into charge per mole of electrons.
> 
> If you use the unrounded value for n(Cu) (4.70866... x 10<sup>-3</sup> mol) at each step, intermediate values differ slightly but the final answer to 3 significant figures remains 5.97 x 10<sup>23</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>. The final answer must be given to 3 significant figures.

parts.problemMd:
**Table 2.1** shows a list of standard electrode potentials at 298 K.

**Table 2.1**

| **Electrode reaction** | ***E***<sup>**θ**</sup>** / V** |
|---|---|
| Ag<sup>+</sup> + e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ Ag | +0.80 |
| Br<sub>2</sub> + 2e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ 2Br<sup>–</sup> | +1.07 |
| F<sub>2</sub> + 2e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ 2F<sup>–</sup> | +2.87 |
| Fe<sup>2+</sup> + 2e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ Fe | –0.44 |
| 2H<sup>+</sup> + 2e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ H<sub>2</sub> | 0.00 |
| Mg<sup>2+</sup> + 2e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ Mg | –2.38 |
| O<sub>2</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O + 4e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ 4OH<sup>–</sup> | +0.40 |
| SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2–</sup> + 4H<sup>+</sup> + 2e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ SO<sub>2</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O | +0.17 |

Use the information in **Table 2.1** to deduce the substances formed at the anode and cathode when 1.0 mol dm<sup>−3</sup> aqueous solutions of the following compounds are electrolysed.

| **compound** | **product at anode** | **product at cathode** |
|---|---|---|
| AgF |   |   |
| FeSO<sub>4</sub> |   |   |
| MgBr<sub>2</sub> |   |   |
parts.solutionMd:
The substances formed at each electrode are:

| **compound** | **product at anode** | **product at cathode** |
|---|---|---|
| AgF | **Final answer:** **O**<sub>**2**</sub>** / Oxygen** | **Final answer:** **Ag / Silver** |
| FeSO<sub>4</sub> | **Final answer:** **O**<sub>**2**</sub>** / Oxygen** | **Final answer:** **H**<sub>**2**</sub>** / Hydrogen** |
| MgBr<sub>2</sub> | **Final answer:** **Br**<sub>**2**</sub>** / Bromine** | **Final answer:** **H**<sub>**2**</sub>** / Hydrogen** |

**[5 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 6 correct answers: 5 marks
> 
> 5 correct answers: 4 marks
> 
> 4 correct answers: 3 marks
> 
> 3 correct answers: 2 marks
> 
> 2 correct answers: 1 mark
> 
> Molecular formulae are required. Atomic symbols alone (e.g. Br, O) are not accepted.

> **[exam-tip]**
> In an aqueous solution, H<sup>+</sup> and OH<sup>–</sup> ions from water are also present and can be discharged. To predict which ion is discharged:
> 
> At the cathode, the cation with the most positive *E*<sup>θ</sup> is discharged.
> 
> - In AgF, Ag<sup>+</sup> (*E*<sup>θ</sup> = +0.80 V) and H<sup>+</sup> (*E*<sup>θ</sup> = 0.00 V) are both present.
> - Ag<sup>+</sup> has the more positive *E*<sup>θ</sup>, so Ag is deposited at the cathode.
> 
> At the anode, the anion discharged depends on its identity:
> 
> - Halide ions (Cl<sup>–</sup>, Br<sup>–</sup>, I<sup>–</sup>) are discharged in preference to OH<sup>–</sup> from water, producing the halogen (Cl<sub>2</sub>, Br<sub>2</sub>, or I<sub>2</sub>).
> - F<sup>–</sup> is never discharged in aqueous solution.
> 
>   - F<sub>2</sub>/F<sup>–</sup> has the highest reduction *E*<sup>θ</sup> in the table (+2.87 V), making F<sup>–</sup> far too difficult to oxidise.
>   - OH<sup>–</sup> from water is preferentially oxidised, forming O<sub>2</sub>.
> - Polyatomic anions (SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2–</sup>, NO<sub>3</sub><sup>–</sup>) are never discharged in preference to OH<sup>–</sup>.
> 
>   - OH<sup>–</sup> is oxidised, forming O<sub>2</sub>.
> 
> Applying these rules:
> 
> - AgF:
> 
>   - F<sup>–</sup> is never discharged in aqueous solution.
>   - So, OH<sup>–</sup> is oxidised → O<sub>2</sub> at the anode.
> - FeSO<sub>4</sub>:
> 
>   - SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2–</sup> is a polyatomic anion.
>   - So, OH<sup>–</sup> is oxidised → O<sub>2</sub> at the anode.
> - MgBr<sub>2</sub>:
> 
>   - Br<sup>–</sup> is a halide.
>   - So, Br<sub>2</sub> is produced at the anode.

parts.problemMd:
Fig. 1.1 shows a lithium–iodine electrochemical cell. These cells are often used in pacemakers as they are reliable and have a life span in the region of 10 years.

![Diagram of a lithium-iodine electrochemical cell showing a lithium electrode and an inert electrode separated by a nickel mesh, labelled as Fig. 1.1](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/24-electrochemistry/24-1-electrolysis/assets/001-diagram-of-a-lithium-iodine-electrochemical-cell.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

It consists of a lithium electrode and an inert electrode immersed in body fluids that are separated by a nickel mesh and collect charge from the anode. It has a high internal resistance which means that only a low current can be drawn.

Explain why the lithium-iodine electrochemical cell is a **dry** cell.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The lithium-iodine electrochemical cell is a dry cell because:
> 
> - There is no water / liquid present in the cell **[1 mark]**
> - Water / liquid could react with the lithium electrode
> **AND**
> (this) could cause the cell to explode
> **OR**
> (this) could cause a build-up of pressure inside the cell **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> This question uses knowledge of Group 1 metal reactivity. Lithium, like all Group 1 metals, reacts vigorously with water to produce a metal hydroxide and hydrogen gas. Since the cell is sealed, hydrogen production would cause a dangerous pressure build-up.
> 
> For both marks, you need two separate points: that there is no liquid in the cell, and why the presence of liquid would be harmful.

parts.problemMd: Construct the overall equation for the reaction taking place at the electrodes of the lithium-iodine electrochemical cell when a current flows.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The overall equation for the lithium-iodine electrochemical cell:
> 
> - 2Li + I<sub>2</sub> → 2Li<sup>+</sup> + 2I<sup>–</sup> **[1 mark]**
> 
> State symbols are not required

> **[exam-tip]**
> Combine the two half-equations, ensuring the electrons cancel:
> 
> - Oxidation (anode): 2Li → 2Li<sup>+</sup> + 2e<sup>–</sup>
> - Reduction (cathode): I<sub>2</sub> + 2e<sup>–</sup> → 2I<sup>–</sup>
> 
> Adding these together cancels the 2e<sup>–</sup>, giving the overall equation 2Li + I<sub>2</sub> → 2Li<sup>+</sup> + 2I<sup>–</sup>.

parts.problemMd:
Table 1.1 lists electrode potentials for some electrode reactions.

**Table 1.1**

| **Electrode reaction** | ***E***<sup>**θ**</sup>** / V** |
|---|---|
| I<sub>2</sub> + 2e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ 2I<sup>–</sup> | + 0.54 |
| Li<sup>+</sup> + e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ Li | – 3.04 |
| Ni<sup>2+</sup> + 2e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ Ni | – 0.25 |

Calculate the *E*<sup>θ</sup><sub>cell</sub> for the lithium-iodine electrochemical cell.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate *E*<sup>θ</sup><sub>cell</sub> for the lithium-iodine electrochemical cell:

*E*<sup>θ</sup><sub>cell</sub> = *E*<sup>θ</sup><sub>reduced</sub> − *E*<sup>θ</sup><sub>oxidised</sub>

*E*<sup>θ</sup><sub>cell</sub> = (+0.54) − (−3.04)

*E*<sup>θ</sup><sub>cell</sub> = **+3.58 V** **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The iodine half-cell (I<sub>2</sub> / I<sup>–</sup>, *E*<sup>θ</sup> = +0.54 V) undergoes reduction as it has the more positive electrode potential. Lithium (Li<sup>+</sup> / Li, *E*<sup>θ</sup> = −3.04 V) is oxidised.
> 
> The Ni<sup>2+</sup> / Ni half-cell is a distractor. It is not involved in the lithium-iodine cell.

parts.problemMd:
A current of 1.5 × 10<sup>-5</sup> A is drawn from this cell.

Calculate the number of days for 0.08 g of the lithium electrode to be used up. Assume the current remains constant throughout this period. Show your working.

The Faraday constant, *F* = 9.65 × 10<sup>4</sup> C mol<sup>–</sup>.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the number of days for 0.08 g of the lithium electrode to be used up:

- Calculate the moles of lithium:

n(Li) = $\frac{0.08}{6.9}$

n(Li) =  = **1.16 × 10**<sup>**-2**</sup>** mol** **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the charge required:

*Q* = n × *F*

*Q* = 1.16 × 10<sup>-2</sup> × 9.65 × 10<sup>4</sup>

*Q* = **1119 C** **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the time in seconds:

*t* = $\frac{1119}{1.5\times10^{-5}}$

*t* = **7.46 × 10**<sup>**7**</sup>** s** **[1 mark]**

- Convert to days:

*t* = $\frac{7.46\times10^{7}}{60\times60\times24}$

*t* = **863 days** **[1 mark]**

parts.problemMd:
A student set up an electrochemical cell using a concentrated sodium chloride solution using a current of 6 A.

State the half-equations occurring at the electrodes during the electrolysis of the concentrated aqueous solution of sodium chloride.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The half-equations at each electrode:
> 
> - Cathode: 2H<sup>+</sup> + 2e<sup>–</sup> → H<sub>2</sub>
> **OR**
> H<sup>+</sup> + e<sup>–</sup> → ½H<sub>2</sub>
> **OR**
> 2H<sub>2</sub>O + 2e<sup>–</sup> → H<sub>2</sub> + 2OH<sup>–</sup> **[1 mark]**
> - Anode: 2Cl<sup>–</sup> → Cl<sub>2</sub> + 2e<sup>–</sup>
> **OR**
> Cl<sup>–</sup> → ½Cl<sub>2</sub> + e<sup>–</sup> **[1 mark]**
> 
> Allow 1 mark if the half-equations are correct but assigned to the wrong electrode

> **[exam-tip]**
> At the cathode (negative electrode), reduction occurs: H<sup>+</sup> ions from water gain electrons to form H<sub>2</sub> gas. At the anode (positive electrode), the concentrated Cl<sup>–</sup> is preferentially discharged to form Cl<sub>2</sub> over OH<sup>–</sup>, because the concentration of Cl<sup>–</sup> is high enough to override the electrode potential difference.
> 
> If you write both half-equations correctly but place them at the wrong electrodes, you can still earn one mark.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A student set up an electrochemical cell using a concentrated sodium chloride solution using a current of 6 A.

Calculate the time, in minutes, to produce 2.00 dm<sup>3</sup> of gas at the **anode** at room temperature and pressure.

The Faraday constant, *F* = 9.65 × 10<sup>4</sup> C mol<sup>–</sup>.

State your answer to 2 significant figures and show your working.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the time to produce 2.00 dm<sup>3</sup> of chlorine gas at the anode:

- Calculate the moles of chlorine:

n(Cl<sub>2</sub>) = $\frac{2.00}{24.0}$

n(Cl<sub>2</sub>) = 0.0833 mol

- Calculate the moles of electrons transferred:

2Cl<sup>–</sup> → Cl<sub>2</sub> + 2e<sup>–</sup>

n(e<sup>–</sup>) = 0.0833 × 2

n(e<sup>–</sup>) = 0.167 mol **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the charge transferred:

*Q* = n × *F*

*Q* = 0.167 × 9.65 × 10<sup>4</sup>

*Q* = 16 100 C **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the time:

*t* = $\frac{16100}{6}$

*t *= 2680 s

- Convert time to minutes:

*t* = $\frac{2680}{60}$

*t *= **45 min** **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Allow 48 min if student uses 22.4 dm<sup>3</sup> mol<sup>–</sup> (STP) instead of 24.0 dm<sup>3</sup> mol<sup>–</sup> (RTP), provided all other steps are correct

> **[exam-tip]**
> At RTP, one mole of gas occupies 24.0 dm<sup>3</sup>. Use this to find moles of Cl<sub>2</sub>.
> 
> The half-equation 2Cl<sup>–</sup> → Cl<sub>2</sub> + 2e<sup>–</sup> shows that 2 moles of electrons are transferred per mole of Cl<sub>2</sub>. Multiply moles of Cl<sub>2</sub> by 2 to get moles of electrons, then use *Q* = n × *F* and *t* = *Q* ÷ *I*. Remember to convert seconds to minutes at the end.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A student set up an electrochemical cell using a concentrated sodium chloride solution using a current of 6 A.

State the half-equations occurring at the electrodes during the electrolysis of the concentrated aqueous solution of sodium chloride.

Anode: 2Cl^– → Cl2 + 2e^–

The student changed the electrolyte to a very dilute sodium chloride solution.

State what change would occur at the anode and give the half equation for the process.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The change at the anode when using very dilute NaCl solution:
> 
> - Oxygen gas / O<sub>2</sub> is produced instead of chlorine **[1 mark]**
> 
> The half-equation at the anode in dilute NaCl solution:
> 
> - 2H<sub>2</sub>O (l) → 4H<sup>+</sup> (aq) + O<sub>2</sub> (g) + 4e<sup>–</sup>
> **OR**
> H<sub>2</sub>O (l) → 2H<sup>+</sup> (aq) + ½O<sub>2</sub> (g) + 2e<sup>–</sup>
> **OR**
> 4OH<sup>–</sup> (aq) → 2H<sub>2</sub>O (l) + O<sub>2</sub> (g) + 4e<sup>–</sup>
> **OR**
> 2OH<sup>–</sup> (aq) → H<sub>2</sub>O (l) + ½O<sub>2</sub> (g) + 2e<sup>–</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> In concentrated NaCl solution, the high Cl<sup>–</sup> concentration causes preferential discharge of Cl<sup>–</sup> at the anode. In very dilute solution, Cl<sup>–</sup> concentration is low and OH<sup>–</sup> / H<sub>2</sub>O is discharged instead, producing O<sub>2</sub>.
> 
> At in-between concentrations, a mixture of both chlorine and oxygen is produced at the anode.

parts.problemMd:
In a different electrolysis experiment, copper(II) sulfate solution was electrolysed using graphite electrodes.

Table 2.1 lists electrode potentials for some electrode reactions.

**Table 2.1**

| **Electrode reaction** | ***E***<sup>**θ**</sup>** / V** |
|---|---|
| Cu<sup>+</sup> + e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ Cu | + 0.52 |
| Cu<sup>2+</sup> + 2e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ Cu | + 0.34 |
| Cu<sup>2+</sup> + e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ Cu<sup>+</sup> | + 0.15 |
| 2H<sub>2</sub>O + 2e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ H<sub>2</sub> + 4OH<sup>–</sup> | – 0.83 |
| O<sub>2</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O + 4e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ 4OH<sup>–</sup> | + 0.40 |
| ½O<sub>2</sub> + 2H<sup>+</sup> + 2e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ H<sub>2</sub>O | + 1.23 |
| SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2–</sup> + 4H<sup>+</sup> + 2e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ SO<sub>2</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O | + 0.17 |
| S<sub>2</sub>O<sub>8</sub><sup>2–</sup> + 2e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ 2SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2–</sup> | + 2.01 |

Explain how the products at the anode and cathode are produced.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Products identified:
> 
> - Anode: oxygen gas / O<sub>2</sub> (g)
> **OR**
> carbon dioxide / CO<sub>2</sub> (g)
> **AND**
> cathode: copper metal / Cu (s) **[1 mark]**
> 
> At the cathode:
> 
> - Cu<sup>2+</sup> (aq) + 2e<sup>–</sup> → Cu (s), *E*<sup>θ</sup> = +0.34 V is preferred over 2H<sub>2</sub>O (l) + 2e<sup>–</sup> → H<sub>2</sub> (g) + 4OH<sup>–</sup> (aq), *E*<sup>θ</sup> = −0.83 V, because Cu<sup>2+</sup> / Cu has a more positive *E*<sup>θ</sup> **[1 mark]**
> 
> At the anode:
> 
> - Sulfate ions cannot be oxidised
> **AND**
> hydroxide / OH<sup>–</sup> ions (from water) are oxidised to form water **[1 mark]**
> - The half-equation at the anode: 2H<sub>2</sub>O (l) → 4H<sup>+</sup> (aq) + O<sub>2</sub> (g) + 4e<sup>–</sup> **[1 mark]**
> - The O<sub>2</sub> produced reacts with the carbon / graphite electrode to form CO<sub>2</sub> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> At the cathode: identify which reduction half-equation has the most positive *E*<sup>θ</sup>. Cu<sup>2+</sup> / Cu (+0.34 V) is more positive than H<sub>2</sub>O / H<sub>2</sub> (−0.83 V), so copper is preferentially deposited.
> 
> At the anode: oxidation occurs at the most positive *E*<sup>θ</sup> for the reverse reaction. Sulfate cannot be oxidised under these conditions. Water / OH<sup>–</sup> is oxidised to give O<sub>2</sub>, which then reacts with the graphite electrode to form CO<sub>2</sub>. This is why graphite electrodes deteriorate during the electrolysis of CuSO<sub>4</sub>(aq).

parts.problemMd:
Table 2.1 lists electrode potentials for the Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub><sup>2–</sup> (aq) / Cr<sup>3+</sup> (aq) and Br<sub>2</sub> (l) / Br<sup>–</sup> (aq) half-cells.

**Table 2.1**

| **Electrode reaction** | ***E***<sup>**θ**</sup>** / V** |
|---|---|
| ½Br<sub>2</sub> (l) + e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ Br<sup>–</sup> (aq) | + 1.09 |
| Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub><sup>2–</sup> (aq) + 14H<sup>+</sup> (aq) + 6e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ 2Cr<sup>3+</sup> (aq) + 7H<sub>2</sub>O (l) | + 1.36 |

Deduce the full equation for the Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub><sup>2–</sup> (aq) / Cr<sup>3+</sup> (aq) and Br<sub>2</sub> (l) / Br<sup>–</sup> (aq) cell.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The full equation for the cell:
> 
> - Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub><sup>2–</sup> (aq) + 14H<sup>+</sup> (aq) + 6Br<sup>–</sup> (aq) → 2Cr<sup>3+</sup> (aq) + 3Br<sub>2</sub> (l) + 7H<sub>2</sub>O (l) **[1 mark]**
> 
> State symbols are not required

> **[exam-tip]**
> Identify which half-equation has the more positive *E*<sup>θ</sup>: that is the reduction (forward direction). The other is reversed to give the oxidation. Multiply each half-equation so the electrons balance, then cancel them to give the overall equation.
> 
> Here:
> 
> - Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub><sup>2–</sup> / Cr<sup>3+</sup> (*E*<sup>θ</sup> = +1.36 V) is reduced
> - Br<sup>–</sup> / Br<sub>2</sub> (*E*<sup>θ</sup> = +1.09 V) is oxidised.
> - Multiply the Br<sup>–</sup> equation by 6 to get 6Br<sup>–</sup> → 3Br<sub>2</sub> + 6e<sup>–</sup>
> - Add to the Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub><sup>2–</sup> equation, and cancel the 6e<sup>–</sup>.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Table 2.1 lists electrode potentials for the Cr~2~O~7~^2–^ (aq) / Cr^3+^ (aq) and Br~2~ (l) / Br^–^ (aq) half-cells.

**Table 2.1**

| **Electrode reaction** | ***E***^**θ**^** / V** |
| --- | :---: |
| ½Br~2~ (l) + e^–^ ⇌ Br^–^ (aq) | + 1.09 |
| Cr~2~O~7~^2–^ (aq) + 14H^+^ (aq) + 6e^–^ ⇌ 2Cr^3+^ (aq) + 7H~2~O (l) | + 1.36 |

Using Table 2.1, calculate the *E*<sup>θ</sup><sub>cell</sub> for the electrochemical cell outlined in part (a).
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate *E*<sup>θ</sup><sub>cell</sub> for the electrochemical cell:

*E*<sup>θ</sup><sub>cell</sub> = *E*<sup>θ</sup><sub>reduced</sub> − *E*<sup>θ</sup><sub>oxidised</sub>

*E*<sup>θ</sup><sub>cell</sub> = 1.36 − 1.09

*E*<sup>θ</sup><sub>cell</sub> = **+0.27 V** **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub><sup>2–</sup> / Cr<sup>3+</sup> has the more positive *E*<sup>θ</sup> (+1.36 V) and undergoes reduction. Br<sub>2</sub> / Br<sup>–</sup> (*E*<sup>θ</sup> = +1.09 V) undergoes oxidation. Apply *E*<sup>θ</sup><sub>cell</sub> = *E*<sup>θ</sup><sub>reduced</sub> − *E*<sup>θ</sup><sub>oxidised</sub>.
> 
> A positive *E*<sup>θ</sup><sub>cell</sub> confirms the reaction is thermodynamically feasible.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Table 2.1 lists electrode potentials for the Cr₂O₇²⁻ (aq) / Cr³⁺ (aq) and Br₂ (l) / Br⁻ (aq) half-cells.

**Table 2.1**

| **Electrode reaction** | ***E***^**θ**^** / V** |
| --- | :---: |
| ½Br₂ (l) + e⁻ ⇌ Br⁻ (aq) | + 1.09 |
| Cr₂O₇²⁻ (aq) + 14H⁺ (aq) + 6e⁻ ⇌ 2Cr³⁺ (aq) + 7H₂O (l) | + 1.36 |

The full equation for the cell:
Cr₂O₇²⁻ (aq) + 14H⁺ (aq) + 6Br⁻ (aq) → 2Cr³⁺ (aq) + 3Br₂ (l) + 7H₂O (l)

*E*^θ^~cell~ = +0.27 V

The electrochemical equation for standard free energy change is given.

Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = −*n*F*E*<sup>θ</sup>

The Faraday constant, *F* = 9.65 × 10<sup>4</sup> C mol<sup>–</sup>.

Use your answers to parts (a) and (b) to deduce whether the reaction of the electrochemical cell is feasible.
parts.solutionMd:
To deduce whether the reaction is feasible:

Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = −*n*F*E*<sup>θ</sup> = −6 × 9.65 × 10<sup>4</sup> × 0.27 = −156 kJ mol<sup>–</sup>

Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> is negative, therefore the reaction is feasible

**[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> n = 6 here because there are 6 electrons transferred in the balanced equation from part (a). Substitute: −6 × 9.65 × 10<sup>4</sup> × 0.27 = −156 330 J mol<sup>–</sup> ≈ −156 kJ mol<sup>–</sup>.
> 
> For feasibility: Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> ≤ 0 means the reaction is spontaneous / feasible. A negative value confirms feasibility.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The electrochemical equation for standard free energy change is given.

Δ*G*^θ^ = −*n*F*E*^θ^

The Faraday constant, *F* = 9.65 × 10^4^ C mol^–^.

An electrochemical cell has a free energy change of −14.475 kJ mol<sup>–</sup>.

Use the information in Table 2.1 to deduce the reactions taking place at each electrode of the electrochemical cell.

**Table 2.1**

| **Electrode reaction** | ***E***<sup>**θ**</sup>** / V** |
|---|---|
| Ag<sup>+</sup> (aq) + e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ Ag (s) | +0.80 |
| Li<sup>+</sup> (aq) + e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ Li (s) | −3.04 |
| ClO<sub>2</sub> (aq) + e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ ClO<sub>2</sub><sup>–</sup> (aq) | +0.95 |
| H<sub>2</sub>O (l) + e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ ½H<sub>2</sub> (g) + OH<sup>–</sup> (aq) | −0.83 |
| Fe<sup>3+</sup> (aq) + e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ Fe<sup>2+</sup> (aq) | +0.77 |
parts.solutionMd:
To deduce the reactions at each electrode:

- Calculate *E*<sup>θ</sup><sub>cell</sub> from Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup>:

*E*<sup>θ</sup><sub>cell</sub> = $\frac{ΔG^{θ}}{-nF}$

*E*<sup>θ</sup><sub>cell</sub> = $\frac{-14475}{-1\times96500}$

*E*<sup>θ</sup><sub>cell</sub> =  **+0.15 V** **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> The pair of half-cells with *E*<sup>θ</sup><sub>cell</sub> = 0.15 V:
> 
> - ClO<sub>2</sub> (aq) + e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ ClO<sub>2</sub><sup>–</sup> (aq), *E*<sup>θ</sup> = +0.95 V
> **AND**
> Ag<sup>+</sup> (aq) + e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ Ag (s), *E*<sup>θ</sup> = +0.80 V
> (difference = 0.95 − 0.80 = 0.15 V) **[1 mark]**
> 
> The reactions at each electrode:
> 
> - Anode: Ag (s) → Ag<sup>+</sup> (aq) + e<sup>–</sup>
> **AND**
> Cathode: ClO<sub>2</sub> (aq) + e<sup>–</sup> → ClO<sub>2</sub><sup>–</sup> (aq) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Rearrange Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = −nF*E*<sup>θ</sup> to give *E*<sup>θ</sup><sub>cell</sub> = Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> / (−nF). Since all half-equations involve 1 electron, n = 1. Substituting gives *E*<sup>θ</sup><sub>cell</sub> = 0.15 V.
> 
> Test pairs from the table until you find two whose *E*<sup>θ</sup> values differ by 0.15 V: ClO<sub>2</sub>/ClO<sub>2</sub><sup>–</sup> (+0.95 V) and Ag<sup>+</sup>/Ag (+0.80 V). The higher *E*<sup>θ</sup> undergoes reduction at the cathode (ClO<sub>2</sub> + e<sup>–</sup> → ClO<sub>2</sub><sup>–</sup>); the lower undergoes oxidation at the anode (Ag → Ag<sup>+</sup> + e<sup>–</sup>).

name: Standard Electrode Potentials E⦵, Standard Cell Potentials E⦵cell & the Nernst Equation

parts.problemMd:
State the standard conditions for the measurement of standard electrode potentials.

Temperature = ..............................

Pressure = ....................................

Ion concentration = ........................
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The standard conditions for measuring standard electrode potentials are:
> 
> - Temperature = 298 K **[1 mark]**
> - Pressure = 1 atm / 101 kPa **[1 mark]**
> - Ion concentration = 1.0 mol dm<sup>–3</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> These standard conditions apply across all of thermodynamics, not just electrochemistry. You will need them for enthalpy, Gibbs free energy, and electrode potential questions.

parts.problemMd:
**Table 4.1**

|   | Half-equation | Standard electrode potential, *E*<sup>θ</sup> / V |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | Ag<sup>+</sup> + e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ Ag | +0.80 |
| **B** | ClO<sup>–</sup> + H<sub>2</sub>O + 2e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ Cl<sup>–</sup> + 2OH<sup>–</sup> | +0.89 |
| **C** | 2H<sub>2</sub>O + 2e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ H<sub>2</sub> + 2OH<sup>–</sup> | –0.83 |

Identify the half-equation from Table 4.1 with the equilibrium position that lies:

i) Furthest left.

[1]

ii) Furthest right.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The half-equation from Table 4.1 with the equilibrium position that lies furthest left is:
> 
> - C / 2H<sub>2</sub>O + 2e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ H<sub>2</sub> + 2OH<sup>–</sup> **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The half-equation from Table 4.1 with the equilibrium position that lies furthest right is:
> 
> - B / ClO<sup>–</sup> + H<sub>2</sub>O + 2e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ Cl<sup>–</sup> + 2OH<sup>–</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The more negative the standard electrode potential, the further the equilibrium lies to the left (the half-cell is less easily reduced). The more positive the value, the further the equilibrium lies to the right (more easily reduced). Here, C has the most negative value (–0.83 V) so lies furthest left; B has the most positive value (+0.89 V) so lies furthest right.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Temperature = 298 K
Pressure = 1 atm / 101 kPa
Ion concentration = 1.0 mol dm^–3^

The standard hydrogen electrode is used as the primary reference electrode for measuring standard electrode potential.

i) Describe a standard hydrogen electrode. Your answer should include the chemicals and conditions used.

[2]

ii) State the standard electrode potential of the standard hydrogen electrode.

*E*<sup>θ</sup> = .......... V

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The standard hydrogen electrode consists of:
> 
> - Hydrogen gas at a pressure of 1 atm / 101 kPa bubbled into / in equilibrium with a 1.0 mol dm<sup>–3</sup> solution of H<sup>+</sup> ions **[1 mark]**
> - With an inert platinum electrode in contact with the hydrogen gas and H<sup>+</sup> ions **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The standard electrode potential of the standard hydrogen electrode is:
> 
> - *E*<sup>θ</sup> = 0 V **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Note that sulfuric acid cannot be used as the electrolyte in a standard hydrogen electrode. H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> is diprotic and does not fully dissociate in its second step, so 1.0 mol dm<sup>–3</sup> H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> does not give [H<sup>+</sup>] = 1.0 mol dm<sup>–3</sup>. A strong monoprotic acid such as HCl gives exactly 1.0 mol dm<sup>–3</sup> H<sup>+</sup>.

parts.solutionMd:
The completed table is:

|---|---|
| non-metal / non-metal ion | Yes |
| **Final answer:** **metal / metal ion** | **Final answer:** **No** |
| **Final answer:** **ion / ion** | **Final answer:** **Yes** |

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for metal / metal ion as a type of half-cell that does not require a platinum electrode
> 
> 1 mark for ion / ion as a type of half-cell that requires a platinum electrode

parts.problemMd:
The direction of electron flow can be determined by comparing the *E*<sup>θ</sup> values of the two half-cells in an electrochemical cell.

State the direction of electron flow in the external circuit of an operating electrochemical cell.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The direction of electron flow in the external circuit is:
> 
> - From the negative electrode to the positive electrode **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Electrons flow from the negative electrode to the positive electrode in the external circuit. Conventional current flows in the opposite direction (positive to negative), so do not confuse the two.

parts.problemMd:
Table 5.2 shows six standard electrode potentials.

**Table 5.2 **

| **Electrode reaction** | ***E***<sup>**θ**</sup>** / V** |
|---|---|
| Cu<sup>+</sup> + e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ Cu | + 0.52 |
| Cu<sup>2+</sup> + 2e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ Cu | + 0.34 |
| Cu<sup>2+</sup> + e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ Cu<sup>+</sup> | + 0.15 |
| Fe<sup>2+</sup> + 2e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ Fe | – 0.44 |
| Fe<sup>3+</sup> + 3e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ Fe | – 0.04 |
| Fe<sup>3+</sup> + e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ Fe<sup>2+</sup> | + 0.77 |

i) Identify a half-cell from Table 5.2 that will ensure that the Cu<sup>+</sup> / Cu half-cell undergoes oxidation.

[1]

ii) Construct the overall equation for the feasible reaction of this electrochemical cell.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The half-cell that will ensure the Cu<sup>+</sup> / Cu half-cell undergoes oxidation is:
> 
> - Fe<sup>3+</sup> / Fe<sup>2+</sup> half-cell **[1 mark]**

ii) The overall equation for the feasible reaction is:

Fe<sup>3+</sup>(aq) + Cu(s) ⇌ Fe<sup>2+</sup>(aq) + Cu<sup>+</sup>(aq)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct reactants: Fe<sup>3+</sup>(aq) and Cu(s)
> 
> 1 mark for correct products: Fe<sup>2+</sup>(aq) and Cu<sup>+</sup>(aq) with correct state symbols throughout

> **[exam-tip]**
> For part (i), for the Cu<sup>+</sup> / Cu half-cell to undergo oxidation, the other half-cell must have a higher *E*<sup>θ</sup> value. Only Fe<sup>3+</sup> + e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ Fe<sup>2+</sup> (+0.77 V) has a higher *E*<sup>θ</sup> than Cu<sup>+</sup> + e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ Cu (+0.52 V).
> 
> For part (ii), construct the overall equation by:
> 
> - Writing the reduction half-equation: Fe<sup>3+</sup>(aq) + e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ Fe<sup>2+</sup>(aq)
> - Reversing the Cu half-equation for oxidation: Cu(s) ⇌ Cu<sup>+</sup>(aq) + e<sup>–</sup>
> - Cancelling the electrons to give: Fe<sup>3+</sup>(aq) + Cu(s) ⇌ Fe<sup>2+</sup>(aq) + Cu<sup>+</sup>(aq)

parts.problemMd:
The standard electrode potentials of the two half-cells are as follows.

[1]

ii) Construct the overall equation for this electrochemical cell.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The electrode that acts as the negative electrode is:
> 
> - Iron / Fe **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The overall equation for this electrochemical cell is:
> 
> - Cu<sup>2+</sup>(aq) + Fe(s) ⇌ Cu(s) + Fe<sup>2+</sup>(aq) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The half-cell with the more negative standard electrode potential acts as the negative electrode and undergoes oxidation. Fe<sup>2+</sup>/Fe (*E*<sup>θ</sup> = −0.44 V) is more negative than Cu<sup>2+</sup>/Cu (*E*<sup>θ</sup> = +0.34 V), so iron is the negative electrode.
> 
> Electrons flow from the negative electrode (Fe) to the positive electrode (Cu) through the external circuit.
> 
> To construct the overall equation, reverse the iron half-equation for oxidation and add to the copper reduction half-equation:
> 
> - Reduction: Cu<sup>2+</sup>(aq) + 2e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ Cu(s)
> - Oxidation: Fe(s) ⇌ Fe<sup>2+</sup>(aq) + 2e<sup>–</sup>
> - Overall: Cu<sup>2+</sup>(aq) + Fe(s) ⇌ Cu(s) + Fe<sup>2+</sup>(aq)

parts.problemMd:
A student set up another electrochemical cell consisting of copper and silver as shown in the following cell representation where the half cell with the greatest negative standard electrode potential is written on the left:

Cu / Cu<sup>2+</sup> ; Ag<sup>+</sup> / Ag

i) Construct a half-equation for the reaction that occurs at the positive electrode.

[1]

ii) Construct a half-equation for the reaction that occurs at the negative electrode.

[1]

iii) Use the half-equations to deduce an overall equation for the cell. Include all state symbols.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The half-equation for the reaction at the positive electrode is:
> 
> - Ag<sup>+</sup>(aq) + e<sup>−</sup> → Ag(s) **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The half-equation for the reaction at the negative electrode is:
> 
> - Cu(s) → Cu<sup>2+</sup>(aq) + 2e<sup>−</sup> **[1 mark]**

iii) The overall equation for the cell is:

Cu(s) + 2Ag<sup>+</sup>(aq) → Cu<sup>2+</sup>(aq) + 2Ag(s)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct overall equation: Cu + 2Ag<sup>+</sup> → Cu<sup>2+</sup> + 2Ag
> 
> 1 mark for all correct state symbols: (s), (aq), (aq), (s)

> **[exam-tip]**
> In the cell representation Cu / Cu<sup>2+</sup> ; Ag<sup>+</sup> / Ag, the left-hand side is the negative electrode (oxidation) and the right-hand side is the positive electrode (reduction).
> 
> To construct the overall equation, multiply the Ag<sup>+</sup> half-equation by 2 so both have the same number of electrons, then add and cancel:
> 
> - Reduction: 2Ag<sup>+</sup>(aq) + 2e<sup>−</sup> → 2Ag(s)
> - Oxidation: Cu(s) → Cu<sup>2+</sup>(aq) + 2e<sup>−</sup>
> - Overall: Cu(s) + 2Ag<sup>+</sup>(aq) → Cu<sup>2+</sup>(aq) + 2Ag(s)

> **[exam-tip]**
> A salt bridge provides an ionic connection between the two half-cells without allowing the solutions to mix. The ions must be mobile to complete the internal circuit.
> 
> Potassium nitrate (KNO<sub>3</sub>) is the standard salt bridge electrolyte because NO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> and K<sup>+</sup> ions do not react with the species in most half-cells. KCl is unsuitable here because Cl<sup>−</sup> ions precipitate with Ag<sup>+</sup> as AgCl(s).

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The apparatus shown was used to measure the standard electrode potential for the reduction of Cr~2~O~7~^2–^ ions to Cr^3+^ ions in acid solution:

Cr~2~O~7~^2–^ (aq) + 14H^+^ (aq) + 6e^–^ ⇌ 2Cr^3+^ (aq) + 7H~2~O (l)

Suggest a suitable solution that could be used as solution **1**.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Solution **1** could be:
> 
> - 1 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> HCl / HNO<sub>3</sub> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Solution 1 is the acid for the standard hydrogen electrode. The H<sup>+</sup> concentration must be exactly 1.00 mol dm<sup>-3</sup>.
> 
> HCl and HNO<sub>3</sub> are strong, monobasic acids that fully ionise, so 1 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> gives exactly 1 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> H<sup>+</sup>. Avoid weak acids (e.g. ethanoic acid) or dibasic acids (e.g. H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>) as neither gives the required H<sup>+</sup> concentration from a 1 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> solution.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The apparatus shown was used to measure the standard electrode potential for the reduction of Cr2O7^2– ions to Cr^3+ ions in acid solution:

Cr2O7^2– (aq) + 14H+ (aq) + 6e– ⇌ 2Cr^3+ (aq) + 7H2O (l)

Solution **2** contains 14.71 g of K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub>.

Calculate the mass of Cr<sub>2</sub>(SO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>3</sub>⋅18H<sub>2</sub>O that should also be used. Show your working.

[*M*<sub>r</sub> values: K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> = 294.2, Cr<sub>2</sub>(SO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>3</sub>⋅18H<sub>2</sub>O = 716.3]
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the mass of Cr<sub>2</sub>(SO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>3</sub>⋅18H<sub>2</sub>O:

- List the known values:

  - Mass of K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> = 14.71 g
  - *M*<sub>r</sub>(K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub>) = 294.2
  - *M*<sub>r</sub>(Cr<sub>2</sub>(SO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>3</sub>⋅18H<sub>2</sub>O) = 716.3
- Calculate the moles of K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub>:

moles = $\frac{\mathrm{mass}}{M_{r}}$

moles = $\frac{14.71}{294.2}$

moles of K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> = 0.0500 mol **[1 mark]**

- The standard solution requires equal molar concentrations of Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub><sup>2–</sup> and Cr<sup>3+</sup>, so 0.0500 mol Cr<sup>3+</sup> is needed:

Each mole of Cr<sub>2</sub>(SO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>3</sub>⋅18H<sub>2</sub>O provides 2 mol Cr<sup>3+</sup>

moles of Cr<sub>2</sub>(SO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>3</sub>⋅18H<sub>2</sub>O = $\frac{0.0500}{2}$ = 0.0250 mol **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the mass:

mass = moles x *M*<sub>r</sub>

mass = 0.0250 x 716.3

mass = **17.9 g** **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Allow 17.91 g (4 sf)
> 
> Allow error carried forward for subsequent marks if the moles of K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> is incorrect

> **[exam-tip]**
> For a standard electrode potential measurement, both the oxidised and reduced species must be at 1.00 mol dm<sup>-3</sup>. This means the molar concentrations of Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub><sup>2–</sup> and Cr<sup>3+</sup> must be equal.
> 
> Since 1 mol Cr<sub>2</sub>(SO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>3</sub>⋅18H<sub>2</sub>O provides 2 mol Cr<sup>3+</sup>, you need half the number of moles of Cr<sub>2</sub>(SO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>3</sub>⋅18H<sub>2</sub>O compared to K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub>.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The apparatus shown was used to measure the standard electrode potential for the reduction of Cr2O7^2– ions to Cr^3+ ions in acid solution:

Cr2O7^2– (aq) + 14H^+ (aq) + 6e^– ⇌ 2Cr^3+ (aq) + 7H2O (l)

Solution 2 contains 14.71 g of K2Cr2O7.

Solution **2** is best acidified with H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> instead of HCl or HBr.

Suggest why.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Solution **2** is best acidified with H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> instead of HCl or HBr because:
> 
> - Dichromate ions / Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub><sup>2–</sup> are strongly oxidising **[1 mark]**
> - Cl<sup>−</sup> / Br<sup>−</sup> ions are more easily oxidised than SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2–</sup> ions **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Potassium dichromate is a strong oxidising agent. Halide ions (Cl<sup>−</sup>, Br<sup>−</sup>) are more easily oxidised than sulfate, so the dichromate would oxidise the acid anion rather than acting as the working oxidant. Sulfate ions are resistant to oxidation, making H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> the correct choice.

parts.solutionMd:
To calculate *E*<sup>θ</sup><sub>cell</sub> and identify the negative electrode:

Ag<sup>+</sup> + e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ Ag  *E*<sup>θ</sup> = +0.80 V

Pt / platinum (Fe<sup>3+</sup>/Fe<sup>2+</sup> half-cell electrode) **[1 mark]**

An electrochemical cell is set up as shown in Fig. 2.1.

Construct an equation to show the reaction taking place in the electrochemical cell in Fig. 2.1.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The equation for the reaction in the electrochemical cell is:
> 
> - Ag<sup>+</sup> (aq) + Fe<sup>2+</sup> (aq) → Ag (s) + Fe<sup>3+</sup> (aq) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Ag<sup>+</sup> (aq) is reduced (gains an electron) and Fe<sup>2+</sup> (aq) is oxidised (loses an electron). The two half-equations each involve 1 electron, so they combine directly:
> 
> - Ag<sup>+</sup> (aq) + e<sup>–</sup> → Ag (s)
> - Fe<sup>2+</sup> (aq) → Fe<sup>3+</sup> (aq) + e<sup>–</sup>
> - Overall: Ag<sup>+</sup> (aq) + Fe<sup>2+</sup> (aq) → Ag (s) + Fe<sup>3+</sup> (aq)

parts.problemMd:
The standard electrode potentials for seven different redox systems are shown in **Table 3.1**.

**Table 3.1**

| **redox system** | **equation** | ***E***<sup>**θ**</sup>** / V** |
|---|---|---|
| **1** | 2H<sup>+</sup>(aq) + 2e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ H<sub>2</sub> (g) | 0.00 |
| **2** | Fe<sup>3+</sup>(aq) + e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ Fe<sup>2+</sup>(aq) | +0.77 |
| **3** | Cu<sup>2+</sup>(aq) + 2e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ Cu(s) | +0.34 |
| **4** | Cl<sub>2</sub>(aq) + 2e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ 2Cl<sup>–</sup>(aq) | +1.36 |
| **5** | O<sub>2</sub> (g) + 4H<sup>+</sup>(aq) + 4e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ 2H<sub>2</sub>O(l) | +1.23 |
| **6** | Al<sup>3+</sup>(aq) + 3e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ Al(s) | −1.66 |
| **7** | I<sub>2</sub>(aq) + 2e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ 2I<sup>–</sup>(aq) | +0.54 |

An electrochemical cell can be made based on redox systems **2** and **3**.

i) Construct the overall equation for the cell reaction.

[1]

ii) Calculate the voltage of this cell.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The overall equation for the cell reaction is:
> 
> - 2Fe<sup>3+</sup> (aq) + Cu (s) → 2Fe<sup>2+</sup> (aq) + Cu<sup>2+</sup> (aq) **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The voltage of this cell is:
> 
> - *E*<sub>cell</sub> (= 0.77 − 0.34) = 0.43 V **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Redox system 2 (Fe<sup>3+</sup>/Fe<sup>2+</sup>, +0.77 V) is more positive than system 3 (Cu<sup>2+</sup>/Cu, +0.34 V), so Fe<sup>3+</sup> is more readily reduced and acts as the oxidising agent. Cu undergoes oxidation.
> 
> To construct the overall equation, write Fe<sup>3+</sup> as reduced (forward) and Cu as oxidised (reverse), multiply to balance electrons, then cancel:
> 
> - 2Fe<sup>3+</sup> (aq) + 2e<sup>–</sup> → 2Fe<sup>2+</sup> (aq)
> - Cu (s) → Cu<sup>2+</sup> (aq) + 2e<sup>–</sup>
> - Overall: 2Fe<sup>3+</sup> (aq) + Cu (s) → 2Fe<sup>2+</sup> (aq) + Cu<sup>2+</sup> (aq)

i) Using redox systems **5**, **6** and **7** **only** in **Table 3.1**, construct the overall equations for **three** reactions that might be feasible.

[3]

ii) Give **two** reasons why these reactions might not take place, even if they are feasible.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
i) The overall equations for **three** reactions that might be feasible are:

- 3O<sub>2</sub> (g) + 12H<sup>+</sup> (aq) + 4Al (s) → 6H<sub>2</sub>O (l) + 4Al<sup>3+</sup> (aq) **[1 mark]**
- 3I<sub>2</sub> (aq) + 2Al (s) → 2Al<sup>3+</sup> (aq) + 6I<sup>–</sup> (aq) **[1 mark]**
- O<sub>2</sub> (g) + 4H<sup>+</sup> (aq) + 4I<sup>–</sup> (aq) → 2H<sub>2</sub>O (l) + 2I<sub>2</sub> (aq) **[1 mark]**

ii) **Two** reasons why these reactions might not take place, even if they are feasible:

- The rate of reaction is slow / *E*<sub>a</sub> is high **[1 mark]**
- Suitable conditions (e.g. catalyst, temperature) are not available **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> For part (i), any three of the three equations above are required. State symbols must be correct throughout for the mark to be awarded.
> 
> For part (ii), allow any two kinetic / conditions-based reasons. Do not accept 'the conditions are not standard' or 'concentration is not 1.0 mol dm<sup>-3</sup>' as a reason for a feasible reaction not proceeding because thermodynamic feasibility already accounts for standard conditions.

> **[exam-tip]**
> A reaction being thermodynamically feasible (positive *E*<sup>θ</sup><sub>cell</sub>) means it is energetically downhill, but this says nothing about the rate. Many feasible reactions have high activation energies and proceed extremely slowly without a catalyst.
> 
> For the three equations, the possible combinations from systems 5, 6, and 7 are: 5 & 6, 6 & 7, and 5 & 7.

Calculate the electrode potential at 298 K of redox system **3** if the concentration of Cu<sup>2+</sup> (aq) ions was 0.0002 mol dm<sup>-3</sup>. Show your working.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the electrode potential of redox system 3 at non-standard conditions:

- State the Nernst equation (from the Data Booklet) and identify the variables:

*E*<sup>θ</sup>(Cu<sup>2+</sup>/Cu) = +0.34 V

z = 2

[Cu<sup>2+</sup>] = 0.0002 mol dm<sup>-3</sup>

The reduced species is the solid metal Cu, which has no concentration term, so the equation simplifies to:

*E* = *E*<sup>θ</sup> + `\frac{0.059}{z}\log_{10}[\text{Cu}^{2+}]`

- Substitute values:

*E* = 0.34 + $\frac{0.059}{2} \mathrm{log}_{10} ( 0 . 0002 )$ **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the logarithm term:

log<sub>10</sub>(0.0002) = −3.699

- Solve the equation:

*E* = 0.34 + (0.0295 x −3.699)

*E* = 0.34 − 0.109 **[1 mark]**

*E* = **+0.23 V** **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Allow *E* = 0.23 V, 0.231 V, or 0.2309 V
> 
> Allow error carried forward if correct substitution but arithmetic error in logarithm step

> **[exam-tip]**
> The Nernst equation is in the Data Booklet: *E* = *E*<sup>θ</sup> + (0.059/*z*) log<sub>10</sub>([oxidised species]/[reduced species]).
> 
> For a metal / metal ion half-cell, the reduced species is the solid metal and its activity = 1, so the term simplifies to just log<sub>10</sub>[Cu<sup>2+</sup>].
> 
> Since [Cu<sup>2+</sup>] = 0.0002 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> < 1.0 mol dm<sup>-3</sup>, log<sub>10</sub>[Cu<sup>2+</sup>] is negative and *E* is less positive than *E*<sup>θ</sup>.

Calculate the standard Gibbs free energy change, and give the units, for the electrochemical cell in part **(b)** and state whether the reaction is feasible.

Show your working.

[4]
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup>:

- List the known values:

  - *E*<sup>θ</sup><sub>cell</sub> = +0.59 V (from part b)
  - *n* = 2 (Ni<sup>2+</sup>/Ni and Cu<sup>2+</sup>/Cu both involve 2 electrons)
  - *F* = 9.65 × 10<sup>4</sup> C mol<sup>−1</sup> (Data Booklet)
- Apply the Gibbs free energy formula:

Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = −*nFE*<sup>θ</sup><sub>cell</sub> **[1 mark]**

Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = −2 × 9.65 × 10<sup>4</sup> × 0.59 **[1 mark]**

Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = −113 870 J mol<sup>−1</sup> **OR** −113.87 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup> **[1 mark]**

The reaction is feasible **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Allow Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = −114 000 J mol<sup>−1</sup> or −114 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup> (3 sf rounding)
> 
> Allow error carried forward from part (b) *E*<sup>θ</sup><sub>cell</sub> value

> **[exam-tip]**
> *n* = 2 because both half-cells involve 2 electrons: Ni<sup>2+</sup> + 2e<sup>−</sup> ⇌ Ni and Cu<sup>2+</sup> + 2e<sup>−</sup> ⇌ Cu.
> 
> The Faraday constant *F* is given in the Data Booklet. Units of Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> as calculated are J mol<sup>−1</sup>; divide by 1000 to convert to kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>.
> 
> A positive *E*<sup>θ</sup><sub>cell</sub> gives a negative Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup>, confirming the reaction is feasible under standard conditions.

  - z = 3
  - [Cr<sup>3+</sup>] = 0.01 mol dm<sup>−3</sup>

*E* = *E*<sup>θ</sup> + `\frac{0.059}{z} \log_{10}[\text{Cr}^{3+}]`

parts.problemMd:
A current of 1.50 A is passed through aqueous CuSO<sub>4</sub> for 25.0 minutes.

Calculate the mass of copper deposited at the cathode. Show your working.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the mass of copper deposited at the cathode:

- List the known values:

  - current, *I* = 1.50 A
  - time, *t* = 25.0 min = 1500 s
  - Faraday constant, *F* = 9.65 × 10<sup>4</sup> C mol<sup>-1</sup>
  - *M*<sub>r</sub> of copper = 63.5
- Calculate the charge passed, *Q*:

*Q* = *I* x *t*

*Q* = 1.50 x 1500

*Q* = 2250 C **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the moles of electrons transferred:

n(e<sup>-</sup>) = $\frac{Q}{F}$

n(e<sup>-</sup>) = $\frac{2250}{9.65\times10^{4}}$

n(e<sup>-</sup>) = 0.02332 mol **[1 mark]**

- Use the half-equation to find the mass of copper deposited:

Cu<sup>2+</sup> (aq) + 2e<sup>-</sup> → Cu (s)

n(Cu) = 0.02332 ÷ 2 = 0.01166 mol

mass = 0.01166 x 63.5

mass = **0.740 g** **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Always convert time to seconds before calculating charge: 25.0 minutes x 60 = 1500 s. The ratio of electrons to copper atoms comes from the half-equation Cu<sup>2+</sup> (aq) + 2e<sup>-</sup> → Cu (s), which shows 2 mol of electrons are needed to deposit 1 mol of copper.

parts.problemMd: Use the Nernst equation from the Data Booklet to calculate the electrode potential (*E*) for the Fe<sup>3+</sup>/Fe<sup>2+</sup> half-cell where [Fe<sup>3+</sup>] = 0.50 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> and [Fe<sup>2+</sup>] = 0.01 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> (*E*<sup>θ</sup> = +0.77 V). Show your working.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the electrode potential of the Fe<sup>3+</sup>/Fe<sup>2+</sup> half-cell:

- List the known values:

  - *E*<sup>θ</sup>(Fe<sup>3+</sup>/Fe<sup>2+</sup>) = +0.77 V
  - [Fe<sup>3+</sup>] = 0.50 mol dm<sup>-3</sup>
  - [Fe<sup>2+</sup>] = 0.01 mol dm<sup>-3</sup>
  - *z* = 1 (one electron transferred: Fe<sup>3+</sup> + e<sup>-</sup> ⇌ Fe<sup>2+</sup>)
- Substitute into the Nernst equation:

*E* = *E*<sup>θ</sup> + $( \frac{0.059}{z} )$ log<sub>10</sub> $\frac{[ \text{oxidised} \text{species} ]}{[ \text{reduced} \text{species} ]}$

*E* = 0.77 + $\frac{0.059}{1}$ log<sub>10</sub> $\frac{0.50}{0.01}$ **[1 mark]**

*E* = 0.77 + 0.059 x log<sub>10</sub> (50)

*E* = 0.77 + (0.059 x 1.699)

*E* = 0.77 + 0.100

*E* = **+0.870 V** **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Check that the oxidised species ([Fe<sup>3+</sup>]) is in the numerator and the reduced species ([Fe<sup>2+</sup>]) is in the denominator of the log term. Here *z* = 1 since only one electron is transferred in the Fe<sup>3+</sup>/Fe<sup>2+</sup> half-equation. The simplified Nernst constant of 0.059 only applies at 298 K.

parts.problemMd:
A cell is constructed using the Fe<sup>3+</sup>/Fe<sup>2+</sup> and Cu<sup>2+</sup>/Cu half-cells under standard conditions. The equation for the overall cell reaction is shown.

2Fe<sup>3+</sup> (aq) + Cu (s) → 2Fe<sup>2+</sup> (aq) + Cu<sup>2+</sup> (aq)

The standard cell potential, *E*<sup>θ</sup><sub>cell</sub>, for this reaction is +0.43 V.

Calculate the standard Gibbs free energy change, Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup>, for this reaction. Give your answer in kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> to three significant figures. Show your working.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the standard Gibbs free energy change, Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup>, for this reaction:

- List the known values:

  - *n* = 2 (2 mol of electrons transferred per mol of Cu oxidised)
  - *F* = 9.65 × 10<sup>4</sup> C mol<sup>-1</sup>
  - *E*<sup>θ</sup><sub>cell</sub> = +0.43 V
- Apply the equation:

Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = −*nFE*<sup>θ</sup><sub>cell</sub> **[1 mark]**

- Substitute values:

Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = −2 x (9.65 × 10<sup>4</sup>) x 0.43

Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = −82 990 J mol<sup>-1</sup>

**[1 mark]**

- Convert to kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>:

Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = −$\frac{82990}{1000}$

Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup> = **−83.0 kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Don't drop the minus sign. A positive *E*<sup>θ</sup><sub>cell</sub> gives a negative Δ*G*<sup>θ</sup>, confirming the reaction is feasible under standard conditions.
> 
> Remember *n* is the number of moles of electrons transferred per mole of reaction as written. Here 2 mol of Fe<sup>3+</sup> are each reduced by 1 electron, so *n* = 2.

parts.problemMd:
Explain why Fig. 3.1 does not represent the standard hydrogen electrode.

![Labelled diagram of the standard hydrogen electrode](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/24-electrochemistry/24-2-standard-electrode-potentials-e-standard-cell-potentials-ecell-and-the-nernst-equation/assets/009-labelled-diagram-of-the-standard-hydrogen-electr.png)

**Fig. 3.1**
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Fig. 3.1 does not represent the standard hydrogen electrode because:
> 
> - Sulfuric acid is a diprotic acid **[1 mark]**
> - The H<sup>+</sup> ion concentration of the solution is not 1.0 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Sulfuric acid undergoes complete first dissociation (H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> → H<sup>+</sup> + HSO<sub>4</sub><sup>-</sup>), but the second dissociation (HSO<sub>4</sub><sup>-</sup> ⇌ H<sup>+</sup> + SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2-</sup>) is only partial. This means a 0.5 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> solution does not give exactly 1.0 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> H<sup>+</sup>.
> 
> For the standard hydrogen electrode, the H<sup>+</sup> concentration must be exactly 1.0 mol dm<sup>-3</sup>, which requires a strong monoprotic acid at 1.0 mol dm<sup>-3</sup>.

parts.problemMd:
The standard electrode potential for Zn<sup>2+</sup> (aq) + 2e<sup>–</sup> → Zn (s) is –0.76 V.

State the meaning of the minus sign in the value of –0.76 V.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The minus sign means:
>

> A negative standard electrode potential means the half-cell acts as a better reducing agent than the standard hydrogen electrode.
> 
> Electrons flow from the more negative electrode to the more positive electrode, from the Zn<sup>2+</sup>/Zn half-cell towards the SHE in the external circuit.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The standard electrode potential for Zn^2+^ (aq) + 2e^–^ → Zn (s) is –0.76 V.

Calculate the length of time, in hours, required to deposit 1.0 g of zinc on the item to be electroplated. Assume the current is a constant 0.1 A throughout this period.

State your answer to 3 significant figures and show your working.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the time required to deposit 1.0 g of zinc:

- List the known values:

  - mass of Zn = 1.0 g
  - *M*<sub>r</sub> of Zn = 65.4 g mol<sup>-1</sup>
  - current, *I* = 0.1 A
  - Faraday constant, *F* = 9.65 × 10<sup>4</sup> C mol<sup>-1</sup>
- Calculate the moles of Zn required:

n(Zn) = $\frac{mass}{M_{r}}$

n(Zn) = $\frac{1.0}{65.4}$

n(Zn) = 0.01529 mol

- Calculate the moles of electrons required:

Zn<sup>2+</sup> (aq) + 2e<sup>-</sup> → Zn (s)

n(e<sup>-</sup>) = 0.01529 × 2

n(e<sup>-</sup>) = 0.03058 mol **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the charge required, *Q*:

*Q* = n(e<sup>-</sup>) × *F*

*Q* = 0.03058 × 9.65 × 10<sup>4</sup>

*Q* = 2951 C **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the time and convert to hours:

*t* = $\frac{Q}{I}$

*t *= $\frac{2951}{0.1}$

*t *= 29 510 s

- Convert to hours:

*t* = $\frac{29510}{3600}$

*t* = **8.20 hours** **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Remember to convert time from seconds to hours at the end by dividing by 3600 (60 × 60).
> 
> The number of moles of electrons comes from the half-equation Zn<sup>2+</sup> (aq) + 2e<sup>-</sup> → Zn (s), which shows 2 mol of electrons are needed per mol of zinc deposited.

parts.problemMd:

A student was asked to plan an experiment to measure the standard electrode potential of the Ag<sup>+</sup> (aq) / Ag (s) half-cell.

i) State the conditions of temperature and pressure under which standard electrode potentials are measured.

ii) Fig. 1.1 shows the diagram drawn by the student.

**Fig. 1.1 **

Complete Table 1.1 to identify **three** mistakes in this diagram and the modifications that should be made to correct them.

**Table 1.1 **

| **Mistake in diagram** | **Modification needed to correct mistake** |
|---|---|
|   |   |
|   |   |
|   |   |

[3]
parts.solutionMd:
## Solution

> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The standard conditions are:
> 
> - 298 K / 25 °C (temperature) AND 101 kPa / 100 kPa / 1 atm (pressure) **[1 mark]**

ii) The completed table identifying the three mistakes is:

| Mistake in diagram | Modification needed to correct mistake |
|---|---|
| **Final answer:** **Ammeter / symbol for ammeter shown in circuit** | **Final answer:** **Replace with a high-resistance voltmeter** |
| **Final answer:** **Ethanoic acid used as the acidic solution** | **Final answer:** **Replace with a solution that is 1.0 mol dm**<sup>**-3**</sup>** with respect to H**<sup>**+**</sup>** (aq)** |

parts.problemMd:
The standard electrode potential, *E*<sup>θ</sup>, of the Ag<sup>+</sup> (aq) / Ag (s) half-cell is +0.80 V.

The electrode potential of an Ag<sup>+</sup> (aq) / Ag (s) half-cell was measured at 25 °C and found to be +0.72 V.

Use the Nernst equation from the Data Booklet to calculate the concentration of silver ions, in mol dm<sup>-3</sup>, in this half-cell. Show your working.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the concentration of silver ions in the half-cell:

- List the known values:

  - *E*<sup>θ</sup>(Ag<sup>+</sup>/Ag) = +0.80 V
  - *E* = +0.72 V
  - *z* = 1 (one electron transferred: Ag<sup>+</sup> + e<sup>-</sup> ⇌ Ag)
  - temperature = 25 °C = 298 K
- Substitute into the Nernst equation:

*E* = *E*<sup>θ</sup> + (0.059/*z*) log<sub>10</sub> [Ag<sup>+</sup> (aq)]

0.72 = 0.80 + (0.059/1) log<sub>10</sub> [Ag<sup>+</sup> (aq)] **[1 mark]**

- Rearrange to find log<sub>10</sub> [Ag<sup>+</sup>]:

log<sub>10</sub> [Ag<sup>+</sup> (aq)] = (0.72 − 0.80) ÷ 0.059

log<sub>10</sub> [Ag<sup>+</sup> (aq)] = −0.08 ÷ 0.059 = −1.356 **[1 mark]**

- Calculate [Ag<sup>+</sup>]:

[Ag<sup>+</sup> (aq)] = 10<sup>−1.356</sup>

[Ag<sup>+</sup> (aq)] = **0.0440 mol dm**<sup>**−3**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For a 1-electron half-reaction (Ag<sup>+</sup> + e<sup>-</sup> ⇌ Ag), *z* = 1, so the Nernst equation simplifies to *E* = *E*<sup>θ</sup> + 0.059 log<sub>10</sub> [Ag<sup>+</sup>].
> 
> Since [Ag<sup>+</sup>] < 1 mol dm<sup>-3</sup>, the log term is negative, making *E* less than *E*<sup>θ</sup> which is consistent with the measured value of +0.72 V being lower than the standard value of +0.80 V.

parts.problemMd:
Table 3.1 lists electrode potentials for some electrode reactions.

**Table 3.1 **

| **Electrode reaction ** | ***E***<sup>**θ**</sup>** / V** |
|---|---|
| Br<sub>2</sub> + 2e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ 2Br<sup>–</sup> | + 1.07 |
| Cl<sub>2</sub> + 2e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ 2Cl <sup>–</sup> | + 1.36 |
| [Co(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup>+ e<sup>–</sup> ⇌  [Co(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> | + 1.81 |
| [Co(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+ </sup>+ e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ [Co(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+ </sup> | + 0.11 |
| Cu<sup>2+</sup> + 2e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ Cu | + 0.34 |
| Fe<sup>2+</sup> + 2e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ Fe | – 0.44 |
| Fe<sup>3+</sup> + e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ Fe<sup>2+</sup> | + 0.77 |
| 2H<sup>+</sup> + 2e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ H<sub>2</sub> | 0.00 |
| I<sub>2</sub> + 2e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ 2I<sup>–</sup> | + 0.54 |
| NO<sub>3</sub><sup>–</sup> + 2H<sup>+</sup> + e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ NO<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O | + 0.81 |
| SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2–</sup> + 4H<sup>+</sup> + 2e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ SO<sub>2</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O | + 0.17 |
| VO<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> + 2H<sup>+</sup> + e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ VO<sup>2+</sup> + H<sub>2</sub>O | +1.00 |

Explain how Table 3.1 could be adapted to show an electrochemical series.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Table 3.1 could be adapted into an electrochemical series by:
> 
> - Placing the reactions in decreasing numerical order of *E*<sup>θ</sup> / ordering from the most positive to the most negative *E*<sup>θ</sup> value **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> An electrochemical series lists electrode reactions in decreasing order of standard electrode potential, with the most positive *E*<sup>θ</sup> at the top and the most negative at the bottom.
> 
> Species at the top have the strongest tendency to be reduced (strongest oxidising agents); species at the bottom have the strongest tendency to be oxidised (strongest reducing agents).

> **[mark-scheme]**
> The halide ion that is the weakest reducing agent is:
> 
> - Cl<sup>-</sup> / chloride (ion) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The weakest reducing agent is the one least easily oxidised.
> 
> From Table 3.1, the halide system with the highest *E*<sup>θ</sup> is Cl<sub>2</sub> + 2e<sup>-</sup> ⇌ 2Cl<sup>-</sup> (*E*<sup>θ</sup> = +1.36 V). The high *E*<sup>θ</sup> means Cl<sub>2</sub> is a strong oxidising agent and Cl<sup>-</sup> is the weakest reducing agent of the halide ions listed.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Sulfate ions cannot oxidise iodide ions because:
> 
> - The *E*<sup>θ</sup> value for the SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2-</sup>/SO<sub>2</sub> system (+0.17 V) is less than the *E*<sup>θ</sup> value for the I<sub>2</sub>/I<sup>-</sup> system (+0.54 V)
> **OR**
> *E*<sup>θ</sup> SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2-</sup>/SO<sub>2</sub> < *E*<sup>θ</sup> I<sub>2</sub>/I<sup>-</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For an oxidation to be feasible, the oxidising agent must have a more positive *E*<sup>θ</sup> than the species being oxidised.
> 
> SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2-</sup> (*E*<sup>θ</sup> = +0.17 V) would need a higher *E*<sup>θ</sup> than the I<sub>2</sub>/I<sup>-</sup> system (+0.54 V) to oxidise I<sup>-</sup>.
> 
> Since 0.17 < 0.54, *E*<sup>θ</sup><sub>cell</sub> would be negative and the reaction is not feasible.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Table 3.1 lists electrode potentials for some electrode reactions.

| **Electrode reaction ** | ***E***^**θ**^** / V** |

| [Co(NH~3~)~6~]^3+ ^+ e^–^ ⇌ [Co(NH~3~)~6~]^2+ ^ | + 0.11 |

| Fe^2+^ + 2e^–^ ⇌ Fe | – 0.44 |
| Fe^3+^ + e^–^ ⇌ Fe^2+^ | + 0.77 |

i) Use Table 3.1 to identify an acid that will oxidise copper. Explain your answer.

[2]

ii) Construct an equation for the reaction.

[1]

iii) Calculate the *E*<sup>θ</sup><sub>cell</sub> for the same overall reaction.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The acid that will oxidise copper is:
> 
> - Nitric acid / HNO<sub>3</sub> **[1 mark]**
> - Because the *E*<sup>θ</sup> value for the NO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup>/NO<sub>2</sub> system (+0.81 V) is greater than the *E*<sup>θ</sup> value for the Cu<sup>2+</sup>/Cu system (+0.34 V) / NO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup> is a better oxidising agent than Cu<sup>2+</sup> **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The equation for the reaction is:
> 
> - Cu (s) + 2NO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup> (aq) + 4H<sup>+</sup> (aq) ⇌ Cu<sup>2+</sup> (aq) + 2NO<sub>2</sub> (g) + 2H<sub>2</sub>O (l) **[1 mark]**
> 
> State symbols are required as this is an ionic equation.
> 
> iii) The *E*<sup>θ</sup><sub>cell</sub> for this reaction is:
> 
> - *E*<sup>θ</sup><sub>cell</sub> = 0.81 − 0.34 = **+0.47 V** **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Only nitric acid will oxidise copper because only the NO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup>/NO<sub>2</sub> system (*E*<sup>θ</sup> = +0.81 V) has a more positive *E*<sup>θ</sup> than Cu<sup>2+</sup>/Cu (+0.34 V).
> 
> The equation is derived by reversing the copper half-equation and doubling the nitrate half-equation to balance electrons.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> The two cobalt(III) complex ions have different standard electrode potentials because:
> 
> - They have different ligands **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Different ligands affect the electron density around the cobalt centre by different amounts (related to ligand field strength). This changes how readily Co<sup>3+</sup> is reduced to Co<sup>2+</sup>, so the *E*<sup>θ</sup> value differs.
> 
> NH<sub>3</sub> is a stronger-field ligand than H<sub>2</sub>O, giving [Co(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup>/<sup>2+</sup> a much lower *E*<sup>θ</sup> (+0.11 V) compared to [Co(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup>/<sup>2+</sup> (+1.81 V).

> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) [Co(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup> will undergo a redox reaction with [Fe(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> because:

ii) The equation for this reaction is:

[Co(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup> (aq) + [Fe(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> (aq) ⇌ [Co(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> (aq) + [Fe(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup> (aq)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for the correct species: [Co(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup> and [Fe(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> on the left; [Co(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> and [Fe(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup> on the right
> 
> 1 mark for (aq) state symbols on all four complex ion species

> **[exam-tip]**
> State symbols are essential for this ionic equation. All four cobalt and iron complex ions are aqueous species, so (aq) must appear on every species.
> 
> A common error is to write the simplified equation Co<sup>3+</sup> + Fe<sup>2+</sup> ⇌ Co<sup>2+</sup> + Fe<sup>3+</sup> without state symbols, which would lose the second equation mark.

parts.problemMd:
pH calculations of buffer solutions use the following equation:

`K_a = \frac{[H^+][A^-]}{[HA]}`

State the assumptions made when using this equation for buffer solutions.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The assumptions made when using this equation for buffer calculations are:
> 
> - The equilibrium concentration of the weak acid, [HA], is equal to the initial concentration of the weak acid **[1 mark]**
> - The equilibrium concentration of the conjugate base, [A<sup>-</sup>], is equal to the initial concentration of the salt **[1 mark]**
> 
> These assumptions hold because the degree of dissociation of the weak acid is negligible, so the contributions to [HA] and [A<sup>-</sup>] from dissociation are insignificant.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Both assumptions stem from the same principle: the weak acid dissociates so slightly that the equilibrium concentrations of HA and A<sup>-</sup> are effectively unchanged from the initial values. If asked to justify the assumptions, state that the degree of dissociation is negligible.

parts.problemMd: Suggest a salt that could be used to form a buffer solution with propanoic acid, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COOH.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> A salt that could be used to form a buffer solution with propanoic acid is:
> 
> - Sodium propanoate / CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COONa
> **OR**
> Potassium propanoate / CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COOK
> **OR**
> Lithium propanoate / CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COOLi **[1 mark]**
> 
> Any other soluble salt containing the CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COO<sup>-</sup> ion is accepted

> **[exam-tip]**
> An acidic buffer requires a weak acid and the salt of that weak acid. The salt must be soluble. Group 1 metal salts (sodium, potassium, lithium) are always soluble and are the standard choices.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

pH calculations of buffer solutions use the following equation:

\$\$K_{a} = \frac{\left[\right. H^{+} \left]\right. \left[\right. A^{-} \left]\right.}{\left[\right. H A \left]\right.}\$\$

A buffer solution contains propanoic acid at a concentration of 0.15 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> and a propanoate salt with [A<sup>-</sup>] = 0.30 mol dm<sup>-3</sup>.

The value of *K*<sub>a</sub> for propanoic acid at 298 K is 1.35 × 10<sup>-5</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup>.

Calculate the pH of this buffer solution at 298 K. Show your working.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the pH of the buffer solution:

- Write the expression for *K*<sub>a</sub>:

`K_a = \frac{[H^+][A^-]}{[HA]}` **[1 mark]**

- Rearrange to find [H<sup>+</sup>]:

`[H^+] = \frac{K_a \times [HA]}{[A^-]}` **[1 mark]**

- Substitute values and calculate [H<sup>+</sup>]:

`[H^+] = \frac{1.35 \times 10^{-5} \times 0.15}{0.30}`

[H<sup>+</sup>] = 6.75 × 10<sup>-6</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup> **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the pH:

pH = –log(6.75 × 10<sup>-6</sup>)

pH = **5.17** **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct *K*<sub>a</sub> expression
> 
> 1 mark for correctly rearranging to find [H<sup>+</sup>]
> 
> 1 mark for [H<sup>+</sup>] = 6.75 × 10<sup>-6</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for pH = 5.17
> 
> Allow error carried forward from an incorrect [H<sup>+</sup>] value if pH = –log[H<sup>+</sup>] is correctly applied

> **[exam-tip]**
> The Henderson-Hasselbalch equation gives an equivalent route:
> 
> pH = p*K*<sub>a</sub> + log([A<sup>-</sup>] / [HA]).
> 
> Here p*K*<sub>a</sub> = –log(1.35 × 10<sup>-5</sup>) = 4.87, and log(0.30 / 0.15) = log 2 = 0.30, giving pH = 4.87 + 0.30 = 5.17.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

pH calculations of buffer solutions use the following equation:

Ka = [H+][A-] / [HA]

Buffer solutions can be tailored to a specific pH by 'coarse-tuning' by changing the acid used, and 'fine-tuning' by altering the ratio of [HA] : [A<sup>-</sup>].

State and explain the effect on the pH of the buffer solution of increasing the concentration of the salt only.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The effect on pH when the concentration of the salt is increased:
> 
> - The pH will increase **[1 mark]**
> - [A<sup>-</sup>] increases, so [H<sup>+</sup>] = *K*<sub>a</sub>[HA] / [A<sup>-</sup>] decreases, therefore pH increases **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Use the expression [H<sup>+</sup>] = *K*<sub>a</sub>[HA] / [A<sup>-</sup>] to reason through the effect: a larger [A<sup>-</sup>] makes the fraction smaller, decreasing [H<sup>+</sup>] and increasing pH. This is 'fine-tuning' as the ratio [HA] : [A<sup>-</sup>] is being shifted towards A<sup>-</sup>.

parts.problemMd: Explain why a 0.10 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> solution of a strong acid has a significantly different pH from a 0.10 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> solution of a weak acid.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The reason why equal concentrations of a strong and weak acid have different pH values:
> 
> - A strong acid fully dissociates / ionises in solution, so [H<sup>+</sup>] is equal to the initial concentration of the acid
> **AND**
> A weak acid only partially dissociates, so [H<sup>+</sup>] is much less than the initial concentration **[1 mark]**
> - The strong acid therefore has a higher [H<sup>+</sup>] and a lower pH than the weak acid **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> pH depends on [H<sup>+</sup>], not on the total concentration of acid molecules.
> 
> A strong acid at 0.10 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> fully dissociates to give [H<sup>+</sup>] = 0.10 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> and pH = 1.0.
> 
> A weak acid at the same concentration only partially dissociates, giving a much lower [H<sup>+</sup>] and a higher pH.

parts.problemMd: Calculate the pH of a 0.1 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> solution of HCl.
parts.solutionMd:
As HCl is a strong acid, it fully dissociates, so [H<sup>+</sup>] = 0.1 mol dm<sup>-3</sup>.

pH = –log<sub>10</sub>(0.1)

pH = **1.0** **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for pH = 1.0
> 
> Allow pH = 1 (without decimal place)

> **[exam-tip]**
> HCl is a strong acid and fully dissociates in water:
> 
> HCl → H<sup>+</sup> + Cl<sup>-</sup>.
> 
> This means [H<sup>+</sup>] = [HCl] = 0.1 mol dm<sup>-3</sup>. Substituting directly into pH = –log<sub>10</sub>[H<sup>+</sup>] gives pH = 1.0.

parts.problemMd:
A sample of 0.1 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> methanoic acid has a *K*<sub>a</sub> value of 1.78 x 10<sup>-4</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup> at 298 K.

i) Write an expression for the acid dissociation constant, *K*<sub>a</sub>, for methanoic acid.

[1]

ii) Calculate the pH of the 0.1 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> methanoic acid. Give your answer to two decimal places and show your working.

[3]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The *K*<sub>a</sub> expression for methanoic acid is:
> 
> - `K_a = \frac{[H^+][HCOO^-]}{[HCOOH]}` **[1 mark]**

ii) To calculate the pH of 0.1 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> methanoic acid:

- Rearrange the *K*<sub>a</sub> expression (applying the assumption that [H<sup>+</sup>] << [HCOOH]):

[H<sup>+</sup>]<sup>2</sup> = *K*<sub>a</sub> x [HCOOH]

[H<sup>+</sup>]<sup>2</sup> = 1.78 x 10<sup>-4</sup> x 0.1

[H<sup>+</sup>]<sup>2</sup> = 1.78 x 10<sup>-5</sup> (mol dm<sup>-3</sup>)<sup>2</sup> **[1 mark]**

- Calculate [H<sup>+</sup>]:

[H<sup>+</sup>] = $\sqrt{1.78\times10^{-5}}$

[H<sup>+</sup>] = 4.22 x 10<sup>-3</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup> **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the pH:

pH = –log<sub>10</sub>(4.22 x 10<sup>-3</sup>)

pH = **2.37** **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for [H<sup>+</sup>]<sup>2</sup> = 1.78 x 10<sup>-5</sup> (mol dm<sup>-3</sup>)<sup>2</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for [H<sup>+</sup>] = 4.22 x 10<sup>-3</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for pH = 2.37
> 
> Allow error carried forward from an incorrect [H<sup>+</sup>] value if pH = –log<sub>10</sub>[H<sup>+</sup>] is correctly applied

> **[exam-tip]**
> The *K*<sub>a</sub> expression must name the specific species (H<sup>+</sup>, HCOO<sup>-</sup>, HCOOH), not a generic HA/A<sup>-</sup> formula.
> 
> In the calculation, the approximation [H<sup>+</sup>]<sup>2</sup> = *K*<sub>a</sub> x [HCOOH] assumes minimal dissociation, so [HCOOH]<sub>eq</sub> ≈ [HCOOH]<sub>initial</sub>.
> 
> Check the assumption holds: here [H<sup>+</sup>] = 4.22 x 10<sup>-3</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup> is much less than 0.1 mol dm<sup>-3</sup>, so the approximation is valid.

parts.problemMd:
The pH of a 0.150 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> solution of piperidine is 11.9.

20.0 cm<sup>3</sup> of 0.200 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> HCl was slowly added to a 20.0 cm<sup>3</sup> sample of 0.150 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> piperidine. The pH was measured throughout the addition. One mole of hydrochloric acid reacts with one mole of piperidine.

i) Calculate the number of moles of HCl remaining at the end of the addition. Show your working.

[2]

ii) Hence calculate [H<sup>+</sup>] and the pH at the end of the addition.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
i) To calculate the moles of HCl remaining at the end of the addition:

- Calculate the initial moles of each reactant:

n(HCl) = $\frac{20.0}{1000}$ x 0.200 =

n(HCl) 4.00 x 10<sup>-3</sup> mol

n(piperidine) = $\frac{20.0}{1000}$ x 0.150

n(piperidine) = 3.00 x 10<sup>-3</sup> mol

**[1 mark]**

- Calculate the moles of HCl remaining:

n(HCl) remaining = 4.00 x 10<sup>-3</sup> – 3.00 x 10<sup>-3</sup> = 1.00 x 10<sup>-3</sup> mol

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for n(HCl) = 4.00 x 10<sup>-3</sup> mol **AND **n(piperidine) = 3.00 x 10<sup>-3</sup> mol
> 
> 1 mark for n(HCl) remaining = 1.00 x 10<sup>-3</sup> mol

ii) To calculate [H<sup>+</sup>] and the pH at the end of the addition (total volume = 40.0 cm<sup>3</sup>):

[H<sup>+</sup>] = $\frac{1.00\times10^{-3}}{0.0400}$

[H<sup>+</sup>] = 0.025 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> **[1 mark]**

pH = –log(0.025)

pH = **1.60** **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for [H<sup>+</sup>] = 0.025 mol dm<sup>-3</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for pH = 1.60
> 
> Allow error carried forward from an incorrect n(HCl) remaining if [H<sup>+</sup>] = n / V is correctly applied

> **[exam-tip]**
> HCl is in excess at the end of the addition, so the excess H<sup>+</sup> ions determine the pH.
> 
> The total volume of the final solution is 20.0 + 20.0 = 40.0 cm<sup>3</sup> = 0.0400 dm<sup>3</sup>.
> 
> Divide the excess moles of HCl by this total volume to find [H<sup>+</sup>].

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The pH of a 0.150 mol dm⁻³ solution of piperidine is 11.9.

20.0 cm³ of 0.200 mol dm⁻³ HCl was slowly added to a 20.0 cm³ sample of 0.150 mol dm⁻³ piperidine. The pH was measured throughout the addition. One mole of hydrochloric acid reacts with one mole of piperidine.

On the following axes shown in Fig. 3.1, sketch how the pH will change during the addition of a total of 20.0 cm<sup>3</sup> of 0.200 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> HCl.

**Fig. 3.1**
parts.solutionMd:
The completed pH curve is:

![Completed pH curve for addition of 0.200 mol dm-3 HCl to 0.150 mol dm-3 piperidine: starts at pH 11.9, with equivalence point at 15.0 cm3 added, ending at pH 1.6](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/25-equilibria/25-1-acids-and-bases/assets/007-completed-ph-curve-for-addition-of-0-200-mol-dm-.jpeg)

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for curve starting at pH 11.9
>
