Barium hydroxide, Ba(OH)<sub>2</sub>, is completely ionised in aqueous solutions. During the addition of 30.0 cm<sup>3</sup> of 0.100 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> Ba(OH)<sub>2</sub> to 20.0 cm<sup>3</sup> of 0.100 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> isocyanic acid, the pH was measured.

Calculate [OH<sup>-</sup>] and the pH of the solution at the end of the addition. Show your working.

On Fig. 2.1, sketch how the pH changes during the addition of a total of 30.0 cm<sup>3</sup> of 0.100 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> Ba(OH)<sub>2</sub> to 20.0 cm<sup>3</sup> of 0.100 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> isocyanic acid.

![Blank graph showing pH (y-axis, 0 to 14) against volume of Ba(OH)2 added in cm3 (x-axis, 0 to 30.0), for sketching the titration curve](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/25-equilibria/25-1-acids-and-bases/assets/003-blank-graph-showing-ph-y-axis-0-to-14-against-vo.png)

**Fig. 2.1**
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate [OH<sup>-</sup>] and the pH at the end of the addition:

- Calculate the initial moles of OH<sup>-</sup> and of HNCO:

moles of OH<sup>-</sup> = 2 x 0.100 x $\frac{30.0}{1000}$ = 6.00 x 10<sup>-3</sup> mol

moles of HNCO = 0.100 x $\frac{20.0}{1000}$ = 2.00 x 10<sup>-3</sup> mol

- Find the moles of OH<sup>-</sup> remaining after neutralisation (in 50.0 cm<sup>3</sup>):

moles of OH<sup>-</sup> remaining = (6.00 – 2.00) x 10<sup>-3</sup> = 4.00 x 10<sup>-3</sup> mol

[OH<sup>-</sup>] = $\frac{4.00\times10^{-3}}{0.0500}$ = 0.0800 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> **[1 mark]**

- Calculate [H<sup>+</sup>] using *K*<sub>w</sub>:

[H<sup>+</sup>] = `\frac{K_w}{[OH^-]}` = $\frac{1.00\times10^{-14}}{0.0800}$ = 1.25 x 10<sup>-13</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup> **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the pH:

pH = –log(1.25 x 10<sup>-13</sup>)

pH = **12.9** **[1 mark]**

The completed pH curve is:

![Completed pH titration curve starting at pH 2.46, with a steep rise at the equivalence point (10.0 cm3 Ba(OH)2 added), reaching a final pH of 12.9](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/25-equilibria/25-1-acids-and-bases/assets/004-completed-ph-titration-curve-starting-at-ph-2-46.jpeg)

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for [OH<sup>-</sup>] = 0.0800 mol dm<sup>-3</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for [H<sup>+</sup>] = 1.25 x 10<sup>-13</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup> and pH = 12.9
> 
> 1 mark for sketch starting at pH = 12.9 is not awarded if [OH<sup>-</sup>] is incorrect
> 
> 1 mark for sketch: curve starts at pH 2.46 (allow 2.5)
> 
> 1 mark for sketch: steep vertical rise (equivalence point) at volume added = 10.0 cm<sup>3</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for sketch: curve finishes at pH 12.9

> **[exam-tip]**
> Ba(OH)<sub>2</sub> provides 2 mol OH<sup>-</sup> per mol Ba(OH)<sub>2</sub>.
> 
> The equivalence point occurs when moles of OH<sup>-</sup> = moles of HNCO: 2 x 0.100 x V/1000 = 2.00 x 10<sup>-3</sup> mol, giving V = 10.0 cm<sup>3</sup>.
> 
> After this point, excess OH<sup>-</sup> raises the pH above 7.
> 
> To find the final pH, use [H<sup>+</sup>] = Kw / [OH<sup>-</sup>] rather than pH = 14 + log[OH<sup>-</sup>]. Both methods give the same answer but the Kw route is more explicit.

parts.problemMd:
This question is about buffer solutions.

Calculate the pH of a buffer solution made by dissolving 0.275 g of benzoic acid (*K*<sub>a</sub> = 6.3 x 10<sup>-5</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup>) and 0.525 g of sodium benzoate in 250 cm<sup>3</sup> of water. Show your working.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the pH of the buffer solution:

- Calculate the moles and concentration of benzoic acid (*M*<sub>r</sub> = 122.0):

moles of C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>COOH = $\frac{0.275}{122.0}$ = 2.25 x 10<sup>-3</sup> mol

[C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>COOH] = $\frac{2.25\times10^{-3}}{0.250}$ = 9.02 x 10<sup>-3</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup>

**[1 mark]**

- Calculate the moles and concentration of sodium benzoate (*M*<sub>r</sub> = 144.0):

moles of C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>COONa = $\frac{0.525}{144.0}$ = 3.65 x 10<sup>-3</sup> mol

[C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>COO<sup>-</sup>] = $\frac{3.65\times10^{-3}}{0.250}$ = 0.0146 mol dm<sup>-3</sup>

**[1 mark]**

- Apply the *K*<sub>a</sub> expression to find [H<sup>+</sup>]:

[H<sup>+</sup>] = *K*<sub>a</sub> x ([C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>COOH] / [C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>COO<sup>-</sup>])

[H<sup>+</sup>] = 6.3 x 10<sup>-5</sup> x (9.02 x 10<sup>-3</sup> / 0.0146)

[H<sup>+</sup>] = 3.90 x 10<sup>-5</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup> **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the pH:

pH = –log(3.90 x 10<sup>-5</sup>)

pH = **4.41** **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct moles **AND **concentration of benzoic acid
> 
> 1 mark for correct moles **AND **concentration of sodium benzoate
> 
> 1 mark for [H<sup>+</sup>] = 3.90 x 10<sup>-5</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup> (allow 3.89–3.90 x 10<sup>-5</sup>)
> 
> 1 mark for pH = 4.41
> 
> Allow moles ratio used directly in place of concentration ratio (volume cancels)

> **[exam-tip]**
> Since both acid and salt are dissolved in the same 250 cm<sup>3</sup>, their volumes are equal and cancel in the ratio [acid]/[salt]. This means moles can be used directly instead of concentrations: [H<sup>+</sup>] = *K*<sub>a</sub> x (moles acid / moles salt).
> 
> The Henderson-Hasselbalch equation gives the same answer:
> 
> pH = p*K*<sub>a</sub> + log([salt] / [acid])
> 
> pH = 4.20 + log(0.0146 / 9.02 x 10<sup>-3</sup>)
> 
> pH = 4.20 + 0.21
> 
> pH = 4.41

parts.problemMd: Calculate the pH of a buffer solution made by mixing together 130 cm<sup>3</sup> of 0.2 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> ethanoic acid (*K*<sub>a</sub> = 1.74 x 10<sup>-5</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup>) and 85 cm<sup>3</sup> of 0.45 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> sodium ethanoate. Show your working.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the pH of the buffer solution:

- Calculate the diluted concentrations after mixing (total volume = 215 cm<sup>3</sup>):

[CH<sub>3</sub>COOH] = 0.2 x $\frac{130}{215}$ = 0.121 mol dm<sup>-3</sup>

[CH<sub>3</sub>COO<sup>-</sup>] = 0.45 x $\frac{85}{215}$ = 0.178 mol dm<sup>-3</sup>

**[1 mark]**

- Apply the *K*<sub>a</sub> expression to find [H<sup>+</sup>]:

[H<sup>+</sup>] = *K*<sub>a</sub> x ([CH<sub>3</sub>COOH] / [CH<sub>3</sub>COO<sup>-</sup>])

[H<sup>+</sup>] = 1.74 x 10<sup>-5</sup> x (0.121 / 0.178)

[H<sup>+</sup>] = 1.18 x 10<sup>-5</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup>

**[1 mark]**

- Calculate the pH:

pH = –log(1.18 x 10<sup>-5</sup>)

pH = **4.93**

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct diluted concentrations of CH<sub>3</sub>COOH **AND **CH<sub>3</sub>COO<sup>-</sup> (allow slight rounding variations)
> 
> 1 mark for [H<sup>+</sup>] = 1.18 x 10<sup>-5</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for pH = 4.93 (allow 4.92–4.93)
> 
> Allow moles used directly instead of concentrations (volume cancels in the ratio)
> 
> Allow error carried forward from incorrect concentrations if the *K*<sub>a</sub> method is correctly applied

> **[exam-tip]**
> When mixing two solutions, the total volume must be used to calculate the new diluted concentrations.
> 
> Alternatively, use moles directly:
> 
> moles CH<sub>3</sub>COOH = 0.2 x 0.130 = 0.026 mol
> 
> moles CH<sub>3</sub>COO<sup>-</sup> = 0.45 x 0.085 = 0.038 mol
> 
> The ratio of moles = ratio of concentrations (same volume), giving the same [H<sup>+</sup>] and pH.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Calculate the pH of a buffer solution made by mixing together 130 cm^3^ of 0.2 mol dm^-3^ ethanoic acid (*K*~a~ = 1.74 x 10^-5^ mol dm^-3^) and 85 cm^3^ of 0.45 mol dm^-3^ sodium ethanoate. Show your working.

1.00 cm<sup>3</sup> of 1.00 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> sodium hydroxide is added to the buffer solution in part **(b)**.

i) State what the comparison of the pH values before and after the addition of NaOH demonstrates about the buffer solution.

[1]

ii) Calculate the new pH of the buffer solution after the addition. Show your working.

[4]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The comparison of pH values before and after addition of NaOH demonstrates:
> 
> - The pH changed by only ~0.02 (from 4.93 to 4.95)
> **AND**
> This demonstrates the buffer successfully resists significant changes in pH when a small amount of alkali is added **[1 mark]**

ii) To calculate the new pH of the buffer after adding 1.00 cm<sup>3</sup> of 1.00 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> NaOH:

- List the initial moles of acid and salt from part **(b)**:

  - moles of CH<sub>3</sub>COOH = 0.121 x 0.215 = 0.026 mol
  - moles of CH<sub>3</sub>COO<sup>-</sup> = 0.178 x 0.215 = 0.038 mol
- Calculate the moles of OH<sup>-</sup> added:

moles of OH<sup>-</sup> = 1.00 x $\frac{1.00}{1000}$ = 1.00 x 10<sup>-3</sup> mol

**[1 mark]**

- Calculate the new moles of acid and salt after the reaction OH<sup>-</sup> + CH<sub>3</sub>COOH → CH<sub>3</sub>COO<sup>-</sup> + H<sub>2</sub>O:

moles of CH<sub>3</sub>COOH = 0.026 – 1.00 x 10<sup>-3</sup> = 0.025 mol

moles of CH<sub>3</sub>COO<sup>-</sup> = 0.038 + 1.00 x 10<sup>-3</sup> = 0.039 mol

**[1 mark]**

- Apply the *K*<sub>a</sub> expression:

[H<sup>+</sup>] = *K*<sub>a</sub> x (moles acid / moles salt) = 1.74 x 10<sup>-5</sup> x (0.025 / 0.039)

[H<sup>+</sup>] = 1.12 x 10<sup>-5</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup>

**[1 mark]**

- Calculate the pH:

pH = –log(1.12 x 10<sup>-5</sup>)

pH = **4.95**

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for moles of OH<sup>-</sup> = 1.00 x 10<sup>-3</sup> mol
> 
> 1 mark for new moles of CH<sub>3</sub>COOH AND CH<sub>3</sub>COO<sup>-</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for [H<sup>+</sup>] = 1.12 x 10<sup>-5</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for pH = 4.95 (allow 4.95–4.96)
> 
> Allow error carried forward from incorrect moles if the *K*<sub>a</sub> method is correctly applied

> **[exam-tip]**
> When NaOH is added to the buffer, OH<sup>-</sup> reacts with the weak acid:
> 
> CH<sub>3</sub>COOH + OH<sup>-</sup> → CH<sub>3</sub>COO<sup>-</sup> + H<sub>2</sub>O.
> 
> This decreases the moles of acid and increases the moles of salt by the same amount. Since both components change by only 1.00 x 10<sup>-3</sup> mol, and the initial moles are much larger, the pH changes by only ~0.02. This is the buffer in action.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Calculate the pH of a buffer solution made by mixing together 130 cm^3^ of 0.2 mol dm^-3^ ethanoic acid (*K*~a~ = 1.74 x 10^-5^ mol dm^-3^) and 85 cm^3^ of 0.45 mol dm^-3^ sodium ethanoate.

Construct two equations for the separate addition of a small volume of acid and a small volume of base to the buffer solution in part **(b)**.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Equation 1: addition of acid to the buffer
> 
> - CH<sub>3</sub>COO<sup>-</sup> (aq) + H<sup>+</sup> (aq) → CH<sub>3</sub>COOH (aq)
> **OR**
> CH<sub>3</sub>COO<sup>-</sup> (aq) + H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> (aq) → CH<sub>3</sub>COOH (aq) + H<sub>2</sub>O (l) **[1 mark]**
> 
> Equation 2: addition of base to the buffer
> 
> - CH<sub>3</sub>COOH (aq) + OH<sup>-</sup> (aq) → CH<sub>3</sub>COO<sup>-</sup> (aq) + H<sub>2</sub>O (l) **[1 mark]**
> 
> State symbols are required for each equation

> **[exam-tip]**
> Buffers resist pH change by reacting with both added acid and added base. The conjugate base (CH<sub>3</sub>COO<sup>-</sup>) mops up added H<sup>+</sup> ions, and the weak acid (CH<sub>3</sub>COOH) reacts with added OH<sup>-</sup> ions. Both equations must include state symbols. Note: adding H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> and H<sub>2</sub>O as a product is also accepted for equation 1.

parts.problemMd:
A saturated solution of silver(I) chloride has a solubility of 1.46 x 10<sup>-3</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup>.

Write the expression for the solubility product, *K*<sub>sp</sub>, for silver(I) chloride.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The expression for the solubility product of silver(I) chloride is:
> 
> - *K*<sub>sp</sub> = [Ag<sup>+</sup> (aq)][Cl<sup>–</sup> (aq)] **[1 mark]**
> 
> State symbols (aq) are required

> **[exam-tip]**
> When writing a *K*<sub>sp</sub> expression, consider the dissolution equation:
> 
> AgCl (s) ⇌ Ag<sup>+</sup> (aq) + Cl<sup>–</sup> (aq)
> 
> The *K*<sub>sp</sub> expression is the product of the ionic concentrations in square brackets.
> 
> For compounds that produce ions with different stoichiometric coefficients, raise each term to the power of its coefficient. For example, for MgCl<sub>2</sub>:
> 
> *K*<sub>sp</sub> = [Mg<sup>2+</sup> (aq)][Cl<sup>–</sup> (aq)]<sup>2</sup>

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A saturated solution of silver(I) chloride has a solubility of 1.46 x 10^-3^ mol dm^-3^.

Write the expression for the solubility product, *K*~sp~, for silver(I) chloride.

Using the information and your answer to part **(a)**, calculate the value of *K*<sub>sp</sub> for silver(I) chloride. State the units of *K*<sub>sp</sub>. Show your working.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the solubility product, *K*<sub>sp</sub>, of silver(I) chloride:

- Substitute into the *K*<sub>sp</sub> expression:

*K*<sub>sp</sub> = [1.46 x 10<sup>-3</sup>][1.46 x 10<sup>-3</sup>]

*K*<sub>sp</sub> = **2.13 x 10**<sup>**-6**</sup> **[1 mark]**

- State the units:

units = mol<sup>2</sup> dm<sup>-6</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for *K*<sub>sp</sub> = 2.13 x 10<sup>-6</sup>
> 
> Allow 2.1 x 10<sup>-6</sup> (2 sf)
> 
> 1 mark for units = mol<sup>2</sup> dm<sup>-6</sup>

> **[exam-tip]**
> To determine the units of *K*<sub>sp</sub>, substitute mol dm<sup>-3</sup> for each concentration term and multiply the powers:
> 
> mol dm<sup>-3</sup> x mol dm<sup>-3</sup> = mol<sup>2</sup> dm<sup>-6</sup>

parts.problemMd:
A saturated solution of iron(II) hydroxide has a solubility of 5.82 x 10<sup>-6</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup>.

i) Write the expression for the solubility product, *K*<sub>sp</sub>, for iron(II) hydroxide.

[1]

ii) Calculate the solubility product and units for iron(II) hydroxide. Show your working.

[3]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The expression for the solubility product of iron(II) hydroxide is:
> 
> - *K*<sub>sp</sub> = [Fe<sup>2+</sup> (aq)][OH<sup>–</sup> (aq)]<sup>2</sup> **[1 mark]**
> 
> State symbols (aq) are required

> **[exam-tip]**
> For Fe(OH)<sub>2</sub>, the dissolution equation is Fe(OH)<sub>2</sub> (s) ⇌ Fe<sup>2+</sup> (aq) + 2OH<sup>–</sup> (aq). The [OH<sup>–</sup>] term is raised to the power of 2 in the *K*<sub>sp</sub> expression.

ii) To calculate the solubility product and units for iron(II) hydroxide:

- Note that [OH<sup>–</sup> (aq)] = 2 x solubility of Fe(OH)<sub>2</sub>:

[OH<sup>–</sup> (aq)] = 2 x 5.82 x 10<sup>-6</sup>

[OH<sup>–</sup> (aq)] = 1.164 x 10<sup>-5</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup>

- Substitute into the *K*<sub>sp</sub> expression:

*K*<sub>sp</sub> = [5.82 x 10<sup>-6</sup>][2 x 5.82 x 10<sup>-6</sup>]<sup>2</sup> **[1 mark]**

*K*<sub>sp</sub> = **7.89 x 10**<sup>**-16**</sup> **[1 mark]**

- State the units:

units = mol<sup>3</sup> dm<sup>-9</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Allow *K*<sub>sp</sub> = 7.88 x 10<sup>-16</sup> or 7.9 x 10<sup>-16</sup>

> **[exam-tip]**
> To determine the units of *K*<sub>sp</sub> with three concentration terms, substitute mol dm<sup>-3</sup> for each:
> 
> mol dm<sup>-3</sup> x (mol dm<sup>-3</sup>)<sup>2</sup> = mol<sup>3</sup> dm<sup>-9</sup>

parts.problemMd:
The general equilibrium expression for the partition coefficient is:

*K*<sub>pc</sub> = `\frac{\left[\text{equilibrium concentration in organic layer / mol dm}^{-3}\right]}{\left[\text{equilibrium concentration in aqueous layer / mol dm}^{-3}\right]}`

100 cm<sup>3</sup> of a 0.500 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> aqueous solution of ethylamine, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>, was shaken with 100 cm<sup>3</sup> of an organic solvent at 25 °C and allowed to reach equilibrium.

CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> (aq) ⇌ CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> (organic solvent)

Only 50.0 cm<sup>3</sup> of the aqueous layer was removed and titrated against 0.500 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> hydrochloric acid. 15.0 cm<sup>3</sup> was required to reach the end point.

CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> (aq) + HCl (aq) → CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup> (aq) + Cl<sup>–</sup> (aq)

Calculate the partition coefficient, *K*<sub>pc</sub>, of ethylamine between the organic solvent and water. Show your working.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the partition coefficient, *K*<sub>pc</sub>, of ethylamine between the organic solvent and water:

- Calculate the moles of ethylamine in the 50.0 cm<sup>3</sup> aliquot from the titration:

*n*(CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>) = *n*(HCl)

*n*(CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>) = 0.500 x 0.0150

*n*(CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>) = 7.50 x 10<sup>-3</sup> mol

- The aliquot was 50.0 cm<sup>3</sup> of 100 cm<sup>3</sup> total aqueous layer, so total moles in the aqueous layer:

*n*(CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>) (aq) = 2 x 7.50 x 10<sup>-3</sup>

*n*(CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>) (aq) = 0.0150 mol

**[1 mark]**

- Calculate the total initial moles of ethylamine and hence the moles in the organic layer:

*n*(CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>) (total) = 0.500 x 0.100

*n*(CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>) (total) = 0.0500 mol

*n*(CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>) (organic) = 0.0500 - 0.0150

*n*(CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>) (organic) = 0.0350 mol

**[1 mark]**

- Calculate the equilibrium concentrations in each layer (volume of each layer = 100 cm<sup>3</sup> = 0.100 dm<sup>3</sup>):

[CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> (aq)] = $\frac{0.0150}{0.100}$

[CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> (aq)] = 0.150 mol dm<sup>-3</sup>

[CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> (organic)] = $\frac{0.0350}{0.100}$

[CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> (organic)] = 0.350 mol dm<sup>-3</sup>

**[1 mark]**

- Calculate the partition coefficient:

*K*<sub>pc</sub> = $\frac{0.350}{0.150}$

*K*<sub>pc</sub> = **2.33**

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for total moles of ethylamine in aqueous layer = 0.0150 mol
> 
> 1 mark for moles of ethylamine in organic layer = 0.0350 mol
> 
> 1 mark for both concentrations correct: [CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> (aq)] = 0.150 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> AND [CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> (organic)] = 0.350 mol dm<sup>-3</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for *K*<sub>pc</sub> = 2.33
> 
> Allow 2.3 (2 sf)

> **[exam-tip]**
> A common error is to treat the aliquot volume (50.0 cm<sup>3</sup>) as the total aqueous layer. The moles from the titration must be doubled because only half the aqueous layer was titrated.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The general equilibrium expression for the partition coefficient is:

Kpc = [equilibrium concentration in organic layer / mol dm^-3] / [equilibrium concentration in aqueous layer / mol dm^-3]

Kpc = 2.33

Use your answer to part **(a)** to state whether ethylamine is more soluble in the aqueous or organic solvent. Explain your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Whether ethylamine is more soluble in the aqueous or organic solvent:
> 
> - Organic solvent **[1 mark]**
> - The value of *K*<sub>pc</sub> is greater than 1 **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> When *K*<sub>pc</sub> > 1, the equilibrium concentration is greater in the organic layer, so the solute (ethylamine) is more soluble in the organic solvent.
> 
> When *K*<sub>pc</sub> < 1, the solute is more soluble in water.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The general equilibrium expression for the partition coefficient is:

*K*~pc~ = [equilibrium concentration in organic layer / mol dm⁻³] / [equilibrium concentration in aqueous layer / mol dm⁻³]

A solution containing 1.00 g of compound **A** in 100 cm<sup>3</sup> of water was shaken with 10.0 cm<sup>3</sup> of ether and allowed to reach equilibrium. 0.60 g of compound **A** is present in the ether layer at equilibrium.

Calculate the partition coefficient of compound **A** between ether and water. Show your working.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the partition coefficient of compound **A** between ether and water:

- Write the *K*<sub>pc</sub> expression:

*K*<sub>pc</sub> = [compound **A** (ether)] / [compound **A** (aq)]

**[1 mark]**

- Calculate the concentration in each layer:

[compound **A** (ether)] = $\frac{0.60}{0.010}$ = 60 g dm<sup>-3</sup>

[compound **A** (aq)] = $\frac{0.40}{0.100}$ = 4.0 g dm<sup>-3</sup>

**[1 mark]**

- Calculate the partition coefficient:

*K*<sub>pc</sub> = $\frac{60}{4.0}$

*K*<sub>pc</sub> = **15**

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for *K*<sub>pc</sub> expression with ether as numerator and aqueous as denominator
> 
> 1 mark for both concentrations: [compound **A** (ether)] = 60 g dm<sup>-3</sup> **AND **[compound **A** (aq)] = 4.0 g dm<sup>-3</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for *K*<sub>pc</sub> = 15

> **[exam-tip]**
> Note that 0.60 g of compound **A** is present in 10.0 cm<sup>3</sup> of ether (not 100 cm<sup>3</sup>). The mass remaining in the aqueous layer is 1.00 - 0.60 = 0.40 g. Convert volumes to dm<sup>3</sup> before calculating concentrations.

parts.problemMd:
The *K*<sub>sp</sub> value for silver bromide, AgBr (s) is 3.3 x 10<sup>-13</sup> at 298 K.

Construct an equation to show the equilibrium present in a saturated solution of silver bromide. Include state symbols.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The equilibrium equation for a saturated solution of silver bromide is:
> 
> - AgBr (s) ⇌ Ag<sup>+</sup> (aq) + Br<sup>–</sup> (aq) **[1 mark]**
> 
> State symbols are required

> **[exam-tip]**
> Silver bromide dissolves to give one Ag<sup>+</sup> ion and one Br<sup>–</sup> ion per formula unit. Including state symbols, (s) for the undissolved solid and (aq) for the dissolved ions, is required for the mark.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The *K*~sp~ value for silver bromide, AgBr (s) is 3.3 x 10^-13^ at 298 K.

Construct an equation to show the equilibrium present in a saturated solution of silver bromide. Include state symbols.

The equilibrium equation for a saturated solution of silver bromide is:

AgBr (s) ⇌ Ag^+^ (aq) + Br^–^ (aq)

State and explain the effect on the concentration of dissolved silver ions when sodium bromide solution is added to a saturated solution of silver bromide.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The effect on the concentration of dissolved silver ions when sodium bromide solution is added:
> 
> - Decreases **[1 mark]**
> - The increase in [Br<sup>–</sup> (aq)] shifts the equilibrium to the left (towards AgBr (s)) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> This is an application of Le Chatelier’s principle. Adding sodium bromide increases the Br<sup>–</sup> concentration. To oppose this change, the equilibrium shifts left, consuming both Ag<sup>+</sup> and Br<sup>–</sup> ions and forming more AgBr (s), so [Ag<sup>+</sup> (aq)] decreases.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The *K*~sp~ value for silver bromide, AgBr (s) is 3.3 x 10^-13^ at 298 K.

Calculate the concentration, in mol dm<sup>-3</sup>, of silver ions at 298 K in a saturated solution of silver bromide. Show your working.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the concentration of silver ions in a saturated solution of silver bromide:

- Let *s* = solubility of AgBr = [Ag<sup>+</sup> (aq)] = [Br<sup>–</sup> (aq)]

- Substitute into the *K*<sub>sp</sub> expression:

*K*<sub>sp</sub> = [Ag<sup>+</sup> (aq)][Br<sup>–</sup> (aq)] = *s*<sup>2</sup> = 3.3 x 10<sup>-13</sup> **[1 mark]**

- Solve for *s*:

[Ag<sup>+</sup> (aq)] = $\sqrt{3.3\times10^{-13}}$

[Ag<sup>+</sup> (aq)] = **5.74 x 10**<sup>**-7**</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for *K*<sub>sp</sub> = *s*<sup>2</sup> = 3.3 x 10<sup>-13</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for [Ag<sup>+</sup> (aq)] = 5.74 x 10<sup>-7</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup>
> 
> Allow 5.7 x 10<sup>-7</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup> (2 sf)

> **[exam-tip]**
> For a 1:1 salt such as AgBr, the two ion concentrations in a saturated solution are equal (both equal to the solubility *s*), so *K*<sub>sp</sub> = *s*<sup>2</sup>. Taking the square root gives the concentration of each ion.

parts.problemMd:
i) State what is meant by partition coefficient.

[2]

ii) Ammonia is soluble in both water and organic solvents.

An aqueous solution of ammonia is shaken with the immiscible organic solvent trichloromethane. The mixture is left to reach equilibrium.

Samples are taken from each layer and titrated with dilute hydrochloric acid.

- A 25.0 cm<sup>3</sup> sample from the trichloromethane layer requires 13.0 cm<sup>3</sup> of 0.100 mol dm<sup>–3</sup> HCl to reach the end-point.
- A 10.0 cm<sup>3</sup> sample from the aqueous layer requires 12.5 cm<sup>3</sup> of 0.100 mol dm<sup>–3</sup> HCl to reach the end-point.

Calculate the partition coefficient, *K*<sub>pc</sub>, of ammonia between trichloromethane and water. Show your working.

[3]

iii) Butylamine, C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>9</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>, is also soluble in both water and organic solvents. Suggest how the numerical value of *K*<sub>pc</sub> of butylamine between trichloromethane and water would compare to the value of *K*<sub>pc</sub> calculated in **(a)(ii)**. Explain your answer.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The partition coefficient is:
> 
> - The ratio of the concentrations of a solute in two immiscible solvents **[1 mark]**
> - At equilibrium **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The partition coefficient expression is *K*<sub>pc</sub> = [solute in organic layer] / [solute in aqueous layer], evaluated once equilibrium is established.

ii) To calculate the partition coefficient, *K*<sub>pc</sub>, of ammonia between trichloromethane and water:

- Calculate [NH<sub>3</sub>] in the aqueous layer:

[NH<sub>3</sub> (aq)] = 0.100 x $\frac{12.5}{10.0}$ = 0.125 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> **[1 mark]**

- Calculate [NH<sub>3</sub>] in the trichloromethane layer:

[NH<sub>3</sub> (organic)] = 0.100 x $\frac{13.0}{25.0}$ = 0.052 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the partition coefficient:

*K*<sub>pc</sub> = $\frac{0.052}{0.125}$

*K*<sub>pc</sub> = **0.416** **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii) 1 mark for [NH<sub>3</sub> (aq)] = 0.125 mol dm<sup>-3</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for [NH<sub>3</sub> (organic)] = 0.052 mol dm<sup>-3</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for *K*<sub>pc</sub> = 0.416
> 
> *K*<sub>pc</sub> = 0.125/0.052 = 2.40 is also accepted if the aqueous layer is used as numerator consistently

> **[exam-tip]**
> To find [NH<sub>3</sub>] in each layer: c = c(HCl) x V(HCl) / V(sample). The Ksp value of 0.416 < 1, meaning ammonia is more soluble in the aqueous layer than in trichloromethane.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> iii) How the *K*<sub>pc</sub> of butylamine between trichloromethane and water compares:
> 
> - If *K*<sub>pc</sub> = 0.416 (organic/aqueous): the *K*<sub>pc</sub> for butylamine is larger than for ammonia
> **OR**
> If *K*<sub>pc</sub> = 2.40 (aqueous/organic): the *K*<sub>pc</sub> for butylamine is smaller than for ammonia **[1 mark]**
> - Butylamine contains a hydrophobic / non-polar butyl (C<sub>4</sub>) chain
> **AND**
> Butylamine is therefore more soluble in trichloromethane than ammonia is **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Butylamine has a longer non-polar hydrocarbon chain compared to ammonia, making it more hydrophobic. Non-polar molecules dissolve preferentially in non-polar organic solvents such as trichloromethane, increasing the relative concentration in the organic layer.

parts.problemMd: Butanamide, C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>7</sub>CONH<sub>2</sub>, is much less basic than butylamine. Explain why.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Why butanamide is much less basic than butylamine:
> 
> - The lone pair on the nitrogen atom is delocalised into the adjacent C=O group / forms part of the extended π system **[1 mark]**
> - The lone pair is therefore less available to accept a proton **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> In amines such as butylamine, the lone pair on nitrogen is localised and readily available to donate to a proton, making them moderately basic. In amides such as butanamide, partial delocalisation of the N lone pair into the adjacent C=O π system significantly reduces its availability, which is why amides are far less basic than amines.

parts.problemMd:
The feasibility of a chemical reaction depends on the standard Gibbs free energy change, Δ*G*<sup>ɵ</sup>. This is dependent on the standard enthalpy and entropy changes, and the temperature.

State and explain whether the following processes will lead to an increase or decrease in entropy.

i) the reaction of magnesium with hydrochloric acid

[1]

ii) the dissolving of solid potassium chloride in water

[1]

iii) the condensing of water from steam

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The reaction of magnesium with hydrochloric acid:
> 
> - Entropy increases
> **AND**
> A gas (H<sub>2</sub>) is produced **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The dissolving of solid potassium chloride in water:
> 
> - Entropy increases
> **AND**
> The ordered solid lattice breaks down to give freely moving ions in solution **[1 mark]**
> 
> iii) The condensing of water from steam:
> 
> - Entropy decreases
> **AND**
> The number of moles of gas decreases / a more ordered liquid is formed **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Entropy is a measure of disorder. Processes that produce gases, dissolve solids, or increase the number of particles increase entropy. Processes that convert gases to liquids or reduce the number of particles decrease entropy.

parts.problemMd:
Magnesium carbonate can be decomposed on heating.

MgCO<sub>3</sub> (s) → MgO (s) + CO<sub>2</sub> (g)      Δ*H*<sup>ɵ</sup> = +117 kJ mol<sup>–1</sup>

Standard entropies are shown in Table 2.1.

**Table 2.1**

| **substance** | MgCO<sub>3</sub> (s) | MgO (s) | CO<sub>2</sub> (g) |
|---|---|---|---|
| *S*<sup>ɵ</sup> / J K<sup>–1</sup> mol<sup>–1</sup> | +65.7 | +26.9 | +214 |

i) Calculate Δ*G*<sup>ɵ</sup> for this reaction at 298 K. Show your working.

[3]

ii) Explain why this reaction is feasible only at high temperatures.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
i) To calculate Δ*G*<sup>ɵ</sup> for the decomposition of MgCO<sub>3</sub> at 298 K:

- Calculate Δ*S*<sup>ɵ</sup>:

Δ*S*<sup>ɵ</sup> = Σ*S*<sup>ɵ</sup>(products) – Σ*S*<sup>ɵ</sup>(reactants)

Δ*S*<sup>ɵ</sup> = (26.9 + 214) – 65.7

Δ*S*<sup>ɵ</sup> = **+175.2** J K<sup>–1</sup> mol<sup>–1</sup> **[1 mark]**

- Substitute into the Gibbs equation:

Δ*G*<sup>ɵ</sup> = Δ*H*<sup>ɵ</sup> – *T*Δ*S*<sup>ɵ</sup> **[1 mark]**

Δ*G*<sup>ɵ</sup> = 117 – (298 x $\frac{175.2}{1000}$)

Δ*G*<sup>ɵ</sup> = **+64.8** kJ mol<sup>–1</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) 1 mark for Δ*S*<sup>ɵ</sup> = +175.2 J K<sup>–1</sup> mol<sup>–1</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for correct application of Δ*G*<sup>ɵ</sup> = Δ*H*<sup>ɵ</sup> – *T*Δ*S*<sup>ɵ</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for Δ*G*<sup>ɵ</sup> = +64.8 kJ mol<sup>–1</sup> (to at least 3 sf)

> **[exam-tip]**
> Δ*S*<sup>ɵ</sup> is in J K<sup>–1</sup> mol<sup>–1</sup> while Δ*H*<sup>ɵ</sup> is in kJ mol<sup>–1</sup>. Divide Δ*S*<sup>ɵ</sup> by 1000 before substituting to ensure consistent units.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii) This reaction is feasible only at high temperatures because:
> 
> - *T*Δ*S*<sup>ɵ</sup> exceeds Δ*H*<sup>ɵ</sup>
> **AND**
> Δ*G*<sup>ɵ</sup> becomes negative **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Both Δ*H*<sup>ɵ</sup> (+117 kJ mol<sup>–1</sup>) and Δ*S*<sup>ɵ</sup> (+175.2 J K<sup>–1</sup> mol<sup>–1</sup>) are positive. Δ*G*<sup>ɵ</sup> = Δ*H*<sup>ɵ</sup> – *T*Δ*S*<sup>ɵ</sup> only becomes negative (feasible) when *T* is large enough that *T*Δ*S*<sup>ɵ</sup> > Δ*H*<sup>ɵ</sup>.

parts.problemMd:
Table 2.2 lists values of solubility products, *K*<sub>**sp**</sub>, of some Group 2 carbonates.

**Table 2.2**

| carbonate | **solubility product in water at 298 K, *****K***<sub>**sp **</sub>**/ mol**<sup>**2**</sup>** dm**<sup>**–6**</sup> |
|---|---|
| MgCO<sub>3</sub> | 1.0 × 10<sup>–5</sup> |
| CaCO<sub>3</sub> | 5.0 × 10<sup>–9</sup> |
| SrCO<sub>3</sub> | 1.1 × 10<sup>–10</sup> |

Deduce the trend in the solubility of the Group 2 carbonates down the group. Justify your answer using the data given.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The trend in solubility of the Group 2 carbonates down the group:
> 
> - Solubility decreases down the group
> **AND**
> *K*<sub>sp</sub> decreases down the group (justified by reference to data in Table 2.2) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> *K*<sub>sp</sub> values with more negative exponents represent smaller numbers and indicate lower solubility. MgCO<sub>3</sub> (*K*<sub>sp</sub> = 1.0 × 10<sup>–5</sup>) is the most soluble; SrCO<sub>3</sub> (*K*<sub>sp</sub> = 1.1 × 10<sup>–10</sup>) is the least soluble.

parts.problemMd:
i) Construct an equation to show the equilibrium for the solubility product of MgCO<sub>3</sub>. Include state symbols.

[1]

ii) With reference to your equation in **(d)(i)**, state what is observed when a few cm<sup>3</sup> of concentrated Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> (aq) are added to a saturated solution of MgCO<sub>3</sub>. Explain your answer.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The equilibrium equation for the solubility product of MgCO<sub>3</sub> is:
> 
> - MgCO<sub>3</sub> (s) ⇌ Mg<sup>2+</sup> (aq) + CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2–</sup> (aq) **[1 mark]**
> 
> State symbols are required; do not accept + (aq) in the equation

> **[exam-tip]**
> MgCO<sub>3</sub> dissolves to give one Mg<sup>2+</sup> ion and one CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2–</sup> ion. The solid MgCO<sub>3</sub> is on the left of the equilibrium; the aqueous ions are on the right. A "+ (aq)" term is not required and is not accepted.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii) When concentrated Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> (aq) is added to a saturated MgCO<sub>3</sub> solution:
> 
> - A white solid / precipitate (of MgCO<sub>3</sub>) forms **[1 mark]**
> - Adding Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> increases [CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2–</sup> (aq)], which shifts the equilibrium to the left **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> provides additional CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2–</sup> ions. By Le Chatelier’s principle, the equilibrium shifts left to reduce [CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2–</sup>], consuming Mg<sup>2+</sup> and CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2–</sup> ions and depositing more solid MgCO<sub>3</sub> as a precipitate.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Table 2.2 lists values of solubility products, *K*~**sp**~, of some Group 2 carbonates.

**Table 2.2**

| carbonate | **solubility product in water at 298 K, *****K***~**sp **~**/ mol**^**2**^** dm**^**–6**^ |
| --- | :---: |
| MgCO~3~ | 1.0 × 10^–5^ |
| CaCO~3~ | 5.0 × 10^–9^ |
| SrCO~3~ | 1.1 × 10^–10^ |

Use the data in Table 2.2 to calculate the solubility of MgCO<sub>3</sub> in water at 298 K, in g dm<sup>–3</sup>. Show your working.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the solubility of MgCO<sub>3</sub> in water at 298 K:

- Let *s* = solubility = [Mg<sup>2+</sup> (aq)] = [CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2–</sup> (aq)]

- Substitute into the *K*<sub>sp</sub> expression:

*K*<sub>sp</sub> = *s*<sup>2</sup> = 1.0 x 10<sup>–5</sup>

*s* = $\sqrt{1.0\times10^{-5}}$ = 3.2 x 10<sup>–3</sup> mol dm<sup>–3</sup> **[1 mark]**

- Convert to g dm<sup>–3</sup> (*M*<sub>r</sub> of MgCO<sub>3</sub> = 84.3):

solubility = 3.2 x 10<sup>–3</sup> x 84.3

solubility = **0.27 g dm**<sup>**–3**</sup>** ****[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for *s* = 3.2 x 10<sup>–3</sup> mol dm<sup>–3</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for solubility = 0.27 g dm<sup>–3</sup>

> **[exam-tip]**
> For a 1:1 salt like MgCO<sub>3</sub>, *K*<sub>sp</sub> = *s*<sup>2</sup>. Take the square root of *K*<sub>sp</sub> to find the molar solubility, then multiply by *M*<sub>r</sub> to convert to g dm<sup>–3</sup>.

parts.problemMd: Describe and explain the variation in the thermal stabilities of the carbonates of the Group 2 elements.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The variation in thermal stability of the Group 2 carbonates:
> 
> - Thermal stability increases down the group
> - The ionic radius of the M<sup>2+</sup> cation increases down the group
> - There is less distortion / polarisation of the CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2–</sup> anion
> - Less weakening of the C–O bonds in the carbonate ion
> 
> **[3 marks]**
> 
> Any three chemical ideas score 2 marks
> 
> Any two chemical ideas score 1 mark

> **[exam-tip]**
> As ionic radius increases down Group 2, charge density of the M<sup>2+</sup> cation decreases. A smaller cation has greater polarising ability and distorts the CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2–</sup> anion more strongly, weakening C–O bonds and lowering the decomposition temperature.

parts.problemMd:
This question is about solubility products.

A 1.70 x 10<sup>-3</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup> solution of calcium nitrate is mixed with an equal volume of 1.50 x 10<sup>-3</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup> potassium sulfate.

Calculate the ionic product and state whether calcium sulfate (*K*<sub>sp</sub> = 2.00 x 10<sup>-5</sup>) will precipitate. Show your working.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the ionic product and determine whether calcium sulfate will precipitate:

- When equal volumes are mixed, each concentration is halved:

[Ca<sup>2+</sup> (aq)] = $\frac{1.70\times10^{-3}}{2}$ = 8.50 x 10<sup>-4</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup>

[SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2-</sup> (aq)] = $\frac{1.50\times10^{-3}}{2}$ = 7.50 x 10<sup>-4</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup>

**[1 mark]**

- Calculate the ionic product:

IP = [Ca<sup>2+</sup>][SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2-</sup>] = 8.50 x 10<sup>-4</sup> x 7.50 x 10<sup>-4</sup>

IP = **6.38 x 10**<sup>**-7**</sup> mol<sup>2</sup> dm<sup>-6</sup>

**[1 mark]**

- Compare IP with *K*<sub>sp</sub>:

6.38 x 10<sup>-7</sup> < 2.00 x 10<sup>-5</sup>

There will be no precipitation as IP < *K*<sub>sp</sub>

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for both concentrations after mixing: [Ca<sup>2+</sup>] = 8.50 x 10<sup>-4</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup> **AND **[SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2-</sup>] = 7.50 x 10<sup>-4</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for IP = 6.38 x 10<sup>-7</sup> (allow 6.375 x 10<sup>-7</sup>)
> 
> 1 mark for IP < *K*<sub>sp</sub> **AND **a conclusion of no precipitation

> **[exam-tip]**
> When equal volumes of two solutions are mixed, the total volume doubles so each concentration is halved.
> 
> Calculate the ionic product (IP) using these diluted concentrations, then compare with *K*<sub>sp</sub>: if IP > *K*<sub>sp</sub>, a precipitate forms; if IP < *K*<sub>sp</sub>, no precipitate forms.

parts.problemMd:
Water with a manganese ion, Mn<sup>2+</sup> (aq), concentration above 1.8 x 10<sup>-6</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup> will cause clothes to stain when being washed. The manganese can precipitate as Mn(OH)<sub>2</sub> (s) which has a *K*<sub>sp</sub> of 4.5 x 10<sup>-14</sup>. This reduces the concentration of Mn<sup>2+</sup> (aq) by the addition of OH<sup>–</sup> ions.

i) Write the expression for *K*<sub>sp</sub>.

[1]

ii) Calculate the concentration of OH<sup>–</sup> ions. Show your working.

[2]

iii) Calculate the minimum pH at 298 K required to prevent clothes from being stained.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The *K*<sub>sp</sub> expression for Mn(OH)<sub>2</sub> is:
> 
> - *K*<sub>sp</sub> = [Mn<sup>2+</sup> (aq)][OH<sup>–</sup> (aq)]<sup>2</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Mn(OH)<sub>2</sub> dissociates to give one Mn<sup>2+</sup> ion and two OH<sup>–</sup> ions. The [OH<sup>–</sup>] term must be raised to the power of 2.

ii) To calculate the concentration of OH<sup>–</sup> ions:

- Substitute [Mn<sup>2+</sup>] = 1.8 x 10<sup>-6</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup> into the *K*<sub>sp</sub> expression:

4.5 x 10<sup>-14</sup> = 1.8 x 10<sup>-6</sup> x [OH<sup>–</sup>]<sup>2</sup> **[1 mark]**

[OH<sup>–</sup>]<sup>2</sup> = $\frac{4.5\times10^{-14}}{1.8\times10^{-6}}$ = 2.5 x 10<sup>-8</sup>

[OH<sup>–</sup>] = **1.58 x 10**<sup>**-4**</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii)
> 
> 1 mark for *K*<sub>sp</sub> = 1.8 x 10<sup>-6</sup> x [OH<sup>–</sup>]<sup>2</sup> or equivalent rearrangement
> 
> 1 mark for [OH<sup>–</sup>] = 1.58 x 10<sup>-4</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup>

iii) To calculate the minimum pH at 298 K:

- Calculate [H<sup>+</sup>] using *K*<sub>w</sub>:

[H<sup>+</sup>] = `\frac{K_w}{[\text{OH}^-]}` = $\frac{1.00\times10^{-14}}{1.58\times10^{-4}}$ = 6.33 x 10<sup>-11</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup> **[1 mark]**

pH = –log(6.33 x 10<sup>-11</sup>)

pH = **10.2** **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> iii)
> 
> 1 mark for [H<sup>+</sup>] = `\frac{K_w}{[\text{OH}^-]}` **OR **[H<sup>+</sup>] = $\frac{1.00\times10^{-14}}{1.58\times10^{-4}}$
> 
> 1 mark for pH = 10.2
> 
> Allow pH calculated as 14 + log(1.58 x 10<sup>-4</sup>) = 10.2

> **[exam-tip]**
> For the pH calculation, *K*<sub>w</sub> = [H<sup>+</sup>][OH<sup>–</sup>] is found in the data booklet at 298 K. Calculate [H<sup>+</sup>] = *K*<sub>w</sub> / [OH<sup>–</sup>], then apply pH = –log[H<sup>+</sup>].
> 
> Alternatively, pOH = –log[OH<sup>–</sup>] = 3.80, and pH = 14 – pOH = 10.2.

parts.problemMd:
Consider the following equilibrium in a saturated solution of AgBr (s):

AgBr (s) ⇌ Ag<sup>+</sup> (aq) + Br<sup>–</sup> (aq)

Explain what will happen to the solubility of AgBr (s) when each of the following substances is added to the solution.

i) AgNO<sub>3</sub>

[2]

ii) Pb(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) When AgNO<sub>3</sub> is added to the saturated solution:
> 
> - Added Ag<sup>+</sup> ions increase [Ag<sup>+</sup> (aq)] (common ion effect) **[1 mark]**
> - Equilibrium shifts to the left towards AgBr (s), reducing the solubility of AgBr **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) When Pb(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> is added to the saturated solution:
> 
> - Pb<sup>2+</sup> ions react with Br<sup>–</sup> ions to form insoluble PbBr<sub>2</sub>, removing Br<sup>–</sup> from the equilibrium **[1 mark]**
> - Equilibrium shifts to the right, increasing the solubility of AgBr **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> When a common ion (Ag<sup>+</sup> or Br<sup>–</sup>) is added, the ionic product exceeds *K*<sub>sp</sub> and the equilibrium shifts left, reducing solubility. When Pb<sup>2+</sup> is added, it forms insoluble PbBr<sub>2</sub>, removing Br<sup>–</sup> and shifting the equilibrium right, increasing solubility.

parts.problemMd: Explain why more Mg(OH)<sub>2</sub> dissolves when hydrochloric acid is added to a saturated solution of Mg(OH)<sub>2</sub>.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Why more Mg(OH)<sub>2</sub> dissolves when hydrochloric acid is added to a saturated solution:
> 
> - H<sup>+</sup> ions from HCl react with OH<sup>–</sup> ions, removing them from solution (forming H<sub>2</sub>O) **[1 mark]**
> - Equilibrium shifts to the right, increasing the solubility of Mg(OH)<sub>2</sub> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Adding H<sup>+</sup> ions from a strong acid removes OH<sup>–</sup> ions from solution via neutralisation. By Le Chatelier’s principle, the equilibrium Mg(OH)<sub>2</sub> (s) ⇌ Mg<sup>2+</sup> (aq) + 2OH<sup>–</sup> (aq) shifts right to restore [OH<sup>–</sup>], dissolving more Mg(OH)<sub>2</sub>.

parts.problemMd:
Calcium phosphate is a sparingly soluble naturally occurring mineral that is a large component of bones and teeth. The *K*<sub>sp</sub> value at 25 °C for calcium phosphate is 2.07 x 10<sup>-33</sup>.

Construct an equation to show the equilibrium present in a saturated solution of calcium phosphate. Include state symbols.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The equilibrium equation for the dissolution of calcium phosphate is:
> 
> - Ca<sub>3</sub>(PO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub> (s) ⇌ 3Ca<sup>2+</sup> (aq) + 2PO<sub>4</sub><sup>3-</sup> (aq) **[1 mark]**
> 
> State symbols are required; equation must be balanced with 3:2 stoichiometry (Ca<sup>2+</sup> to PO<sub>4</sub><sup>3-</sup>)

> **[exam-tip]**
> Calcium phosphate contains Ca<sup>2+</sup> (charge 2+) and PO<sub>4</sub><sup>3-</sup> (charge 3-). Three Ca<sup>2+</sup> ions and two PO<sub>4</sub><sup>3-</sup> ions balance the charges (6+ = 6-), giving the formula Ca<sub>3</sub>(PO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub>.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Calcium phosphate is a sparingly soluble naturally occurring mineral that is a large component of bones and teeth. The Ksp value at 25 °C for calcium phosphate is 2.07 x 10^-33.

The equilibrium equation for the dissolution of calcium phosphate is:
Ca3(PO4)2 (s) ⇌ 3Ca^2+ (aq) + 2PO4^3- (aq)

Use your answer to part **(a)** to calculate the concentration, in mol dm<sup>-3</sup>, of the calcium and phosphate ions in solution. Show your working.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the concentrations of ions in a saturated solution of calcium phosphate:

- Let *x* = solubility of Ca<sub>3</sub>(PO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub>, so [Ca<sup>2+</sup> (aq)] = 3*x* and [PO<sub>4</sub><sup>3-</sup> (aq)] = 2*x*

- Write the *K*<sub>sp</sub> expression and substitute:

*K*<sub>sp</sub> = [Ca<sup>2+</sup> (aq)]<sup>3</sup>[PO<sub>4</sub><sup>3-</sup> (aq)]<sup>2</sup>

*K*<sub>sp</sub> = (3*x*)<sup>3</sup>(2*x*)<sup>2</sup> **[1 mark]**

- Expand and set equal to *K*<sub>sp</sub>:

2.07 x 10<sup>-33</sup> = 27*x*<sup>3</sup> x 4*x*<sup>2</sup>

2.07 x 10<sup>-33</sup> = 108*x*<sup>5</sup> **[1 mark]**

- Solve for *x*:

*x*<sup>5</sup> = $\frac{2.07\times10^{-33}}{108}$

*x*<sup>5</sup> = 1.92 x 10<sup>-35</sup>

*x* = `\sqrt[5]{1.92 \times 10^{-35}}`

*x* = 1.14 x 10<sup>-7</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup> **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the equilibrium concentrations:

[Ca<sup>2+</sup> (aq)] = 3 x 1.14 x 10<sup>-7</sup> = **3.42 x 10**<sup>**-7**</sup>** mol dm**<sup>**-3**</sup>

[PO<sub>4</sub><sup>3-</sup> (aq)] = 2 x 1.14 x 10<sup>-7</sup> = **2.28 x 10**<sup>**-7**</sup>** mol dm**<sup>**-3**</sup>

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for *K*<sub>sp</sub> = (3*x*)<sup>3</sup>(2*x*)<sup>2</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for 108*x*<sup>5</sup> = 2.07 x 10<sup>-33</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for *x* = 1.14 x 10<sup>-7</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for both concentrations: [Ca<sup>2+</sup> (aq)] = 3.42 x 10<sup>-7</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup> **AND **[PO<sub>4</sub><sup>3-</sup> (aq)] = 2.28 x 10<sup>-7</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup>

> **[exam-tip]**
> Express each ion concentration in terms of *x* (the solubility).
> 
> Since Ca<sub>3</sub>(PO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub> gives 3 Ca<sup>2+</sup> and 2 PO<sub>4</sub><sup>3-</sup> per formula unit, [Ca<sup>2+</sup>] = 3*x*<sup>3</sup> and [PO<sub>4</sub><sup>3-</sup>] = 2*x*<sup>*2*</sup>*. *

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Let x = solubility of Ca~3~(PO~4~)~2~, so [Ca^2+^ (aq)] = 3x and [PO~4~^3-^ (aq)] = 2x

x = 1.14 x 10^-7^ mol dm^-3^

[Ca^2+^ (aq)] = 3 x 1.14 x 10^-7^ = 3.42 x 10^-7^ mol dm^-3^

[PO~4~^3-^ (aq)] = 2 x 1.14 x 10^-7^ = 2.28 x 10^-7^ mol dm^-3^

Use your answer to part **(b)** to calculate the mass of solute, in grams, in 150 cm<sup>3</sup> of solution at 25 °C. Show your working.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the mass of calcium phosphate, Ca<sub>3</sub>(PO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub>, dissolved in 150 cm<sup>3</sup> of solution:

- Use *x* = 1.14 x 10<sup>-7</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup> (solubility of Ca<sub>3</sub>(PO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub>) to find moles in 150 cm<sup>3</sup>:

*n*(Ca<sub>3</sub>(PO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub>) = 1.14 x 10<sup>-7</sup> x 0.150

*n*(Ca<sub>3</sub>(PO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub>) = 1.71 x 10<sup>-8</sup> mol **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the mass (*M*<sub>r</sub> of Ca<sub>3</sub>(PO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub> = 310.3):

mass = 1.71 x 10<sup>-8</sup> x 310.3

mass = **5.31 x 10**<sup>**-6**</sup> g **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for *n*(Ca<sub>3</sub>(PO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub>) = 1.71 x 10<sup>-8</sup> mol
> 
> 1 mark for mass = 5.31 x 10<sup>-6</sup> g
> 
> Allow 5.30 x 10<sup>-6</sup> g depending on *M*<sub>r</sub> used
> 
> Allow error carried forward from part (b) if *x* is used consistently

> **[exam-tip]**
> The value of *x* from part (b) is the molar solubility of Ca<sub>3</sub>(PO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub> in mol dm<sup>-3</sup>.
> 
> Convert 150 cm<sup>3</sup> to 0.150 dm<sup>3</sup>, multiply by *x* to get moles, then multiply by *M*<sub>r</sub> to get mass.

parts.problemMd:
Silver chromate, Ag<sub>2</sub>CrO<sub>4</sub>, is a chemical compound of silver and hexavalent chromium that is used in photography.

It has a solubility product, *K*<sub>sp</sub>, of 9.0 x 10<sup>-12</sup> at 25 °C.

Write the *K*<sub>sp</sub> expression for Ag<sub>2</sub>CrO<sub>4</sub>.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The *K*<sub>sp</sub> expression for Ag<sub>2</sub>CrO<sub>4</sub> is:
> 
> - *K*<sub>sp</sub> = [Ag<sup>+</sup> (aq)]<sup>2</sup>[CrO<sub>4</sub><sup>2-</sup> (aq)] **[1 mark]**
> 
> [Ag<sup>+</sup> (aq)] must be squared
> 
> State symbols (aq) are required

> **[exam-tip]**
> Ag<sub>2</sub>CrO<sub>4</sub> dissociates to give two Ag<sup>+</sup> ions and one CrO<sub>4</sub><sup>2-</sup> ion. The concentration of Ag<sup>+</sup> must be raised to the power of 2 in the *K*<sub>sp</sub> expression.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Silver chromate, Ag~2~CrO~4~, is a chemical compound of silver and hexavalent chromium that is used in photography.

It has a solubility product, *K*~sp~, of 9.0 x 10^-12^ at 25 °C.

Write the *K*~sp~ expression for Ag~2~CrO~4~.

The *K*~sp~ expression for Ag~2~CrO~4~ is:

*K*~sp~ = [Ag^+^ (aq)]^2^[CrO~4~^2-^ (aq)]

Use your answer to part **(a)** to calculate the solubility, in mol dm<sup>-3</sup>, of Ag<sub>2</sub>CrO<sub>4</sub> in 0.020 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> K<sub>2</sub>CrO<sub>4</sub> (aq). Show your working.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the solubility of Ag<sub>2</sub>CrO<sub>4</sub> in 0.020 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> K<sub>2</sub>CrO<sub>4</sub> (aq):

- Let *s* = solubility of Ag<sub>2</sub>CrO<sub>4</sub>; [Ag<sup>+</sup> (aq)] = 2*s* and [CrO<sub>4</sub><sup>2-</sup> (aq)] ≈ 0.020 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> (common ion)

- Substitute into the *K*<sub>sp</sub> expression:

*K*<sub>sp</sub> = (2*s*)<sup>2</sup> x 0.020 = 9.0 x 10<sup>-12</sup> **[1 mark]**

- Rearrange and solve:

4*s*<sup>2</sup> = $\frac{9.0\times10^{-12}}{0.020}$ = 4.5 x 10<sup>-10</sup> **[1 mark]**

*s*<sup>2</sup> = 1.125 x 10<sup>-10</sup>

*s* = $\sqrt{1.125\times10^{-10}}$ = **1.06 x 10**<sup>**-5**</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for *K*<sub>sp</sub> = (2*s*)<sup>2</sup> x 0.020 (correct substitution with common ion)
> 
> 1 mark for 4*s*<sup>2</sup> = 4.5 x 10<sup>-10</sup> or equivalent rearrangement
> 
> 1 mark for *s* = 1.06 x 10<sup>-5</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup>

> **[exam-tip]**
> In the presence of a common ion (CrO<sub>4</sub><sup>2-</sup> from K<sub>2</sub>CrO<sub>4</sub>), the [CrO<sub>4</sub><sup>2-</sup>] is approximated as 0.020 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> since the Ag<sub>2</sub>CrO<sub>4</sub> contribution is negligible.
> 
> Substituting [Ag<sup>+</sup>] = 2*s* and [CrO<sub>4</sub><sup>2-</sup>] = 0.020 gives *K*<sub>sp</sub> = 4*s*<sup>2</sup> x 0.020.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Silver chromate, Ag₂CrO₄, is a chemical compound of silver and hexavalent chromium that is used in photography.

It has a solubility product, *K*sp, of 9.0 x 10⁻¹² at 25 °C.

10.0 cm<sup>3</sup> of 1.0 x 10<sup>-4</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup> AgNO<sub>3</sub> (aq) was mixed with 10.0 cm<sup>3</sup> of 0.020 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> K<sub>2</sub>CrO<sub>4</sub> (aq).

Calculate the ionic product of Ag<sub>2</sub>CrO<sub>4</sub> and state whether a precipitate of silver chromate will form. Show your working.
parts.solutionMd:
To determine whether a precipitate of Ag<sub>2</sub>CrO<sub>4</sub> will form on mixing:

- Calculate the concentrations after mixing (total volume = 10.0 + 10.0 = 20.0 cm<sup>3</sup>):

[Ag<sup>+</sup> (aq)] = $\frac{1.0\times10^{-4}\times10.0}{20.0}$ = 5.0 x 10<sup>-5</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup>

[CrO<sub>4</sub><sup>2-</sup> (aq)] = $\frac{0.020\times10.0}{20.0}$ = 0.010 mol dm<sup>-3</sup>

**[1 mark]**

- Calculate the ionic product:

IP = [Ag<sup>+</sup>]<sup>2</sup>[CrO<sub>4</sub><sup>2-</sup>] = (5.0 x 10<sup>-5</sup>)<sup>2</sup> x 0.010

IP = **2.5 x 10**<sup>**-11**</sup>

**[1 mark]**

- Compare IP with *K*<sub>sp</sub>:

2.5 x 10<sup>-11</sup> > 9.0 x 10<sup>-12</sup>

A precipitate of Ag<sub>2</sub>CrO<sub>4</sub> will form because IP > *K*<sub>sp</sub>

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for both concentrations after mixing: [Ag<sup>+</sup>] = 5.0 x 10<sup>-5</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup> **AND **[CrO<sub>4</sub><sup>2-</sup>] = 0.010 mol dm<sup>-3</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for IP = 2.5 x 10<sup>-11</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for IP > *K*<sub>sp</sub> **AND **a conclusion that a precipitate forms

> **[exam-tip]**
> When two equal volumes are mixed, each concentration is halved. Use: c<sub>mixed</sub> = c<sub>original</sub> x V<sub>original</sub> / V<sub>total</sub>.
> 
> If IP > *K*<sub>sp</sub>, the solution is supersaturated and a precipitate forms. If IP < *K*<sub>sp</sub>, no precipitate forms.

name: Simple Rate Equations, Orders of Reaction & Rate Constants

parts.problemMd:
The rate equation for the reaction between reactants **X**, **Y** and **Z** is shown below.

rate = *k *[**X**]<sup>2</sup> [**Y**]

State the orders with respect to **X**, **Y** and **Z**.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The orders with respect to each reactant are:
> 
> - **X**: second / 2nd order / order 2 **[1 mark]**
> - **Y**: first / 1st order / order 1 **[1 mark]**
> - **Z**: zero order / order 0 **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The order of reaction for each reactant is found from the power to which its concentration is raised in the rate equation.
> 
> - [**X**] is raised to the power of 2, so **X** is second order
> - [**Y**] is raised to the power of 1, so **Y** is first order
> - **Z** does not appear in the rate equation, so it is zero order. Changing [**Z**] has no effect on the rate

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The rate equation for the reaction between reactants **X**, **Y** and **Z** is shown below.

rate = *k *[**X**]^2^ [**Y**]

State the overall order of this reaction.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The overall order of this reaction is:
> 
> - 3 / third / 3rd (order) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The overall order is the sum of the individual orders with respect to each reactant: 2 (**X**) + 1 (**Y**) + 0 (**Z**) = 3.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The rate equation for the reaction between reactants X, Y and Z is shown below.

rate = k[X]²[Y]

The rate of reaction is 3.72 x 10<sup>-5</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup> s<sup>-1</sup> when the

- concentration of **X** is 0.01 mol dm<sup>-3</sup>
- concentration of **Y** is 0.02 mol dm<sup>-3</sup>
- concentration of **Z** is 0.04 mol dm<sup>-3</sup>

Calculate the rate constant, *k*, for this reaction. State the units of *k*. Show your working.
parts.solutionMd:
The rate constant, *k*, is calculated by rearranging the rate equation.

- List the known values:

  - rate = 3.72 × 10<sup>-5</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup> s<sup>-1</sup>
  - [**X**] = 0.01 mol dm<sup>-3</sup>
  - [**Y**] = 0.02 mol dm<sup>-3</sup>
- Rearrange rate = *k*[**X**]<sup>2</sup>[**Y**] for *k* and substitute values:

`k = \frac{3 . 72 \times 10^{- 5}}{\left(\right. 0 . 01 \left.\right)^{2} \times 0 . 02}` **[1 mark]**

*k* = **18.6 ****[1 mark]**

- Units of *k*:

dm<sup>6</sup> mol<sup>-2</sup> s<sup>-1</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct substitution into the rearranged rate equation
> 
> 1 mark for *k* = 18.6
> 
> 1 mark for correct units dm<sup>6</sup> mol<sup>-2</sup> s<sup>-1</sup>

> **[exam-tip]**
> Rearrange the rate equation to make *k* the subject: *k* = rate / ([**X**]<sup>2</sup>[**Y**]).
> 
> A common mistake is forgetting to apply the power of 2 to [**X**] before substituting. Always check each concentration term matches its power in the rate equation.
> 
> To determine the units, substitute units into the rearranged expression and cancel:
> 
> - Units of *k* = mol dm<sup>-3</sup> s<sup>-1</sup> / ((mol dm<sup>-3</sup>)<sup>2</sup> × mol dm<sup>-3</sup>) = dm<sup>6</sup> mol<sup>-2</sup> s<sup>-1</sup>

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The rate equation for the reaction between reactants X, Y and Z is shown below.

rate = k[X]²[Y]

The rate of reaction is 3.72 x 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹ when the
- concentration of X is 0.01 mol dm⁻³
- concentration of Y is 0.02 mol dm⁻³
- concentration of Z is 0.04 mol dm⁻³

The experiment was repeated but the initial concentration of **X** was doubled, all other concentrations remained the same.

State and explain the effect on the rate of reaction.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The effect on the rate of reaction is:
> 
> - Rate quadruples / increases by a factor of 4 / (becomes) 1.488 × 10<sup>-4</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup> s<sup>-1</sup> **[1 mark]**
> - (Because) reaction is second / 2nd order with respect to **X**, so doubling [**X**] multiplies rate by 2<sup>2</sup> = 4 **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Because the reaction is second order with respect to **X**, doubling [**X**] multiplies the rate by 2<sup>2</sup> = 4, not by 2.
> 
> You can verify numerically: 3.72 × 10<sup>-5</sup> × 4 = 1.488 × 10<sup>-4</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup> s<sup>-1</sup>.

parts.problemMd:
Bromide ions and bromate(V) ions react in acidic conditions to form aqueous bromine in the following equation.

5Br<sup>–</sup> (aq) + BrO<sub>3</sub><sup>–</sup> (aq) + 6H<sup>+</sup> (aq) → 3Br<sub>2</sub> (aq) + 3H<sub>2</sub>O (l)

A series of experiments was carried out at a given temperature to find the rate equation for the reaction.

The results from experiments using different hydrogen ion concentrations are shown in Fig. 2.1.

![Graph showing rate of reaction against hydrogen ion concentration as a curved line increasing from the origin](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/26-reaction-kinetics/26-1-simple-rate-equations-orders-of-reaction-and-rate-constants/assets/010-graph-showing-rate-of-reaction-against-hydrogen-.png)

**Fig. 2.1**

Use the information in Fig. 2.1 to deduce the order of reaction with respect to hydrogen ions.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The order of reaction with respect to hydrogen ions is:
> 
> - 2 / 2nd / second order **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> On a rate-concentration graph, the shape of the curve indicates the order:
> 
> - Zero order: horizontal line (rate does not change with concentration)
> - First order: straight line through the origin (rate proportional to concentration)
> - Second order: upward curve (rate increases as the square of concentration)
> 
> The curve in Fig. 2.1 steepens as [H<sup>+</sup>] increases, which is consistent with second order.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Bromide ions and bromate(V) ions react in acidic conditions to form aqueous bromine in the following equation.

5Br⁻ (aq) + BrO₃⁻ (aq) + 6H⁺ (aq) → 3Br₂ (aq) + 3H₂O (l)

Experiments using different bromide concentrations showed that the order of reaction with respect to bromide ions was first order.

On the graph in Fig. 2.2, sketch a graph to show how the concentration of bromide ions would change during the course of a reaction.

![Blank concentration-time graph for bromide ions with axes labelled](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/26-reaction-kinetics/26-1-simple-rate-equations-orders-of-reaction-and-rate-constants/assets/011-blank-concentration-time-graph-for-bromide-ions-.png)

**Fig. 2.2**
parts.solutionMd:
The concentration-time graph for bromide ions is:

![Concentration-time graph for bromide ions showing a shallow curve decreasing from initial concentration to near zero](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/26-reaction-kinetics/26-1-simple-rate-equations-orders-of-reaction-and-rate-constants/assets/012-concentration-time-graph-for-bromide-ions-showin.png)

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for a shallow curve, decreasing as time increases

> **[exam-tip]**
> For a first order reaction, concentration decreases as a smooth exponential decay curve that gets shallower over time. The curve must start at the initial [Br<sup>-</sup>] and approach (but not reach) zero.
> 
> Zero order gives a straight line with constant gradient. Do not draw a straight line here.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Bromide ions and bromate(V) ions react in acidic conditions to form aqueous bromine in the following equation.

5Br⁻ (aq) + BrO₃⁻ (aq) + 6H⁺ (aq) → 3Br₂ (aq) + 3H₂O (l)

A series of experiments was carried out at a given temperature to find the rate equation for the reaction.

The order of reaction with respect to hydrogen ions is: 2 / 2nd / second order

Experiments using different bromide concentrations showed that the order of reaction with respect to bromide ions was first order.

Overall, the reaction between bromide ions and bromate(V) ions in acidic conditions is fourth order.

i) Deduce the order with respect to bromate(V) ions.

[1]

ii) Using your answer to part **(a)** and the information in part **(b)**, construct the rate equation for the reaction.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The order with respect to bromate(V) ions is:
> 
> - 1 / 1st / first order **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The rate equation for the reaction is:
> 
> - Rate = *k*[Br<sup>-</sup>][BrO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup>][H<sup>+</sup>]<sup>2</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> To find the bromate(V) order, use the total overall order. The reaction is fourth order overall: Br<sup>-</sup> contributes 1, H<sup>+</sup> contributes 2, so BrO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup> = 4 - 1 - 2 = 1.
> 
> For the rate equation, include each reactant raised to its order as the power. A first order term appears as [species]<sup>1</sup>, which is conventionally written as [species] (no superscript needed).

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Overall, the reaction between bromide ions and bromate(V) ions in acidic conditions is fourth order.

ii) Using your answer to part (a) and the information in part (b), construct the rate equation for the reaction.

The rate equation for the reaction is:

Rate = k[Br^-][BrO3^-][H^+]^2

Bromide ions and bromate(V) ions react in acidic conditions to form aqueous bromine in the following equation.

5Br<sup>–</sup> (aq) + BrO<sub>3</sub><sup>–</sup> (aq) + 6H<sup>+</sup> (aq) → 3Br<sub>2</sub> (aq) + 3H<sub>2</sub>O (l)

i) Using your answer to part **(c)**, construct an expression for the rate constant for the reaction between bromide ions and bromate(V) ions in acidic conditions.

[1]

ii) Suggest suitable units for the rate constant.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The expression for the rate constant is:
> 
> - $\mathrm{k} = \frac{rate}{[ Br^{ - } ] [ BrO_{3}^{ - } ] [ \mathrm{H} ^{ + } ] ^{2} }$ **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) Suitable units for the rate constant are:
> 
> - dm<sup>9</sup> mol<sup>-3</sup> s<sup>-1</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Rearrange the rate equation to make *k* the subject: *k* = rate / ([Br<sup>-</sup>][BrO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup>][H<sup>+</sup>]<sup>2</sup>).
> 
> To determine the units, substitute units into the expression for *k* and cancel:
> 
> - *k* = mol dm<sup>-3</sup> s<sup>-1</sup> / ((mol dm<sup>-3</sup>)(mol dm<sup>-3</sup>)(mol dm<sup>-3</sup>)<sup>2</sup>) = dm<sup>9</sup> mol<sup>-3</sup> s<sup>-1</sup>

parts.problemMd:
Hydrogen peroxide, H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>, is a colourless liquid. It is widely used in cosmetic and medical products. It is an effective disinfectant and bleaching agent.

Hydrogen peroxide is unstable and will decompose slowly to form water and oxygen. The rate of decomposition can be increased using manganese(IV) oxide as a catalyst.

2H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> (aq) → 2H<sub>2</sub>O (l) + O<sub>2</sub> (g)

The graph in Fig. 3.1 shows how hydrogen peroxide decomposes in the presence of manganese(IV) oxide.

![Concentration-time graph showing the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide over time in the presence of manganese(IV) oxide catalyst](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/26-reaction-kinetics/26-1-simple-rate-equations-orders-of-reaction-and-rate-constants/assets/007-concentration-time-graph-showing-the-decompositi.png)

**Fig. 3.1**

Define the term half-life of a reaction.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The half-life of a reaction is:
> 
> - The time taken for the concentration of a reactant to halve / fall to half its original value **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> This is a definition you need to know precisely. The key elements are:
> 
> 1. The time taken...
> 2. ...for the concentration of a reactant to fall to half its original value.
> 
> Avoid phrases like "the time for the reaction to be half complete" as the half-life specifically refers to concentration, not the overall extent of reaction.

parts.solutionMd:
To show that the reaction is first order with respect to hydrogen peroxide:

Using the graph in Fig. 3.2, determine

>

ii) The rate constant can be determined by either method:

- Rate constant clearly linked to rate: `k = \frac{rate}{[H_{2}O_{2}]}`
**OR**
Rate constant clearly linked to half-life: $k = \frac{ln2}{t_{1/2}}$ **[1 mark]**

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Hydrogen peroxide, H~2~O~2~, is a colourless liquid. It is widely used in cosmetic and medical products. It is an effective disinfectant and bleaching agent.

Hydrogen peroxide is unstable and will decompose slowly to form water and oxygen. The rate of decomposition can be increased using manganese(IV) oxide as a catalyst.

2H~2~O~2~ (aq) → 2H~2~O (l) + O~2~ (g)

To show that the reaction is first order with respect to hydrogen peroxide:

Rate = *k*[H~2~O~2~]

When the initial concentration of hydrogen peroxide was halved, state what the effect, if any, on the half-life of this reaction would be.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The effect on the half-life is:
> 
> - No effect (on the half-life) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For a first order reaction, the half-life is constant and independent of the initial concentration. Halving the starting concentration of H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> does not change the time taken for that concentration to halve again.
> 
> This is a defining characteristic of first order kinetics. In contrast, for a zero order reaction, the half-life decreases as the concentration decreases.

parts.problemMd:
The initial rate of the reaction of chlorine dioxide, ClO<sub>2</sub>, and fluorine, F<sub>2</sub>, is measured in a series of experiments at a constant temperature.

2 ClO<sub>2</sub> + F<sub>2</sub> → 2ClO<sub>2</sub>F

The results obtained are shown in Table 1.1.

**Table 1.1**

| **experiment** | **[ClO**<sub>**2**</sub>**] / mol dm**<sup>**-3**</sup> | **[F**<sub>**2**</sub>**] / mol dm**<sup>**-3**</sup> | **initial rate / mol dm**<sup>**-3**</sup>** s**<sup>**-1**</sup> |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0.010 | 0.060 | 2.20 × 10<sup>-3</sup> |
| 2 | 0.025 | 0.060 | to be calculated |
| 3 | to be calculated | 0.040 | 7.04 × 10<sup>-3</sup> |

The rate equation is rate = *k*[ClO<sub>2</sub>][F<sub>2</sub>].

i) Define the term order of reaction with respect to a particular reagent.

[1]

ii) Use the results of experiment 1 to calculate the rate constant, *k*, for this reaction. State the units of *k*. Show your working.

*k* = ............................. units .............................

[2]

iii) Use the data in Table 1.1 to calculate the initial rate in experiment 2.

initial rate = ...................................... mol dm<sup>-3</sup> s<sup>-1</sup>

[1]

iv) Use the data in Table 1.1 to calculate [ClO<sub>2</sub>] in experiment 3.

[ClO<sub>2</sub>] = ............................................ mol dm<sup>-3</sup>

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The order of reaction with respect to a particular reagent is:
> 
> - The power to which the concentration of that reactant is raised in the rate equation
> **OR**
> The index / exponent / power of the reactant's concentration in the rate equation **[1 mark]**

ii) To calculate the rate constant, *k*, using the data from experiment 1:

- List the known values:

  - rate = 2.20 × 10<sup>-3</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup> s<sup>-1</sup>
  - [ClO<sub>2</sub>] = 0.010 mol dm<sup>-3</sup>
  - [F<sub>2</sub>] = 0.060 mol dm<sup>-3</sup>
- Rearrange rate = *k*[ClO<sub>2</sub>][F<sub>2</sub>] for *k* and substitute values:

$k = \frac{2.20\times10^{-3}}{0.010\times0.060}$

*k* = **3.7 ****[1 mark]**

- Units of *k*:

mol<sup>-1</sup> dm<sup>3</sup> s<sup>-1</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii)
> 
> 1 mark for *k* = 3.7 (accept 3.66–3.70)
> 
> 1 mark for units mol<sup>-1</sup> dm<sup>3</sup> s<sup>-1</sup>

iii) The initial rate in experiment 2 is found using *k*:

rate = *k*[ClO<sub>2</sub>][F<sub>2</sub>]

rate = 3.7 × 0.025 × 0.060

rate = 5.50 × 10<sup>-3</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup> s<sup>-1</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> iii)
> 
> 1 mark for rate = 5.50 × 10<sup>-3</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup> s<sup>-1</sup> (allow 5.55 × 10<sup>-3</sup> if using rounded *k*)

iv) [ClO<sub>2</sub>] in experiment 3 is found by rearranging the rate equation:

- Rearrange rate = *k*[ClO<sub>2</sub>][F<sub>2</sub>] for [ClO<sub>2</sub>] and substitute values:

[ClO<sub>2</sub>] = $\frac{7.04\times10^{-3}}{3.7\times0.040}$

[ClO<sub>2</sub>] = 0.048 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> iv) 1 mark for [ClO<sub>2</sub>] = 0.048 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> (accept 0.047–0.049)
> 
> Allow error carried forward from an incorrect *k* in parts iii and iv.

> **[exam-tip]**
> For part (i): the order refers to the power in the rate equation, not the stoichiometric coefficient in the balanced equation. They are frequently different.
> 
> For parts (ii)–(iv): always rearrange the rate equation to make the unknown the subject before substituting values.
> 
> To find the units of *k*, substitute units into the rearranged expression and cancel:
> 
> - *k* = mol dm<sup>-3</sup> s<sup>-1</sup> / ((mol dm<sup>-3</sup>)(mol dm<sup>-3</sup>)) = mol<sup>-1</sup> dm<sup>3</sup> s<sup>-1</sup>
> 
> For part (iii): use the unrounded *k* value for the most accurate answer. Using rounded *k* = 3.7 gives 5.55 × 10<sup>-3</sup>, which is also accepted.
> 
> For part (iv): rearrange for [ClO<sub>2</sub>] = rate / (*k* × [F<sub>2</sub>]). Divide by BOTH *k* AND [F<sub>2</sub>] as a common mistake is omitting one of them.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The initial rate of the reaction of chlorine dioxide, ClO2, and fluorine, F2, is measured in a series of experiments at a constant temperature.

2 ClO2 + F2 → 2ClO2F

The rate equation is rate = k[ClO2][F2].

i) Define the term rate-determining step.

[1]

ii) The mechanism of the reaction between ClO<sub>2</sub> and F<sub>2</sub> has two steps.

Suggest equations for the two steps of this mechanism.

step 1 ..............................................................................

step 2 ...............................................................................

[1]

iii) State and explain which of the two steps is the rate-determining step.

rate-determining step = ..........................

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The rate-determining step is:
> 
> - The slowest step in a multi-step reaction **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) Equations for the two steps of the mechanism:
> 
> Step 1: ClO<sub>2</sub> + F<sub>2</sub> → ClO<sub>2</sub>F<sub>2</sub>
> Step 2: ClO<sub>2</sub> + ClO<sub>2</sub>F<sub>2</sub> → 2ClO<sub>2</sub>F
> 
> **OR**
> 
> Step 1: ClO<sub>2</sub> + F<sub>2</sub> → ClO<sub>2</sub>F + F
> Step 2: ClO<sub>2</sub> + F → ClO<sub>2</sub>F **[1 mark]**
> 
> iii) The rate-determining step is:
> 
> - Step 1
> **AND**
> Stoichiometry of step 1 (1 mol ClO<sub>2</sub> and 1 mol F<sub>2</sub>) is consistent with the rate equation **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For part (i): the rate-determining step controls the overall rate because it is the slowest step. Only the species that react in this step affect the rate.
> 
> For part (ii): the two steps must add together to give the overall equation. The intermediate formed in step 1 must appear as a reactant in step 2 and cancel when the steps are added.
> 
> For part (iii): identify the rate-determining step by comparing the stoichiometry of each step with the rate equation rate = *k*[ClO<sub>2</sub>][F<sub>2</sub>]. Step 1 has exactly one ClO<sub>2</sub> and one F<sub>2</sub>, matching first order in each. Step 2 involves the intermediate (not in the rate equation), so it cannot be rate-determining.

parts.problemMd: Describe the effect of temperature change on the rate of a reaction and the rate constant.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The effect of temperature change on the rate of a reaction and the rate constant is:
> 
> - As temperature increases, both the rate of reaction and the rate constant / *k* increase **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Increasing temperature increases both the rate AND the rate constant *k*. Note that *k* is not a fixed value as it depends on temperature and increases exponentially as temperature rises.
> 
> This question asks you to "describe", which means that you do not need to explain why in terms of activation energy. A description of the direction of change is sufficient.

parts.problemMd:
This question is about the reactions of different unknown compounds. Two compounds, **X** and **Y**, were reacted together. The initial rate of reaction was measured when compound **X** and compound **Y** were reacted together. The temperature was kept constant and the results of the experiments are shown in **Table 2.1**. **Table 2.1** | **experiment** | **[X] / mol dm****-3** | **[Y] / mol dm****-3** | **rate of reaction**

[1] ii) State the order of the reaction with respect to **Y**. [1] iii) State the overall order of the reaction. [1] iv) Construct the rate equation for the reaction. [1]
parts.solutionMd:
i) To deduce the order of reaction with respect to **X**:

- Use experiments 1 and 2:

  - [X] increases by a factor of 1.5
  - [Y] is constant
  - Rate increases by a factor of 1.5
  - The rate is proportional to [X]
  - Therefore, the order of reaction with respect to **X** is 1 / first **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for X is 1st order

i) To deduce the order of reaction with respect to **Y**:

- Use experiments 2 and 3:

  - [Y] increases by a factor of 1.5
  - [X] is constant
  - Rate increases by a factor of 1.5
  - The rate is proportional to [Y]
  - Therefore, the order of reaction with respect to **Y** is 1 / first **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> iii) The overall order of reaction is:
> 
> - 2 **[1 mark]**
> 
> iv) The rate equation is:
> 
> - rate = *k*[X][Y] **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> When determining the order of a reactant, look for a pair of experiments where only that reactant's concentration changes.
> 
> For the rate equation, always include *k* and use square brackets to show concentration. First order terms are written as [X], not [X]<sup>1</sup>.

parts.problemMd:
Three separate experiments were carried out at 400K with different starting concentrations of A and B. The results are shown in **Table 2.2.** **Table 2.2** | **experiment ** | **[A] / mol dm****-3** | **[B] / mol dm****-3** | **rate of reaction**
**/ mol dm****-3**** s****-1** | |---|---|---|---| | 1 | 0.50 | 0.30 | 7.6 x 10-4 | | 2 | 0.25 | 0.30 | 1.9 x 10-4 | | 3 | 0.25 | 0.60 | 3.8 x 10-3 | i) Deduce the order of reaction with respect to each reactant. Explain your reasoning. [2] ii) Construct the rate equation for this reaction. Calculate the rate constant, k. State the units of k. Show your working. [4]
parts.solutionMd:
i) To deduce the order of reaction with respect to **A**:

- Use experiments 1 and 2:

  - [A] decreases by a factor of 2
  - [B] is constant
  - Rate decreases by a factor of 4
  - Since halving [A] quarters the rate, A is second order **[1 mark]**

To deduce the order of reaction with respect to **B**:

- Use experiments 2 and 3:

  - [B] increases by a factor of 2
  - [A] is constant
  - Rate increases by a factor of 2
  - The rate is proportional to [X]
  - Therefore, the order of reaction with respect to **B** is 1 / first **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for A is 2nd order / order 2
> 
> 1 mark for B is 1st order / order 1

ii) The rate equation is:

rate = *k*[A]<sup>2</sup>[B] **[1 mark]**

To calculate *k*:

*k* = `\frac{rate}{\left[A\right]^{2}\left[B\right]}`

*k* = `\frac{7.6 \times 10^{-4}}{\left(0.50\right)^{2}\left(0.30\right)}` **[1 mark]**

*k* = **0.010 ****[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for rate = *k*[A]<sup>2</sup>[B]
> 
> 1 mark for correct substitution into the rearranged rate equation
> 
> 1 mark for k = 0.010 (accept: 1.0 × 10<sup>-2</sup>)
> 
> 1 mark for mol<sup>-2</sup> dm<sup>6</sup> s<sup>-1</sup>

> **[exam-tip]**
> When calculating *k*, remember to square [A] in the denominator. A common error is using [A] rather than [A]<sup>2</sup>.

parts.problemMd:
The overall rate equation for a reaction is rate = *k*[P]<sup>2</sup>[Q]

i) State what the units would be of the rate constant, *k*, in this reaction.

[1]

ii) State the overall order of the reaction above.

[1]

> 
> - mol<sup>-2</sup> dm<sup>6</sup> s<sup>-1</sup> **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The overall order of the reaction is:
> 
> - 3 **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> To find the units of *k*, rearrange the rate equation to make *k* the subject, then substitute units for rate (mol dm<sup>-3</sup> s<sup>-1</sup>) and concentration (mol dm<sup>-3</sup>). Cancel mol dm<sup>-3</sup> where possible.

parts.problemMd:
Chemists measured the rate of a chemical reaction in a series of experiments between compounds C and D at a fixed temperature as shown in **Table 2.3**. **Table 2.3** | **experiment** | **[C] / mol dm****-3** | **[D] / mol dm****-3** | **rate of reaction**

parts.solutionMd:
i) To deduce the order of reaction with respect to C and D:

- Use experiments 1 and 2:

  - [C] increases by a factor of 3
  - [D] is constant
  - Rate increases by a factor of 9
  - C is second order **[1 mark]**

  - [C] increases by a factor of 2
  - [D] increases by a factor of 2
  - Rate increases by a factor of 4
  - The [C] should cause a rate increase of factor 4 alone
  - Therefore, D is zero order **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for C = 2nd order / order 2 **AND **D = zero order / order 0

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii) The overall rate equation is:
> 
> - rate = *k*[C]<sup>2</sup> **[1 mark]**
> 
> rate = *k*[C]<sup>2</sup>[D]<sup>0</sup> is not accepted as  [D] must not appear in the rate equation for a zero order species.
