In octahedral complexes, d<sub>x</sub><sup><sub>2</sub></sup><sub>-y</sub><sup><sub>2</sub></sup> and d<sub>z</sub><sup><sub>2</sub></sup> have higher energy; in tetrahedral complexes these same orbitals have lower energy, with d<sub>xy</sub>, d<sub>xz</sub> and d<sub>yz</sub> taking the higher energy positions.

parts.problemMd: Define the term transition element.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> A transition element is:
> 
> - (A d-block element that can) form one or more stable ions with an incomplete d subshell **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> This is a standard definition you are required to know. Note that zinc and scandium are not transition elements: Zn<sup>2+</sup> has a full 3d subshell (d<sup>10</sup>) and Sc<sup>3+</sup> has an empty 3d subshell (d<sup>0</sup>), so neither meets the definition.

parts.problemMd:
Ammonia, NH<sub>3</sub>, acts as a monodentate ligand in many transition element complexes.

i) Define the term monodentate ligand.

[2]

ii) Aqueous silver ions, Ag<sup>+</sup> (aq), react with aqueous ammonia, NH<sub>3</sub> (aq), to form a linear complex.

State the formula of this complex. Include its charge.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) A monodentate ligand is defined as:
> 
> - A species / molecule / ion that forms one dative covalent / coordinate bond to a central metal ion **[1 mark]**
> - Using a lone pair of electrons to form the bond **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The formula of this complex, including its charge, is:
> 
> - [Ag(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>]<sup>+</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Monodentate ligands form only one coordinate bond to the central metal ion. Common examples include:
> 
> - Water (H<sub>2</sub>O)
> - Ammonia (NH<sub>3</sub>)
> - Chloride ions (Cl<sup>-</sup>)
> - Cyanide ions (CN<sup>-</sup>).
> 
> The linear [Ag(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>]<sup>+</sup> complex forms because Ag<sup>+</sup> adopts linear geometry with two coordinate bonds. Since NH<sub>3</sub> carries no charge, the overall charge of the complex equals the charge on the silver ion.

parts.problemMd:
There are two isomeric complex ions with the formula [Cr(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>]<sup>+</sup>. One is green and the other is violet.

i) State the type of stereoisomerism shown by these two complex ions.

[1]

ii) Explain why these complex ions are coloured, and why their colours are different.

[4]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The type of stereoisomerism shown is:
> 
> - Cis-trans / geometrical (stereoisomerism) **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) These complex ions are coloured and have different colours because:
> 
> - Ligands split the d-orbitals into two sets of non-degenerate energy levels **[1 mark]**
> - Visible light is absorbed when an electron is promoted / excited from a lower to a higher energy d-orbital **[1 mark]**
> - The observed colour is the complement of the colour of light absorbed **[1 mark]**
> - The two isomers have different spatial arrangements of ligands, giving different d-orbital splitting energies (Δ*E*), so different wavelengths of light are absorbed **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The four marking points for colour are always the same:
> 
> 1. d-orbital splitting by ligands
> 2. Visible light absorbed / electron promoted
> 3. Complementary colour observed
> 4. Different spatial arrangement of ligands → different Δ*E* → different wavelength absorbed.
> 
> Learn these four points and you will always score full marks on this type of question.
> 
> ![Cis and trans isomers of [Cr(NH3)4Cl2]+ showing the two different spatial arrangements of chloride ligands around the octahedral chromium centre](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/28-chemistry-of-transition-elements/28-3-colour-of-complexes/assets/002-cis-and-trans-isomers-of-cr-nh3-4cl2-showing-the.jpeg)

The two stereoisomers of [Ni(en)<sub>3</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> are:

**[2 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Ethane-1,2-diamine, H₂NCH₂CH₂NH₂, is represented as en.

Ethane-1,2-diamine is a useful reagent in organic chemistry.

i) Explain why ethane-1,2-diamine acts as a Brønsted–Lowry base.

[2]

ii) Construct an equation for the reaction of ethane-1,2-diamine with an excess of hydrochloric acid.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) Ethane-1,2-diamine acts as a Brønsted–Lowry base because:
> 
> - The nitrogen atoms have lone pairs of electrons **[1 mark]**
> - These lone pairs accept protons / are donated to protons (from the acid) **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The equation for the reaction with excess hydrochloric acid is:
> 
> - H<sub>2</sub>NCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> + 2HCl → ClH<sub>3</sub>NCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>3</sub>Cl **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> A Brønsted–Lowry base accepts protons using a lone pair of electrons. Ethane-1,2-diamine has two NH<sub>2</sub> groups, each with a lone pair on nitrogen, so it can accept two protons in total. With excess HCl, both amino groups are protonated. You can also write the ionic equation: H<sub>2</sub>NCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> + 2H<sup>+</sup> → (H<sub>3</sub>NCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>3</sub>)<sup>2+</sup>

parts.problemMd:
This question is about the geometry and colours of transition element complexes.

Explain why transition elements have variable oxidation states but Group 1 elements do not.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Transition elements have variable oxidation states but Group 1 elements do not because:
> 
> - In transition elements, the 4s and 3d subshells are close in energy / successive ionisation energies increase gradually **[1 mark]**
> - In Group 1 elements, the second electron is removed from a much lower energy level / there is a large increase in ionisation energy between the first and second ionisation energies **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> You should be able to explain variable oxidation states in terms of successive ionisation energies. For transition elements, the small differences between ionisation energies mean that several oxidation states are energetically accessible. For Group 1 elements, the second ionisation energy is far higher than the first because the electron is removed from a stable noble gas core, so only the +1 oxidation state is observed.

parts.problemMd:
Transition element compounds are often coloured. For example, [Cr(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup> is green.

Explain why transition element complexes are coloured.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Transition element complexes are coloured because:
> 
> - Ligands cause the d-orbitals to split into two sets of non-degenerate energy levels **[1 mark]**
> - Visible light is absorbed when an electron is promoted / excited from a lower to a higher energy d-orbital **[1 mark]**
> - The observed colour is the complement of the colour of light absorbed **[1 mark]**
> - The wavelength of light absorbed depends on the size of the d-orbital splitting energy (Δ*E*), which depends on the identity and number of ligands **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> These four marking points come up every time a question asks why transition element complexes are coloured. Learn them in order:
> 
> 1. d-orbital splitting by ligands
> 2. Visible light absorbed / electron promoted
> 3. Complementary colour observed
> 4. Different ligands give different Δ*E*, hence different colours.
> 
> If the question only asks why the complex is coloured (not why different complexes have different colours), points 1–3 are sufficient.

parts.problemMd:
Zinc and cobalt ions react with water to form the complexes [Zn(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> and [Co(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup>.

i) Explain why water is able to act as a ligand in forming these complexes.

[2]

ii) State the geometry of the [Co(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> complex ion.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) Water is able to act as a ligand because:
> 
> - Oxygen has a lone pair of electrons **[1 mark]**
> - Which it donates to form a dative covalent / coordinate bond with the metal ion **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The geometry of [Co(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> is:
> 
> - Octahedral **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> A ligand must be able to donate a lone pair of electrons to form a coordinate bond with the central metal ion — it acts as a Lewis base. Water uses the lone pairs on the oxygen atom for this purpose. With six water ligands, [Co(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> adopts an octahedral geometry to place the six coordinate bonds as far apart as possible.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Transition element complexes are coloured because:

- Ligands cause the d-orbitals to split into two sets of non-degenerate energy levels
- Visible light is absorbed when an electron is promoted / excited from a lower to a higher energy d-orbital
- The observed colour is the complement of the colour of light absorbed
- The wavelength of light absorbed depends on the size of the d-orbital splitting energy (ΔE), which depends on the identity and number of ligands

Explain why solutions containing [Zn(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> are colourless.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> [Zn(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> is colourless because:
> 
> - The Zn<sup>2+</sup> ion has a completely full 3d subshell (d<sup>10</sup>) **[1 mark]**
> - No d-d electron transitions can occur / no electrons can be promoted between d-orbitals **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Zinc is not a transition element because Zn<sup>2+</sup> has the electron configuration [Ar]3d<sup>10</sup>, which is a full 3d subshell.
> 
> For a complex to be coloured, d-orbital splitting must occur and an electron must be able to move between the two sets.
> 
> With a completely full d subshell, this is impossible, so no visible light is absorbed and the solution appears colourless. Contrast this with Co<sup>2+</sup>, which has the configuration [Ar]3d<sup>7</sup> (a partially filled 3d subshell) and can absorb visible light.

parts.problemMd:
i) Explain why aqueous nickel(II) ions, Ni<sup>2+</sup>(aq), are green.

[4]

ii) Explain why aqueous scandium(III) ions, Sc<sup>3+</sup>(aq), are colourless.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) Aqueous Ni<sup>2+</sup> ions are green because:
> 
> - Ligands cause the d-orbitals to split into two sets of non-degenerate energy levels **[1 mark]**
> - Visible light is absorbed when an electron is promoted / excited from a lower to a higher energy d-orbital **[1 mark]**
> - Ni<sup>2+</sup> has a partially filled 3d subshell, so d-d electron transitions can occur **[1 mark]**
> - The observed colour (green) is the complement of the colour of light absorbed **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) Aqueous Sc<sup>3+</sup> ions are colourless because:
> 
> - Sc<sup>3+</sup> has an empty 3d subshell (d<sup>0</sup>), so no d-d electron transitions can occur **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Scandium is not a transition element because Sc<sup>3+</sup> has the electron configuration [Ar], it has no 3d electrons at all.
> 
> Without any electrons in the d-orbitals, no d-d transitions are possible and no visible light is absorbed, so Sc<sup>3+</sup> solutions are colourless.
> 
> Nickel(II) has the configuration [Ar]3d<sup>8</sup>, which is a partially filled 3d subshell, so it can form coloured complexes.

parts.problemMd: Explain why the addition of an excess of aqueous ammonia to aqueous copper(II) ions causes a change in the colour of the solution.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Adding excess aqueous ammonia to aqueous copper(II) ions causes a colour change because:
> 
> - (Four of the) water ligands are replaced by ammonia ligands / ligand exchange occurs **[1 mark]**
> - The d-orbital splitting energy (Δ*E*) between the two sets of d-orbitals changes because it depends on the identity of the ligand **[1 mark]**
> - A different wavelength / frequency of light is absorbed, so a different colour is observed **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> First recognise that adding excess ammonia causes ligand exchange: water ligands in [Cu(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> are replaced by ammonia ligands to form [Cu(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>2</sub>]<sup>2+</sup>.
> 
> Different ligands cause different extents of d-orbital splitting, so the energy gap changes. Since a different wavelength of light is absorbed, the complementary colour seen changes, and the solution appears a deeper blue.

parts.problemMd:
The [Fe(CN)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>4-</sup> complex ion contains iron and cyanide ligands.

i) Deduce the oxidation state of iron in [Fe(CN)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>4-</sup>. Show your working.

[1]

ii) Draw the arrangement of electrons in the 3d and 4s subshells of the iron ion in [Fe(CN)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>4-</sup>, using arrow-in-box notation.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
i) To deduce the oxidation state of iron in [Fe(CN)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>4-</sup>:

Fe + (6 x -1) = -4

Fe = +2 **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for +2 with working shown (CN<sup>-</sup> = -1 stated or implied; Fe + 6(-1) = -4 seen)

ii) The arrangement of electrons in the 3d and 4s subshells of the Fe<sup>2+</sup> ion is:

![Fe2+ orbital box diagram showing the 3d subshell with six electrons arranged as three pairs in the lower three boxes and empty 4s subshell, with [Ar] noble gas core notation](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/28-chemistry-of-transition-elements/28-3-colour-of-complexes/assets/001-fe2-orbital-box-diagram-showing-the-3d-subshell-.png)

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for six electrons correctly arranged in the 3d subshell with empty 4s and [Ar] noble gas core notation

> **[exam-tip]**
> To find the oxidation state, recall that each CN<sup>-</sup> ligand carries a -1 charge. With six CN<sup>-</sup> ligands, total charge from ligands = 6 x (-1) = -6. The overall complex charge is -4, so: Fe + (-6) = -4, giving Fe = +2.
> 
> For the orbital diagram, Fe<sup>2+</sup> has the configuration [Ar]3d<sup>6</sup> — the 4s subshell is empty because electrons are removed from 4s before 3d. Include [Ar] at the start to indicate the noble gas core.

parts.problemMd:
Cobalt is a transition element with atomic number 27.

Complete the electronic configurations of a Co atom and a Co<sup>2+</sup> ion.

Co atom   1s<sup>2</sup> 2s<sup>2</sup> 2p<sup>6</sup>  ..................................

Co<sup>2+</sup> ion   1s<sup>2</sup> 2s<sup>2</sup> 2p<sup>6</sup>  ..................................
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The electronic configurations of a Co atom and a Co<sup>2+</sup> ion are:
> 
> - Co atom: 1s<sup>2</sup> 2s<sup>2</sup> 2p<sup>6</sup> 3s<sup>2</sup> 3p<sup>6</sup> 3d<sup>7</sup> 4s<sup>2</sup>
> **OR**
> 1s<sup>2</sup> 2s<sup>2</sup> 2p<sup>6</sup> 3s<sup>2</sup> 3p<sup>6</sup> 4s<sup>2</sup> 3d<sup>7</sup> **[1 mark]**
> - Co<sup>2+</sup> ion: 1s<sup>2</sup> 2s<sup>2</sup> 2p<sup>6</sup> 3s<sup>2</sup> 3p<sup>6</sup> 3d<sup>7</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Although the Periodic Table suggests electrons fill in the order 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 4s, 3d, the correct filling order is 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 3d, 4s. The 3d orbital is slightly lower in energy than 4s, so 3d fills before 4s.
> 
> You can check your answer by adding up all the electrons:
> 
> 2 + 2 + 6 + 2 + 6 + 7 + 2 = 27
> 
> When writing the Co<sup>2+</sup> ion configuration, remember that 4s electrons are lost before 3d electrons. Co<sup>2+</sup> has 25 electrons, so the 4s electrons are removed first, giving 1s<sup>2</sup> 2s<sup>2</sup> 2p<sup>6</sup> 3s<sup>2</sup> 3p<sup>6</sup> 3d<sup>7</sup>.

parts.problemMd:
When aqueous ammonia, NH<sub>3</sub> (aq), is added to [Co(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> (aq), dropwise at first and then in excess, two distinct chemical reactions occur. For each reaction, state the expected observations and construct an equation.

i) Addition of a few drops of NH<sub>3</sub> (aq)

observation .............................................................................

equation ..................................................................................

[2]

ii) Addition of an excess of NH<sub>3</sub> (aq)

observation .............................................................................

equation ..................................................................................

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) Observations and equation for addition of a few drops of NH<sub>3</sub> (aq):
> 
> - Observation: blue / blue-green precipitate **[1 mark]**
> - [Co(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> (aq) + 2NH<sub>3</sub> (aq) ⇌ Co(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>4</sub>(OH)<sub>2</sub> (s) + 2NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> (aq)
> **OR**
> [Co(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> (aq) + 2OH<sup>-</sup> (aq) ⇌ Co(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>4</sub>(OH)<sub>2</sub> (s) + 2H<sub>2</sub>O (l) **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) Observations and equation for addition of excess NH<sub>3</sub> (aq):
> 
> - Observation: (straw) yellow / brown solution **[1 mark]**
> - Co(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>4</sub>(OH)<sub>2</sub> (s) + 6NH<sub>3</sub> (aq) ⇌ [Co(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> (aq) + 4H<sub>2</sub>O (l) + 2OH<sup>-</sup> (aq)
> **OR**
> Co(OH)<sub>2</sub> (s) + 6NH<sub>3</sub> (aq) ⇌ [Co(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> (aq) + 2OH<sup>-</sup> (aq) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Cobalt(II) and copper(II) are the two transition metals commonly tested for ligand substitution reactions with aqueous ammonia.
> 
> Cobalt(II) undergoes complete substitution with six water ligands replaced by six ammonia ligands, forming [Co(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup>. In contrast, copper(II) undergoes partial substitution with only four of the six water ligands replaced.
> 
> The [Co(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> complex is unstable in air and readily oxidises to form a blue [Co(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup> solution. You may be asked about this in a follow-on question.

parts.problemMd:
EDTA<sup>4-</sup> is a hexadentate ligand. When a solution of EDTA<sup>4-</sup> is added to a solution containing [Co(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup>, a new complex is formed. The formula of this complex is [CoEDTA]<sup>2-</sup>.

i) Explain what is meant by the term hexadentate ligand.

[2]

ii) State the type of reaction occurring here.

[1]

iii) Write an expression for the stability constant, *K*<sub>stab</sub>, of [CoEDTA]<sup>2-</sup> in this reaction.

[1]

iv) The numerical value of the *K*<sub>stab</sub> of [CoEDTA]<sup>2-</sup> is 7.7 x 10<sup>4</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup> dm<sup>3</sup> at 298 K.

Deduce what this value indicates about the stability of [CoEDTA]<sup>2-</sup> compared to [Co(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup>.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The meaning of the term hexadentate ligand:
> 
> - A ligand that can donate six lone pairs of electrons (to a central metal atom / ion) **[1 mark]**
> - To form six dative (covalent) / coordinate bonds **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The type of reaction is:
> 
> - Ligand exchange / substitution / replacement / displacement **[1 mark]**
> 
> iii) The stability constant expression for [CoEDTA]<sup>2-</sup> is:
> 
> - *K*<sub>stab</sub> = [[CoEDTA]<sup>2-</sup>] / ([[Co(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup>][[EDTA]<sup>4-</sup>]) **[1 mark]**
> 
> iv) The value of *K*<sub>stab</sub> indicates that:
> 
> - [CoEDTA]<sup>2-</sup> is (very) stable / more stable than [Co(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> A ligand is a species that donates a lone pair of electrons to a central metal atom or ion to form a coordinate (dative covalent) bond. The prefix tells you how many lone pairs it can donate: mono (1), bi (2), and so on up to hexa (6).
> 
> Since all six water ligands in [Co(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> are replaced by one EDTA<sup>4-</sup> ligand, this is a ligand exchange reaction. The equation is:
> 
> [Co(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> + EDTA<sup>4-</sup> ⇌ [CoEDTA]<sup>2-</sup> + 6H<sub>2</sub>O
> 
> The *K*<sub>stab</sub> expression follows from this equation in the same way as any equilibrium expression. Water is not included because it is the solvent:
> 
> *K*<sub>stab</sub> = [[CoEDTA]<sup>2-</sup>] / ([[Co(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup>][[EDTA]<sup>4-</sup>])
> 
> The greater the value of *K*<sub>stab</sub>, the more stable the complex ion is relative to the aquo complex it replaced.

parts.problemMd:
Several platinum complexes, including oxoplatin, iproplatin, ormaplatin and satraplatin, are used as anti-cancer drugs. The central platinum ions in the four complexes shown in **Fig. 1.1** all have the same geometry and oxidation state.

![Structural diagrams of four platinum anti-cancer drug complexes: oxoplatin, iproplatin, ormaplatin and satraplatin](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/28-chemistry-of-transition-elements/28-4-stereoisomerism-in-transition-element-complexes/assets/004-structural-diagrams-of-four-platinum-anti-cancer.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

State the oxidation state of the platinum ion and the geometry of these complexes.

oxidation state of the platinum ion ..................................................

geometry of the complexes ..................................................
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The oxidation state and geometry of the platinum complexes are:
> 
> - Oxidation state of the platinum ion = +4 **[1 mark]**
> - Geometry of the complexes = Octahedral **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> To deduce the oxidation state of platinum, use oxoplatin as it contains familiar ligands. The charge contributions are:
> 
> - OH<sup>-</sup> contributes -1
> - Cl<sup>-</sup> contributes -1
> - NH<sub>3</sub> contributes 0 (neutral ligand)
> 
> Since the overall charge on the complex is 0:
> 
> Pt + 2(-1) + 2(-1) + 2(0) = 0
> 
> Pt - 4 = 0
> 
> Pt = +4
> 
> All four complexes have 6 coordinate bonds, so the geometry must be octahedral.

i) Some transition elements and their compounds behave as catalysts. Explain why transition elements behave as catalysts.

[2]

ii) Catalysis can be classified as heterogeneous or homogeneous. Complete Table 1.1 by placing **one **tick (`✓`) in each row to indicate the type of catalysis in each reaction.

**Table 1.1**

|   | **type of catalysis** |   |

| Fe in the Haber process |   |   |
| Fe<sup>2+</sup> in the I<sup>–</sup> / S<sub>2</sub>O<sub>8</sub><sup>2–</sup> reaction |   |   |
| NO<sub>2</sub> in the oxidation of SO<sub>2</sub> |   |   |

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) Transition elements are able to act as catalysts because:
> 
> - Transition elements have more than one stable oxidation state **[1 mark]**
> - There are vacant d-orbitals that can accept lone pairs from reactant molecules
> **OR**
> They can form dative bonds with ligands **[1 mark]**

ii) The completed Table 1.1:

|   | **type of catalysis** |   |
|---|---|---|
| **reaction** | **heterogeneous** | **homogeneous** |
| Fe in the Haber process | `\checkmark` |   |
| Fe<sup>2+</sup> in the I<sup>–</sup> / S<sub>2</sub>O<sub>8</sub><sup>2–</sup> reaction |   | `\checkmark` |
| NO<sub>2</sub> in the oxidation of SO<sub>2</sub> |   | `\checkmark` |

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for all three rows correct

> **[exam-tip]**
> For part (i), the two key properties that allow transition elements to act as catalysts are their ability to adopt multiple oxidation states (allowing them to act as both electron donors and acceptors in reaction cycles) and their vacant d-orbitals (which allow reactant molecules to form coordinate bonds with the metal).
> 
> For part (ii), a heterogeneous catalyst is in a different phase from its reactants. Iron in the Haber process is a solid while the reactant gases N<sub>2</sub> and H<sub>2</sub> are in the gas phase.
> 
> A homogeneous catalyst is in the same phase as the reactants. Fe<sup>2+</sup> ions and the I<sup>–</sup>/S<sub>2</sub>O<sub>8</sub><sup>2–</sup> reactants are all aqueous. NO<sub>2</sub> and SO<sub>2</sub> are both gases.

parts.problemMd:
A solution containing a mixture of Sn<sup>2+</sup> (aq) and Sn<sup>4+</sup> (aq) is added to a solution containing a mixture of Fe<sup>2+</sup> (aq) and Fe<sup>3+</sup> (aq).

Table 2.2 lists electrode potentials for some electrode reactions of these ions.

**Table 2.2**

| **electrode reaction** | ***E***<sup>**ɵ**</sup>** / V** |
|---|---|
| Fe<sup>2+</sup> + 2e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ Fe | –0.44 |
| Fe<sup>3+</sup> + 3e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ Fe | –0.04 |
| Fe<sup>3+</sup> + e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ Fe<sup>2+</sup> | +0.77 |
| Sn<sup>2+</sup> + 2e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ Sn | –0.14 |
| Sn<sup>4+</sup> + 2e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ Sn<sup>2+</sup> | +0.15 |

*E*<sup>ɵ</sup> data from the table can be used to predict the reaction that takes place when the two solutions are mixed.

i) Construct an equation for this reaction.

[1]

ii) Calculate *E*<sup>ɵ</sup><sub>cell</sub> for this reaction.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The equation for this reaction:
> 
> - Sn<sup>2+</sup> + 2Fe<sup>3+</sup> → Sn<sup>4+</sup> + 2Fe<sup>2+</sup> **[1 mark]**
> 
> State symbols are not required.
> 
> ii) The standard cell potential:
> 
> - *E*<sup>ɵ</sup><sub>cell</sub> = 0.77 – 0.15 = **+0.62 V** **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For the equation, compare the *E*<sup>ɵ</sup> values: Sn<sup>2+</sup>/Sn<sup>4+</sup> (+0.15 V) is less positive than Fe<sup>3+</sup>/Fe<sup>2+</sup> (+0.77 V). The less positive electrode acts as the anode (oxidation), so Sn<sup>2+</sup> is oxidised to Sn<sup>4+</sup>. The Fe<sup>3+</sup> half-equation runs in the forward direction (reduction). Balance electrons: 2 moles of Fe<sup>3+</sup> are reduced per mole of Sn<sup>2+</sup> oxidised.
> 
> For *E*<sup>ɵ</sup><sub>cell</sub>, use:
> 
> *E*<sup>ɵ</sup><sub>cell</sub> = *E*<sup>ɵ</sup><sub>reduction</sub> – *E*<sup>ɵ</sup><sub>oxidation</sub>:
> 
> *E*<sup>ɵ</sup><sub>cell</sub> = (+0.77) – (+0.15) = +0.62 V

parts.problemMd:
Hexaaquairon(III) ions are pale violet. They form a colourless complex with fluoride ions, F<sup>–</sup>, as shown in equilibrium **1**, and a deep-red complex with thiocyanate ions, SCN<sup>–</sup>, as shown in equilibrium **2**.

equilibrium **1:**

[Fe(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup> + F<sup>–</sup> ⇌ [Fe(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>5</sub>F]<sup>2+</sup> + H<sub>2</sub>O

violet ⇌ colourless

*K*<sub>stab</sub> = 2.0 × 10<sup>5</sup> mol<sup>–1</sup> dm<sup>3</sup>

equilibrium **2:**

[Fe(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup> + SCN<sup>–</sup> ⇌ [Fe(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>5</sub>SCN]<sup>2+</sup> + H<sub>2</sub>O

violet ⇌ deep-red

*K*<sub>stab</sub> = 1.0 × 10<sup>3</sup> mol<sup>–1</sup> dm<sup>3</sup>

The following two experiments are carried out.

Experiment 1: A few drops of KSCN (aq) are added to 5 cm<sup>3</sup> of Fe<sup>3+</sup> (aq), followed by a few drops of KF (aq).

Experiment 2: A few drops of KF (aq) are added to 5 cm<sup>3</sup> of Fe<sup>3+</sup> (aq), followed by a few drops of KSCN (aq).

i) State and explain the sequence of colour changes you would observe in each of Experiment 1 and Experiment 2.

[4]

ii) State the type of reaction occurring during the experiments in **(d)(i)**.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The colour changes observed are:
> 
> Experiment 1:
> 
> - Violet to deep-red (adding KSCN forms the thiocyanate complex) **[1 mark]**
> - Deep-red to colourless (adding KF displaces the thiocyanate complex) **[1 mark]**
> 
> Experiment 2:
> 
> - Violet to colourless (adding KF forms the fluoride complex), remaining colourless on addition of KSCN **[1 mark]**
> 
> Explanation:
> 
> - *K*<sub>stab</sub> of [Fe(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>5</sub>F]<sup>2+</sup> > *K*<sub>stab</sub> of [Fe(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>5</sub>SCN]<sup>2+</sup>
> **OR**
> 2.0 × 10<sup>5</sup> > 1.0 × 10<sup>3</sup>, so the fluoride complex is more stable and displaces the thiocyanate complex **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The type of reaction:
> 
> - Ligand exchange / substitution / displacement **[1 mark]**
> 
> In Experiment 2, the fluoride complex is not displaced by SCN<sup>–</sup> because the F<sup>–</sup> complex has the larger *K*<sub>stab</sub> value.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Work through each experiment step by step.
> 
> Experiment 1: the pale violet [Fe(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup> turns deep-red when KSCN is added, forming [Fe(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>5</sub>SCN]<sup>2+</sup>. When KF is then added, the solution becomes colourless because the fluoride complex ([Fe(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>5</sub>F]<sup>2+</sup>, *K*<sub>stab</sub> = 2.0 × 10<sup>5</sup> mol<sup>–1</sup> dm<sup>3</sup>) is more stable than the thiocyanate complex (*K*<sub>stab</sub> = 1.0 × 10<sup>3</sup> mol<sup>–1</sup> dm<sup>3</sup>) and displaces it.
> 
> Experiment 2: the pale violet solution turns colourless when KF is added. When KSCN is then added, there is no colour change. The fluoride complex has the larger *K*<sub>stab</sub> value and cannot be displaced by SCN<sup>–</sup>.
> 
> For part (ii), any reaction in which one ligand replaces another is called ligand exchange or ligand substitution.

parts.problemMd:
Solutions of iron(III) salts are acidic due to the equilibrium shown.

[Fe(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+ </sup>(aq) ⇌ [Fe(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>5</sub>(OH)]<sup>2+ </sup>(aq) + H<sup>+</sup> (aq)

K<sub>a</sub> = 8.9 × 10<sup>–4</sup> mol dm<sup>–3</sup>

Calculate the pH of a 0.25 mol dm<sup>–3</sup> FeCl<sub>3 </sub>solution. Show your working.

pH = ..........................................................
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the pH of a 0.25 mol dm<sup>–3</sup> FeCl<sub>3</sub> solution:

- Find [H<sup>+</sup>]:

[H<sup>+</sup>]<sup>2</sup> = *K*<sub>a</sub> × [Fe<sup>3+</sup>]

[H<sup>+</sup>]<sup>2</sup> = 8.9 × 10<sup>–4</sup> × 0.25

[H<sup>+</sup>]<sup>2</sup> = 2.225 × 10<sup>–4</sup>

[H<sup>+</sup>] = $\sqrt{2.225\times10^{-4}}$

[H<sup>+</sup>] = 0.0149 mol dm<sup>–3 </sup>**[1 mark]**

- Calculate pH:

pH = –log(0.0149)

pH = **1.83** **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for [H<sup>+</sup>] = 0.0149 mol dm<sup>–3</sup> (accept 0.01492)
> 
> 1 mark for pH in the range 1.8–1.83

> **[exam-tip]**
> For this weak acid calculation, use:
> 
> [H<sup>+</sup>]<sup>2</sup> = *K*<sub>a</sub> × [HA]
> 
> This assumes [H<sup>+</sup>] equals [A<sup>–</sup>] (both produced in equal amounts) and that the equilibrium concentration of the weak acid equals the initial concentration, since the degree of dissociation is small.
> 
> Here, [Fe(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup> acts as the weak acid, so [HA]<sub>initial</sub> = 0.25 mol dm<sup>–3</sup>. Take the square root to find [H<sup>+</sup>], then use pH = –log[H<sup>+</sup>].

parts.problemMd: Define the term ligand.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> A ligand is a molecule or ion that:
> 
> - Contains a lone pair of electrons **[1 mark]**
> - Donates a lone pair to a central metal ion to form a coordinate / dative (covalent) bond **[1 mark]**
> 
> A ligand must be described as a molecule or ion, not just a species
> 
> Stating only 'donates electrons' without specifying a lone pair is not accepted.

> **[exam-tip]**
> A complete definition requires two elements: that the ligand possesses a lone pair of electrons, and that it donates that lone pair to the metal ion to form a coordinate bond.

parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The stability constant, *K*<sub>stab</sub>, is:
> 
> - The equilibrium constant for the formation of a complex ion (from a central metal ion and its ligands) **[1 mark]**
> - In aqueous solution / in a solvent / from its constituent ions or molecules in solution **[1 mark]**
> 
> Answers referring to the equilibrium constant for the dissociation of a complex are not accepted
> 
> ii) The stability constant expression for [Ni(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> is:
> 
> - *K*<sub>stab</sub> = [[Ni(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup>] / ([Ni<sup>2+</sup>][NH<sub>3</sub>]<sup>6</sup>)
> **OR**
> *K*<sub>stab</sub> = [[Ni(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup>] / ([[Ni(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup>][NH<sub>3</sub>]<sup>6</sup>) **[1 mark]**
> 
> Water is not included in the denominator unless the hexaaqua ion is treated as the reactant

> **[exam-tip]**
> When writing a stability constant expression, write the complex formation equation first to identify which species appear in the numerator and denominator and the correct power for each ligand.
> 
> A common mistake is forgetting the ligand coefficient. Here, six ammonia molecules coordinate to the nickel ion, so [NH<sub>3</sub>] must be raised to the power of 6.

parts.problemMd:

Nickel(II) forms the complex ion [Ni(en)<sub>3</sub>]<sup>2+</sup>. This complex exists as two stereoisomers.

i) Define the term bidentate ligand.

[2]

ii) Draw three-dimensional diagrams to show the two stereoisomers of [Ni(en)<sub>3</sub>]<sup>2+</sup>.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) A bidentate ligand is:
> 
> - A molecule or ion that can donate two lone pairs of electrons **[1 mark]**
> - To form two coordinate / dative (covalent) bonds with the same central metal ion **[1 mark]**

ii) The three-dimensional diagrams showing the two stereoisomers of [Ni(en)<sub>3</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> are:

![Diagram showing two nickel complexes with ethylenediamine (en) ligands in a distorted octahedral geometry, each carrying a 2+ charge.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/28-chemistry-of-transition-elements/28-5-stability-constants-kstab/assets/001-diagram-showing-two-nickel-complexes-with-ethyle.png)

**OR**

![Diagram of two nickel complexes, each with a nickel ion bonded to four NH2 groups forming a square planar configuration, with 2+ charge overall.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/28-chemistry-of-transition-elements/28-5-stability-constants-kstab/assets/002-diagram-of-two-nickel-complexes-each-with-a-nick.png)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for a correct three-dimensional diagram of one isomer showing octahedral geometry, using wedges and dashes, with each bidentate ligand linking adjacent (cis) positions on the metal ion
> 
> 1 mark for the second isomer drawn as a non-superimposable mirror image of the first (same connectivity, opposite handedness)

parts.problemMd:
The complex [Ni(EDTA)]<sup>2–</sup> is significantly more stable than the complex [Ni(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup>.

By considering the ligand exchange reaction between [Ni(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> and EDTA<sup>4–</sup>, explain this difference in stability in terms of entropy changes.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The difference in stability in terms of entropy changes:
> 
> - [Ni(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> + EDTA<sup>4–</sup> ⇌ [Ni(EDTA)]<sup>2–</sup> + 6NH<sub>3</sub> **[1 mark]**
> - The number of particles / moles of species increases from 2 (on the left) to 7 (on the right), so entropy increases / Δ*S* is positive **[1 mark]**
> - The positive Δ*S* makes Δ*G* more negative (via Δ*G* = Δ*H* − *T*Δ*S*), making the ligand exchange more feasible / the EDTA complex more stable **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The chelate effect: polydentate ligands like EDTA displace multiple monodentate ligands in a single exchange step, increasing the total number of particles in solution and therefore increasing entropy.
> 
> Even if the enthalpy changes are similar, the more positive Δ*S* for EDTA displacement makes Δ*G* more negative, favouring formation of [Ni(EDTA)]<sup>2–</sup>.

parts.problemMd:
When chromium(III) sulfate dissolves in water, a violet solution containing the [Cr(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup> ion forms.

i) State the bond angles found in this complex ion.

[1]

ii) Explain why the chromium(III) complex ion is coloured.

[4]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The bond angle is:
> 
> - 90° **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> [Cr(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup> is octahedral as six identical water ligands arranged symmetrically around the Cr<sup>3+</sup> ion. All six ligand-metal-ligand bond angles between adjacent ligands are 90°.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii) The chromium(III) complex ion is coloured because:
> 
> - The water ligands cause the 3d orbitals to split into two energy levels of different energies **[1 mark]**
> - Light / radiation in the visible region of the electromagnetic spectrum is absorbed **[1 mark]**
> - The absorbed energy promotes electrons from the lower 3d energy level to the higher 3d energy level **[1 mark]**
> - The complementary colour / violet light is transmitted / observed **[1 mark]**
> 
> 'Green light is transmitted' is not accepted

> **[exam-tip]**
> In an isolated transition metal atom the five 3d orbitals are degenerate (equal energy). When a complex ion forms, the ligands split the 3d orbitals into two energy levels. Light of a wavelength matching this energy gap is absorbed, promoting an electron to the higher level. The remaining complementary colour is transmitted and observed.
> 
> A common error is to state that colour arises because electrons 'return to their ground state and emit light', but this describes emission spectra (flame tests), not complex ion colour.
> 
> Also note: the question specifies [Cr(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup>, which appears violet, not green. Stating the wrong transmitted colour will lose the final mark.

parts.problemMd:
Ethylenediaminetetraacetate, EDTA<sup>4−</sup>, shown in Fig. 1.1, is a polydentate ligand.

![Structural formula of EDTA showing two nitrogen atoms each connected to two CH2COO- groups and linked by an ethylene bridge](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/28-chemistry-of-transition-elements/28-5-stability-constants-kstab/assets/003-structural-formula-of-edta-showing-two-nitrogen-.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

When a solution of EDTA<sup>4−</sup> is added to a solution of [Cr(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup> ions, a new complex ion is formed.

[Cr(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup> + EDTA<sup>4–</sup> ⇌ [Cr(EDTA)]<sup>–</sup> + 6H<sub>2</sub>O

i) Name the type of reaction occurring here.

[1]

ii) Write an expression for the stability constant, *K*<sub>stab</sub>, of [Cr(EDTA)]<sup>–</sup> in this reaction.

[1]

iii) The numerical value of the *K*<sub>stab</sub> of [Cr(EDTA)]<sup>–</sup> is 2.51 × 10<sup>23</sup> in this reaction.

Suggest what this indicates about the position and entropy of the equilibrium.

[3]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The type of reaction occuring is:
> 
> - Ligand exchange / substitution / displacement / replacement **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The stability constant expression for [Cr(EDTA)]<sup>–</sup> is:
> 
> - *K*<sub>stab</sub> = [[Cr(EDTA)]<sup>–</sup>] / ([[Cr(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup>][EDTA<sup>4–</sup>]) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Identify the product ([Cr(EDTA)]<sup>–</sup>) and the two reactants ([Cr(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup> and EDTA<sup>4–</sup>) from the equation given in the question. Write the product concentration in the numerator and the reactant concentrations in the denominator. Water is excluded as the solvent.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> iii) The large value of *K*<sub>stab</sub> for [Cr(EDTA)]<sup>–</sup> indicates:
> 
> - The equilibrium lies far to the right / [Cr(EDTA)]<sup>–</sup> is more stable than [Cr(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup>
> **OR**
> The forward reaction is very feasible / spontaneous / goes to completion **[1 mark]**
> - Δ*S*<sub>system</sub> is positive / entropy increases **[1 mark]**
> - The number of moles / particles increases from 2 (reactants) to 7 (products)
> **OR**
> 2 moles of reactants form 7 moles of products **[1 mark]**
> 
> Explaining only the entropy change without addressing the position of equilibrium is not accepted for full marks

> **[exam-tip]**
> A large *K*<sub>stab</sub> means the equilibrium strongly favours products.
> 
> The entropy change follows from the ligand exchange equation: 2 species on the left (the hexaaqua complex and EDTA<sup>4–</sup>) produce 7 on the right (1 Cr-EDTA complex + 6 water molecules), so the number of particles increases and Δ*S* is positive.
> 
> This is the chelate effect: replacing six monodentate ligands with one hexadentate ligand in a single step greatly increases entropy and drives the reaction forward.

parts.problemMd:
Chromium(III) picolinate, shown in Fig. 1.2, is a neutral complex that can be prepared from the weak acid, picolinic acid.

![Structural formula of chromium(III) picolinate showing a Cr3+ ion coordinated to three picolinate ligands in an octahedral arrangement](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/28-chemistry-of-transition-elements/28-5-stability-constants-kstab/assets/004-structural-formula-of-chromium-iii-picolinate-sh.png)

**Fig. 1.2**

Chromium(III) picolinate is used in tablets as a nutritional supplement for chromium.

i) Draw the structure of the ligand in chromium(III) picolinate.

[1]

ii) A typical tablet of chromium(III) picolinate contains 200 μg of chromium.

Calculate the mass, in g, of chromium(III) picolinate in a typical tablet. Give your answer to three significant figures. Show your working.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
i) The structure of the ligand in chromium(III) picolinate is:

![Structure of the picolinate ligand showing a pyridine ring with a deprotonated carboxylate group (COO–) at the 2-position, and a lone pair on the nitrogen for coordination](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/28-chemistry-of-transition-elements/28-5-stability-constants-kstab/assets/005-structure-of-the-picolinate-ligand-showing-a-pyr.png)

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for the picolinate ligand: pyridine ring with deprotonated carboxylate (COO<sup>–</sup>) at position 2, without a negative charge on the nitrogen
> 
> The negative charge on the nitrogen is not accepted

> **[exam-tip]**
> The picolinate ligand is picolinic acid (pyridine-2-carboxylic acid) after deprotonation of the COOH group.
> 
> Three of nitrogen's five valence electrons are used in bonding within the pyridine ring, leaving a lone pair that forms the coordinate bond with Cr<sup>3+</sup>.
> 
> The nitrogen does not carry a formal negative charge, only the carboxylate oxygen does.

ii) To calculate the mass, in g, of chromium(III) picolinate in a typical tablet:

- State the *M*<sub>r</sub> of chromium(III) picolinate:

*M*<sub>r</sub> = 418.0

- Calculate moles of chromium (1 μg = 10<sup>–6</sup> g):

n(Cr) = $\frac{200\times10^{-6}}{52.0}$

n(Cr) = 3.85 x 10<sup>–6</sup> mol

**[1 mark]**

- Calculate mass of chromium(III) picolinate:

mass = 3.85 x 10<sup>–6</sup> x 418.0

mass = **1.61 x 10**<sup>**–3**</sup> g **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for *M*<sub>r</sub>(chromium(III) picolinate) = 418.0 **AND** moles of chromium = 3.85 x 10<sup>–6</sup> mol
> 
> 1 mark for mass = 1.61 x 10<sup>–3</sup> g (to 3 s.f.)

> **[exam-tip]**
> The *M*<sub>r</sub> of chromium(III) picolinate requires care: the picolinate ligand has *M*<sub>r</sub> = 122.1, and three coordinate to the Cr<sup>3+</sup> ion (plus one proton lost per ligand), giving *M*<sub>r</sub> = 52.0 + (3 x 122.0) = 418.0. Remember 1 μg = 10<sup>–6</sup> g.

parts.problemMd:
Compound **L** is a complex with the empirical formula CrN<sub>4</sub>H<sub>12</sub>Cl<sub>3</sub>

The formula of compound **L** contains one chloride ion and a complex ion **M**, which has two stereoisomers.

i) Deduce the formula of complex ion **M**.

[1]

ii) Draw three-dimensional diagrams to show the two stereoisomers of complex ion **M**.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The formula of complex ion **M** is:
> 
> - [Cr(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>]<sup>+</sup> / [CrN<sub>4</sub>H<sub>12</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>]<sup>+</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Compound **L** has the empirical formula CrN<sub>4</sub>H<sub>12</sub>Cl<sub>3</sub> and contains one ionically-bonded chloride ion. Removing this gives complex ion **M** the composition CrN<sub>4</sub>H<sub>12</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub> with a 1+ charge. The N<sub>4</sub>H<sub>12</sub> portion is four NH<sub>3</sub> ligands, giving the formula [Cr(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>]<sup>+</sup>.

ii) The three-dimensional diagrams showing the two stereoisomers of complex ion **M** are:

![Three-dimensional diagrams of cis-[Cr(NH3)4Cl2]+ and trans-[Cr(NH3)4Cl2]+ showing correct wedge-dash notation with 1+ charges indicated on both isomers](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/28-chemistry-of-transition-elements/28-5-stability-constants-kstab/assets/006-three-dimensional-diagrams-of-cis-cr-nh3-4cl2-an.png)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for a correct 3D diagram of one isomer with 4NH<sub>3</sub> and 2Cl ligands, correct wedge-dash notation, and 1+ charge shown
> 
> 1 mark for the second isomer drawn as the other geometric isomer (*cis* or *trans*), correctly labelled, with 1+ charge shown

> **[exam-tip]**
> [Cr(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>]<sup>+</sup> is octahedral and exists as *cis* (both Cl adjacent, 90° apart) and *trans* (both Cl opposite, 180° apart) isomers. Draw each with 2 'out wedges', 2 'in wedges', and 2 bonds in the plane of the paper.
> 
> Make sure the 1+ charge appears on both structures. A common error is to omit the charge or to draw cis and trans incorrectly by placing the Cl ligands in the wrong positions.

name: Formulas, Functional Groups & the Naming of Organic Compounds
section: 29. An Introduction to A Level Organic Chemistry

parts.problemMd:
The structural formulae of four different organic compounds are shown in Table 1.1.

**Table 1.1**

| **Structural formula** | **IUPAC name** |
|---|---|
| C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> |   |
| CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CHO |   |
| CH<sub>3</sub>NHCH<sub>3</sub> |   |
| CH<sub>3</sub>CH(NH<sub>2</sub>)CO<sub>2</sub>H |   |

Complete Table 1.1 by stating the systematic (IUPAC) name for each compound.
parts.solutionMd:
The completed table is:

| **Structural formula** | **IUPAC name** |
|---|---|
| C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> | **Final answer:** **methylbenzene** |
| CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CHO | **Final answer:** **pentanal** |
| CH<sub>3</sub>NHCH<sub>3</sub> | **Final answer:** **dimethylamine** |
| CH<sub>3</sub>CH(NH<sub>2</sub>)CO<sub>2</sub>H | **Final answer:** **2-aminopropanoic acid** |

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for methylbenzene
> 
> 1 mark for pentanal
> 
> 1 mark for dimethylamine
> 
> 1 mark for 2-aminopropanoic acid

> **[exam-tip]**
> For C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>:
> 
> - C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub> tells you this is a benzene ring
> - The five hydrogen atoms in the structure tell you that one hydrogen atom has been substituted, in this case for a CH<sub>3</sub> group
> - Therefore it is methylbenzene
> 
> For CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CHO:
> 
> - The CHO group at the end of the molecule indicates the compound is an aldehyde
> - There are five carbon atoms in the straight chain, so the name is pentanal
> 
> For CH<sub>3</sub>NHCH<sub>3</sub>:
> 
> - The NH atom indicates that this is an amine
> - There are two CH<sub>3</sub> groups bonded to the nitrogen atom, so dimethyl- should be in the name
> - Therefore the name is dimethylamine
> 
> For CH<sub>3</sub>CH(NH<sub>2</sub>)CO<sub>2</sub>H:
> 
> - This compound is an amino acid
> - There are three carbon atoms in the chain with a carboxylic acid group, CO<sub>2</sub>H
> - This group takes priority so is named last: propanoic acid
> - There is also a NH<sub>2</sub> group (amine group) bonded to the second carbon
> - Therefore the name is 2-aminopropanoic acid

parts.problemMd: Butanoyl chloride reacts with cold water to form butanoic acid. State the name of the mechanism for this reaction.

parts.problemMd:
Compounds **K**, **L** and **M** are organic compounds with different properties.

| **K** | **L** | **M** |
|---|---|---|
| ![Structural diagram of phenol, showing a benzene ring with an attached hydroxyl (OH) group at one carbon position](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/29-an-introduction-to-a-level-organic-chemistry/29-1-formulas-functional-groups-and-the-naming-of-organic-compounds/assets/001-structural-diagram-of-phenol-showing-a-benzene-r.png) | ![Skeletal formula of ethanoyl chloride, showing a carbonyl group with oxygen above, chlorine below, and a single methyl group to the left](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/29-an-introduction-to-a-level-organic-chemistry/29-1-formulas-functional-groups-and-the-naming-of-organic-compounds/assets/002-skeletal-formula-of-ethanoyl-chloride-showing-a-.png) | ![Line drawing of the organic molecule 2‑phenyl‑2‑aminopropane, showing a benzene ring attached to a branched carbon chain ending with an NH₂ group](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/29-an-introduction-to-a-level-organic-chemistry/29-1-formulas-functional-groups-and-the-naming-of-organic-compounds/assets/003-line-drawing-of-the-organic-molecule-2-phenyl-2-.png) |

State the systematic name of compounds **K**, **L** and **M**.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The systematic name of each compound:
> 
> - compound **K** = phenol **[1 mark]**
> - compound **L** = ethanoyl chloride **[1 mark]**
> - compound **M** = 2-phenylpropylamine **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Compound **K** is the well-known compound phenol, so this name should be memorised.
> 
> Compound **L** is an acyl chloride:
> 
> - Acyl chlorides have the suffix -oyl chloride
> - The carbon chain is 2 carbons long, so the stem is eth-
> - The chain contains only single bonds, so the name includes -an-
> - Overall: eth + an + oyl chloride = ethanoyl chloride
> 
> Compound **M** has a phenyl ring attached to carbon-2 of a three-carbon chain ending in an amine group:
> 
> - The 2-phenyl- prefix indicates the benzene ring at carbon-2
> - The propylamine suffix indicates a three-carbon chain with a terminal amine
> - Overall: 2-phenyl + propylamine = 2-phenylpropylamine

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The reaction pathway for the formation of an N-substituted amide is shown in a three-step synthesis in Fig. 2.1. In step 1, the major product of the reaction is formed.

The IUPAC names of compounds **W** and **X**:
- **W** is propene
- **X** is 2-chloropropane

5.0 g of compound **W** was used to produce compound **X**. The percentage yield was 64%.

i) Calculate the mass, in grams, of compound **X**. Give your answer to 1 decimal place. Show your working.

[3]

ii) State **two** reasons why the percentage yield of the reaction is not 100%.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the mass of compound **X**:

- List the known values:

  - mass of W = 5.0 g
  - M<sub>r</sub> of W (propene) = 42
  - M<sub>r</sub> of X (2-chloropropane) = 78.5
  - percentage yield = 64%
- Calculate the moles of compound **W**:

n(W) = $\frac{mass}{M_{r}}$

n(W) = $\frac{5.0}{42}$

n(W) = 0.119 mol **[1 mark]**

- Mole ratio W : X = 1 : 1, so n(X) theoretical = 0.119 mol

- Calculate the theoretical mass of compound **X**:

mass(X) = n(X) x M<sub>r</sub>(X)

mass(X) = 0.119 x 78.5

mass(X) = 9.34 g **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the actual mass of compound **X** using the percentage yield:

actual mass = theoretical mass x $\frac{\mathrm{percentage} \mathrm{yield}}{100}$

actual mass = 9.34 x $\frac{64}{100}$

actual mass = **6.0 g** **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Allow error carried forward in steps 2 and 3 if a correct method is used with an incorrect moles value from step 1.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Percentage yield = (actual yield / theoretical yield) x 100.
> 
> Give your answer to the number of decimal places specified. Take care to use an unrounded intermediate value where possible: 5.0 / 42 x 78.5 x 0.64 = 5.98... g, which rounds to 6.0 g (1 dp).

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii) Two reasons why the percentage yield is not 100%:
> 
> Any **two** from (1 mark for each point):
> 
> - By-products are formed in this reaction
> - Reaction has not gone to completion
> - Alternative chemical pathways exist
> - Formation of intermediates
> 
> **[2 marks]**

> - The CHO / aldehyde group changes from trigonal planar to tetrahedral (the CHOHCN / hydroxynitrile group) **[1 mark]**
> - The C=O bond breaks, forming two single bonds (to OH and CN groups)
> **AND**
> The carbon atom is now surrounded by 4 single bonding pairs, resulting in a tetrahedral shape **[1 mark]**
> 
> Chirality:
> 
> - CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CHO / butanal has no chiral centres
> **AND**
> The organic product / 2-hydroxypentanenitrile has one chiral centre **[1 mark]**
> - The C=O bond breaks, forming two single bonds to OH and CN groups
> **AND**
> The carbon atom now has four different atoms or groups of atoms attached **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CHO is the aldehyde butanal, which has no chiral centres because no carbon has four different atoms or groups attached.
> 
> The aldehyde carbon has a trigonal planar shape due to the C=O double bond.
> 
> Aldehydes undergo an addition reaction with HCN to form hydroxynitrile compounds. The product here is 2-hydroxypentanenitrile (note that the CN group adds a carbon to the chain, making it five carbons rather than four).
> 
> After the reaction, the former carbonyl carbon has four different groups attached (H, OH, CN, and CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>-), so it becomes a chiral centre.

parts.problemMd:
In a second reaction, CH<sub>3</sub>OH reacts with CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COCl.

i) State the name of the mechanism involved in this reaction. Describe the steps in the mechanism to support your answer.

[5]

ii) State the systematic name of the organic product of this reaction.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The name of the mechanism and its steps:
> 
> - (Nucleophilic) addition-elimination **[1 mark]**
> 
> Description of the mechanism steps:
> 
> - The lone pair on CH<sub>3</sub>OH / methanol acts as a nucleophile, attacking the δ+ carbonyl carbon
> **AND**
> One C=O bond breaks heterolytically, giving both electrons to the oxygen atom **[1 mark]**
> - A lone pair from the O<sup>-</sup> reforms the C=O bond
> **AND**
> The C-Cl bond breaks heterolytically, releasing a chloride ion **[1 mark]**
> - The O-H bond breaks heterolytically, giving both electrons to the electron-deficient oxygen / O<sup>+</sup> atom
> **AND**
> H<sup>+</sup> is lost **[1 mark]**
> - Overall, an HCl molecule is eliminated **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The systematic name of the organic product:
> 
> - Methyl butanoate **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The reaction of an alcohol with an acyl chloride produces an ester and HCl via nucleophilic addition-elimination.
> 
> Each step of the mechanism requires precise reference to lone pairs, bond breaking, and the charges formed.
> 
> For naming the ester product:
> 
> - Methanol gives the methyl- prefix
> - Butanoyl chloride gives the -butanoate suffix
> - Product: methyl butanoate
