name: Characteristic Organic Reactions
section: 29. An Introduction to A Level Organic Chemistry

parts.problemMd:
This question is about benzene.

Describe and explain the shape of benzene.

In your answer, include:

- the bond angle between carbon atoms
- the hybridisation of the carbon atoms
- how orbital overlap forms σ and π bonds between the carbon atoms
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The shape of benzene can be described and explained as follows:
> 
> - Bond angle between carbon atoms: 120° **[1 mark]**
> - Hybridisation of carbon atoms: sp<sup>2</sup> **[1 mark]**
> - σ bonds formed by end-on overlap of sp<sup>2</sup> orbitals
> **AND**
> π bonds formed by sideways overlap of p orbitals above and below the plane of the ring **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Each carbon in benzene forms three σ bonds using its sp<sup>2</sup> hybrid orbitals: one to each neighbouring ring carbon and one to a hydrogen atom. These bonds lie in the plane of the ring at 120° to each other.
> 
> Each carbon also has one unhybridised p orbital pointing perpendicular to the ring plane. These p orbitals overlap sideways with the p orbitals on neighbouring carbons to form the π system. Because all six p orbitals overlap equally, the π electrons are delocalised across the whole ring rather than fixed between specific carbon pairs.
> 
> A key consequence of this delocalisation is that all six C–C bond lengths in benzene are equal, with a value between a C–C single bond (0.154 nm) and a C=C double bond (0.134 nm). Students sometimes lose the third mark by describing either σ or π bond formation but not both.

parts.problemMd:
Benzene can be nitrated by warming it with a mixture of concentrated sulfuric acid and concentrated nitric acid.

The mechanism for the reaction is shown in Fig. 1.1.

![Reaction mechanism showing nitration of benzene: benzene ring attacked by nitronium ion, forming sigma complex, then deprotonation to give nitrobenzene](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/29-an-introduction-to-a-level-organic-chemistry/29-2-characteristic-organic-reactions/assets/004-reaction-mechanism-showing-nitration-of-benzene-.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

i) Name the mechanism of this nitration reaction.

[1]

ii) Write an equation for the reaction between H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> and HNO<sub>3</sub> that generates the electrophile for this reaction.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The mechanism of this nitration reaction is:
> 
> - Electrophilic substitution **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The mechanism is electrophilic because the attacking species, NO<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>, is electron-deficient and attacks the electron-rich benzene ring. It is substitution rather than addition because the hydrogen atom is replaced by the NO<sub>2</sub> group, preserving the aromaticity of the ring. Addition would break the delocalised π system and is strongly disfavoured.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii) The equation for the generation of the electrophile is:
> 
> - HNO<sub>3</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> → NO<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> + HSO<sub>4</sub><sup>-</sup> + H<sub>2</sub>O **[1 mark]**
> 
> The two-step representation: H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> + HNO<sub>3</sub> → H<sub>2</sub>NO<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup> + HSO<sub>4</sub><sup>-</sup> followed by H<sub>2</sub>NO<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup> → NO<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> + H<sub>2</sub>O is accepted

> **[exam-tip]**
> In this equation, concentrated sulfuric acid acts as an acid, donating a proton (H<sup>+</sup>) to nitric acid. The protonated nitric acid (H<sub>2</sub>NO<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup>) is unstable and loses water to form the nitronium ion, NO<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>. It is this NO<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> ion that acts as the electrophile and attacks the benzene ring in the mechanism shown in Fig. 1.1.

parts.problemMd:
Benzene can be used to synthesise (4-aminophenyl)ethanoic acid which is a drug that can be used to treat chronic inflammation of the intestines.

i) Draw the structure of (4-aminophenyl)ethanoic acid.

[1]

ii) One of the intermediate products made during the synthesis of (4-aminophenyl)ethanoic acid is the molecule shown in Fig. 1.2.

![Chemical structure of 4‑nitrotoluene: a benzene ring with a methyl group at the top and a nitro group at the opposite, para position](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/29-an-introduction-to-a-level-organic-chemistry/29-2-characteristic-organic-reactions/assets/005-chemical-structure-of-4-nitrotoluene-a-benzene-r.png)

**Fig. 1.2**

Give the systematic name of the molecule shown in Fig. 1.2.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
i) The structure of (4-aminophenyl)ethanoic acid is:

![Structure of (4-aminophenyl)ethanoic acid showing a benzene ring with an amino group at the para position and a CH2COOH group](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/29-an-introduction-to-a-level-organic-chemistry/29-2-characteristic-organic-reactions/assets/006-structure-of-4-aminophenyl-ethanoic-acid-showing.png)

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for the correct structure of (4-aminophenyl)ethanoic acid

> **[exam-tip]**
> Work through the name systematically to build up the structure:
> 
> - "ethanoic acid" indicates a –CH<sub>2</sub>COOH group attached to a benzene ring (phenylethanoic acid)
> - "4-amino" indicates an –NH<sub>2</sub> group at the para (4-) position of the ring, directly opposite the –CH<sub>2</sub>COOH group
> 
> Start by drawing phenylethanoic acid, with the –CH<sub>2</sub>COOH group attached to C-1 of the benzene ring:
> 
> Then add the –NH<sub>2</sub> group at C-4 to give the final structure:

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii) The systematic name of the molecule shown in Fig. 1.2 is:
> 
> - 4-nitromethylbenzene **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The molecule in Fig. 1.2 is methylbenzene with a nitro group (–NO<sub>2</sub>) substituted onto the ring. When naming, take the carbon bearing the methyl group as C-1. The nitro group is directly opposite, at C-4, giving the name 4-nitromethylbenzene.

parts.problemMd:
Noradrenaline, shown in Fig. 1.3, is a hormone and neurotransmitter which contains a benzene ring. It is released during stress to stimulate the heart and increase blood pressure.

![Chemical structure of noradrenaline](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/29-an-introduction-to-a-level-organic-chemistry/29-2-characteristic-organic-reactions/assets/007-chemical-structure-of-noradrenaline.png)

**Fig. 1.3**

Name three functional groups in the noradrenaline molecule in addition to the arene group.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Three functional groups in noradrenaline in addition to the arene group are:
> 
> - Phenol **[1 mark]**
> - (Secondary) alcohol **[1 mark]**
> - (Primary) amine **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Noradrenaline contains three functional groups in addition to the arene group:
> 
> 1. Phenol: the –OH group attached directly to the benzene ring. This is a separate functional group from alcohol and must be named specifically as phenol.
> 2. Secondary alcohol: the –OH group attached to a carbon that is bonded to two other carbon atoms. Because the central carbon has two C–C bonds, it is a secondary alcohol, not a primary one.
> 3. Primary amine: the –NH<sub>2</sub> group, where the nitrogen is bonded to one carbon chain (one R group) and two hydrogen atoms.
> 
> A common error is to name the phenol –OH as an alcohol. In CIE mark schemes, phenol and alcohol are distinct functional groups and cannot be substituted for each other.

parts.problemMd:
Benzene, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>6</sub>, undergoes electrophilic substitution.

i) State what is meant by the term electrophile.

[1]

ii) Write an equation for the reaction between benzene and concentrated nitric acid.

[1]

iii) Identify the electrophile in this reaction.

[1]

iv) Write an equation to show how this electrophile is generated.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The meaning of the term electrophile:
> 
> - A species that accepts / receives an electron pair / electron pair acceptor / electron-deficient species **[1 mark]**
> 
> Answers referring only to positive charge without mention of electron pairs are not accepted

> **[exam-tip]**
> The key distinction between an electrophile and a nucleophile is the direction of the electron pair: electrophiles accept pairs, nucleophiles donate them.
> 
> Electrophiles do not need to carry a full positive charge. A partial positive charge (δ+) is sufficient; for example, the carbon in a polar C–X bond can act as an electrophile.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii) The equation for the reaction between benzene and concentrated nitric acid:
> 
> - C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>6</sub> + HNO<sub>3</sub> → C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>NO<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O **[1 mark]**
> 
> State symbols are not required

> **[exam-tip]**
> This reaction is called nitration and produces nitrobenzene, a pale yellow liquid.
> 
> Concentrated sulfuric acid acts as a catalyst, so it does not appear in the overall equation; it is regenerated at the end of the mechanism.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> iii) The electrophile in this reaction:
> 
> - NO<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> / the nitronium ion **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The electrophile is the nitronium ion, NO<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>, not nitric acid itself. Nitric acid must first react with concentrated sulfuric acid to generate NO<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> before the substitution reaction can proceed.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> iv) The equation showing how this electrophile is generated:
> 
> - HNO<sub>3</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> → NO<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> + HSO<sub>4</sub><sup>-</sup> + H<sub>2</sub>O **[1 mark]**
> 
> State symbols are not required

> **[exam-tip]**
> Nitric acid acts as a Brønsted–Lowry base in this step, accepting a proton from concentrated sulfuric acid. This is unusual for nitric acid, which is normally an acid, but it occurs because concentrated sulfuric acid is a stronger acid.
> 
> The HSO<sub>4</sub><sup>-</sup> ion can donate a proton back at the end of the mechanism, regenerating H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>. This explains why sulfuric acid is described as a catalyst.

parts.problemMd:
Benzene is a highly unsaturated molecule.

i) Explain why benzene undergoes substitution reactions rather than addition reactions.

[3]

ii) Write an equation for the reaction of benzene with chlorine. State the conditions required for this reaction.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) Explain why benzene undergoes substitution rather than addition reactions:
> 
> Any **three** from (1 mark for each point):
> 
> - The electrons in benzene are delocalised across all six carbon atoms in the ring
> - Delocalisation confers extra stability to the benzene ring
> - Addition reactions would disrupt / break the delocalised electron system
> - Disrupting delocalisation would require more energy than is released, making addition energetically unfavourable
> - Substitution reactions preserve the delocalised / aromatic ring structure
> 
> **[3 marks]**
> 
> Answers referring to benzene having localised double bonds are not accepted

> **[exam-tip]**
> The stability gained through delocalisation is sometimes called the delocalisation energy or resonance energy. It is this extra stability that makes addition reactions thermodynamically unfavourable compared to substitution reactions, as addition would destroy the aromatic system.
> 
> When explaining this in the exam, link your points clearly: delocalised electrons give stability, and addition would destroy this stability. Saying only "benzene is stable" without explaining why does not gain the mark.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii) The equation for the reaction of benzene with chlorine, and the conditions required:
> 
> - C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>6</sub> + Cl<sub>2</sub> → C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>Cl + HCl **[1 mark]**
> - AlCl<sub>3</sub> as a catalyst, anhydrous conditions **[1 mark]**
> 
> FeCl<sub>3</sub> / iron(III) chloride is accepted as an alternative catalyst
> 
> State symbols are not required

> **[exam-tip]**
> The aluminium chloride catalyst is sometimes called a halogen carrier. It polarises the Cl–Cl bond to generate a Cl<sup>+</sup> electrophile, which then attacks the benzene ring.
> 
> Anhydrous conditions are essential because AlCl<sub>3</sub> reacts vigorously with water. If moisture is present, the catalyst is destroyed and the reaction will not proceed.

parts.problemMd:
An aromatic organic compound with molecular formula C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>8</sub> reacts with bromine in the presence of UV light to produce a compound with molecular formula C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>7</sub>Br.

i) Name the type of reaction.

[1]

ii) Draw the structures of the reactant and product.

[2]

iii) Suggest the formula of one other organic product that could form in this reaction.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The type of reaction is:
> 
> - Free radical substitution **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The clue here is the presence of UV light, which provides the energy needed to initiate free radical substitution. This reaction occurs at the methyl group (side chain), not on the benzene ring itself. Bromine reacts with alkyl hydrogens under UV light, not with the delocalised ring.

ii) The structures of the reactant and product are:

![Structural diagrams showing methylbenzene as the reactant and (bromomethyl)benzene as the product of free radical substitution with bromine](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/29-an-introduction-to-a-level-organic-chemistry/29-2-characteristic-organic-reactions/assets/003-structural-diagrams-showing-methylbenzene-as-the.png)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for the correct structure of the reactant: methylbenzene / toluene, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>
> 
> 1 mark for the correct structure of the product: (bromomethyl)benzene, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Br

> **[exam-tip]**
> The molecular formula C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>8</sub> corresponds to methylbenzene: a benzene ring with one methyl group. The degree of unsaturation is 4, consistent with a benzene ring.
> 
> When UV light initiates the reaction, a bromine radical abstracts a hydrogen from the methyl group, not from the ring. The benzene ring is too stable to undergo addition or radical substitution under these conditions.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> iii) One other organic product that could form is:
> 
> Any **one** from:
> 
> - C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CHBr<sub>2</sub> / C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>6</sub>Br<sub>2</sub>
> - C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CBr<sub>3</sub> / C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>5</sub>Br<sub>3</sub>
> - C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub> / C<sub>14</sub>H<sub>14</sub>
> 
> **[1 mark]**
> 
> HBr is not accepted as it is an inorganic product

> **[exam-tip]**
> Further substitution can occur with excess bromine and UV light, where one or two more hydrogen atoms in the methyl group can be replaced, giving C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CHBr<sub>2</sub> and C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CBr<sub>3</sub>.
> 
> The final alternative product, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>, forms when two benzyl radicals combine in the termination step.

parts.problemMd:
Propanal reacts with potassium cyanide, followed by dilute acid, to form the hydroxynitrile CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH(OH)CN.

State the systematic name of CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH(OH)CN.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The systematic name of CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH(OH)CN is:
> 
> - 2-hydroxybutanenitrile **[1 mark]**
> 
> The 'e' at the end of butane must be included; '2-hydroxybutannitrile' is not accepted

> **[exam-tip]**
> The name is built in three steps: identify the parent chain (4 carbons including the CN carbon = butane), add the nitrile suffix keeping the 'e' (butane + nitrile = butanenitrile), then number the hydroxy group from the nitrile end (OH is on C-2 = 2-hydroxy).
> 
> The most common error is dropping the 'e' to write '2-hydroxybutannitrile', which is not accepted.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Propanal reacts with potassium cyanide, followed by dilute acid, to form the hydroxynitrile CH~3~CH~2~CH(OH)CN.

Name the mechanism for this reaction.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The mechanism for this reaction is:
> 
> - Nucleophilic addition **[1 mark]**
> 
> Both words are required for the mark

> **[exam-tip]**
> Both words, nucleophilic and addition, must be present. Writing only one will not gain the mark.
> 
> This mechanism applies whenever a nucleophile attacks the C=O group of an aldehyde or ketone. The addition part reflects that the nucleophile adds across the C=O double bond rather than substituting an existing group.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Propanal reacts with potassium cyanide, followed by dilute acid, to form the hydroxynitrile CH3CH2CH(OH)CN.

The mechanism for this reaction is: Nucleophilic addition

Explain why propanal undergoes this type of mechanism.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Propanal undergoes this mechanism because:
> 
> - The C=O bond is polar
> **OR**
> O is more electronegative than C
> **OR**
> C is δ+ and O is δ−  **[1 mark]**
> - Nucleophiles / CN<sup>-</sup> are electron pair donors 
> **AND** 
> They are attracted to the electron-deficient C<sup>δ+</sup> carbon **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> These two marks are sequential: the first establishes why the carbon is susceptible to attack (polar C=O bond, δ+ carbon), and the second explains why a nucleophile is attracted to it (electron pair donors are drawn to δ+ centres).
> 
> For the second mark, both parts are required: you must state that CN<sup>-</sup> / nucleophiles are electron pair donors, and that they are attracted to the δ+ carbon. Stating only one of these will not gain the mark.

parts.problemMd:
Under suitable conditions, 3-nitrobenzaldehyde can be formed by the reaction of benzaldehyde with appropriate reagents.

i) State the name of the mechanism, and the reagents and conditions, for the formation of 3-nitrobenzaldehyde.

mechanism ................................................................................

reagents ................................................................................

conditions ................................................................................

[3]

ii) Draw the fully displayed formula of 3-nitrobenzaldehyde. On your diagram, draw a circle around each functional group.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The name of the mechanism, reagents and conditions for this nitration reaction are:
> 
> - Mechanism: electrophilic substitution **[1 mark]**
> - Reagents: concentrated nitric acid
> **AND**
> Concentrated sulfuric acid **[1 mark]**
> - Conditions: heat / reflux
> **AND**
> Temperature in the range 25–60 °C **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> This reaction is a nitration, which is a type of electrophilic aromatic substitution in which a nitro group (–NO<sub>2</sub>) replaces a hydrogen atom on the benzene ring.
> 
> Both acids are required. The sulfuric acid acts as a catalyst by protonating the nitric acid to generate the nitronium ion (NO<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>), which is the electrophile in the mechanism.
> 
> The temperature must be controlled carefully. Too high a temperature leads to polynitration, where more than one nitro group is added to the ring.
> 
> When numbering the carbon atoms, count the benzene carbon bearing the aldehyde group as C-1. The –CHO group is an electron-withdrawing meta-director, so the nitro group is added at C-3.

ii) The fully displayed formula of 3-nitrobenzaldehyde with the functional groups circled is:

![The fully displayed formula of 3-nitrobenzaldehyde with circles around the aldehyde group, nitro group, and benzene ring](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/29-an-introduction-to-a-level-organic-chemistry/29-2-characteristic-organic-reactions/assets/001-the-fully-displayed-formula-of-3-nitrobenzaldehy.png)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for a correct fully displayed formula of 3-nitrobenzaldehyde
> 
> 1 mark for all three functional groups correctly circled

> **[exam-tip]**
> The three functional groups to circle are:
> 
> - The aldehyde group (–CHO)
> - The nitro group (–NO<sub>2</sub>)
> - The benzene ring
> 
> The benzene ring is the most commonly missed functional group. It counts as a functional group in its own right.
> 
> Take care with the nitro group in the fully displayed formula. It contains two N–O bonds: one N=O double bond and one N–O single bond, with the oxygen bearing a negative charge. Make sure the correct number of bonds is shown before circling.

parts.problemMd:
Benzaldehyde, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CHO, is the simplest aromatic aldehyde with a characteristic smell of almonds or cherries.

i) State the hybridisation of the carbon atom in the aldehyde group and predict the C–C=O bond angle.

hybridisation ................................................................................

bond angle ................................................................................

[2]

ii) A student suggests that a molecule of benzaldehyde is not planar because there is free rotation around the C–C bond connecting the benzene ring to the aldehyde group.

Explain why the student is incorrect.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The hybridisation and C–C=O bond angle in benzaldehyde are:
> 
> - Hybridisation: sp<sup>2</sup> **[1 mark]**
> - C–C=O bond angle: 120° **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The carbon atom in the aldehyde group (–CHO) has three groups attached: the ring carbon, the hydrogen, and the oxygen (via the double bond, which counts as one group). Three groups around a central atom corresponds to sp<sup>2</sup> hybridisation and a trigonal planar arrangement, giving bond angles of 120°.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii) To explain why the student is incorrect:
> 
> - The p-orbital on the carbon atom of the aldehyde group overlaps / delocalises with the π system of the benzene ring **[1 mark]**
> - This gives the C–C bond partial double bond character, which restricts rotation **[1 mark]**
> 
> Writing π orbital instead of p-orbital in the first marking point is accepted
> 
> The statement that lone pairs on the oxygen atom delocalise into the ring is not accepted for the first marking point.
> 
> References to hydrogen bonding or van der Waals' forces are not accepted

> **[exam-tip]**
> The student's error is treating the C–C bond connecting the ring to the aldehyde group as a simple single bond, like those found in alkanes. In benzaldehyde, this is not the case.
> 
> The p-orbital on the carbonyl carbon (the C of –CHO) is parallel to the p-orbitals of the benzene ring. These orbitals overlap sideways, extending the delocalised π system across the C–C bond. This gives the C–C bond partial double bond character, which restricts rotation and holds the molecule in a planar conformation.
> 
> A common error is to state that lone pairs on the oxygen delocalise into the ring. This is what happens in phenol (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH), not benzaldehyde. In benzaldehyde, it is the p-orbital on the carbonyl carbon that overlaps with the ring, not lone pairs on oxygen.

parts.problemMd:
Methylbenzene reacts with ethanoyl chloride in the presence of an AlCl<sub>3</sub> catalyst.

i) Draw the structure of the major organic product of this reaction.

[1]

ii) Deduce the total number of σ and π bonds in one molecule of this organic product.

σ bonds ..............................

π bonds ..............................

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
i) The major organic product of this reaction is:

![Structure of 4-methylacetophenone, the major organic product of the Friedel-Crafts acylation of methylbenzene with ethanoyl chloride, showing the acetyl group at the para position](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/29-an-introduction-to-a-level-organic-chemistry/29-2-characteristic-organic-reactions/assets/002-structure-of-4-methylacetophenone-the-major-orga.png)

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for the correct structure of the major organic product, with the acetyl group (CH<sub>3</sub>CO–) at the 4/para position of the methylbenzene ring
> 
> The 2/ortho product is not accepted as the major product.

> **[exam-tip]**
> This is a Friedel-Crafts acylation. The ethanoyl chloride reacts with the AlCl<sub>3</sub> catalyst to form the acylium ion (CH<sub>3</sub>CO<sup>+</sup>):
> 
> CH<sub>3</sub>COCl + AlCl<sub>3</sub> → CH<sub>3</sub>CO<sup>+</sup> + AlCl<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup>
> 
> The CH<sub>3</sub> group on methylbenzene is an electron-donating ortho/para director, so substitution occurs at the ortho or para positions. The para product is the major product because the ortho positions have greater steric hindrance from the adjacent ring hydrogens.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii) The total number of σ and π bonds in one molecule of the organic product is:
> 
> - σ bonds = 20
> **AND**
> π bonds = 4 **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Every covalent bond contains a sigma bond, including the sigma component of every double bond.
> 
> To count sigma bonds: count every bond in the structure. 4-methylacetophenone has 20 bonds in total, so there are 20 sigma bonds.
> 
> To count pi bonds: count each double bond once. Using a Kekulé structure, the benzene ring contains 3 C=C double bonds, plus 1 C=O double bond in the acetyl group, giving 4 pi bonds in total.

parts.problemMd: Draw the displayed formula of benzene.
parts.solutionMd:
The displayed formula of benzene is:

![Kekulé structure of benzene with alternating single and double bonds](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/29-an-introduction-to-a-level-organic-chemistry/29-3-shapes-of-aromatic-organic-molecules--and--bonds/assets/004-kekul-structure-of-benzene-with-alternating-sing.png)

**OR**

![Delocalised structure of benzene with a circle inside a regular hexagon](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/29-an-introduction-to-a-level-organic-chemistry/29-3-shapes-of-aromatic-organic-molecules--and--bonds/assets/005-delocalised-structure-of-benzene-with-a-circle-i.png)

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for a correct displayed formula of benzene showing all six C–H bonds and all six C–C bonds. Both the Kekulé structure and the delocalised (circle) representation are accepted.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The fully displayed formula must show all atoms and all bonds. For benzene (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>6</sub>), draw all six C–H bonds and all six C–C bonds explicitly.
> 
> You can draw benzene as a hexagon with alternating single and double bonds (Kekulé structure) or as a regular hexagon with a circle inside to represent the delocalised π electrons.

parts.problemMd: State the bond angle in a benzene molecule.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The bond angle in benzene is:
> 
> - 120° **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Each carbon atom in benzene is bonded to three other atoms, creating three regions of electron density. These arrange in a trigonal planar geometry, giving bond angles of 120°. There are no lone pairs on the carbon atoms to distort this angle.

parts.problemMd: State the type of hybridisation of the carbon atoms in benzene.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The type of hybridisation of the carbon atoms in benzene is:
> 
> - sp<sup>2</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> sp<sup>2</sup> hybridisation means that one s orbital and two p orbitals combine to form three sp<sup>2</sup> hybrid orbitals arranged at 120° to each other in a plane. Each carbon in benzene also has one unhybridised p orbital perpendicular to this plane, which participates in the delocalised π system.
> 
> Compare with sp<sup>3</sup> hybridised carbon (e.g. methane), where all four orbitals hybridise to give a tetrahedral geometry with 109.5° bond angles.

parts.problemMd:
State the systematic (IUPAC) name for compounds W, X and Y.

![Three substituted benzene compounds labelled W, X and Y](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/29-an-introduction-to-a-level-organic-chemistry/29-3-shapes-of-aromatic-organic-molecules--and--bonds/assets/001-three-substituted-benzene-compounds-labelled-w-x.png)
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The systematic (IUPAC) names for compounds W, X and Y are:
> 
> - W = 4-chloromethylbenzene **[1 mark]**
> - X = 3-nitrobenzoic acid **[1 mark]**
> - Y = propylbenzene **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The benzene ring is the main functional group in compounds W and Y, so the suffix is -benzene.
> 
> In W, the prefixes chloro- and methyl- are needed. The methyl group assumes position 1 and the chloro- group is given a position in relation to this, i.e. 4.
> 
> In Y, the prefix propyl- is used to represent the –CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> group.
> 
> For compound X, the benzene ring has the –COOH group attached, so its suffix is benzoic acid. It also has the NO<sub>2</sub> group attached, so the prefix nitro- is needed, and its position is given in relation to the –COOH group.

parts.problemMd:
State the systematic (IUPAC) name for compound Z.

![Structural formula of 2,4-dibromophenol labelled compound Z](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/29-an-introduction-to-a-level-organic-chemistry/29-3-shapes-of-aromatic-organic-molecules--and--bonds/assets/002-structural-formula-of-2-4-dibromophenol-labelled.jpeg)
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The systematic (IUPAC) name for compound Z is:
> 
> - 2,4-dibromophenol **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The benzene ring contains an –OH group, so the main stem is phenol.
> 
> Starting from the OH group (on carbon 1, as this is the dominant functional group) and counting anticlockwise, there are two bromine atoms on carbons 2 and 4. This is the lowest numbered version as counting clockwise would give 4 and 6.

parts.problemMd: State the bond angle in a benzene molecule.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The bond angle in benzene is:
> 
> - 120° **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Each carbon atom in benzene is sp<sup>2</sup> hybridised and bonded to three other atoms. The three areas of electron density arrange themselves as far apart as possible, giving a trigonal planar arrangement and a bond angle of 120°.

parts.problemMd:
In benzene, each of the carbon atoms is sp<sup>2</sup> hybridised.

i) Describe how neighbouring carbon atoms form σ bonds.

[1]

ii) Neighbouring carbon atoms also form π bonds. Describe how these π bonds are formed.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) σ bonds between neighbouring carbon atoms are formed by:
> 
> - End-on / axial overlap of sp<sup>2</sup> hybridised orbitals **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) π bonds between neighbouring carbon atoms are formed by:
> 
> - Sideways / lateral overlap of adjacent p orbitals (above and below the plane of the ring) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Each carbon atom has three sp<sup>2</sup> hybridised orbitals (formed from one s and two p orbitals), arranged at 120° to each other in a plane. These sp<sup>2</sup> orbitals overlap end-on with the sp<sup>2</sup> orbitals of neighbouring carbon atoms and the s orbital of the hydrogen atom, forming σ bonds.
> 
> Each carbon atom also has one unhybridised p orbital, perpendicular to the plane of the molecule. These p orbitals overlap sideways with adjacent p orbitals, forming π bonds. The resulting electrons become delocalised around the ring.

parts.problemMd:
State the systematic (IUPAC) name for each of the following aromatic compounds.

![Two aromatic compounds labelled X and Y](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/29-an-introduction-to-a-level-organic-chemistry/29-3-shapes-of-aromatic-organic-molecules--and--bonds/assets/003-two-aromatic-compounds-labelled-x-and-y.png)
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The systematic (IUPAC) names are:
> 
> - compound X: 1-chloro-2-methylbenzene **[1 mark]**
> - compound Y: 3,5-dichlorophenylamine **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> To name compound X, the chloro and methyl groups are listed in alphabetical order, with the methyl group at position 1.
> 
> To name compound Y, the dominant functional group is the amine group. When bonded directly to a benzene ring, this gives the parent name phenylamine. The two chloro groups are at positions 3 and 5.

parts.problemMd: Explain why the benzene ring is planar.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The benzene ring is planar because:
> 
> - All carbon atoms in C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>6</sub> / benzene are sp<sup>2</sup> hybridised **[1 mark]**
> - Forming a trigonal planar / triangular planar arrangement
> **AND**
> (With) bond angles of 120° **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Hybridisation explains the shape of molecules. sp<sup>2</sup> hybridisation produces three equivalent orbitals arranged at 120° in a plane, giving a trigonal planar geometry. Since all six carbon atoms in benzene are sp<sup>2</sup> hybridised, the entire ring lies in one plane.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

compound X: 1-chloro-2-methylbenzene

Compound X can be formed from benzene in a two-step reaction.

State the reagents and conditions required for each step.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The reagents and conditions for each step are:
> 
> - step 1 reagents: CH<sub>3</sub>Cl and AlCl<sub>3</sub> **[1 mark]**
> - step 1 conditions: anhydrous **[1 mark]**
> - step 2 reagents: Cl<sub>2</sub> and AlCl<sub>3</sub> **[1 mark]**
> - step 2 conditions: anhydrous **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For benzene to react, a powerful electrophile must be generated. The delocalised π system is very stable and will only react with powerful electrophiles. AlCl<sub>3</sub> acts as a Lewis acid catalyst (halogen carrier) by generating an electrophilic species from the reagent.
> 
> Step 1 is a Friedel-Crafts alkylation: benzene reacts with CH<sub>3</sub>Cl / AlCl<sub>3</sub> to form methylbenzene.
> 
> Step 2 is a Friedel-Crafts halogenation: methylbenzene reacts with Cl<sub>2</sub> / AlCl<sub>3</sub> to form compound X as a mixture of 2- and 4-chloromethylbenzene.
> 
> Anhydrous conditions are essential: water hydrolyses AlCl<sub>3</sub>, destroying its catalytic activity.

parts.problemMd: State the bond angle in a benzene molecule.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The bond angle in benzene is:
> 
> - 120° **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Each carbon atom in benzene is sp<sup>2</sup> hybridised and bonded to three other atoms. The three areas of electron density arrange themselves as far apart as possible, giving a trigonal planar arrangement and a bond angle of 120°.

parts.problemMd: Explain why benzene, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>6</sub>, does not react with aqueous bromine, whereas hexene, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>, reacts readily.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Hexene reacts with aqueous bromine but benzene does not because:
> 
> - The π bond in hexene / C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub> contains localised electrons / an area of high electron density **[1 mark]**
> - The π bond in hexene / C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub> induces a partial positive (δ+) and partial negative (δ–) in the Br<sub>2</sub> molecule **[1 mark]**
> - The δ+ Br / bromine atom is attracted to the π bond in hexene / C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>, forming a carbocation intermediate **[1 mark]**
> - The carbocation intermediate attracts the δ– Br / bromine atom **[1 mark]**
> - In benzene / C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>6</sub>, there are no localised electrons / areas of high electron density, so it cannot polarise the Br<sub>2</sub> molecule
> **OR**
> In benzene / C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>6</sub>, the electrons are delocalised with no areas of high electron density, so it cannot polarise the Br<sub>2</sub> molecule **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Alkenes undergo electrophilic addition with halogen molecules because the localised π bond has high electron density that readily polarises the Br<sub>2</sub> molecule. Benzene's delocalised electrons cannot do this as a halogen carrier such as AlBr<sub>3</sub> is needed to generate a sufficiently powerful electrophile for benzene to react.

parts.problemMd:
Benzene reacts with liquid bromine in the presence of a suitable catalyst.

State the name of the mechanism for this reaction.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The mechanism for this reaction is:
> 
> - Electrophilic substitution **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Benzene's delocalised π electron system is very stable. Unlike alkenes, it does not undergo electrophilic addition (which would disrupt the stabilising ring), but instead undergoes electrophilic substitution, which restores the delocalised ring after each step.

parts.problemMd:
Hydroxypropanoic acid has two position isomers.

i) Draw the structural formulae of the two position isomers of hydroxypropanoic acid and state the systematic name of each.

[2]

ii) State which of these isomers exhibits optical isomerism.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
i) The two position isomers of hydroxypropanoic acid are:

3-hydroxypropanoic acid:

![Structural formula of 3-hydroxypropanoic acid with the hydroxyl group on C3](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/29-an-introduction-to-a-level-organic-chemistry/29-4-isomerism-optical/assets/011-structural-formula-of-3-hydroxypropanoic-acid-wi.png)

2-hydroxypropanoic acid:

![Structural formula of 2-hydroxypropanoic acid with the hydroxyl group on C2](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/29-an-introduction-to-a-level-organic-chemistry/29-4-isomerism-optical/assets/012-structural-formula-of-2-hydroxypropanoic-acid-wi.png)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for the correct name and structure of 3-hydroxypropanoic acid
> 
> 1 mark for the correct name and structure of 2-hydroxypropanoic acid

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii) The isomer that exhibits optical isomerism is:
> 
> - 2-hydroxypropanoic acid
> **OR**
> Lactic acid **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The two position isomers differ only in the location of the –OH group: C2 in 2-hydroxypropanoic acid and C3 in 3-hydroxypropanoic acid. The –OH cannot sit on the same carbon as the –COOH group, so only two positions are possible.
> 
> To identify the optically active isomer, look for a carbon carrying four different groups (the chiral centre). In 2-hydroxypropanoic acid, C2 carries –H, –OH, –CH<sub>3</sub>, and –COOH: four different groups, so it is chiral. In 3-hydroxypropanoic acid, C3 carries two H atoms, so it cannot be a chiral centre.

parts.problemMd:
Fig. 1.1 shows the structures of three amino acids.

![Structural formulae of glycine, cysteine and aspartate](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/29-an-introduction-to-a-level-organic-chemistry/29-4-isomerism-optical/assets/013-structural-formulae-of-glycine-cysteine-and-aspa.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

Identify the amino acid in Fig. 1.1 that does not exhibit optical isomerism.

> 
> - Glycine / Gly **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> An optically active compound contains a chiral centre: a carbon bonded to four different atoms or groups. Of the three amino acids in Fig. 1.1, glycine is the only one where the central carbon carries two hydrogen atoms. Because two of its substituents are identical, glycine has no chiral centre and does not exhibit optical isomerism.

parts.problemMd:
Serine, shown in Fig. 1.2, exhibits optical isomerism.

![Structural formula of serine showing the chiral centre](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/29-an-introduction-to-a-level-organic-chemistry/29-4-isomerism-optical/assets/014-structural-formula-of-serine-showing-the-chiral-.png)

**Fig. 1.2**

Draw three-dimensional diagrams to show the two optical isomers of serine.
parts.solutionMd:
The two optical isomers of serine are:

![Three-dimensional diagrams of the two optical isomers of serine shown as non-superimposable mirror images](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/29-an-introduction-to-a-level-organic-chemistry/29-4-isomerism-optical/assets/015-three-dimensional-diagrams-of-the-two-optical-is.png)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for a correct three-dimensional diagram of one optical isomer of serine, with the chiral carbon at the centre bearing four different groups (–H, –OH, –NH<sub>2</sub>, –CH<sub>2</sub>OH) shown using wedge-and-dash notation
>

> 
> Allow other valid orientations of the groups provided the two structures are non-superimposable mirror images of each other

> **[exam-tip]**
> The chiral centre in serine is the central carbon, which carries –H, –NH<sub>2</sub>, –COOH, and –CH<sub>2</sub>OH. Place this carbon at the centre of your diagram and draw four bonds arranged tetrahedrally: two standard bonds in the plane of the page, one wedge bond (coming towards you) and one dash bond (going away from you).
> 
> The second optical isomer is the mirror image of the first. The simplest way to generate it is to keep two groups in the same position and swap the other two. The key check is that no rotation of one structure should allow it to be superimposed onto the other.

parts.problemMd:
Leucine is an optically active amino acid with the molecular formula (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CHCH<sub>2</sub>CH(NH<sub>2</sub>)COOH.

Draw the displayed formula of leucine.
parts.solutionMd:
The displayed formula of leucine is:

![Displayed formula of leucine showing all bonds including C–C, C–H, O–H and N–H bonds](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/29-an-introduction-to-a-level-organic-chemistry/29-4-isomerism-optical/assets/001-displayed-formula-of-leucine-showing-all-bonds-i.png)

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for the correct fully-displayed formula of leucine with all bonds shown, including the O–H bond in the carboxylic acid group and the N–H bonds in the amino group

> **[exam-tip]**
> A displayed formula shows every bond in the molecule as a line. The most commonly missed bonds are the O–H in the –COOH group and both N–H bonds in the –NH<sub>2</sub> group. Check your diagram includes all of these before moving on.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Leucine is an optically active amino acid with the molecular formula (CH~3~)~2~CHCH~2~CH(NH~2~)COOH.

Leucine exists as stereoisomers.

i) Explain what is meant by the term stereoisomerism.

[2]

ii) Describe how the two optical isomers of leucine can be distinguished.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The meaning of the term stereoisomerism:
> 
> - Molecules with the same structural formula / same atoms bonded to each other in the same order **[1 mark]**
> - But with a different arrangement of atoms in space **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The two optical isomers of leucine can be distinguished:
> 
> - By passing plane-polarised light through solutions of each isomer / by using a polarimeter **[1 mark]**
> - Each optical isomer / enantiomer rotates the plane of polarised light in opposite directions **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For the definition of stereoisomerism, two points are needed:
> 
> 1. The molecules have the same structural formula (the same atoms bonded in the same order)
> 2. They differ in the spatial arrangement of those atoms.
> 
> Saying only 'different arrangement' without specifying it is a spatial difference will not score the second mark.
> 
> For distinguishing optical isomers, focus on the one physical property that sets them apart: their effect on plane-polarised light. One enantiomer rotates the plane clockwise and the other rotates it anticlockwise. A racemic mixture contains equal amounts of both, so the rotations cancel and there is no net effect on the light.

parts.problemMd:
Propranolol is an optically active drug. Its structure is shown in Fig. 2.1.

![Skeletal formula of propranolol](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/29-an-introduction-to-a-level-organic-chemistry/29-4-isomerism-optical/assets/005-skeletal-formula-of-propranolol.png)

**Fig. 2.1**

i) Deduce the molecular formula of propranolol.

[1]

ii) On Fig. 2.1, indicate the chiral centre with an asterisk (*).

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The molecular formula of propranolol is:
> 
> - C<sub>16</sub>H<sub>21</sub>NO<sub>2</sub>
> **OR**
> C<sub>16</sub>H<sub>21</sub>O<sub>2</sub>N **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> To count atoms in a skeletal formula, go through carbon by carbon. In a skeletal formula, each line end and intersection represents a carbon, and H atoms on carbon are implied (not shown). The fused ring system in propranolol has carbons shared between the two rings, so be careful not to count those shared carbons twice.

ii) The chiral centre of propranolol is:

![Skeletal formula of propranolol with an asterisk indicating the chiral centre on the carbon bearing the hydroxyl group](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/29-an-introduction-to-a-level-organic-chemistry/29-4-isomerism-optical/assets/006-skeletal-formula-of-propranolol-with-an-asterisk.png)

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for identifying the chiral centre as the carbon attached to the –OH group, with four different groups (–H, –OH, –OCH<sub>2</sub>– chain, and –CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)– chain).

> **[exam-tip]**
> To identify the chiral centre, look for the only carbon bonded to four different groups. The carbon attached to the –OH group carries –H, –OH, the –OCH<sub>2</sub>– chain, and the –CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)– group: all four are different, making it the chiral centre. Other carbons in propranolol either form part of the aromatic ring or carry identical substituents.

parts.problemMd: Explain why a racemic mixture of propranolol has no effect on plane-polarised light.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> A racemic mixture of propranolol has no effect on plane-polarised light because:
> 
> - A racemic mixture contains equal amounts of each enantiomer / optical isomer **[1 mark]**
> - The rotation of plane-polarised light by each enantiomer is equal in magnitude but opposite in direction, so the effects cancel out **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The key word here is 'equal': a racemic mixture has a 50:50 ratio of the two enantiomers. One enantiomer rotates plane-polarised light clockwise by a given angle; the other rotates it anticlockwise by the same angle. Because the amounts are equal, these rotations exactly cancel, giving no net rotation.
> 
> If the mixture were not a 50:50 ratio (for example, if it contained more of one enantiomer), it would still rotate plane-polarised light and would not be described as a racemic mixture.

parts.problemMd: Explain why it is often important that chiral drugs, such as propranolol, are administered as a single pure enantiomer rather than as a racemic mixture.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> It is often important because:
> 
> - Each enantiomer has / may have different biological activity / interacts differently with biological receptors **[1 mark]**
> - One enantiomer may have unwanted / harmful side effects
> **OR**
> Administering a single enantiomer increases the potency / effectiveness of the drug **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Enantiomers have identical physical and chemical properties in achiral environments, but biological receptors are chiral. This means the two enantiomers of a drug can interact very differently with receptors in the body. In some drugs, one enantiomer provides the therapeutic benefit while the other is inactive or causes side effects. By administering the pure active enantiomer, the required dose is lower and the risk of side effects is reduced.

parts.problemMd:
Chiral catalysts are often used in the manufacturing process of drugs.

i) State the purpose of using a chiral catalyst in drug synthesis.

[1]

ii) State one advantage and one disadvantage of using a chiral catalyst.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The purpose of using a chiral catalyst in drug synthesis:
> 
> - To ensure that only one enantiomer is produced / formed **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) One advantage and one disadvantage of using a chiral catalyst:
> 
> One advantage:
> 
> - Only small amounts of catalyst are needed
> **OR**
> The catalyst can be reused / recycled **[1 mark]**
> 
> One disadvantage:
> 
> - Chiral catalysts are expensive / costly to produce **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The advantages and disadvantages of a chiral catalyst follow the same pattern as any catalyst: small quantities are required and the catalyst is not consumed in the reaction, so it can be recovered and reused. The specific purpose in chiral synthesis is selectivity: only one enantiomer is formed, avoiding the need to separate a racemic mixture afterwards.
> 
> Enzymes are biological chiral catalysts. They can achieve very high enantiomeric purity but may require carefully controlled reaction conditions (pH, temperature, aqueous environment) that are not always practical for industrial synthesis.

parts.problemMd:
Two isomers of C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>6</sub>O are shown below in Fig. 3.1.

![Structural formulae of propanal (compound A, an aldehyde) and propanone (compound B, a ketone)](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/29-an-introduction-to-a-level-organic-chemistry/29-4-isomerism-optical/assets/003-structural-formulae-of-propanal-compound-a-an-al.png)

**Fig. 3.1**

i) State the systematic (IUPAC) name of compound **A** and of compound **B**.

[2]

ii) State the name of the mechanism for the reaction between compound **A** and HCN.

[1]

iii) Describe the mechanism for the reaction between compound **A** and HCN. Include all relevant curly arrows, lone pairs, and partial charges in your diagram.

[4]

iv) State the systematic name of the organic product formed in this reaction.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The systematic (IUPAC) names of compounds **A** and **B** are:
> 
> - **A**: propanal **[1 mark]**
> - **B**: propanone **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The name of the mechanism is:
> 
> - Nucleophilic addition **[1 mark]**

iii) The mechanism for the reaction between compound **A** and HCN is:

![Nucleophilic addition mechanism showing the cyanide ion attacking the carbonyl carbon of propanal, with curly arrows for electron movement, formation of the alkoxide intermediate, and protonation to give 2-hydroxybutanenitrile](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/29-an-introduction-to-a-level-organic-chemistry/29-4-isomerism-optical/assets/004-nucleophilic-addition-mechanism-showing-the-cyan.png)

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for a curly arrow drawn from the lone pair of :CN<sup>-</sup> to the δ<sup>+</sup> carbon atom of compound A
> 
> 1 mark for a curly arrow drawn from the C=O bond to the δ<sup>-</sup> oxygen atom
> 
> 1 mark for the correct negatively charged intermediate with O<sup>-</sup> and CN bonded to the former carbonyl carbon
> 
> 1 mark for a curly arrow drawn from the lone pair of O<sup>-</sup> to an H<sup>+</sup> ion, forming the final product
> 
> HCN alone is not accepted as the nucleophile. The cyanide ion (:CN<sup>-</sup>) is the nucleophile.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> iv) The systematic name of the organic product is:
> 
> - 2-hydroxybutanenitrile **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Compound A is an aldehyde (the carbonyl group is at the end of the chain); compound B is a ketone (the carbonyl group is internal). Both can undergo nucleophilic addition with HCN.
> 
> For the mechanism in part iii), the nucleophile is the cyanide ion CN<sup>-</sup>, which attacks the δ<sup>+</sup> carbon of the C=O group. Your diagram must show:
> 
> - The lone pair on :CN<sup>-</sup> with a curly arrow going to the δ<sup>+</sup> carbon.
> - → A curly arrow from the C=O bond going to the δ<sup>-</sup> oxygen (forming O<sup>-</sup>).
> - → The complete intermediate with O<sup>-</sup> and CN bonded to the former carbonyl carbon.
> - → A curly arrow from the lone pair on O<sup>-</sup> going to H<sup>+</sup>, forming the final –OH group.
> 
> For part iv), the product is a hydroxynitrile. The –CN group becomes part of the carbon chain (extending it by one carbon), so the parent chain is 4 carbons long. The –OH is on C2 and the nitrile is the principal functional group: 2-hydroxybutanenitrile.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Two isomers of C~3~H~6~O are shown below in Fig. 3.1.

**Fig. 3.1**

Compound **A**: propanal (an aldehyde)
Compound **B**: propanone (a ketone)

Compound **B** also reacts with HCN.

i) State the systematic name of the organic product formed.

[1]

ii) Explain why the organic product in b(i) does not exhibit optical isomerism.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The systematic name of the organic product:
> 
> - 2-hydroxy-2-methylpropanenitrile **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The product does not exhibit optical isomerism because:
> 
> - The central carbon of the product is bonded to two identical methyl / –CH<sub>3</sub> groups **[1 mark]**
> - Optical isomerism requires a chiral centre; this compound has no carbon bonded to four different groups **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> When propanone (compound B) reacts with HCN, the product is 2-hydroxy-2-methylpropanenitrile. The central carbon (C2) carries –OH, –CN, and two –CH<sub>3</sub> groups. Because two of its substituents are identical, C2 is not a chiral centre, and the compound cannot exhibit optical isomerism.
> 
> This contrasts with the product from compound A (propanal), where C2 after HCN addition carries –H, –OH, –CN, and –CH<sub>3</sub>: four different groups, giving a chiral centre and therefore a pair of optical isomers.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Two isomers of C~3~H~6~O are shown below in Fig. 3.1.

**Fig. 3.1**

Compound A is propanal (an aldehyde) and compound B is propanone (a ketone).

Explain why the reaction between compound **A** and HCN produces a racemic mixture.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The reaction between compound A and HCN produces a racemic mixture because:
> 
> - Compound A / the carbonyl group is planar
> **OR**
> The carbonyl carbon is sp<sup>2</sup> hybridised **[1 mark]**
> - The nucleophile / CN<sup>-</sup> ion can attack from above or below the plane of the carbonyl group with equal probability **[1 mark]**
> - A chiral centre is created with four different groups attached, giving equal amounts of both enantiomers **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The key is the geometry of the carbonyl group. The carbonyl carbon in compound A is sp<sup>2</sup> hybridised and the molecule is planar around that carbon. This means the incoming nucleophile (CN<sup>-</sup>) can approach from either side of the plane with equal probability. Attack from above gives one enantiomer; attack from below gives the mirror image. Since both are equally probable, equal amounts of each enantiomer form, giving a racemic mixture.

parts.problemMd:

Compound A is propanal (an aldehyde) and compound B is propanone (a ketone).

The reaction between compound A and HCN produces a racemic mixture because:
- Compound A / the carbonyl group is planar OR The carbonyl carbon is sp^2^ hybridised
- The nucleophile / CN^-^ ion can attack from above or below the plane of the carbonyl group with equal probability
- A chiral centre is created with four different groups attached, giving equal amounts of both enantiomers

Explain why the racemic mixture formed in this reaction has no effect on plane-polarised light.
parts.solutionMd:

> The racemic mixture has no effect on plane-polarised light because:
>

> **OR**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Each enantiomer rotates plane-polarised light by the same angle but in opposite directions. Because the racemic mixture contains exactly equal amounts of both, the clockwise rotation from one enantiomer is exactly cancelled by the anticlockwise rotation of the other. The overall effect on the light is zero.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

This question is about the chemistry of limonene.

Limonene is a naturally occurring hydrocarbon found in citrus fruits, with the molecular formula C~10~H~16~.

Limonene exists as a pair of enantiomers:

- One enantiomer is responsible for a strong orange smell
- The other enantiomer is responsible for a lemon smell

Suggest why receptors in the human nose can distinguish between the orange and lemon enantiomers of limonene.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Receptors in the human nose can distinguish between the enantiomers of limonene because:
> 
> - Each enantiomer has a different three-dimensional shape / structure **[1 mark]**
> - Receptors in the human nose have a specific three-dimensional shape
> **OR**
> Receptors in the human nose are stereospecific **[1 mark]**
> - Only one enantiomer fits a given receptor / the two enantiomers fit different receptors **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> This question draws on the concept of molecular shape complementarity, the same principle as enzyme-substrate specificity in biology. Enantiomers have the same physical properties such as melting and boiling points, but different three-dimensional arrangements, which is why they interact differently with chiral environments such as receptors.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Limonene is a naturally occurring hydrocarbon found in citrus fruits, with the molecular formula C~10~H~16~.

Limonene can undergo full hydrogenation to form menthane as shown.

![Equation showing limonene reacting with two molecules of hydrogen gas to form menthane by complete hydrogenation](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/29-an-introduction-to-a-level-organic-chemistry/29-4-isomerism-optical/assets/009-equation-showing-limonene-reacting-with-two-mole.png)

For the complete hydrogenation of an impure sample of 3.00 g of limonene at room temperature and pressure, 870 cm<sup>3</sup> of hydrogen was required.

Calculate, showing your working, the percentage purity of limonene.

percentage purity = ........................ %
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the percentage purity of the limonene sample:

- Convert the volume of H<sub>2</sub> and calculate moles of H<sub>2</sub>:

870 cm<sup>3</sup> = 0.870 dm<sup>3</sup>

moles H<sub>2</sub> = $\frac{0.870}{24.0}$

moles H<sub>2</sub> = 0.03625 mol

**[1 mark]**

- Use the molar ratio to find moles of limonene (limonene : H<sub>2</sub> = 1 : 2):

moles limonene = $\frac{0.03625}{2}$

moles limonene = 0.018125 mol

**[1 mark]**

- Calculate M<sub>r</sub> of limonene and the mass of pure limonene:

M<sub>r</sub> (limonene) = (12.0 x 10) + (1.0 x 16) = 136 g mol<sup>-1</sup>

mass of limonene = 0.018125 x 136

mass of limonene = 2.465 g

**[1 mark]**

- Calculate the percentage purity:

$\text{percentage purity} = \frac{\text{mass of pure limonene}}{\text{total mass of impure sample}} \times 100$

percentage purity = $\frac{2.465}{3.00}$ x 100

percentage purity = **82.2%**

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct moles of H<sub>2</sub> = 0.03625 mol (accept 0.0363 or 0.0362) **AND** correct unit conversion 870 cm<sup>3</sup> = 0.870 dm<sup>3</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for correct moles of limonene = 0.018125 mol
> 
> 1 mark for correct mass of limonene = 2.465 g
> 
> 1 mark for correct percentage purity = 82.2%
> 
> Allow error carried forward from any step within the calculation

> **[exam-tip]**
> Retrieve the molar volume at RTP (24.0 dm<sup>3</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>) from the Data Booklet; it is not provided in the question.
> 
> Show all steps clearly: convert the volume of H<sub>2</sub> to dm<sup>3</sup>, use the 1:2 molar ratio from the equation to find moles of limonene, calculate the mass of pure limonene using M<sub>r</sub>, and then apply the percentage purity formula.

parts.problemMd:
Benzene can react with aluminium bromide, AlBr<sub>3</sub>, and bromoethane, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Br, to form ethylbenzene.

Construct an equation for the formation of the CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> species.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The equation for the formation of the CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> species is:
> 
> - CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Br + AlBr<sub>3</sub> → CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> + AlBr<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup> **[1 mark]**
> 
> AlCl<sub>3</sub> is not accepted

> **[exam-tip]**

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Benzene can react with aluminium bromide, AlBr~3~, and bromoethane, CH~3~CH~2~Br, to form ethylbenzene.

State the name of the mechanism for the formation of ethylbenzene from benzene and aluminium bromide.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The name of the mechanism for this reaction is:
> 
> - Electrophilic substitution **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Benzene undergoes electrophilic substitution rather than addition because substitution allows the delocalised π system to be restored. Addition would permanently break the ring's delocalisation, destroying the extra stability this provides.
> 
> Do not confuse the mechanism name (electrophilic substitution) with the reaction type (Friedel-Crafts alkylation). Both describe aspects of this reaction but are not interchangeable.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Benzene can react with aluminium bromide, AlBr3, and bromoethane, CH3CH2Br, to form ethylbenzene.

Describe the mechanism for the conversion of benzene into ethylbenzene using the CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> electrophile. Include all relevant curly arrows and charges.
parts.solutionMd:
The mechanism for the conversion of benzene into ethylbenzene is:

![Electrophilic substitution mechanism showing a curly arrow from the benzene ring to the C+ of the ethyl carbocation, the carbocation intermediate with a horseshoe partial delocalisation and positive charge, and a curly arrow from the C–H bond restoring the ring with loss of H+](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/30-hydrocarbons/30-1-arenes/assets/016-electrophilic-substitution-mechanism-showing-a-c.png)

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for a curly arrow from the π system of the benzene ring to the C<sup>+</sup> of the CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> ion (arrow must start from the ring, not from inside it)
> 
> 1 mark for the correct intermediate structure: horseshoe opening towards the sp<sup>3</sup> carbon, positive charge inside the ring system, with CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub> and H both attached to the sp<sup>3</sup> carbon
> 
> 1 mark for a curly arrow from the C–H bond back into the ring, restoring the delocalised π system, with H<sup>+</sup> shown as lost

> **[exam-tip]**
> Common errors in electrophilic substitution mechanisms:
> 
> - Starting the first curly arrow from inside the ring rather than from the ring circle
> - Placing the positive charge on the wrong carbon in the CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> electrophile. It must be on the terminal carbon
> - Drawing the horseshoe extending past carbons 2 and 6 in the intermediate

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Benzene can react with aluminium bromide, AlBr~3~, and bromoethane, CH~3~CH~2~Br, to form ethylbenzene.

The equation for the formation of the CH~3~CH~2~^+^ species is:
CH~3~CH~2~Br + AlBr~3~ → CH~3~CH~2~^+^ + AlBr~4~^–^

State why anhydrous conditions are required for this reaction.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Anhydrous conditions are required because:
> 
> - Water reacts with / hydrolyses the AlBr<sub>3</sub> catalyst, preventing formation of the electrophile **[1 mark]**
> 
> Allow: water would deactivate / destroy the catalyst

> **[exam-tip]**
> AlBr<sub>3</sub> is a Lewis acid that is rapidly destroyed by water. Even trace moisture reacts with the catalyst before it can generate the CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> electrophile, so the reaction cannot proceed. Anhydrous solvents and glassware are essential for all Friedel-Crafts reactions.

parts.problemMd: Construct an equation for the reaction of benzene with concentrated nitric acid to form nitrobenzene and water.
parts.solutionMd:
An equation for the reaction is:

C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>6</sub> + HNO<sub>3</sub> → C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>NO<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O

> 
> 1 mark for correct formulas for the products: C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>NO<sub>2</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>O

> **[exam-tip]**
> This is an electrophilic substitution reaction. A nitro group (–NO<sub>2</sub>) replaces one hydrogen atom on the benzene ring.

parts.problemMd: State the type of reaction that benzene will typically undergo.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Benzene typically undergoes:
> 
> - Electrophilic substitution **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Benzene undergoes electrophilic substitution rather than addition because substitution restores the delocalised π system. Addition would permanently break the ring's extra stability.
> 
> The three types of substitution to know are: free radical (alkanes + halogens), electrophilic (benzene ring reactions), and nucleophilic (halogenoalkanes + nucleophiles).

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

State the name of the mechanism that benzene will undergo if reacted with bromine in the presence of a halogen carrier to form bromobenzene, C~6~H~5~Br.

Construct an equation to show how the halogen carrier generates the Br<sup>+</sup> ion in order to allow the reaction in part **(a)** to occur.
parts.solutionMd:
An equation showing the generation of the Br<sup>+</sup> ion is:

AlBr<sub>3</sub> + Br<sub>2</sub> → AlBr<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup> + Br<sup>+</sup>

**OR**

FeBr<sub>3</sub> + Br<sub>2</sub> → FeBr<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup> + Br<sup>+</sup>

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct reactants: AlBr<sub>3</sub> + Br<sub>2</sub> or FeBr<sub>3</sub> + Br<sub>2</sub>
> 
> 1 mark for correct products: AlBr<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup> + Br<sup>+</sup> or FeBr<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup> + Br<sup>+</sup>

> **[exam-tip]**
> The halogen carrier acts as a Lewis acid, accepting one bromine atom from Br<sub>2</sub> to generate the Br<sup>+</sup> electrophile. AlBr<sub>3</sub> and FeBr<sub>3</sub> are equally acceptable.
> 
> The catalyst is regenerated at the end when the complex ion reacts with the H<sup>+</sup> lost from the ring:
> 
> AlBr<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup> + H<sup>+</sup> → AlBr<sub>3</sub> + HBr.

4-nitromethylbenzene can be prepared via an electrophilic substitution reaction as shown in Fig. 1.1.

[1]

ii) Construct an equation for the reaction between HNO<sub>3</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> that forms the electrophile for this reaction.

[1]

iii) Describe how the structure and bonding of the six-membered ring in intermediate **T** differ from those in methylbenzene. In your answer refer to the hybridisation, the π bonding and the bond angles in the ring system.

[3]
parts.solutionMd:
i) The structure of the isomer by-product is:

![Skeletal formula of 2-nitromethylbenzene showing a benzene ring with a methyl group and a nitro group at adjacent (2-) positions](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/30-hydrocarbons/30-1-arenes/assets/025-skeletal-formula-of-2-nitromethylbenzene-showing.png)

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii) The equation for the formation of the electrophile is:
> 
> - HNO<sub>3</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> → H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> + NO<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> + 2HSO<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup> 
> **OR**
> HNO<sub>3</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> → NO<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> + HSO<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup> + H<sub>2</sub>O **[1 mark]**
> 
> iii) Differences between the six-membered ring in intermediate T and in methylbenzene:
> 
> Any **three** from (1 mark for each point):
> 
> - The delocalised / π system extends over only five carbons in **T**
> **OR**
> The delocalised / π system extends over all six carbons in methylbenzene
> 
> - There are only four π-electrons in (the delocalised system of) **T**
> **OR**
> There are six π-electrons in (the delocalised system of) methylbenzene
> 
> - One carbon is sp<sup>3</sup> hybridised in **T**
> **OR**
> Only five carbons are sp<sup>2</sup> hybridised in **T**
> **OR**
> All six ring carbons are sp<sup>2</sup> hybridised in methylbenzene
> 
> - One carbon has a bond angle of 109.5° / tetrahedral in **T**
> **OR**
> Not all bond angles are 120° in **T**
> **OR**
> All bond angles are 120° in methylbenzene
> 
> **[3 marks]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The methyl group is an ortho/para director. Substitution at the 4-position gives 4-nitromethylbenzene; at the 2-position gives the by-product.
> 
> Intermediate T is the carbocation formed when NO<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> bonds to the ring. One ring carbon switches from sp<sup>2</sup> to sp<sup>3</sup>, breaking the full delocalisation. The other five carbons remain sp<sup>2</sup> and the π electrons are partially delocalised over them.

parts.problemMd:
Benzene can undergo electrophilic substitution with ethanoyl chloride in the presence of aluminium chloride.

i) Construct an equation to show the formation of the electrophile.

[1]

ii) Describe the mechanism for the reaction. Include all relevant curly arrows and charges.

[3]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The equation for the formation of the electrophile is:
> 
> - CH<sub>3</sub>COCl + AlCl<sub>3</sub> → CH<sub>3</sub>CO<sup>+</sup> + AlCl<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup> **[1 mark]**

ii) The mechanism for the Friedel-Crafts acylation is:

![Friedel-Crafts acylation mechanism showing a curly arrow from the benzene ring to the C+ of the acylium ion, the carbocation intermediate with horseshoe partial delocalisation and positive charge, and a curly arrow from the C–H bond restoring the ring with loss of H+](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/30-hydrocarbons/30-1-arenes/assets/017-friedel-crafts-acylation-mechanism-showing-a-cur.jpeg)

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for a curly arrow from the π system of the benzene ring to the C<sup>+</sup> of the acylium ion (the + must be on the carbonyl carbon of COCH<sub>3</sub>, not the methyl carbon)
> 
> 1 mark for the correct intermediate structure: horseshoe covering more than half of the ring but not extending past carbons 2 and 6, with a positive charge correctly placed inside the ring
> 
> 1 mark for a curly arrow from the C–H bond back into the ring **AND** the correct product structure **AND** H<sup>+</sup> shown

> **[exam-tip]**
> The acylium ion (CH<sub>3</sub>CO<sup>+</sup>) is generated from the reaction of ethanoyl chloride with AlCl<sub>3</sub>. The positive charge is on the carbonyl carbon, not the methyl carbon.
> 
> All electrophilic substitution mechanisms follow the same pattern. The most common errors are starting the first curly arrow from inside the ring, misplacing the + in the intermediate, and omitting H<sup>+</sup>.

The organic product from part **(a)** can be reduced to form an alcohol.

Name a suitable reducing agent. Construct an equation for this reduction, using [H] to represent the reducing agent.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> A suitable reducing agent is:
> 
> - NaBH<sub>4</sub> / LiAlH<sub>4</sub>
> **OR** H<sub>2</sub> with Ni / Pd / Pt **[1 mark]**
> 
> An equation for the reduction is:
> 
> - C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>COCH<sub>3</sub> + 2[H] → C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CH(OH)CH<sub>3</sub> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The product from part (a) is phenyl methyl ketone (acetophenone). Reduction of a ketone with NaBH<sub>4</sub> or LiAlH<sub>4</sub> gives a secondary alcohol. The [H] notation represents the equivalent of one hydrogen atom from the reducing agent.

parts.problemMd: Explain why Friedel-Crafts acylation gives a mono-substituted product, while Friedel-Crafts alkylation may give a mixture of poly-substituted products.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Friedel-Crafts acylation gives only a mono-substituted product because:
> 
> - The acyl product contains an electron-withdrawing –COR group, which deactivates the benzene ring towards further electrophilic substitution **[1 mark]**
> - In alkylation, the product contains an electron-donating alkyl group, which activates the ring and allows further substitution to occur (polyalkylation) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The acyl group withdraws electron density from the ring through the C=O bond, making the ring less reactive towards electrophiles. An alkyl group donates electron density into the ring by the inductive effect, increasing reactivity and making poly-substitution more likely.
> 
> This is a key practical advantage of acylation: it always gives a single, predictable mono-substituted product.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Benzene can undergo electrophilic substitution with ethanoyl chloride in the presence of aluminium chloride.

i) Construct an equation to show the formation of the electrophile.

The equation for the formation of the electrophile is:
CH3COCl + AlCl3 → CH3CO+ + AlCl4–

Explain how the aluminium chloride catalyst reforms at the end of the electrophilic substitution reaction.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The aluminium chloride catalyst reforms because:
> 
> - H<sup>+</sup> is produced during electrophilic substitution when the benzene ring is restored **[1 mark]**
> - H<sup>+</sup> + AlCl<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup> → HCl + AlCl<sub>3</sub> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> AlCl<sub>3</sub> is consumed when it accepts Cl<sup>–</sup> to generate the acylium ion, forming AlCl<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup>. The H<sup>+</sup> lost from the ring in the final step then reacts with AlCl<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup> to regenerate AlCl<sub>3</sub> and release HCl. The catalyst is therefore reformed and can participate in further reaction cycles.

The mechanism for reaction 2 (electrophilic aromatic substitution) is:

parts.problemMd:
Benzene reacts with concentrated nitric acid in the presence of concentrated sulfuric acid.

Describe the structure and bonding of a benzene molecule, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>6</sub>. In your answer, refer to:

- the hybridisation of the carbon atoms
- the bond angles within the ring
- how the *σ* and *π* bonds are formed.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The structure and bonding of a benzene molecule can be described as:
> 
> - The carbon atoms are sp<sup>2</sup> hybridised **[1 mark]**
> - The molecule is planar (or a flat hexagon)
> **AND**
> the bond angle is 120° **[1 mark]**
> - The σ bonds are formed by the head-on (or end-on) overlap of (sp<sup>2</sup>) orbitals **[1 mark]**
> - The π bonds (or delocalised system) are formed by the sideways overlap of p-orbitals (creating electron density above and below the plane of the ring) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> When describing benzene, avoid drawing or implying **alternating double bonds**. Examiners are looking for the idea of a **delocalised π system** spread over all six carbon atoms, not localised C=C bonds.
> 
> A good way to check your answer is to mention **both** the planar structure **and** the π electron cloud above and below the ring. Together, these explain benzene’s unusual stability compared with alkenes.

parts.problemMd:

i) Construct an equation to show the generation of the electrophile.

[1]

[4]

> i) An equation to show the generation of the electrophile is:
> 
> - HNO<sub>3</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> → NO<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> + 2HSO<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup> + H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>
> **OR**
> HNO<sub>3</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> → NO<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> + HSO<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup> + H<sub>2</sub>O **[1 mark]**

ii) The mechanism for the formation of nitrobenzene is:

![Benzene ring undergoes nitration with NO2+, forms an intermediate with NO2 and H+, resulting in nitrobenzene and hydrogen ion](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/30-hydrocarbons/30-1-arenes/assets/001-benzene-ring-undergoes-nitration-with-no2-forms-.png)

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct name of mechanism: electrophilic substitution
> 
> 1 mark for a curly arrow from the delocalised π-system of the benzene ring to the NO<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> ion (arrow must start from the ring circle and point to the N atom or + charge)
> 
> 1 mark for correct structure of the intermediate: horseshoe delocalisation opening towards the sp<sup>3</sup> carbon **AND** positive charge clearly inside the horseshoe/ring system **AND** H and NO<sub>2</sub> attached to the sp<sup>3</sup> carbon
>
