parts.problemMd:
i) State the relative order of increasing acidity for ethanol, phenol, and ethanoic acid.

[1]

ii) Identify the electronic effect of the alkyl group that makes the ethoxide ion less stable than the phenoxide ion.

[1]

iii) Describe the distribution of the negative charge in the ethanoate ion that makes it the most stable of these three conjugate bases.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The relative order of increasing acidity is:
> 
> - Ethanol < phenol < ethanoic acid **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The electronic effect of the alkyl group that makes the ethoxide ion less stable than the phenoxide ion is:
> 
> - Positive inductive effect
> **OR**
> +*I* effect
> **OR**
> Electron-donating effect **[1 mark]**
> 
> iii) The distribution of the negative charge in the ethanoate ion that makes it the most stable of these three conjugate bases is:
> 
> - Charge is spread equally over both oxygen atoms
> **OR**
> The p-orbital on the carbon atom overlaps with the p-orbitals on both oxygen atoms
> **OR**
> The negative charge / π-electrons are delocalised over the COO<sup>−</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> When comparing acid strengths, always think in terms of **conjugate base stability**. The strongest acid forms the **most stable conjugate base**.
> 
> Look for features that stabilise negative charge, such as **delocalisation** and the presence of **electronegative atoms**, and avoid explanations based only on acidity strength or pH without reference to molecular structure.

parts.problemMd: Predict the major product formed when phenol reacts with dilute nitric acid.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The major product is:
> 
> - 4-nitrophenol
> **OR**
> 2-nitrophenol **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Phenol reacts with dilute nitric acid at room temperature to give a mixture of 2-nitrophenol and 4-nitrophenol. The -OH group activates the benzene ring and directs substitution to the 2- and 4-positions.
> 
> Although 4-nitrophenol is usually formed in greater proportion due to reduced steric hindrance, both products are expected and credited at this level in line with the specification.

parts.problemMd:
Benzene can be converted into 3-chlorobenzoic acid in a multi-step synthesis.

Suggest a **three-step** synthetic route for this conversion. In your answer, identify the reagents and conditions for each step and draw the structures of the intermediate compounds formed.
parts.solutionMd:
One suitable three-step synthetic route for the conversion of benzene into 3-chlorobenzoic acid is:

**Step 1** — Friedel-Crafts alkylation to give methylbenzene:

**Step 2** — Oxidation of the methyl side chain to give benzoic acid:

![Chemical structure of benzoic acid, showing a hexagonal benzene ring connected to a COOH group](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/30-hydrocarbons/30-1-arenes/assets/003-chemical-structure-of-benzoic-acid-showing-a-hex.png)

Reagents: alkaline KMnO<sub>4</sub>, heat; then acidify

**Step 3** — Electrophilic chlorination of the ring to give 3-chlorobenzoic acid:

Reagents: Cl<sub>2</sub> with AlCl<sub>3</sub> (or FeCl<sub>3</sub>) catalyst

**[5 marks]**

> 
> 1 mark for the correct intermediate structure of methylbenzene (toluene)
> 
> 1 mark for step 2 reagents: alkaline KMnO<sub>4</sub>, heat, then acidify
> 
> 1 mark for the correct intermediate structure of benzoic acid
> 
> 1 mark for step 3 reagents: Cl<sub>2</sub> **AND** AlCl<sub>3</sub> / FeCl<sub>3</sub>

> **[exam-tip]**
> The order of the steps matters. If chlorination is done while the ring has a −CH<sub>3</sub> group, the methyl group directs substitution to the 2- and 4-positions.
>

parts.problemMd:
The nitration of benzene forms the basis for the synthesis of dyes and explosives.

i) Construct an equation for the generation of the electrophile.

[1]

ii) State which reactant is acting as a Brønsted-Lowry base and justify your answer.

[1]

iii) Identify the conjugate acid in the reaction.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The equation for the generation of the electrophile is:
> 
> - 2H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> + HNO<sub>3</sub> → 2HSO<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup> + H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> + NO<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>
> **OR**
> HNO<sub>3</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> → NO<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> + HSO<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup> + H<sub>2</sub>O **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The reactant acting as a Brønsted-Lowry base and the justification are:
> 
> - Nitric acid / HNO<sub>3</sub>
> **AND**
> It accepts a proton from sulfuric acid / H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> **[1 mark]**
> 
> H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> is not accepted as the Brønsted-Lowry base.
> 
> iii) The conjugate acids in the reaction are:
> 
> - H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>
> **AND**
> NO<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> A Brønsted-Lowry base accepts a proton.
> 
> - HNO<sub>3</sub> accepts H<sup>+</sup> from H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>, so HNO<sub>3</sub> is the base.
> - H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> donates the proton, making it the acid.
> 
> The intermediate H<sub>2</sub>NO<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup> decomposes immediately to H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> and NO<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>. Both are conjugate acids because each formed by gaining H<sup>+</sup>.

parts.problemMd: Explain why benzene can generally only undergo substitution reactions.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Benzene undergoes substitution rather than addition because:
> 
> - Addition requires breaking the delocalised π system to form new bonds **[1 mark]**
> - Breaking the delocalised π system requires significant energy input **[1 mark]**
> - The C–H bond at the ring is not part of the delocalised π system **[1 mark]**
> - Substituting H leaves the delocalised π system intact **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Benzene's delocalised π system gives it extra stability. Addition would permanently destroy this, which is energetically unfavourable. Substitution replaces only the H atom (not part of the π system), so the ring's full delocalisation is restored after reaction.

> This question tests knowledge of directing effects. The two products have the same molecular formula but are different structural isomers because the position of bromination on the ring depends on which substituent is present when bromination takes place.

> As a general rule:
> 
> - Electron-donating groups (e.g. –NH<sub>2</sub>) make the ring more reactive and direct incoming electrophiles to the 2- and 4-positions
> - Electron-withdrawing groups (e.g. –NO<sub>2</sub>) make the ring less reactive and direct incoming electrophiles to the 3-position

parts.solutionMd:
The IUPAC name and structure of Compound **Z** are:

4-amino-3,5-dichlorobenzoic acid:

![Structure of Compound Z: 4-amino-3,5-dichlorobenzoic acid showing the benzene ring with COOH at position 1, Cl at positions 3 and 5, and NH~2~ at position 4](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/31-halogen-compounds/31-1-halogen-compounds/assets/009-structure-of-compound-z-4-amino-3-5-dichlorobenz.jpeg)

>

parts.problemMd:
Chlorobenzene is formed by bubbling chlorine gas into benzene at room temperature in the presence of anhydrous AlCl<sub>3</sub>.

Explain, by the use of equations, how AlCl<sub>3</sub> acts as a catalyst in the chlorination of benzene.
parts.solutionMd:
To explain how AlCl<sub>3</sub> acts as a catalyst in the chlorination of benzene:

- Construct the equation for generation of the electrophile:

Cl<sub>2</sub> + AlCl<sub>3</sub> → Cl<sup>+</sup> + AlCl<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup> **[1 mark]**

- Construct the equation for the electrophilic substitution of benzene:

Cl<sup>+</sup> + C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>6</sub> → C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>Cl + H<sup>+</sup> **[1 mark]**

- Construct the equation showing regeneration of the catalyst:

H<sup>+</sup> + AlCl<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup> → HCl + AlCl<sub>3</sub> **[1 mark]**

- AlCl<sub>3</sub> is used in the first step
**AND**
AlCl<sub>3</sub> is regenerated in the final step **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> State symbols are not required

> **[exam-tip]**
> AlCl<sub>3</sub> acts as a Lewis acid (halogen carrier). It accepts Cl<sup>–</sup> from Cl<sub>2</sub> to generate the Cl<sup>+</sup> electrophile, then recovers it from H<sup>+</sup> in the final step to reform AlCl<sub>3</sub> and release HCl. This completes the catalytic cycle: AlCl<sub>3</sub> is consumed in step 1 but regenerated in step 3, so the overall amount of AlCl<sub>3</sub> is unchanged.

parts.problemMd:
Nitrobenzene undergoes further substitution considerably more slowly than chlorobenzene. In nitrobenzene, the incoming group joins the benzene ring in the 3-position, whereas in chlorobenzene the incoming group joins to the benzene ring in the 4-position. Use these ideas to suggest the structures of the intermediate compounds **Y** and **Z** in the following synthesis of 4-chlorophenylamine.

![Synthesis pathway from benzene to 4-chlorophenylamine showing intermediate compounds Y and Z with reactions A, B, and a reduction step](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/31-halogen-compounds/31-1-halogen-compounds/assets/001-synthesis-pathway-from-benzene-to-4-chlorophenyl.png)
parts.solutionMd:
The structures of Compounds **Y** and **Z** are:

Compound **Y** (chlorobenzene):

![Structure of chlorobenzene showing a benzene ring with a Cl substituent](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/31-halogen-compounds/31-1-halogen-compounds/assets/002-structure-of-chlorobenzene-showing-a-benzene-rin.png)

Compound **Z** (4-chloronitrobenzene):

![Structure of 4-chloronitrobenzene showing a benzene ring with Cl at position 4 and a NO2 group at position 1](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/31-halogen-compounds/31-1-halogen-compounds/assets/003-structure-of-4-chloronitrobenzene-showing-a-benz.png)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct structure of Compound Y: chlorobenzene
> 
> 1 mark for correct structure of Compound Z: 4-chloronitrobenzene

> **[exam-tip]**
> The order matters: chlorination must occur before nitration so that the –Cl group directs the –NO<sub>2</sub> into the 4-position
> 
> To decide which step comes first, work backwards from the final product (4-chlorophenylamine) and consider the directing effects:
> 
> The –Cl group is 2,4-directing, so if chlorination occurs first, nitration is directed to the 4-position. This gives 4-chloronitrobenzene (Compound Z). Reduction of the –NO<sub>2</sub> group then gives 4-chlorophenylamine.
> 
> If nitration had occurred first, the –NO<sub>2</sub> group would direct chlorination to the 3-position, giving 3-chloronitrobenzene, which would produce 3-chlorophenylamine after reduction (not the desired product).

parts.problemMd: Suggest the structure of the organic product formed when 4-chlorophenylamine reacts with bromine water.

The structure of the organic product is:

**[1 mark]**

> 
> Br atoms must be at positions 2 and 6

> **[exam-tip]**
> The –NH<sub>2</sub> group is strongly electron-donating and o/p directing. For unsubstituted aniline, reaction with bromine water gives 2,4,6-tribromoaniline.
> 
> In 4-chlorophenylamine, the 4-position (para to –NH<sub>2</sub>) is already occupied by –Cl. Only positions 2 and 6 (ortho to –NH<sub>2</sub>) are available, so the product is 2,6-dibromo-4-chlorophenylamine.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Fig. 3.1 shows two reactions of methylbenzene.

Reaction 1 shows chlorination of the ring with Cl~2~/AlCl~3~ (electrophilic substitution), and Reaction 2 shows chlorination of the methyl group side chain with Cl~2~/UV light (free radical substitution)

Fig. 3.2 shows Reaction 3 showing the conversion of 4-methylbenzoic acid (a carboxylic acid) to the corresponding acyl chloride using a suitable reagent

The three chloro-compounds **A**, **B** and **C** vary in their ease of hydrolysis.

i) Place a tick in the box in Table 3.1 corresponding to the correct relative rates of hydrolysis. [the symbol '>' means 'faster than'].

**Table 3.1**

|   | Place **one** tick only in this column |
|---|---|
| **A** > **B** > **C** |   |
| **A** > **C** > **B** |   |
| **B** > **A** > **C** |   |
| **B** > **C** > **A** |   |
| **C** > **B** > **A** |   |
| **C** > **A** > **B** |   |

[1]

ii) Suggest an explanation for these differences in reactivity.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The correct order of ease of hydrolysis:
> 
> - **C** > **B** > **A** **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The explanation for the differences in reactivity:
> 
> - Compound **C** (acyl chloride) is most reactive: the carbon atom is highly δ+ due to bonding to two electronegative atoms (Cl and =O)
> **OR**
> an addition-elimination mechanism is possible **[1 mark]**
> - Compound **A** (aryl chloride) is least reactive: a lone pair on the Cl atom is delocalised into the π system of the benzene ring, giving the C–Cl bond partial double-bond character and making it very strong **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Hydrolysis involves nucleophilic attack by OH<sup>–</sup> on the carbon atom. Ease of hydrolysis depends on how accessible and electron-deficient that carbon is:
> 
> Compound **C** (acyl chloride) is most reactive: the carbon is highly δ+ (bonded to two electronegative groups: Cl and C=O), and an addition-elimination mechanism is available.
> 
> Compound **B** (chloroalkyl benzene) is intermediate: the C–Cl bond is polar and accessible, but the carbon is less activated than in an acyl chloride.
> 
> Compound **A** (aryl chloride) is least reactive: the lone pair on Cl is delocalised into the benzene ring π system, creating partial double-bond character that significantly strengthens the C–Cl bond.

parts.problemMd:

parts.solutionMd:

> 
> - Ethanol / C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH **[1 mark]**
> - Concentrated sulfuric acid / conc H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (catalyst) **[1 mark]**
> - Heat / heat under reflux **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) An equation to show the formation of ethyl ethanoate is:
> 
> - C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH + CH<sub>3</sub>COOH ⇌ CH<sub>3</sub>COOC<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O **[1 mark]**
>

> **[exam-tip]**
> Fischer esterification requires three things: the alcohol, the carboxylic acid, and concentrated sulfuric acid as the acid catalyst. Heat is also needed to drive the reaction forward at a practical rate.
> 
> The reaction is reversible (⇌), so a large excess of one reactant or continuous removal of water drives the equilibrium towards the ester product.
> 
> The equation follows the pattern: alcohol + carboxylic acid ⇌ ester + water.

Describe the mechanism for the reaction in part **(a)**.

Include all relevant curly arrows, lone pairs, and dipoles.
parts.solutionMd:
The mechanism for nucleophilic addition-elimination is:

![Nucleophilic addition-elimination mechanism for the reaction of propan-2-ol with ethanoyl chloride, showing curly arrows, lone pairs, dipoles, and tetrahedral intermediate](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/32-hydroxy-compounds/32-1-alcohols/assets/005-nucleophilic-addition-elimination-mechanism-for-.webp)

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for a curly arrow from the lone pair on the O–H oxygen to the δ+ carbonyl carbon
> 
> 1 mark for a curly arrow from the C=O bond to the δ– carbonyl oxygen
> 
> 1 mark for a correct tetrahedral intermediate structure
> 
> 1 mark for correct curly arrows on the intermediate showing loss of Cl<sup>-</sup> and restoration of the C=O bond

> **[exam-tip]**
> This mechanism is nucleophilic addition-elimination. There are two stages:
> 
> 1. Addition: the lone pair on the oxygen of propan-2-ol attacks the δ+ carbonyl carbon; the C=O breaks to form a tetrahedral intermediate with O<sup>-</sup> and Cl still attached.
> 2. Elimination: the C–Cl bond breaks (Cl<sup>-</sup> leaves); the C=O re-forms as electrons from O<sup>-</sup> move back onto carbon.
> 
> Curly arrows must start from a lone pair or a bond and point towards a positive or partial-positive centre. Show all δ+ and δ– on the C=O and C–Cl bonds clearly before drawing your arrows.

parts.problemMd:
Aldehydes can be prepared from acyl chlorides. A sample of an aldehyde is suspected to be contaminated with unreacted CH<sub>3</sub>COCl.

[1]

> 
> ii) The observation for a positive test is:
> 
> - (Immediate) white precipitate **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The acyl chloride reacts with water in the silver nitrate solution to release HCl, which then reacts with silver ions to form white silver chloride (AgCl). Aldehydes do not react in this way, so a positive test (precipitate) confirms the presence of unreacted acyl chloride.
> 
> The reaction sequence is:
> 
> CH<sub>3</sub>COCl + H<sub>2</sub>O → CH<sub>3</sub>COOH + HCl
> 
> Ag<sup>+</sup> (aq) + Cl<sup>-</sup> (aq) → AgCl (s)
> 
> Note that the precipitate forms immediately with an acyl chloride, whereas a halogenoalkane would require warming. This rapid reaction is a characteristic property of acyl chlorides.

**Extract:**

Phenol reacts with ethanoyl chloride to form a new product.

Describe the mechanism for the reaction occurring in part **(a)**.

Include all relevant curly arrows, lone pairs, and dipoles.

parts.problemMd: Explain why phenol acts as a weak acid.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Phenol acts as a weak acid because:
> 
> - The lone pair on the oxygen atom delocalises into the benzene / aromatic π system **[1 mark]**
> - This weakens the O–H bond / stabilises the phenoxide ion (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>O<sup>-</sup>) **[1 mark]**
> - The H<sup>+</sup> ion can be donated / released more easily **[1 mark]**
> 
> Phenol is a weak acid, so the equilibrium C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH ⇌ C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>O<sup>-</sup> + H<sup>+</sup> lies to the left; accept references to partial dissociation

> **[exam-tip]**
> Phenol is a weak acid because it only partially dissociates in aqueous solution. The explanation requires three linked ideas:
> 
> 1. Delocalisation: the lone pair on oxygen spreads into the ring π system.
> 2. Effect on O–H bond: this weakens the O–H bond and stabilises the phenoxide ion formed when H<sup>+</sup> leaves.
> 3. Result: H<sup>+</sup> can be released, but the equilibrium lies to the left, making phenol weak rather than strong.
> 
> Do not describe phenol as fully dissociating — that would make it a strong acid. The stability of the phenoxide ion, provided by delocalisation, is the key driving factor.

parts.problemMd: State the name of the reaction mechanism for the reaction of phenol with bromine water.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The name of the reaction mechanism for the reaction of phenol with bromine water is:
> 
> - Electrophilic substitution **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> A lone pair of electrons on the oxygen atom overlaps with the delocalised π system of the benzene ring, increasing the electron density around the ring. This makes phenol particularly susceptible to attack by electrophiles, which is why it undergoes electrophilic substitution more readily than benzene.

parts.problemMd:
Phenol undergoes bromination when reacted with bromine water. Benzene also undergoes bromination but requires different conditions.

State the conditions needed for the bromination of phenol and the conditions needed for the bromination of benzene.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The conditions needed for the bromination of phenol and for the bromination of benzene are:
> 
> - Bromination of phenol: Room temperature **[1 mark]**
> 
> - Bromination of benzene: Pure bromine
> **AND**
> Aluminium bromide / AlBr<sub>3</sub> (catalyst) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> A lone pair of electrons on the oxygen atom overlaps with the π bonding system of the benzene ring, increasing electron density in the ring. This makes phenol more susceptible to attack by electrophiles, so it reacts with bromine water at room temperature without a catalyst. Benzene requires pure bromine (rather than bromine water) and a halogen carrier catalyst such as AlBr<sub>3</sub>.

parts.problemMd:
Phenol behaves as a weak acid.

i) Construct the equation for the reaction of phenol with sodium hydroxide.

[1]

ii) Construct the equation for the reaction of phenol with sodium metal.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The equation for the reaction of phenol with sodium hydroxide is:
> 
> - C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH + NaOH → C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>O<sup>-</sup>Na<sup>+</sup> + H<sub>2</sub>O **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The equation for the reaction of phenol with sodium metal is:
> 
> - 2C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH + 2Na → 2C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>O<sup>-</sup>Na<sup>+</sup> + H<sub>2</sub> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> These are acid–base reactions:
> 
> Acid + base → salt + water (phenol + NaOH)
> 
> Acid + metal → salt + hydrogen gas (phenol + Na)
> 
> The product in both reactions is sodium phenoxide, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>O<sup>-</sup>Na<sup>+</sup>. The phenoxide ion (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>O<sup>-</sup>) forms an ionic bond with Na<sup>+</sup>.

parts.problemMd:
Explain why phenol is a weak acid.

You should include an equation in your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Phenol acts as a weak acid because:
> 
> - Phenol can donate the H atom from the O–H group to form the phenoxide ion **[1 mark]**
> 
> - C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH + H<sub>2</sub>O ⇌ C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>O<sup>-</sup> + H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>
> **OR**
> C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH ⇌ C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>O<sup>-</sup> + H<sup>+</sup> **[1 mark]**
> 
> - The phenoxide ion is stable because the negative charge is delocalised (spread) over the entire ion **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Acids donate protons. Although phenol is a weak acid, it can still lose the H from the –OH group to form the phenoxide ion. The equilibrium lies to the left (phenol is not fully ionised), making it weakly acidic.

parts.problemMd: Describe and explain how the acidities of ethanol and phenol compare with that of water.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> A comparison of the acidities of ethanol and phenol with that of water:
> 
> - Ethanol is less acidic than water **[1 mark]**
> - The ethyl group is electron-donating, concentrating more negative charge on the oxygen atom of the ethoxide ion **[1 mark]**
> - Phenol is more acidic than water **[1 mark]**
> - The phenoxide ion is more stable than hydroxide because the negative charge is delocalised over the ring **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The order of acidity (least to most acidic): ethanol < water < phenol
> 
> In phenol, the phenoxide ion (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>O<sup>-</sup>) has its charge spread over the benzene ring via delocalisation. This reduces the tendency to accept H<sup>+</sup> back, making phenol more acidic than water.
> 
> In ethanol, the ethoxide ion (C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>O<sup>-</sup>) has charge concentrated on oxygen because the ethyl group is electron-donating. The higher charge density means H<sup>+</sup> is more strongly attracted back, making ethanol less acidic than water.

- **Stage 2:** React phenylamine with nitric(III) acid and hydrochloric acid to form a diazonium salt
- **Stage 3:** Thermal decomposition of the diazonium salt to form phenol, hydrochloric acid, and nitrogen gas

Stage 1:

parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The balanced equations for each stage are:
> 
> Stage 1:
> 
> - NaNO<sub>2</sub> + HCl → HNO<sub>2</sub> + NaCl **[1 mark]**
> 
> Stage 2:
> 
> - C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> + HNO<sub>2</sub> + HCl → C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>N<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>Cl<sup>-</sup> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O
> **OR**
> C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> + NaNO<sub>2</sub> + 2HCl → C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>N<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>Cl<sup>-</sup> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O + NaCl **[1 mark]**
> 
> Stage 3:
> 
> - C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>N<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>Cl<sup>-</sup> + H<sub>2</sub>O → C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH + HCl + N<sub>2</sub> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Stage 1: sodium nitrite reacts with hydrochloric acid to produce nitric(III) acid (nitrous acid) and sodium chloride.

> Stage 3: the diazonium salt undergoes thermal decomposition in the presence of water to give phenol, hydrochloric acid, and nitrogen gas.

parts.problemMd:
This question is about the reactions of phenol and benzene.

Explain the difference in bromination of phenol and benzene. In your answer, include structures of any organic products formed in the reaction.
parts.solutionMd:
The structure of 2,4,6-tribromophenol is:

![2,4,6-tribromophenol](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/32-hydroxy-compounds/32-2-phenol/assets/027-2-4-6-tribromophenol.jpeg)

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for the correct structure of 2,4,6-tribromophenol
> 
> The difference in bromination of phenol and benzene, including structures of any organic products formed:
> 
> - Phenol has a lone pair on the oxygen atom that (partially) delocalises into the π system of the benzene ring **[1 mark]**
> 
> - The π electrons of benzene are delocalised over the ring **[1 mark]**
> 
> - Phenol has a higher electron density in the ring than benzene **[1 mark]**
> 
> - Benzene cannot polarise the Br–Br bond
> **OR**
> Phenol can polarise the Br–Br bond (allow: δ<sup>+</sup> Br or Br<sup>+</sup> electrophile) **[1 mark]**
> 
> - Bromination of benzene requires a halogen carrier catalyst such as FeBr<sub>3</sub> / AlBr<sub>3</sub> and pure bromine **[1 mark]**
> 
> - Phenol reacts with bromine water at room temperature to form 2,4,6-tribromophenol **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> This question covers a lot of content. Break your answer into sections:
> 
> **Bromination of phenol**:
> 
> - The lone pair on the oxygen atom delocalises into the π ring, increasing electron density.
> - This allows phenol to polarise the Br–Br bond and react with bromine water at room temperature without a catalyst, giving 2,4,6-tribromophenol.
> 
> **Bromination of benzene**:
> 
> - The π electrons are delocalised but the electron density is lower than in phenol.
> - Benzene cannot polarise Br–Br on its own and requires pure bromine and a halogen carrier catalyst (FeBr<sub>3</sub> or AlBr<sub>3</sub>), giving bromobenzene.
> 
> **Directing effects**:
> 
> - The –OH group is an activating group that directs electrophiles to the 2, 4 and 6 positions, which is why three bromine atoms are substituted in phenol but only one in benzene.

mass = ............... g

[3]
parts.solutionMd:

*M*<sub>r</sub> of 2-nitrophenol = 139.0

*M*<sub>r</sub> of phenol = 94.0

parts.problemMd:
Phenol reacts with sodium to form a salt and hydrogen gas in an acid-base reaction.

Explain why phenol behaves as a weak acid.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Phenol behaves as a weak acid because:
> 
> - The O–H bond breaks; H<sup>+</sup> is donated and the phenoxide ion, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>O<sup>-</sup>, is formed **[1 mark]**
> - A lone pair on the oxygen atom (partially) delocalises into the π system of the benzene ring **[1 mark]**
> - This stabilises the phenoxide ion / the negative charge is delocalised (spread) over the ring **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The delocalisation of the oxygen lone pair into the ring is the key difference between phenol and simple alcohols. It weakens the O–H bond compared to alcohols, making phenol acidic. However, phenol is still a weak acid because the equilibrium lies to the left, so it does not fully ionise in water.
> 
> The formula of the phenoxide ion is C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>O<sup>-</sup>. The dissociation equation is:
> 
> C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH ⇌ C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>O<sup>-</sup> + H<sup>+</sup>
> 
> You may also be asked to calculate the pH of a phenol solution from a given concentration using the K<sub>a</sub> expression.

Dilute HNO<sub>3</sub> at room temperature is sufficient. The –COOH group is ring-deactivating, but the activating effect of the –OH dominates.
> 
> Step 2 converts the nitro group (–NO<sub>2</sub>) to an amine (–NH<sub>2</sub>) by reduction. Sn/HCl is the reducing agent and heat under reflux provides the energy. Under acidic conditions the amine product is protonated (–NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup>), so excess NaOH is added in the final step to deprotonate it and give the free amine –NH<sub>2</sub>.

parts.problemMd: State the relative acidities of benzoic acid and phenol. Explain your reasoning.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The relative acidities of benzoic acid and phenol are:
> 
> - Benzoic acid is a stronger acid than phenol **[1 mark]**
> - The C=O group in benzoic acid withdraws electron density from the O–H bond (negative inductive effect) **[1 mark]**
> - This weakens the O–H bond, making it easier to release H<sup>+</sup> / the proton **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The stronger an acid, the more easily it donates a proton (H<sup>+</sup>). In benzoic acid, the adjacent C=O group withdraws electron density from the O–H bond, stabilising the benzoate anion and making proton release easier.
> 
> In phenol, the oxygen lone pair is donated into the benzene ring, which reduces the electron density available on the oxygen. However, phenol has no carbonyl group to further weaken the O–H bond, so it is a weaker acid than benzoic acid (though stronger than aliphatic alcohols).

State the relative order of acidity of benzoic acid, phenylmethanol and 4-methylphenol shown in Fig. 1.1, starting with the most acidic. Explain your reasoning.

**Fig. 1.1**
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The relative order of acidity and reasoning are:
> 
> - Benzoic acid > 4-methylphenol > phenylmethanol **[1 mark]**
> - The benzoate ion is stabilised by delocalisation of negative charge over two electronegative oxygen atoms 
> **OR**
> The C=O group withdraws electron density from the O–H bond **[1 mark]**
> - The 4-methylphenoxide ion is stabilised by delocalisation of the oxygen lone pair into the benzene ring **[1 mark]**
> - The alkoxide ion of phenylmethanol is destabilised by the electron-donating CH<sub>2</sub> group 
> **OR**
> The alkyl group donates electron density to the oxygen, making it less stable **[1 mark]**

The phenoxide ion is less stable as the charge is delocalised into carbon atoms in the ring. The alkoxide ion from phenylmethanol is destabilised by the electron-donating effect of the benzyl group.

i) Draw the structure of the repeat unit of Nylon 6,6.

[2]

ii) Polyesters and polyamides are biodegradable polymers, whereas polyalkenes are generally non-biodegradable.

Explain this difference in terms of the structure and reactivity of the polymer chains.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
i) The structure of the repeat unit of Nylon 6,6 is:

![Chemical structure of the Nylon 6,6 repeat unit showing the amide linkage –NH–CO– connecting a hexamethylene diamine chain and an adipoyl chain](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/33-carboxylic-acids-and-derivatives/33-1-carboxylic-acids/assets/005-chemical-structure-of-the-nylon-6-6-repeat-unit-.png)

Structure of repeat unit: −NH(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>6</sub>NH−CO(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>4</sub>CO−

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - Correct amide linkage shown, i.e. –NH–CO– **[1 mark]**
> - Correct carbon backbone on both sides of the amide link, i.e. –NH(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>6</sub>NH– and –CO(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>4</sub>CO– **[1 mark]**
> 
> Acceptable representation includes, for example:
> −NH(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>6</sub>NH−CO(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>4</sub>CO−

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii) Polyesters and polyamides are biodegradable polymers, whereas polyalkenes are generally non-biodegradable because:
> 
> - Polyesters / polyamides contain polar ester / amide linkages which can be hydrolysed (by acids, alkalis, or bacteria) **[1 mark]**
> - Polyalkenes contain non-polar C–C bonds and C–H bonds which are chemically unreactive and cannot be hydrolysed **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> When explaining biodegradability, focus on bond type and reactivity rather than just stating the compound breaks down. Polar ester and amide bonds are susceptible to hydrolysis because water molecules can attack the δ<sup>+</sup> carbonyl carbon. Non-polar C–C and C–H bonds in polyalkenes have no such dipole and do not react with water.

parts.problemMd:
Esters can be formed from carboxylic acids and acyl chlorides.

Construct an equation for the formation of the ester formed from methanol and propanoic acid.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> An equation for the formation of the ester from methanol and propanoic acid is:
> 
> - CH<sub>3</sub>OH + CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COOH → CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COOCH<sub>3</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The first part of the ester name comes from the alcohol: methanol gives the methyl- group. The second part comes from the carboxylic acid: propanoic acid gives the -propanoate group. The ester formed is methyl propanoate.
> 
> During the reaction, a water molecule is lost and an ester linkage (-COO-) forms between the two groups. This type of reaction is a condensation reaction.
> 
> In the structural formula, the -CO- portion comes from the carboxylic acid and the -O- portion comes from the alcohol, giving CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COOCH<sub>3</sub>.

parts.problemMd:
Propanoyl chloride can be prepared from propanoic acid.

i) Construct an equation for the preparation of propanoyl chloride from propanoic acid and phosphorus(V) chloride.

[1]

ii) Give **one** observation of this reaction.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) An equation for the preparation of propanoyl chloride from propanoic acid and phosphorus(V) chloride is:
> 
> - CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COOH + PCl<sub>5</sub> → CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COCl + POCl<sub>3</sub> + HCl **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) One observation of this reaction is:
> 
> - White fumes / steamy fumes / misty fumes (of HCl) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Acyl chlorides are prepared from their corresponding carboxylic acid, so propanoyl chloride is produced from propanoic acid.
> 
> Three different reagents can be used in this preparation: PCl<sub>5</sub>, PCl<sub>3</sub> (with heat), and SOCl<sub>2</sub>. You should be able to construct equations for the preparation of an acyl chloride using all three.
> 
> The white fumes are hydrogen chloride gas (HCl), which is produced alongside the acyl chloride and phosphoryl chloride (POCl<sub>3</sub>).

parts.problemMd: Name and outline a mechanism for the reaction between methanol and propanoyl chloride to form methyl propanoate.
parts.solutionMd:
The name and mechanism for the reaction between methanol and propanoyl chloride to form methyl propanoate:

Name = (nucleophilic) addition-elimination

![Nucleophilic addition step of addition-elimination mechanism: curly arrow from methanol lone pair to δ+ carbonyl carbon of propanoyl chloride, and curly arrow from C=O bond to O, giving tetrahedral intermediate with negatively charged O and positively charged methanol oxygen](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/33-carboxylic-acids-and-derivatives/33-2-esters/assets/004-nucleophilic-addition-step-of-addition-eliminati.png)

**[5 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for naming the mechanism: (Nucleophilic) Addition-elimination
> 
> 1 mark for a curly arrow from the lone pair on the oxygen (of the OH) to the carbon atom of C=O **AND **δ+ on C of C=O and δ− on O of C=O
> 
> 1 mark for a curly arrow from C=O bond to the O of the C=O bond
> 
> 1 mark for three correct curly arrows in the second stage **AND **a lone pair on the O atom
> 
> 1 mark for the correct structure of the ion including the two charges

> **[exam-tip]**
> The alcohol acts as a nucleophile in this reaction. The lone pair on the oxygen of methanol attacks the δ+ carbonyl carbon, and an HCl molecule is eliminated in the second step.
> 
> Make sure your curly arrows are clear and double-headed. The first mechanism mark requires both the curly arrow from the lone pair **AND **the partial charges (δ+ on C and δ− on O of C=O) to be shown.
> 
> The mechanism is called addition-elimination because the nucleophile first adds to the carbonyl carbon, forming a tetrahedral intermediate, and then the chloride ion is eliminated.

parts.problemMd: State **two** advantages of using propanoyl chloride over propanoic acid in the preparation of esters in industry.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Two advantages of using propanoyl chloride over propanoic acid in the preparation of esters in industry:
> 
> Any **two** from (1 mark for each point):
> 
> - The reactions with acyl chlorides are quicker / faster
> - The acyl chloride reactions go to completion / are irreversible / do not form an equilibrium mixture
> - A higher yield of ester is obtained
> - No catalyst is required
> 
> **[2 marks]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> A reaction that forms an equilibrium mixture will result in a lower yield of product, because the reverse reaction continuously converts products back into reactants. Acyl chlorides avoid this problem as they react irreversibly, producing a higher yield in a shorter time.

parts.problemMd:
Methanoic acid, HCO<sub>2</sub>H, has a similar acid strength to propanoic acid.

Describe a chemical test to distinguish between these two acids. Name the acid which gives a positive result in this test and describe the observations that would be made.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> A chemical test to distinguish between the two acids, and the expected observations, are:
> 
> Any **one** of the following sets (1 mark for the chemical test and 1 mark for the acid/observation):
> 
> Set 1:
> 
> - Chemical test: Tollens' reagent
> - Acid/observation: Methanoic acid gives a silver mirror / black precipitate / grey solid
> 
> **OR**
> 
> Set 2:
> 
> - Chemical test: Fehling's solution
> - Acid/observation: Methanoic acid gives a red / orange precipitate / solid
> 
> **[2 marks]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Tollens' reagent and Fehling's solution both react with methanoic acid because the carbonyl carbon has a hydrogen directly bonded to it, as shown in the displayed formulae.
> 
> ![Displayed formulae of methanoic acid (left, H-C(=O)-OH) and propanoic acid (right, CH3CH2COOH), showing that methanoic acid has a hydrogen directly bonded to its carbonyl carbon, unlike propanoic acid](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/33-carboxylic-acids-and-derivatives/33-2-esters/assets/002-displayed-formulae-of-methanoic-acid-left-h-c-o-.jpeg)
> 
> This allows methanoic acid to behave like an aldehyde and act as a reducing agent.
> 
> Propanoic acid does not give a positive result because, although its carbon is doubly bonded to oxygen, it does not have a hydrogen directly attached to the carbonyl carbon.

parts.problemMd:
The ester phenyl propanoate, C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>, can be made from phenol and propanoic acid in a two step synthesis.

The first step produces an acyl chloride.

For this two step synthesis:

i) Draw the structure of the product of the first step.

[1]

ii) State the reagents and conditions needed for each step of the synthesis.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
i) The product of the first step:

![Displayed formula of propanoyl chloride (CH3CH2COCl), the acyl chloride product of reacting propanoic acid with PCl5, showing C=O and C-Cl bonds at the terminal carbon](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/33-carboxylic-acids-and-derivatives/33-2-esters/assets/003-displayed-formula-of-propanoyl-chloride-ch3ch2co.jpeg)

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for the correct structure of propanoyl chloride

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii) The reagents and conditions needed for each step are:
> 
> Step 1 (propanoic acid to propanoyl chloride):
> 
> - PCl<sub>5</sub>
> **OR**
> PCl<sub>3</sub> (+ heat)
> **OR**
> SOCl<sub>2</sub> (added to propanoic acid) **[1 mark]**
> 
> Step 2 (propanoyl chloride to phenyl propanoate):
> 
> - Add the product of Step 1 to phenol in NaOH **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> In order to form an acyl chloride, propanoic acid can react with solid phosphorus(V) chloride (PCl<sub>5</sub>), liquid phosphorus(III) chloride (PCl<sub>3</sub>, with heat), or liquid sulfur dichloride oxide (SOCl<sub>2</sub>).
> 
> Acyl chlorides are more reactive than carboxylic acids and are therefore often used as starting materials in ester synthesis. With phenols, the reaction requires heat and must be carried out in the presence of a base. The base deprotonates the phenol to form a phenoxide ion, which is a better nucleophile than the phenol molecule itself.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The ester phenyl propanoate, C~2~H~5~CO~2~C~6~H~5~, can be made from phenol and propanoic acid in a two step synthesis.

The first step produces an acyl chloride.

Explain why an acyl chloride should be formed first for the reaction in part **(b)**.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> An acyl chloride should be formed first because:
> 
> Any **one** from:
> 
> - Faster reaction
> - Reaction of phenol and carboxylic acid / propanoic acid does not go to completion
> 
> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Carboxylic acids are less reactive than acyl chlorides, so the direct reaction between propanoic acid and phenol is slow and reversible. Acyl chlorides react faster and irreversibly, giving a higher yield. The esterification of acyl chlorides proceeds via an addition-elimination mechanism, which is why the reaction goes to completion.

parts.problemMd:
Esters are responsible for various sweet, flowery and fruity smells. Some confectionery products use synthetic esters to achieve their aroma.

A student reacted acids and alcohols together to form ethyl methanoate (raspberry essence) and ethyl butanoate (pineapple essence).

Construct word and symbol equations to show the reactions that would produce these esters.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The word and symbol equations for the formation of ethyl methanoate (raspberry essence) and ethyl butanoate (pineapple essence) are:
> 
> - Ethanol + methanoic acid → ethyl methanoate + water
> **AND**
> CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH + HCOOH → HCOOCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O **[1 mark]**
> - Ethanol + butanoic acid → ethyl butanoate + water
> **AND**
> CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH + CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COOH → CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COOCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Remember that acid + alcohol → ester + water.
> 
> The alcohol gives the alkyl part of the ester name (ethanol = ethyl-) and the acid gives the carboxylate part (methanoic acid = -methanoate; butanoic acid = -butanoate).

parts.problemMd:
Octyl ethanoate can be manufactured or extracted from oranges and grapefruits. It is a flammable ester with a boiling point of 211 <sup>o</sup>C, a flash point of 86 <sup>o</sup>C and a density of 0.87 g/cm<sup>3</sup>.

A student reacted an acid and an alcohol in the presence of concentrated sulphuric acid to make an immiscible sample of octyl ethanoate. They added warm, aqueous sodium carbonate solution to remove any excess acid.

i) Explain why distillation would **not** work to safely obtain the octyl ethanoate.

[2]

ii) Describe the equipment that the student could use to safely obtain their octyl ethanoate and explain how this equipment would work.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) Distillation would not allow the student to safely obtain their octyl ethanoate because:
> 
> Any **two** from (1 mark for each point):
> 
> - The ester / octyl ethanoate is flammable
> **AND**
> it could ignite using a Bunsen burner / its flash point is below its boiling point
> - The high boiling point of the ester / octyl ethanoate
> **AND**
> means that the aqueous portion would boil off / would leave behind any dissolved materials in the ester / octyl ethanoate
> - There is a risk that the ester / octyl ethanoate could distil across with the water
> 
> **[2 marks]**
> 
> ii) The equipment that the student could use to safely obtain their octyl ethanoate is:
> 
> - A separating funnel **[1 mark]**
> - (Because) the ester / octyl ethanoate does not dissolve in water
> **OR**
> (Because) the ester / octyl ethanoate forms an organic layer
> **OR**
> (Because) the ester / octyl ethanoate floats on top of the other chemicals **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> This question gives you a lot of information about octyl ethanoate: it is flammable (flash point 86 °C), has a high boiling point (211 °C), and has a density of 0.87 g/cm<sup>3</sup>, meaning it is less dense than water and immiscible with it.
> 
> The flash point (86 °C) is well below the boiling point (211 °C), so the ester would ignite before it could be distilled safely using a Bunsen burner.
> 
> To safely purify the octyl ethanoate, focus on its low density and immiscibility with water. A separating funnel allows the organic layer to be separated from the aqueous layer without any heating.

parts.problemMd:
Propan-2-ol reacts with ethanoic acid in the presence of a suitable catalyst

i) Construct an equation for the reaction, name the organic product and clearly show its structure

[3]

ii) Suggest a suitable homogeneous catalyst for the reaction.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
i) The equation for the reaction between propan-2-ol and ethanoic acid, showing the structure of the organic product:

CH<sub>3</sub>CH(OH)CH<sub>3</sub> + CH<sub>3</sub>COOH → CH<sub>3</sub>COOCH(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O

![Displayed formula equation showing propan-2-ol reacting with ethanoic acid to form propan-2-yl ethanoate and water, with the ester linkage (-C(=O)-O-) formed between the acid carbonyl and alcohol oxygen](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/33-carboxylic-acids-and-derivatives/33-2-esters/assets/001-displayed-formula-equation-showing-propan-2-ol-r.png)

The organic product is **propan-2-yl ethanoate**

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) Marks are awarded for:
> 
> 1 mark for correct structural / displayed formulae for reactants
> 
> 1 mark for correct structural / displayed formula of the products (ester and water)
> 
> 1 mark for correct organic product name: propan-2-yl ethanoate **OR **1-methylethyl ethanoate

> **[exam-tip]**
> Naming esters from secondary alcohols can be challenging. The alcohol provides the first part of the name (propan-2-ol = propan-2-yl) and the acid provides the second part (ethanoic acid = ethanoate). The ester is propan-2-yl ethanoate, also accepted as 1-methylethyl ethanoate.
> 
> You will usually be awarded marks if you have used a mixture of displayed and structural formulae, for example drawing the displayed formula of the ester but writing the structural formula of water as H<sub>2</sub>O.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii) A suitable homogeneous catalyst for the reaction is:
> 
> - Concentrated sulphuric acid / concentrated H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Concentrated sulphuric acid is the answer CIE expects here. It acts as a homogeneous catalyst because the catalyst and both reactants are in the same liquid phase.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Propan-2-ol reacts with ethanoic acid in the presence of a suitable catalyst

i) Construct an equation for the reaction, name the organic product and clearly show its structure

The equation for the reaction between propan-2-ol and ethanoic acid, showing the structure of the organic product:

CH~3~CH(OH)CH~3~ + CH~3~COOH → CH~3~COOCH(CH~3~)~2~ + H~2~O

The organic product is **propan-2-yl ethanoate**

The same organic product, from part (c), was synthesised using an alternative method.

Name an alternative reagent to react with the alcohol to form the organic product in part (c) and name the other product formed as part of the reaction.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Any **one** of the following sets (1 mark for the reagent and 1 mark for the other product):
> 
> Set 1:
> 
> - Reagent: Ethanoyl chloride
> - Other product: HCl / hydrogen chloride / hydrochloric acid
> 
> **OR**
> 
> Set 2:
> 
> - Reagent: Ethanoic anhydride
> - Other product: Ethanoic acid / CH<sub>3</sub>COOH
> 
> **[2 marks]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The three methods of esterification you are expected to know are:
> 
> - Acid + alcohol → ester + water (reversible, requires concentrated H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>)
> - Acyl chloride + alcohol → ester + HCl (fast, irreversible)
> - Acid anhydride + alcohol → ester + carboxylic acid (fast, less hazardous than acyl chlorides)
> 
> You can also be expected to outline the mechanism for any of these methods. The acyl chloride and acid anhydride routes both proceed via addition-elimination.

parts.problemMd:
This question is about derivatives of carboxylic acids.

Fig. 1.1 shows the structure of a carboxylic acid derivative.

![Displayed formula of butanoyl chloride showing the four-carbon chain with a C=O group bonded to chlorine](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/33-carboxylic-acids-and-derivatives/33-3-acyl-chlorides/assets/004-displayed-formula-of-butanoyl-chloride-showing-t.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

State the systematic name of the carboxylic acid derivative shown in Fig. 1.1.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The systematic name of the carboxylic acid derivative in Fig. 1.1 is:
> 
> - Butanoyl chloride **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The compound in Fig. 1.1 is an acyl chloride. To name an acyl chloride, take the name of the parent carboxylic acid and replace "-ic acid" with "-oyl chloride". The longest chain (including the carbonyl carbon) has four carbons, so the parent acid is butanoic acid, giving **butanoyl chloride**.

parts.problemMd:
Ethanoyl chloride reacts with ethanol to form ethyl ethanoate as shown in Fig. 1.2.

![Reaction equation showing ethanoyl chloride reacting with ethanol to form ethyl ethanoate and HCl](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/33-carboxylic-acids-and-derivatives/33-3-acyl-chlorides/assets/005-reaction-equation-showing-ethanoyl-chloride-reac.png)

**Fig. 1.2**

i) State the name of the other product formed in this reaction.

[1]

ii) This reaction can be described as an esterification reaction or an acylation reaction.

Explain why this reaction can also be described as a condensation reaction.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The name of the other product formed:
> 
> - Hydrogen chloride / HCl **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) This reaction is classified as a condensation reaction because:
> 
> - A small molecule / hydrogen chloride / HCl is eliminated **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> A condensation reaction is one in which two molecules join together and a small molecule is eliminated.
> 
> When an acyl chloride reacts with an alcohol, HCl is the small molecule eliminated. Compare this with the direct esterification of a carboxylic acid with an alcohol, where water (H<sub>2</sub>O) is eliminated instead.
> 
> Both are condensation reactions and both produce an ester.

parts.problemMd:
Ethanoyl chloride can also react with ammonia to form ethanamide.

Construct an equation for this reaction.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The equation for this reaction is:
> 
> - CH<sub>3</sub>COCl + 2NH<sub>3</sub> → CH<sub>3</sub>CONH<sub>2</sub> + NH<sub>4</sub>Cl
> **OR**
> CH<sub>3</sub>COCl + NH<sub>3</sub> → CH<sub>3</sub>CONH<sub>2</sub> + HCl **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Both equations are accepted by CIE. When excess ammonia is present, the HCl produced immediately reacts with a second NH<sub>3</sub> molecule to form ammonium chloride, NH<sub>4</sub>Cl. The equation using 2NH<sub>3</sub> is the more complete answer when excess ammonia is specified.

parts.problemMd:
During the preparation of propanoyl chloride, SO<sub>2</sub> and HCl were also produced.

State the names of the two reactants used to form propanoyl chloride.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The two reactants used to form propanoyl chloride are:
> 
> - Propanoic acid **[1 mark]**
> - Sulfur dichloride oxide / thionyl chloride (SOCl<sub>2</sub>) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The by-products SO<sub>2</sub> and HCl tell you which reagent was used. SOCl<sub>2</sub> (thionyl chloride) produces SO<sub>2</sub> and HCl as by-products:
> 
> CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COOH + SOCl<sub>2</sub> → CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COCl + SO<sub>2</sub> + HCl
> 
> The other reagents that convert carboxylic acids to acyl chlorides are PCl<sub>5</sub> (by-products: POCl<sub>3</sub> + HCl) and PCl<sub>3</sub> (by-product: H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>3</sub>).

parts.problemMd:
Propanoyl chloride is used for the synthesis of other organic compounds.

Draw the skeletal formula for propanoyl chloride.
parts.solutionMd:
The skeletal formula for propanoyl chloride is:

![Skeletal formula of propanoyl chloride](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/33-carboxylic-acids-and-derivatives/33-3-acyl-chlorides/assets/006-skeletal-formula-of-propanoyl-chloride.png)

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for the correct skeletal formula of propanoyl chloride

> **[exam-tip]**
> You must be able to draw the skeletal formula for acyl chlorides. The acyl chloride functional group is a carbonyl carbon (C=O) bonded to a chlorine atom. For propanoyl chloride, the three-carbon chain has the acyl chloride group at one end.

parts.problemMd:
i) State the names of the two products formed when propanoyl chloride undergoes hydrolysis.

[2]

ii) State the name of the mechanism by which hydrolysis occurs.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The two products formed when propanoyl chloride undergoes hydrolysis are:
> 
> - Propanoic acid **[1 mark]**
> - HCl / hydrochloric acid **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The name of the mechanism is:
> 
> - Addition-elimination / nucleophilic addition-elimination **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The hydrolysis of an acyl chloride always produces the corresponding carboxylic acid and HCl. Water acts as the nucleophile, attacking the electrophilic carbonyl carbon atom, before HCl is eliminated.
> 
> For higher-mark questions, you may be asked to draw the full mechanism for this reaction.

parts.problemMd: Explain why propanoyl chloride will more readily undergo hydrolysis compared to 2-chloropropane.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The reason propanoyl chloride hydrolyses more readily is:
> 
> - The carbonyl carbon is bonded to two highly electronegative atoms (oxygen and chlorine) / the carbonyl carbon is highly electron-deficient (δ+) **[1 mark]**
> - It strongly attracts nucleophiles / is highly susceptible to nucleophilic attack by water **[1 mark]**
> 
> 'The C-Cl bond is weaker' is not accepted without reference to the electron-deficient carbonyl carbon

> **[exam-tip]**
> In 2-chloropropane, the carbon bonded to chlorine is attached to only one electronegative atom. In propanoyl chloride, the carbonyl carbon is attached to both oxygen and chlorine. This creates a much larger δ+ charge on the carbonyl carbon, making it far more susceptible to nucleophilic attack by water.
> 
> Note that the C-Cl bond in an acyl chloride is indeed weaker than in an alkyl chloride, but this alone is not the accepted explanation here. The answer must reference the electron deficiency of the carbonyl carbon and its susceptibility to nucleophilic attack.

parts.problemMd:
Acyl chlorides are commonly used carboxylic acid derivatives.

Ethanoyl chloride reacts with an excess of ammonia.

A student proposes the following equation to represent the reaction:

CH<sub>3</sub>COCl + NH<sub>3</sub>  →  CH<sub>3</sub>CONH<sub>2</sub> + HCl

Correct and explain the student's error.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The correct equation for the reaction of ethanoyl chloride with excess ammonia is:
> 
> - CH<sub>3</sub>COCl + 2NH<sub>3</sub> → CH<sub>3</sub>CONH<sub>2</sub> + NH<sub>4</sub>Cl **[1 mark]**
> 
> The student's equation is incorrect because:
> 
> - The excess ammonia reacts with the HCl produced, because ammonia is a base
> **AND**
> Ammonium chloride is formed as the second product (not hydrogen chloride) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The student's equation would have been correct if ethanoyl chloride reacted with a single equivalent of ammonia only. The use of excess ammonia means a second molecule of NH<sub>3</sub> acts as a base and reacts with the HCl produced, forming NH<sub>4</sub>Cl as the ionic salt product.

parts.problemMd:
i) Explain why butanoic acid is a weaker acid than 2-chlorobutanoic acid.

[2]

ii) Draw the skeletal formula for 2-chlorobutanoic acid.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) Butanoic acid is a weaker acid than 2-chlorobutanoic acid because:
> 
> - The chlorine atom withdraws electron density from the –COOH group **[1 mark]**
> - (Therefore,) the O–H bond is weakened, making it easier for 2-chlorobutanoic acid to lose an H<sup>+</sup> ion **[1 mark]**

ii) The skeletal formula for 2-chlorobutanoic acid is:

![Skeletal formula of 2-chlorobutanoic acid with Cl substituent at the alpha carbon](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/33-carboxylic-acids-and-derivatives/33-3-acyl-chlorides/assets/002-skeletal-formula-of-2-chlorobutanoic-acid-with-c.png)

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for the correct skeletal formula of 2-chlorobutanoic acid

> **[exam-tip]**
> Acids ionise in water by losing an H<sup>+</sup> proton from the –OH group. The weaker the O–H bond, the more readily the proton is lost and the stronger the acid.
> 
> In 2-chlorobutanoic acid, the electronegative chlorine at C2 withdraws electron density from the nearby –COOH group through the sigma bonds (inductive effect). This weakens the O–H bond further compared to butanoic acid, making 2-chlorobutanoic acid a stronger acid.

parts.problemMd:
Butanoyl chloride can undergo hydrolysis.

Describe the mechanism for the hydrolysis of butanoyl chloride. Include charges, dipoles, lone pairs of electrons and curly arrows, as appropriate.
parts.solutionMd:
The mechanism for the hydrolysis of butanoyl chloride is:

![Curly arrow mechanism diagram showing nucleophilic addition-elimination of water with butanoyl chloride to form butanoic acid and HCl](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/33-carboxylic-acids-and-derivatives/33-3-acyl-chlorides/assets/003-curly-arrow-mechanism-diagram-showing-nucleophil.png)

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for a curly arrow from the lone pair on the oxygen atom of H<sub>2</sub>O to the δ+ carbonyl carbon **AND** δ+ shown on the carbonyl carbon
> 
> 1 mark for a curly arrow from the C=O bond to the oxygen atom of the C=O group
> 
> 1 mark for all three curly arrows drawn correctly **AND** a lone pair shown on the oxygen atom of H<sub>2</sub>O
> 
> 1 mark for a correct structure of the tetrahedral intermediate (including both charges)

> **[exam-tip]**
> This is a nucleophilic addition-elimination mechanism. The water molecule acts as the nucleophile, with its lone pair attacking the δ+ carbonyl carbon. After the addition step forms the tetrahedral intermediate, the elimination step regenerates the C=O bond as HCl is eliminated to give butanoic acid.
> 
> Make sure your curly arrows are double-headed and you clearly show the δ+ on the carbonyl carbon.

parts.problemMd: State and explain the relative ease of hydrolysis for butanoyl chloride, chlorobenzene and 1-chlorobutane.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The correct order of ease of hydrolysis (most reactive first) is:
> 
> - Butanoyl chloride > 1-chlorobutane > chlorobenzene **[1 mark]**
> 
> Explanation for the order of butanoyl chloride and 1-chlorobutane:
> 
> - Butanoyl chloride has a carbon atom bonded to two electronegative atoms (oxygen and chlorine) **[1 mark]**
> - (Therefore,) the carbonyl carbon is more strongly δ+ than the carbon in 1-chlorobutane, making it more susceptible to nucleophilic attack **[1 mark]**
> 
> Explanation for the position of chlorobenzene:
> 
> - A lone pair of electrons from the Cl atom overlaps with the delocalised π electrons in the benzene ring **[1 mark]**
> - (Therefore,) the C–Cl bond acquires partial double-bond character and is stronger / harder to break **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Acyl chlorides can be hydrolysed readily at room temperature by water. Alkyl chlorides such as 1-chlorobutane require heating under reflux with aqueous alkali, because hydroxide ions are stronger nucleophiles than water and are needed to break the C–Cl bond.
> 
> Aryl chlorides such as chlorobenzene are the least reactive towards hydrolysis. One of the lone pairs on the Cl atom overlaps with the delocalised π system of the benzene ring, giving the C–Cl bond partial double-bond character. This makes the C–Cl bond significantly stronger and much harder to break.

parts.problemMd:
Ethanoyl chloride can react with primary aliphatic and aromatic amines to produce different amides.

i) Explain why ethanoyl chloride is more reactive towards ethylamine than phenylamine.

[2]

ii) Name the products of both reactions and classify the nitrogen in each product.

[3]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) Ethanoyl chloride reacts more readily with ethylamine than phenylamine because:
> 
> - Ethylamine is a stronger nucleophile than phenylamine
> **OR**
> Phenylamine is a weaker nucleophile than ethylamine **[1 mark]**
> - The alkyl group in ethylamine donates electron density to N, making the lone pair more available for nucleophilic attack
> **OR**
> The N lone pair in phenylamine is delocalised into the benzene ring, making it less available for nucleophilic attack **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The products and classification of nitrogen are:
> 
> - N-ethylethanamide **[1 mark]**
> - N-phenylethanamide **[1 mark]**
> - The nitrogen in both products is secondary / 2° **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For part (i): the reactivity of an amine as a nucleophile depends on how available the lone pair on N is. Alkyl groups (in ethylamine) donate electron density to N via the inductive effect, increasing lone pair availability. In phenylamine, the N lone pair is partially delocalised into the benzene π system, reducing its availability for nucleophilic attack.
> 
> For part (ii): when naming secondary amides from acyl chloride reactions, identify the chain attached to N (ethyl / phenyl) and the chain containing the carbonyl (ethan-). The product names take the form N-[alkyl/aryl]ethanamide. Both nitrogen atoms are secondary because N is bonded to two carbon atoms in the amide.

parts.problemMd: Explain why amines can act as bases.

> A base is defined as a proton acceptor or electron-pair donor.
> 
> An amine accepts a proton (H<sup>+</sup> ion) by donating its lone pair of electrons from the nitrogen atom to form a dative (coordinate) bond. This is why amines are classified as bases.

ii) Describe the mechanism for this reaction. Include all relevant curly arrows, lone pairs, and dipoles.

[4]

> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The name of the mechanism:
> 
> - (Nucleophilic) addition-elimination **[1 mark]**

ii) The mechanism for the reaction between ethanoyl chloride and methylamine is:

![Nucleophilic addition-elimination mechanism between ethanoyl chloride and methylamine, showing lone pair on nitrogen attacking carbonyl carbon, tetrahedral intermediate with charges, and elimination of chloride to give N-methylethanamide](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/34-nitrogen-compounds/34-1-primary-and-secondary-amines/assets/001-nucleophilic-addition-elimination-mechanism-betw.png)

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii)
> 
> 1 mark for curly arrow from lone pair on N atom to δ+ C atom AND curly arrow from C=O bond to O atom, with correct dipole shown on C=O
> 
> 1 mark for correct tetrahedral intermediate with positive charge on N and negative charge on O

parts.problemMd:
Methylamine can be prepared from chloromethane.

i) State the reagents and conditions required for this synthesis.

[3]

ii) State the name of the mechanism for this reaction.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:

> 
> - Excess ammonia / NH<sub>3</sub> **[1 mark]**
> - Ethanolic solvent / ethanol **[1 mark]**
> - Heat under pressure **[1 mark]**
>

> 
> - Nucleophilic substitution **[1 mark]**

> 
> The excess ammonia also reacts with the HCl produced to form NH<sub>4</sub>Cl, removing it from the reaction mixture and preventing it from reacting with the methylamine.
> 
> This is a nucleophilic substitution reaction in which the nitrogen lone pair in ammonia attacks the carbon bearing the Cl, replacing Cl<sup>-</sup> as the leaving group.

parts.problemMd:
The structural formulae of four isomeric amines, **A**–**D**, with the molecular formula C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>9</sub>N are given in Table 2.1.

**Table 2.1**

|   | **formula** | **systematic name** | **type of amine** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A** | CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NHCH<sub>3</sub> | *N*-methylethanamine |   |
| **B** | (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>N |   | tertiary |
| **C** | CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> |   |   |
| **D** | CH<sub>3</sub>CH(NH<sub>2</sub>)CH<sub>3</sub> |   |   |

Complete Table 2.1 to give the name and type of each amine. Each amine is primary, secondary, or tertiary.
parts.solutionMd:
The completed table is:

|   | **formula** | **systematic name** | **type of amine** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A** | CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NHCH<sub>3</sub> | *N*-methylethanamine | **Final answer:** **secondary** |
| **B** | (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>N | **Final answer:** **trimethylamine / N,N-dimethylmethanamine** | tertiary |
| **C** | CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> | **Final answer:** **propan-1-amine / propylamine** | **Final answer:** **primary** |
| **D** | CH<sub>3</sub>CH(NH<sub>2</sub>)CH<sub>3</sub> | **Final answer:** **propan-2-amine / 2-aminopropane** | **Final answer:** **primary** |

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for A = secondary **AND **B = trimethylamine / N,N-dimethylmethanamine
> 
> 1 mark for C = propan-1-amine / propylamine **AND **primary
> 
> 1 mark for D = propan-2-amine / 2-aminopropane **AND **primary

> **[exam-tip]**
> (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>N has three methyl groups on the nitrogen atom, making it a tertiary amine. It is commonly called trimethylamine; the IUPAC name is N,N-dimethylmethanamine.
> 
> CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> is a propane chain with the amine group at carbon-1, making it a primary amine. Its IUPAC name is propan-1-amine.
> 
> CH<sub>3</sub>CH(NH<sub>2</sub>)CH<sub>3</sub> has the amine group at carbon-2, making it a primary amine. Its IUPAC name is propan-2-amine; 2-aminopropane is also accepted.
> 
> Primary amines have an –NH<sub>2</sub> group on one alkyl group. Secondary amines have an –NH group between two alkyl groups. Tertiary amines have three alkyl groups on the nitrogen.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The structural formulae of four isomeric amines, **A**–**D**, with the molecular formula C~3~H~9~N are given in Table 2.1.

**Table 2.1**

|   | **formula** | **systematic name** | **type of amine** |
| :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| **A** | CH~3~CH~2~NHCH~3~ | *N*-methylethanamine |   |
| **B** | (CH~3~)~3~N |   | tertiary |
| **C** | CH~3~CH~2~CH~2~NH~2~ |   |   |
| **D** | CH~3~CH(NH~2~)CH~3~ |   |   |

State which of amines **A** and **D** is the stronger base. Explain your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Amine **A** is the stronger base:
> 
> - Amine A is the stronger base
> **AND**
> it has two alkyl groups donating electron density to the nitrogen atom **[1 mark]**
> - The increased electron density on the N atom makes the lone pair more available to accept a proton / H<sup>+</sup> **[1 mark]**
> 
> The reverse argument explaining why amine D is a weaker base is accepted.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Amine A is a secondary amine and amine D is a primary amine. Secondary amines are stronger bases than primary amines because they have more alkyl groups donating electron density to the lone pair on the nitrogen atom.

parts.problemMd:
State the relative order of basicity of ammonia, hexylamine, and phenylamine. Explain your reasoning.

most basic  ......................... > ......................... > ......................... least basic
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The relative order of basicity (most basic to least basic) is:
> 
> - Hexylamine > ammonia > phenylamine **[1 mark]**
> 
> Explanation:
> 
> - The hexyl / alkyl group is electron-donating (positive inductive effect)
> **AND**
> this increases the electron density on the nitrogen atom **[1 mark]**
> - The lone pair on the nitrogen atom in phenylamine is delocalised into the benzene ring
> **AND**
> this decreases the electron density on the nitrogen atom **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> When comparing the basicity of amines:
> 
> - Alkyl groups donate electrons (positive inductive effect), increasing the electron density on nitrogen. This makes the lone pair more available to accept a proton, so hexylamine is a stronger base than ammonia.
> - In phenylamine, the lone pair on nitrogen delocalises into the benzene ring, reducing the electron density on nitrogen. This makes the lone pair less available, so phenylamine is a weaker base than ammonia.

parts.problemMd:
Three nitrogen-containing molecules, ammonia, NH<sub>3</sub>, phenylamine, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>, and *N*-methylethanamine, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NHCH<sub>3</sub>, are drawn below in Fig. 1.1.

![Three amine molecules: ammonia (NH3), phenylamine (C6H5NH2), and N-methylethanamine (CH3CH2NHCH3), shown as structural diagrams](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/34-nitrogen-compounds/34-2-phenylamine-and-azo-compounds/assets/017-three-amine-molecules-ammonia-nh3-phenylamine-c6.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

i) State the relative order of basicity of the three amine molecules shown in Fig. 1.1.

least basic ......................... < ......................... < ......................... most basic

[1]

ii) Explain your answer to part (i).

[4]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The relative order of basicity, from least to most basic, is:
> 
> - Phenylamine < ammonia < *N*-methylethanamine **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The explanation for the order of basicity is:
> 
> - Alkyl groups donate electron density towards the N atom in *N*-methylethanamine / the methyl and ethyl groups have a positive inductive effect **[1 mark]**
> - The lone pair on N in *N*-methylethanamine is more available to accept a proton / bond with H<sup>+</sup> **[1 mark]**
> - In phenylamine, the lone pair on N overlaps with / becomes delocalised into the π system of the benzene ring **[1 mark]**
> - The lone pair on N in phenylamine is therefore less available to accept a proton **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Base strength depends on the availability of the lone pair on the nitrogen atom to accept H<sup>+</sup>.
> 
> For *N*-methylethanamine: two alkyl groups donate electron density towards N through the positive inductive effect, making the lone pair more available. This makes it the strongest base of the three.
> 
> For phenylamine: N is bonded directly to the benzene ring. The lone pair overlaps with the delocalised π electron system, partially withdrawing it from N and reducing its availability to bond with H<sup>+</sup>. This makes phenylamine the weakest base, weaker even than ammonia, which has no interaction with an aromatic ring system.

parts.problemMd:
Phenylamine, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>, can be produced from nitrobenzene, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>NO<sub>2</sub>.

State the name of the type of reaction and the reagents and conditions required for this conversion.

type of reaction ...............................................................

reagents ...............................................................

conditions ...............................................................
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The type of reaction and the reagents and conditions are:
> 
> - Type of reaction: Reduction **[1 mark]**
> - Reagents: Tin / Sn
> **AND**
> concentrated HCl / hydrochloric acid **[1 mark]**
> - Conditions: Heat / heat under reflux
> **AND**
> NaOH (aq) / sodium hydroxide solution **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The conversion of nitrobenzene to phenylamine is a core syllabus reaction involving reduction of the nitro group (–NO<sub>2</sub>) to an amino group (–NH<sub>2</sub>).
> 
> The tin and concentrated HCl reduce the nitrobenzene under heat. The strongly acidic conditions produce a phenylammonium salt rather than the free amine. Aqueous sodium hydroxide is then added to deprotonate the salt and release phenylamine.

parts.problemMd:
Phenylamine, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>, can be used in the manufacture of azo dyes. In the first step, phenylamine reacts with hydrochloric acid and nitrous acid, HNO<sub>2</sub>, to form a diazonium salt.

C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> + HCl + HNO<sub>2</sub> → C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>N<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>Cl<sup>−</sup> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O

In the second step, the diazonium salt solution is added to an alkaline solution of a phenol coupling agent to form the azo dye.

i) The diazonium salt, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>N<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>Cl<sup>−</sup>, is unstable. State the essential temperature condition required to prevent the diazonium salt from decomposing during this reaction.

[1]

ii) Draw the structure of the diazonium salt formed in this reaction. The nitrogen-containing group must be shown fully displayed.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The essential temperature condition is:
> 
> - Below 10 °C / between 0 °C and 10 °C / ice-cold conditions **[1 mark]**

ii) The structure of the diazonium salt is:

![Structural formula of benzenediazonium chloride, showing a phenyl group bonded to two nitrogen atoms connected by a triple bond, with a positive charge on the terminal N atom and Cl minus as the counterion](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/34-nitrogen-compounds/34-2-phenylamine-and-azo-compounds/assets/018-structural-formula-of-benzenediazonium-chloride-.png)

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct N≡N<sup>+</sup> triple bond AND positive charge on the terminal N atom AND Cl<sup>−</sup> counterion

> **[exam-tip]**
> The diazonium salt must be kept below 10 °C at all times. Above this temperature it decomposes. The N<sub>2</sub> group leaves as nitrogen gas, and the diazonium ion reacts with water to form phenol, destroying the intermediate before it can be used in the coupling reaction.
> 
> The nitrogen-containing group in the diazonium ion is –N≡N<sup>+</sup>. The two nitrogens are connected by a triple bond, with the positive charge on the terminal N atom furthest from the benzene ring. The counterion is Cl<sup>−</sup>.

**Extract:**

Phenylamine, C6H5NH2, can be used in the manufacture of azo dyes. In the first step, phenylamine reacts with hydrochloric acid and nitrous acid, HNO2, to form a diazonium salt.

C6H5NH2 + HCl + HNO2 → C6H5N2+Cl− + 2H2O

In the second step, the diazonium salt solution is added to an alkaline solution of a phenol coupling agent to form the azo dye.

In the second step of azo dye production, the diazonium salt reacts with an alkaline solution of a phenol coupling agent.

Draw the skeletal formula of the azo dye formed if the coupling agent used is 2,6-dimethylphenol.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
The skeletal formula of the azo dye is:

![Skeletal formula of the azo dye formed from benzenediazonium chloride and 2,6-dimethylphenol, showing two aromatic rings connected by an N=N azo linkage, with the diazonium ring attached at the para position of the 2,6-dimethylphenol ring and the OH group retained](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/34-nitrogen-compounds/34-2-phenylamine-and-azo-compounds/assets/019-skeletal-formula-of-the-azo-dye-formed-from-benz.png)

parts.problemMd:
4-methylphenylamine can be manufactured from methylbenzene in two steps.

Draw the skeletal formula of the intermediate organic compound formed in step 1.
parts.solutionMd:
The skeletal formula of the intermediate is:

>
