parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

4-methylphenylamine can be manufactured from methylbenzene in two steps.

State the reagents and conditions required for step 1.

reagents ...............................................................

conditions ...............................................................
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The reagents and conditions for step 1 are:
> 
> - Concentrated nitric acid / conc HNO<sub>3</sub>
> **AND**
> concentrated sulfuric acid / conc H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> **[1 mark]**
> - Heat / reflux between 30–50 °C **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> A nitrating mixture of concentrated HNO<sub>3</sub> and concentrated H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> generates the nitronium ion (NO<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>), which acts as the electrophile in the electrophilic substitution reaction.
> 
> Because the methyl group activates the benzene ring towards electrophilic substitution, nitration of methylbenzene requires a lower temperature than for plain benzene (55 °C). A temperature of 30–50 °C achieves mono-nitration while reducing the risk of a di-nitrated product forming.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

4-methylphenylamine can be manufactured from methylbenzene in two steps.

Step 2 involves heating the intermediate under reflux with tin and concentrated hydrochloric acid.

Explain why aqueous sodium hydroxide must also be added to obtain 4-methylphenylamine.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Sodium hydroxide is required because:
> 
> - The reduction in strongly acidic conditions produces the protonated amine / 4-methylphenylammonium salt rather than the free amine **[1 mark]**
> - Aqueous sodium hydroxide deprotonates the ammonium salt / acts as a base to neutralise the acid and liberate the free amine **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> When the nitro group is reduced using Sn and concentrated HCl, the acidic conditions immediately protonate the –NH<sub>2</sub> group as it forms, producing a 4-methylphenylammonium salt. The nitrogen's lone pair accepts H<sup>+</sup> from the acid.
> 
> To obtain the free amine, aqueous NaOH is added after the reduction step. It accepts the H<sup>+</sup> from the ammonium ion (acting as a Brønsted–Lowry base), releasing the neutral 4-methylphenylamine.

parts.problemMd:
The azo dye 4-hydroxyazobenzene, C<sub>12</sub>H<sub>10</sub>N<sub>2</sub>O, can be produced from phenylamine as shown in Fig. 3.1.

![Reaction scheme for the synthesis of 4-hydroxyazobenzene from phenylamine: phenylamine reacts in step 1 to form benzenediazonium chloride, which undergoes coupling in step 2 to form 4-hydroxyazobenzene](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/34-nitrogen-compounds/34-2-phenylamine-and-azo-compounds/assets/002-reaction-scheme-for-the-synthesis-of-4-hydroxyaz.png)

**Fig. 3.1**

Step 1 requires nitrous acid, HNO<sub>2</sub>, which is generated in situ.

i) State the reagents and conditions required for step 1.

reagents ...............................................................

conditions ...............................................................

[2]

ii) Construct an equation for the reaction that takes place in step 1.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The reagents and conditions required for step 1 are:
> 
> - NaNO<sub>2</sub> / sodium nitrite
> **AND**
> HCl / dilute hydrochloric acid **[1 mark]**
> - Temperature below 10 °C / ice / ice-cold conditions **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The equation for step 1 is:
> 
> - C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> + HNO<sub>2</sub> + HCl → C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>N<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>Cl<sup>−</sup> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O
> **OR**
> C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> + NaNO<sub>2</sub> + 2HCl → C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>N<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>Cl<sup>−</sup> + NaCl + 2H<sub>2</sub>O **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Nitrous acid (HNO<sub>2</sub>) is unstable and must be generated in situ by mixing sodium nitrite (NaNO<sub>2</sub>) with dilute hydrochloric acid immediately before use.
> 
> The temperature condition (below 10 °C) is for the stability of the diazonium salt product, not for the formation of nitrous acid. Above 10 °C, the diazonium ion rapidly decomposes by reacting with water to form phenol and nitrogen gas.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The azo dye 4-hydroxyazobenzene, C~12~H~10~N~2~O, can be produced from phenylamine as shown in Fig. 3.1.

Reaction scheme for the synthesis of 4-hydroxyazobenzene from phenylamine: phenylamine reacts in step 1 to form benzenediazonium chloride, which undergoes coupling in step 2 to form 4-hydroxyazobenzene

> 
> - Phenol / C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> 4-hydroxyazobenzene contains an –OH group on one of the aromatic rings, which originates from phenol, the coupling partner. Phenol is dissolved in alkaline conditions (NaOH (aq)) to form the more reactive phenoxide ion (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>O<sup>−</sup>) before coupling.
> 
> A common error is to suggest a compound that already contains nitrogen. The diazonium salt provides both nitrogen atoms in the –N=N– azo group. The coupling reagent simply needs to be an electron-rich aromatic compound activated by an electron-donating group such as –OH or –NR<sub>2</sub>.

parts.problemMd:
When heated, phenylamine reacts with iodomethane to form compound **B**, *N*-methylphenylamine.

i) Describe the mechanism for the formation of the *N*-methylphenylammonium iodide salt from the reaction of phenylamine and iodomethane. Include all relevant curly arrows, lone pairs, and dipoles.

[3]

ii) A further reaction occurs with an excess of iodomethane to form compound **C**, *N,N*-dimethylphenylamine.

Explain what this implies about the relative basicity of phenylamine and compound **B**.

[3]
parts.solutionMd:
i) The mechanism for the formation of the *N*-methylphenylammonium iodide salt is:

![Mechanism diagram showing nucleophilic substitution: the lone pair on the N atom of phenylamine attacks the delta positive carbon of iodomethane while the C-I bond breaks heterolytically, forming N-methylphenylammonium iodide salt with positive charge on N and I minus as a separate species](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/34-nitrogen-compounds/34-2-phenylamine-and-azo-compounds/assets/008-mechanism-diagram-showing-nucleophilic-substitut.jpg)

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for curly arrow from the lone pair on N of phenylamine to the δ+ carbon of iodomethane
> 
> 1 mark for curly arrow from the C–I bond to the I atom
> 
> 1 mark for correct product showing positive charge on the N atom **AND** I<sup>−</sup> / iodide ion as a separate species

> **[exam-tip]**
> This is a nucleophilic substitution reaction. Phenylamine (the nucleophile, lone pair on N) attacks iodomethane (the electrophile, δ+ on C):
> 
> - One curly arrow from the lone pair on N to the δ+ carbon of CH<sub>3</sub>I
> - One curly arrow from the C–I bond to I
> - Product: *N*-methylphenylammonium iodide salt with positive charge on N and I<sup>−</sup> as a separate ion

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii) This implies about the relative basicity:
> 
> - Compound **B** / *N*-methylphenylamine is a stronger base than phenylamine **[1 mark]**
> - The methyl group in compound **B** donates electron density towards the N atom / positive inductive effect of the methyl group **[1 mark]**
> - The lone pair on N in compound **B** is therefore more available to accept a proton than in phenylamine **[1 mark]**
> 
> Both compounds contain a phenyl ring, so the delocalising effect of the ring on the N lone pair applies equally to both. The only structural difference is the methyl group in compound **B**.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Since both phenylamine and compound **B** contain the phenyl ring, the delocalisation of the N lone pair into the π system applies equally to both. The only difference is the methyl group in compound **B**, which donates electron density towards N (positive inductive effect), making the lone pair more available to accept H<sup>+</sup>. This makes compound **B** a stronger base, which explains why excess iodomethane is required to form compound **C**.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The acid-base indicator methyl red is an azo dye synthesised from 2-nitrobenzaldehyde and phenylamine. Fig. 1.1 shows the first stages of this synthesis.

Synthesis scheme for methyl red showing: 2-nitrobenzaldehyde undergoes step 1 (oxidation) to give 2-nitrobenzoic acid, then step 2 (reduction) to give compound A (2-aminobenzoic acid), which undergoes step 3 (diazotization) and coupling with phenylamine to give methyl red

Explain why the temperature used in step 3 must be kept between 0 °C and 10 °C.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The temperature must be kept between 0 °C and 10 °C because:
> 
> - Above 10 °C, the diazonium salt decomposes / reacts with water / forms a phenol / nitrogen gas is evolved **[1 mark]**
> - Below 0 °C, the reaction rate is too slow / the diazotization does not proceed at a practical rate **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The 0–10 °C range is a compromise between two competing requirements:
> 
> - The upper limit (below 10 °C) prevents the diazonium salt from decomposing. Above this temperature the N–N<sup>+</sup> group leaves as nitrogen gas and the diazonium ion reacts with water to form a phenol derivative, destroying the intermediate before it can be used.
> - The lower limit (above 0 °C) ensures the reaction proceeds fast enough to be practical.
> 
> This temperature constraint applies to any diazotization step in diazonium salt chemistry.

parts.problemMd:
Fig. 1.2 shows the structure of indigotin. It can be synthesised from 2-nitrobenzaldehyde and propanone in aqueous sodium hydroxide.

![Structural formula of indigotin, a blue dye with a symmetric bicyclic structure containing two indole units connected by a C=C double bond, with NH and C=O groups](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/34-nitrogen-compounds/34-2-phenylamine-and-azo-compounds/assets/009-structural-formula-of-indigotin-a-blue-dye-with-.png)

![Skeletal formula of indigotin showing the two fused ring systems connected by a central C=C bond](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/34-nitrogen-compounds/34-2-phenylamine-and-azo-compounds/assets/010-skeletal-formula-of-indigotin-showing-the-two-fu.png)

**Fig. 1.2**

i) Complete the equation for this reaction, shown in Fig. 1.3.

![Incomplete equation for the synthesis of indigotin from 2-nitrobenzaldehyde and propanone in aqueous NaOH, with blank spaces for balancing coefficients and products](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/34-nitrogen-compounds/34-2-phenylamine-and-azo-compounds/assets/011-incomplete-equation-for-the-synthesis-of-indigot.png)

**Fig. 1.3**

[1]

ii) Calculate the mass of 2-nitrobenzaldehyde required to produce 12.0 g of indigotin from this reaction. The percentage yield is 82.0%. Show your working.

[3]
parts.solutionMd:
i) The completed equation is:

![Balanced equation for the synthesis of indigotin from 2 molecules of 2-nitrobenzaldehyde and 2 molecules of propanone in aqueous NaOH, giving indigotin plus 2 sodium ethanoate and water](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/34-nitrogen-compounds/34-2-phenylamine-and-azo-compounds/assets/012-balanced-equation-for-the-synthesis-of-indigotin.png)

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct balancing: 2 propanone + 2 NaOH; products include 2 CH<sub>3</sub>COO<sup>−</sup>Na<sup>+</sup> and H<sub>2</sub>O

> **[exam-tip]**
> Propanone (CH<sub>3</sub>COCH<sub>3</sub>, 3 carbons) contributes one carbon to each of the two five-membered rings in indigotin. Two propanone molecules are needed, each losing a CH<sub>3</sub> group that becomes sodium ethanoate (CH<sub>3</sub>COO<sup>−</sup>Na<sup>+</sup>). Balance NaOH and water last.

ii) To calculate the mass of 2-nitrobenzaldehyde required:

- Find *M*<sub>r</sub> values:

*M*<sub>r</sub> of 2-nitrobenzaldehyde = (7 x 12) + (5 x 1) + 14 + (3 x 16)

*M*<sub>r</sub> of 2-nitrobenzaldehyde = 151 g mol<sup>−1</sup>

*M*<sub>r</sub> of indigotin = (16 x 12) + (10 x 1) + (2 x 14) + (2 x 16)

*M*<sub>r</sub> of indigotin = 262 g mol<sup>−1</sup>

**[1 mark]**

- Find theoretical mass and moles of indigotin (100% yield):

mass at 100% yield = $\frac{100}{82.0} \times 12 . 0$

mass at 100% yield = 14.63 g

moles of indigotin = $\frac{14.63}{262}$

moles of indigotin = 0.05585 mol

**[1 mark]**

- Find mass of 2-nitrobenzaldehyde:

molar ratio 2 : 1 from equation

moles of 2-nitrobenzaldehyde = 0.05585 x 2

moles of 2-nitrobenzaldehyde = 0.1171 mol

mass = 0.1171 x 151

mass = **17.7 g**

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for the *M*<sub>r</sub> of 2-nitrobenzaldehyde **AND ** indigotin
> 
> 1 mark for the moles of indigotin
> 
> 1 mark for the mass of 2-nitrobenzaldehyde
> 
> Allow error carried forward from an incorrect *M*<sub>r</sub> value in subsequent steps

> **[exam-tip]**
> The 82.0% yield means 12.0 g is only 82.0% of the theoretical maximum. Scale up first (12.0 ÷ 0.820 = 14.63 g), then use *M*<sub>r</sub> and the 2 : 1 molar ratio to find the mass of starting material.

parts.problemMd:
Amides can be formed from amines. An example is shown in the following reaction scheme where compound **X** reacts with methylamine to form *N*-methylpropanamide and hydrogen chloride.

compound **X** + CH<sub>3</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> → CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CONHCH<sub>3</sub> + HCl

Deduce the structural formula of compound **X**.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The structural formula of compound **X** is:
> 
> - CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COCl **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Amides are formed by the reaction of an amine with an acyl chloride. In this case, the primary amine CH<sub>3</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> reacts with propanoyl chloride, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COCl, to form the substituted amide and hydrochloric acid.

parts.problemMd: *N*-methylpropanamide can undergo reduction forming compound **Y** and water. State the reagent required for this reaction.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The reagent required for this reduction is:
> 
> - LiAlH<sub>4</sub> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> *N*-methylpropanamide is a substituted amide. When reduced with LiAlH<sub>4</sub>, it forms a secondary amine (compound **Y**) and water.
> 
> LiAlH<sub>4</sub> is a strong enough reducing agent for this reaction. NaBH<sub>4</sub> is not strong enough to reduce amides.

parts.problemMd:
Fig. 1.2 shows the reduction of benzamide to form benzylamine.

![Structural formulae of benzamide and benzylamine with an arrow showing LiAlH4 reduction between them](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/34-nitrogen-compounds/34-3-amides/assets/008-structural-formulae-of-benzamide-and-benzylamine.png)

**Fig. 1.2**

i) State which of these two compounds is the weaker base. Explain your answer.

[3]

ii) State the name or formula of a suitable reducing agent for this reduction.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The weaker base and explanation:
> 
> - Benzamide **[1 mark]**
> - The carbonyl / C=O group is electron-withdrawing **[1 mark]**
> - The lone pair on the nitrogen atom is less available to donate / less available to accept a proton **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) A suitable reducing agent is:
> 
> - LiAlH<sub>4</sub> / lithium aluminium hydride **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Benzamide is a weaker base than benzylamine because the carbonyl group (C=O) adjacent to the nitrogen is electron-withdrawing. This reduces the electron density on the nitrogen atom, making the lone pair less available to accept a proton.
> 
> Both compounds contain the electron-withdrawing benzene ring, but this affects both equally. The key difference is the C=O group in benzamide, which is absent in benzylamine.
> 
> LiAlH<sub>4</sub> is required for the reduction of amides to amines. NaBH<sub>4</sub> is not strong enough to reduce the C=O group in an amide.

parts.problemMd:

parts.solutionMd:

Structural formula of N-ethylethanamide showing an ethanoyl group connected via an NH group to an ethyl group

Construct an equation to show the alkaline hydrolysis of *N*-ethylethanamide.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The equation for the alkaline hydrolysis of *N*-ethylethanamide is:
> 
> - CH<sub>3</sub>CONHCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> + NaOH → CH<sub>3</sub>COONa + CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Alkaline hydrolysis of a substituted (N-substituted) amide produces the carboxylate salt and the amine.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The structure of *N*-ethylethanamide is shown in Fig. 2.1.

![Structural formula of N-ethylethanamide showing an ethanoyl group connected via an NH group to an ethyl group](https://cdn.savemyexams.com/uploads/2024/03/n-ethylethanamide.png)

State the relative order of basicity of diethylamine, *N*-ethylethanamide and ammonia in aqueous solution. Explain your reasoning.

least basic ......................... > .........................  > .........................  most basic
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The relative order of basicity (least to most basic) and explanation:
> 
> - *N*-ethylethanamide < ammonia < diethylamine **[1 mark]**
> 
> Explanation:
> 
> - Alkyl groups donate electron density to the nitrogen atom, increasing the availability of the lone pair **[1 mark]**
> - The carbonyl group withdraws electron density from the nitrogen atom, reducing the availability of the lone pair **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The order of basicity depends on how available the nitrogen lone pair is to accept a proton:
> 
> Alkyl groups:
> 
> - Donate electron density through the inductive effect
> - Increase electron density on nitrogen, making the lone pair more available
> - Diethylamine (two ethyl groups) is a stronger base than ammonia
> 
> Carbonyl group:
> 
> - Withdraws electron density through the inductive effect
> - Decreases electron density on nitrogen, making the lone pair less available
> - *N*-ethylethanamide (carbonyl group adjacent to N) is the weakest base of the three
> 
> Be careful: exam questions sometimes swap the "least basic" and "most basic" labels. Always check which end of the table you are filling from.

parts.problemMd:
Methylamine reacts with propanoyl chloride to form CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CONHCH<sub>3</sub>.

i) State the name of the mechanism for this reaction.

[1]

An incomplete mechanism for this reaction is shown in Fig. 3.1.

![Incomplete addition-elimination mechanism diagram showing methylamine approaching propanoyl chloride with blank spaces for curly arrows, lone pairs, dipoles, and the second product](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/34-nitrogen-compounds/34-3-amides/assets/001-incomplete-addition-elimination-mechanism-diagra.png)

**Fig. 3.1**

ii) Complete the mechanism in Fig. 3.1. Include all relevant curly arrows, lone pairs, and dipoles. Also show the formula of the second product formed.

[5]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The name of the mechanism is:
> 
> - (Nucleophilic) addition-elimination **[1 mark]**

ii) The completed mechanism is:

![Completed addition-elimination mechanism showing methylamine reacting with propanoyl chloride, with all curly arrows, lone pairs, dipoles, formal charges on the intermediate, and HCl identified as the second product](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/34-nitrogen-compounds/34-3-amides/assets/002-completed-addition-elimination-mechanism-showing.png)

**[5 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii)
> 
> 1 mark for the correct dipole on the C=O bond **AND **the lone pair on the amine nitrogen
> 
> 1 mark for the curly arrow from the amine nitrogen to the δ+ carbon **AND **a curly arrow from the C=O bond to the δ– oxygen
> 
> 1 mark for the correct formal charges: – on oxygen and + on nitrogen in the intermediate **AND **the lone pair on the oxygen in the intermediate
> 
> 1 mark for the curly arrow from the N–H bond to the + nitrogen **AND **a curly arrow from the C–Cl bond to the chlorine **AND **A curly arrow from the oxygen lone pair to the C–O bond
> 
> 1 mark for HCl identified as the second product

> **[exam-tip]**
> The addition-elimination mechanism proceeds in two stages:
> 
> Addition:
> 
> - The lone pair on the nitrogen of methylamine attacks the δ+ carbonyl carbon.
> - The C=O π bond breaks, the oxygen becomes negatively charged (–), and the nitrogen becomes positively charged (+).
> 
> Elimination:
> 
> - A proton is transferred from the + nitrogen to the – oxygen, then the C–Cl bond breaks as Cl– leaves, and the C=O bond reforms. HCl is produced as the second product.
> 
> Make sure you include all three curly arrows in the elimination stage: N–H to + N, C–Cl to Cl, and O lone pair to C–O.

parts.problemMd:
Electrophoresis is an analytical technique which separates ions by placing them in an electrical field.

Describe how a sample of amino acids can be separated using this technique.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> A sample of amino acids can be separated using this technique by:
> 
> - A sample of amino acids is placed between two oppositely charged electrodes **[1 mark]**
> - The positively charged ions will move towards the negative electrode
> **AND**
> The negatively charged ions will move towards the positive electrode **[1 mark]**
> - Larger ions move more slowly
> **OR**
> Smaller ions move more quickly **[1 mark]**
> - Highly charged ions move more quickly
> **OR**
> Ions with a low charge move slowly **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> This question asks you to describe how amino acids are separated, not how they are identified.
> 
> After electrophoresis, an electropherogram is produced. This is a series of bands on the paper or gel, where each band corresponds to a particular species. The distance each band has moved from the origin indicates the relative size and charge of that species.

parts.problemMd:
Much research has been carried out in recent years investigating the exact structure of silk. The silk of a spider's web is at least five times as strong as steel, and twice as elastic as nylon. The silk fibre is composed of many identical protein chains, which are mainly made from the amino acids glycine, alanine and serine, shown in Fig. 1.1, with smaller amounts of four other amino acids.

![Structural formulae of glycine, alanine and serine](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/34-nitrogen-compounds/34-4-amino-acids/assets/007-structural-formulae-of-glycine-alanine-and-serin.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

Amino acids can exist as zwitterions. Draw the zwitterion structure for glycine.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The zwitterion structure of glycine is:
> 
> - NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup>CH<sub>2</sub>COO<sup>–</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> When an amino acid forms a zwitterion, the hydrogen ion from the –COOH group is transferred to the –NH<sub>2</sub> group. This produces a molecule with both a positive charge (on the nitrogen) and a negative charge (on the oxygen), but with no overall charge.
> 
> To draw the zwitterion of glycine: move the H from –COOH to –NH<sub>2</sub>, add a positive charge to give –NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup>, and add a negative charge to give –COO<sup>–</sup>.
> 
> Do not show individual single bonds in the structural formula.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Much research has been carried out in recent years investigating the exact structure of silk. The silk of a spider's web is at least five times as strong as steel, and twice as elastic as nylon. The silk fibre is composed of many identical protein chains, which are mainly made from the amino acids glycine, alanine and serine, shown in Fig. 1.1, with smaller amounts of four other amino acids.

![Structural formulae of glycine, alanine and serine](https://cdn.savemyexams.com/uploads/2024/03/xLItzEXi_glycine-alanine-serine.png)

{align=center} **Fig. 1.1**

Amino acids can act as acids or bases. Construct equations to show:

i) the reaction between alanine and HCl (aq),

[1]

ii) the reaction between serine and NaOH (aq).

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The equation for the reaction between alanine and HCl (aq) is:
> 
> - H<sub>2</sub>NCH(CH<sub>3</sub>)COOH + HCl → <sup>+</sup>H<sub>3</sub>NCH(CH<sub>3</sub>)COOH + Cl<sup>–</sup> **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The equation for the reaction between serine and NaOH (aq) is:
> 
> - H<sub>2</sub>NCH(CH<sub>2</sub>OH)COOH + NaOH → H<sub>2</sub>NCH(CH<sub>2</sub>OH)COONa + H<sub>2</sub>O **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Amino acids exist as zwitterions in solution. Think of the amino acid as having two separate functional groups: an acidic –COOH group and a basic –NH<sub>2</sub> group.
> 
> When HCl is added, the H<sup>+</sup> ion protonates the –NH<sub>2</sub> group to give –NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup>. The –COOH group remains unchanged.
> 
> When NaOH is added, the OH<sup>–</sup> ion deprotonates the –COOH group to give –COO<sup>–</sup>, with the Na<sup>+</sup> forming the sodium salt. Water is produced.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Much research has been carried out in recent years investigating the exact structure of silk. The silk fibre is composed of many identical protein chains, which are mainly made from the amino acids glycine, alanine and serine, shown in Fig. 1.1, with smaller amounts of four other amino acids.

i) Draw the structural formula of a portion of the silk protein, showing three amino acid residues. Label a peptide bond on your structure.

[3]

ii) State the polymer **type** of silk protein.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
i) The structural formula of a portion of the silk protein, with a peptide bond labelled, is:

![Structural formula of a silk protein chain showing three amino acid residues connected by peptide bonds](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/34-nitrogen-compounds/34-4-amino-acids/assets/008-structural-formula-of-a-silk-protein-chain-showi.png)

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct CO–NH bonding, including at least one C=O bond
> 
> 1 mark for at least one peptide bond labelled
> 
> 1 mark for 3 amino acid residues shown

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii) The polymer **type** of silk protein is:
> 
> - Condensation
> **OR**
> Polyamide **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The amine group of one amino acid reacts with the carboxylic acid group of the next. A water molecule is lost (condensation reaction) and a peptide bond (C(=O)–NH) forms between them.
> 
> The structural formula you draw must contain 3 residues. A residue is an amino acid that has lost a water molecule when forming the chain. The three residues do not all need to be different, but should be glycine, alanine or serine.
> 
> A polyamide is a condensation polymer containing amide (peptide) bonds. Silk and nylon are both polyamides.

parts.problemMd:
The *M*<sub>r</sub> of a silk protein molecule is about 600,000. Assuming it is made from equal amounts of the three amino acids in Fig. 1.1, calculate the average number of amino acid residues in the protein chain. Show your working.

[*M*<sub>r</sub> (glycine) = 75;   *M*<sub>r</sub> (alanine) = 89;     *M*<sub>r</sub> (serine) = 105]

number of residues .............................................
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the average number of amino acid residues in the protein chain:

- List the known values:

  - *M*<sub>r</sub>(glycine) = 75
  - *M*<sub>r</sub>(alanine) = 89
  - *M*<sub>r</sub>(serine) = 105
  - *M*<sub>r</sub>(protein chain) = 600 000
- Determine the *M*<sub>r</sub> of one repeating unit of three amino acid residues (each residue loses one water molecule when forming the chain):

(75 − 18) + (89 − 18) + (105 − 18)

= 57 + 71 + 87 = 215

**[1 mark]**

- Calculate the number of three-residue sets in the protein chain:

$\frac{600000}{215}$

= 2791

**[1 mark]**

- Calculate the total number of amino acid residues:

2791 x 3 = **8372**

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for calculating the *M*<sub>r</sub> of one repeating unit of three amino acid residues: 215
> 
> 1 mark for calculating the number of three-residue sets in the protein chain: 2791
> 
> 1 mark for calculating the total number of amino acid residues: 8372

> **[exam-tip]**
> When an amino acid joins a protein chain via a peptide bond, one water molecule (*M*<sub>r</sub> = 18) is lost per residue. Subtract 18 from each amino acid *M*<sub>r</sub> to find the residue *M*<sub>r</sub>.
> 
> The second step gives the number of repeating three-residue sets. Multiply by 3 to get the total number of individual amino acid residues.
> 
> If you did not subtract 18 from each *M*<sub>r</sub> value (using 75 + 89 + 105 = 269 instead of 215), you would still score 2 marks if the method for steps 2 and 3 is correct.

parts.problemMd:
A mixture of amino acids may be separated using electrophoresis. A typical practical set-up is shown in Fig. 2.1.

![Diagram of an electrophoresis apparatus](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/34-nitrogen-compounds/34-4-amino-acids/assets/004-diagram-of-an-electrophoresis-apparatus.png)

**Fig. 2.1**

When the power supply is switched on, some amino acids may not move, but remain stationary. Suggest an explanation for this observation.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Some amino acids remain stationary because:
> 
> Any **two** from (1 mark per point):
> 
> - The amino acid is uncharged / neutral / a zwitterion **OR** charges balance / are equal
> - It is equally attracted by the anode / + and the cathode / – **OR**
> It is attracted by neither the anode nor the cathode
> - The pH of the buffer is at the isoelectric point / IEP of the amino acid
> 
> **[2 marks]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> When a sample of amino acids is placed between two oppositely charged electrodes:
> 
> - The positively charged amino acids will move toward the negative electrode
> - The negatively charged amino acids will move toward the positive electrode
> - Amino acids with an overall neutral charge will remain stationary
> 
> If the pH of the buffer is at the isoelectric point of the amino acid, neither the positively nor negatively charged ions will dominate and the amino acid will exist as a neutral zwitterion

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Tryptophan is a naturally occurring α-amino acid. Its structure is shown below.

Deduce the molecular formula for tryptophan and write a balanced equation for the reaction of tryptophan with dilute nitric acid.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The molecular formula and equation are:
> 
> - Molecular formula: C<sub>11</sub>H<sub>12</sub>N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> **[1 mark]**
> - Equation: C<sub>11</sub>H<sub>12</sub>N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> + HNO<sub>3</sub> → C<sub>11</sub>H<sub>13</sub>N<sub>3</sub>O<sub>5</sub> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> When an amino group reacts with a dilute acid it is protonated:
> 
> RNH<sub>2</sub> + H<sup>+</sup> → RNH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup>
> 
> Tryptophan has only one basic amino group, which is the α-amino group (–NH<sub>2</sub>) attached to the central carbon
> 
> The nitrogen in the indole ring is part of the aromatic π system; its lone pair is delocalised into the ring and cannot be protonated by dilute acid
> 
> Adding one mole of HNO<sub>3</sub> contributes 1H, 1N, and 3O to the molecular formula of tryptophan, giving the ammonium nitrate salt C<sub>11</sub>H<sub>13</sub>N<sub>3</sub>O<sub>5</sub>

parts.problemMd: State the names of **two** classes of organic molecules that can take part in condensation polymerisation.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Two classes of organic molecules that can take part in condensation polymerisation include:
> 
> Any **two** from (1 mark for each point):
> 
> - Dicarboxylic acids
> - Hydroxy acids / hydroxycarboxylic acids
> - Diols
> - Diamines
> - Amino acids
> - Diacyl chlorides / dioyl chlorides
> 
> **[2 marks]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> To undergo condensation polymerisation, each monomer must have two reactive functional groups, either two identical groups (one at each end) or two complementary groups that can react with each other.
> 
> The key combinations are:
> 
> - Carboxylic acid (or acyl chloride) + alcohol forms a polyester
> - Carboxylic acid (or acyl chloride) + amine forms a polyamide.
> 
> In both cases a small molecule (water or HCl) is eliminated at each step.
> 
> Amino acids can self-polymerise because every amino acid already contains both –NH<sub>2</sub> and –COOH groups in the same molecule.

The structural formulae of the two monomers are:

![Structural formulae of the two monomers: benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid and ethane-1,2-diol](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/35-polymerisation/35-1-condensation-polymerisation/assets/012-structural-formulae-of-the-two-monomers-benzene-.png)

**Extract:**

The structure of a synthetic polyester is shown below.

Draw the structural formulae of the **two** monomers used to make this polyester.

One of the monomers is benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid. State the systematic name of the other monomer.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The systematic name of the other monomer is:
> 
> - Ethane-1,2-diol **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The other monomer has two alcohol groups (–OH), one on each carbon, so it is a diol. The two-carbon chain gives the stem ethane, and the locants 1,2 show the –OH groups are on adjacent carbons.
> 
> Diols and dicarboxylic acids are the two key monomers for making polyesters by condensation polymerisation.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

One of the monomers is benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid. State the systematic name of the other monomer.

The systematic name of the other monomer is: Ethane-1,2-diol

State the name of the other product formed during the reaction between the two monomers in **(b)**.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The other product formed during the reaction is:
> 
> - Water **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Every time an ester linkage forms between a –COOH group and an –OH group, one water molecule is eliminated. This is why the reaction is called condensation polymerisation.

parts.problemMd:

Fig. 2.2 shows the structures of three molecules, **R**, **S**, and **T**.

![Three organic molecules labelled R, S, and T — R is a diamine, S and T have different functional groups](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/35-polymerisation/35-1-condensation-polymerisation/assets/013-three-organic-molecules-labelled-r-s-and-t-r-is-.png)

State which of the molecules, **R**, **S**, or **T**, reacts with benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid to form a polyamide.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The molecule that reacts with benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid to form a polyamide is:
> 
> - **R** **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**

Valylalanine, shown in Fig. 1.1, is a dipeptide.

![Structural formula of valylalanine dipeptide showing the amide bond between valine and alanine residues](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/35-polymerisation/35-1-condensation-polymerisation/assets/016-structural-formula-of-valylalanine-dipeptide-sho.png)

parts.problemMd:
Polyamides can form strong fibres suitable for weaving. Polyalkenes are generally too weak for this purpose.

Fig. 1.3 shows the structure of serine, an amino acid that forms polyamide links.

![Structural formula of serine showing the amino group, carboxylic acid group, and hydroxyl side chain](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/35-polymerisation/35-1-condensation-polymerisation/assets/020-structural-formula-of-serine-showing-the-amino-g.png)

**Fig. 1.3**

Explain why polyamides are suitable for use as weaving fibres but polyalkenes are not. In your answer, refer to the intermolecular forces between the polymer chains.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Why polyamides are suitable for weaving fibres but polyalkenes are not:
> 
> - Polyamides have hydrogen bonding between chains
> **OR**
> Polyalkenes have no hydrogen bonding between chains **[1 mark]**
> - Polyalkenes only have (weak) van der Waals forces between chains **[1 mark]**
> - Hydrogen bonds are much stronger than van der Waals forces
> **OR**
> Polyalkenes require much less energy to separate the chains **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Hydrogen bonding can form between the –C=O and –N–H groups on adjacent polyamide chains. Polyalkenes have no N, O, or F atoms, so no hydrogen bonding is possible.
> 
> The first mark is for identifying the type of force in each polymer. The second mark is for naming van der Waals forces specifically in polyalkenes. The third mark is for explicitly comparing the strengths.
> 
> Van der Waals forces are weak because they require large electron clouds or high molecular mass to become significant. Polyalkene chains can slide past each other relatively easily.

parts.problemMd: Explain how the molecule NH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COCl can undergo condensation polymerisation.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Why NH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COCl can undergo condensation polymerisation:
> 
> - The molecule contains two different functional groups: an amine (–NH<sub>2</sub>) and an acyl chloride (–COCl) **[1 mark]**
> - These two groups react with each other, forming an amide linkage and eliminating HCl **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> A molecule can self-polymerise if it contains two complementary reactive groups, one at each end. Here, the –NH<sub>2</sub> at one molecule reacts with the –COCl of the next molecule, building up the polymer chain.
> 
> Each step eliminates HCl (not water), but it is still called condensation polymerisation because a small molecule is lost each time a new bond forms.

parts.problemMd:
Polyurethanes are polymers made by the reaction of a diisocyanate with a diol, as shown in Fig. 2.1. R<sup>1</sup> and R<sup>2</sup> are hydrocarbon groups.

![General structure of a polyurethane polymer showing the urethane linkage –NH–CO–O– formed between a diisocyanate and a diol](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/35-polymerisation/35-1-condensation-polymerisation/assets/021-general-structure-of-a-polyurethane-polymer-show.png)

**Fig. 2.1**

Lycra<sup>®</sup> in Fig. 2.2 is a polyurethane formed from the diisocyanate **P** and HOCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH.

![Repeat unit of Lycra polyurethane showing the urethane linkage and the specific R groups from diisocyanate P and ethane-1,2-diol](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/35-polymerisation/35-1-condensation-polymerisation/assets/022-repeat-unit-of-lycra-polyurethane-showing-the-ur.png)

**Fig. 2.2**

i) State the molecular formula of diisocyanate **P**.

[1]

ii) Draw **one** repeat unit of Lycra<sup>®</sup>. The newly formed linkages must be shown fully displayed.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The molecular formula of diisocyanate **P** is:
> 
> - C<sub>15</sub>H<sub>10</sub>N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> To find the molecular formula of **P**, look at the Lycra repeat unit.
> 
> It shows two benzene rings connected by a –CH<sub>2</sub>– group, each bearing one –NCO group.
> 
> Count:
> 
> - 13 C from rings and bridge plus 2 from –NCO groups = 15 C total
> - 10 H (4 per disubstituted ring x2 plus 2 on –CH<sub>2</sub>–)
> - 2 N and 2 O from the two –NCO groups.

ii) One repeat unit of Lycra<sup>®</sup> is:

![Repeat unit of Lycra polyurethane showing the –NH–CO–O– urethane linkages, the diphenylmethane group from diisocyanate P, and the ethylene group from ethane-1,2-diol](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/35-polymerisation/35-1-condensation-polymerisation/assets/023-repeat-unit-of-lycra-polyurethane-showing-the-nh.png)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for for the correct –NH–CO–O– urethane linkage shown fully displayed.
> 
> 1 mark for the remainder of repeat unit correct (R<sup>1</sup> = diphenylmethane group, R<sup>2</sup> = –CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>–) with continuation bonds.

> **[exam-tip]**
> R<sup>1</sup> comes from the diisocyanate (the diphenylmethane group between the two NCO-derived N atoms), and R<sup>2</sup> comes from the diol (–CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>– from ethane-1,2-diol).
> 
> The urethane linkage –NH–CO–O– must be drawn with the N–H and C=O and C–O all explicitly shown to earn the first mark.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Lycra® in Fig. 2.2 is a polyurethane formed from the diisocyanate P and HOCH₂CH₂OH.

Polyurethanes are polymers made by the reaction of a diisocyanate with a diol, as shown in Fig. 2.1. R¹ and R² are hydrocarbon groups.

Fibres of Lycra<sup>®</sup> are strong due to the intermolecular forces between the polymer chains. Complete the table to state two types of intermolecular force responsible for this property, and the groups involved.

| **Intermolecular force** | **Group(s) involved** |
|---|---|
|   |   |
|   |   |
parts.solutionMd:
The completed table is:

| **Intermolecular force** | **Group(s) involved** |
|---|---|
| Hydrogen bonding | –NH |
| Van der Waals forces / induced dipole–dipole forces | –C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>4</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>– / benzene rings |

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for hydrogen bonding **AND** –NH group correctly identified.
> 
> 1 mark for van der Waals forces (accept induced dipole–dipole / London dispersion) **AND** –C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>4</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>– or benzene/aromatic rings correctly identified.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Hydrogen bonding occurs between the H on the –NH group of one chain and the lone pair on the C=O of an adjacent chain. Both the force and the group must be correct for the mark.
> 
> The –C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>4</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>– section contains only C and H, so no polar bonds, making the strongest force here van der Waals. Large aromatic groups produce relatively strong van der Waals forces.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Examples of commercially important synthetic polymers:
> 
> - Synthetic polyamide: Nylon / Kevlar / Nomex **[1 mark]**
> - Synthetic polyester: Terylene / PET / polylactic acid (PLA) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> You should be able to recall at least one commercial example of each type from your A level studies. Nylon (polyamide) and Terylene (polyester) are the most commonly cited.

parts.problemMd:
Fig. 2.3 shows the repeat unit of Nylon 66.

![Repeat unit of Nylon 66 polyamide showing the amide linkage between the hexamethylenediamine and adipic acid derived segments](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/35-polymerisation/35-1-condensation-polymerisation/assets/024-repeat-unit-of-nylon-66-polyamide-showing-the-am.png)

**Fig. 2.3**

Nylon 66 is heated under reflux with dilute sulfuric acid.

Draw the skeletal formulae of the **two** organic products formed.
parts.solutionMd:
The two organic products formed from the acid hydrolysis of Nylon 66 are:

![Skeletal formulae of the two hydrolysis products: the protonated hexamethylenediamine salt with two –NH~3~^+^ groups, and adipic acid (hexanedioic acid) with two –COOH groups](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/35-polymerisation/35-1-condensation-polymerisation/assets/025-skeletal-formulae-of-the-two-hydrolysis-products.jpeg)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct skeletal formula of the diamine product with both –NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup> groups (protonated under acidic conditions).
> 
> 1 mark for correct skeletal formula of hexanedioic acid (adipic acid) with both –COOH groups.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Under acidic conditions (dilute H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>, heated under reflux), the amide bonds are hydrolysed. Each –CO–NH– bond breaks to give a –COOH group and a –NH<sub>2</sub> group. In acidic solution the amine is immediately protonated to –NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup>.
> 
> The two products are: (1) the protonated diamine (hexane-1,6-diamine with both ends as –NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup>) and (2) hexanedioic acid (adipic acid, HOOC(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>4</sub>COOH).
> 
> If alkaline hydrolysis (NaOH) were used instead, the products would be different: the diamine would be neutral (–NH<sub>2</sub>) and the diacid would be deprotonated (carboxylate salt, –COO<sup>-</sup>Na<sup>+</sup>).

parts.problemMd: Explain how ethane-1,2-diamine acts as a Brønsted–Lowry base.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> How ethane-1,2-diamine acts as a Brønsted–Lowry base:
> 
> - The nitrogen atoms have lone pairs of electrons
> **AND**
> Which can accept a proton (H<sup>+</sup>) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> A Brønsted–Lowry base is any species that accepts a proton. Ethane-1,2-diamine has two nitrogen atoms, each with a lone pair. Either lone pair can accept H<sup>+</sup> from an acid.
> 
> Both conditions are needed for the mark: the lone pair must be identified and the proton acceptance stated.

parts.problemMd: Construct an equation to show the reaction of ethane-1,2-diamine with an excess of hydrochloric acid.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The equation for the reaction of ethane-1,2-diamine with excess hydrochloric acid is:
> 
> - H<sub>2</sub>NCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> + 2HCl → ClH<sub>3</sub>NCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>3</sub>Cl
> **OR**
> C<sub>2</sub>N<sub>2</sub>H<sub>8</sub> + 2HCl → C<sub>2</sub>N<sub>2</sub>H<sub>10</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> With excess HCl, both –NH<sub>2</sub> groups are protonated. Each nitrogen accepts one H<sup>+</sup> from HCl, forming the dihydrochloride salt. Make sure you use 2HCl to show both groups react.
> 
> The product has the formula C<sub>2</sub>N<sub>2</sub>H<sub>10</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>. The original H<sub>8</sub> gains two extra H atoms (one per NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup>), and two Cl<sup>-</sup> ions balance the charge.

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct amide bond (–CO–NH–) shown fully displayed.
> 
> 1 mark for correct overall structure with exactly two repeat units and continuation bonds at both ends.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Ethanedioic acid (HOOCCOOH) provides a very short two-carbon diacid. The repeat unit has no carbon atoms between the two amide links on the acid side. Draw the –CO–NH– linkage with N–H explicitly shown.

parts.problemMd:
Fig. 1.1 shows a general dicarboxylic acid and a general diol.

**Fig. 1.1**

Draw **one** repeat unit of the polyester formed from these monomers. The newly formed linkage must be shown fully displayed.
parts.solutionMd:
The repeat unit of the polyester is:

![Repeat unit of the general polyester formed from a dicarboxylic acid and a diol, showing the ester linkage –CO–O– and continuation bonds](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/35-polymerisation/35-1-condensation-polymerisation/assets/009-repeat-unit-of-the-general-polyester-formed-from.png)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct ester linkage (–CO–O–) shown fully displayed.
>

> The ester linkage –CO–O– forms when the –COOH of the diacid reacts with one –OH of the diol. Draw both the C=O and the C–O–C explicitly.

parts.problemMd: In terms of *n*, state the number of molecules of water formed in the condensation polymerisation of *n* molecules of a dicarboxylic acid and *n* molecules of a diol.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> In terms of *n*, the number of molecules of water formed is:
> 
> - 2*n* − 1 **[1 mark]**
> 
> Allow 2*n* (if candidate treats the polymer as having no free end groups).

> **[exam-tip]**
> Try small values to find the pattern:
> 
> - For *n* = 1 (one acid + one diol): one ester bond forms, releasing 1 water
> - For *n* = 2: three ester bonds form, releasing 3 water molecules
> - For *n* = 3: five water molecules. The pattern is 2*n* − 1.
> 
> The 2*n* answer arises if you assume a fully cyclic or infinite-chain polymer where both ends have also reacted. Both answers can be credited.

parts.problemMd: Construct an equation for the condensation polymerisation of propanedioyl dichloride and butane-1,4-diol. Your equation should use structural formulae for the monomers and the repeat unit.
parts.solutionMd:
The equation for the condensation polymerisation is:

![Equation for the condensation polymerisation of propanedioyl dichloride and butane-1,4-diol, showing the structural formulae of both monomers (each with stoichiometry n), the polyester repeat unit in square brackets with n, and (2n−1) HCl as by-product](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/35-polymerisation/35-1-condensation-polymerisation/assets/010-equation-for-the-condensation-polymerisation-of-.png)

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct structural formulae of both monomers with stoichiometry *n*.
> 
> 1 mark for correct structural formula of the repeat unit in square brackets with *n*.
> 
> 1 mark for (2*n* − 1) HCl as the by-product.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Propanedioyl dichloride has the structure ClCO–CH<sub>2</sub>–COCl, a three-carbon chain with an acyl chloride (–COCl) group at each end. Draw it as a structural formula showing all bonds in the functional groups.
> 
> Butane-1,4-diol is HO–CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>–OH: four carbons with –OH at each end.
> 
> Each –COCl + –OH reaction forms one ester linkage and releases one HCl. For *n* of each monomer, (2*n* − 1) HCl molecules are eliminated overall.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Construct an equation for the condensation polymerisation of propanedioyl dichloride and butane-1,4-diol. Your equation should use structural formulae for the monomers and the repeat unit.

Propanedioyl dichloride has the structure ClCO–CH~2~–COCl, a three-carbon chain with an acyl chloride (–COCl) group at each end.

Butane-1,4-diol is HO–CH~2~CH~2~CH~2~CH~2~–OH: four carbons with –OH at each end.

State the systematic names of an alternative pair of monomers that could be used to produce the same polymer chain as in **(c)**.

Monomer 1 ..................................................................................................

Monomer 2 ..................................................................................................
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> An alternative pair of monomers that could produce the same polymer chain is:
> 
> - Monomer 1: propanedioic acid / malonic acid **[1 mark]**
> - Monomer 2: butane-1,4-diol **[1 mark]**
> 
> Monomers can be in either order

> **[exam-tip]**
> The polymer from part **(c)** has ester linkages from a three-carbon diacid and a four-carbon diol. Propanedioyl dichloride (an acyl chloride) can be replaced by propanedioic acid, which forms the same ester linkage via condensation with the –OH group.

> You cannot simply swap the diacid and diol (e.g. butanedioyl dichloride + propane-1,3-diol) as that produces a different polymer with a different repeat unit length.

parts.problemMd:
Lactic acid has the structural formula CH<sub>3</sub>CHOHCOOH.

i) State the names of the **two** functional groups present in lactic acid.

[1]

ii) State the systematic name of lactic acid.

[1]

iii) State the type of stereoisomerism shown by lactic acid.

[1]

iv) Draw three-dimensional structures for the two stereoisomers of lactic acid.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The two functional groups present in lactic acid are:
> 
> - Alcohol / hydroxyl
> **AND**
> Carboxylic acid / carboxyl **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The systematic name of lactic acid is:
> 
> - 2-hydroxypropanoic acid **[1 mark]**
> 
> iii) The type of stereoisomerism shown by lactic acid is:
> 
> - Optical (isomerism) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For part i): both groups must be named for the mark, either systematic (hydroxyl / carboxyl) or common names (–OH group / carboxylic acid group) are accepted.
> 
> For part ii): work from the structural formula. 3 carbons (prop-), a carboxylic acid at C1 (-oic acid), and an –OH at C2 (2-hydroxy-) gives 2-hydroxypropanoic acid.
> 
> For part iii): optical isomerism arises because C2 is a chiral centre. It has four different groups attached: –CH<sub>3</sub>, –H, –OH, and –COOH.

iv) The three-dimensional structures of the two stereoisomers of lactic acid are:

![Two three-dimensional wedge-and-dash structures of the optical isomers of lactic acid, showing the chiral carbon centre with four different groups arranged as non-superimposable mirror images](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/35-polymerisation/35-1-condensation-polymerisation/assets/001-two-three-dimensional-wedge-and-dash-structures-.png)

**[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Nomex® and Kevlar® are two examples of polyamides containing benzene rings. Nomex® is made from 1,3-diaminobenzene and benzene-1,3-dicarboxylic acid.

parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The polymer with the higher melting point is:
> 
> - Kevlar<sup>®</sup> **[1 mark]**
> 
> Explanation:
> 
> - The 1,4-substitution in Kevlar creates straight, linear polymer chains, so adjacent chains can pack more closely together. The 1,3-substitution in Nomex creates a kinked chain, so chains pack less closely.
> **AND**
> Closer packing makes the hydrogen bonds between chains more effective / stronger, requiring more energy to separate the chains **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The key difference between Kevlar and Nomex is the substitution pattern: Kevlar uses 1,4-substitution (para), giving a straight chain; Nomex uses 1,3-substitution (meta), giving a kinked chain.
> 
> You can also give the reverse argument: Nomex has the lower melting point because its kinked chains pack less closely, giving weaker and fewer hydrogen bonds between chains.
> 
> Both marks require you to link chain shape to packing to intermolecular force strength to melting point. Simply stating "Kevlar is straighter" without explaining why that affects the melting point is not sufficient for the second mark.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Glycine and serine are amino acids with the systematic names 2-aminoethanoic acid and 2-amino-3-hydroxypropanoic acid respectively.

Glycine and serine can react to form condensation polymers containing ester and amide linkages.

State the names of the functional groups that react to form:

i) an ester linkage

[1]

ii) an amide linkage

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The functional groups that react to form an ester linkage are:
> 
> - Hydroxyl / –OH
> **AND**
> carboxylic acid / –COOH **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The functional groups that react to form an amide linkage are:
> 
> - Amine / amino / –NH₂
> **AND**
> carboxylic acid / –COOH **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> An ester linkage forms from a reaction between a hydroxyl group (–OH) and a carboxylic acid group (–COOH). Only serine has a hydroxyl group, so ester formation requires at least one serine monomer.
> 
> An amide linkage forms from a reaction between an amine group (–NH<sub>2</sub>) and a carboxylic acid group (–COOH). Both glycine and serine have these groups, so amide linkages can form between any combination of the two amino acids.

parts.problemMd: State what is meant by the term *hydrolysis*.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The meaning of the term hydrolysis is:
> 
> - The breakdown of a compound by reaction with water **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The word *hydrolysis* comes from the Greek roots *hydro* (water) and *lysis* (breaking apart). Remembering this helps you recall the definition without memorising it word for word.

parts.problemMd: State the reagents and conditions required for the acid hydrolysis of a polyamide.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The reagents and conditions for the acid hydrolysis of a polyamide are:
> 
> - Dilute acid (dilute HCl / dilute H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>) **[1 mark]**
> - Heat under reflux **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Acid hydrolysis of a polyamide requires H<sup>+</sup> ions as a catalyst and heat under reflux to supply enough energy to break the amide bonds. Without the acid catalyst, hydrolysis is extremely slow at any practical temperature.

Explain why clothing made from nylon is easily damaged by spillages of strong acids or strong alkalis.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The reason why nylon clothing is easily damaged by strong acids and alkalis:
> 
> - The amide linkages in nylon can be hydrolysed by strong acids and strong alkalis **[1 mark]**
> - Hydrolysis breaks the polymer chains, destroying the structural integrity of the fabric / creating holes in the fabric **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Nylon is a polyamide, which means it contains amide bonds (–CO–NH–). Strong acids and alkalis catalyse the hydrolysis of these bonds, breaking the long polymer chains into shorter fragments. Once the polymer chains are broken, the fabric loses its structural integrity.
> 
> This is why polyamide fabrics and equipment should be kept away from corrosive chemicals in the laboratory.

**Fig. 1.2**

Explain why Nomex has a higher melting point than nylon.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The reason why Nomex has a higher melting point than nylon:
> 
> - The benzene rings make the Nomex chains more rigid and planar, allowing the chains to pack together more closely **[1 mark]**
> - This results in stronger intermolecular forces (van der Waals' forces / hydrogen bonding) between chains, requiring more energy to overcome **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Melting point depends on the strength of intermolecular forces between polymer chains. The more closely chains can pack, the stronger the forces between them.
> 
> Nylon has a flexible aliphatic backbone, while Nomex contains rigid, planar benzene rings. The planar rings allow Nomex chains to pack together more tightly than the flexible chains in nylon, creating stronger van der Waals' forces and more hydrogen bonding between chains.

parts.problemMd:
Table 1.1 shows the structural formulae of three amino acids.

**Table 1.1**

| **Amino Acid** | **Structural formula** |
|---|---|
| **T** | CH<sub>3</sub>CH(NH<sub>2</sub>)CO<sub>2</sub>H |
| **U** | C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH(NH<sub>2</sub>)CO<sub>2</sub>H |
| **V** | H<sub>2</sub>N(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>4</sub>CH(NH<sub>2</sub>)CO<sub>2</sub>H |

State which of the amino acids, **T**, **U** or **V**, has the highest pH in an aqueous solution, and explain your answer.

amino acid ......................................................

explanation ......................................................
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The amino acid with the highest pH in aqueous solution:
> 
> - Amino acid V **[1 mark]**
> - It has two amine / NH<sub>2</sub> groups (which can be protonated) **OR** it has an additional amine / NH<sub>2</sub> group on its side chain / R group (compared to T and U) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> A higher pH means a more basic solution. Amino acids are amphoteric, but if the amine group count exceeds the carboxylic acid count, the amino acid produces a more basic solution.
> 
> Amino acid V has two –NH<sub>2</sub> groups and one –COOH group, giving it a greater capacity to accept protons than T or U (which each have one –NH<sub>2</sub> and one –COOH group). More proton acceptance means a higher pH.

parts.problemMd: State how many different dipeptides could be formed from a reaction mixture consisting of amino acids **T** and **U**.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The number of different dipeptides that could be formed from amino acids T and U:
> 
> - 4 / four **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> A dipeptide contains two amino acid residues. The four possibilities when two different amino acids (T and U) are present are:
> 
> - T–T
> - U–U
> - T–U
> - U–T
> 
> Note that T–U and U–T are different dipeptides because the amino acid at the N-terminus differs. Students often forget the self-combinations (T–T and U–U) or forget that order matters.

parts.problemMd: Despite containing a high proportion of carbon and hydrogen atoms, many polypeptides are soluble in water. Explain why. In your answer, you should refer to the functional groups present in a polypeptide chain.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The reason why polypeptides are soluble in water despite their high C and H content:
> 
> - Hydrogen bonds form between the polar N–H and C=O groups (peptide bonds) in the polypeptide chain and water molecules **[1 mark]**
> - This allows the polypeptide to interact with and dissolve in water **[1 mark]**
> 
> Allow ion-dipole attractions between the NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup> and CO<sub>2</sub><sup>–</sup> end groups of the zwitterion and polar water molecules for the first marking point

> **[exam-tip]**
> Although the majority of a polypeptide chain is made up of C–C and C–H bonds (which are non-polar), the peptide bonds (–CO–NH–) contain polar C=O and N–H groups. These groups can form hydrogen bonds with water.
> 
> In addition, amino acids exist as zwitterions at physiological pH, with NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup> and CO<sub>2</sub><sup>–</sup> end groups. These charged groups form strong ion-dipole interactions with water molecules, further aiding solubility.

parts.problemMd:
One of the steps in the manufacture of ibuprofen is shown in Fig. 1.2.

![Reaction scheme showing the Friedel-Crafts acylation step in ibuprofen synthesis from compound X to compound Y](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/36-organic-synthesis/36-1-organic-synthesis/assets/041-reaction-scheme-showing-the-friedel-crafts-acyla.png)

**Fig. 1.2**

i) Write an equation to show how AlCl<sub>3</sub> generates the electrophile for the conversion of **X** into **Y**.

[1]

ii) Draw the mechanism for the conversion of **X** into **Y**. Include all necessary curly arrows and charges.

[3]

iii) Write an equation to show how the AlCl<sub>3</sub> is regenerated.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The equation to show how AlCl<sub>3</sub> generates the electrophile:
> 
> - CH<sub>3</sub>COCl + AlCl<sub>3</sub> → CH<sub>3</sub>CO<sup>+</sup> + AlCl<sub>4</sub><sup>-</sup> **[1 mark]**

ii) The mechanism for the conversion of **X** into **Y** is:

![Curly arrow mechanism for Friedel-Crafts acylation of compound X producing compound Y](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/36-organic-synthesis/36-1-organic-synthesis/assets/042-curly-arrow-mechanism-for-friedel-crafts-acylati.png)

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for a curly arrow from the ring system to the positively charged carbon of CH<sub>3</sub>CO<sup>+</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for the correct intermediate structure with a positive charge shown
> 
> 1 mark for a curly arrow from the C–H bond into the ring AND loss of H<sup>+</sup>

> **[mark-scheme]**
> iii) The equation to show how AlCl<sub>3</sub> is regenerated:
> 
> - H<sup>+</sup> + AlCl<sub>4</sub><sup>-</sup> → HCl + AlCl<sub>3</sub> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> You need to know how AlCl<sub>3</sub> acts as a catalyst to form the positive ion required for the reaction, including the equations to form the electrophile and to reform the AlCl<sub>3</sub> catalyst.
> 
> For the mechanism (ii):
> 
> - The curly arrows must start from inside the delocalised ring and point to the bond being formed
> - The intermediate must show a positive charge
> - The bond forms between the carbon of the ring and the carbonyl carbon of CH<sub>3</sub>CO<sup>+</sup> — the arrow must point to the carbon, not the oxygen
> - The origin and destination of curly arrows must be clear and unambiguous
> - Mechanisms are a good way to pick up marks, so it is worth practising them

parts.problemMd:
Cuminyl alcohol can be synthesised from benzene by the following route shown in Fig. 2.1.

![Synthesis route for cuminyl alcohol from benzene via Friedel-Crafts alkylation, Friedel-Crafts acylation, iodoform reaction, and LiAlH4 reduction](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/36-organic-synthesis/36-1-organic-synthesis/assets/021-synthesis-route-for-cuminyl-alcohol-from-benzene.png)

**Fig. 2.1**

Suggest reagents and conditions for steps 1–4.

step 1 ...................................................

step 2 ...................................................

step 3 ...................................................

step 4 ...................................................
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The reagents and conditions for each step are:
> 
> - Step 1: (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CHCl and AlCl<sub>3</sub> / CH<sub>3</sub>CH=CH<sub>2</sub> and AlCl<sub>3</sub> / heat **[1 mark]**
> - Step 2: CH<sub>3</sub>COCl and AlCl<sub>3</sub> / heat **[1 mark]**
> - Step 3: NaOH and I<sub>2</sub> / Cl<sub>2</sub> / Br<sub>2</sub>, then H<sup>+</sup> **[1 mark]**
> - Step 4: LiAlH<sub>4</sub> in dry ether **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Steps 1 and 2 both involve Friedel-Crafts electrophilic substitution of the benzene ring.
> 
> Step 1 adds an isopropyl group (alkylation). A halogen carrier catalyst such as AlCl<sub>3</sub> is needed to generate the carbocation electrophile:
> 
> AlCl<sub>3</sub> + (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CHCl → AlCl<sub>4</sub><sup>-</sup> + (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CH<sup>+</sup>
> 
> Step 2 adds an acyl group (acylation). An acyl chloride and halogen carrier are required:
> 
> AlCl<sub>3</sub> + CH<sub>3</sub>COCl → AlCl<sub>4</sub><sup>-</sup> + CH<sub>3</sub>CO<sup>+</sup>
> 
> Step 3 converts the methyl ketone to a carboxylic acid via the haloform (iodoform) reaction:
> 
> R-CO-CH<sub>3</sub> + 3I<sub>2</sub> + 4OH<sup>-</sup> → CHI<sub>3</sub> + RCOO<sup>-</sup> + 3I<sup>-</sup> + 3H<sub>2</sub>O
> 
> The carboxylate RCOO<sup>-</sup> is then acidified with H<sup>+</sup> to give RCOOH.
> 
> Step 4 uses LiAlH<sub>4</sub> in dry ether to reduce the carboxylic acid to a primary alcohol.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Cuminyl alcohol can be synthesised from benzene by the following route shown in Fig. 2.1.

Step 2: CH3COCl and AlCl3 / heat

Step 2 adds an acyl group (acylation). An acyl chloride and halogen carrier are required:

AlCl3 + CH3COCl → AlCl4^-^ + CH3CO^+^

Draw the reaction mechanism for step 2.
parts.solutionMd:
The reaction mechanism for step 2 is:

![Curly arrow mechanism for Friedel-Crafts acylation electrophilic substitution showing arenium intermediate and loss of H+](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/36-organic-synthesis/36-1-organic-synthesis/assets/022-curly-arrow-mechanism-for-friedel-crafts-acylati.jpeg)

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for a curly arrow from the ring system to the positively charged carbon of CH<sub>3</sub>CO<sup>+</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for the correct arenium intermediate structure with a positive charge, the horseshoe covering more than half the ring but not extending past carbons 2 and 6
> 
> 1 mark for a curly arrow from the C–H bond back into the ring
> 
> 1 mark for the correct benzene product AND H<sup>+</sup> shown
> 
> The origin and destination of curly arrows must be clear and unambiguous, or the marks are not awarded.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Common mistakes in benzene electrophilic substitution mechanisms:
> 
> - Not drawing the hydrogen that is being substituted
> - Drawing the substituted hydrogen in the wrong position
> - Forgetting to place the positive charge in the correct position on the intermediate
> - Drawing the ring inside the intermediate structure incorrectly
> 
> The general mechanism: the electrophile attacks the pi system of benzene, forming a positively charged arenium (carbocation) intermediate. A curly arrow then shows the C–H bond electrons returning to restore aromaticity, releasing H<sup>+</sup>.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Cuminyl alcohol can be synthesised from benzene by the following route shown in Fig. 2.1.

Deduce the number of peaks that would be present in the <sup>13</sup>C NMR spectrum of cuminyl alcohol.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The number of <sup>13</sup>C NMR peaks in cuminyl alcohol is:
> 
> - 7 peaks **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Look for symmetry within the molecule to identify equivalent carbon environments, as these give only one peak between them.
> 
> Cuminyl alcohol (4-isopropylbenzyl alcohol) has 7 distinct carbon environments:
> 
> - C1: ring carbon bearing the CH<sub>2</sub>OH group
> - C2 and C6: equivalent ring carbons (ortho to CH<sub>2</sub>OH, meta to isopropyl)
> - C3 and C5: equivalent ring carbons (ortho to isopropyl)
> - C4: ring carbon bearing the isopropyl group
> - CH<sub>2</sub>: the methylene carbon of CH<sub>2</sub>OH
> - CH: the methine carbon of the isopropyl group
> - CH<sub>3</sub>: both methyl groups of the isopropyl group are equivalent

> **[mark-scheme]**
> The synthesis of ethanal from ethane:
> 
> i) Step 1: Ethane → chloroethane
> 
> - Reagent: Cl<sub>2</sub> / chlorine **[1 mark]**
> - Conditions: UV light / high temperature **[1 mark]**
> - Reaction type: free radical substitution / halogenation **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) Step 2: Chloroethane → ethanol
> 
> - Reagent: aqueous NaOH / NaOH(aq) / aqueous KOH / KOH(aq) **[1 mark]**
> - Conditions: heat under reflux **[1 mark]**
> - Reaction type: nucleophilic substitution / hydrolysis **[1 mark]**
> 
> iii) Step 3: Ethanol → ethanal
> 
> - Reagent: acidified potassium dichromate(VI) / K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub>
> **OR**
> Acidified potassium manganate(VII) / KMnO<sub>4</sub> **[1 mark]**
> - Conditions: distillation **[1 mark]**
> - Reaction type: oxidation **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The conversion of an alkane to a haloalkane is hard to control industrially, as it is difficult to prevent multiple products from forming. It is included here to test your ability to apply knowledge of organic reactions to synthesis problems.
> 
> The mechanism types are shown in brackets in the mark scheme but are not essential for the mark.
> 
> The dichromate ion, Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub><sup>2-</sup>, is the oxidising species, so sodium dichromate(VI) is also an acceptable reagent for step 3.

parts.problemMd:
The following reaction pathway in Fig. 3.1 is used to produce compounds **A** and **B**, which when reacted together, form a branched ester molecule, compound **C**.

Suggest suitable reagents and conditions for the synthesis of compound **A** via step 1 and give the name for this type of reaction.

![Reaction pathway showing oxidation of an aldehyde to carboxylic acid (compound A) via step 1, and reduction of a ketone to secondary alcohol (compound B) via step 2, followed by esterification to form compound C](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/36-organic-synthesis/36-1-organic-synthesis/assets/028-reaction-pathway-showing-oxidation-of-an-aldehyd.png)

**Fig. 3.1**
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Suitable reagents and conditions for the synthesis of compound **A** via step 1:
> 
> - K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> / potassium dichromate(VI)
> **OR**
> KMnO<sub>4</sub> / potassium manganate(VII) **[1 mark]**
> - H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> / acidified / with acid **[1 mark]**
> - Oxidation **[1 mark]**
> 
> Sodium dichromate(VI) is also accepted for the first marking point.
> 
> Ions such as Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub><sup>2-</sup> are not accepted as a reagent must be something that can be found on a laboratory shelf.

> **[exam-tip]**
> An ester is commonly made from a carboxylic acid and an alcohol.
> 
> A carboxylic acid cannot be produced from a ketone, so compound **A** must come from the oxidation of an aldehyde.
> 
> The question asks for the names of reagents, not ions. Writing Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub><sup>2-</sup> alone would not score the mark.

> 
> 1 mark for correct dibrominated product structure from Br<sub>2</sub> (aq)
> 
> 1 mark for electrophilic substitution as the reaction type for Br<sub>2</sub> (aq)

>

> 
> 1 mark for oxidation as the reaction type for I<sub>2</sub> / NaOH (aq)

> **[exam-tip]**
> Na (s) reacts with the phenolic -OH group, breaking the O–H bond to form the phenoxide -O<sup>-</sup>Na<sup>+</sup>.
> 
> Bromine water reacts with the phenol group via electrophilic substitution. The -OH group is 2,4,6-directing; however, position 4 is occupied by the ketone side chain, so bromine substitutes at positions 2 and 6.
> 
> I<sub>2</sub> / NaOH (aq) is used in the iodoform reaction. The methyl ketone group reacts: first, all three H-atoms on the CH<sub>3</sub> group are replaced by iodine to form a -CI<sub>3</sub> group; the alkaline solution then hydrolyses this intermediate to give the carboxylate salt (-COONa) and yellow CHI<sub>3</sub> precipitate. Under alkaline conditions, the phenol is simultaneously deprotonated to give the phenoxide (-ONa). Both groups must be shown in the product structure.

ii) The mechanism for step 1 is:

![Curly arrow mechanism for Friedel-Crafts alkylation of benzene with bromomethane electrophile showing arenium intermediate and loss of H+](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/36-organic-synthesis/36-1-organic-synthesis/assets/044-curly-arrow-mechanism-for-friedel-crafts-alkylat.png)

The correct structure of compound A (methylbenzene)

Concentrated sulphuric acid and concentrated nitric acid are used to form the ion required for step 2.

The following equilibrium is the first step in the formation of the ion:

H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> + HNO<sub>3</sub> ⇋ HSO<sub>4</sub><sup>-</sup> + H<sub>2</sub>NO<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup>

i) State the roles of each acid in this reaction.

[2]

ii) Use your answer to part **(i)** to suggest the relative strengths of the acids.

[1]

iii) Different isomers with the molecular formula C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>7</sub>NO<sub>2</sub> can be formed during step 2.

Draw the structure of the isomer **B**. Explain your answer.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The roles of each acid in this reaction:
> 
> - Sulfuric acid acts as a Brønsted–Lowry acid
> **AND**
> It donates a proton / H<sup>+</sup> to nitric acid **[1 mark]**
> 
> - Nitric acid acts as a Brønsted–Lowry base
> **AND**
> It accepts a proton / H<sup>+</sup> from sulfuric acid **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The relative strengths of the acids:
> 
> - Sulfuric acid is stronger than nitric acid (as it donates a proton to nitric acid)
> **OR**
> Nitric acid is weaker than sulfuric acid (as it accepts a proton from sulfuric acid) **[1 mark]**

iii) The structure of isomer **B** is:

![Skeletal structure of 4-nitromethylbenzene (compound B, p-nitrotoluene)](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/36-organic-synthesis/36-1-organic-synthesis/assets/045-skeletal-structure-of-4-nitromethylbenzene-compo.png)

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for the correct structure of isomer **B**
> 
> Explanation
> 
> - The methyl / CH<sub>3</sub> group on methylbenzene activates positions 2, 4 and 6 on the ring
> **AND**
> The nitro / NO<sub>2</sub> group must attach to carbon-4 to form the product of step 3 **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The reversible arrow in the equilibrium is not directly relevant to answering part (i). So, focus on which species loses and which gains a proton.
> 
> The overall equation for nitronium ion formation is:
> 
> HNO<sub>3</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> → NO<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> + 2HSO<sub>4</sub><sup>-</sup> + H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>
>

parts.solutionMd:

> The reagents and conditions for steps 3 to 5 of the synthesis are:
> 
> Step 3:
> 
> - Hot alkaline KMnO<sub>4</sub> / potassium manganate(VII), heat under reflux, then dilute acid / dilute H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> / H<sup>+</sup> **[1 mark]**
>
