parts.problemMd:
A chemist prepares and analyses some esters.

The chemist prepares an ester by reacting propan-2-ol with ethanoic anhydride.

Using structural formulae, construct an equation for the reaction of propan-2-ol with ethanoic anhydride.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The equation, using structural formulae:
> 
> - (CH<sub>3</sub>CO)<sub>2</sub>O + CH<sub>3</sub>CH(OH)CH<sub>3</sub> → CH<sub>3</sub>COOCH(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> + CH<sub>3</sub>COOH **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The reaction of an alcohol with an acid anhydride produces an ester and the corresponding carboxylic acid, not water. The most common mistake is writing water as the second product by analogy with esterification using a carboxylic acid.
> 
> Take care with the structural formulae: isopropyl ethanoate (CH<sub>3</sub>COOCH(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>) and ethanoic acid (CH<sub>3</sub>COOH) must both be written correctly.

parts.problemMd:
A sample contains a mixture of two esters contaminated with an alkane and an alcohol.

The chemist attempts to separate the four organic compounds in the mixture using gas chromatography. The stationary phase in the gas chromatograph column is a liquid alkane.

i) Explain how a liquid stationary phase separates organic compounds in a mixture.

[1]

ii) Deduce the relative retention times of these four compounds using the alkane stationary phase. Explain your answer.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) A liquid stationary phase separates organic compounds by:
> 
> - Their relative solubility in the stationary phase **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) Deducing relative retention times:
> 
> - Both esters have the same functional groups
> **AND**
> they will have similar retention times **[1 mark]**
> - The alcohol is not soluble in the non-polar alkane stationary phase leading to a short retention time
> **AND**
> the alkane contaminant is highly soluble in the alkane stationary phase leading to a long retention time **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Separation in GC depends on the relative solubility of compounds in the mobile and stationary phases.
> 
> - Non-polar compounds (e.g. alkanes) are strongly attracted to a non-polar (alkane) stationary phase → longer retention times
> - Polar compounds (e.g. alcohols) are weakly attracted to a non-polar stationary phase → shorter retention times
> - Esters are polar but less so than alcohols; the two esters have the same functional groups so similar solubility → similar retention times
> 
> Without further information you can only state that the two esters will have similar (not identical) retention times.

parts.problemMd:
An ester is isolated from a perfume and analysed.

The percentage by mass of the ester is: carbon 66.63%, hydrogen 11.18% and oxygen 22.19%.

The mass spectrum and proton (<sup>1</sup>H) NMR spectrum of the ester are shown in Fig. 2.1 and Fig. 2.2 respectively.

![Mass spectrum of ester isolated from perfume](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/37-analytical-techniques/37-4-proton-1h-nmr-spectroscopy/assets/018-mass-spectrum-of-ester-isolated-from-perfume.png)

**Fig. 2.1**

![Proton NMR spectrum of ester isolated from perfume](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/37-analytical-techniques/37-4-proton-1h-nmr-spectroscopy/assets/019-proton-nmr-spectrum-of-ester-isolated-from-perfu.png)

**Fig. 2.2**

i) Calculate the molecular formula of the ester. Show your working.

[3]

ii) Use Fig. 2.1, Fig. 2.2 and the Data Booklet to deduce the skeletal formula of the ester. Explain your reasoning.

[5]
parts.solutionMd:
i) To calculate the molecular formula of the ester:

- Divide each percentage by the relative atomic mass to find the molar ratio:

C = $\frac{66.63}{12.0}$ = 5.55

H = $\frac{11.18}{1.0}$ = 11.18

O = $\frac{22.19}{16.0}$ = 1.39

**[1 mark]**

- Divide by the smallest value (1.39) to find the empirical formula:

C = $\frac{5.55}{1.39}$ = 4

H = $\frac{11.18}{1.39}$ = 8

O = $\frac{1.39}{1.39}$ = 1

- So, the empirical formula:

C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O

**[1 mark]**

- Calculate *M*<sub>r</sub> of the empirical unit:

*M*<sub>r</sub> of C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O = (4 x 12.0) + (8 x 1.0) + 16.0

*M*<sub>r</sub> of C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O = 72.0

- Confirm using the M<sup>+</sup> peak in Fig. 2.1:

m/e = 144

144 = 72.0 x 2

molecular formula = **C**<sub>**8**</sub>**H**<sub>**16**</sub>**O**<sub>**2**</sub>

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for the correct molar ratio of C (5.55) **AND** H (11.18) **AND** O (1.39)
> 
> 1 mark for the correct empirical formula of C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O
> 
> 1 mark for identifying the peak at m/e = 144 **AND** a correct molecular formula of C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>16</sub>O<sub>2</sub>

ii) To deduce the skeletal formula of the ester:

- δ 3.8 ppm: –O–CH<sub>2</sub>– (2H, quartet; adjacent CH<sub>3</sub> gives n = 3, n + 1 = 4)
- δ 2.2 ppm: –CH<sub>2</sub>–C=O (2H, singlet; adjacent quaternary carbon bears no H atoms)
- δ 1.3 ppm: –O–CH<sub>2</sub>–CH<sub>3</sub> (3H, triplet; adjacent CH<sub>2</sub> gives n = 2, n + 1 = 3)
- δ 0.9 ppm: (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>C– (9H, singlet; integration of 9 confirms three equivalent methyl groups; adjacent quaternary carbon bears no H atoms, confirming tert-butyl group)

The skeletal formula of the ester is:

![Skeletal formula of ethyl 3,3-dimethylbutanoate](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/37-analytical-techniques/37-4-proton-1h-nmr-spectroscopy/assets/020-skeletal-formula-of-ethyl-3-3-dimethylbutanoate.png)

**[5 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for identifying δ 3.8 ppm as –O–CH<sub>2</sub>–, with supporting explanation/information
> 
> 1 mark for identifying δ 2.2 ppm: –CH<sub>2</sub>–C=O, with supporting explanation/information
> 
> 1 mark for identifying δ 1.3 ppm: –O–CH<sub>2</sub>–CH<sub>3</sub>, with supporting explanation/information
> 
> 1 mark for identifying δ 0.9 ppm: (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>C–, with supporting explanation/information
> 
> 1 mark for the correct skeletal formula of ethyl 3,3-dimethylbutanoate

> **[exam-tip]**
> Work through the problem systematically:
> 
> 1. Calculate the empirical formula from % composition
> 2. Confirm the molecular formula using the M<sup>+</sup> peak at m/e = 144
> 3. Use the NMR spectrum to identify structural fragments
> 
> For the NMR fragment identification:
> 
> The peaks at δ 3.8 (quartet, 2H) and δ 1.3 (triplet, 3H) together identify an –O–CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> ethyl ester group (δ 3.2–4.0 ppm = alkyl next to electronegative atom; δ 0.9–1.7 ppm = alkyl).
> 
> The peak at δ 2.2 (singlet, 2H) identifies a –CH<sub>2</sub>– adjacent to both the ester carbonyl and a quaternary carbon (δ 2.2–3.0 ppm = alkyl next to C=O; singlet because the adjacent quaternary carbon bears no H atoms).
> 
> The peak at δ 0.9 (singlet, 9H) is the key diagnostic for the tert-butyl group. Nine equivalent protons with no adjacent H-bearing carbon means three identical CH<sub>3</sub> groups on a quaternary carbon, –C(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Compound **X** contains carbon, hydrogen and oxygen only. It has a relative molecular mass (*M*~r~) of 88.

The infra-red spectrum of **X** shows a strong absorption at 1745 cm^−1^ but no absorption between 3200 cm^−1^ and 3650 cm^−1^.

The proton (^1^H) NMR spectrum of **X** is shown in Fig 8.1

Proton NMR spectrum with a quartet at 4.1 ppm, a singlet at 2.0 ppm, and a triplet at 1.3 ppm, displayed along a delta scale from 5 to 0 ppm.

i) Using the IR data, identify the functional group present in **X**. Explain your answer.

[2]

ii) Use the proton (<sup>1</sup>H) NMR spectrum to deduce the structural formula of **X**.

Explain how you reached your conclusion by referring to the chemical shifts and splitting patterns of the peaks.

[4]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The functional group in **X** is:
> 
> - Ester / R−COO−R′ **[1 mark]**
> - Absorption at 1745 cm<sup>-1</sup> is characteristic of a C=O stretch of an ester (carboxyl C=O range: 1710–1750 cm<sup>-1</sup>); no O–H absorption (3200–3650 cm<sup>-1</sup>) confirms the absence of a carboxylic acid **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The structural formula of **X** is:
> 
> - CH<sub>3</sub>COOCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> (ethyl ethanoate) **[1 mark]**
>

> Signals around δ 4 ppm usually suggest protons adjacent to an oxygen atom, while a singlet near δ 2 ppm often indicates a methyl group adjacent to a carbonyl group.
> 
> Only refer to IR evidence if it is explicitly provided in the question.

parts.problemMd:
A different compound, **Y**, contains a halogen atom. The mass spectrum of **Y** shows two molecular ion peaks, M<sup>+</sup> and [M+2]<sup>+</sup>, of approximately equal height (1:1 ratio).

i) State the identity of the halogen present in **Y**.

[1]

ii) Explain why the M<sup>+</sup> and [M+2]<sup>+</sup> peaks appear in this ratio.

[2]

> i) The halogen present in **Y** is:
> 
> - Bromine / Br **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The M<sup>+</sup> and [M+2]<sup>+</sup> peaks appear in a 1:1 ratio because:
> 
> - Bromine exists as two isotopes, <sup>79</sup>Br and <sup>81</sup>Br **[1 mark]**

parts.problemMd: Explain why isotopes of the same element have different physical properties.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Isotopes of the same element have different physical properties because:
> 
> - Isotopes have different numbers of neutrons / different mass numbers **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Physical properties such as density, melting point, and boiling point depend on the mass of the atom. Since isotopes differ in their number of neutrons, they have different masses and therefore different physical properties.

parts.problemMd: Explain why the chemical properties of <sup>35</sup>Cl and <sup>37</sup>Cl are identical.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The chemical properties of <sup>35</sup>Cl and <sup>37</sup>Cl are identical because:
> 
> - They have the same electronic configuration / same number of electrons / same number of outer shell electrons **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Chemical properties are determined by the arrangement of electrons, particularly the outer shell electrons that take part in bonding and reactions. Since isotopes of the same element have the same atomic number, they have the same number of electrons and the same electronic configuration, giving identical chemical properties.

parts.problemMd:

parts.problemMd:
A mass spectrometer can be used to determine the isotopic abundances of an element. The mass spectrum of a sample of silicon shows that it contains three isotopes, <sup>28</sup>Si, <sup>29</sup>Si and <sup>30</sup>Si.

i) Define the term *isotope*.

[1]

ii) The isotopic abundances of the sample are shown in Table 1.2.

**Table 1.2**

| **Isotope** | **Percentage abundance / %** |
|---|---|
| <sup>28</sup>Si | 92.23 |
| <sup>29</sup>Si | 4.68 |
| <sup>30</sup>Si | 3.09 |

Calculate the relative atomic mass, *A*<sub>r</sub>, of this sample of silicon. Give your answer to two decimal places.

*A*<sub>r</sub> = ......

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) Isotopes are:
> 
> - Atoms of the same element with the same number of protons / same atomic number but different numbers of neutrons / different mass numbers **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Always include both parts of the definition — same number of protons and different numbers of neutrons. Stating only one part will not score the mark.
> 
> Do not confuse isotopes with ions: isotopes differ in neutron number, not in electron number or charge.

ii) To calculate the relative atomic mass, *A*<sub>r</sub>, of silicon:

*A*<sub>r</sub> = $\frac{(92.23\times28)+(4.68\times29)+(3.09\times30)}{100}$

*A*<sub>r</sub> = $\frac{2582.44+135.72+92.70}{100}$

*A*<sub>r</sub> = **28.11** **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for *A*<sub>r</sub> = 28.11

> **[exam-tip]**
> To calculate relative atomic mass, multiply each isotope's mass number by its percentage abundance, add the results together, then divide by 100.
> 
> The question asks for two decimal places, so round 28.1086... to 28.11.

parts.problemMd: Sodium is an element in Period 3. State and explain the trend in atomic radius across Period 3.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The trend in atomic radius across Period 3, and the reason, are:
> 
> - Decreases **[1 mark]**
> 
> Explanation:
> 
> - The atomic / proton number / nuclear charge increases **[1 mark]**
> - Shielding remains the same / similar across the period
> **OR**
> Electrons are added to the same principal quantum shell **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Across Period 3, each element has one more proton than the last, increasing the nuclear charge. The extra electrons are added to the same outer shell, so shielding stays roughly constant. The stronger nuclear pull on the same outer electrons contracts the atom, so atomic radius decreases.

parts.problemMd:
Chlorine is an element in Period 3 which has an atomic radius of 0.099 nm. The chloride ion has an ionic radius of 0.181 nm.

Explain the difference between the two radii.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The chloride ion has a larger radius than chlorine because:
> 
> - The Cl<sup>-</sup> ion has the same nuclear charge / same number of protons (17) but one more electron / more electrons (18) **[1 mark]**
> - Greater electron-electron repulsion / the outer electrons experience a reduced effective nuclear charge, causing the electron cloud to expand **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Chlorine gains one electron to form Cl<sup>-</sup>, giving it 17 protons but 18 electrons. The nuclear charge stays the same, but there is now more electron-electron repulsion in the outer shell. This repulsion pushes the electrons further from the nucleus, increasing the ionic radius compared to the atomic radius.

parts.problemMd:
Chlorine and sulfur are elements in Period 3.

Explain why the atomic radius of a chlorine atom is smaller than that of a sulfur atom.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The atomic radius of a chlorine atom is smaller than that of a sulfur atom because:
> 
> - Chlorine has a greater nuclear charge / more protons than sulfur **[1 mark]**
> - The outer electrons in both atoms occupy the same shell / shielding is similar
> **AND**
> The greater nuclear charge in chlorine draws the outer electrons closer to the nucleus **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Both sulfur and chlorine are in Period 3 and have the same number of electron shells. Chlorine has one more proton than sulfur, giving it a greater nuclear charge. Since the outer electrons in both atoms are in the same (third) shell, shielding is similar. The higher nuclear charge in chlorine therefore pulls the outer electrons closer to the nucleus, reducing the atomic radius.

parts.problemMd:
Table 4.1 below shows the atomic radii for the elements of Period 2, Li to F.

**Table 4.1**

| **Element** | **Li** | **Be** | **B** | **C** | **N** | **O** | **F** |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Atomic radius / pm** | 152 | 112 | 88 | 77 | 70 | 66 | 64 |

i) State and explain the trend in atomic radius across Period 2.

[3]

ii) Suggest why the atomic radius of neon cannot be determined in the same way as the other Period 2 elements.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The trend in atomic radius across Period 2 is:
> 
> - Atomic radius decreases (from Li to F) **[1 mark]**
> - Nuclear charge increases across Period 2
> **AND**
> Shielding is similar / constant across the period / electrons are added to the same shell **[1 mark]**
> - There is a stronger attraction between the nucleus and outer electrons **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> This is a three-point answer:
> 
> - State the trend
> - Give the cause
> - Explain why
> 
> Make sure you state that atomic radius decreases before giving the explanation, or you risk missing the first marking point.
> 
> The key phrase for the second marking point is that shielding remains roughly constant across the period because all new electrons enter the same shell (the 2nd shell).
> 
> This means the increasing nuclear charge acts more effectively on the outer electrons, pulling them closer.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii) The atomic radius of neon cannot be determined in the same way because:
> 
> - Neon does not form covalent bonds / exists as single atoms / is monoatomic **[1 mark]**
> - Atomic radius is defined as half the distance between the nuclei of two covalently bonded atoms of the same element **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The atomic radius values in the table are covalent radii, measured as half the bond length between two atoms of the same element. Since neon is a noble gas and does not form bonds, no bond length can be measured and this method cannot be applied.

parts.problemMd: Explain why the first ionisation energy of boron is lower than the first ionisation energy of beryllium.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The first ionisation energy of boron is lower than that of beryllium because:
> 
> - The outer electron of B is in the 2p subshell
> **AND**
> The outer electron of Be is in the 2s subshell **[1 mark]**
> - The 2p subshell is at higher energy / further from the nucleus / more shielded by the 2s electrons than the 2s subshell
> **AND**
> Less energy is required to remove the outer electron of B **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The key is subshell type, not electron count. Although B has more protons than Be, the extra electron is in the higher-energy 2p subshell, which is further from the nucleus and partially shielded by the 2s electrons. This makes the 2p electron easier to remove than Be's 2s electron.
> 
> The electronic configurations are:
> 
> - Be: 1s<sup>2</sup> 2s<sup>2</sup>
> - B: 1s<sup>2</sup> 2s<sup>2</sup> 2p<sup>1</sup>

mass = (6 x 1.673 × 10<sup>−27</sup>) + (6 x 1.675 × 10<sup>−27</sup>) + (6 x 9.000 × 10<sup>−31</sup>)

mass = **2.009 × 10**<sup>**−26**</sup>** kg ****[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**

>

> 
> Allow 2.010 × 10<sup>−26</sup> kg if intermediate values are rounded to 4 s.f.
> 
> 2.009 × 10<sup>−23</sup> kg is not accepted; an answer in grams must be converted to kg.

> **[exam-tip]**
> In a neutral atom, the number of electrons equals the number of protons. The carbon-12 isotope has proton number 6, so it contains 6 protons, 6 electrons, and 12 − 6 = 6 neutrons.

parts.problemMd:
A sample of carbon contains three isotopes, <sup>12</sup>C, <sup>13</sup>C and <sup>14</sup>C.

State **one** similarity and **one** difference in the properties of these isotopes of carbon. Explain your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> One similarity in the properties of the isotopes of carbon:
> 
> - (The carbon isotopes have) the same chemical properties
> **AND**
> The same electronic configuration / the same number of electrons **[1 mark]**
> 
> One difference in the properties of the isotopes of carbon:
> 
> - (The carbon isotopes have) different physical properties
> **AND**
> A different number of neutrons / different mass numbers **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Chemical properties depend on the arrangement of electrons. All three isotopes of carbon have proton number 6 and therefore the same number of electrons and electronic configuration, so they react identically.
> 
> Physical properties such as density and boiling point depend on mass. <sup>12</sup>C has 6 neutrons, <sup>13</sup>C has 7 neutrons and <sup>14</sup>C has 8 neutrons, so each has a slightly different mass and therefore slightly different physical properties.

parts.problemMd:
A sample of element **E** contains five isotopes. The percentage abundance of four of the isotopes is shown in Table 2.2.

**Table 2.2**

| **isotope of E** | **percentage abundance / %** |
|---|---|
| <sup>46</sup>E | 8.02 |
| <sup>47</sup>E | 7.31 |
| <sup>48</sup>E | 73.81 |
| <sup>49</sup>E |   |
| <sup>50</sup>E | 5.32 |

i) Calculate the percentage abundance of <sup>49</sup>E.

[1]

ii) Calculate the relative atomic mass, *A*<sub>r</sub>, of element **E**. Give your answer to one decimal place. Show your working.

[2]

iii) Identify element **E**.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
i) The percentage abundance of <sup>49</sup>E is:

100 − (8.02 + 7.31 + 73.81 + 5.32)

100 − 94.46

**5.54% ****[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> i)
> 
> 1 mark for the correct percentage abundance of <sup>49</sup>E: 5.54%

ii) To calculate the *A*<sub>r</sub> of element E:

- State the formula:

*A*<sub>r</sub> = `\frac{\sum(\text{relative isotopic mass} \times \% \text{ abundance})}{100}`

- Substitute values:

*A*<sub>r</sub> = $\frac{(8.02\times46)+(7.31\times47)+(73.81\times48)+(5.54\times49)+(5.32\times50)}{100}$ **[1 mark]**

*A*<sub>r</sub> = **47.9 ****[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii)
> 
> 1 mark for correct substitution using the value from part (i)
> 
> 1 mark for *A*<sub>r</sub> = 47.9 (to 1 d.p.)
> 
> Allow error carried forward from part (i) if the method is correct.
> 
> (0.0802 x 46) + (0.0731 x 47) + (0.7381 x 48) + (0.0554 x 49) + (0.0532 x 50) is also accepted
> 
> iii) Element **E** is:
> 
> - Titanium / Ti **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For part (i), the percentage abundances of all five isotopes must sum to 100%:
> 
> - percentage abundance of <sup>49</sup>E = 100 − (8.02 + 7.31 + 73.81 + 5.32) = 5.54%
> 
> For part (ii), you can use fractional abundances instead. Divide each percentage by 100 and sum (relative isotopic mass x fractional abundance) without dividing by 100 at the end. Both methods give the same answer.
> 
> For part (iii), find the element with *A*<sub>r</sub> closest to 47.9 on the Periodic Table. This is titanium (Ti, proton number 22).

| Li | 519 |
| **Final answer:** **Mg** | 736 |

**[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> First ionisation energy generally increases across a period and decreases down a group.
> 
> Na (Period 3, Group 1) has a lower first ionisation energy than Mg (Period 3, Group 2) because Mg has a higher nuclear charge.

parts.problemMd: Explain why the first ionisation energy of aluminium is lower than the first ionisation energy of magnesium.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The first ionisation energy of aluminium is lower than that of magnesium because:
> 
> - The outer electron in aluminium is in a 3p sub-shell / orbital, whereas in magnesium it is in a 3s sub-shell / orbital **[1 mark]**
> - The 3p sub-shell / orbital is higher in energy / further from the nucleus / more shielded than the 3s sub-shell / orbital, so less energy is required to remove the electron **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> This tests a classic anomaly in the first ionisation energy trend across Period 3.
> 
> The first mark requires you to name the specific sub-shell for each element: aluminium's outer electron is in 3p, magnesium's is in 3s.
> 
> The second mark follows from this: the 3p sub-shell is at higher energy than 3s, so less energy is needed to remove aluminium's outer electron.
> 
> The same reasoning explains the Period 2 anomaly: boron has a lower first ionisation energy than beryllium because boron's outer electron is in a 2p orbital, whereas beryllium's is in 2s.

parts.problemMd: State the full electronic configuration of a chromium atom.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**

>

The expected configuration would be [Ar] 3d<sup>4</sup> 4s<sup>2</sup>, but one electron is promoted from 4s into 3d to achieve a half-filled 3d subshell (3d<sup>5</sup>), which is energetically more stable.

parts.problemMd:
This question is about the chromium(III) ion, $\text{Cr} pre_{24} pre^{52^{3} +}$.

i) Deduce the number of protons, neutrons, and electrons in a <sup>52</sup>Cr<sup>3+</sup> ion.

protons ..........................

neutrons ..........................

electrons ..........................

[1]

ii) State the full electronic configuration of a chromium(III) ion.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The number of protons, neutrons, and electrons in a <sup>52</sup>Cr<sup>3+</sup> ion:
> 
> - 24 protons
> **AND**
> 28 neutrons
> **AND **
> 21 electrons **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The full electronic configuration of a chromium(III) ion is:
> 
> - 1s<sup>2</sup> 2s<sup>2</sup> 2p<sup>6</sup> 3s<sup>2</sup> 3p<sup>6</sup> 3d<sup>3</sup>
> **OR**
> [Ar] 3d<sup>3</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For part (i):
> 
> Protons equal the atomic number (24).
> 
> Neutrons = mass number − atomic number = 52 − 24 = 28.
> 
> The 3+ charge means three electrons have been lost, so electrons = 24 − 3 = 21.
> 
> For part (ii):
> 
> When transition metal atoms form positive ions, electrons are always removed from 4s before 3d.
> 
> Once 3d begins to fill, repulsion raises the energy of 4s above 3d, making it the outermost subshell.
> 
> Chromium starts as [Ar] 3d<sup>5</sup> 4s<sup>1</sup>, so Cr<sup>3+</sup> loses the 4s electron first, then two 3d electrons, giving [Ar] 3d<sup>3</sup>.

![Completed electron box notation for selenium showing 4s with two paired electrons and 4p with one paired orbital and two singly-occupied orbitals](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/1-atomic-structure/1-3-electrons-energy-levels-and-atomic-orbitals/assets/007-completed-electron-box-notation-for-selenium-sho.png)

parts.problemMd:
In the blast furnace, carbon reacts with a limited supply of oxygen to form carbon monoxide.

Write an equation for this reaction.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The equation for this reaction is:
> 
> - 2C (s) + O<sub>2</sub> (g) → 2CO (g) **[1 mark]**
> 
> State symbols are not required.

> **[exam-tip]**
> This reaction is the incomplete combustion of carbon. With a limited supply of oxygen, carbon reacts to form carbon monoxide rather than carbon dioxide. The complete combustion of carbon produces CO<sub>2</sub> only.
> 
> State symbols are not required, but including them is good practice. Carbon is a solid and both oxygen and carbon monoxide are gases under these conditions.

i) Complete Fig. 5.2 to show the electronic configuration of a carbon atom in the ground state.

**Fig. 5.2**

[1]

ii) A molecule of carbon monoxide, CO, contains a triple covalent bond.

Deduce the hybridisation of the carbon atom in carbon monoxide.

[1]

iii) Describe how the σ and π bonds form in a molecule of carbon monoxide. Refer to orbital overlap in your answer.

[3]
parts.solutionMd:
i) The completed electronic configuration for carbon in the ground state is:

![Completed electrons-in-boxes diagram showing ground state carbon: 1s with paired electrons, 2s with paired electrons, and two separate 2p orbitals each with one electron of parallel spin](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/1-atomic-structure/1-3-electrons-energy-levels-and-atomic-orbitals/assets/011-completed-electrons-in-boxes-diagram-showing-gro.jpeg)

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for ground state carbon: 1s<sup>2</sup> 2s<sup>2</sup> 2p<sup>2</sup> with two electrons in separate 2p orbitals with parallel spins (Hund's rule)
> 
> ii) The hybridisation of the carbon atom in carbon monoxide is:
> 
> - sp **[1 mark]**
> 
> iii) The σ and π bonds in carbon monoxide form as follows:
> 
> - sp hybrid orbitals on C and O overlap end-on to form the σ bond **[1 mark]**
> - Unhybridised 2p orbitals on C and O overlap sideways / laterally to form each π bond **[1 mark]**
> - Two π bonds are formed as C and O each have two unhybridised 2p orbitals **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For part i):
> 
> - In the ground state, the two 2p electrons in carbon occupy separate orbitals with parallel spins (Hund's rule).
> - The excited state (1s<sup>2</sup> 2s<sup>1</sup> 2p<sup>3</sup>) has one electron promoted from 2s to 2p, but the syllabus only requires the ground state configuration.
> 
> For part ii):
> 
> - sp hybridisation involves the mixing of one 2s orbital and one 2p orbital to form two sp hybrid orbitals.
> - The remaining two 2p orbitals stay unhybridised.
> - The triple bond in CO consists of one σ bond and two π bonds.
> 
> For part iii):
> 
> - The σ bond forms by end-on (head-on) overlap of sp orbitals, giving electron density along the internuclear axis.
> - Each π bond forms by sideways (lateral) overlap of parallel unhybridised p orbitals, giving electron density above and below the internuclear axis.

parts.problemMd:
An isotope of element **X** has two more protons and two more neutrons than an atom of <sup>41</sup>K.

Deduce the identity of element **X**.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Element **X** is:
> 
> - Scandium / Sc / <sup>45</sup>Sc **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Potassium (K) has atomic number 19 and mass number 41. Adding two more protons gives atomic number 21, which is scandium (Sc). Adding two more neutrons gives mass number 45, so the specific isotope is <sup>45</sup>Sc.
> 
> The element name (Scandium) or symbol (Sc) is sufficient to identify element X. The isotope notation <sup>45</sup>Sc is also accepted.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> The full electronic configurations are:
> 
> - K<sup>+</sup>: 1s<sup>2</sup> 2s<sup>2</sup> 2p<sup>6</sup> 3s<sup>2</sup> 3p<sup>6</sup> **[1 mark]**
> - Ti: 1s<sup>2</sup> 2s<sup>2</sup> 2p<sup>6</sup> 3s<sup>2</sup> 3p<sup>6</sup> 3d<sup>2</sup> 4s<sup>2</sup> **[1 mark]**
> - Co: 1s<sup>2</sup> 2s<sup>2</sup> 2p<sup>6</sup> 3s<sup>2</sup> 3p<sup>6</sup> 3d<sup>7</sup> 4s<sup>2</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> K<sup>+</sup> has lost one electron from K (19 electrons), giving it 18 electrons, which is the same configuration as argon.
> 
> For transition metals (Ti and Co), the 4s subshell fills before 3d when building up the configuration. In the written notation, the 3d is written after 3p (principal quantum number order). Ti (Z = 22) has 22 electrons; Co (Z = 27) has 27 electrons.

parts.problemMd:
i) Construct equations to represent the first ionisation energy of potassium and the second ionisation energy of scandium.

first ionisation energy of K .....................................................................

second ionisation energy of Sc .................................................................

[2]

ii) State the full electronic configuration of an Sc<sup>2+</sup> ion.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The equations for the ionisation energies are:
> 
> - First ionisation energy of K: K (g) → K<sup>+</sup> (g) + e<sup>-</sup> **[1 mark]**
> - Second ionisation energy of Sc: Sc<sup>+</sup> (g) → Sc<sup>2+</sup> (g) + e<sup>-</sup> **[1 mark]**
> 
> Equations without state symbols are not accepted.
> 
> ii) The full electronic configuration of an Sc<sup>2+</sup> ion is:
> 
> - 1s<sup>2</sup> 2s<sup>2</sup> 2p<sup>6</sup> 3s<sup>2</sup> 3p<sup>6</sup> 3d<sup>1</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Each ionisation energy equation removes exactly one mole of electrons from one mole of gaseous species. The second ionisation energy of Sc starts from Sc<sup>+</sup> (g), not Sc (g) as the first electron has already been removed.
> 
> Sc has the full electronic configuration 1s<sup>2</sup> 2s<sup>2</sup> 2p<sup>6</sup> 3s<sup>2</sup> 3p<sup>6</sup> 3d<sup>1</sup> 4s<sup>2</sup>. The Sc<sup>2+</sup> ion loses both 4s electrons first (4s empties before 3d when forming transition metal ions), leaving 1s<sup>2</sup> 2s<sup>2</sup> 2p<sup>6</sup> 3s<sup>2</sup> 3p<sup>6</sup> 3d<sup>1</sup>.

parts.problemMd:
Table 2.1 shows successive ionisation energies of element **Z**, which is in Period 3.

**Table 2.1**

| ionisation | 1st | 2nd | 3rd | 4th | 5th |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **ionisation energy / kJ mol^-1^** | 786 | 1576 | 3232 | 4356 | 16091 |

i) Explain why the first ionisation energy generally increases across Period 3.

[2]

ii) Deduce the group of the Periodic Table to which element **Z** belongs. Explain your answer.

Group ................................

Explanation ........................................................................................

[3]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The first ionisation energy generally increases across Period 3 because:
> 
> - Nuclear charge / number of protons increases across Period 3 **[1 mark]**
> - Electron shielding remains approximately constant / electrons are added to the same shell so shielding from inner shells is unchanged **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) Element **Z** belongs to:
> 
> - Group 14 / Group 4 **[1 mark]**
> - There is a large increase between the 4th and 5th ionisation energies **[1 mark]**
> - The 5th electron is removed from an inner shell (n = 2), closer to the nucleus and more tightly held than the 4th electron (in the outer shell, n = 3) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For part (i): across Period 3, each successive element has one more proton, increasing the nuclear charge. All Period 3 elements have three electron shells, so shielding from inner electrons remains approximately constant. The increased nuclear charge with similar shielding pulls outer electrons more tightly, increasing the ionisation energy.
> 
> Note that there are two slight downward steps in the Period 3 trend: between Mg and Al (3s to 3p) and between P and S (paired 3p electron easier to remove). These are exceptions to the general trend.
> 
> For part (ii): a large jump in successive ionisation energies marks the point where the next electron is being removed from a closer inner shell. The jump between the 4th and 5th IE means the element has 4 electrons in its outer shell, placing it in Group 14.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> The full electronic configurations are:
> 
> - Mg: 1s<sup>2</sup> 2s<sup>2</sup> 2p<sup>6</sup> 3s<sup>2</sup> **[1 mark]**
> - Mg<sup>2+</sup>: 1s<sup>2</sup> 2s<sup>2</sup> 2p<sup>6</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Mg is in Period 3, Group 2, with 12 electrons. The configuration 1s<sup>2</sup> 2s<sup>2</sup> 2p<sup>6</sup> 3s<sup>2</sup> fills all subshells up to and including 3s.
> 
> Mg<sup>2+</sup> has lost two electrons from the 3s subshell, leaving 10 electrons. Its configuration (1s<sup>2</sup> 2s<sup>2</sup> 2p<sup>6</sup>) is the same as neon.

parts.problemMd: Construct an equation to represent the first ionisation energy of magnesium. Include state symbols.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The equation for the first ionisation energy of magnesium is:
> 
> - Mg (g) → Mg<sup>+</sup> (g) + e<sup>-</sup> **[1 mark]**
> 
> Equations without state symbols are not accepted.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The first ionisation energy removes one mole of electrons from one mole of gaseous atoms. All species must be in the gaseous state, which means that the (g) state symbols are required. Only one electron is removed per equation.

parts.problemMd: Explain why the second ionisation energy of magnesium is higher than the first ionisation energy.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The second ionisation energy of magnesium is higher than the first because:
> 
> - The electron is removed from a positive ion (Mg<sup>+</sup>) rather than a neutral atom (Mg) **[1 mark]**
> - There is greater electrostatic attraction between the nucleus and the outer electron in Mg<sup>+</sup>, so more energy is required to remove it **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> After the first ionisation, the nucleus still has a charge of 12+ but there are only 11 electrons remaining. Each remaining electron therefore experiences a stronger effective nuclear attraction than in the neutral atom.
> 
> This pattern applies generally: each successive ionisation energy is higher than the previous one because each electron is removed from a more positively charged ion with stronger nuclear attraction.

parts.problemMd:
Complete Table 1.1 to show the composition of the given species.

**Table 1.1**

| atomic number | nucleon number | number of electrons | number of protons | number of neutrons | species |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 9 |   | 10 |   |   | <sup>19</sup>F<sup>-</sup> |
|   |   | 23 | 26 | 32 |   |
parts.solutionMd:
The completed table is:

| atomic number | nucleon number | number of electrons | number of protons | number of neutrons | species |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 9 | **Final answer:** **19** | 10 | **Final answer:** **9** | **Final answer:** **10** | <sup>19</sup>F<sup>-</sup> |
| **Final answer:** **26** | **Final answer:** **58** | 23 | 26 | 32 | **Final answer:** <sup>**58**</sup>**Fe**<sup>**3+**</sup> |

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for all three answers in row 1 correct: nucleon number 19, protons 9, neutrons 10
> 
> 1 mark for all three answers in row 2 correct: atomic number 26, nucleon number 58, species <sup>58</sup>Fe<sup>3+</sup>

> **[exam-tip]**
> Atomic number = number of protons. Nucleon number = protons + neutrons. For ions, the number of electrons differs from the number of protons: negative ions have gained electrons and positive ions have lost them.
> 
> For row 1 (<sup>19</sup>F<sup>-</sup>): atomic number 9 gives protons = 9. The <sup>-</sup> charge means one electron gained, so electrons = 10. Neutrons = nucleon number - protons = 19 - 9 = 10.
> 
> For row 2 (Fe<sup>3+</sup>): atomic number = protons = 26 (iron). Nucleon number = protons + neutrons = 26 + 32 = 58. The <sup>3+</sup> charge means three electrons lost, confirming electrons = 26 - 3 = 23. Species: <sup>58</sup>Fe<sup>3+</sup>.

parts.problemMd:
Lithium and potassium are Group 1 metals.

State the isotopic symbol and the full electronic configuration for a potassium ion, K<sup>+</sup>, with a nucleon number of 39.

symbol .......................................................................

electronic configuration .............................................................................
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The isotopic symbol and full electronic configuration for K<sup>+</sup> (nucleon number 39) are:
> 
> - Symbol: <sup>39</sup>K<sup>+</sup> **[1 mark]**
> - Electronic configuration: 1s<sup>2</sup> 2s<sup>2</sup> 2p<sup>6</sup> 3s<sup>2</sup> 3p<sup>6</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The isotopic symbol includes the mass number (nucleon number) as a superscript before the element symbol and the charge as a superscript after: <sup>39</sup>K<sup>+</sup>.
> 
> K has 19 electrons; K<sup>+</sup> has lost one electron, leaving 18 electrons in the configuration 1s<sup>2</sup> 2s<sup>2</sup> 2p<sup>6</sup> 3s<sup>2</sup> 3p<sup>6</sup>. This is the same configuration as argon.

parts.problemMd:
Beams of protons, neutrons and electrons behave differently in an electric field due to their differing properties. Fig. 1.1 shows the path of a beam of electrons in an electric field.

On Fig. 1.1, draw and label the paths of a beam of protons and a beam of neutrons in the same field.

![Diagram of an electric field showing two charged plates with the curved path of a beam of electrons deflecting towards the positive plate, labelled electrons](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/1-atomic-structure/1-4-ionisation-energy/assets/006-diagram-of-an-electric-field-showing-two-charged.png)

**Fig. 1.1**
parts.solutionMd:
The completed diagram is:

![Completed electric field diagram showing: electrons curving towards the positive plate, protons curving with less deflection towards the negative plate, and neutrons travelling in a straight undeflected line, all labelled](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/1-atomic-structure/1-4-ionisation-energy/assets/007-completed-electric-field-diagram-showing-electro.jpeg)

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for a straight undeflected path labelled neutrons
> 
> 1 mark for a path curving towards the negative plate labelled protons
> 
> 1 mark for the proton path showing clearly less deflection than the electron path

> **[exam-tip]**
> Neutrons have no charge, so they are not deflected by the electric field and travel straight through.
> 
> Protons have a positive charge, so they are deflected towards the negative plate (opposite direction to electrons). Protons are approximately 1840 times heavier than electrons, so they are deflected much less for the same field strength.
> 
> Electrons have a negative charge and are deflected towards the positive plate. Their small mass means they curve more sharply than protons.

parts.problemMd:
Table 1.2 shows the 5th to 8th successive ionisation energies of three elements, **X**, **Y** and **Z**, which are in Period 3 of the Periodic Table.

**Table 1.2**

| element | 5th IE / kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> | 6th IE / kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> | 7th IE / kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> | 8th IE / kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **X** | 6274 | 21269 | 25398 | 29855 |
| **Y** | 7012 | 8496 | 27107 | 31671 |
| **Z** | 6542 | 9362 | 11018 | 33606 |

i) Deduce the group of the Periodic Table to which element **Y** belongs. Explain your answer.

Group ...............................

Explanation ..............................

[2]

ii) State and explain the general trend in first ionisation energies across Period 3.

[2]

iii) Explain why the first ionisation energy of element **Y** is less than that of element **X**.

[2]

iv) Complete the full electronic configuration of an atom of element **Z**.

1s<sup>2</sup> .................

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) Element **Y** belongs to:
> 
> - Group 16 / Group 6 **[1 mark]**
> - Large increase between the 6th and 7th ionisation energies **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The general trend in first ionisation energies across Period 3:
> 
> - First ionisation energy generally increases across Period 3 / increases from Na to Ar **[1 mark]**
> - Nuclear charge / number of protons increases; shielding remains approximately constant / electrons are added to the same shell **[1 mark]**
> 
> iii) The first ionisation energy of **Y** is less than that of **X** because:
> 
> - **Y** has a paired electron in a 3p orbital (3p<sup>4</sup> configuration) / one 3p orbital in **Y** is doubly occupied **[1 mark]**
> - Electron pair repulsion makes the paired electron easier to remove / reduces the ionisation energy of **Y** **[1 mark]**
> 
> iv) The full electronic configuration of an atom of element **Z** is:
> 
> - (1s<sup>2</sup>) 2s<sup>2</sup> 2p<sup>6</sup> 3s<sup>2</sup> 3p<sup>5</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For part (i): to deduce the group number from successive ionisation energy data, look for the large jump. For Y, the jump is between the 6th and 7th values (8496 to 27107), meaning the 7th electron is in an inner shell. Y therefore has 6 outer electrons and belongs to Group 16.
> 
> For part (ii): note there are two slight downward steps in Period 3 (Na to Mg to Al, and P to S) but the overall trend is an increase. These exceptions involve subshell changes and spin-pair repulsion.
> 
> For part (iii): X is in Group 15 (3p<sup>3</sup>, half-filled with one electron in each 3p orbital). Y is in Group 16 (3p<sup>4</sup>, with one 3p orbital doubly occupied). The paired electrons in Y repel each other, making the first electron easier to remove than expected from nuclear charge alone.
> 
> For part (iv): the large jump for Z is between the 7th and 8th values (11018 to 33606), so Z has 7 outer electrons and belongs to Group 17 (chlorine). Its electronic configuration is 1s<sup>2</sup> 2s<sup>2</sup> 2p<sup>6</sup> 3s<sup>2</sup> 3p<sup>5</sup>.

parts.problemMd:
All elements have a value for a first ionisation energy.

i) Define the term first ionisation energy of an element.

[2]

ii) Construct an equation to represent the first ionisation energy of aluminium. Include state symbols.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The first ionisation energy of an element is:
> 
> - The enthalpy / energy needed to remove one mole of electrons from one mole of gaseous atoms **[1 mark]**
> - To form one mole of gaseous 1+ ions / ions with +1 charge **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The equation for the first ionisation energy of aluminium is:
> 
> - Al (g) → Al<sup>+</sup> (g) + e<sup>-</sup> **[1 mark]**
> 
> Equations without state symbols do not gain the mark.

> **[exam-tip]**
> When writing an ionisation energy equation, always start with the neutral gaseous atom, not a positive ion. For the 1st ionisation energy, you remove the 1st mole of electrons from neutral Al (g) atoms to form Al<sup>+</sup> (g) ions. A common mistake is to write Al<sup>+</sup> on the left-hand side, which would represent the second ionisation energy.
> 
> The number of the ionisation energy tells you which mole of electrons is being removed: the 1st IE removes the 1st mole of electrons to form 1+ ions; the 2nd IE removes the 2nd mole of electrons to form 2+ ions, and so on.
> 
> State symbols are essential in ionisation energy equations. The definition specifically requires gaseous atoms and gaseous ions, so (g) on all species is part of the correct answer.

parts.problemMd:
Table 3.1 shows successive ionisation energies of an element **A**, found in Period 3 of the Periodic Table.

**Table 3.1**

| ionisation | 1st | 2nd | 3rd | 4th | 5th | 6th | 7th | 8th |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ionisation energy / kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> | 1012 | 1904 | 2914 | 4964 | 6274 | 21 268 | 25 431 | 29 872 |

Use data from Table 3.1 to deduce the identity of element **A**. Explain your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The identity of element **A** and the evidence for it are:
> 
> - Phosphorus / P **[1 mark]**
> - There is a large jump in ionisation energy between the 5th and 6th ionisation energies / after the 5th ionisation energy **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> To deduce the identity of an element from successive ionisation energy data, look for the large jump, the point where the ionisation energy increases significantly compared to the previous steps.
> 
> Here, the values from the 1st to the 5th IE increase by roughly 1000 to 2000 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> each time. The jump from the 5th to the 6th is nearly 15 000 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>, far larger than any previous step. This means the 6th electron is much harder to remove because it is in an inner shell, closer to the nucleus.
> 
> A common mistake is to identify the element as being in Group 6 because the large jump occurs between the 5th and 6th IEs. But if the jump comes after the 5th IE, there are 5 outer electrons, placing the element in Group 15 / Group V. The electronic configuration of phosphorus is 1s<sup>2</sup> 2s<sup>2</sup> 2p<sup>6</sup> 3s<sup>2</sup> 3p<sup>3</sup>, confirming it has 5 electrons in its outer shell.

parts.problemMd:
Fig. 3.1 shows the trend in ionisation energy for Period 3 of the Periodic Table.

![Graph of first ionisation energy plotted against element for Period 3, from sodium to argon, showing a general increase with anomalies at aluminium and sulfur](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/1-atomic-structure/1-4-ionisation-energy/assets/005-graph-of-first-ionisation-energy-plotted-against.png)

**Fig. 3.1**

i) State and explain the general trend in first ionisation energies across Period 3.

[3]

ii) Explain the deviations from the trend shown in Fig. 3.1.

[3]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The general trend and reasons for it are:
> 
> - There is a general increase in first ionisation energy across Period 3 **[1 mark]**
> - Nuclear charge increases / a proton is added to the nucleus **AND** shielding stays the same / electrons are added to the same shell **[1 mark]**
> - Atomic radius decreases **OR** outermost / outer / highest energy / valence electrons are closer to the nucleus **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The deviations from the trend are:
> 
> - Aluminium deviates because its outermost / highest energy / valence electron is in a 3p orbital **[1 mark]**
> - The 3p orbital is further from the nucleus **OR** the 3p orbital has a slightly higher energy than the 3s orbital **[1 mark]**
> - Sulfur deviates because its outermost / outer / highest energy / valence electron is paired / shares an orbital with another electron **AND** there is repulsion between the electrons in the orbital **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For the general trend across Period 3, your answer needs three elements:
> 
> 1. State that IE generally increases
> 2. Explain it using nuclear charge and shielding
> 3. Bring in the consequence (smaller atomic radius or outer electrons closer to the nucleus). Make sure you give both the increased nuclear charge and the unchanged shielding together, as both are needed for that one mark.
> 
> Aluminium (Group 13) and sulfur (Group 16) are the two anomalies in this trend, and they arise for different reasons.
> 
> - For Al, the outer electron is in a 3p orbital, which is at higher energy than the 3s orbital of Mg, so it is easier to remove.
> - For S, one 3p orbital holds a paired electron; the repulsion between those two electrons makes it easier to remove one compared to the half-filled 3p orbitals in P.
> 
> The same reasoning applies in Period 2: boron has a lower 1st IE than beryllium, and oxygen has a lower 1st IE than nitrogen, for the same reasons.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The first ionisation energy of an element is:
- The enthalpy / energy needed to remove one mole of electrons from one mole of gaseous atoms
- To form one mole of gaseous 1+ ions / ions with +1 charge

The equation for the first ionisation energy of aluminium is:
- Al (g) → Al^+^ (g) + e^-^

Explain why the second ionisation energy of aluminium is greater than the first ionisation energy.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The second ionisation energy of aluminium is greater because:
> 
> Any **one** from:
> 
> - Electrons are removed from a positive ion rather than a neutral atom
> - The electron being removed is closer to the nucleus
> - The Al<sup>+</sup> ion is smaller than the Al atom
> - The electron is being removed from a 3s orbital rather than a 3p orbital
> 
> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Successive ionisation energies always increase because once an electron has been removed, the remaining electrons experience a stronger effective nuclear charge. There are the same number of protons but fewer electrons, so each remaining electron is held more tightly.
> 
> For aluminium specifically, there is a second factor: the 2nd electron is removed from a 3s orbital rather than a 3p orbital. The 3s orbital is at a lower energy and sits closer to the nucleus than the 3p orbital, so removing an electron from it requires more energy. This is why the 2nd IE of Al is noticeably higher than the 1st.

X<sup>+</sup> (g) → X<sup>2+</sup> (g) + e<sup>-</sup>

>

> **[exam-tip]**

parts.problemMd:

> **[exam-tip]**

parts.problemMd:
Ionisation energies provide evidence for the electronic structure of atoms.

i) Define the term first ionisation energy.

[2]

ii) Construct an equation to represent the second ionisation energy of magnesium. Include state symbols.

[1]

iii) Explain the trend in first ionisation energies across Period 3 (sodium to argon). Refer to nuclear charge and shielding in your answer.

[3]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The first ionisation energy is:
> 
> - The enthalpy / energy required to remove one mole of electrons from one mole of gaseous atoms **[1 mark]**
> - To form one mole of gaseous 1+ ions / ions with a +1 charge **[1 mark]**
> 
> Marks cannot be awarded if energy is described as released.
> 
> ii) The equation for the second ionisation energy of magnesium is:
> 
> - Mg<sup>+</sup> (g) → Mg<sup>2+</sup> (g) + e<sup>-</sup> **[1 mark]**
> 
> iii) The trend in first ionisation energies across Period 3 is:
> 
> - Nuclear charge / number of protons increases across the period **[1 mark]**
> - Shielding by inner shells remains approximately constant **OR** electrons are added to the same shell **[1 mark]**
> - Attraction between the nucleus and outer electron increases, so more energy is needed to remove the electron **OR** effective nuclear charge increases, so more energy is needed to remove the electron **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For ionisation energy definitions, precision matters. A common slip is writing that energy is "released". Ionisation is endothermic, so energy is always required. Also make sure you specify gaseous atoms and gaseous 1+ ions; the gaseous state is part of the definition.
> 
> For the second ionisation energy equation, start from the 1+ ion, not the neutral atom. The first electron has already been removed, so the equation begins with Mg<sup>+</sup> (g).
> 
> For the trend across Period 3, avoid simply stating that IE increases. The marks are for the explanation: nuclear charge increases while shielding stays approximately the same, because electrons are added to the same shell rather than a new one. This increases the attraction to the outer electron, so more energy is needed to remove it.

parts.problemMd:
Silicon(IV) oxide, SiO<sub>2</sub>, and phosphorus(III) chloride, PCl<sub>3</sub>, have different structures and physical properties.

i) Describe the structure and bonding of silicon(IV) oxide.

[2]

ii) Predict the shape and bond angle of a molecule of phosphorus(III) chloride.

[2]

iii) Explain the difference in melting points between silicon(IV) oxide and phosphorus(III) chloride in terms of their structure and bonding.

[3]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The structure and bonding of silicon(IV) oxide is:
> 
> - Structure: giant molecular
> **OR**
> Giant covalent
> **OR**
> Macromolecular **[1 mark]**
> - Bonding: each Si is bonded to 4 O atoms and each O atom is bonded to 2 Si atoms **[1 mark]**
> 
> Describing the structure as simple molecular, ionic lattice or metallic does not score the first mark.
> 
> ii) The shape and bond angle of a molecule of phosphorus(III) chloride are:
> 
> - Shape: trigonal pyramidal **[1 mark]**
> - Bond angle: 107°
> **OR**
> 107.5° **[1 mark]**
> 
> iii) The difference in melting points between silicon(IV) oxide and phosphorus(III) chloride is because:
> 
> - SiO<sub>2</sub> has many strong covalent bonds that must be broken **[1 mark]**
> - PCl<sub>3</sub> has weak intermolecular forces (London / van der Waals') between molecules which must be overcome **[1 mark]**
> - More energy is needed to melt SiO<sub>2</sub> than PCl<sub>3</sub>, so SiO<sub>2</sub> has a much higher melting point **[1 mark]**
> 
> Breaking covalent bonds in PCl<sub>3</sub> means the second and third marks cannot be awarded.

> **[exam-tip]**
> For shapes and bond angles, start by counting bonding pairs and lone pairs on the central atom.
> 
> In PCl<sub>3</sub>, phosphorus forms three bonds and keeps one lone pair. Lone pairs repel bonding pairs more strongly than bonding pairs repel each other, which reduces the bond angle from 109.5° to about 107°.
> 
> A common bonding mistake is mixing up what breaks when a substance melts.
> 
> - In giant covalent structures (for example SiO<sub>2</sub>), you must break strong covalent bonds within the lattice.
> - In simple molecular substances (for example PCl<sub>3</sub>), the covalent bonds stay intact and you only overcome weak intermolecular forces.

parts.problemMd:
Fig. 1.1 shows the elements from the first three periods of the Periodic Table.

![Periodic table showing elements from the first three periods, hydrogen to argon](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/1-atomic-structure/1-4-ionisation-energy/assets/008-periodic-table-showing-elements-from-the-first-t.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

Identify an element that fits each of the following descriptions:

i) An element that forms a 2<sup>-</sup> ion with the same electronic configuration as Ne

[1]

ii) The Period 3 element with the highest boiling point

[1]

iii) The element from the first three periods with the largest atomic radius

[1]

iv) The element from the first three periods with the highest first ionisation energy

[1]

v) The Period 3 element with the successive ionisation energies shown in Table 1.1

**Table 1.1**

| ionisation number | 1st | 2nd | 3rd | 4th |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ionisation energy / kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> | 738 | 1451 | 7733 | 10 541 |

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The elements are:
> 
> i) Oxygen / O **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) Silicon / Si **[1 mark]**
> 
> iii) Sodium / Na **[1 mark]**
> 
> iv) Helium / He **[1 mark]**
> 
> v) Magnesium / Mg **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> i) Oxygen has the electronic configuration 1s<sup>2</sup> 2s<sup>2</sup> 2p<sup>4</sup>. Gaining 2 electrons forms O<sup>2-</sup> with configuration 1s<sup>2</sup> 2s<sup>2</sup> 2p<sup>6</sup>, which is the same as neon.
> 
> ii) Silicon has a giant covalent structure. Much more energy is needed to break the strong covalent bonds throughout the lattice compared to the metallic bonding in Na to Al, or the weak van der Waals forces between molecules in P to Ar.
> 
> iii) Sodium has the largest atomic radius of the first three periods. It has 3 electron shells (more than any element in Periods 1 or 2) and the lowest nuclear charge of the Period 3 elements, so its outer electrons are held least tightly.
> 
> iv) Helium has the highest first ionisation energy from H to Ar. It has only one shell of electrons very close to the nucleus, and two protons providing a strong nuclear attraction. Although neon has more protons, helium's outer electrons are in shell 1 (not shell 2), so they are held more strongly.
> 
> v) The large jump occurs between the 2nd and 3rd ionisation energies, indicating that the 3rd electron is in an inner shell. The element has 2 outer electrons and is therefore in Group 2. The Period 3 Group 2 element is magnesium.

Fig. 1.2 shows the first ionisation energies for six consecutive elements labelled **A**–**F**.

**Fig. 1.2**

Complete the graph to show the first ionisation energies of elements **G**–**K**.
parts.solutionMd:
The completed graph is:

![Graph showing first ionisation energies of elements A to K, with G and I starting new sub-periods and a drop from G to H due to spin-pair repulsion](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/1-atomic-structure/1-4-ionisation-energy/assets/010-graph-showing-first-ionisation-energies-of-eleme.png)

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for G plotted above F **AND** H plotted between F and G
> 
> 1 mark for I plotted above H and below A **AND** J plotted above I and below B
> 
> 1 mark for K plotted below C

> **[exam-tip]**
> Element B is the noble gas in the sequence, because there is a large drop after B to C. The outer electron of C is in a new, higher energy shell at the start of a new period, so C is a Group 1 element.
> 
> From C onwards, the pattern repeats across the next period. G starts at a similar level to C (both are Group 1), then the IE generally increases toward J (noble gas), with two characteristic dips: one from D to E (outer electron moves from s to p subshell, higher energy and further from nucleus) and one from G to H (spin-pair repulsion in a doubly occupied p orbital lowers the IE of H below G).
> 
> K starts the following period and will have a lower IE than C or G, because it has one more shell of electrons further from the nucleus.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Fig. 1.2 shows the first ionisation energies for six consecutive elements labelled **A**–**F**.

Explain why the value of the first ionisation energy for **D** is greater than for **C**.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The first ionisation energy of **D** is greater than that of **C** because:
> 
> - **D** has one more proton / higher nuclear charge **OR** the outer electron in **D** is closer to the nucleus **[1 mark]**
> - The electrons being removed from **D** and **C** are in the same (s) subshell **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> In this sequence, B is the noble gas (it has the highest IE before a large drop to C), so C is a Group 1 element starting a new period and D is the Group 2 element that follows. D has one more proton than C but the same number of inner shells, so its outer electron experiences a stronger nuclear attraction.
> 
> The key point to include is that both C and D have their outer electrons in the same s subshell, so shielding is the same for both. The only difference is nuclear charge, which makes D's outer electron harder to remove.

parts.problemMd:
Successive ionisation energies provide evidence for the arrangement of electrons in atoms. In Table 2.1, the successive ionisation energies of oxygen are given.

**Table 2.1**

| ionisation | 1st | 2nd | 3rd | 4th | 5th | 6th | 7th | 8th |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ionisation energy / kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> | 1314 | 3388 | 5301 | 7469 | 10 989 | 13 327 | 71 337 | 84 080 |

i) Construct an equation to represent the third ionisation energy of oxygen. Include state symbols.

[2]

ii) Explain how this data shows evidence of two energy shells in oxygen.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
i) The equation for the third ionisation energy of oxygen is:

O<sup>2+</sup> (g) → O<sup>3+</sup> (g) + e<sup>-</sup>

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct formulae: O<sup>2+</sup> (g) → O<sup>3+</sup> (g) + e<sup>-</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for correct state symbols: (g) on all three species
> 
> ii) The data shows evidence of two energy shells because:
> 
> - There is a very large jump / increase in ionisation energy between the 6th and 7th ionisation energies **[1 mark]**
> - This indicates the 7th electron is removed from a different / inner shell / energy level, closer to the nucleus **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For the third ionisation energy equation, start from the 2+ ion as two electrons have already been removed. The equation shows one mole of electrons removed from one mole of gaseous O<sup>2+</sup> ions to form O<sup>3+</sup> ions. State symbols on all three species are required.
> 
> To interpret successive IE data for evidence of shells, look for the largest jump. Here the values increase gradually from the 1st to the 6th IE (all within the outer shell), then there is a dramatic rise from the 6th (13 327 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>) to the 7th (71 337 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>). This jump indicates the 7th electron is being removed from a shell much closer to the nucleus. Since there are 6 electrons in the outer shell and 2 in the inner shell, this is consistent with oxygen having two energy shells.

parts.problemMd:
Give the full electronic configuration of the following atoms and ions.

i) Te

[1]

ii) Zn<sup>2+</sup>

[1]

iii) Cu<sup>2+</sup>

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The full electronic configuration of Te is:
> 
> - 1s<sup>2</sup> 2s<sup>2</sup> 2p<sup>6</sup> 3s<sup>2</sup> 3p<sup>6</sup> 3d<sup>10</sup> 4s<sup>2</sup> 4p<sup>6</sup> 4d<sup>10</sup> 5s<sup>2</sup> 5p<sup>4</sup> **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The full electronic configuration of Zn<sup>2+</sup> is:
> 
> - 1s<sup>2</sup> 2s<sup>2</sup> 2p<sup>6</sup> 3s<sup>2</sup> 3p<sup>6</sup> 3d<sup>10</sup> **[1 mark]**
> 
> iii) The full electronic configuration of Cu<sup>2+</sup> is:
> 
> - 1s<sup>2</sup> 2s<sup>2</sup> 2p<sup>6</sup> 3s<sup>2</sup> 3p<sup>6</sup> 3d<sup>9</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Always write full electronic configurations in order of principal quantum number (n = 1, 2, 3, 4...), placing 3d before 4s and 4d before 5s in the written form, even though the s subshells fill first.
> 
> For ions, the s subshell empties before the d subshell. Zinc is [Ar] 3d<sup>10</sup> 4s<sup>2</sup> as a neutral atom; forming Zn<sup>2+</sup> removes both 4s electrons, leaving [Ar] 3d<sup>10</sup>.
> 
> Copper has an anomalous configuration: [Ar] 3d<sup>10</sup> 4s<sup>1</sup> rather than [Ar] 3d<sup>9</sup> 4s<sup>2</sup>, because a completely full 3d subshell provides extra stability. When forming Cu<sup>2+</sup>, the 4s<sup>1</sup> electron is removed first, then one 3d electron, giving [Ar] 3d<sup>9</sup>. The other anomalous first-row transition metal is chromium, which has a half-filled 3d subshell: [Ar] 3d<sup>5</sup> 4s<sup>1</sup>.

ii) Construct an equation to represent the third ionisation energy of zirconium, Zr. Include state symbols.

> 
> - [Kr] 4d<sup>2</sup> **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The equation for the third ionisation energy of zirconium is:
