parts.problemMd:
Define the following terms.

Relative atomic mass

[2]

Relative isotopic mass

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The definition of relative atomic mass:
> 
> - The weighted average / mean mass of an atom of the element / one mole of atoms of the element **[1 mark]**
> - Relative to / compared to 1/12 (of the mass) of (an atom of) carbon-12
> **OR**
> On a scale where carbon-12 has a mass of (exactly) 12 (units)
> **OR**
> Where one mole of carbon-12 has a mass of exactly 12 g **[1 mark]**
> 
> The definition of relative isotopic mass:
> 
> - The mass of an atom / isotope / one mole of (atoms of) a specific isotope **[1 mark]**
> - Relative to / compared to 1/12 (of the mass) of (an atom of) carbon-12
> **OR**
> On a scale where carbon-12 has a mass of (exactly) 12 (units) **[1 mark]**
> 
> The formula $\frac{\text{average mass of one atom}}{1/12\text{the mass of one carbon-12 atom}}$ is accepted for both marks for relative atomic mass.

> **[exam-tip]**
> These definitions are frequently tested in CIE examinations. Learn both the single-atom and mole-scale versions so you can adapt to how the question phrases the requirement.
> 
> For relative atomic mass, the key points are: (1) it is a weighted average (accounting for isotope abundances), and (2) it is measured relative to carbon-12. Both marks require both components to be present.
> 
> The key distinction between relative atomic mass and relative isotopic mass is that relative atomic mass is the weighted average across all naturally occurring isotopes, while relative isotopic mass refers to one specific isotope only.
> 
> These two definitions are unlikely to appear together in the same examination paper.

parts.problemMd:
i) State the symbols used for relative atomic mass and relative molecular mass.

[1]

ii) Describe how to calculate the relative molecular mass of a compound.

[1]

iii) State the difference between relative molecular mass and relative formula mass.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The symbols for relative atomic mass and relative molecular mass:
> 
> - *A*<sub>r</sub> 
> **AND**
> *M*<sub>r</sub> **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) To calculate the relative molecular mass of a compound:
> 
> - Add the relative atomic masses / *A*<sub>r</sub> values of all atoms in the molecule **[1 mark]**
> 
> iii) The difference between relative molecular mass and relative formula mass:
> 
> - Relative molecular mass is used for molecular compounds
> **AND**
> Relative formula mass is used for ionic compounds / compounds that contain ions **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The symbols *A*<sub>r</sub> and *M*<sub>r</sub> are equivalent to the full terms relative atomic mass and relative molecular mass respectively. Both forms appear in examination questions and mark schemes.
> 
> Relative formula mass is used for ionic compounds such as NaCl and MgO, which do not exist as discrete molecules. Relative molecular mass applies to compounds with distinct covalent molecules such as H<sub>2</sub>O and CO<sub>2</sub>.

parts.problemMd:
Ionic compounds such as sodium chloride are arranged in a giant three-dimensional lattice structure, with a regular and repeating pattern of positive and negative ions.

State the formula unit of sodium chloride.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The formula unit of sodium chloride:
> 
> - NaCl **[1 mark]**
> 
> The formula unit is the simplest formula for an ionic compound. Ionic compounds form giant lattice structures rather than discrete molecules.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Ionic compounds such as NaCl do not exist as individual molecules. The formula unit represents the simplest ratio of ions in the compound. Other examples: SiO<sub>2</sub> for silicon dioxide, C for diamond.

parts.problemMd:
Complete Table 1.1

**Table 1.1**

| **Chemical** | **Formula** | **Relative molecular / formula mass** |
|---|---|---|
| Magnesium oxide | MgO |   |
| Sulfuric acid | H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> |   |
| Ammonium phosphate | (NH<sub>4</sub>)<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>4</sub> |   |
| Copper(II) sulfate pentahydrate | CuSO<sub>4</sub>•5H<sub>2</sub>O |   |
parts.solutionMd:
The completed table is:

| **Chemical** | **Formula** | **Relative molecular / formula mass** |
|---|---|---|
| Magnesium oxide | MgO | **Final answer:** **40.3** |
| Sulfuric acid | H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> | **Final answer:** **98.1** |
| Ammonium phosphate | (NH<sub>4</sub>)<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>4</sub> | **Final answer:** **149.0** |
| Copper(II) sulfate pentahydrate | CuSO<sub>4</sub>•5H<sub>2</sub>O | **Final answer:** **249.6** |

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for MgO = 40.3
> 
> 1 mark for H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> = 98.1
> 
> 1 mark for (NH<sub>4</sub>)<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>4</sub> = 149.0
> 
> 1 mark for CuSO<sub>4</sub>•5H<sub>2</sub>O = 249.6

> **[exam-tip]**
> Use the relative atomic mass values from your data booklet rather than memorised values, as the precision may differ.
> 
> For compounds with brackets, such as (NH<sub>4</sub>)<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>4</sub>, work out the mass of each bracket group first, then multiply by the subscript.
> 
> - The NH<sub>4</sub> group: 14.0 + (4 × 1.0) = 18.0
> - Three groups: 3 × 18.0 = 54.0
> - The PO<sub>4</sub> group: 31.0 + (4 × 16.0) = 95.0
> - Total: 54.0 + 95.0 = 149.0
> 
> For hydrated salts such as CuSO<sub>4</sub>•5H<sub>2</sub>O, treat the water of crystallisation separately.
> 
> - CuSO<sub>4</sub>: 63.5 + 32.1 + (4 × 16.0) = 159.6
> - Five water molecules: 5 × 18.0 = 90.0
> - Total: 159.6 + 90.0 = 249.6

parts.problemMd:
The element chromium has several naturally occurring isotopes whose abundances are shown in Table 1.1

**Table 1.1**

| **Mass number** | **% abundance** |
|---|---|
| 50 | 4.345 |
| 52 | 83.789 |
| 53 | 9.501 |
| 54 | 2.365 |

Calculate the relative atomic mass of chromium to two decimal places.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the relative atomic mass of chromium:

- Calculate *A*<sub>r</sub> using the weighted average:

*A*<sub>r</sub> = $\frac{(4.345\times50)+(83.789\times52)+(9.501\times53)+(2.365\times54)}{100}$

*A*<sub>r</sub> = $\frac{5205.5}{100}$ **[1 mark]**

*A*<sub>r</sub> = **52.06** **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Always check that your calculated Ar makes sense against the data: the most abundant isotope of chromium is <sup>52</sup>Cr (83.8%), so the average mass must be very close to 52. An answer of 52.06 is consistent with this.
> 
> The question asks for two decimal places specifically. Even if your answer rounds to a whole number, write the required decimal places, for example 52.00 rather than 52.

parts.problemMd:
Chromium can form a variety of compounds. Chromium(III) chloride hydrate is the dark green complex [CrCl<sub>2</sub>(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>4</sub>]Cl.

Write the full electronic configuration for the chromium ion in this compound.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The full electronic configuration of the Cr<sup>3+</sup> ion is:
> 
> - 1s<sup>2</sup> 2s<sup>2</sup> 2p<sup>6</sup> 3s<sup>2</sup> 3p<sup>6</sup> 3d<sup>3</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The Roman numeral (III) in the compound name tells you the chromium ion has a 3+ charge. Starting from the ground state chromium atom (1s<sup>2</sup> 2s<sup>2</sup> 2p<sup>6</sup> 3s<sup>2</sup> 3p<sup>6</sup> 3d<sup>5</sup> 4s<sup>1</sup>), remove three electrons. Electrons are removed from the 4s subshell before the 3d subshell when forming transition metal ions, so removing 1 from 4s and 2 from 3d gives the 3d<sup>3</sup> configuration.
> 
> Write configurations in principal quantum number order: n = 1, then n = 2, then n = 3. This means 3d is always written before 4s in the final configuration.

parts.problemMd: Calculate the relative molecular mass of [CrCl<sub>2</sub>(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>4</sub>]Cl.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the relative molecular mass of [CrCl<sub>2</sub>(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>4</sub>]Cl:

- Identify the atoms: 1 Cr, 3 Cl (2 inside the brackets + 1 outside), 4 H<sub>2</sub>O

- Calculate *M*<sub>r</sub>:

*M*<sub>r</sub> = 52.0 + (3 × 35.5) + (4 × 18.0)

*M*<sub>r</sub> = 52.0 + 106.5 + 72.0

*M*<sub>r</sub> = **230.5** **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Take care when reading the formula [CrCl<sub>2</sub>(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>4</sub>]Cl: there are two Cl atoms inside the coordination sphere plus one Cl outside the brackets, giving 3 Cl atoms in total.
> 
> For the water molecules inside the complex, treat each H<sub>2</sub>O as having Mr = 18.0, then multiply by the number of water molecules: 4 × 18.0 = 72.0.

parts.problemMd:
Nitrous oxide is used as a sedative in dentistry and has the formula N<sub>2</sub>O. Different sources of N<sub>2</sub>O contain different ratios of <sup>14</sup>N and <sup>15</sup>N.

State the name of the instrument used to distinguish between <sup>14</sup>N and <sup>15</sup>N and outline two characteristic differences seen in the analysis of <sup>14</sup>N and <sup>15</sup>N.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The instrument used to distinguish between <sup>14</sup>N and <sup>15</sup>N:
> 
> - Mass spectrometer **[1 mark]**
> 
> Two characteristic differences in the mass spectrum of <sup>14</sup>N and <sup>15</sup>N:
> 
> - <sup>14</sup>N and <sup>15</sup>N have different mass/charge (m/z) ratios
> **AND**
> Different relative abundances (peak heights) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> In a mass spectrum of nitrogen with two isotopes, each isotope produces a separate peak: <sup>14</sup>N at m/z = 14 and <sup>15</sup>N at m/z = 15. The height of each peak reflects the relative abundance of that isotope.
> 
> Mass spectrometry has two main applications at A Level:
> 
> - Determining relative atomic mass from isotope data
> - Identifying organic molecules from fragmentation patterns, which is covered in later topics.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Nitrous oxide is used as a sedative in dentistry and has the formula N~2~O. Different sources of N~2~O contain different ratios of ^14^N and ^15^N.

A sample of nitrous oxide was enriched so that it contained 4% by mass of <sup>15</sup>N. Calculate the relative molecular mass of the resulting nitrous oxide.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the relative molecular mass of the enriched nitrous oxide:

- Calculate the relative atomic mass of N in the enriched sample:

*A*<sub>r</sub>(N) = $\frac{(4\times15.00)+(96\times14.00)}{100}$

*A*<sub>r</sub>(N) = $\frac{1404}{100}$ = 14.04 **[1 mark]**

- Calculate *M*<sub>r</sub> of N<sub>2</sub>O using this value of *A*<sub>r</sub>(N):

*M*<sub>r</sub> = (2 × 14.04) + 16.00

*M*<sub>r</sub> = **44.08** **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The enrichment percentage (4% <sup>15</sup>N by mass) can be treated directly as the percentage abundance of <sup>15</sup>N. The remaining 96% is <sup>14</sup>N.
> 
> Apply the weighted average formula to find Ar(N) first, then use this value in the Mr calculation for N<sub>2</sub>O. Do not use the standard Ar(N) = 14.01 from the data booklet, as this sample has been deliberately enriched in <sup>15</sup>N.

parts.problemMd:
An atom has twice as many protons, and twice as many neutrons, as an atom of <sup>15</sup>N.

Determine the chemical symbol for this atom, including the mass number, and deduce the number of electrons.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The atom with twice the protons and neutrons of <sup>15</sup>N:
> 
> - Chemical symbol including mass number: <sup>30</sup>Si **[1 mark]**
> - Number of electrons in the neutral atom: 14 **[1 mark]**
> 
> <sup>15</sup>N has 7 protons and 8 neutrons; doubling gives 14 protons and 16 neutrons; atomic number 14 is silicon; mass number = 14 + 16 = 30.

> **[exam-tip]**
> From the periodic table, nitrogen has atomic number 7, so <sup>15</sup>N has 7 protons and 15 - 7 = 8 neutrons.
> 
> Doubling both gives 14 protons and 16 neutrons. Atomic number 14 is silicon (Si), and mass number = 14 + 16 = 30, giving the symbol <sup>30</sup>Si.
> 
> In a neutral atom, the number of electrons equals the number of protons: 14 electrons. Do not confuse mass number with electron count.

parts.problemMd:
Ethanoic acid has a relative molecular mass of 60.0.

Define the term relative molecular mass.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The definition of relative molecular mass:
> 
> - The mass of a molecule / the (weighted) average / mean mass of the molecule(s) / the mass of one mole of molecules **[1 mark]**
> - Relative to / compared to 1/12 (of the mass) of (an atom of) carbon-12
> **OR**
> On a scale where carbon-12 has a mass of (exactly) 12 (units) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The definition of Mr has two required components: what is being measured (the mass of a molecule or average mass of molecules) and the reference standard (carbon-12). Both components are needed for full marks.
> 
> The reference to carbon-12 can be phrased in two equivalent ways: "relative to 1/12 the mass of a carbon-12 atom" or "on a scale where carbon-12 = 12 units."

parts.problemMd: State the empirical formula of ethanoic acid.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The empirical formula of ethanoic acid:
> 
> - CH<sub>2</sub>O **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The molecular formula of ethanoic acid is C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>O<sub>2</sub>. The empirical formula is the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms. All three subscripts share a common factor of 2, so dividing each by 2 gives CH<sub>2</sub>O.
> 
> Do not confuse the empirical formula with the structural formula (CH<sub>3</sub>COOH) or the molecular formula (C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>O<sub>2</sub>).

parts.problemMd:
Ethanoic acid reacts with aqueous sodium carbonate to form a neutral salt solution and a gas.

i) Name the salt produced in this reaction.

[1]

ii) Calculate its relative formula mass.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The name of the salt produced in this reaction:
> 
> - Sodium ethanoate **[1 mark]**

ii) To calculate the relative formula mass of sodium ethanoate (CH<sub>3</sub>COONa):

*M*<sub>r</sub> = 12.0 + (3 × 1.0) + 12.0 + (2 × 16.0) + 23.0

*M*<sub>r</sub> = **82.0** **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Ethanoic acid (CH<sub>3</sub>COOH) reacts with sodium carbonate (Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>) to form sodium ethanoate (CH<sub>3</sub>COONa), water and carbon dioxide. The gas produced is CO<sub>2</sub>.
> 
> For the relative formula mass, count the atoms in CH<sub>3</sub>COONa carefully: 2 C, 3 H, 2 O and 1 Na. Working: 12.0 + 3.0 + 12.0 + 32.0 + 23.0 = 82.0.

parts.problemMd:
Table 3.1 shows the number of protons, neutrons and electrons of some isotopes and ions of copper.

**Table 3.1**

| **Species** | **Protons** | **Neutrons** | **Electrons** |
|---|---|---|---|
|   |   | 34 | 27 |
| <sup>65</sup>Cu<sup>+</sup> | 29 |   |   |

i) Complete Table 3.1.

[2]

ii) State the full electronic configuration of the Cu<sup>+</sup> ion.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
i) The completed Table 3.1:

| **Species** | **Protons** | **Neutrons** | **Electrons** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Final answer:** <sup>**63**</sup>**Cu**<sup>**2+**</sup> | **Final answer:** **29** | 34 | 27 |
| <sup>65</sup>Cu<sup>+</sup> | 29 | **Final answer:** **36** | **Final answer:** **28** |

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for all values in the <sup>63</sup>Cu<sup>2+</sup> row correct: species = <sup>63</sup>Cu<sup>2+</sup>, protons = 29
> 
> 1 mark for all values in the <sup>65</sup>Cu<sup>+</sup> row correct: neutrons = 36, electrons = 28

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii) The full electronic configuration of the Cu<sup>+</sup> ion:
> 
> - 1s<sup>2</sup> 2s<sup>2</sup> 2p<sup>6</sup> 3s<sup>2</sup> 3p<sup>6</sup> 3d<sup>10</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For completing Table 3.1: the number of protons in copper is always 29 (atomic number = 29). For Row 1, electrons (27) < protons (29) by 2, indicating Cu<sup>2+</sup>. Mass number = 29 + 34 = 63, giving <sup>63</sup>Cu<sup>2+</sup>. For Row 2, <sup>65</sup>Cu<sup>+</sup> has mass number 65, so neutrons = 65 - 29 = 36. Cu<sup>+</sup> has lost 1 electron: 29 - 1 = 28 electrons.
> 
> For the Cu<sup>+</sup> electronic configuration: copper has an anomalous ground state of [Ar] 3d<sup>10</sup> 4s<sup>1</sup> (not the expected [Ar] 3d<sup>9</sup> 4s<sup>2</sup>) because a fully filled 3d subshell provides extra stability. Forming Cu<sup>+</sup> removes the single 4s<sup>1</sup> electron, leaving a complete 3d<sup>10</sup> configuration: 1s<sup>2</sup> 2s<sup>2</sup> 2p<sup>6</sup> 3s<sup>2</sup> 3p<sup>6</sup> 3d<sup>10</sup>. Write configurations in principal quantum number order: 3d is written before 4s.

parts.problemMd:
<sup>63</sup>Cu has a relative isotopic mass of 62.9296 and <sup>65</sup>Cu has a relative isotopic mass of 64.9278. The relative atomic mass of copper is 63.546.

Calculate the percentage abundance of each isotope of copper. Show your working.

Express your answer to an appropriate number of significant figures.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the percentage abundances of <sup>63</sup>Cu and <sup>65</sup>Cu:

- Let the fractional abundance of <sup>63</sup>Cu = *x*, so the fractional abundance of <sup>65</sup>Cu = (1 - *x*)

- Set up the weighted average equation using Ar(Cu) = 63.546:

63.546 = (62.9296 × *x*) + (64.9278 × (1 - *x*))

**[1 mark]**

- Expand and rearrange:

63.546 = 62.9296*x* + 64.9278 - 64.9278*x*

-1.3818 = -1.9982*x*

**[1 mark]**

- Solve for *x*:

*x* = $\frac{1.3818}{1.9982}$ = 0.69152

<sup>63</sup>Cu = **69.152%** **AND** <sup>65</sup>Cu = **30.848% ****[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correctly setting up the weighted average equation
> 
> 1 mark for obtaining -1.9982x = -1.3818 (or equivalent rearrangement)
> 
> 1 mark for both final answers correct to 5 significant figures: <sup>63</sup>Cu = 69.152%, <sup>65</sup>Cu = 30.848%
> 
> Both percentages must be given for the final mark.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Since the total abundance of all isotopes must equal 100%, the fractional abundance of <sup>65</sup>Cu = 1 - *x* where *x* is the fractional abundance of <sup>63</sup>Cu. This allows you to solve for *x* using a single equation.
> 
> Always express your final answer to the same number of significant figures as the least precise data value. The relative isotopic masses are given to 6 sig figs and the relative atomic mass to 5 sig figs, so give both percentages to 5 significant figures.
> 
> Check your answer: most naturally occurring copper is <sup>63</sup>Cu (about 69%), so an answer near 69% for <sup>63</sup>Cu is expected.

parts.problemMd: Explain why isotopes of copper have the same chemical properties but different densities.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The explanation for same chemical reactions but different densities in copper isotopes:
> 
> - Isotopes of copper have the same number of electrons / the same electronic configuration **[1 mark]**
> - Isotopes of copper have different mass numbers / different numbers of neutrons **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Chemical properties are determined by the number and arrangement of electrons. Density depends on mass: more neutrons means greater nuclear mass and therefore greater density.
> 
> Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons. The number of electrons (and therefore the electronic configuration) is unchanged between isotopes of the same element, so chemical reactivity is identical.
> 
> Physical properties such as density, melting point and boiling point are affected by mass. Heavier isotopes have greater mass per atom, leading to slightly higher density. This is why <sup>65</sup>Cu is denser than <sup>63</sup>Cu.

parts.problemMd:
Copper(II) chloride reacts with sodium phosphate to form two salts only.

Write a balanced equation for this reaction.
parts.solutionMd:
The balanced equation for the reaction between copper(II) chloride and sodium phosphate:

3CuCl<sub>2</sub> + 2Na<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>4</sub> → Cu<sub>3</sub>(PO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub> + 6NaCl

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct formulae for all reactants and products: CuCl<sub>2</sub>, Na<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>4</sub>, Cu<sub>3</sub>(PO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub>, NaCl
> 
> 1 mark for correct balancing: coefficients 3, 2, 1, 6
> 
> State symbols are not required.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The trickiest formula is copper(II) phosphate. The copper ion is Cu<sup>2+</sup> and the phosphate ion is PO<sub>4</sub><sup>3-</sup>.
> 
> To form a neutral compound: 3 Cu<sup>2+</sup> (charge +6) and 2 PO<sub>4</sub><sup>3-</sup> (charge -6). The formula is Cu<sub>3</sub>(PO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub>, so brackets around PO<sub>4</sub> are essential.
> 
> To balance:
> 
> - Start with sodium (2Na<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>4</sub> gives 6 Na, so 6NaCl)
> - Balance copper (3CuCl<sub>2</sub> gives 3 Cu, consistent with Cu<sub>3</sub>(PO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub>).
> - Check chlorine: 3 x 2 = 6 Cl, giving 6 NaCl.

parts.problemMd: State the number of particles in one mole of a chemical.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The number of particles in one mole of a chemical:
> 
> - 6.02 x 10<sup>23 </sup>
> **OR **
> 6.022 x 10<sup>23</sup>**[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> This value is Avogadro's constant, symbol *L*. It is printed in the data booklet at the back of every CIE exam paper so you do not need to memorise it.
> 
> The current CIE data booklet gives *L* = 6.022 × 10<sup>23</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>. Always use this value to at least 3 significant figures in your calculations.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

State the number of particles in one mole of a chemical.

The number of particles in one mole of a chemical: 6.02 x 10^23 OR 6.022 x 10^23

i) State the number and type of atoms present in a molecule of water.

[2]

ii) Calculate the total number of particles and atoms present in one mole of water.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The number and type of atoms in a molecule of water:
> 
> - 3 / three atoms **[1 mark]**
> - 2 / two hydrogen atoms **AND** 1 / one oxygen atom **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The total number of particles and atoms in one mole of water:
> 
> - Particles = 6.022 × 10<sup>23</sup> **AND** atoms = 1.807 × 10<sup>24</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For part i), stating the total number of atoms (3) alone scores 1 mark. Identifying both hydrogen (×2) and oxygen (×1) is needed for the second mark.
> 
> For part ii), "particles" here means molecules of water. Each molecule contains 3 atoms, so: atoms = 3 × 6.022 × 10<sup>23</sup> = 1.807 × 10<sup>24</sup>.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The number of particles in one mole of a chemical: 6.022 × 10^23

i) State the number and type of ions present in one mole of sodium carbonate, Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>.

[2]

ii) Calculate the number of metal ions present in two moles of sodium carbonate.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The ions present in one mole of sodium carbonate, Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>:
> 
> - 2 sodium / Na<sup>+</sup> ions **[1 mark]**
> - 1 carbonate / CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2-</sup> ion **[1 mark]**

ii) To calculate the number of sodium (metal) ions in two moles of sodium carbonate:

- Calculate Na<sup>+</sup> ions in one mole of Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>:

2 × 6.022 × 10<sup>23</sup> = 1.204 × 10<sup>24</sup> **[1 mark]**

- Double for two moles:

2 × 1.204 × 10<sup>24</sup> = **2.409 × 10**<sup>**24**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> In Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>, the subscript 2 indicates 2 sodium ions per formula unit, so one mole contains 2 × *L* sodium ions. For two moles, double this value.
> 
> The carbonate ion CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2-</sup> has a 2- charge, which balances the overall 2+ total charge from two Na<sup>+</sup> ions per formula unit.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

State the number of particles in one mole of a chemical.

The number of particles in one mole of a chemical: 6.02 x 10²³ OR 6.022 x 10²³

This value is Avogadro's constant, symbol L. L = 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹.

i) State the conditions when one mole of a gas occupies a volume of 24.0 dm<sup>3</sup>.

[2]

ii) Complete Table 2.1.

**Table 2.1**

| **Gas** | **Number of moles** | **Volume of gas (dm**<sup>**3**</sup>**)** | **Number of molecules present** |
|---|---|---|---|
| Nitrogen | 2.0 | 48.0 |   |
| Sulfur dioxide |   | 1.8 |   |
| Carbon monoxide |   |   | 9.03 × 10<sup>23</sup> |

[5]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The conditions when one mole of a gas occupies a volume of 24.0 dm<sup>3</sup>:
> 
> - 20 <sup>o</sup>C
> **OR**
> Room temperature **[1 mark]**
> - 1 atmosphere
> **OR**
> Room pressure **[1 mark]**

ii) The completed Table 2.1:

| **Gas** | **Number of moles** | **Volume of gas (dm**<sup>**3**</sup>**)** | **Number of molecules present** |
|---|---|---|---|
| Nitrogen | 2.0 | 48.0 | **Final answer:** **1.204 × 10**<sup>**24**</sup> |
| Sulfur dioxide | **Final answer:** **0.075** | 1.8 | **Final answer:** **4.517 × 10**<sup>**22**</sup> |
| Carbon monoxide | **Final answer:** **1.50** | **Final answer:** **36.0** | 9.03 × 10<sup>23</sup> |

**[5 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for number of nitrogen molecules = 1.204 × 10<sup>24</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for moles of sulfur dioxide = 0.075
> 
> 1 mark for number of sulfur dioxide molecules = 4.517 × 10<sup>22</sup> (accept 4.51 to 4.52 × 10<sup>22</sup>)
> 
> 1 mark for moles of carbon monoxide = 1.50
> 
> 1 mark for volume of carbon monoxide = 36.0 dm<sup>3</sup>

> **[exam-tip]**
> At room temperature and pressure, all gases occupy 24.0 dm<sup>3</sup> per mole. Use moles = volume ÷ 24.0 to convert between volume (dm<sup>3</sup>) and moles.
> 
> For sulfur dioxide: moles = $\frac{1.8}{24.0}$ = 0.075 mol, then molecules = 0.075 × 6.022 × 10<sup>23</sup> = 4.517 × 10<sup>22</sup>.
> 
> For carbon monoxide: moles = $\frac{9.03\times10^{23}}{6.022\times10^{23}}$ = 1.50 mol, then volume = 1.50 × 24.0 = 36.0 dm<sup>3</sup>.
> 
> Always use *L* = 6.022 × 10<sup>23</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup> from the CIE data booklet. Express answers to 3 or 4 significant figures consistent with the data provided.

parts.problemMd:
5.0 g of an unknown Group 2 nitrate was decomposed to produce 0.0843 mol of gas.

2X(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> (s) → 2XO (s) + 4NO<sub>2</sub> (g) + O<sub>2</sub> (g)

i) Calculate the amount, in mol, of the unknown Group 2 nitrate.

[1]

ii) Calculate the number of ions in 0.03372 mol of the unknown Group 2 nitrate.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
i) To calculate the amount, in mol, of the unknown Group 2 nitrate:

- From the equation, ratio of X(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> to total gas = 2:5 (4 NO<sub>2</sub> + 1 O<sub>2</sub>)

moles of X(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> = $\frac{0.0843}{5}$ × 2

moles of X(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> = **0.03372 mol** **[1 mark]**

ii) To calculate the number of ions in 0.03372 mol of the unknown Group 2 nitrate:

- X(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> contains 3 ions per formula unit: 1 X<sup>2+</sup> **AND** 2 NO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup> **[1 mark]**

number of ions = 0.03372 × 3 × 6.022 × 10<sup>23</sup>

number of ions = **6.09 × 10**<sup>**22**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For part i), the key step is counting the total moles of gas from the equation: 4 moles of NO<sub>2</sub> and 1 mole of O<sub>2</sub> = 5 moles of gas per 2 moles of X(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>. The ratio is 2:5.
> 
> For part ii), always count all ions in the formula. X(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> gives one X<sup>2+</sup> and two NO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup> = 3 ions per formula unit. Multiply moles by 3, then by *L* = 6.022 × 10<sup>23</sup>.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

5.0 g of an unknown Group 2 nitrate was decomposed to produce 0.0843 mol of gas.

2X(NO~3~)~2~ (s) → 2XO (s) + 4NO~2~ (g) + O~2~ (g)

moles of X(NO~3~)~2~ = 0.03372 mol

Identify the unknown element X.
parts.solutionMd:
To identify the unknown element X:

- Calculate *M*<sub>r</sub> of X(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>:

*M*<sub>r</sub> = $\frac{\mathrm{mass}}{\mathrm{moles}}$

*M*<sub>r</sub> = $\frac{5.0}{0.03372}$

*M*<sub>r</sub> = 148.3

**[1 mark]**

- Determine the relative atomic mass of X:

*A*<sub>r</sub>(X) = 148.3 - (2 × 62.0)

*A*<sub>r</sub>(X) = 24.3

X = **magnesium / Mg**

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for *M*<sub>r</sub> of X(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> = 148.3 (accept 148.0 to 148.5)
> 
> 1 mark for *A*<sub>r</sub>(X) = 24.3 **AND** identification as magnesium / Mg
> 
> Allow error carried forward from moles in part i)

> **[exam-tip]**
> Molar mass = mass ÷ moles = 5.0 ÷ 0.03372 = 148.3 g mol<sup>-1</sup>.
> 
> This is the *M*<sub>r</sub> of X(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>.
> 
> Subtract the mass of two nitrate groups: *M*<sub>r</sub>(NO<sub>3</sub>) = 14.0 + (3 × 16.0) = 62.0. Two nitrate groups: 2 × 62.0 = 124.0. Remaining mass = 148.3 - 124.0 = 24.3, which matches magnesium (*A*<sub>r</sub> = 24.3).

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

2X(NO~3~)~2~ (s) → 2XO (s) + 4NO~2~ (g) + O~2~ (g)

X = magnesium / Mg

Using your answer to part (b), calculate the mass, in grams, of the metal oxide produced in the complete decomposition of 0.03372 mol of X(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>.

Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the mass of the metal oxide produced:

- Determine moles of XO:

ratio X(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> : XO = 1:1

moles of XO = 0.03372 mol **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the mass of MgO (*M*<sub>r</sub> = 24.3 + 16.0 = 40.3):

mass = 0.03372 × 40.3

mass = **1.36 g** **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for moles of XO / MgO = 0.03372 mol
> 
> 1 mark for mass = 1.36 g
> 
> Allow error carried forward from part (i) moles and from identification in part (b)

> **[exam-tip]**
> From the equation 2X(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> → 2XO + 4NO<sub>2</sub> + O<sub>2</sub>, the molar ratio of X(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> to XO is 1:1. Moles of MgO equal the moles of Mg(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> used.
> 
> *M*<sub>r</sub>(MgO) = 24.3 + 16.0 = 40.3. Mass = 0.03372 × 40.3 = 1.36 g (3 significant figures).

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

5.0 g of an unknown Group 2 nitrate was decomposed to produce 0.0843 mol of gas.

2X(NO3)2 (s) → 2XO (s) + 4NO2 (g) + O2 (g)

X = magnesium / Mg

State whether strontium nitrate would need to be heated more or less strongly than **X**(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> to decompose. Explain your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> To decompose strontium nitrate:
> 
> - Heat more strongly** [1 mark]**
> - Strontium nitrate is more thermally stable than X(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>
> **OR** 
> Thermal stability increases down Group 2 **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Going down Group 2, more heat is needed to break down the nitrate ions
> 
> - The thermal stability of the Group 2 nitrates increases down the group
> 
> The smaller positive ions at the top of the groups polarise the anions more than the larger ions at the bottom
> 
> The higher the charge and the smaller the ion, the higher the polarising power
> 
> The more polarised they are, the more likely they are to thermally decompose as the bonds in the nitrate ions become weaker

parts.problemMd:
Barium sulfate is a white insoluble solid and is used in stomach X-rays and as a pigment for paint.

Calculate the number of particles in 74 mg of barium sulfate.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the number of particles in 74 mg of barium sulfate:

- Convert mass to grams and calculate moles of BaSO<sub>4</sub>:

moles = $\frac{mass}{M_{r}}$

moles = $\frac{0.074}{137.3+32.1+(4\times16.0)}$

moles = $\frac{0.074}{233.4}$

moles = 3.17 x 10<sup>-4</sup> mol **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the number of particles:

particles = moles x *L*

particles = 3.17 x 10<sup>-4</sup> x 6.022 x 10<sup>23</sup>

particles = **1.91 x 10**<sup>**20**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for moles of BaSO<sub>4</sub> = 3.17 x 10<sup>-4</sup> mol
> 
> 1 mark for number of particles = 1.91 x 10<sup>20</sup>

> **[exam-tip]**
> To find the number of particles, multiply the number of moles by the Avogadro constant, *L* = 6.022 x 10<sup>23</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>.
> 
> Remember to convert the mass from mg to g before calculating moles: 74 mg = 0.074 g.

parts.problemMd: State the ionic equation for the formation of barium sulfate.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The ionic equation for the formation of barium sulfate is:
> 
> - Ba<sup>2+</sup> (aq) + SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2-</sup> (aq) → BaSO<sub>4</sub> (s) **[1 mark]**
> 
> State symbols are required

> **[exam-tip]**
> Barium sulfate is insoluble in water and forms as a white precipitate; its state symbol is (s). The barium and sulfate ions are both aqueous (aq) before the reaction.

parts.problemMd:
A different barium compound, barium carbonate, was reacted with hydrochloric acid.

i) Write the balanced symbol equation for this reaction.

[1]

ii) 0.03 moles of carbon dioxide were formed in this reaction. Calculate the number of hydrogen ions that reacted.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The balanced symbol equation for the reaction of barium carbonate with hydrochloric acid:
> 
> - BaCO<sub>3</sub> (s) + 2HCl (aq) → BaCl<sub>2</sub> (aq) + H<sub>2</sub>O (l) + CO<sub>2</sub> (g) **[1 mark]**
> 
> State symbols are required

ii) To calculate the number of hydrogen ions that reacted:

- Moles of H<sup>+</sup> = 0.03 x 2 = 0.06 mol **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the number of H<sup>+</sup> ions:

number = moles x *L*

number = 0.06 x 6.022 x 10<sup>23</sup>

number = **3.613 x 10**<sup>**22**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for moles of H<sup>+</sup> = 0.06 mol
> 
> 1 mark for number of H<sup>+</sup> ions = 3.613 x 10<sup>22</sup>

> **[exam-tip]**
> HCl fully dissociates in solution: HCl → H<sup>+</sup> + Cl<sup>-</sup>. The moles of H<sup>+</sup> equals the moles of HCl. Since the equation shows 2 mol HCl per mol BaCO<sub>3</sub>, and 0.03 mol CO<sub>2</sub> was produced (1:1 ratio with BaCO<sub>3</sub>), moles of H<sup>+</sup> = 0.03 x 2 = 0.06 mol.

parts.problemMd:
When magnesium reacts with hydrochloric acid, the following reaction occurs:

Mg (s) + 2HCl (aq) → MgCl<sub>2</sub> (aq) + H<sub>2</sub> (g)

During the reaction, the hydrogen produced occupies 103 cm<sup>3</sup> at 25.0 °C and 100 kPa.

Calculate the amount, in moles, of hydrogen gas produced during the reaction.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the amount, in moles, of hydrogen gas produced:

- List the known values:

  - *P* = 100 kPa = 100 000 Pa
  - *V* = 103 cm<sup>3</sup> = 1.03 x 10<sup>-4</sup> m<sup>3</sup>
  - *T* = 25.0 °C = 298 K
  - *R* = 8.31 J mol<sup>-1</sup> K<sup>-1</sup>
- Rearrange *PV* = *nRT* for *n*:

$n = \frac{PV}{RT}$

**[1 mark]**

- Substitute values with correct units:

$n = \frac{100000\times0.000103}{8.31\times298}$

**[1 mark]**

- Calculate *n*:

*n* = **4.16 x 10**<sup>**-3**</sup>** mol** **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct rearrangement of *PV* = *nRT* to find *n*
> 
> 1 mark for correct substitution with *P* in Pa, *V* in m<sup>3</sup>, and *T* in K
> 
> 1 mark for *n* = 4.16 x 10<sup>-3</sup> mol (allow 4.157 x 10<sup>-3</sup> mol if *R* = 8.314 is used)

> **[exam-tip]**
> Always write out *PV* = *nRT* and your rearranged form before substituting; the equation and rearrangement often carry a mark in CIE papers.
> 
> Three unit conversions are needed before substituting:
> 
> - Pressure: kPa to Pa (multiply by 1000): 100 kPa = 100 000 Pa
> - Volume: cm<sup>3</sup> to m<sup>3</sup> (divide by 10<sup>6</sup>): 103 cm<sup>3</sup> = 1.03 x 10<sup>-4</sup> m<sup>3</sup>
> - Temperature: °C to K (add 273): 25.0 °C = 298 K
> 
> Give your answer to 3 significant figures to match the precision of the data given.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

When magnesium reacts with hydrochloric acid, the following reaction occurs:

Mg (s) + 2HCl (aq) → MgCl₂ (aq) + H₂ (g)

A student completed the same reaction as in part **(a)**, using 3.75 g of magnesium.

Calculate the mass, in grams, of magnesium chloride produced by the student during this reaction. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the mass of magnesium chloride produced:

- Calculate moles of Mg:

moles = $\frac{mass}{A_{r}}$

moles = $\frac{3.75}{24.3}$

moles = 0.15432 mol **[1 mark]**

- Apply the Mg : MgCl<sub>2</sub> = 1 : 1 ratio:

moles of MgCl<sub>2</sub> = 0.15432 mol

- Calculate the mass of MgCl<sub>2</sub>:

mass = moles x *M*<sub>r</sub>

mass of MgCl<sub>2</sub> = 0.15432 x 95.3

mass of MgCl<sub>2</sub> = **14.7 g** **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for moles of Mg = 0.15432 mol **OR **0.154 mol
> 
> 1 mark for mass of MgCl<sub>2</sub> = 14.7 g
> 
> Allow error carried forward from an incorrect number of moles of Mg

> **[exam-tip]**
> The molar ratio of Mg to MgCl<sub>2</sub> in the equation is 1:1, so moles of MgCl<sub>2</sub> = moles of Mg.
> 
> The molar mass of MgCl<sub>2</sub> = 24.3 + (2 x 35.5) = 95.3 g mol<sup>-1</sup>.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

When magnesium reacts with hydrochloric acid, the following reaction occurs:

Mg (s) + 2HCl (aq) → MgCl2 (aq) + H2 (g)

A student completed the same reaction as in part (a), using 3.75 g of magnesium.

Calculate the number of hydrogen atoms produced during the student's reaction in part **(b)**.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the number of hydrogen atoms produced:

- The ratio MgCl<sub>2</sub> : H<sub>2</sub> = 1 : 1, so moles of H<sub>2</sub> = 0.15432 mol

- Calculate the number of H<sub>2</sub> molecules:

molecules = moles x *L*

molecules = 0.15432 x 6.022 x 10<sup>23</sup>

molecules = 9.293 x 10<sup>22</sup> **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the number of H atoms:

H atoms = 9.293 x 10<sup>22</sup> x 2

H atoms = **1.859 x 10**<sup>**23**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for number of H<sub>2</sub> molecules = 9.293 x 10<sup>22</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for number of H atoms = 1.859 x 10<sup>23</sup>
> 
> Answer values rounded to 3 significant figures are accepted

> **[exam-tip]**
> The question asks for hydrogen *atoms*, not molecules. Each H<sub>2</sub> molecule contains 2 atoms, so multiply the number of molecules by 2.
> 
> Use the moles of Mg from part **(b)** — the molar ratio Mg : H<sub>2</sub> = 1 : 1, so moles of H<sub>2</sub> = moles of Mg.

Complete Table 1.1.

The completed Table 1.1 is:

| Phosphate | **Final answer:** **PO**<sub>**4**</sub><sup>**3-**</sup> |

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 3 marks for all 8 answers correct
> 
> 2 marks for 4–7 answers correct
> 
> 1 mark for 1–3 answers correct

> **[exam-tip]**
> All ions in this table must be memorised for CIE 9701; they are not provided in the Data Booklet.
> 
> You can use the Periodic Table to deduce ionic charges: oxygen forms O<sup>2-</sup>, halogens form X<sup>-</sup>, Group 1 metals form M<sup>+</sup>, and Group 2 metals form M<sup>2+</sup>.
> 
> Roman numerals indicate the charge of a metal ion, such as zinc(II) for Zn<sup>2+</sup>. Silver does not require a Roman numeral as it forms only one common ion, Ag<sup>+</sup>.

parts.problemMd:
Complete Table 1.2.

**Table 1.2**

| Sodium chloride | NaCl |
| Potassium oxide |   |
|   | Al<sub>2</sub>(CO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub> |
| Copper(II) nitrate |   |
parts.solutionMd:
The completed Table 1.2 is:

| **Ionic compound** | **Formula** |
|---|---|
| Sodium chloride | NaCl |
| Potassium oxide | **Final answer:** **K**<sub>**2**</sub>**O** |
| **Final answer:** **Aluminium carbonate** | Al<sub>2</sub>(CO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub> |
| Copper(II) nitrate | **Final answer:** **Cu(NO**<sub>**3**</sub>**)**<sub>**2**</sub> |

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for formula of potassium oxide: K<sub>2</sub>O
> 
> 1 mark for name: aluminium carbonate
> 
> 1 mark for formula of copper(II) nitrate: Cu(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>

> **[exam-tip]**
> To work out the formula of an ionic compound, balance the charges of the component ions.
> 
> Potassium is in Group 1, so K<sup>+</sup>; oxide is O<sup>2-</sup>. Two K<sup>+</sup> ions balance one O<sup>2-</sup> ion, giving K<sub>2</sub>O.
> 
> For compounds with complex ions in brackets, the subscript outside the bracket shows how many of that ion are present: Cu(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> contains two NO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup> ions.

parts.problemMd:
Aqueous silver nitrate should not be acidified with hydrochloric acid as it forms a white precipitate of silver chloride, AgCl, and nitric acid.

i) Write the chemical equation for the reaction of silver nitrate with hydrochloric acid. Your answer should include state symbols.

[2]

ii) Silver ions from the silver nitrate and chloride ions from the hydrochloric acid are responsible for the formation of silver chloride.

Ag<sup>+</sup> + Cl<sup>-</sup> → AgCl

Suggest why the nitrate ions and hydrogen ions do not appear in this ionic equation.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
i) The balanced chemical equation for the reaction is:

AgNO<sub>3</sub> (aq) + HCl (aq) → AgCl (s) + HNO<sub>3</sub> (aq)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for all correct chemical formulae: AgNO<sub>3</sub>, HCl, AgCl, HNO<sub>3</sub>
> 
> 1 mark for all state symbols correct: (aq), (aq), (s), (aq)

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii) The nitrate and hydrogen ions do not appear in the ionic equation because:
> 
> Any **one **from:
> 
> - They are spectator ions
> - They do not take part in the reaction
> - They are not involved in the formation of silver chloride
> 
> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> State symbols are always required unless the question says otherwise. Silver nitrate and hydrochloric acid are aqueous (aq); silver chloride is a precipitate (s).
> 
> An ionic equation shows only the ions directly involved in forming the product. Nitrate and hydrogen ions are spectator ions; their state, charge, and oxidation number are unchanged by the reaction, so they are not included.

parts.problemMd:
Aqueous barium chloride should not be acidified with sulfuric acid as it forms a white precipitate of barium sulfate and hydrochloric acid.

i) Write the chemical equation for the reaction of barium chloride with sulfuric acid. Your answer should include state symbols.

[2]

ii) Write the ionic equation for the formation of barium sulfate.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
i) The balanced chemical equation for the reaction is:

BaCl<sub>2</sub> (aq) + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (aq) → BaSO<sub>4</sub> (s) + 2HCl (aq)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for all correct chemical formulae: BaCl<sub>2</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>, BaSO<sub>4</sub>, HCl
> 
> 1 mark for correct balancing **AND** all state symbols correct: (aq), (aq), (s), (aq)

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii) The ionic equation for the formation of barium sulfate is:
> 
> - Ba<sup>2+</sup> (aq) + SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2-</sup> (aq) → BaSO<sub>4</sub> (s) **[1 mark]**
> 
> State symbols are required

> **[exam-tip]**
> BaCl<sub>2</sub> releases two Cl<sup>-</sup> ions, so two HCl are produced on the right to balance the equation.
> 
> Spectator ions (Cl<sup>-</sup> and H<sup>+</sup>) are removed from the ionic equation; only the ions forming the precipitate, Ba<sup>2+</sup> and SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2-</sup>, are shown.

parts.problemMd: Define the terms empirical formula and molecular formula.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Empirical formula and molecular formula are:
> 
> - Empirical formula: the simplest whole number ratio of atoms of each element in a compound **[1 mark]**
> - Molecular formula: the actual number of atoms of each element in one molecule of a compound **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> These are 1-mark definitions that appear frequently in CIE papers.
> 
> - For empirical formula, the key phrase is "simplest whole number ratio."
> - For molecular formula, be specific: "actual number of atoms of each element in one molecule". "Actual ratio," is too vague.
> 
> The empirical formula and molecular formula can be identical.
> 
> For example, H<sub>2</sub>O and CO<sub>2</sub> cannot be simplified further. This means that their empirical and molecular formulas are the same.

parts.problemMd:
Three organic compounds are shown in Fig. 5.1.

![Displayed structural formulas of acetic acid, glucose and lactic acid](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/2-atoms-molecules-and-stoichiometry/2-3-formulas/assets/002-displayed-structural-formulas-of-acetic-acid-glu.png)

**Fig. 5.1**

i) State the molecular formula of each compound.

Acetic acid ..............................

Glucose ..............................

Lactic acid ..............................

[3]

ii) State the empirical formula of all three compounds.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The molecular formula of each compound:
> 
> - Acetic acid: C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>O<sub>2</sub> **[1 mark]**
> - Glucose: C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>6</sub> **[1 mark]**
> - Lactic acid: C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>6</sub>O<sub>3</sub> **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The empirical formula of all three compounds:
> 
> - CH<sub>2</sub>O **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For part i, count the atoms directly from the displayed structural formula in Fig. 5.1.
> 
> - Acetic acid has 2C, 4H, 2O
> - Glucose has 6C, 12H, 6O
> - For lactic acid, note that the structure shown is not a fully displayed formula. Skeletal carbons and one hydrogen are not drawn explicitly. The complete structure has 3 carbons, 6 hydrogens, and 3 oxygens, giving C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>6</sub>O<sub>3</sub>.
> 
> For part ii, all three compounds have the same C:H:O ratio of 1:2:1. The simplest whole number ratio gives the empirical formula CH<sub>2</sub>O, even though their molecular formulas are all different. This shows why the empirical formula alone cannot uniquely identify a compound.

parts.problemMd:
An unknown hydrocarbon contains 85.7% carbon. The relative molecular mass of the unknown hydrocarbon is 56.0.

i) Calculate the empirical formula of the unknown hydrocarbon. Show your working.

[3]

ii) Determine the molecular formula of the unknown hydrocarbon. Show your working.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
i) To calculate the empirical formula of the unknown hydrocarbon:

- Determine the percentage of hydrogen:

%H = 100 − 85.7

%H = 14.3%

- Divide each percentage by the relative atomic mass (A<sub>r</sub>):

moles of C = $\frac{85.7}{12.0}$ = 7.142

moles of H = $\frac{14.3}{1.0}$ = 14.3

**[1 mark]**

- Divide by the smallest value (7.142) to find the simplest ratio:

C: $\frac{7.142}{7.142}$ = 1

H: $\frac{14.3}{7.142}$ = 2.00

**[1 mark]**

Empirical formula = **CH**<sub>**2**</sub>

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> i)
> 
> 1 mark for the correct moles of carbon (7.142) **AND **hydrogen (14.3)
> 
> 1 mark for the correct ratio values of carbon (1) **AND **hydrogen (2)
> 
> 1 mark for the correct empirical formula (CH<sub>2</sub>)
> 
> Workings must be shown

ii) To determine the molecular formula of the unknown hydrocarbon:

- Calculate the mass of one empirical formula unit and the multiplier:

M<sub>r</sub> of CH<sub>2</sub> = 12.0 + 2(1.0) = 14.0

$\frac{56.0}{14.0}$ = 4 **[1 mark]**

Molecular formula = **C**<sub>**4**</sub>**H**<sub>**8**</sub> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii) Allow error carried forward from an incorrect empirical formula in part (i)

> **[exam-tip]**
> For empirical formula calculations from percentage composition, assume a 100 g sample. This converts percentage values directly to masses in grams.
> 
> Always use A<sub>r</sub> values to one decimal place from the CIE Data Booklet (C = 12.0, H = 1.0). Rounding atomic masses introduces errors that compound across calculation stages.
> 
> Show the division step explicitly (% ÷ A<sub>r</sub> = moles). This step carries a mark, and writing only the result is not sufficient when working is required.
> 
> To go from empirical formula to molecular formula: calculate the M<sub>r</sub> of the empirical formula unit, divide the given M<sub>r</sub> by this to find the multiplier, then multiply each subscript.

parts.problemMd: State the difference between an anhydrous salt and a hydrated salt.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The difference between an anhydrous salt and a hydrated salt:
> 
> - An anhydrous salt contains no water of crystallisation
> **OR**
> A hydrated salt contains water of crystallisation **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The prefix *hydr-* in "hydrated" refers to water. A hydrated salt contains water molecules incorporated into its crystal structure (water of crystallisation). An anhydrous salt has had all such water removed, typically by heating.
> 
> Water of crystallisation is chemically bonded within the crystal lattice in a fixed ratio, shown by the formula notation, e.g. CaSO<sub>4</sub>•2H<sub>2</sub>O for hydrated gypsum.

parts.problemMd:
Gypsum is a salt that can contain water of crystallisation. In its anhydrous form, the chemical formula of gypsum is CaSO<sub>4</sub>. 1.80 g of water is added to 6.81 g of gypsum to form the hydrated salt, CaSO<sub>4</sub>•xH<sub>2</sub>O.

Calculate the value of x in CaSO<sub>4</sub>•xH<sub>2</sub>O. Show your working.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the value of x in CaSO<sub>4</sub>•xH<sub>2</sub>O:

- Calculate the molar mass of CaSO<sub>4</sub>:

M<sub>r</sub>(CaSO<sub>4</sub>) = 40.1 + 32.1 + 4(16.0) = 136.2

- Calculate the moles of CaSO<sub>4</sub>:

moles of CaSO<sub>4</sub> = $\frac{6.81}{136.2}$ = 0.05000 mol **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the molar mass of H<sub>2</sub>O:

M<sub>r</sub>(H<sub>2</sub>O) = 2(1.0) + 16.0 = 18.0

- Calculate the moles of H<sub>2</sub>O:

moles of H<sub>2</sub>O = $\frac{1.80}{18.0}$ = 0.1000 mol **[1 mark]**

- Find the mole ratio and state the value of x:

ratio CaSO<sub>4</sub> : H<sub>2</sub>O = $\frac{0.05000}{0.05000}$ : $\frac{0.1000}{0.05000}$ = 1 : 2

x = **2** **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Accept x = 2 from a consistent method even if intermediate values differ slightly due to rounding.
> 
> CaSO<sub>4</sub>•2H<sub>2</sub>O is accepted as an alternative to x = 2.
> 
> The value of x must be a whole number.
> 
> Allow error carried forward from an incorrect number of moles of CaSO<sub>4</sub> as long as the ratio method is applied correctly.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Water of crystallisation calculations follow the same approach as empirical formula calculations, convert masses to moles, then find the simplest whole number ratio.
> 
> Always calculate *M*<sub>r</sub> from the formula using Data Booklet values. For CaSO<sub>4</sub>: Ca (40.1) + S (32.1) + 4 × O (16.0) = 136.2.
> 
> The value of x must always be a whole number. If your calculation gives a non-integer result (e.g. 1.98), round to the nearest integer and state clearly that x = 2.

parts.problemMd:
Cobalt(II) sulfate is used in storage batteries, electroplating baths and as an additive to soils and animal feeds.

A sample of hydrated cobalt sulfate, CoSO<sub>4</sub>•xH<sub>2</sub>O, has a relative formula mass of 173.0.

Calculate a value for 'x'.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the value of x in CoSO<sub>4</sub>•xH<sub>2</sub>O:

- Calculate the *M*<sub>r</sub> of anhydrous CoSO<sub>4</sub>:

*M*<sub>r</sub>(CoSO<sub>4</sub>) = 58.9 + 32.1 + 4(16.0) = 155.0

- Calculate the mass of water in the hydrated salt:

mass of water = *M*<sub>r</sub> of anhydrous CoSO<sub>4</sub>•xH<sub>2</sub>O - *M*<sub>r</sub> of anhydrous CoSO<sub>4</sub>

mass of water = 173.0 − 155.0 
mass of water = 18.0

**[1 mark]**

- Divide by the *M*<sub>r</sub> of water to find x:

x = $\frac{18.0}{18.0}$

x = **1**

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for both *M*<sub>r</sub>(CoSO<sub>4</sub>) = 155.0 and mass of H<sub>2</sub>O = 18.0
> 
> 1 mark for x = 1 **OR** CoSO<sub>4</sub>•H<sub>2</sub>O / CoSO<sub>4</sub>•1H<sub>2</sub>O

> **[exam-tip]**
> This question gives you the *M*<sub>r</sub> of the hydrated salt directly. To find x, subtract the *M*<sub>r</sub> of the anhydrous salt from the given *M*<sub>r</sub> to find the mass contributed by the water, then divide by 18.0 (*M*<sub>r</sub> of H<sub>2</sub>O).
> 
> You can also set up the equation: 155.0 + 18.0x = 173.0, then solve for x. Both approaches give the same answer.
> 
> Always calculate *M*<sub>r</sub>(CoSO<sub>4</sub>) from Data Booklet values: Co (58.9) + S (32.1) + 4 × O (16.0) = 155.0.

parts.problemMd:
A student completed an experiment to determine the value of 'x' in a hydrated salt.

They heated a solid sample of the salt, CoSO<sub>4</sub>.xH<sub>2</sub>O, in a crucible for 60 seconds and recorded the following set of results.

**Table 2.1**

| Mass of empty crucible (g) | 29.22 |
|---|---|
| Mass of crucible and solid before heating (g) | 32.67 |
| Mass of crucible and solid after heating (g) | 32.02 |

Use the data obtained by the student in Table 2.1 to calculate a value for 'x'.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the value of x in CoSO<sub>4</sub>.xH<sub>2</sub>O:

- Calculate the masses of anhydrous CoSO<sub>4</sub> and water removed:

mass of CoSO<sub>4</sub> = 32.02 − 29.22 = 2.80 g

mass of H<sub>2</sub>O = 32.67 − 32.02 = 0.65 g

**[1 mark]**

- Calculate the moles of each compound:

moles of CoSO<sub>4</sub> = $\frac{2.80}{155.0}$ = 0.01806 mol

moles of H<sub>2</sub>O = $\frac{0.65}{18.0}$ = 0.03611 mol

**[1 mark]**

- Find the mole ratio:

ratio CoSO<sub>4</sub> : H<sub>2</sub>O = $\frac{0.01806}{0.01806}$ : $\frac{0.03611}{0.01806}$ = 1 : 1.998

**[1 mark]**

x = **2** **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct mass of anhydrous CoSO<sub>4</sub> = 2.80 g **AND **correct mass of H<sub>2</sub>O lost = 0.65 g; both required
> 
> 1 mark for correct moles of CoSO<sub>4</sub> = 0.01806 mol **AND **correct moles of H<sub>2</sub>O = 0.03611 mol; both required
> 
> 1 mark for correct mole ratio ≈ 1 : 2
> 
> 1 mark for x = 2, given as a whole number
> 
> 1 : 1.99 or similar mole ratios from unrounded moles are accepted
> 
> An alternative method that also achieves full marks: calculate the *M*<sub>r</sub> of the hydrated salt (mass of sample ÷ moles of CoSO<sub>4</sub>), subtract *M*<sub>r</sub>(CoSO<sub>4</sub>) = 155.0, then divide by 18.0 to find x.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The mass of anhydrous salt is found from the mass after heating minus the empty crucible (32.02 − 29.22 = 2.80 g). The mass of water removed is the difference in mass of the crucible and solid before and after heating (32.67 − 32.02 = 0.65 g). A common mistake is to subtract the wrong pair of readings.
> 
> Keep full, unrounded intermediate values on your calculator. Do not round the moles before finding the ratio, as rounding errors may prevent the ratio from being clearly close to 1 : 2. Only round the final answer for x to the nearest whole number.
> 
> The calculated value of x = 2 is much lower than the actual value (x = 7 for CoSO<sub>4</sub>•7H<sub>2</sub>O) because the student only heated for 60 seconds, which was not long enough to drive off all the water of crystallisation.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A student completed an experiment to determine the value of 'x' in a hydrated salt.

They heated a solid sample of the salt, CoSO~4~.xH~2~O, in a crucible for 60 seconds and recorded the following set of results.

**Table 2.1**

| Mass of empty crucible (g) | 29.22 |
| --- | :---: |
| Mass of crucible and solid before heating (g) | 32.67 |
| Mass of crucible and solid after heating (g) | 32.02 |

The actual value for x in CoSO<sub>4</sub>.xH<sub>2</sub>O is 7.

i) Suggest **one** reason for the difference between your calculated value in **part (b)** and the actual value.

[1]

ii) Explain how you could improve the experiment the student did, using the same equipment, to achieve a value closer to the correct value for x.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) One reason for the calculated value being lower than the actual value:
> 
> Any **one** from:
> 
> - Failure to remove / drive off all of the water of crystallisation
> - Not heated to constant mass
> - Heated for an insufficient time (60 seconds is not long enough)
> 
> **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) How the experiment could be improved:
> 
> - Heat to constant mass
> **OR**
> Continue heating and reweighing until successive readings agree **[1 mark]**
> - To ensure that all / more of the water of crystallisation has been removed / driven off **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For part i, the student heated for only 60 seconds. The time was too short to drive off all the water of crystallisation, so the calculated x is lower than the actual value.
> 
> For part ii, "heat to constant mass" is the standard improvement for this experiment. State both the procedure (heat, cool, weigh, repeat until successive masses agree) and the reason (ensures all water of crystallisation has been removed). Both points are needed for full marks.

parts.problemMd:
Cobalt(II) sulfate undergoes a displacement reaction with magnesium because magnesium is a more reactive metal than cobalt.

Write an **ionic **equation for this reaction. State symbols are **not** required.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The ionic equation for the displacement reaction:
> 
> - Co<sup>2+</sup> + Mg → Mg<sup>2+</sup> + Co **[1 mark]**
> 
> State symbols are not required.

> **[exam-tip]**
> In an ionic equation, spectator ions are removed. Sulfate (SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2-</sup>) appears in both CoSO<sub>4</sub> and MgSO<sub>4</sub> and does not change, so it is a spectator ion and is excluded.
> 
> The overall equation is:
> 
> CoSO<sub>4</sub> + Mg → MgSO<sub>4</sub> + Co
> 
> Removing the sulfate spectator ion gives the ionic equation:
> 
> Co<sup>2+</sup> + Mg → Mg<sup>2+</sup> + Co
> 
> Magnesium and cobalt are both uncharged metals in this equation, so only the aqueous ions carry charges.

parts.problemMd:
Chevreul's salt or copper(I, II) sulfite dihydrate, Cu<sub>3</sub>(SO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>•2H<sub>2</sub>O, is an unusual hydrated salt as it contains copper in both of its common oxidation states.

The first step in the formation of Chevreul's salt is the reaction of aqueous copper sulfate with a solution of potassium metabisulfite, K<sub>2</sub>S<sub>2</sub>O<sub>5</sub>.

Complete the equation for the reaction to form the anhydrous Chevreul's salt.

_CuSO<sub>4</sub> + _K<sub>2</sub>S<sub>2</sub>O<sub>5</sub> → _Cu<sub>3</sub>(SO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> + 4K<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> + _SO<sub>2</sub>
parts.solutionMd:
The completed equation is:

**3**CuSO<sub>4</sub> + **4**K<sub>2</sub>S<sub>2</sub>O<sub>5</sub> → Cu<sub>3</sub>(SO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> + 4K<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> + **5**SO<sub>2</sub>

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for coefficient 3 (CuSO<sub>4</sub>)
> 
> 1 mark for coefficient 4 (K<sub>2</sub>S<sub>2</sub>O<sub>5</sub>) **AND **coefficient 5 (SO<sub>2</sub>)

> **[exam-tip]**
> To balance this equation, start with copper. The product Cu<sub>3</sub>(SO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> contains 3 copper atoms, so 3CuSO<sub>4</sub> is needed on the reactant side.
> 
> With 4K<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> as a fixed product, you need 4K<sub>2</sub>S<sub>2</sub>O<sub>5</sub> to provide the 8 potassium atoms. This also brings in 8 sulfur atoms from the metabisulfite.
> 
> Count total sulfur on the reactant side: 3 (from 3CuSO<sub>4</sub>) + 8 (from 4K<sub>2</sub>S<sub>2</sub>O<sub>5</sub>) = 11. Sulfur on the product side: 2 (in Cu<sub>3</sub>(SO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>) + 4 (in 4K<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>) = 6. The remaining 5 sulfur atoms appear as 5SO<sub>2</sub>.

parts.problemMd:
The chemical formula of Chevreul's salt is sometimes written as Cu<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>3</sub>•CuSO<sub>3</sub>•2H<sub>2</sub>O to show that it contains copper(I) sulfite and copper(II) sulfite.

Calculate the percentage by mass of copper(I) ions in copper(I) sulfite.

Show your working.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the percentage by mass of copper(I) ions in Cu<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>3</sub>:

- Calculate the *M*<sub>r</sub> of copper(I) sulfite, Cu<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>3</sub>:

*M*<sub>r</sub>(Cu<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>3</sub>) = 2(63.5) + 32.1 + 3(16.0)

*M*<sub>r</sub>(Cu<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>3</sub>) = 207.1 **[1 mark]**

- Apply the percentage by mass formula:

% by mass = $\frac{A_{r}\times\mathrm{number} \mathrm{of} \mathrm{atoms}}{\mathrm{mass} \mathrm{of} \mathrm{compound}}$ x 100

% by mass of Cu<sup>+</sup> = $\frac{2\times63.5}{207.1} \times 100$ **[1 mark]**

% by mass of Cu<sup>+</sup> = **61.3%** **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for the *M*<sub>r</sub> of copper(I) sulfite, Cu<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>3</sub>: 207.1
> 
> 1 mark for correct substitution of values into the % by mass equation
> 
> 1 mark for a correct final answer of 61.3%

> **[exam-tip]**
> Copper(I) sulfite has the formula Cu<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>3</sub> (not CuSO<sub>3</sub>). Copper(I) has a +1 charge, so two Cu<sup>+</sup> ions are needed to balance the 2− charge of the sulfite ion (SO<sub>3</sub><sup>2-</sup>).

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Chevreul's salt or copper(I, II) sulfite dihydrate, Cu₃(SO₃)₂•2H₂O, is an unusual hydrated salt as it contains copper in both of its common oxidation states.

The chemical formula of Chevreul's salt is sometimes written as Cu₂SO₃•CuSO₃•2H₂O to show that it contains copper(I) sulfite and copper(II) sulfite.

Chevreul's salt can react with ammonia solution to form a deep blue solution of the tetraamminecopper(II) complex, [Cu(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> (aq). It can also react with hydrochloric acid to form a white solid of copper(I) chloride, water and sulfur dioxide.

Write an **ionic** equation for the formation of copper(I) chloride from Chevreul's salt. Include state symbols.
parts.solutionMd:
The ionic equation for the formation of copper(I) chloride:

Cu<sup>+</sup> (aq) + Cl<sup>-</sup> (aq) → CuCl (s)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct ionic equation
> 
> 1 mark for correct state symbols: (aq), (aq), (s)
> 
> Multiples of the equation, e.g. 2Cu<sup>+</sup> (aq) + 2Cl<sup>-</sup> (aq) → 2CuCl (s), are accepted

> **[exam-tip]**
> Chevreul's salt contains both copper(I) sulfite (Cu<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>3</sub>) and copper(II) sulfite (CuSO<sub>3</sub>). The question specifies that copper(I) chloride forms, so it is the Cu<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>3</sub> component that reacts with HCl.
> 
> The molecular equation is:
> 
> Cu<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>3</sub> + 2HCl → 2CuCl + SO<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O
> 
> For the ionic equation, include only the species that change. The key reaction is Cu<sup>+</sup> combining with Cl<sup>-</sup> to form insoluble CuCl. Since Cu<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>3</sub> contains two Cu<sup>+</sup> ions, this also gives:
> 
> 2Cu<sup>+</sup> (aq) + 2Cl<sup>-</sup> (aq) → 2CuCl (s).

parts.problemMd:
When Chevreul's salt is heated in an inert atmosphere, it is stable to around 200 <sup>o</sup>C. Above this temperature, a variety of compounds can be produced although the final product of sustained heating at high temperatures is copper(II) oxide.

During the heating process, a sample of the mixture is taken. After separation, the most common compound was analysed and found to contain 39.8% copper, 20.1% sulfur and the rest oxygen.

Calculate the empirical formula of the most common compound. Show your working.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the empirical formula of the most common compound:

- Calculate the percentage of oxygen:

%O = 100 − 39.8 − 20.1 = 40.1% **[1 mark]**

- Divide each percentage by the relative atomic mass (*A*<sub>r</sub>):

moles of Cu = $\frac{39.8}{63.5}$ = 0.6268

moles of S = $\frac{20.1}{32.1}$ = 0.6262

moles of O = $\frac{40.1}{16.0}$ = 2.506

**[1 mark]**

- Divide by the smallest value (0.6262) to find the simplest ratio:

Cu: $\frac{0.6268}{0.6262}$ = 1.001

S: $\frac{0.6262}{0.6262}$ = 1

O: $\frac{2.506}{0.6262}$ = 4.002

Empirical formula = **CuSO**<sub>**4**</sub>

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for %O = 40.1%
> 
> 1 mark for all three mole values correctly calculated by dividing by the respective *A*<sub>r</sub>
> 
> 1 mark for the ratio (1 : 1 : 4) **AND **the correct empirical formula CuSO<sub>4</sub>
> 
> Use *A*<sub>r</sub> values to one decimal place: Cu = 63.5, S = 32.1, O = 16.0

> **[exam-tip]**
> The percentage of oxygen is not given directly; calculate it: %O = 100 − 39.8 − 20.1 = 40.1%.
> 
> Use *A*<sub>r</sub> values to one decimal place from the CIE Data Booklet (Cu = 63.5, not 64). Rounding *A*<sub>r</sub> values before dividing introduces errors.
> 
> The ratios of 1.001 and 4.002 are very close to integers, so always round to the nearest whole number when the ratio is clearly near an integer. The empirical formula CuSO<sub>4</sub> is the anhydrous form of copper(II) sulfate.

parts.problemMd:
A synthetic carbohydrate was isotopically labelled with carbon-13.

Analysis of a 12 g sample of the carbohydrate found it to contain 6.93 g carbon, 0.80 g hydrogen and the remainder was oxygen.

Calculate the empirical formula of the carbohydrate. Show your working.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the empirical formula of the carbohydrate:

- Calculate the mass of oxygen:

mass of O = 12.00 − 6.93 − 0.80

mass of O = 4.27 g

**[1 mark]**

- Divide each mass by the relative atomic mass (*A*<sub>r</sub>):

  - Note: carbon-13 has *A*<sub>r</sub> = 13.0

moles of C = $\frac{6.93}{13.0}$ = 0.5331

moles of H = $\frac{0.80}{1.0}$ = 0.80

moles of O = $\frac{4.27}{16.0}$ = 0.2669

**[1 mark]**

- Divide by the smallest value (0.2669) to find the simplest ratio:

C: $\frac{0.5331}{0.2669}$ = 1.997

H: $\frac{0.80}{0.2669}$ = 2.998

O: $\frac{0.2669}{0.2669}$ = 1

Empirical formula = **C**<sub>**2**</sub>**H**<sub>**3**</sub>**O**

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for the mass of O: 4.27 g
> 
> 1 mark for the correct moles of carbon (using *A*<sub>r</sub>(C) = 13.0), hydrogen and oxygen
> 
> 1 mark for the correct empirical formula: C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>3</sub>O

> **[exam-tip]**
> The key detail here is that the carbon is carbon-13, so *A*<sub>r</sub>(C) = 13.0, not 12.0. This is intentional. Using *A*<sub>r</sub> = 12.0 gives the awkward ratio 2.16 : 3 : 1, which should prompt you to re-read the question.
> 
> Always calculate the missing element's mass before starting. Here: mass of O = 12.00 − 6.93 − 0.80 = 4.27 g.
> 
> Keep the full, unrounded mole values on your calculator when dividing by the smallest to find the ratio. The values 1.997 and 2.998 round cleanly to 2 and 3, confirming the empirical formula C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>3</sub>O.

parts.problemMd:
The fermentation of glucose, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>6</sub>, produces ethanol and carbon dioxide.

Construct an equation for this reaction.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The balanced equation for fermentation of glucose:
> 
> - C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>6</sub> → 2C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH + 2CO<sub>2</sub> **[1 mark]**
> 
> State symbols are not required.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Fermentation converts glucose to ethanol and carbon dioxide in a 1 : 2 : 2 molar ratio. This ratio is used directly in the percentage yield calculation in part (c).
> 
> Hydration of ethene is the other main industrial method for producing ethanol: CH<sub>2</sub>=CH<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O → CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH. Both routes are covered in the organic chemistry topics later in the specification.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The fermentation of glucose, C~6~H~12~O~6~, produces ethanol and carbon dioxide.

The balanced equation for fermentation of glucose:
C~6~H~12~O~6~ → 2C~2~H~5~OH + 2CO~2~

During the fermentation process in the reaction in part (b), 312 g of ethanol was produced from 1.5 kg of glucose.

Calculate the percentage yield of this reaction. Give your answer to 3 significant figures. Show your working.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the percentage yield of ethanol:

- Calculate the moles of glucose (convert 1.5 kg to g first):

moles = $\frac{mass ( \mathrm{g} )}{M_{r} }$

moles of glucose = $\frac{1500}{180.0}$

moles of glucose = 8.333 mol

**[1 mark]**

- Calculate the theoretical moles and mass of ethanol (molar ratio 1 : 2):

moles of ethanol = 8.333 × 2

moles of ethanol = 16.667 mol

mass = moles x *M*<sub>r</sub>

theoretical mass of ethanol = 16.667 × 46.0

theoretical mass of ethanol = 766.7 g

**[1 mark]**

- Calculate the percentage yield:

percentage yield = $\frac{\mathrm{actual} \mathrm{yield}}{\mathrm{theoretical} \mathrm{yield}}$ x 100

percentage yield = $\frac{312}{766.7}$ × 100

percentage yield = **40.7%**

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for the moles of glucose: 8.333 mol
> 
> 1 mark for moles of ethanol: 16.667 mol **AND **theoretical mass of ethanol: 766.7 g
> 
> 1 mark for the correct percentage yield: 40.7%
> 
> Allow error carried forward from an incorrect molar ratio in part (b), applied consistently throughout.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Always convert kg to g before calculating moles: 1.5 kg = 1500 g.
> 
> Keep the full, unrounded moles of glucose on your calculator throughout. Using 8.3 mol instead of 8.333 mol leads to a theoretical mass of 763.6 g and a final answer of 40.9%, which is incorrect due to early rounding and will lose marks.

parts.problemMd:
Magnesium carbonate is a common antacid that is used to neutralise excess stomach acid, HCl.

MgCO<sub>3</sub> (s) + 2HCl (aq) → MgCl<sub>2</sub> (aq) + CO<sub>2</sub> (g) + H<sub>2</sub>O (l)

5.31 g of magnesium carbonate reacts completely with an excess of hydrochloric acid.

Calculate the volume, in dm<sup>3</sup>, of carbon dioxide produced at room conditions. Show your working.

Volume of CO<sub>2</sub> = .................. dm<sup>3</sup>
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the volume of CO<sub>2</sub> produced at room conditions:

- Calculate the moles of MgCO<sub>3</sub>:

moles = $\frac{\mathrm{mass}}{M_{r}}$

moles of MgCO<sub>3</sub> = $\frac{5.31}{84.3}$

moles of MgCO<sub>3</sub> = 0.06299 mol **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the volume of CO<sub>2</sub> (moles CO<sub>2</sub> = moles MgCO<sub>3</sub>):

volume = moles x molar gas volume

volume CO<sub>2</sub> = 0.06299 x 24.0

volume CO<sub>2</sub> = **1.51 dm**<sup>**3**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Allow error carried forward for the volume if an incorrect number of moles is used consistently.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The *M*<sub>r</sub> of MgCO<sub>3</sub> = 24.3 + 12.0 + 3(16.0) = 84.3. You need to calculate this from the CIE Data Booklet atomic masses.
> 
> From the equation, MgCO<sub>3</sub> and CO<sub>2</sub> are in a 1 : 1 molar ratio, so moles of CO<sub>2</sub> = moles of MgCO<sub>3</sub>.
> 
> 1 mol of any gas occupies 24.0 dm<sup>3</sup> at room conditions.

parts.problemMd:
Another magnesium salt, magnesium sulfate, can exist in hydrated or anhydrous forms.

6.31 g of a sample of magnesium sulfate, MgSO<sub>4</sub>.xH<sub>2</sub>O, was strongly heated until a mass of 3.61 g of solid remained with no further change in mass recorded.

Calculate the value of x. Show your working.

x = .....................
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the number of moles of water of crystallisation, x:

- Calculate the moles of MgSO<sub>4</sub> (anhydrous residue):

moles = $\frac{\mathrm{mass}}{M_{r}}$

moles MgSO<sub>4</sub> = $\frac{3.61}{120.4}$

moles MgSO<sub>4</sub> = 0.02999 mol **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the moles of H<sub>2</sub>O lost on heating:

mass H<sub>2</sub>O = 6.31 − 3.61 = 2.70 g

moles H<sub>2</sub>O = $\frac{2.70}{18.0}$ = 0.1500 mol **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the molar ratio MgSO<sub>4</sub> : H<sub>2</sub>O:

ratio = $\frac{0.1500}{0.02999}$ = 5.00

MgSO<sub>4</sub> : H<sub>2</sub>O = 1 : 5

x = **5 ****[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> x must be given as an integer.
> 
> MgSO<sub>4</sub>.5H<sub>2</sub>O is an accepted final answer
> 
> Allow error carried forward from incorrect moles in steps 1 and 2 provided method is correct.

> **[exam-tip]**
> This is an empirical formula question applied to a hydrated salt. After heating, the solid that remains is anhydrous MgSO<sub>4</sub>. The mass lost is the water that was driven off.
> 
> Calculate moles of MgSO<sub>4</sub> from the residue mass and moles of H<sub>2</sub>O from the mass loss. The ratio of moles H<sub>2</sub>O : moles MgSO<sub>4</sub> gives x directly.
> 
> x must always be a whole number. If your ratio is not close to an integer, check you have used the correct *M*<sub>r</sub> values: MgSO<sub>4</sub> = 120.4 and H<sub>2</sub>O = 18.0.

parts.problemMd:
Another sample of hydrated magnesium sulfate, MgSO<sub>4</sub>.xH<sub>2</sub>O, is found to contain 51.1% water by mass.

Calculate the value of x. Show your working.

x = .....................
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate x in MgSO<sub>4</sub>.xH<sub>2</sub>O containing 51.1% water by mass:

- Assume a 100 g sample; identify the mass of each component:

mass H<sub>2</sub>O = 51.1 g

mass MgSO<sub>4</sub> = 48.9 g

- Calculate the moles of each component:

moles = $\frac{\mathrm{mass}}{M_{r}}$

moles MgSO<sub>4</sub> = $\frac{48.9}{120.4}$ = 0.4061 mol **[1 mark]**

moles H<sub>2</sub>O = $\frac{51.1}{18.0}$ = 2.839 mol **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the molar ratio MgSO<sub>4</sub> : H<sub>2</sub>O:

ratio = $\frac{2.839}{0.4061}$ = 6.99 ≈ 7

MgSO<sub>4</sub> : H<sub>2</sub>O = 1 : 7

x = **7 ****[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> x must be given as an integer. Allow 6.99 rounded to 7.
> 
> MgSO<sub>4</sub>.7H<sub>2</sub>O is an accepted final answer
> 
> Allow error carried forward from incorrect moles in steps 1 and 2 provided method is correct.

> **[exam-tip]**
> When given percentage composition, treat the percentages as masses by assuming a 100 g sample. This converts percentages directly into grams.
> 
> The calculation then follows the same steps as the previous part: find moles of each component and take the ratio.
> 
> MgSO<sub>4</sub>.7H<sub>2</sub>O is Epsom salt, so x = 7 is a well-known hydrated salt. Keep full calculator values for all intermediate steps. Only round x to an integer at the very end.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Another magnesium salt, magnesium sulfate, can exist in hydrated or anhydrous forms.

6.31 g of a sample of magnesium sulfate, MgSO~4~.xH~2~O, was strongly heated until a mass of 3.61 g of solid remained with no further change in mass recorded.

Calculate the value of x. Show your working.

State the effect on the calculated value of x if the salt was not heated to constant mass. Explain your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The effect of not heating to constant mass on the value of x:
> 
> - Some water remains in the salt / the salt remains partially hydrated / not all water is driven off **[1 mark]**
> - The calculated moles of water are too low
> **AND**
> The value of x is too small **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Think through the chain of consequences. If the salt is not fully dehydrated, the mass loss appears smaller than the true value, so fewer moles of water are recorded.
> 
> The mark scheme expects two separate points. The first mark is for identifying that some water remains (the direct cause). The second mark requires both linked consequences together: calculated moles of water too low **AND **x too small.

parts.problemMd:
A sample of a caffeinated drink contains 34 mg of caffeine, *M*<sub>r</sub> = 194.0 g mol<sup>-1</sup>.

Calculate the amount, in mol, of caffeine in the sample. Show your working.

amount of caffeine = .................... mol
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the amount of caffeine in the sample:

- Convert mass to grams: 34 mg = 0.034 g

amount of caffeine = $\frac{0.034}{194.0}$

amount of caffeine = **1.75 x 10**<sup>**-4**</sup> mol **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Allow 1.74–1.76 x 10<sup>-4</sup> mol.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Always check the units given in the question. The mass here is in milligrams; convert to grams before dividing by *M*<sub>r</sub>: 34 mg ÷ 1000 = 0.034 g.

parts.problemMd:
Caffeine contains 49.48% carbon, 5.20% hydrogen and 28.85% nitrogen by mass. The remainder is oxygen.

Calculate the empirical formula of caffeine. Show your working.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the empirical formula of caffeine:

- Find % oxygen by mass:

%O = 100 − 49.48 − 5.20 − 28.85

%O = 16.47%

- Divide each % by *A*<sub>r</sub> to find moles:

moles C = $\frac{49.48}{12.0}$ = 4.123

moles H = $\frac{5.20}{1.0}$ = 5.200

moles N = $\frac{28.85}{14.0}$ = 2.061

**[1 mark]**

moles O = $\frac{16.47}{16.0}$ = 1.029

**[1 mark]**

- Divide each by the smallest value (moles O = 1.029):

C : H : N : O = $\frac{4.123}{1.029}$ : $\frac{5.200}{1.029}$ : $\frac{2.061}{1.029}$ : $\frac{1.029}{1.029}$

C : H : N : O = 4 : 5 : 2 : 1

empirical formula = **C**<sub>**4**</sub>**H**<sub>**5**</sub>**N**<sub>**2**</sub>**O**

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct moles of carbon, hydrogen and nitrogen
> 
> 1 mark for correct moles of oxygen
> 
> 1 mark for correct empirical formula
> 
> Allow error carried forward from a correct method with incorrect moles.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The oxygen percentage is not given; you must calculate it: 100 − 49.48 − 5.20 − 28.85 = 16.47%.
> 
> Show all working clearly. If any individual mole calculation is wrong, you can still gain marks for a correct method.
> 
> The full calculation can be set out as a table:
> 
> | Element | C | H | N | O |
> |---|---|---|---|---|
> | % | 49.48 | 5.20 | 28.85 | 16.47 |
> | *A*<sub>r</sub> | 12.0 | 1.0 | 14.0 | 16.0 |
> | Moles | 4.123 | 5.200 | 2.061 | 1.029 |
> | Ratio | 4 | 5.05 ≈ 5 | 2 | 1 |
> 
> Always divide by the smallest moles value to get the ratio. Keep full calculator values throughout, only round to whole numbers at the ratio step.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A sample of a caffeinated drink contains 34 mg of caffeine, Mr = 194.0 g mol^-1.

Caffeine contains 49.48% carbon, 5.20% hydrogen and 28.85% nitrogen by mass. The remainder is oxygen.

Calculate the empirical formula of caffeine.

Use your answer to (b) and the *M*<sub>r</sub> of caffeine given in part (a) to deduce the molecular formula of caffeine. Show your working.
parts.solutionMd:
To deduce the molecular formula of caffeine:

- Calculate the *M*<sub>r</sub> of empirical formula C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>5</sub>N<sub>2</sub>O:

*M*<sub>r</sub>(C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>5</sub>N<sub>2</sub>O) = (4 x 12.0) + (5 x 1.0) + (2 x 14.0) + 16.0

*M*<sub>r</sub>(C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>5</sub>N<sub>2</sub>O) = 97.0

- Find the multiplier:

multiplier = $\frac{194.0}{97.0}$ = 2.00 ≈ 2

molecular formula = **C**<sub>**8**</sub>**H**<sub>**10**</sub>**N**<sub>**4**</sub>**O**<sub>**2**</sub> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Allow error carried forward from an incorrect empirical formula in (b) provided method is correct.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Divide the *M*<sub>r</sub> of caffeine (194.0) by the *M*<sub>r</sub> of the empirical formula (97.0) to find the multiplier. Here, 194.0 / 97.0 = 2, so the molecular formula is 2 x C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>5</sub>N<sub>2</sub>O = C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>10</sub>N<sub>4</sub>O<sub>2</sub>.

parts.problemMd:
Apatite is a general term used for a family of various calcium phosphate compounds commonly found in rocks and minerals, bones and teeth.

i) State the formula of calcium phosphate.

[1]

ii) Hydroxylapatite, Ca<sub>5</sub>(PO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>3</sub>OH, is one member of the apatite family and is a major component of bone.

Deduce the oxidation number of phosphorus in hydroxylapatite, Ca<sub>5</sub>(PO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>3</sub>OH. Show your working.

[2]

iii) Another member of the apatite family is chlorapatite.

Suggest the formula of chlorapatite.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The formula of calcium phosphate is:
> 
> - Ca<sub>3</sub>(PO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub> **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) Deducing the oxidation number of phosphorus in hydroxylapatite:
> 
> - P + 4(–2) = –3 **[1 mark]**
> - P = +5 **[1 mark]**
> 
> iii) The formula of chlorapatite is:
> 
> - Ca<sub>5</sub>(PO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>3</sub>Cl **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
