parts.problemMd:
0.144 g of C<sub>60</sub> is placed in a 100 cm<sup>3</sup> container of hydrogen gas at a temperature of 20 °C and a pressure of 1.00 × 10<sup>5</sup> Pa.

The container is heated to make the C<sub>60</sub> and hydrogen gas react. The reaction occurs as shown in the equation.

C<sub>60</sub> (s) + xH<sub>2</sub> (g) → C<sub>60</sub>H<sub>2x</sub> (s)

After the reaction, the container is allowed to cool to 20 °C. The pressure decreases to 2.21 × 10<sup>4</sup> Pa. All of the C<sub>60</sub> has reacted.

i) Name the type of reaction that occurs.

[1]

ii) Calculate the amount, in moles, of C<sub>60</sub> that reacts. Show your working.

[1]

iii) Calculate the amount, in moles, of hydrogen gas that reacted with the C<sub>60</sub>. Show your working.

[3]

iv) Use your answers from (c)(ii) and (c)(iii) to deduce the molecular formula of the hydrocarbon, C<sub>60</sub>H<sub>2x</sub>. Show your working.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The type of reaction:
> 
> - Addition / hydrogenation **[1 mark]**

ii) To calculate the moles of C<sub>60</sub>:

- Calculate the *M*<sub>r</sub> of C<sub>60</sub>:

*M*<sub>r</sub>(C<sub>60</sub>) = 12 × 60

*M*<sub>r</sub>(C<sub>60</sub>) = 720 g mol<sup>-1</sup>

- Calculate the moles of C<sub>60</sub>:

moles = $\frac{mass}{M_{r}}$

n(C<sub>60</sub>) = $\frac{0.144}{720}$

n(C<sub>60</sub>) = **2.00 × 10**<sup>**-4**</sup> mol **[1 mark]**

iii) To calculate the moles of H<sub>2</sub> that reacted:

- Calculate the pressure of H<sub>2</sub> consumed (= decrease in pressure):

*p*(H<sub>2</sub>) = 1.00 × 10<sup>5</sup> − 2.21 × 10<sup>4</sup>

*p*(H<sub>2</sub>) = 7.79 × 10<sup>4</sup> Pa

- Convert units:

*V* = 100 cm<sup>3</sup> = 1.00 × 10<sup>-4</sup> m<sup>3</sup>

*T* = 20 + 273 = 293 K

**[1 mark]**

- Rearrange *pV* = *nRT *and substitute:

n = $\frac{pV}{RT}$

n(H<sub>2</sub>) = $\frac{7.79\times10^{4}\times1.00\times10^{-4}}{8.31\times293}$

**[1 mark]**

- Calculate the moles:

n(H<sub>2</sub>) = **3.20 × 10**<sup>**-3**</sup> **mol**

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correctly calculating the pressure of H<sub>2</sub> consumed (7.79 × 10<sup>4</sup> Pa) **AND **converting pressure and temperature to SI units
> 
> 1 mark for rearranging the ideal gas equation **AND **substituting the values
> 
> 1 mark for correctly calculating the moles (3.20 × 10<sup>-3</sup> mol)

iv) To deduce the molecular formula:

- Find the molar ratio of C<sub>60</sub> to H<sub>2</sub>:

C<sub>60</sub> : H<sub>2</sub> = 2.00 × 10<sup>-4</sup> : 3.20 × 10<sup>-3</sup>

C<sub>60</sub> : H<sub>2</sub> = 1 : 16 **[1 mark]**

- Determine x and write the molecular formula:

x = 16, so H<sub>2x</sub> = H<sub>32</sub>

molecular formula = **C**<sub>**60**</sub>**H**<sub>**32**</sub>** ****[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Allow error carried forward from part (ii) and part (iii)

> **[exam-tip]**
> The decrease in pressure after the reaction equals the pressure of the H<sub>2</sub> that was consumed, since C<sub>60</sub> is a solid and does not contribute to gas pressure.
> 
> To convert cm<sup>3</sup> to m<sup>3</sup>: divide by 10<sup>6</sup>.
> 
> The *M*<sub>r</sub> of C<sub>60</sub> is 12 × 60 = 720 g mol<sup>-1</sup>.

parts.problemMd:
Silicon shows the same type of bonding and structure as diamond.

Silicon reacts with magnesium to form Mg<sub>2</sub>Si.

Solid Mg<sub>2</sub>Si reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid to form gaseous SiH<sub>4</sub> and a solution of magnesium chloride.

i) Construct an equation for this reaction. Include state symbols.

[2]

ii) Predict the shape of the SiH<sub>4</sub> molecule.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
i) The equation for the reaction, including state symbols, is:

Mg<sub>2</sub>Si (s) + 4HCl (aq) → SiH<sub>4</sub> (g) + 2MgCl<sub>2</sub> (aq)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> i)
> 
> 1 mark for correct species **AND** correct balancing
> 
> 1 mark for all four correct state symbols
> 
> ii) The shape of the SiH<sub>4</sub> molecule is:
> 
> - Tetrahedral **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The state symbols can be deduced from the question: Mg<sub>2</sub>Si is described as solid, HCl is a dilute acid (aqueous), SiH<sub>4</sub> is described as gaseous, and magnesium chloride forms in solution (aqueous).
> 
> SiH<sub>4</sub> has the same structure as CH<sub>4</sub>.Silicon is in Group 14, so it forms 4 bonds with 4 hydrogen atoms. With 4 bonding pairs and no lone pairs, VSEPR theory predicts a tetrahedral shape with bond angles of 109.5°.

parts.problemMd:
Copper and iodine are both solids which have different physical and chemical properties.

Each element has the same face-centred crystal structure which is shown below.

![Face-centred cubic crystal structure diagram showing particles as black balls arranged in a regular lattice](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/4-states-of-matter/4-2-bonding-and-structure/assets/006-face-centred-cubic-crystal-structure-diagram-sho.png)

The particles present in such a crystal may be atoms, molecules, anions or cations. In the diagram above, the particles present are represented by the black balls.

Which type of particles are present in the iodine crystal? Give their formula.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The particles present in the iodine crystal are:
> 
> - Molecules **[1 mark]**
> 
> The formula is:
> 
> - I<sub>2</sub> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Group 17 elements such as iodine exist as diatomic molecules — two atoms share electrons to achieve a full outer shell, giving the formula I<sub>2</sub>.

parts.problemMd:
When separate samples of copper or iodine are heated to 50 °C, the copper remains as a solid while the iodine turns into a vapour.

Explain, in terms of the forces present in the solid structure, why copper remains a solid at 50 °C.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Copper remains solid at 50 °C because:
> 
> - Cations are held in a sea of delocalised electrons **[1 mark]**
> - By strong metallic bonds **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Metallic bonds exist between the positive metal ions (cations) and the delocalised electrons that move freely throughout the lattice.
> 
> A large amount of energy is required to overcome these strong bonds, hence copper has a very high melting point (1085 °C), which is well above 50 °C.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

When separate samples of copper or iodine are heated to 50 °C, the copper remains as a solid while the iodine turns into a vapour.

Explain, in terms of the forces present in the solid structure, why iodine turns into a vapour when heated to 50 °C.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Iodine turns into a vapour when heated to 50 °C because:
> 
> - There are instantaneous dipole-induced dipole forces / London dispersion forces between molecules **[1 mark]**
> - These forces are weak (so require little energy to overcome them) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Be specific about the type of intermolecular force. Van der Waals' forces is used as a generic term in the specification and is not an acceptable answer here.
> 
> The weak London dispersion forces between I<sub>2</sub> molecules mean that relatively little energy is needed to separate them, allowing iodine to vaporise at a low temperature.

parts.problemMd:
Calculate the volume, in cm<sup>3</sup>, that 5.00 g of iodine vapour occupies at 185 °C and a pressure of 100 kPa.

Assume iodine vapour behaves as an ideal gas.

The gas constant *R* = 8.31 J K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>

Show your working. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.solutionMd:
- Calculate the *M*<sub>r</sub> of iodine vapour:

*M*<sub>r</sub>(I<sub>2</sub>) = 2 × 126.9 = 253.8

- Calculate the moles of iodine vapour:

moles = $\frac{\mathrm{mass}}{M_{r}}$

moles of iodine vapour  = $\frac{5.00}{253.8}$

moles of iodine vapour  = 0.01970 mol

**[1 mark]**

- Convert units:

*T *= 185 + 273 = 458 K

*p *= 100 kPa = 1.00 × 10<sup>5</sup> Pa

**[1 mark]**

- Rearrange *pV *= *nRT *to find *V *and substitute:

*V *= $\frac{nRT}{p}$

*V *= $\frac{0.01970\times8.31\times458}{1.00\times10^{5}}$

**[1 mark]**

- Convert to cm<sup>3</sup>:

*V *= 7.50 × 10<sup>-4</sup> m<sup>3</sup> × 10<sup>6</sup>

*V* = **750 cm**<sup>**3**</sup>

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for the moles of iodine vapour
> 
> 1 mark for correct conversions of temperature **AND **pressure to SI units
> 
> 1 mark for correctly rearranging *pV* = *nRT* **AND **correct substitution of values into the rearranged equation
> 
> 1 mark for the final volume in cm<sup>3</sup>

> **[exam-tip]**
> To convert °C to K, add 273.
> 
> To convert kPa to Pa, multiply by 1000.
> 
> *V* from *pV *= *nRT *will be in m<sup>3</sup>. To convert to cm<sup>3</sup>, multiply by 10<sup>6</sup>.

parts.problemMd:
Although copper is a relatively unreactive metal, when it is heated to a high temperature in an excess of chlorine, copper(II) chloride is formed.

i) State the role of chlorine in this reaction.

[1]

ii) When a mixture of copper and iodine is heated to a high temperature, no reaction occurs. Suggest a reason for this difference.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The role of chlorine in this reaction:
> 
> - Oxidising agent **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) No reaction occurs when copper and iodine are heated because:
> 
> - Iodine is a weaker oxidising agent than chlorine **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> An oxidising agent oxidises another substance as it gains electrons and is itself reduced. In this reaction, chlorine is reduced from Cl<sub>2</sub> (oxidation state 0) to Cl<sup>-</sup> (−1) as it oxidises copper.
> 
> Iodine is less electronegative than chlorine and is a weaker oxidising agent, so it cannot oxidise copper under these conditions.

parts.problemMd:
Until 1985, carbon was thought to exist in only two structural forms or allotropes. In 1985 another form, buckminsterfullerene, was discovered, in which the carbon exists as spherical molecules.

The other two forms of carbon have very different structures.

i) Name these two forms.

[1]

ii) Give **three** differences in physical properties between these two forms.

[3]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The two forms are:
> 
> - Diamond
> **AND**
> Graphite
> 
> **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) Any **three** from (1 mark for each difference):
> 
> - Graphite can conduct electricity but diamond cannot
> - Graphite is soft / slippery but diamond is hard
> - Graphite is black but diamond is transparent / colourless
> - Graphite is less dense than diamond
> - Graphite has a lower melting point than diamond
> 
> **[3 marks]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Make sure you refer to both graphite and diamond for each difference — a statement about only one of them will not gain a mark.
> 
> In graphite, each carbon atom is bonded to only three other carbon atoms, leaving one electron per atom delocalised. This allows graphite to conduct electricity and makes it softer, as the layers can slide over each other.

parts.problemMd:
The diagram shows the structure of buckminsterfullerene.

![Diagram showing the spherical structure of buckminsterfullerene (C60), with 60 carbon atoms arranged in interlocking pentagons and hexagons](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/4-states-of-matter/4-2-bonding-and-structure/assets/005-diagram-showing-the-spherical-structure-of-buckm.png)

The molecule of buckminsterfullerene contains 60 carbon atoms.

Suggest a reason why buckminsterfullerene reacts with hydrogen under suitable conditions and give a formula for the product.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Buckminsterfullerene reacts with hydrogen because:
> 
> - Each carbon is bonded to three other carbons / has three bonding locations
> **OR**
> It is unsaturated / contains double bonds **[1 mark]**
> - C<sub>60</sub>H<sub>60</sub> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Each carbon in C<sub>60</sub> uses three of its four outer electrons to bond with three neighbouring carbons. The remaining electron can form a double bond, making the molecule unsaturated and able to react with hydrogen.
> 
> If each of the 60 carbon atoms forms one additional bond with a hydrogen atom, the formula of the product is C<sub>60</sub>H<sub>60</sub>.

parts.problemMd:
In 2010, two scientists from the University of Manchester were awarded the Nobel Prize for Physics for their work on graphene, a 'nano-material' and new structural form of carbon.

i) Graphene is in the form of sheets of carbon one atom thick.

Calculate the number of carbon atoms present in a sheet of graphene with a mass of one thousandth of a gram (0.001 g). Show your working.

[1]

ii) The number of hexagons in a large sheet of graphene can be assumed to be one half of the number of carbon atoms. Each hexagon has an area of 690 nm<sup>2</sup>.

Calculate the area of the sheet of graphene in (i). Show your working.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
i) To calculate the number of carbon atoms:

- Calculate the moles of carbon:

moles = $\frac{\mathrm{mass}}{A_{r}}$

moles of C = $\frac{0.001}{12.0}$

moles of C = 8.33 × 10<sup>-5</sup> mol

- Calculate the number of atoms of carbon:

number of atoms = moles × Avogadro's constant

number of atoms of C = 8.33 × 10<sup>-5</sup> × 6.022 × 10<sup>23</sup>

number of atoms of C = **5.02 × 10**<sup>**19**</sup>

**[1 mark]**

ii) To calculate the area of the sheet:

- Calculate the number of hexagons:

number of hexagons = $\frac{5.02\times10^{19}}{2}$

number of hexagons = 2.51 × 10<sup>19</sup> **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the area:

area = 690 × 2.51 × 10<sup>19</sup>

area = **1.73 × 10**<sup>**22**</sup>** nm**<sup>**2**</sup>** ****[1 mark]**

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Until 1985, carbon was thought to exist in only two structural forms or allotropes. In 1985 another form, buckminsterfullerene, was discovered, in which the carbon exists as spherical molecules.

The molecule of buckminsterfullerene contains 60 carbon atoms.

Graphene is in the form of sheets of carbon one atom thick.

Explain whether you would expect samples of graphene and buckminsterfullerene to be electrical conductors.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Graphene and buckminsterfullerene as electrical conductors:
> 
> - Graphene would conduct electricity because it has delocalised / free electrons **[1 mark]**
> - Buckminsterfullerene would not conduct electricity because it consists of simple molecules **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Although buckminsterfullerene contains delocalised electrons within each C<sub>60</sub> molecule, these electrons are confined to individual molecules and cannot flow through the entire structure to carry charge.
> 
> In graphene, the delocalised electrons extend across the whole sheet and are free to move, allowing electrical conduction.

parts.problemMd:
This question is about the melting points of different chemicals.

The melting and boiling points of calcium and chlorine are given in Table 4.1.

**Table 4.1**

| **Element** | **Melting point / K** | **Boiling point / K** |
|---|---|---|
| Chlorine | 172 | 239 |
| Calcium | 1115 | 1757 |

i) In terms of structure and bonding, compare the boiling points of chlorine and calcium.

[3]

ii) Explain why calcium can conduct electricity but chlorine cannot.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) Comparing the boiling points of chlorine and calcium:
> 
> - Chlorine is a simple molecular substance
> **AND**
> Calcium is a giant metallic structure / contains positive Ca<sup>2+</sup> ions in a sea of delocalised electrons **[1 mark]**
> - Chlorine has weak van der Waals / id-id forces between Cl<sub>2</sub> molecules
> **AND**
> Calcium has strong metallic bonds **[1 mark]**
> - More energy is required to break metallic bonds in calcium than to overcome the weak van der Waals forces in chlorine **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) Explaining the electrical conductivity of calcium and chlorine:
> 
> - Calcium has delocalised electrons that can move and carry charge
> **AND**
> Chlorine has no mobile electrons or ions to carry charge **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> When comparing boiling points, always refer to both the type of structure AND the type of forces/bonds present.
> 
> Chlorine molecules contain covalent bonds. It is the weak van der Waals forces between molecules that are overcome on boiling, not the covalent bonds.
> 
> Metals have delocalised electrons in both solid and liquid states, so they conduct electricity in both states.

parts.problemMd:
Sulfur dioxide and magnesium oxide are both oxides. The melting point of sulfur dioxide is –72 <sup>o</sup>C and the melting point of magnesium oxide is 2852 <sup>o</sup>C.

i) Explain, with reference to structure and bonding, the difference in the melting points of sulfur dioxide and magnesium oxide.

[3]

ii) Hydrogen fluoride, HF, and hydrogen chloride, HCl, both have simple molecular structures. The melting point of HF is −83.6 <sup>o</sup>C and the melting point of HCl is −114.2 <sup>o</sup>C.

Explain why HF has a higher melting point than HCl.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) Explaining the difference in melting points of SO<sub>2</sub> and MgO:
> 
> - Magnesium oxide / MgO is a giant ionic structure
> **AND**
> Sulfur dioxide / SO<sub>2</sub> is a simple molecular structure **[1 mark]**
> - The ionic bonds in MgO are much stronger than the weak van der Waals / intermolecular forces between SO<sub>2</sub> molecules **[1 mark]**
> - More energy is required to break the strong ionic bonds in MgO than to overcome the weak van der Waals forces in SO<sub>2</sub> **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) Explaining why HF has a higher melting point than HCl:
> 
> - HF has hydrogen bonding between molecules
> **AND**
> HCl only has weak van der Waals / id-id forces between molecules **[1 mark]**
> - More energy is required to overcome the hydrogen bonds in HF than the van der Waals forces in HCl **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> When comparing substances with different structures, always identify both structures explicitly.
> 
> Hydrogen bonding occurs when hydrogen is bonded to a highly electronegative atom (F, O or N).
> 
> Always link the strength of bonding/forces back to the energy needed to break them, which explains the relative melting/boiling points.

parts.problemMd:
Silver chloride is used in photography films as well as having antiseptic properties.

i) Describe the structure and bonding in silver chloride.

[2]

ii) Explain why silver chloride has a relatively high melting point.

[3]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) Describing the structure and bonding in silver chloride:
> 
> - Silver chloride / AgCl has a giant ionic lattice structure **[1 mark]**
> - Strong electrostatic attraction / ionic bonds between oppositely charged Ag<sup>+</sup> and Cl<sup>–</sup> ions **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) Explaining the high melting point of silver chloride:
> 
> - There is strong electrostatic attraction between the oppositely charged Ag<sup>+</sup> and Cl<sup>–</sup> ions in the giant ionic lattice **[1 mark]**
> - A large number of ionic bonds must be broken / overcome throughout the lattice **[1 mark]**
> - This requires large amounts of energy / heat **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The melting point of an ionic compound is determined by the strength of the electrostatic attraction between the oppositely charged ions in the lattice.
> 
> For a high melting point ionic compound, always state:
> 
> 1. The type of structure
> 2. The strength of the ionic bonds
> 3. The energy needed to break them
> 
> Do not confuse the electronegativity difference (which predicts whether a bond is ionic or covalent) with the strength of the ionic bond itself.

parts.problemMd:
Diamond and ice are types of crystals.

i) Describe the structure and bonding in diamond.

[2]

ii) Describe the structure and bonding in ice.

[1]

iii) Explain why diamond has a much higher melting point than ice.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) Describing the structure and bonding in diamond:
> 
> - Diamond has a giant covalent / macromolecular lattice structure **[1 mark]**
> - Each carbon atom is covalently bonded to four others in a tetrahedral arrangement **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) Describing the structure and bonding in ice:
> 
> - Ice has a simple molecular structure with hydrogen bonds between water molecules **[1 mark]**
> 
> iii) Explaining why diamond has a much higher melting point than ice:
> 
> - In diamond, strong covalent bonds between carbon atoms must be broken **[1 mark]**
> - In ice, weaker hydrogen bonds between molecules are overcome, so less energy is required **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Both diamond and ice contain covalent bonds. In diamond, these are between C atoms in the lattice. In ice (H<sub>2</sub>O), the covalent bonds are within each water molecule.
> 
> When ice melts, it is the hydrogen bonds between water molecules that are broken, not the covalent O–H bonds within the molecules.
> 
> Always use 'overcome' for intermolecular forces and 'broken' for covalent/ionic bonds to be precise in your language.

parts.problemMd:
Mercury is a naturally occurring element that is a liquid at room temperature and pressure. Some of its physical properties are shown in Table 5.1.

**Table 5.1**

| **Appearance at room temperature** | shiny silver liquid |
|---|---|
| **Melting point / **<sup>**o**</sup>**C** | -38.8 |
| **Boiling point / **<sup>**o**</sup>**C** | 356.7 |
| **Electrical conductivity** | good |

Compare and explain the electrical conductivity of mercury and sodium chloride in both the solid state and when melted.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Comparing the electrical conductivity of mercury and sodium chloride:
> 
> - Mercury conducts electricity in both solid and liquid states
> **AND**
> Sodium chloride does not conduct in the solid state but does conduct when molten **[1 mark]**
> - Mercury has delocalised electrons that are mobile in both states and carry electrical charge **[1 mark]**
> - Sodium chloride has Na<sup>+</sup> and Cl<sup>–</sup> ions that are mobile when molten but fixed in the lattice when solid, and only mobile ions can carry charge **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> This is a comparison question, so address each substance in turn to keep your answer clear and logical.
> 
> Metals have delocalised electrons which can carry charge in both the solid and liquid state.
> 
> Solid ionic compounds cannot conduct because the ions are held in fixed positions by strong electrostatic forces. Only when molten do the ions become free to move.

parts.problemMd:
The strength of ionic bonding in different compounds can be compared by using the amount of energy required to separate the ions, as shown in Table 5.2.

**Table 5.2**

| **Compound** | **Amount of energy required to separate the ions / kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup> |
|---|---|
| LiF | 1031 |
| NaF | 787 |
| MgF<sub>2</sub> | 2962 |

Using the data from Table 5.2, explain how changes in the cation affect the strength of ionic bonding in an ionic compound.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explaining the effect of changes in the cation on the strength of ionic bonding:
> 
> - The higher the charge on the cation, the greater the charge density and the stronger the ionic bonding
> **AND**
> A higher amount of energy is needed to separate Mg<sup>2+</sup> in MgF<sub>2</sub> than Li<sup>+</sup> / Na<sup>+</sup> in LiF / NaF **[1 mark]**
> - The smaller the ionic radius of the cation, the stronger the ionic bonding between the ions
> **AND**
> Li<sup>+</sup> has a smaller ionic radius, so a higher energy is needed to separate the ions in LiF than in NaF **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> You must use the data from the table in your answer and refer specifically to the ions (Li<sup>+</sup>, Na<sup>+</sup>, Mg<sup>2+</sup>), not to the atoms.
> 
> Two factors affect the strength of ionic bonding:
> 
> - Ionic charge (higher charge → stronger bonding)
> - Ionic radius (smaller radius → stronger bonding).
> 
> A smaller ionic radius means the centres of the ions are closer together, resulting in stronger electrostatic forces of attraction.

parts.problemMd:
Sodium chloride and iodine are both solids. Sodium chloride does not melt until it reaches a temperature of 1074 K yet iodine sublimes when heated gently, giving off purple vapours. Sodium chloride will conduct electricity when molten and iodine is a very poor conductor of electricity.

i) State the type of structure and bonding of iodine and sodium chloride.

[2]

ii) Explain why iodine is volatile.

[2]

iii) Explain the differences in electrical conductivity of sodium chloride and iodine.

[3]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The type of structure and bonding of iodine and sodium chloride is:
> 
> - Iodine has a simple molecular structure with weak van der Waals / id-id forces between I<sub>2</sub> molecules **[1 mark]**
> - Sodium chloride has a giant ionic lattice structure with ionic bonds / strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged Na<sup>+</sup> and Cl<sup>–</sup> ions **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) Iodine is volatile because:
> 
> - Iodine has weak van der Waals / id-id forces between I<sub>2</sub> molecules **[1 mark]**
> - These weak forces are easily overcome at low temperatures, allowing iodine to vaporise / sublime easily **[1 mark]**
> 
> iii) The difference in electrical conductivity is because:
> 
> - Iodine has no ions or free electrons to carry electrical charge **[1 mark]**
> - Molten sodium chloride has Na<sup>+</sup> and Cl<sup>–</sup> ions that are free to move and carry electrical charge **[1 mark]**
> - Solid sodium chloride cannot conduct as the ions are held in fixed positions in the lattice **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The four types of crystalline structure are:
> 
> - Simple molecular
> - Giant covalent (macromolecular)
> - Ionic
> - Metallic
> 
> When explaining volatility, refer to the weak van der Waals forces between molecules being overcome, not the covalent bonds within the molecules.
> 
> Iodine has no charged species (no ions, no free electrons), so it cannot conduct electricity.
> 
> Sodium chloride can only conduct when molten or dissolved in water, as in these states the ions are mobile.

parts.problemMd:
Graphene, graphite and diamond are all forms of solid carbon.

Explain, in terms of structure and bonding, why graphene and graphite are good electrical conductors but diamond is a poor electrical conductor.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explaining the electrical conductivity of graphene, graphite and diamond:
> 
> - In both graphene and graphite, each carbon atom is covalently bonded to three others, leaving one delocalised electron per carbon atom **[1 mark]**
> - These delocalised electrons are mobile and can carry electrical charge in graphene and graphite **[1 mark]**
> - In diamond, each carbon atom is covalently bonded to four others in a tetrahedral arrangement **[1 mark]**
> - All four outer electrons are used in covalent bonds / there are no delocalised electrons in diamond, so diamond cannot conduct electricity **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The key difference between graphene/graphite and diamond is the number of covalent bonds each carbon atom forms: 3 in graphene/graphite (leaves 1 delocalised) vs 4 in diamond (none delocalised).
> 
> Both graphene and graphite have delocalised electrons, so mention both in your answer.
> 
> Delocalised electrons are mobile and act as the charge carriers in graphene and graphite, just as they do in metals.

parts.problemMd:
Standard enthalpy changes include enthalpy of formation, enthalpy of combustion and enthalpy of neutralisation.

i) Define the term standard enthalpy change of formation.

[2]

ii) Construct an equation that represents the standard enthalpy change of formation of ammonia, NH<sub>3</sub>. Include state symbols.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The standard enthalpy change of formation is:
> 
> - The enthalpy change when one mole of a compound is formed from its elements **[1 mark]**
> - In their standard states, under standard conditions (298 K and 100 kPa) **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The equation representing the standard enthalpy change of formation of ammonia is:
> 
> - ½N<sub>2</sub> (g) + 1½H<sub>2</sub> (g) → NH<sub>3</sub> (g) **[1 mark]**
> 
> Equations using integers (e.g. N<sub>2</sub> (g) + 3H<sub>2</sub> (g) → 2NH<sub>3</sub> (g)) are not accepted as they do not represent the formation of one mole of NH<sub>3</sub>

> **[exam-tip]**
> For part i), both marking points must be included to score both marks. The enthalpy change involves forming one mole of a compound from its elements, and the elements must be in their standard states — the most stable form of each element at 298 K and 100 kPa. For example, the standard state of carbon is graphite (not diamond), and the standard state of bromine is liquid Br<sub>2</sub> (not gas).
> 
> For part ii), CIE accepts fractional coefficients in enthalpy of formation equations. The equation must produce exactly one mole of NH<sub>3</sub>. Using N<sub>2</sub> (g) + 3H<sub>2</sub> (g) → 2NH<sub>3</sub> (g) does not score the mark because it represents the formation of two moles.

parts.problemMd: State what is meant by standard conditions in enthalpy measurements.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Standard conditions in enthalpy measurements are:
> 
> - A temperature of 298 K
> **AND**
> A pressure of 100 kPa **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> A common error is to give the temperature in degrees Celsius (25 °C) rather than kelvin. CIE requires the temperature in kelvin (298 K) and the pressure in kPa (100 kPa).

parts.problemMd:
The equation for the reaction between dilute sulfuric acid and aqueous sodium hydroxide is shown.

H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (aq) + 2NaOH (aq) → Na<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (aq) + 2H<sub>2</sub>O (l)

Explain why the enthalpy change for this reaction does not represent the standard enthalpy change of neutralisation.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The enthalpy change does not represent the standard enthalpy change of neutralisation because:
> 
> - The standard enthalpy change of neutralisation is defined as the enthalpy change when one mole of water is formed from the reaction of an acid and a base **[1 mark]**
> - This reaction produces two moles of water / the equation must be halved so that only one mole of water is produced **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The key criterion for the standard enthalpy change of neutralisation is that exactly one mole of water must be formed. The identity of the acid and base does not matter.
> 
> Always check the coefficient of water in any neutralisation equation. If it is not 1, the equation does not directly represent the standard enthalpy change of neutralisation.

parts.problemMd:
Freon 21 is a hydrochlorofluorocarbon that was used as a propellant and refrigerant but later withdrawn from use because of its effect on ozone depletion. The formula is CHCl<sub>2</sub>F.

Freon 21 is produced by reacting hydrogen fluoride with trichloromethane in the following reaction:

CHCl<sub>3</sub> (g) + HF (g) → CHCl<sub>2</sub>F (g) + HCl (g)

Use the data in Table 2.1 to calculate the standard enthalpy change of reaction, Δ*H*°<sub>r</sub>, for this reaction. Show your working.

| Compound | Standard enthalpy change of formation, Δ*H*°<sub>f</sub> / kJ mol<sup>–1</sup> |
|---|---|
| CHCl<sub>3</sub> (g) | –103.2 |
| CHCl<sub>2</sub>F (g) | –284.1 |
| HF (g) | –273.3 |
| HCl (g) | –92.3 |

**Table 2.1**
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the standard enthalpy change of reaction, Δ*H*°<sub>r</sub>:

- State the relationship:

Δ*H*°<sub>r</sub> = ΣΔ*H*°<sub>f</sub> (products) − ΣΔ*H*°<sub>f</sub> (reactants)

- Substitute the values from Table 2.1:

Δ*H*°<sub>r</sub> = [(–284.1) + (–92.3)] − [(–103.2) + (–273.3)] **[1 mark]**

Δ*H*°<sub>r</sub> = –376.4 − (–376.5)

Δ*H*°<sub>r</sub> = **+0.1 kJ mol**<sup>**–1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct substitution: [(–284.1) + (–92.3)] − [(–103.2) + (–273.3)]
> 
> 1 mark for correct final answer: +0.1 kJ mol<sup>–1</sup> (allow 0.1 kJ mol<sup>–1</sup>)

> **[exam-tip]**
> The formula for calculating the standard enthalpy change of reaction using standard enthalpies of formation is:
> 
> Δ*H*°<sub>r</sub> = ΣΔ*H*°<sub>f</sub> (products) − ΣΔ*H*°<sub>f</sub> (reactants)
> 
> All four values in the table are negative. Be careful with the signs when subtracting a group of negative values — use brackets around each set of products and reactants to avoid sign errors.
> 
> The answer is very close to zero (+0.1 kJ mol<sup>–1</sup>), meaning the reaction is approximately thermoneutral. This affects how you draw the reaction pathway diagram in part (b): the two horizontal lines should be at almost the same height.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Freon 21 is a hydrochlorofluorocarbon that was used as a propellant and refrigerant but later withdrawn from use because of its effect on ozone depletion. The formula is CHCl₂F.

Freon 21 is produced by reacting hydrogen fluoride with trichloromethane in the following reaction:

CHCl₃ (g) + HF (g) → CHCl₂F (g) + HCl (g)

ΔH°r = +0.1 kJ mol⁻¹

On Fig. 2.1, sketch a reaction pathway diagram for this reaction. Label the diagram to show the enthalpy change of reaction, Δ*H*°<sub>r</sub>, and the activation energy, *E*<sub>a</sub>.

![Blank reaction pathway diagram with energy on the y-axis and reaction coordinate on the x-axis](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/5-chemical-energetics/5-1-enthalpy-change-h/assets/011-blank-enthalpy-profile-graph-with-vertical-axis-.png)

**Fig. 2.1**
parts.solutionMd:
The completed reaction pathway diagram is:

![Reaction pathway diagram showing reactants and products at almost the same energy level with a curved hump above; ΔH°r labelled as a near-zero energy difference between reactants and products, and Ea labelled as an upward arrow from the reactants level to the peak of the curve](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/5-chemical-energetics/5-1-enthalpy-change-h/assets/016-reaction-pathway-diagram-showing-reactants-and-p.png)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for a correctly drawn reaction profile with reactants and products labelled and at approximately the same energy level (Δ*H*°<sub>r</sub> ≈ 0), with a smooth curve showing a hump
> 
> 1 mark for activation energy *E*<sub>a</sub> correctly labelled as an upward arrow from the reactants energy level to the peak of the curve

> **[exam-tip]**
> Since the standard enthalpy change of reaction from part (a) is +0.1 kJ mol<sup>–1</sup>, which is very close to zero, the reactants and products should be drawn at almost identical heights. If you draw them far apart, you have not correctly applied the calculated value.
> 
> The activation energy is always shown as an arrow from the energy level of the reactants up to the peak of the curve. It represents the minimum energy that reactant particles must have to react.

parts.problemMd: Define the term activation energy.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The definition of activation energy is:
> 
> - The minimum energy required for a reaction to occur / the minimum energy that colliding particles must possess for a successful collision **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The activation energy, *E*<sub>a</sub>, is shown on a reaction pathway diagram as an arrow from the energy level of the reactants to the peak of the curve. It represents the energy barrier that reacting particles must overcome for the reaction to proceed.

parts.problemMd: Define the term bond energy.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The definition of bond energy is:
> 
> - The energy required to break one mole of a specified bond **[1 mark]**
> - In a gaseous molecule, averaged over a range of similar compounds **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The definition must include both marking points:
> 
> - Bond energy relates to breaking one mole of a specific bond
> - It is an average value taken from a variety of gaseous molecules.
> 
> The average is necessary because the exact energy depends on the molecular environment. A C–H bond in methane has a slightly different energy from a C–H bond in ethanol. Bond energies are always positive (endothermic) because breaking bonds always requires an input of energy.

parts.problemMd: Suggest why the value of Δ*H*<sub>r</sub> calculated using bond energies may differ from the value obtained by experiment.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The calculated value may differ from the experimental value because:
> 
> - Bond energies are average values (taken over a range of compounds and molecular environments) and not exact values for the specific bonds in the molecules **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Bond energy data tables list average values calculated from many different compounds. For example, the C–H bond energy is an average of the C–H bond energy in methane, ethane, ethanol, and many other molecules. The actual C–H bond energy in a specific molecule may differ slightly from this average, introducing a small error into the calculated enthalpy change.

parts.problemMd:
Use the data given in Table 3.1 to calculate the enthalpy change for the hydration of ethene to form ethanol. Show your working.

CH<sub>2</sub>=CH<sub>2</sub> (g) + H<sub>2</sub>O (g) → CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH (l)

**Table 3.1**

| Bond | Bond energy / kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> |
|---|---|
| C–C | 346 |
| C=C | 614 |
| C–H | 414 |
| C–O | 358 |
| O–H | 463 |
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the enthalpy change for the hydration of ethene:

- List the bonds broken (endothermic) in the reactants:

E(C=C) = 1 x 614 = 614 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>

E(C–H) = 4 x 414 = 1656 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>

E(O–H) = 2 x 463 = 926 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>

Total bonds broken = 614 + 1656 + 926 = 3196 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> **[1 mark]**

- List the bonds formed (exothermic) in the products:

E(C–C) = 1 x 346 = 346 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>

E(C–H) = 5 x 414 = 2070 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>

E(C–O) = 1 x 358 = 358 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>

E(O–H) = 1 x 463 = 463 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>

Total bonds formed = 346 + 2070 + 358 + 463 = 3237 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the enthalpy change:

Δ*H*<sub>r</sub> = total bonds broken − total bonds formed

Δ*H*<sub>r</sub> = 3196 − 3237

Δ*H*<sub>r</sub> = **−41 kJ mol**<sup>**−1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct total bonds broken: 3196 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for correct total bonds formed: 3237 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for correct final answer: −41 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>

> **[exam-tip]**
> Drawing out the full structural formulae of the reactants and products helps you identify every bond.
> 
> ![Structural equation showing ethene reacting with water to form ethanol, with carbon–carbon double bond becoming single and –OH group added](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/5-chemical-energetics/5-1-enthalpy-change-h/assets/017-structural-equation-showing-ethene-reacting-with.jpeg)
> 
> In ethene (CH<sub>2</sub>=CH<sub>2</sub>), there are four C–H bonds and one C=C bond. Water (H<sub>2</sub>O) has two O–H bonds.
> 
> In ethanol (CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH), there are five C–H bonds, one C–C bond, one C–O bond, and one O–H bond.

parts.problemMd:
Ethane reacts with bromine to form 1,2-dibromoethane and hydrogen bromide.

Construct an equation for this reaction. Hence, use the data in Table 3.2 to calculate the enthalpy change for this reaction. Show your working.

| Bond | Bond enthalpy / kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> |
|---|---|
| C–C | 346 |
| C–H | 414 |
| C–Br | 285 |
| H–Br | 366 |
| Br–Br | 193 |

**Table 3.2**
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the enthalpy change for the reaction of ethane with bromine:

- Construct the balanced equation:

CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> (g) + 2Br<sub>2</sub> (g) → CH<sub>2</sub>BrCH<sub>2</sub>Br (g) + 2HBr (g) **[1 mark]**

- List the bonds broken (endothermic) in the reactants:

E(C–C) = 1 x 346 = 346 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>

E(C–H) = 6 x 414 = 2484 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>

E(Br–Br) = 2 x 193 = 386 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>

Total bonds broken = 346 + 2484 + 386 = 3216 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> **[1 mark]**

- List the bonds formed (exothermic) in the products:

E(C–C) = 1 x 346 = 346 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>

E(C–H) = 4 x 414 = 1656 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>

E(C–Br) = 2 x 285 = 570 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>

E(H–Br) = 2 x 366 = 732 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>

Total bonds formed = 346 + 1656 + 570 + 732 = 3304 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the enthalpy change:

Δ*H*<sub>r</sub> = total bonds broken − total bonds formed

Δ*H*<sub>r</sub> = 3216 − 3304

Δ*H*<sub>r</sub> = **−88 kJ mol**<sup>**−1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for a correctly balanced equation: CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> (g) + 2Br<sub>2</sub> (g) → CH<sub>2</sub>BrCH<sub>2</sub>Br (g) + 2HBr (g)
> 
> 1 mark for correct total bonds broken: 3216 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for correct total bonds formed: 3304 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for correct final answer: −88 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>

> **[exam-tip]**
> Drawing out the structural formulae helps identify all the bonds in each molecule.
> 
> ![Reaction scheme: ethane reacting with two bromine molecules to form 1,2-dibromoethane and two hydrogen bromide molecules, drawn as structural formulae.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/5-chemical-energetics/5-1-enthalpy-change-h/assets/018-reaction-scheme-ethane-reacting-with-two-bromine.jpeg)
> 
> Ethane (CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>) has one C–C bond and six C–H bonds.
> 
> The product 1,2-dibromoethane (CH<sub>2</sub>BrCH<sub>2</sub>Br) has one C–C bond, four C–H bonds, and two C–Br bonds. Notice that the C–C bond appears on both sides of the calculation and effectively cancels out as it has not changed during the reaction.

parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the energy change, *q*:

- Write the equation and substitute known values:

*q* = *mc*Δ*T*

*q* = 875 x 4.18 x 2.5 **[1 mark]**

- Calculate *q* and convert to kJ:

*q* = $\frac{9143.75}{1000}$

*q* = **9.1 kJ (to 2 s.f.) ****[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> An answer in J only, without conversion to kJ, is not accepted

> **[exam-tip]**
> The unit in the answer space is kJ, so make sure to divide your answer in J by 1000.
>

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

butan-1-ol, C~4~H~9~OH (*M*~r~ = 74.12 g mol^-1^)

**Table 2.1**

| Mass of butan-1-ol / g | 2.20 |
| --- | :---: |
| Volume of water / cm^3^ | 875 |
| Initial temperature of water / °C | 22.5 |
| Final temperature of water / °C | 25.0 |

(Specific heat capacity of water = 4.18 J g^-1^ K^-1^)

Use the data to calculate the energy change, *q*, for the reaction.

Determine the enthalpy of combustion of butan-1-ol using Table 2.1 and your answer to part **(b)**.

Give your answer to three significant figures.

parts.solutionMd:
To determine the enthalpy of combustion of butan-1-ol:

- Calculate the moles of butan-1-ol burned:

*n* = $\frac{mass}{M_{r}}$

moles of butan-1-ol burned = $\frac{2.20}{74.12}$

moles of butan-1-ol burned = 0.02968 mol **[1 mark]**

- Calculate Δ*H*:

Δ*H* = $\frac{q}{n}$

Δ*H* = $\frac{9143.75}{0.02968}$

Δ*H* = 308077.8 J mol<sup>-1</sup> **[1 mark]**

- Convert to kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> and apply sign:

Δ*H*<sub>c</sub> = $\frac{308077.8}{1000}$

Δ*H*<sub>c</sub> = **−308 kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup>** (to 3 s.f.) ****[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Values given to 3 (or more) significant figures during the working steps are accepted; but any values given to 2 (or less) significant figures are not accepted
> 
> Allow error carried forward from part (b) if the method is correct
> 
> A correct final answer, including the negative sign, with no working shown still gains full marks.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Do not round intermediate values. Use *q* = 9143.75 J (not 9100 J) to avoid accumulating rounding errors.
> 
> Using *q* = 9100 J from part (b) gives −307 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> and loses the final mark.

parts.problemMd:
Molecules of NO<sub>2</sub> can be formed by the reaction between N<sub>2</sub> and O<sub>2</sub>. The bond between the N and O atoms in NO<sub>2</sub> is a double covalent bond.

The enthalpy change of reaction for this reaction is +497 kJ mol<sup>–1</sup>. Calculate the bond energy, in kJ mol<sup>–1</sup>, of the N=O bond.

Show your working.

Use relevant data from **Table 3.2**.

**Table 3.2**

| **Bond** | **Bond energy / kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup> |
|---|---|
| N≡N | 941 |
| O=O | 495 |

Bond energy of the N=O bond = ............................. kJ mol<sup>–1</sup>
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the bond energy of the N=O bond:

- The equation for the reaction is:

N<sub>2</sub> (g) + 2O<sub>2</sub> (g) → 2NO<sub>2</sub> (g)

- Calculate the total energy for bonds broken:

1 × N≡N = 941 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>

2 × O=O = 2 × 495 = 990 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>

Total bonds broken = +1931 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> **[1 mark]**

- Set up the Δ*H*<sub>r</sub> equation:

Δ*H*<sub>r</sub> = Σ(bonds broken) − Σ(bonds formed)

+497 = +1931 − 4(N=O) **[1 mark]**

- Solve for the bond energy of N=O:

4(N=O) = 1931 − 497

4(N=O) = 1434

N=O = $\frac{1434}{4}$

N=O = **358.5 kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The reaction equation is N<sub>2</sub> (g) + 2O<sub>2</sub> (g) → 2NO<sub>2</sub> (g), so 1 N≡N bond and 2 O=O bonds are broken, and 4 N=O bonds are formed.
> 
> Work step by step:
> 
> - Find the total bond energy for bonds broken
> - Set up the Δ*H*<sub>r</sub> equation
> - Solve for the N=O bond energy

parts.problemMd:
The boiling points of carbon dioxide and nitrogen dioxide are -78.5 <sup>o</sup>C and 21 <sup>o</sup>C respectively.

Suggest a reason for the difference.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> A reason for the difference in boiling points between carbon dioxide and nitrogen dioxide:
> 
> - The van der Waals / intermolecular forces are (much) stronger in NO<sub>2</sub> / weaker in CO<sub>2</sub> **[1 mark]**
> 
> Plus, any **one** from:
> 
> - NO<sub>2</sub> has permanent dipole-dipole attractions between molecules; CO<sub>2</sub> does not
> - NO<sub>2</sub> is polar but CO<sub>2</sub> is not
> - In CO<sub>2</sub> the molecule is symmetrical and the dipoles cancel out / there is no net dipole
> 
> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The C=O bond is actually more polar than the N=O bond (greater electronegativity difference), but NO<sub>2</sub> has a lone pair on nitrogen that makes it a bent molecule, whereas CO<sub>2</sub> is linear.
> 
> The linear shape of CO<sub>2</sub> causes the bond dipoles to cancel, giving no net dipole. So, CO<sub>2</sub> only has weaker dispersion (London) forces, resulting in a much lower boiling point.

parts.problemMd:
Construct an equation that represents the standard enthalpy change of formation of nitrogen monoxide, NO.

Include state symbols.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The equation for the standard enthalpy change of formation of nitrogen monoxide, NO:
> 
> - ½N<sub>2</sub> (g) + ½O<sub>2</sub> (g) → NO (g) **[1 mark]**
>

> **[exam-tip]**
> The standard enthalpy change of formation requires exactly 1 mole of product to be formed.
> 
> Writing N<sub>2</sub> (g) + O<sub>2</sub> (g) → 2NO (g) is a common error. This produces 2 moles of NO rather than 1, so it does not represent the standard enthalpy change of formation.

parts.problemMd:
Propane gas is used widely as a fuel which can be used in camping gas stoves. The enthalpy of combustion for propane is −2219.2 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>.

Calculate the minimum mass of fuel needed to bring 150 cm<sup>3</sup> of water from 25.0°C to its boiling point of 100.0°C.

Show your working.

................... g
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the minimum mass of propane needed:

- Calculate the energy required to heat the water:

*q* = *mc*Δ*T*

*q* = 150 x 4.18 x 75

*q* = 47025 J

- Convert from J to kJ:

*q* = $\frac{47025}{1000}$

*q* = 47.025 kJ **[1 mark]**

- Rearrange the Δ*H* equation for *n*:

Δ*H* = $\frac{q}{n}$

*n* = $\frac{q}{ΔH}$

- Calculate the moles of propane required:

*n* = $\frac{47.025}{2219.2}$

*n* = 0.02119 mol **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the *M*<sub>r</sub> of propane:

*M*<sub>r</sub> of propane = (3 × 12) + (8 × 1)

*M*<sub>r</sub> of propane = 44.0 g mol<sup>-1</sup>

- Calculate the mass of propane:

mass = moles × *M*<sub>r</sub>

mass of propane = 0.02119 x 44.0

mass of propane = **0.93 g** **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Allow error carried forward if method is correct

parts.problemMd:
The enthalpy change of solution for ammonium chloride can be measured using calorimetry. 12.04 g of ammonium chloride is dissolved in 125.0 cm<sup>3</sup> of water at 19.5 °C.

The standard enthalpy change of solution of ammonium chloride is +15.1 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>. Calculate the energy change, *q*, in J, when 12.04 g of ammonium chloride is dissolved in 125.0 cm<sup>3</sup> of water.

Show your working.

*q* = ................................. J
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the energy change, *q*, in J:

- Calculate the moles of ammonium chloride:

moles = $\frac{\mathrm{mass}}{M_{r}}$

*n*(NH<sub>4</sub>Cl) = $\frac{12.04}{53.5}$

*n*(NH<sub>4</sub>Cl) = 0.2250 mol **[1 mark]**

- Convert Δ*H*<sub>sol</sub> from kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> to J mol<sup>-1</sup>:

Δ*H*<sub>sol</sub> = 15.1 x 1000

Δ*H*<sub>sol</sub> = 15100 J mol<sup>-1</sup>

- Calculate the energy change:

*q* = *n* x Δ*H*<sub>sol</sub>

*q* = 0.2250 x 15 100

*q* = **3397.5 J** (to 3 s.f.) **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> The final answer must be given to 2 or more significant figures
> 
> Δ*H*<sub>sol</sub> must be converted from kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> to J mol<sup>-1</sup> (×1000) to score the second mark

> **[exam-tip]**
> Work backwards from Δ*H*<sub>sol</sub> to find the energy change for the actual amount used (0.225 mol, not 1 mol).

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The enthalpy change of solution for ammonium chloride can be measured using calorimetry. 12.04 g of ammonium chloride is dissolved in 125.0 cm^3^ of water at 19.5 °C.

The standard enthalpy change of solution of ammonium chloride is +15.1 kJ mol^-1^.

Use your answer to part (a) to calculate the final temperature, in °C, of the solution.

The specific heat capacity of the solution is 4.18 J g<sup>-1</sup> K<sup>-1</sup>.

Show your working.

Final temperature = ................................. °C
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the final temperature of the solution:

- Calculate the temperature change:

*q* = *mc*Δ*T*

Δ*T* = $\frac{q}{mc}$

Δ*T* = $\frac{3398}{125.0\times4.18}$

Δ*T* = 6.5 °C **[1 mark]**

- The dissolution is endothermic, so the temperature decreases:

*T*<sub>final</sub> = 19.5 °C − 6.5 °C

*T*<sub>final</sub> = **13.0 °C** **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Allow error carried forward from part (a) if method is correct

> **[exam-tip]**
> The positive enthalpy of solution (+15.1 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>) tells you that dissolution is endothermic. Heat is absorbed from the surroundings, so the temperature of the solution decreases.
> 
> Subtract the temperature change from the initial temperature to find the final temperature.

parts.problemMd:
Use the data in Table 2.1 to calculate the enthalpy change of reaction for the hydrogenation of propene.

Show your working.

**Table 2.1**

| **Bond** | **Bond energy / kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup> |
|---|---|
| H–H | 435 |
| C–H | 413 |
| C–C | 347 |
| C=C | 619 |

Enthalpy of hydrogenation, Δ*H*<sub>r</sub> = ................................. kJ mol<sup>–1</sup>
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the enthalpy change of reaction for the hydrogenation of propene:

- Construct the equation for the hydrogenation:

CH<sub>3</sub>CH=CH<sub>2</sub> (g) + H<sub>2</sub> (g) → C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub> (g)

**[1 mark]**

- Identify and calculate bonds broken:

Bonds broken = 1 × C=C + 1 × H–H

Bonds broken = 619 + 435

Bonds broken = +1054 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>

- Identify and calculate bonds formed:

Bonds formed = 1 × C–C + 2 × C–H

Bonds formed = 347 + 2(413)

Bonds formed = −1173 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>

**[1 mark]**

- Calculate Δ*H*<sub>r</sub>:

Δ*H*<sub>r</sub> = +1054 + (−1173)

Δ*H*<sub>r</sub> = **−119 kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup>

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct hydrogenation equation: CH<sub>3</sub>CH=CH<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub> → C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub>
> 
> 1 mark for bonds broken = +1054 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> (C=C + H–H) **AND** bonds formed = −1173 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> (C–C + 2 × C–H)
> 
> 1 mark for Δ*H*<sub>r</sub> = −119 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>
> 
> Allow the full bond energy approach (using all bonds in propene and propane) for full marks if method and answer are correct

> **[exam-tip]**
> Only bonds that change in the reaction need to be counted. In the hydrogenation of propene, the C=C becomes C–C and H–H is broken while two new C–H bonds form. Bonds in CH<sub>3</sub> groups are identical on both sides and cancel out.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

**Table 2.1**

| **Bond** | **Bond energy / kJ mol**^**-1**^ |
| :---: | :---: |
| H–H | 435 |
| C–H | 413 |
| C–C | 347 |
| C=C | 619 |

Use the data in Table 2.1 to suggest, with a reason, whether the polymerisation of propene is exothermic or endothermic
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The polymerisation of propene is
> 
> - Exothermic 
> **OR**
> There is a net release of energy **[1 mark]**
> - One C=C bond is broken and two C–C bonds are formed
> **OR**
> One C=C bond is weaker than two C–C bonds (619 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> vs 2 × 347 = 694 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For each repeat unit of the polymer, one C=C bond breaks and two new C–C bonds form.
> 
> The energy released in forming two C–C bonds (2 × 347 = 694 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>) is greater than the energy required to break one C=C bond (619 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>), giving a net release of energy.

parts.problemMd:
Carbon, hydrogen and ethene each undergo complete combustion in oxygen.

| Equation | Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>c</sub> / kJ mol<sup>–1</sup> |
|---|---|
| C (s) + O<sub>2</sub> (g) → CO<sub>2</sub> (g) | −393.7 |
| H<sub>2</sub> (g) + ½O<sub>2</sub> (g) → H<sub>2</sub>O (l) | −285.9 |
| C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub> (g) + 3O<sub>2</sub> (g) → 2CO<sub>2</sub> (g) + 2H<sub>2</sub>O (l) | −1411.0 |

Use the data to calculate the standard enthalpy change of formation, Δ*H*<sup>*θ*</sup><sub>f</sub>, in kJ mol<sup>–1</sup>, of ethene at 298 K.

Show your working.

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>f</sub> = ................................. kJ mol<sup>–1</sup>
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the standard enthalpy change of formation, Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>f</sub>, of ethene:

- Apply Hess’s Law:

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>f</sub> = 2Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>c</sub>(C) + 2Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>c</sub>(H<sub>2</sub>) − Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>c</sub>(C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>) **[1 mark]**

- Substitute values and calculate:

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>f</sub> = 2(−393.7) + 2(−285.9) − (−1411.0)

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>f</sub> = −787.4 − 571.8 + 1411.0

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>f</sub> = **+51.8 kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for applying Hess’s Law correctly: Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>f</sub> = 2Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>c</sub>(C) + 2Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>c</sub>(H<sub>2</sub>) − Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>c</sub>(C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>)
> 
> Allow 1 mark for a correctly labelled Hess cycle showing the correct route
> 
> ![Diagram of Hess’s law: 2C(s) + 2H₂(g) → C₂H₄(g), arrows to 2CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l) with enthalpy values −393.7×2, −285.9×2 and −1411.0 kJ](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/5-chemical-energetics/5-1-enthalpy-change-h/assets/014-diagram-of-hess-s-law-2c-s-2h-g-c-h-g-arrows-to-.png)
> 
> 1 mark for a final positive Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>f</sub> value = +51.8 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>

> **[exam-tip]**
> Use Hess’s Law: the enthalpy change for the direct route (formation of ethene from its elements) equals the enthalpy change via combustion.
> 
> Construct the formation equation from the definition. 1 mole of compound formed from its elements in their standard states:
> 
> 2C (s) + 2H<sub>2</sub> (g) → C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub> (g)
> 
> Remember to multiply the combustion values by the stoichiometric coefficients in the formation equation before combining them.

parts.problemMd:
Compound **A** is a liquid containing carbon, hydrogen and oxygen. Quantitative analysis shows that **A** has the empirical formula CH<sub>2</sub>O.

A sample of **A** with a mass of 0.240 g is vaporised. At 80.0 °C and 101 kPa, the vapour occupies a volume of 116 cm<sup>3</sup>.

Calculate the relative molecular mass, *M*<sub>r</sub>, of **A**.

Show your working.

*M*<sub>r</sub> = .............
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the relative molecular mass, *M*<sub>r</sub>, of **A**:

- Convert units to SI:

*V* = 116 cm<sup>3</sup> = 116 × 10<sup>-6</sup> m<sup>3</sup>

*T* = 80.0 °C = 353 K

*p* = 101 kPa = 101 000 Pa

**[1 mark]**

- Calculate the number of moles, *n*, using *pV* = *nRT*:

*n* = $\frac{pV}{RT}$

*n* = $\frac{101000\times(116\times10^{-6})}{8.31\times353}$

*n* = 3.99 × 10<sup>-3</sup> mol

**[1 mark]**

- Calculate *M*<sub>r</sub>:

*M*<sub>r</sub> = $\frac{\mathrm{mass}}{\mathrm{moles}}$

*M*<sub>r</sub> = $\frac{0.240}{3.99\times10^{-3}}$

*M*<sub>r</sub> = **60.1 (to 3 s.f.)**

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct conversions of volume, temperature **AND **pressure to SI units
> 
> Answers given to more than 3 significant figures are accepted, if supported by workings

> **[exam-tip]**
> Watch units carefully.
> 
> If you use *R* = 8.31, you must use SI units. This means converting **kPa to Pa**, **cm**<sup>**3**</sup>** to m**<sup>**3**</sup>, and **°C to K** before substituting into *pV* = *nRT*.
> 
> A missed conversion (especially pressure or volume) is the most common reason these questions lose marks.

parts.problemMd:
Methyl methanoate, HCOOCH<sub>3</sub>, is a liquid ester.

i) Define the term standard enthalpy change of formation.

[2]

ii) The standard enthalpy changes of combustion, Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>c</sub>, in **Table 2.1** are for complete combustion to CO<sub>2</sub> (g) and H<sub>2</sub>O (l) under standard conditions.

**Table 2.1**

| Substance | Standard enthalpy change of combustion, Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>c</sub> / kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> |
|---|---|
| C (s) | –394 |
| H<sub>2</sub> (g) | –286 |
| HCOOCH<sub>3</sub> (l) | –975 |

The enthalpy of formation of methyl methanoate refers to the reaction:

2C (s) + 2H<sub>2</sub> (g) + O<sub>2</sub> (g) → HCOOCH<sub>3</sub> (l)

Use the data in Table 2.1 to calculate the standard enthalpy change of formation, Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>f</sub>, of liquid methyl methanoate.

Show your working.

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>f</sub> = ........................ kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>

[3]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) Standard enthalpy change of formation is:
> 
> - The enthalpy change when one mole / 1 mol of a compound is formed from its elements **[1 mark]**
> - In their standard states under standard conditions **[1 mark]**

ii) To calculate the standard enthalpy change of formation, Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>f</sub>, of liquid methyl methanoate:

- State the relationship used:

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>f</sub> + Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>c</sub>(compound) = Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>c</sub>(reactants)  **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the total enthalpy of combustion of the reactants:

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>c</sub>(reactants) = (2 x C) + (2 x H<sub>2</sub>)

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>c</sub>(reactants) = (2 x -394) + (2 x -286)

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>c</sub>(reactants) = −1360 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> **[1 mark]**

- Calculate Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>f</sub>:

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>f</sub> = −1360 − (−975)

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>f</sub> = **−385 kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>f</sub> + Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>c</sub>(compound) = Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>c</sub>(reactants)
> 
> 1 mark for Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>c</sub>(reactants) = (2 x C) + (2 x H<sub>2</sub>) **OR** Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>c</sub>(reactants) = (2 x 394) + (2 x -286) **OR** Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>c</sub>(reactants) = −1360 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for a final negative Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>f</sub> value = −385 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>
> 
> 3 marks can be awarded for a correct final answer with or without working
> 
> Only 1 mark is awarded for a final answer of +385 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>

> **[exam-tip]**
> In formation definitions, do not forget the two precision points:
> 
> 1. One mole / 1 mol
> 2. Standard states under standard conditions.
> 
> In the Hess calculation, the most common error is missing the stoichiometry from the formation equation. Multiply the combustion values by the coefficients first (here, 2 for C and 2 for H<sub>2</sub>) before combining them with the ester’s combustion value.

parts.problemMd:
The equation for the formation of gaseous methyl methanoate from gaseous atoms is shown.

2C (g) + 4H (g) + 2O (g) → HCOOCH<sub>3</sub> (g)

Use bond energy data from the Data Booklet to calculate the enthalpy change for this reaction.

Show your working.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the enthalpy change for this reaction:

- The reactants are gaseous atoms, so there are no bonds to break:

Δ*H*<sub>(bonds broken)</sub> = 0

- Identify the bonds formed in HCOOCH<sub>3</sub> (g):

1 × C=O

2 × C–O

4 × C–H

**[1 mark]**

- Use bond energies from the Data Booklet to calculate the total energy of bonds formed:

Δ*H*<sub>(bonds formed)</sub> = −(C=O + (2 × C–O) + (4 × C–H))

Δ*H*<sub>(bonds formed)</sub> = −((740) + (2 × 360) + (4 × 410))

Δ*H*<sub>(bonds formed)</sub> = **−3100 kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup>

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct identification of all bonds formed in HCOOCH<sub>3</sub>(g): 1 × C=O, 2 × C–O, 4 × C–H
> 
> 1 mark for a final negative Δ*H*<sub>(bonds formed)</sub> value = - 3100 (kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>)
> 
> 2 marks can be awarded for a correct final answer with or without working

> **[exam-tip]**
> Since the reactants are gaseous atoms, this is a bond formation only question as there are no bonds to break. The enthalpy change is the negative of the total bond energies for all bonds formed.
> 
> The most common mistakes are:
> 
> - Treating it like a normal bond energy cycle and trying to “break” bonds in the reactants
> - Missing one of the C–O bonds in the ester group
> - Forgetting the negative sign

parts.problemMd:
Use the data in Table 1.1 to calculate the standard enthalpy change of combustion of butane, Δ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>c</sub>. Show your working.

**Table 1.1**

| **Substance** | **Standard enthalpy change of formation, **Δ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>f</sub>** / kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup> |
|---|---|
| CO<sub>2</sub> (g) | −393.5 |
| C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub> (g) | −125 |
| H<sub>2</sub>O (l) | −286 |

Δ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>c</sub> (C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub>) = .........................................kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the standard enthalpy change of combustion of butane, Δ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>c</sub>:

- Apply the Hess's law expression:

Δ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>c</sub> = −Δ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>f</sub> [C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub> (g)] + 4Δ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>f</sub> [CO<sub>2</sub> (g)] + 5Δ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>f</sub> [H<sub>2</sub>O (l)] **[1 mark]**

- Substitute values from Table 1.1:

Δ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>c</sub> = −(−125) + 4(−393.5) + 5(−286)

Δ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>c</sub> = **−2879 kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct expression with correct stoichiometric coefficients
> 
> 1 mark for −2879 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>

> **[exam-tip]**
> The balanced combustion equation for butane is:

> 
> Take care with signs. Subtracting the enthalpy of formation of the reactant means subtracting a negative value, making it positive: −(−125) = +125.

parts.problemMd:
Use the bond energies given in Table 1.2 to calculate the standard enthalpy change of combustion of butane. Show your working.

**Table 1.2**

| **Bond** | **Bond energy / kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup> |
|---|---|
| C−C | 348 |
| C−H | 410 |
| C=O | 743 |
| H−O | 463 |
| O=O | 495 |

Δ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>c</sub> (C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub>) = .........................................kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the standard enthalpy change of combustion of butane using bond energies:

- Identify and total the bonds broken (in reactants):

3 x C−C: 3 x 348 = +1044 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>

10 x C−H: 10 x 410 = +4100 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>

6.5 x O=O: 6.5 x 495 = +3217.5 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>

Total bonds broken = +8361.5 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> **[1 mark]**

- Identify and total the bonds formed (in products):

8 x C=O: 8 x 743 = −5944 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>

10 x H−O: 10 x 463 = −4630 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>

Total bonds formed = −10574 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the enthalpy change:

Δ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>c</sub> = (+8361.5) + (−10574)

Δ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>c</sub> = **−2212.5 kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for total bonds broken = +8361.5 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> (3 x C−C, 10 x C−H, 6.5 x O=O with correct values)
> 
> 1 mark for total bonds formed = −10574 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> (8 x C=O, 10 x H−O with correct values)
> 
> 1 mark for −2212.5 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>

> **[exam-tip]**
> Start by writing the balanced combustion equation for butane:
> 
> C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub> (g) + 6.5O<sub>2</sub> (g) → 4CO<sub>2</sub> (g) + 5H<sub>2</sub>O (g)
> 
> Bond energies always refer to gaseous species, so water is treated as gaseous in this calculation. This is why the answer differs from the thermochemical value in part (b), which uses liquid water products.
> 
> Count the bonds carefully. Butane (C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub>) has 3 C−C bonds and 10 C−H bonds. Each CO<sub>2</sub> molecule has 2 C=O bonds (8 total for 4 molecules), and each H<sub>2</sub>O molecule has 2 O−H bonds (10 total for 5 molecules).
> 
> Bond energies are average values taken from a range of similar compounds, so the calculated value is only an approximation of the true enthalpy change.

parts.problemMd:
Propane gas is commonly used as a fuel for outdoor cooking. It can be produced in a number of ways, including from the addition reaction of propyne gas with hydrogen. Propyne has the formula CHCCH<sub>3</sub> and includes a triple bond.

Construct an equation for the formation of propane from propyne. Include state symbols.
parts.solutionMd:
The equation for the formation of propane from propyne is:

CHCCH<sub>3</sub> (g) + 2H<sub>2</sub> (g) → CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> (g)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**

> 
> 1 mark for all correct state symbols: (g), (g), (g)

> **[exam-tip]**
> Propyne contains a C$\equiv$C triple bond, which requires 2 moles of H<sub>2</sub> for complete addition: first to give propene, then to give propane.
> 
> You do not need to know the alkyne homologous series, but you should be able to apply your knowledge of addition reactions to the structural information given in the question.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Propane gas is commonly used as a fuel for outdoor cooking. It can be produced in a number of ways, including from the addition reaction of propyne gas with hydrogen. Propyne has the formula CHCCH3 and includes a triple bond.

The equation for the formation of propane from propyne is:

CHCCH3 (g) + 2H2 (g) → CH3CH2CH3 (g)

Table 2.1 lists the relevant standard enthalpy change of combustion data for the formation of propane from propyne.

**Table 2.1**

|   | **Standard enthalpy change of combustion, **Δ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>c</sub>** / kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup> |
|---|---|
| **Hydrogen** | −285.8 |
| **Propane** | −2220 |
| **Propyne** | −1940 |

Calculate the standard enthalpy change of reaction, Δ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>r</sub>, for the formation of propane from propyne. Show your working.

Δ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>r</sub> = .........................................kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the standard enthalpy change of reaction, Δ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>r</sub>, for the formation of propane from propyne:

- Apply the Hess's law expression using combustion data:

Δ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>r</sub> = ΣΔ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>c</sub>(reactants) − ΣΔ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>c</sub>(products) **[1 mark]**

- Substitute values from Table 2.1:

Δ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>r</sub> = [Δ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>c</sub>(propyne) + 2 x Δ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>c</sub>(H<sub>2</sub>)] − Δ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>c</sub>(propane)

Δ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>r</sub> = [(−1940) + 2(−285.8)] − (−2220) **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the result:

Δ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>r</sub> = −2511.6 + 2220

Δ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>r</sub> = **−291.6 kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct expression: ΣΔ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>c</sub>(reactants) − ΣΔ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>c</sub>(products), or equivalent Hess cycle approach
> 
> 1 mark for correct substitution with x2 multiplier for H<sub>2</sub>
> 
> 1 mark for −291.6 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>

> **[exam-tip]**
> When combustion data is provided, the Hess's law expression is:
> 
> Δ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>r</sub> = ΣΔ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>c</sub>(reactants) − ΣΔ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>c</sub>(products)
> 
> This is the reverse of the formation data expression (Δ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>r</sub> = ΣΔ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>f</sub>(products) − ΣΔ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>f</sub>(reactants)). Take care not to confuse the two.
> 
> The stoichiometry from part (a) matters here. The balanced equation shows 2 mol H<sub>2</sub> are consumed, so Δ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>c</sub>(H<sub>2</sub>) must be multiplied by 2.

> Bond energies in the Data Booklet are average values calculated from many different compounds containing the same type of bond. For example, the C−H bond energy is derived from many different molecules, so it does not represent any one C−H bond exactly. This is why a calculated bond energy value is only an approximation.

parts.problemMd:
Enthalpy changes of combustion can be determined using calorimetry or calculated using Hess cycles.

Fig. 3.1 shows the equipment used to determine the standard enthalpy change of combustion, Δ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>c</sub>, of 2-methylpropan-2-ol, C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>9</sub>OH, using a calorimeter containing 75.0 g of water.

![Spirit burner calorimetry experiment setup showing a spirit burner beneath a metal can containing water](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/5-chemical-energetics/5-2-hesss-law/assets/008-spirit-burner-calorimetry-experiment-setup-showi.png)

**Fig. 3.1**

Table 3.1 shows the results of the experiment.

**Table 3.1**

|   | **Initial** | **Final** | **Change** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Mass of spirit burner / g** | 267.35 | 266.78 |   |
| **Temperature of water / °C** | 19.5 | 65.3 |   |

Calculate the standard enthalpy change of combustion, Δ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>c</sub>, of 2-methylpropan-2-ol. Include the sign and units. Show your working.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the standard enthalpy change of combustion, Δ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>c</sub>, of 2-methylpropan-2-ol:

- Calculate the mass of 2-methylpropan-2-ol burned and the temperature change of the water:

mass burned = 267.35 − 266.78 = 0.57 g
**AND**
temperature change = 65.3 − 19.5 = 45.8 °C

**[1 mark]**

- Calculate the heat energy transferred to the water using *q* = *mc*Δ*T*:

*q* = 75.0 x 4.18 x 45.8

*q* = 14 358 J **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the *M*<sub>r</sub> of 2-methylpropan-2-ol, C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>9</sub>OH:

*M*<sub>r</sub> = (4 x 12.0) + (10 x 1.0) + 16.0 = 74.0 **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the moles of 2-methylpropan-2-ol burned:

moles = $\frac{0.57}{74.0}$

moles = 7.703 x 10<sup>-3</sup> mol **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the standard enthalpy change of combustion:

Δ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>c</sub> = $\frac{-14358}{7.703\times10^{-3}}$

Δ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>c</sub> = **−1864 kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for both mass change = 0.57 g **AND **temperature change = 45.8 °C
> 
> 1 mark for q = 14 358 J
> 
> 1 mark for *M*<sub>r</sub> = 74.0 g mol<sup>-1</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for moles = 7.703 x 10<sup>-3</sup> mol
> 
> 1 mark for −1864 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>

> **[exam-tip]**
> The mass used in *q* = *mc*Δ*T* is the mass of water (75.0 g), not the mass of 2-methylpropan-2-ol burned. The mass of the spirit burner decreases because fuel is consumed.
> 
> The combustion reaction is exothermic, so the enthalpy change is negative.
> 
> To find the moles burned, use:
> 
> moles = $\frac{\mathrm{mass} \mathrm{of} \mathrm{fuel} \mathrm{burne}d}{M_{r}}$ =$\frac{0.57}{74.0}$

parts.problemMd: Define the term *standard enthalpy of combustion*, Δ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>c</sub>.
parts.solutionMd:

> - With all reactants and products in their standard states

> Be careful not to confuse products and reactants in thermodynamic definitions.
>

parts.problemMd: Construct an equation for the complete combustion of propan-1-ol, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH (l). Include state symbols.

>

> **[exam-tip]**
> A common mistake is to leave out the oxygen from a combustion equation — complete combustion always requires oxygen.
> 
> If you are not using fractions to balance the equation, you must double the number of moles of all other chemicals.
> 
> Double-check your balancing once you have written your equation.
> 
> Many chemical calculations work from a balanced symbol equation, so if your equation is incorrect, any subsequent calculations will also contain errors.

> 1 mark for correct final answer: −2020.7 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>
> 
> Allow error carried forward if an incorrect substitution leads to a consistent final answer.

> **[exam-tip]**

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Urea, CO(NH~2~)~2~, is a naturally occurring substance which can be hydrolysed with water to form ammonia and carbon dioxide.

The standard enthalpy changes of formation of relevant species are given in Table 1.1.

**Table 1.1**

| **compound** | Δ*H*^ϴ^~f~** / kJ mol**^**-1**^ |
| :---: | :---: |
| H~2~O (l) | −285.8 |
| CO(NH~2~)~2~ (aq) | −320.5 |
| CO~2~ (g) | −393.5 |
| NH~3~ (aq) | −81.0 |
| CO(NH~2~)~2~ (s) | −333.1 |

Use the data in Table 1.1 to calculate the standard enthalpy change of reaction, Δ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>r</sub>, for the hydrolysis of aqueous urea. Show your working.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the standard enthalpy change of reaction, Δ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>r</sub>, for the hydrolysis of aqueous urea:

- Apply the enthalpy of formation equation:

Δ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>r</sub> = ΣΔ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>f</sub> (products) − ΣΔ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>f</sub> (reactants) **[1 mark]**

- Substitute values from Table 1.1:

Δ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>r</sub> = [(−393.5) + 2(−81.0)] − [(−320.5) + (−285.8)]

Δ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>r</sub> = (−555.5) − (−606.3)

Δ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>r</sub> = **+50.8 kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct formula: Δ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>r</sub> = ΣΔ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>f</sub> products − ΣΔ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>f</sub> reactants
> 
> 1 mark for correct final answer: +50.8 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>
> 
> Allow error carried forward if an incorrect substitution leads to a consistent final answer.

> **[exam-tip]**
> As you go around the Hess cycle, add the enthalpy value if you follow the arrow and subtract it if you go against the arrow.
> 
> Using brackets around the terms helps to avoid careless calculation errors.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Urea, CO(NH~2~)~2~, is a naturally occurring substance which can be hydrolysed with water to form ammonia and carbon dioxide.

The standard enthalpy changes of formation of relevant species are given in Table 1.1.

**Table 1.1**

| **compound** | Δ*H*^ϴ^~f~** / kJ mol**^**-1**^ |
| :---: | :---: |
| H~2~O (l) | −285.8 |
| CO(NH~2~)~2~ (aq) | −320.5 |
| CO~2~ (g) | −393.5 |
| NH~3~ (aq) | −81.0 |
| CO(NH~2~)~2~ (s) | −333.1 |

Use the data in Table 1.1 to calculate the standard enthalpy change of combustion, Δ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>c</sub>, of solid urea, given the following equation. Show your working.

2CO(NH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>2</sub> (s) + 3O<sub>2</sub> (g) → 2CO<sub>2</sub> (g) + 2N<sub>2</sub> (g) + 4H<sub>2</sub>O (l)
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the standard enthalpy change of combustion of solid urea, Δ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>c</sub>:

- Apply the enthalpy of formation equation:

Δ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>c</sub> = ΣΔ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>f</sub> (products) − ΣΔ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>f</sub> (reactants) **[1 mark]**

- Substitute values from Table 1.1 for the equation as written (2 mol of urea):

Δ*H* = [2(−393.5) + 2(0) + 4(−285.8)] − [2(−333.1) + 3(0)] **[1 mark]**

Δ*H* = (−787.0 − 1143.2) − (−666.2) = −1264.0 kJ

- Divide by 2 to give the standard enthalpy change of combustion per mole of urea:

Δ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>c</sub> = **−632.0 kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct formula: Δ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>c</sub> = ΣΔ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>f</sub> products − ΣΔ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>f</sub> reactants
> 
> 1 mark for correct substitution using Δ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>f</sub>[CO(NH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>2</sub> (s)] = −333.1 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> and Δ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>f</sub>[N<sub>2</sub> (g)] = Δ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>f</sub>[O<sub>2</sub> (g)] = 0
> 
> 1 mark for correct final answer per mole: −632.0 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>
> 
> Allow error carried forward if an incorrect substitution leads to a consistent final answer per mole of urea.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The equation given shows the combustion of 2 moles of urea. The standard enthalpy of combustion is always defined per mole of substance, so remember to divide the calculated Δ*H* by 2 at the end.
> 
> Oxygen and nitrogen both have Δ*H*<sup>ϴ</sup><sub>f</sub> = 0 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> as they are elements in their standard states.

parts.problemMd:

Complete Table 1.1 to show the oxidation number of sulfur in each compound.
