parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Ethanoic acid can be reacted with methanol to form methyl ethanoate, and an equilibrium mixture is formed.

CH~3~COOH (l) + CH~3~OH (l) ⇌ CH~3~COOCH~3~ (l) + H~2~O (l)

The reaction is usually carried out in the presence of an acid catalyst.

In an experiment to determine *K*<sub>c</sub> a student placed together in a conical flask 0.20 mol of ethanoic acid, 0.20 mol of methanol, and 0.01 mol of hydrogen chloride catalyst.

The flask was sealed and kept at 25 °C for ten days. After this time, the student titrated all of the contents of the flask with 1.80 mol dm<sup>–3</sup> KOH. At the end-point, 26.30 cm<sup>3</sup> of KOH had been used.

i) Construct a balanced equation for the reaction between ethanoic acid and potassium hydroxide.

[1]

ii) Suggest a suitable choice of indicator for the titration.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The balanced equation for the reaction between ethanoic acid and potassium hydroxide:
> 
> - CH<sub>3</sub>COOH + KOH → CH<sub>3</sub>COOK + H<sub>2</sub>O **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) A suitable indicator for this titration:
> 
> - Phenolphthalein **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> This is a weak acid–strong base neutralisation. The equivalence point is above pH 7 because the salt formed (CH<sub>3</sub>COOK) is slightly alkaline through hydrolysis. Phenolphthalein is therefore the correct indicator choice.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Ethanoic acid can be reacted with methanol to form methyl ethanoate, and an equilibrium mixture is formed.

CH~3~COOH (l) + CH~3~OH (l) ⇌ CH~3~COOCH~3~ (l) + H~2~O (l)

In an experiment to determine *K*~c~ a student placed together in a conical flask 0.20 mol of ethanoic acid, 0.20 mol of methanol, and 0.01 mol of hydrogen chloride catalyst.

The flask was sealed and kept at 25 °C for ten days. After this time, the student titrated all of the contents of the flask with 1.80 mol dm^–3^ KOH. At the end-point, 26.30 cm^3^ of KOH had been used.

The student carried out the following calculations.

i) Calculate the amount, in moles, of KOH used in the titration.

[1]

ii) State the amount, in moles, of KOH that reacted with the hydrogen chloride.

[1]

iii) Hence calculate the amount, in moles, of KOH that reacted with the ethanoic acid.

[1]

iv) Use your results from parts **(i)**, **(ii)** and **(iii)** to calculate the amount, in moles, of ethanoic acid present at equilibrium.

Hence complete the table below.

[2]

|   | CH<sub>3</sub>COOH | CH<sub>3</sub>OH | CH<sub>3</sub>COOCH<sub>3</sub> | H<sub>2</sub>O |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Initial amount / mol | 0.20 | 0.20 | 0 | 0 |
| Equilibrium amount / mol |   |   |   |   |

v) Use your results to calculate a value for *K*<sub>c</sub> for this reaction. State its units.

*K*<sub>c</sub> = ........................

units = .......................

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
i) To calculate the amount, in moles, of KOH used in the titration:

moles of KOH = 1.80 x $\frac{26.30}{1000}$

moles of KOH = 0.04734 mol **[1 mark]**

ii) The amount, in moles, of KOH that reacted with HCl:

moles of KOH = moles of HCl

moles of HCl = 0.01 mol **[1 mark]**

iii) To calculate the amount, in moles, of KOH that reacted with ethanoic acid:

moles of KOH reacted with CH<sub>3</sub>COOH = 0.04734 − 0.01

moles of KOH reacted with CH<sub>3</sub>COOH = 0.03734 mol **[1 mark]**

iv) To calculate the moles of CH<sub>3</sub>COOH consumed:

moles of CH<sub>3</sub>COOH consumed= 0.20 − 0.03734

moles of CH<sub>3</sub>COOH consumed= 0.16266 mol

The completed table is:

|   | CH<sub>3</sub>COOH | CH<sub>3</sub>OH | CH<sub>3</sub>COOCH<sub>3</sub> | H<sub>2</sub>O |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Initial amount / mol | 0.20 | 0.20 | 0 | 0 |
| Change / mol | −0.16266 | −0.16266 | +0.16266 | +0.16266 |
| Equilibrium amount / mol | **Final answer:** **0.03734** | **Final answer:** **0.03734** | **Final answer:** **0.16266** | **Final answer:** **0.16266** |

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct equilibrium amounts of CH<sub>3</sub>COOH and CH<sub>3</sub>OH (0.03734 mol each)
> 
> 1 mark for correct equilibrium amounts of CH<sub>3</sub>COOCH<sub>3</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>O (0.16266 mol each)
> 
> Allow error carried forward from part iii) for the equilibrium amounts

v) To calculate *K*<sub>c</sub>:

*K*<sub>c</sub> = `(left square bracket CH _ 3 COOCH _ 3 right square bracket left square bracket H _ 2 O right square bracket)/(left square bracket CH _ 3 COOH right square bracket left square bracket CH _ 3 OH right square bracket)`

*K*<sub>c</sub> = $\frac{0.16266\times0.16266}{0.03734\times0.03734}$

*K*<sub>c</sub> = **18.97** **[1 mark]**

Units = **no units** **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Allow error carried forward from parts iii)  and iv) for the *K*<sub>c</sub> calculation.

> **[exam-tip]**
> In this reaction, the total volume cancels out in the *K*<sub>c</sub> expression because there is 1 mol of each species on each side. This means you can substitute molar amounts directly into the expression without converting to concentrations.
> 
> For the titration: both neutralisation reactions (KOH + CH<sub>3</sub>COOH and KOH + HCl) have a 1:1 ratio, so moles of KOH equal moles of each acid separately.

parts.problemMd:
The student performed another titration between the ethanoic acid used in the formation of the ester and the potassium hydroxide solution. The volume of potassium hydroxide added from the burette was recorded.

Sketch a pH titration curve for this reaction.
parts.solutionMd:
The pH titration curve for this reaction is:

![Weak acid–strong base pH titration curve showing pH starting above 3, rising gradually, with a steep S-shaped section above pH 7 at the equivalence point, and ending around pH 13](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/7-equilibria/7-1-chemical-equilibria-reversible-reactions-and-dynamic-equilibrium/assets/004-weak-acid-strong-base-ph-titration-curve-showing.jpeg)

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for the curve starting above pH 3 (reflecting a weak acid, not fully dissociated)
> 
> 1 mark for the equivalence point above pH 7
> 
> 1 mark for the curve ending around pH 13 (strong base in excess)
> 
> 1 mark for an S-shaped curve with a near-vertical section at the equivalence point, with alkali added on the x-axis

> **[exam-tip]**
> This is a weak acid–strong base titration (ethanoic acid + KOH). Key features to draw:
> 
> - The starting pH is above 3 (weak acid is only partially dissociated)
> - The equivalence point is above pH 7 (the salt formed, potassium ethanoate, undergoes slight hydrolysis to give an alkaline solution)
> - The curve shows a characteristic S-shape with a steep vertical section at the equivalence point.

parts.problemMd:
The following dynamic equilibrium was reached at temperature *T* in a closed container.

3A (g) + 2B (g) ⇌ 2C (g)    Δ*H* = −65 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>

The value of *K*<sub>c</sub> for the reaction was 255 mol<sup>-3</sup> dm<sup>9</sup> when the equilibrium mixture contained 3.34 mol of **A** and 4.28 mol of **C**.

i) Explain what is meant by the term *dynamic equilibrium*.

[2]

ii) Write an expression for the equilibrium constant, *K*<sub>c</sub>, for this reaction.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The term *dynamic equilibrium* means:
> 
> - The rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the reverse reaction **[1 mark]**
> - The concentrations of reactants and products remain constant **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The expression for *K*<sub>c</sub>:
> 
> - *K*<sub>c</sub> = $\frac{[ C ] ^{2} }{[ A ] ^{3} [ B ] ^{2} }$ **[1 mark]**
> 
> Square brackets must be used for concentrations; round brackets are not accepted.

> **[exam-tip]**
> For part i), two distinct points are required for 2 marks: the equal rates point and the constant concentrations point. Stating only one will score 1 mark.
> 
> For part ii), products go in the numerator and reactants in the denominator. The powers match the stoichiometric coefficients: [C]<sup>2</sup>, [A]<sup>3</sup>, and [B]<sup>2</sup>.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The following dynamic equilibrium was reached at temperature *T* in a closed container.

3A (g) + 2B (g) ⇌ 2C (g)    Δ*H* = −65 kJ mol^-1^

The value of *K*~c~ for the reaction was 255 mol^-3^ dm^9^ when the equilibrium mixture contained 3.34 mol of **A** and 4.28 mol of **C**.

Calculate the concentration of **B** in the equilibrium mixture if the volume of the container is 8.00 dm<sup>3</sup>. Give your answer to 3 significant figures. Show your working.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the concentration of **B** in the equilibrium mixture:

- Calculate the concentrations of **A** and **C** by dividing moles by volume:

[**A**] = $\frac{3.34}{8.00}$ = 0.4175 mol dm<sup>-3</sup>

[**C**] = $\frac{4.28}{8.00}$ = 0.535 mol dm<sup>-3</sup>

**[1 mark]**

- Write the *K*<sub>c</sub> expression and rearrange to make [**B**]<sup>2</sup> the subject:

*K*<sub>c</sub> = $\frac{[ C ] ^{2} }{[ A ] ^{3} [ B ] ^{2} }$

[**B**]<sup>2</sup> = [**C**]<sup>2</sup> / ([**A**]<sup>3</sup> x *K*<sub>c</sub>) **[1 mark]**

- Substitute values and calculate [**B**]<sup>2</sup>:

[**B**]<sup>2</sup> = $\frac{[ 0.535 ]^{2}}{[ 0.4175 ]^{3} \times 255}$

[**B**]<sup>2</sup> = 0.01542 **[1 mark]**

- Take the square root to find [**B**]:

[**B**] = **0.124** mol dm<sup>-3</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for [**A**] = 0.4175 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> **AND** [**C**] = 0.535 mol dm<sup>-3</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for correct rearranged expression: [**B**]<sup>2</sup> = [**C**]<sup>2</sup> / ([**A**]<sup>3</sup> x *K*<sub>c</sub>)
> 
> 1 mark for [**B**]<sup>2</sup> = 0.0154
> 
> 1 mark for [**B**] = 0.124 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> (3 s.f.)
> 
> Allow error carried forward from incorrect concentrations if the rearrangement method is correct.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The first step is to convert moles to concentrations by dividing by the volume. Using moles directly in the *K*<sub>c</sub> expression instead of concentrations is the most common error in this type of question.
> 
> After rearranging, calculate [**B**]<sup>2</sup> first, then take the square root. Forgetting the square root at the end is a common final step error.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The following dynamic equilibrium was reached at temperature *T* in a closed container.

3A (g) + 2B (g) ⇌ 2C (g)    Δ*H* = −65 kJ mol^-1^

State and explain the effect of an increase in temperature on the equilibrium concentration of **B**.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The effect of an increase in temperature on the equilibrium concentration of **B**:
> 
> - The concentration of **B** increases **[1 mark]**
> - Increasing temperature favours the reverse / endothermic reaction **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The forward reaction is exothermic (Δ*H* = −65 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>). By Le Chatelier's principle, increasing temperature shifts the position of equilibrium in the direction that opposes the change, favouring the reverse (endothermic) reaction. This consumes C and produces more A and B, so the concentration of **B** increases.
> 
> State the effect first (concentration increases), then give the reason using Le Chatelier's principle. Both points are required for full marks.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The following dynamic equilibrium was reached at temperature *T* in a closed container.

3A (g) + 2B (g) ⇌ 2C (g)    Δ*H* = −65 kJ mol^-1^

The value of *K*~c~ for the reaction was 255 mol^-3^ dm^9^ when the equilibrium mixture contained 3.34 mol of **A** and 4.28 mol of **C**.

Calculate the value of the equilibrium constant for the following reaction at temperature *T*. Show your working.

2**C** (g) ⇌ 3**A** (g) + 2**B** (g)
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the value of *K*<sub>c</sub> for the reverse reaction:

- This reaction is the reverse of the original equilibrium, so *K*<sub>c</sub> (reverse) = $\frac{1}{K_{c}\text{(forward)}}$:

*K*<sub>c</sub> = $\frac{1}{255}$

*K*<sub>c</sub> = **3.92 x 10**<sup>**-3**</sup> mol<sup>3</sup> dm<sup>-9</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for *K*<sub>c</sub> = 1/255 = 3.92 × 10<sup>-3</sup> mol<sup>3</sup> dm<sup>-9</sup>
> 
> Allow 0.00392 mol<sup>3</sup> dm<sup>-9</sup>

> **[exam-tip]**
> When an equation is reversed, the *K*<sub>c</sub> value is inverted: *K*<sub>c</sub> (reverse) = 1 / *K*<sub>c</sub> (forward) = 1/255 = 3.92 × 10<sup>-3</sup>.
> 
> For units: the forward reaction (3A + 2B ⇌ 2C) has Δ*n* = 2 − 5 = −3, giving units of mol<sup>-3</sup> dm<sup>9</sup>. The reverse reaction has Δ*n* = +3, so units are mol<sup>3</sup> dm<sup>-9</sup>.

parts.problemMd:
The graph in **Fig. 2.1** shows the effect of pressure and temperature on the equilibrium yield of a gaseous product.

![Graph (Fig. 2.1) showing equilibrium yield / % against temperature for three pressures (5 MPa, 20 MPa and 30 MPa). At each pressure, yield decreases as temperature increases and is greatest at the lowest pressure (5 MPa).](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/7-equilibria/7-1-chemical-equilibria-reversible-reactions-and-dynamic-equilibrium/assets/002-graph-fig-2-1-showing-equilibrium-yield-against-.png)

**Fig. 2.1**

Use **Fig. 2.1** to deduce whether the forward reaction is exothermic or endothermic. Explain your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Using Fig. 2.1 to deduce whether the forward reaction is exothermic or endothermic:
> 
> - The forward reaction is exothermic **[1 mark]**
> - As temperature increases, the equilibrium yield decreases, so the equilibrium shifts to oppose the increase in temperature by favouring the reverse / endothermic reaction **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> From Fig. 2.1, the equilibrium yield decreases as temperature increases at all pressures. By Le Chatelier's principle, this means the system opposes the temperature increase by favouring the endothermic (reverse) reaction, which lowers the yield. The forward reaction must therefore be exothermic.
> 
> Structure your answer clearly: state the conclusion (exothermic), then justify it using evidence from the graph and Le Chatelier's principle.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The graph in **Fig. 2.1** shows the effect of pressure and temperature on the equilibrium yield of a gaseous product.

{align=center} **Fig. 2.1**

At each pressure, yield decreases as temperature increases and is greatest at the lowest pressure (5 MPa).

Use **Fig. 2.1** to deduce whether the forward reaction produces an increase or a decrease in the number of moles of gas. Explain your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Using Fig. 2.1 to deduce the change in moles of gas in the forward reaction:
> 
> - The forward reaction produces an increase in the number of moles of gas **[1 mark]**
> - As pressure increases, the equilibrium yield decreases, so the equilibrium shifts to the side with fewer moles of gas (left / backward reaction)
> **OR**
> as pressure decreases, the equilibrium yield increases, so the equilibrium shifts to the side with more moles of gas (right / forward reaction) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> From Fig. 2.1, yield is greatest at the lowest pressure (5 MPa) and lowest at the highest pressure (30 MPa). By Le Chatelier's principle, increasing pressure shifts the equilibrium to the side with fewer moles of gas. Since higher pressure gives lower yield (less product), the product side must have more moles of gas than the reactant side — the forward reaction increases the number of moles of gas.

parts.problemMd:
**Fig. 2.2** shows the relationship between temperature and *K*<sub>c</sub> for a different dynamic equilibrium.

![Graph (Fig. 2.2) showing Kc against temperature. Kc decreases as temperature increases, indicating the forward reaction is exothermic.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/7-equilibria/7-1-chemical-equilibria-reversible-reactions-and-dynamic-equilibrium/assets/003-graph-fig-2-2-showing-kc-against-temperature-kc-.png)

**Fig. 2.2**

Use the information in **Fig. 2.2** to deduce whether the forward reaction is exothermic or endothermic. Explain your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Using Fig. 2.2 to deduce whether the forward reaction is exothermic or endothermic:
> 
> - The forward reaction is exothermic **[1 mark]**
> - As temperature increases, *K*<sub>c</sub> decreases, so the equilibrium shifts to the left / favours the reverse / endothermic reaction at higher temperatures **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> *K*<sub>c</sub> can only change with temperature. If *K*<sub>c</sub> decreases as temperature increases, the concentration of products decreases relative to reactants. By Le Chatelier's principle, the system opposes the increase in temperature by favouring the endothermic (reverse) reaction, so the forward reaction must be exothermic.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

**Fig. 2.2** shows the relationship between temperature and *K*~c~ for a different dynamic equilibrium.

Graph (Fig. 2.2) showing Kc against temperature. Kc decreases as temperature increases, indicating the forward reaction is exothermic.

The equilibrium in **Fig. 2.2** is used to manufacture a gaseous product industrially.

Suggest one reason why the industrial temperature may be higher than the temperature that gives the maximum equilibrium yield.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> One reason why the industrial temperature may be higher than the temperature that gives the maximum equilibrium yield:
> 
> - A higher temperature increases the rate of reaction **[1 mark]**
> - The rate at the temperature of maximum yield is too slow to be economically viable / to produce product at an acceptable rate **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> This is the classic industrial compromise between rate and yield. At the temperature that gives maximum equilibrium yield, the reaction may be so slow that very little product forms per unit time, making the process uneconomical. A higher temperature sacrifices some equilibrium yield but greatly increases the rate of product formation.
> 
> A one-mark answer stating 'to increase the rate' is not sufficient on its own — you must explain why a slower rate at the optimum yield temperature is a problem (economic viability or unacceptably slow production).

parts.problemMd:
At high temperatures, gaseous phosphorus(V) chloride dissociates according to the following equation:

PCl<sub>5</sub> (g) ⇌ PCl<sub>3</sub> (g) + Cl<sub>2</sub> (g)

At 550 K, the equilibrium amount of each gas is shown in Table 3.1.

**Table 3.1**

| **Chemical** | PCl<sub>5</sub> (g) | PCl<sub>3</sub> (g) | Cl<sub>2</sub> (g) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Equilibrium moles** | 0.192 | 0.822 | 0.822 |

Calculate the total pressure of the reaction, if *K*<sub>p</sub> = 526 kPa. Give your answer to an appropriate number of significant figures. Show your working.

*P* = ........................... kPa
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the total pressure of the equilibrium mixture:

- Calculate the total moles:

total moles = 0.192 + 0.822 + 0.822

total moles = 1.836 mol **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the mole fractions:

x(PCl<sub>5</sub>) = $\frac{0.192}{1.836}$ = 0.1046

x(PCl<sub>3</sub>) = x(Cl<sub>2</sub>) = $\frac{0.822}{1.836}$ = 0.4477

**[1 mark]**

- Write the *K*<sub>p</sub> expression and substitute partial pressures in terms of *P*:

*K*<sub>p</sub> = $\frac{p\mathrm{PCl}_{3}\timesp\mathrm{Cl}_{2}}{p\mathrm{Cl}_{5}}$

526 = $\frac{(0.4477\timesP)\times(0.4477\timesP)}{(0.1046\timesP)}$

526 = $\frac{(0.4477)^{2}\timesP}{0.1046}$ **[1 mark]**

- Rearrange and solve for *P*:

*P* = $\frac{526\times0.1046}{0.4477^{2}}$

*P* = **274** kPa (3 s.f.) **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for total moles = 1.836 mol
> 
> 1 mark for mole fractions: x(PCl<sub>5</sub>) = 0.1046 **AND** x(PCl<sub>3</sub>) = x(Cl<sub>2</sub>) = 0.4477
> 
> 1 mark for correct algebraic substitution showing *K*<sub>p</sub> = (0.4477)<sup>2</sup> x *P* / 0.1046
> 
> 1 mark for *P* = 274 kPa (allow 274–275 kPa, 3 s.f.)
> 
> Allow error carried forward from incorrect mole fractions if the algebraic method is correct.

> **[exam-tip]**
> When total pressure is unknown, represent it as *P* in the partial pressure expressions: p = mole fraction x *P*. Substituting into *K*<sub>p</sub> gives a linear expression in *P* (the *P*<sup>2</sup> terms in numerator and denominator cancel for this reaction), which can be rearranged directly.
> 
> PCl<sub>3</sub> and Cl<sub>2</sub> have equal equilibrium moles, so their mole fractions are equal. The *K*<sub>p</sub> expression therefore simplifies to (0.4477)<sup>2</sup> x *P* / 0.1046.

parts.problemMd:
Nitrogen dioxide decomposes according to the following equation:

2NO<sub>2</sub> (g) ⇌ 2NO (g) + O<sub>2</sub> (g)

At 700 K, the equilibrium amount of each gas is shown in Table 3.2.

**Table 3.2**

| **Chemical** | NO<sub>2</sub> (g) | NO (g) | O<sub>2</sub> (g) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Equilibrium moles** | 0.920 | 0.0600 | 0.0400 |

Calculate the total pressure of the reaction, if *K*<sub>p</sub> = 9.8 x 10<sup>-3</sup> kPa. Show your working.

*P* = ................... kPa
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the total pressure of the equilibrium mixture:

- Calculate the total moles:

total moles = 0.920 + 0.0600 + 0.0400 = 1.020 mol **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the mole fractions:

x(NO<sub>2</sub>) = $\frac{0.920}{1.020}$ = 0.9020

x(NO) = $\frac{0.0600}{1.020}$ = 0.05882

x(O<sub>2</sub>) = $\frac{0.0400}{1.020}$ = 0.03922

**[1 mark]**

- Write the *K*<sub>p</sub> expression and substitute partial pressures in terms of *P*:

*K*<sub>p</sub> = (pNO)<sup>2</sup> x pO<sub>2</sub> / (pNO<sub>2</sub>)<sup>2</sup>

9.8 x 10<sup>-3</sup> = (0.05882 x *P*)<sup>2</sup> x (0.03922 x *P*) / (0.9020 x *P*)<sup>2</sup>

9.8 x 10<sup>-3</sup> = (0.05882)<sup>2</sup> x 0.03922 x *P* / (0.9020)<sup>2</sup> **[1 mark]**

- Solve for *P*:

9.8 x 10<sup>-3</sup> = 1.668 x 10<sup>-4</sup> x *P*

*P* = **58.8** kPa **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for total moles = 1.02 mol
> 
> 1 mark for mole fractions: x(NO<sub>2</sub>) = 0.9020, x(NO) = 0.05882, x(O<sub>2</sub>) = 0.03922
> 
> 1 mark for correct algebraic substitution showing *P*<sup>2</sup> terms cancel to give a linear expression in *P*
> 
> 1 mark for *P* = 58.8 kPa (allow 58.7–58.9 kPa)
> 
> Allow error carried forward from incorrect mole fractions if the algebraic method is correct.

> **[exam-tip]**
> In this *K*<sub>p</sub> expression, (pNO)<sup>2</sup> appears in the numerator and (pNO<sub>2</sub>)<sup>2</sup> in the denominator. When substituting p = mole fraction x *P*, the *P*<sup>2</sup> terms cancel, leaving a single *P* term that can be rearranged directly.
> 
> Work through the algebra carefully: expand each bracket, identify cancelling *P*<sup>2</sup> terms, then collect the remaining *P* terms before dividing to find *P*.

parts.problemMd:
Hydrogen iodide can undergo thermal decomposition according to the following equation:

2HI (g) ⇌ H<sub>2</sub> (g) + I<sub>2</sub> (g)

The value of *K*<sub>p</sub> for this reaction at 700 K is 0.0185.

Calculate the total pressure when the partial pressure of hydrogen iodide, at equilibrium, is 133 kPa. Give your answer to an appropriate number of significant figures. Show your working.

*P* = ......................... kPa
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the total pressure when pHI = 133 kPa:

- Write the *K*<sub>p</sub> expression:

*K*<sub>p</sub> = pH<sub>2</sub> x pI<sub>2</sub> / pHI<sup>2</sup> **[1 mark]**

- Recognise that H<sub>2</sub> and I<sub>2</sub> are produced in a 1:1 ratio, so pH<sub>2</sub> = pI<sub>2</sub>. Simplify the expression:

*K*<sub>p</sub> = pH<sub>2</sub><sup>2</sup> / pHI<sup>2</sup> **[1 mark]**

- Rearrange and calculate pH<sub>2</sub>:

0.0185 = pH<sub>2</sub><sup>2</sup> / 133<sup>2</sup>

pH<sub>2</sub><sup>2</sup> = 0.0185 x 133<sup>2</sup> = 327.2

pH<sub>2</sub> = pI<sub>2</sub> = $\sqrt{327.2}$ = 18.1 kPa **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the total pressure:

*P* = pHI + pH<sub>2</sub> + pI<sub>2</sub>

*P* = 133 + 18.1 + 18.1 = **169** kPa **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for *K*<sub>p</sub> = pH<sub>2</sub> x pI<sub>2</sub> / pHI<sup>2</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for recognising pH<sub>2</sub> = pI<sub>2</sub> and simplifying to *K*<sub>p</sub> = pH<sub>2</sub><sup>2</sup> / pHI<sup>2</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for pH<sub>2</sub> = pI<sub>2</sub> = 18.1 kPa (allow 18.0–18.1 kPa)
> 
> 1 mark for *P* = 169 kPa (3 s.f.) (allow 169–170 kPa)
> 
> Allow error carried forward from incorrect pH<sub>2</sub> if the method is correct.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The key insight is that H<sub>2</sub> and I<sub>2</sub> are produced in a 1:1 molar ratio (from the stoichiometry 2HI ⇌ H<sub>2</sub> + I<sub>2</sub>), so their partial pressures at equilibrium are equal. This allows the *K*<sub>p</sub> expression to simplify to *K*<sub>p</sub> = pH<sub>2</sub><sup>2</sup> / pHI<sup>2</sup>, which can be rearranged directly without needing mole fractions.
> 
> *K*<sub>p</sub> for this reaction is dimensionless (no units) because Δ*n* = 0 — equal moles of gas on each side. The partial pressures and total pressure are all in kPa.

parts.problemMd:
Dinitrogen tetroxide decomposes according to the following equilibrium:

N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> (g) ⇌ 2NO<sub>2</sub> (g)

The value of *K*<sub>p</sub> for this reaction at 300 K is 385 kPa.

The equilibrium mixture contained 2.40 mol of nitrogen dioxide after an initial 3.00 mol of dinitrogen tetroxide were heated at 300 K.

Calculate the partial pressures of N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> (g) and NO<sub>2</sub> (g). Give your answer to an appropriate number of significant figures. Show your working.

*p*N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> = ................... kPa

*p*NO<sub>2</sub> = ................... kPa
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the partial pressures of N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> (g) and NO<sub>2</sub> (g):

- Deduce the equilibrium moles of N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>:

|   | N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> (g) | NO<sub>2</sub> (g) |
|---|---|---|
| Initial moles | 3.00 | 0 |
| Change / mol | −1.20 | +2.40 |
| Equilibrium moles | **1.80** | **2.40** |

**[1 mark]**

- Calculate the total moles and mole fractions:

total moles = 1.80 + 2.40 = 4.20 mol

x(N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>) = $\frac{1.80}{4.20}$ = 0.4286

x(NO<sub>2</sub>) = $\frac{2.40}{4.20}$ = 0.5714

**[1 mark]**

- Write the *K*<sub>p</sub> expression and substitute partial pressures in terms of *P*:

*K*<sub>p</sub> = pNO<sub>2</sub><sup>2</sup> / pN<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>

385 = (0.5714 x *P*)<sup>2</sup> / (0.4286 x *P*)

385 = (0.5714)<sup>2</sup> x *P* / 0.4286 **[1 mark]**

- Solve for total pressure *P*:

*P* = 385 x 0.4286 / (0.5714)<sup>2</sup> = **505** kPa **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the partial pressures:

*p*N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> = 0.4286 x 505 = **217** kPa

*p*NO<sub>2</sub> = 0.5714 x 505 = **289** kPa

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> equilibrium moles = 1.80 mol
> 
> 1 mark for mole fractions: x(N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>) = 0.4286 **AND** x(NO<sub>2</sub>) = 0.5714
> 
> 1 mark for correct algebraic substitution showing *P*<sup>2</sup> cancels to give a linear expression in *P*
> 
> 1 mark for total pressure *P* = 505 kPa (allow 505–506 kPa)
> 
> 1 mark for *p*N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> = 217 kPa (allow 216–217) **AND** *p*NO<sub>2</sub> = 289 kPa (allow 288–289)
> 
> Allow error carried forward from incorrect mole fractions or incorrect *P* if the method is correct.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The equilibrium moles of N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> must be found first. Since NO<sub>2</sub> and N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> react in a 2:1 ratio, the change in N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> = 2.40/2 = 1.20 mol, giving 3.00 − 1.20 = 1.80 mol at equilibrium.
> 
> Once total pressure *P* is found by the algebraic method, multiply each mole fraction by *P* to obtain the individual partial pressures.
> 
> Answers should be given to 3 significant figures, consistent with the data provided.

parts.problemMd: State what is meant by a Brønsted–Lowry acid.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> A Brønsted–Lowry acid is:
> 
> - A species that donates a proton / H<sup>+</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> A Brønsted–Lowry acid is a proton / H<sup>+</sup> donor. A Brønsted–Lowry base is a proton / H<sup>+</sup> acceptor. Remember that in an equilibrium, both the forward and reverse reactions involve Brønsted–Lowry acid–base pairs.

parts.problemMd:
Identify the two species that act as Brønsted–Lowry bases in the following reaction.

HSO<sub>4</sub><sup>-</sup> (aq) + H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> (aq) ⇌ H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (aq) + H<sub>2</sub>O (l)
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The two species that act as Brønsted–Lowry bases are:
> 
> - HSO<sub>4</sub><sup>-</sup>
> **AND**
> H<sub>2</sub>O **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> In an equilibrium reaction, each direction involves a Brønsted–Lowry acid and a Brønsted–Lowry base.
> 
> In the forward reaction:
> 
> - HSO<sub>4</sub><sup>-</sup> accepts a proton from H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> to form H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>
> - So, HSO<sub>4</sub><sup>-</sup> is the Brønsted–Lowry base.
> 
> In the reverse reaction:
> 
> - H<sub>2</sub>O accepts a proton from H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> to form H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>
> - So, H<sub>2</sub>O is the Brønsted–Lowry base.

parts.problemMd:
Identify the species that acts as a Brønsted–Lowry acid in the following reaction.

CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2-</sup> (aq) + H<sup>+</sup> (aq) ⇌ HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup> (aq)
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The species that acts as a Brønsted–Lowry acid is:
> 
> - HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> A Brønsted–Lowry acid is a proton donor.
> 
> In the reverse reaction, HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup> donates H<sup>+</sup> to form CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2-</sup>, making it the Brønsted–Lowry acid. In the forward reaction, H<sup>+</sup> is the proton donor.
> 
> The question asks which species in the equilibrium acts as an acid, and identifying HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup> shows understanding of the reverse reaction direction.

parts.problemMd:
Propanoic acid, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>H, is a weak acid.

Construct an equation to show the dissociation of propanoic acid in water.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Propanoic acid dissociates as follows:
> 
> - CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>H (aq) ⇌ CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COO<sup>-</sup> (aq) + H<sup>+</sup> (aq)
> **OR** CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>H (aq) + H<sub>2</sub>O (l) ⇌ CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COO<sup>-</sup> (aq) + H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> (aq) **[1 mark]**
> 
> The equilibrium arrow (⇌) must be used; a single-headed arrow (→) is not accepted.
> 
> State symbols are not required.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Propanoic acid is a weak acid, which means that it only partially dissociates in aqueous solution.
> 
> Use the reversible arrow ⇌, not a single-headed arrow →.
> 
> Either form of the equation is accepted: with H<sup>+</sup> or with H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> for the hydrogen ion in solution.

parts.problemMd:
KOH (aq) is added from a burette to HCl (aq) in a beaker.

On Fig. 6.1, sketch the pH curve for this reaction.

![An empty graph with volume of KOH (aq) added (cm³) on the x-axis and pH on the y-axis, used to sketch a titration curve](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/7-equilibria/7-2-brnsted-lowry-theory-of-acids-and-bases/assets/003-an-empty-graph-with-volume-of-koh-aq-added-cm-on.png)

**Fig. 6.1**
parts.solutionMd:
The completed pH curve is:

![A pH titration curve for a strong acid–strong base reaction: starts at low pH, rises steeply through the equivalence point at pH 7, and levels off at high pH](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/7-equilibria/7-2-brnsted-lowry-theory-of-acids-and-bases/assets/004-a-ph-titration-curve-for-a-strong-acid-strong-ba.jpeg)

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for the curve starting between pH 0–3
> 
> 1 mark for the equivalence point at pH 7
> 
> 1 mark for the curve ending between pH 12–14

> **[exam-tip]**
> HCl is a strong acid (starting pH 0–3) and KOH is a strong base (finishing pH 12–14).
> 
> The equivalence point for a strong acid–strong base titration is at pH 7.
> 
> The steep vertical section should be centred on pH 7. So, make sure the point of inflection is at this value.

parts.problemMd:
A titration was performed between ethanoic acid, CH<sub>3</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>H (aq), and sodium hydroxide, NaOH (aq).

**Table 6.1**

| **Indicator** | **pH range** |
|---|---|
| Pentamethoxy red | 1.2–3.2 |
| Naphthyl red | 3.7–5.0 |
| 4-nitrophenol | 5.6–7.0 |
| Cresol purple | 7.6–9.2 |

i) Construct an equation for the reaction between ethanoic acid and sodium hydroxide.

[1]

ii) Use the information in Table 6.1 to identify a suitable indicator for this titration.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The equation for this reaction is:
> 
> - CH<sub>3</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>H (aq) + NaOH (aq) → CH<sub>3</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>Na (aq) + H<sub>2</sub>O (l) **[1 mark]**
> 
> State symbols are not required.
> 
> ii) A suitable indicator for this titration is:
> 
> - Cresol purple **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The salt formed in this reaction is sodium ethanoate, CH<sub>3</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>Na, which partially hydrolyses in water to give an alkaline solution.
> 
> This means the equivalence point is above pH 7. Therefore, any indicator that changes colour in the acidic or neutral range would give an inaccurate endpoint. Cresol purple (pH 7.6–9.2) is the only indicator in Table 6.1 whose range covers the alkaline equivalence point.

parts.problemMd: Apart from using a pH probe or indicator, describe **one** chemical test that could be used to show that hydrochloric acid is a stronger acid than ethanoic acid of the same concentration. State the expected observation for each acid.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Any **one** of the following sets (1 mark for each point):
> 
> Set 1
> 
> - Test the electrical conductivity of each acid
> - Hydrochloric acid conducts electricity better / has a lower resistance than ethanoic acid
> 
> **OR**
> 
> Set 2
> 
> - Add a reactive metal / carbonate / hydrogen carbonate to each acid
> - Hydrochloric acid shows greater effervescence / faster rate of reaction than ethanoic acid
> 
> **OR**
> 
> Set 3
> 
> - Add the same volume of sodium hydroxide solution to each acid and measure the temperature change
> - Hydrochloric acid produces a greater temperature rise than ethanoic acid
> 
> **[2 marks]**
> 
> Describing a titration method for Set 3 is not accepted.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Any method that produces a measurable difference between the two acids is valid, but you must state both the test and the expected observation for each acid to gain both marks.
> 
> HCl is fully dissociated (strong acid) while CH<sub>3</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>H is only partially dissociated (weak acid) at the same concentration. This difference in [H<sup>+</sup>] drives all of these observations.

parts.problemMd:
i) State what is meant by a Brønsted–Lowry base.

[1]

ii) Explain what is meant by a weak acid.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) A Brønsted–Lowry base is a species that:
> 
> - Accepts a proton / H<sup>+</sup> **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) A weak acid is:
> 
> - A proton / H<sup>+</sup> donor **[1 mark]**
> - That only partially ionises / dissociates in water (to give H<sup>+</sup>) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> These definitions are frequently examined. For a Brønsted–Lowry base, the key word is “accepts” a proton. For a weak acid, you need both parts of the definition: it is a proton donor AND it only partially dissociates in water. Missing out either part will lose a mark.

parts.problemMd:
A student titrated 0.10 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> acid into a conical flask containing 25.0 cm<sup>3</sup> of 0.10 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> of a base, recording the pH with each addition of acid. The student repeated the procedure using different combinations of acids and bases.

![A graph showing three pH titration curves labelled X, Y, and Z, with volume of acid added (cm³) on the x-axis and pH on the y-axis](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/7-equilibria/7-2-brnsted-lowry-theory-of-acids-and-bases/assets/002-a-graph-showing-three-ph-titration-curves-labell.png)

**Fig. 5.1**

Identify the curve in Fig. 5.1 that represents the titration of:

i) Ammonia and ethanoic acid.

[1]

ii) Ammonia and nitric acid.

[1]

iii) Sodium hydroxide and propanoic acid.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The curves that represent each acid-base combination are:
> 
> i) Ammonia and ethanoic acid:
> 
> - X **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) Ammonia and nitric acid:
> 
> - Z **[1 mark]**
> 
> iii) Sodium hydroxide and propanoic acid:
> 
> - Y **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Look at the starting pH to identify the base (strong base starts pH 11–13; weak base starts pH 7–10) and the ending pH to identify the acid (strong acid ends pH 0–3; weak acid ends pH 4–7). Matching both gives the correct curve.
> 
> Curve X:
> 
> - Weak base (NH<sub>3</sub>) + weak acid (CH<sub>3</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>H)
> - Starts pH 7–10, ends pH 4–7.
> 
> Curve Z:
> 
> - Weak base (NH<sub>3</sub>) + strong acid (HNO<sub>3</sub>)
> - Starts pH 7–10, ends pH 0–3.
> 
> Curve Y:
> 
> - Strong base (NaOH) + weak acid (CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>H)
> - Starts pH 11–13, ends pH 4–7.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A student titrated 0.10 mol dm^-3^ acid into a conical flask containing 25.0 cm^3^ of 0.10 mol dm^-3^ of a base, recording the pH with each addition of addition of acid. The student repeated the procedure using different combinations of acids and bases.

Identify the curve in Fig. 5.1 that represents the titration of:

i) Ammonia and ethanoic acid.

ii) Ammonia and nitric acid.

iii) Sodium hydroxide and propanoic acid.

Curve Z represents ammonia and nitric acid.

Identify which indicator in Table 5.2 would be most suitable for curve Z. Explain your answer.

**Table 5.2**

| **Indicator** | **pH range** |
|---|---|
| Methyl orange | 3.1–4.4 |
| Phenolphthalein | 8.3–10.0 |
| Bromothymol blue | 6.0–7.6 |
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The most suitable indicator for curve Z is:
> 
> - Methyl orange **[1 mark]**
> - Curve Z is a strong acid–weak base titration, so the equivalence point is below pH 7
> **OR**
> Methyl orange changes colour between pH 3.1–4.4, which covers the equivalence point **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Curve Z represents nitric acid (strong acid) added to ammonia (weak base), where the equivalence point is below pH 7.
> 
> The indicator must change colour within the steep section of the curve. Methyl orange (pH 3.1–4.4) is the only indicator in Table 5.2 with a range below pH 7.

parts.problemMd:
Water is amphoteric and will react with nitric acid and ammonia.

i) Construct an equation to show how water reacts with ammonia.

[1]

ii) State what is meant by the term amphoteric.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The equation for the reaction of water with ammonia is:
> 
> - H<sub>2</sub>O (l) + NH<sub>3</sub> (aq) ⇌ NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> (aq) + OH<sup>-</sup> (aq) **[1 mark]**
> 
> The equilibrium arrow (⇌) must be used since this is a reversible reaction.
> 
> State symbols are not required.
> 
> ii) A species that is amphoteric:
> 
> - Can behave as both a Brønsted–Lowry acid and a Brønsted–Lowry base **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> In the equation for part (i), water acts as a Brønsted–Lowry acid because it donates a proton to ammonia.
> 
> Water is amphoteric because it can also accept a proton (acting as a base, as in its reaction with acids).

parts.problemMd:
**A** and **B** are two solutions of the same concentration that have pH values of 3 and 6 respectively.

i) Identify the stronger acid. Calculate the concentration of hydrogen ions in each solution.

[2]

ii) Calculate the ratio of the hydrogen ion concentrations in **A** and **B**.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
i) The stronger acid is **A** **[1 mark]**

To calculate [H<sup>+</sup>] for each solution using [H<sup>+</sup>] = 10<sup>-pH</sup>:

[H<sup>+</sup>]<sub>A</sub> = 10<sup>-3</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup>

[H<sup>+</sup>]<sub>B</sub> = 10<sup>-6</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup>

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for identifying **A** as the stronger acid
> 
> 1 mark for both [H<sup>+</sup>] values.

ii) To calculate the ratio [H<sup>+</sup>]<sub>A</sub> : [H<sup>+</sup>]<sub>B</sub>:

10<sup>-3</sup> ÷ 10<sup>-6</sup> = 10<sup>3</sup> = 1000

Ratio = **1000 : 1** **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Accept 10<sup>3</sup> : 1 for the ratio in part (ii).

> **[exam-tip]**
> The stronger acid has the lower pH at the same concentration, indicating a higher [H<sup>+</sup>] and greater dissociation.
> 
> To convert pH to [H<sup>+</sup>], use [H<sup>+</sup>] = 10<sup>-pH</sup>.
> 
> Take care with the direction of the ratio in part (ii) as the question asks for [H<sup>+</sup>]<sub>A</sub> : [H<sup>+</sup>]<sub>B</sub>, so the answer is 1000 : 1. Note that 10<sup>-3</sup> is 1000 times larger than 10<sup>-6</sup>, not smaller.

parts.problemMd:
The variation of conductivity and concentration of a strong and weak monoprotic acid are shown in Fig. 2.1.

![A graph showing conductivity on the vertical axis against concentration on the horizontal axis for two monoprotic acids labelled 1 and 2; Acid 1 shows a linear relationship while Acid 2 shows a curved relationship that levels off at higher concentrations](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/7-equilibria/7-2-brnsted-lowry-theory-of-acids-and-bases/assets/007-a-graph-showing-conductivity-on-the-vertical-axi.png)

**Fig. 2.1**

Use the information in Fig. 2.1 to deduce which acid is strong and which is weak. Explain your reasoning.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> From Fig. 2.1, the identities of the acids are:
> 
> - Acid **1** is the strong acid
> **AND**
> Acid **2** is the weak acid **[1 mark]**
> 
> The reasoning is:
> 
> Any **two** from (1 mark for each point):
> 
> - Acid **1** shows a linear relationship between concentration and conductivity
> - The number of ions in Acid **1** is proportional to its concentration / doubling the concentration of Acid **1** doubles the number of ions present
> - Acid **1** is fully ionised at all concentrations shown
> - Acid **2** reaches a maximum conductivity at low concentration
> - Doubling the concentration of Acid **2** does not double the number of ions present
> 
> **[2 marks]**
> 
> The reverse arguments (describing Acid **2** as the weak acid) are equally acceptable.

> **[exam-tip]**
> A strong acid fully ionises at all concentrations. So, conductivity increases linearly with concentration (more ions = higher conductivity).
> 
> A weak acid only partially ionises, and the degree of ionisation decreases as concentration increases, so conductivity does not increase proportionally.
> 
> When giving reasoning, you should address both acids or refer to the specific features of Fig. 2.1 that support your answer.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The variation of conductivity and concentration of a strong and weak monoprotic acid are shown in Fig. 2.1.

Acid 1 is the strong acid
Acid 2 is the weak acid

State how the volume of 0.2 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> NaOH required to neutralise 20 cm<sup>3</sup> of 0.1 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> acid **1** compares to the volume required to neutralise the same volume of 0.1 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> acid **2**.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The volume of NaOH required:
> 
> - Both acids require the same volume of NaOH (aq) / both require 10 cm<sup>3</sup> of 0.2 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> NaOH **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The strength of an acid does not affect its concentration.
> 
> Both acids are 0.1 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> and both are monoprotic, so 20 cm<sup>3</sup> of each contains the same number of moles of acid.
> 
> The same moles of H<sup>+</sup> are available for neutralisation, requiring the same volume of NaOH solution regardless of acid strength.

parts.problemMd:
Glycolic acid, C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>O<sub>3</sub>, is an organic acid sometimes used to remove limescale, CaCO<sub>3</sub>, from electric kettles and coffee machines.

State and explain one difference that would be observed when samples of calcium carbonate react with the same concentration of sulfuric acid and glycolic acid.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> One difference that would be observed is:
> 
> - Slower rate of reaction with glycolic acid than with sulfuric acid
> **OR**
> Less effervescence / fewer bubbles with glycolic acid than with sulfuric acid
> **OR**
> A smaller temperature rise with glycolic acid than with sulfuric acid **[1 mark]**
> 
> This is because:
> 
> - Glycolic acid is a weak acid / only partially dissociates in water, giving a lower [H<sup>+</sup>] than sulfuric acid at the same concentration **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Organic acids are generally weak acids, which means that they only partially ionise in water.
> 
> At the same concentration, a weak acid has a lower [H<sup>+</sup>] than a strong acid, so its reaction rate with CaCO<sub>3</sub> is slower. Both the observation (slower reaction / less effervescence) and the reason (weak acid / partial dissociation) are required for full marks.

parts.problemMd: A solution of hydrochloric acid has a pH of 1 and a solution of carbonic acid has a pH of 5. Calculate the ratio of hydrogen ion concentrations of hydrochloric acid to carbonic acid.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the ratio of [H<sup>+</sup>] in hydrochloric acid to [H<sup>+</sup>] in carbonic acid:

- Convert pH to [H<sup>+</sup>] using [H<sup>+</sup>] = 10<sup>-pH</sup>:

For HCl: [H<sup>+</sup>] = 10<sup>-1</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup>

For H<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>: [H<sup>+</sup>] = 10<sup>-5</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup>

**[1 mark]**

- Calculate the ratio:

10<sup>-1</sup> ÷ 10<sup>-5</sup> = 10<sup>4</sup>

Ratio = **10 000 : 1** **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for both [H<sup>+</sup>] values
> 
> 1 mark the correct ratio
> 
> Accept 10<sup>4</sup> : 1 for the ratio.
> 
> The ratio must be expressed as HCl : H<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>, so the answer 1 : 10 000 is not accepted.

> **[exam-tip]**
> To convert pH to [H<sup>+</sup>], use [H<sup>+</sup>] = 10<sup>-pH</sup>.
> 
> In part (ii), take care with the direction of the ratio as the question asks for HCl : H<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>, so HCl (lower pH, higher [H<sup>+</sup>]) must come first. 10<sup>-1</sup> is 10<sup>4</sup> times larger than 10<sup>-5</sup>, giving a ratio of 10 000 : 1.

parts.problemMd: Apart from measuring the pH, describe two methods that could be used to distinguish between equimolar solutions of carbonic acid and hydrochloric acid. State the expected observation for each method.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Any **two** of the following sets (1 mark for the method, 1 mark for the observation):
> 
> Set 1
> 
> - Add a named reactive metal (e.g. magnesium) to each solution
> - The metal reacts faster / produces more bubbles with HCl than with H<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> / the metal does not react noticeably with H<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>
> 
> **OR**
> 
> Set 2
> 
> - Add solid sodium carbonate / sodium hydrogen carbonate to each solution
> - More vigorous effervescence with HCl / the carbonate does not dissolve noticeably in H<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>
> 
> **OR**
> 
> Set 3
> 
> - Test the electrical conductivity of each solution
> - HCl has greater conductivity / lower resistance than H<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>
> 
> **[4 marks]**
> 
> You would not be expected to know specific reactions of carbonic acid; comparison of strong vs. weak acid behaviour is sufficient.

> **[exam-tip]**
> For each method, you must state both the test and the expected observation for each acid to gain both marks.
> 
> HCl is a strong acid (fully dissociated, higher [H<sup>+</sup>]) while H<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> is a weak acid (partially dissociated, lower [H<sup>+</sup>]). This difference drives all the observable distinctions.

parts.problemMd:
A student carried out two acid-base titrations. The pH ranges of four indicators are given in Table 1.1.

**Table 1.1**

| **Indicator** | **pH range** |
|---|---|
| methyl red | 4.2–6.3 |
| bromothymol blue | 6.0–7.6 |
| bromocresol green | 3.8–5.4 |
| phenolphthalein | 8.2–10.0 |

In the first titration, 0.200 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> aqueous ammonia is added from a burette to 10.0 cm<sup>3</sup> of 0.200 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> HCl (aq).

Sketch the pH curve for this reaction.
parts.solutionMd:
The completed pH curve is:

![A pH titration curve for a strong acid–weak base reaction: starts between pH 0–2, rises steeply at 10 cm³ with equivalence point at approximately pH 5, and levels off between pH 9–11](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/7-equilibria/7-2-brnsted-lowry-theory-of-acids-and-bases/assets/005-a-ph-titration-curve-for-a-strong-acid-weak-base.png)

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for the initial pH between 0–2
> 
> 1 mark for the vertical section at 10 cm<sup>3</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for the curve tailing off between pH 9–11

> **[exam-tip]**
> HCl is a strong acid, which means that the initial pH should be between 0–2.
> 
> Ammonia is a weak base, which means that the curve tails off between pH 9–11.
> 
> Both solutions are 0.200 mol dm<sup>-3</sup>, so equal volumes react: the equivalence point is at 10 cm<sup>3</sup> of ammonia added. This is a strong acid–weak base titration, so the equivalence point is below pH 7 (approximately pH 5).

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A student carried out two acid-base titrations. The pH ranges of four indicators are given in Table 1.1.

**Table 1.1**

| **Indicator** | **pH range** |
| --- | :---: |
| methyl red | 4.2–6.3 |
| bromothymol blue | 6.0–7.6 |
| bromocresol green | 3.8–5.4 |
| phenolphthalein | 8.2–10.0 |

In the first titration, 0.200 mol dm^-3^ aqueous ammonia is added from a burette to 10.0 cm^3^ of 0.200 mol dm^-3^ HCl (aq).

Using Table 1.1, explain why methyl red is a suitable indicator for the first titration but phenolphthalein is not.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Methyl red is a suitable indicator for this titration but phenolphthalein is not because:
> 
> - Methyl red changes colour at the equivalence point / where the sharpest pH change occurs **[1 mark]**
> - Phenolphthalein changes colour between pH 8.2–10.0, which does not correspond to the equivalence point / steepest part of the curve **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For a strong acid–weak base titration, the equivalence point is below pH 7 (approximately pH 5).
> 
> A suitable indicator must change colour within the steep section of the curve. Check whether the indicator's pH range in Table 1.1 overlaps with the equivalence point.

parts.problemMd:
In the second titration, 0.100 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> ethanoic acid is added from a burette to 25.0 cm<sup>3</sup> of 0.200 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> NaOH (aq).

Sketch the pH curve for this reaction.

The completed pH curve is:

> 1 mark for the vertical section at 50 cm<sup>3</sup>

> Ethanoic acid is a weak acid, which means that the curve tails off between pH 3–5.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A student carried out two acid-base titrations. The pH ranges of four indicators are given in Table 1.1.

**Table 1.1**

| **Indicator** | **pH range** |
| --- | :---: |
| methyl red | 4.2–6.3 |
| bromothymol blue | 6.0–7.6 |
| bromocresol green | 3.8–5.4 |
| phenolphthalein | 8.2–10.0 |

In the second titration, 0.100 mol dm^-3^ ethanoic acid is added from a burette to 25.0 cm^3^ of 0.200 mol dm^-3^ NaOH (aq).

Using Table 1.1, explain why phenolphthalein is a suitable indicator for the second titration but methyl red is not.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Phenolphthalein is a suitable indicator for this titration but methyl red is not because:
> 
> - Phenolphthalein changes colour at the equivalence point / where the sharpest pH change occurs **[1 mark]**
> - Methyl red changes colour between pH 4.2–6.3, which does not correspond to the equivalence point / steepest part of the curve **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For a weak acid–strong base titration, the equivalence point is above pH 7.
> 
> Phenolphthalein (pH 8.2–10.0) changes colour in the alkaline range and is suitable; methyl red (pH 4.2–6.3) changes colour in the acidic range and would give an incorrect endpoint.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

In the first titration, 0.200 mol dm^-3^ aqueous ammonia is added from a burette to 10.0 cm^3^ of 0.200 mol dm^-3^ HCl (aq).

In the second titration, 0.100 mol dm^-3^ ethanoic acid is added from a burette to 25.0 cm^3^ of 0.200 mol dm^-3^ NaOH (aq).

Explain why the equivalence point of the titration in part (a) is below pH 7, and why the equivalence point of the titration in part (c) is above pH 7.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The equivalence points differ because of the salts formed:
> 
> For the titration in part (a):
> 
> - The salt formed at the equivalence point is ammonium chloride, NH<sub>4</sub>Cl **[1 mark]**
> - NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> is a weak acid that partially hydrolyses in water, producing an acidic solution **[1 mark]**
> 
> For the titration in part (c):
> 
> - The salt formed at the equivalence point is sodium ethanoate, CH<sub>3</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>Na **[1 mark]**
> - CH<sub>3</sub>CO<sub>2</sub><sup>-</sup> is a weak base that partially hydrolyses in water, producing an alkaline solution **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> At the equivalence point, all the acid and base have been neutralised. The pH is determined by the salt formed:
> 
> - If the cation is from a weak base (e.g. NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> from NH<sub>3</sub>), it partially hydrolyses to give H<sup>+</sup>, making the solution acidic.
> - If the anion is from a weak acid (e.g. CH<sub>3</sub>CO<sub>2</sub><sup>-</sup> from CH<sub>3</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>H), it partially hydrolyses to give OH<sup>-</sup>, making the solution alkaline.

parts.problemMd: Malonic acid is a weak dicarboxylic acid with the formula C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>4</sub>O<sub>4</sub>. Draw the displayed formula of malonic acid.
parts.solutionMd:
The displayed formula of malonic acid is:

![The displayed formula of malonic acid showing two carboxyl groups (-COOH) at each end connected by a central -CH2- group, with all bonds shown](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/7-equilibria/7-2-brnsted-lowry-theory-of-acids-and-bases/assets/008-the-displayed-formula-of-malonic-acid-showing-tw.png)

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for the correct displayed formula showing all bonds, including both -COOH groups and the central -CH<sub>2</sub>- group

> **[exam-tip]**
> Malonic acid is a dicarboxylic acid, which means that it has two –COOH groups connected by a central –CH<sub>2</sub>– group. The displayed formula must show every bond explicitly, including all C–H bonds.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Malonic acid is a weak dicarboxylic acid with the formula C~3~H~4~O~4~.

Ethanoic acid and malonic acid are in aqueous solution at the same concentration. State and explain which acid has the higher pH.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The acid with the higher pH at the same concentration is:
> 
> - Ethanoic acid **[1 mark]**
> 
> This is because:
> 
> - Malonic acid is diprotic and produces more H<sup>+</sup> ions per mole than ethanoic acid
> **OR**
> Ethanoic acid is monoprotic and produces fewer H<sup>+</sup> ions per mole than malonic acid **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> A higher pH means a lower [H<sup>+</sup>]. At the same concentration, malonic acid releases more H<sup>+</sup> because it is diprotic (two –COOH groups, each able to donate a proton). Ethanoic acid is monoprotic (one –COOH group), so it produces fewer H<sup>+</sup> ions and has the higher pH.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Ethanoic acid and malonic acid are in aqueous solution at the same concentration. State and explain which acid has the higher pH.

Ethanoic acid has the higher pH because malonic acid is diprotic and produces more H+ ions per mole than ethanoic acid.

Apart from measuring the pH, suggest one experiment that could be used to distinguish between equimolar solutions of malonic acid and ethanoic acid. State the expected observation.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> One experiment that could distinguish the two acids is:
> 
> Any **one** from:
> 
> - Test the electrical conductivity of each solution
> **AND**
> Malonic acid shows higher conductivity / lower resistance
> - Add a reactive metal (e.g. magnesium) to each solution
> **AND**
> Malonic acid produces bubbles at a faster rate
> - Add a metal oxide or carbonate to each solution
> **AND**
> Malonic acid reacts at a faster rate
> 
> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Malonic acid is diprotic, so at the same concentration it has a higher [H<sup>+</sup>] than ethanoic acid. Any method that detects this difference in [H<sup>+</sup>] is valid. You must state both the test and the expected observation to gain the mark.

parts.problemMd:
30.0 cm<sup>3</sup> of 0.075 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> CH<sub>3</sub>COOH with a pH of 2.93 is added to 10.0 cm<sup>3</sup> of 0.150 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> KOH with a pH of 13.1.

On the following axes, sketch the pH curve for this addition.

![An empty graph with volume of CH~3~COOH added (cm³) on the x-axis and pH on the y-axis, used to sketch a titration curve](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/7-equilibria/7-2-brnsted-lowry-theory-of-acids-and-bases/assets/009-an-empty-graph-with-volume-of-ch-3-cooh-added-cm.jpeg)
parts.solutionMd:
The completed pH curve is:

![A pH titration curve for a weak acid added to a strong base: starts at pH 13.1, falls steeply at 20 cm³ with equivalence point above pH 7, and levels off at pH 2.93](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/7-equilibria/7-2-brnsted-lowry-theory-of-acids-and-bases/assets/010-a-ph-titration-curve-for-a-weak-acid-added-to-a-.jpeg)

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for the starting pH at 13.1
> 
> 1 mark for the vertical section at 20 cm<sup>3</sup> **AND** the midpoint of the vertical section above pH 7
> 
> 1 mark for the final pH at 2.93

> **[exam-tip]**
> The acid (0.075 mol dm<sup>-3</sup>) is added to the base (0.150 mol dm<sup>-3</sup>), so the pH starts high and decreases.
> 
> To find the equivalence volume:
> 
> Vol<sub>a</sub> x Conc<sub>a</sub> = Vol<sub>b</sub> x Conc<sub>b</sub>
> 
> Vol<sub>a</sub> x 0.075 = 10.0 x 0.150
> 
> Vol<sub>a</sub> = 20.0 cm<sup>3</sup>

parts.problemMd:
This question is about effective reactions and reaction rates.

According to collision theory, state **two **conditions that particles need for an effective collision to occur.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> According to collision theory, the two conditions for an effective collision are:
> 
> - Sufficient energy
> **OR**
> Energy greater than or equal to the activation energy / *E* ≥ *E*<sub>a</sub>; **[1 mark]**
> - (To be in the) correct orientation; **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For a chemical reaction to occur, the colliding particles must satisfy both conditions: correct orientation AND sufficient energy (*E* ≥ *E*<sub>a</sub>). A collision with the right orientation but insufficient energy will not result in a reaction, and vice versa.

parts.problemMd:
An increase in concentration means that there are more particles per unit volume.

In terms of collisions, explain how this increases the rate of reaction.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> In terms of collisions, increasing the concentration increases the rate of reaction by:
> 
> - Increasing the frequency of (effective / successful) collisions per unit time
> **OR**
> Increasing the number of (effective / successful) collisions per unit time
> **OR**
> Having particles collide (effectively / successfully) more often **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The key phrase is "frequency of effective collisions", not just "more collisions." CIE mark schemes require both the frequency (per unit time) and the effectiveness aspect. Writing "more collisions" without "per unit time" or "effective" is unlikely to score the mark.
> 
> If the question describes a decrease in concentration, write "less frequent effective collisions". The logic reverses but the required terminology stays the same.

parts.problemMd:
Aqueous hydrogen peroxide, H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>, decomposes to form oxygen and water.

2H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> (aq) → 2H<sub>2</sub>O (l) + O<sub>2</sub> (g)

A student investigates the decomposition of a hydrogen peroxide solution as outlined below.

- The student adds 25.00 cm<sup>3</sup> of H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> (aq) to a conical flask.
- The student adds a small spatula measure of manganese dioxide, MnO<sub>2</sub>.
- They quickly connect the flask to a gas syringe.
- The student measures the volume of oxygen every 100 seconds.

i) State the role of the manganese dioxide in this reaction.

[1]

The student obtained the following results.

| **Time / s** | 0 | 100 | 200 | 300 | 400 | 500 | 600 | 700 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Volume of O**~**2**~** / cm**^**3**^ | 0.0 | 7.0 | 13.5 | 18.0 | 21.0 | 22.5 | 23.0 | 23.0 |

ii) Calculate the average rate of reaction, in cm<sup>3</sup> s<sup>-1</sup>, for the first 100 seconds of the reaction.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The role of the manganese dioxide in this reaction is:
> 
> - Catalyst
> **OR**
> To increase the rate of reaction **[1 mark]**

ii) To calculate the average rate of reaction for the first 100 seconds:

average rate = $\frac{\mathrm{change} \mathrm{in} \mathrm{volume}}{\mathrm{change} \mathrm{in} \mathrm{time}}$

average rate = 7.0 ÷ 100

average rate = **0.07 cm**<sup>**3**</sup>** s**<sup>**-1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Units required; answers without units are not accepted

> **[exam-tip]**
> The catalyst (manganese dioxide) is not consumed in the reaction. It speeds up the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide by providing an alternative reaction pathway of lower activation energy, so more particles have sufficient energy to react.

parts.problemMd:
The student plotted a graph of volume of O<sub>2</sub> against time.

![Graph showing volume of oxygen produced against time in the catalytic decomposition of hydrogen peroxide](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/8-reaction-kinetics/8-1-rate-of-reaction/assets/009-graph-showing-volume-of-oxygen-produced-against-.png)

Use the student's graph and tangent to find the rate of the reaction, in cm<sup>3</sup> s<sup>–1</sup>, at t = 300 s.

Show your working.
parts.solutionMd:
To find the rate of the reaction at t = 300 s:

- Read the coordinates of two points on the tangent at t = 300 s:

Volume at 200 s = 14.5 cm<sup>3</sup>

Volume at 400 s = 21.5 cm<sup>3</sup>

**[1 mark]**

- Calculate the change in volume:

change in volume = 21.5 − 14.5 = **7** cm<sup>3</sup> **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the rate of reaction:

rate = $\frac{7}{200}$

rate = **0.035 cm**<sup>**3**</sup>** s**<sup>**-1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for tangent coordinates: volume at 200 s = 14.5 cm<sup>3</sup> **AND** volume at 400 s = 21.5 cm<sup>3</sup>
> 
> Other coordinate pairs read from the tangent are accepted if they lead to the correct gradient
> 
> Allow rates in the range 0.033–0.038 cm<sup>3</sup> s<sup>-1</sup> for the third mark
> 
> Correct units (cm<sup>3</sup> s<sup>-1</sup>) required for the third mark

> **[exam-tip]**
> The rate at a specific time equals the gradient of the tangent to the curve at that point:
> 
> rate = $\frac{ΔV}{Δt}$
> 
> When reading off the tangent, choose two points that are far apart on the line to reduce the percentage error in your readings. Extend the tangent as far as possible across the graph.
> 
> Note that the tangent is drawn at t = 300 s and the coordinates are read from the tangent line itself, not from the curve.

parts.problemMd:
A platinum-rhodium catalyst is used in the reaction forming nitrogen(II) oxide from ammonia.

4NH<sub>3</sub> (g) + 5O<sub>2</sub> (g) ⇌ 4NO (g) + 6H<sub>2</sub>O (g)

i) State what is meant by the term **heterogeneous catalyst**.

[1]

ii) Explain why a catalyst has no effect on the yield of the products in the reaction.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The term 'heterogeneous catalyst' means:
> 
> - (A catalyst that is in) a different phase / state to the reactants; **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) A catalyst has no effect on the yield of the products because:
> 
> - (A catalyst) increases the rate of both the forward and reverse reactions equally
> **OR**
> (A catalyst) does not shift the position of equilibrium; **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Heterogeneous catalysts are very common in industry. The platinum-rhodium catalyst in car catalytic converters and the iron catalyst in the Haber process are both heterogeneous, as they are solid catalysts with gaseous reactants.
> 
> A catalyst lowers the activation energy by the same amount for both the forward and reverse reactions. The proportion of molecules with sufficient energy increases equally in both directions, so the position of equilibrium is unchanged and the yield is unaffected.

parts.problemMd:
A group of students were completing a practical, investigating the factors which affect the rate of the following chemical reaction.

**A (s) + B (aq) → C (g)**

The students collected the gas produced and plotted the graph shown in Fig. 1.1.

![Graph showing volume of gas evolved over time for the original reaction, with a curve starting at the origin that rises and levels off at point R](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/8-reaction-kinetics/8-1-rate-of-reaction/assets/010-graph-showing-volume-of-gas-evolved-over-time-fo.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

i) State and explain what the letter **R** represents on the student's graph.

[1]

ii) In the original reaction above, the students used 0.5 g of **A** and 50 cm<sup>3</sup> of 1.0 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> of **B**. Sketch a curve on the graph in Fig 1.1 to show how the total volume of gas collected would change if the students still used 0.5 g of **A**, but used 50 cm<sup>3</sup> of 2.0 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> of **B**.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The letter **R** represents:
> 
> - The rate of reaction is zero at this point
> **OR**
> The reaction is complete / has stopped / no more product is produced
> **OR**
> All the reactants have been used up / reacted **[1 mark]**

ii) The sketch of the curve for 0.5 g of **A** and 50 cm<sup>3</sup> of 2.0 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> of **B** is:

![Graph showing the original curve and a new steeper curve that levels off at double the volume, representing the reaction with double the concentration of B](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/8-reaction-kinetics/8-1-rate-of-reaction/assets/011-graph-showing-the-original-curve-and-a-new-steep.png)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for a curve steeper than the original that starts at the origin
> 
> 1 mark for the curve levelling off at double the height of the original curve

> **[exam-tip]**
> At point R, the gradient of the graph is zero because the rate of reaction is zero. At least one reactant has been fully consumed.
> 
> Doubling the concentration of B doubles the moles of B in the reaction mixture (since the volume is unchanged). B is the limiting reagent in the original reaction, so doubling its moles doubles the total volume of gas produced, i.e. the plateau is at double the original height.
> 
> The steeper initial gradient shows a faster rate because higher concentration of B means more particles per unit volume and more frequent effective collisions.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A group of students were completing a practical, investigating the factors which affect the rate of the following chemical reaction.

A (s) + B (aq) → C (g)

The students collected the gas produced and plotted the graph shown in Fig. 1.1.

Fig. 1.1

i) State and explain what the letter R represents on the student's graph.

Explain why the gradient of the curve in part **(b) **decreases as the time of the reaction progresses.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The gradient of the curve decreases as the reaction progresses because:
> 
> - The concentration of reactants decreases
> **OR**
> The reactants are used up; **[1 mark]**
> - The frequency of effective collisions decreases
> **OR**
> The rate of reaction / rate of formation of gas decreases; **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> As the reaction proceeds, reactant particles are consumed. Fewer reactant particles means fewer particles per unit volume, so collisions between A and B become less frequent. Since effective collisions decrease in frequency, the rate falls and the graph gradient decreases.
> 
> When all reactant particles have been consumed, the gradient reaches zero (point R on the graph from part (b)).

parts.problemMd:
Another way to increase the rate of reaction is to increase the temperature.

Explain why a small increase in temperature has a large effect on the initial rate of a chemical reaction.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> A small increase in temperature causes a large increase in the rate of reaction because:
> 
> - A much higher proportion / many more molecules have energy greater than or equal to the activation energy (*E* ≥ *E*<sub>a</sub>); **[1 mark]**
> - The frequency of effective collisions (per unit time) increases significantly; **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> CIE mark schemes require reference to the proportion of molecules with energy greater than or equal to the activation energy (*E* ≥ *E*<sub>a</sub>). Simply stating "particles have more energy" or "kinetic energy increases" is not sufficient for the first mark.
> 
> The Boltzmann distribution curve is asymmetric, so even a small temperature rise shifts the curve so that the area to the right of *E*<sub>a</sub> increases disproportionately. This is why a small temperature increase produces such a large effect on the rate of reaction.

parts.problemMd:
This question is about how different factors affect the rate of a chemical reaction.

A reaction between reactant molecules can only occur when collisions between the reactant molecules are effective.

i) Explain what is meant by the term effective collision.

[1]

ii) State **two** factors that could cause an ineffective collision.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) An effective collision is:
> 
> - A collision that results in a reaction / products being formed **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) Two factors that could cause an ineffective collision are:
> 
> - The (reactant) particles do not collide in the correct orientation; **[1 mark]**
> - The (reactant) particles do not have energy greater than or equal to the activation energy (*E*<sub>a</sub>); **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> An effective collision requires two conditions simultaneously: correct orientation AND sufficient energy (*E* ≥ *E*<sub>a</sub>). An ineffective collision fails one or both conditions.
> 
> Note that most collisions are ineffective as particles collide constantly, but only a small fraction have both the right orientation and sufficient energy at the same moment.

parts.problemMd:
A student made the following statement about factors that affect the rate of a chemical reaction.

'The rate of a reaction increases with temperature as there are more collisions'

Discuss why this statement is only true to an extent and what other factors need to be considered to fully explain how the rate of a reaction is affected by temperature.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Discussing the statement about temperature and rate:
> 
> - As temperature increases, there are more collisions (so the statement is partially correct) **[1 mark]**
> - The rate depends on the frequency of effective collisions, not just the total number of collisions **[1 mark]**
> - As temperature increases, the (average) kinetic energy / speed of the particles increases **[1 mark]**
> - This increases the frequency of collisions (per unit time) **[1 mark]**
> - A higher proportion of particles have energy ≥ *E*<sub>a</sub>, resulting in more frequent effective collisions **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The statement in the question is correct as far as it goes because higher temperature does produce more collisions. The error is in the reasoning: more collisions alone do not fully explain the increase in rate.
> 
> The critical distinction is between total collisions and effective collisions. Rate depends on effective collisions (those with *E* ≥ *E*<sub>a</sub> in the correct orientation). A small temperature rise causes a disproportionately large proportion of molecules to gain sufficient energy, amplifying the effect on rate well beyond what the collision frequency increase alone would predict.

parts.problemMd:
Hydrogen and oxygen can react to form water in an exothermic reaction.

2H<sub>2 </sub>(g) + O<sub>2</sub> (g) → 2H<sub>2</sub>O (g)

The rate of this reaction depends on the pressure as well as the temperature.

Describe and explain the effect of increasing the pressure on this reaction.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The effect of increasing the pressure on the rate of reaction is:
> 
> - The rate increases **[1 mark]**
> - There are more molecules / particles per unit volume / the molecules are closer together, so the frequency of (effective) collisions (per unit time) increases **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> When explaining concentration or pressure effects on rate, always include "per unit volume" when describing the particle density as stating "more molecules" alone is not sufficient. The key chain is:
> 
> - more particles per unit volume
> - → more frequent collisions
> - → more frequent effective collisions
> - → faster rate.
> 
> Avoid writing "there are more molecules" without specifying "per unit volume" or "per dm<sup>3</sup>" as this is a common reason marks are lost in this type of question.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Hydrogen and oxygen can react to form water in an exothermic reaction.

2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(g)

If the rate of reaction increases suddenly, an explosion can occur.

A highly exothermic reaction, such as the reaction in **(c)**, is at more risk of exploding than a less exothermic reaction.

Suggest why.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> A highly exothermic reaction is at greater risk of exploding than a less exothermic reaction because:
> 
> - When the reaction starts, the temperature of the reactant particles increases more (than in a less exothermic reaction) **[1 mark]**
> - Many more particles have energy greater than or equal to the activation energy (*E* ≥ *E*<sub>a</sub>), so the rate increases more rapidly **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> "Suggest" questions require you to apply your knowledge to an unfamiliar situation. Here, the chain of reasoning is:
> 
> - more exothermic
> - → more energy released
> - → greater temperature rise
> - → larger proportion of particles exceed *E*<sub>a</sub>
> - → rate increases more rapidly
> - → greater risk of a runaway reaction.
> 
> The key insight is that the temperature increase is self-reinforcing: as more particles react, more heat is released, which raises the temperature further. A positive feedback cycle that can lead to explosion.

parts.problemMd:
A series of experiments was carried out to investigate the factors which affect the rate of reaction between calcium carbonate and dilute hydrochloric acid.

CaCO<sub>3</sub> (s) + 2HCl (aq) → CaCl<sub>2</sub> (aq) + H<sub>2</sub>O (l) + CO<sub>2</sub> (g)

- 50.0 cm<sup>3</sup> of hydrochloric acid was added to 10 g of small pieces of calcium carbonate (an excess) in a conical flask placed on an electronic balance.
- The loss in mass of the flask and its contents was recorded every 30 seconds for 10 minutes.
- The experiment was repeated using a different concentration of hydrochloric acid or a different temperature.
- The results are shown in Table 3.1

**Table 3.1**

| **Experiment** | **Concentration of hydrochloric acid / mol d**<sup>**-3**</sup> | **Temperature / °C** |
|---|---|---|
| **1** | 0.50 | 20 |
| **2** | 0.50 | 60 |
| **3** | 1.00 | 20 |

The results of Experiment **1** are shown in Fig. 3.1.

![Graph of mass lost in grams against time in seconds for Experiment 1, showing a curve that rises then plateaus, ready for Experiments 2 and 3 to be drawn](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/8-reaction-kinetics/8-1-rate-of-reaction/assets/004-graph-of-mass-lost-in-grams-against-time-in-seco.png)

**Fig. 3.1**

Draw curves on the graph in Fig 3.1 to show the results you would expect for Experiments **2** and **3**.

Label the curves **2** and **3**.
parts.solutionMd:
The curves for Experiments **2** and **3** drawn on Fig. 3.1 are:

![Graph showing three curves: Experiment 1 as the original curve, Experiment 2 steeper and reaching the same maximum mass loss, and Experiment 3 steeper and reaching double the maximum mass loss](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/8-reaction-kinetics/8-1-rate-of-reaction/assets/005-graph-showing-three-curves-experiment-1-as-the-o.png)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for Experiment 2: a curve steeper than Experiment 1 that reaches the same final mass loss as Experiment 1 (approximately 0.5 g)
> 
> 1 mark for Experiment 3: a curve steeper than Experiment 1 that reaches double the final mass loss (approximately 1.0 g)
>

> **[exam-tip]**
> Compare pairs of experiments to identify what has changed:
> 
> Experiments 1 and 2:
> 
> - Only temperature changes (0.50 mol dm<sup>-3</sup>, 20°C → 60°C).
> - Higher temperature → faster rate (steeper curve).
> - Same amounts of CaCO<sub>3</sub> and HCl → same mass loss.
