parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A series of experiments was carried out to investigate the factors which affect the rate of reaction between calcium carbonate and dilute hydrochloric acid.

CaCO~3~ (s) + 2HCl (aq) → CaCl~2~ (aq) + H~2~O (l) + CO~2~ (g)

- 50.0 cm^3^ of hydrochloric acid was added to 10 g of small pieces of calcium carbonate (an excess) in a conical flask placed on an electronic balance.
- The loss in mass of the flask and its contents was recorded every 30 seconds for 10 minutes.
- The experiment was repeated using a different concentration of hydrochloric acid or a different temperature.
- The results are shown in Table 3.1

**Table 3.1**

| **Experiment** | **Concentration of hydrochloric acid / mol d**^**-3**^ | **Temperature / °C** |
| :---: | :---: | :---: |
| **1** | 0.50 | 20 |
| **2** | 0.50 | 60 |
| **3** | 1.00 | 20 |

Determine the initial rate of reaction for Experiment **1**.

You must show your working on the graph in Fig 3.2. Include units in your answer.

![Graph of mass lost in grams against time in seconds for Experiment 1, ready for a tangent to be drawn at t = 0 to determine the initial rate](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/8-reaction-kinetics/8-1-rate-of-reaction/assets/006-graph-of-mass-lost-in-grams-against-time-in-seco.png)

**Fig 3.2**
parts.solutionMd:
To determine the initial rate of reaction for Experiment **1:**

- Draw a tangent to the curve at t = 0:

![Graph of mass lost against time for Experiment 1, with a tangent line drawn at t = 0 to determine the initial rate of reaction](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/8-reaction-kinetics/8-1-rate-of-reaction/assets/007-graph-of-mass-lost-against-time-for-experiment-1.png)

- Calculate the gradient / initial rate:

initial rate = $\frac{change \text{in} \text{mass} \text{lost} ( \mathrm{g} )}{change \text{in} \text{time} ( \mathrm{s} )}$

initial rate = $\frac{1.0g}{312s}$

initial rate = **3.21 × 10**<sup>**-3**</sup>** g s**<sup>**-1**</sup>** **

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for tangent drawn to the curve at t = 0 AND tangent extends to at least 120 s
> 
> 1 mark for gradient calculation in the range 3.13 × 10<sup>-3</sup> to 3.53 × 10<sup>-3</sup> (e.g. gradient = 1.0 ÷ 312 = 3.21 × 10<sup>-3</sup>)
> 
> 1 mark for correct units: g s<sup>-1</sup> or g / s

> **[exam-tip]**
> For the initial rate, draw the tangent at t = 0 because the straight line should touch the curve at the very start, where the gradient is steepest.
> 
> Extend the tangent as far as possible across the graph to minimise reading errors.
> 
> Note that each small square on the x-axis is worth 12 s. Read the axis scale carefully before calculating the gradient. The units mark (g s<sup>-1</sup>) is independent of the numerical value, so always state units even if uncertain about the calculation.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A series of experiments was carried out to investigate the factors which affect the rate of reaction between calcium carbonate and dilute hydrochloric acid.

CaCO~3~ (s) + 2HCl (aq) → CaCl~2~ (aq) + H~2~O (l) + CO~2~ (g)

- 50.0 cm^3^ of hydrochloric acid was added to 10 g of small pieces of calcium carbonate (an excess) in a conical flask placed on an electronic balance.
- The loss in mass of the flask and its contents was recorded every 30 seconds for 10 minutes.
- The experiment was repeated using a different concentration of hydrochloric acid or a different temperature.
- The results are shown in Table 3.1

**Table 3.1**

| **Experiment** | **Concentration of hydrochloric acid / mol d**^**-3**^ | **Temperature / °C** |
| :---: | :---: | :---: |
| **1** | 0.50 | 20 |
| **2** | 0.50 | 60 |
| **3** | 1.00 | 20 |

The results of Experiment **1** are shown in Fig. 3.1.

Calculate the average rate of reaction over the first 240 seconds of Experiment 1.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the average rate of reaction over the first 240 seconds of Experiment 1:

average rate = mass lost ÷ time

average rate = 0.5 ÷ 240

average rate = **0.0021 g s**<sup>**-1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Allow 0.00208 or 0.002083 g s<sup>-1</sup>
>

>

> **[exam-tip]**

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A series of experiments was carried out to investigate the factors which affect the rate of reaction between calcium carbonate and dilute hydrochloric acid.

CaCO~3~ (s) + 2HCl (aq) → CaCl~2~ (aq) + H~2~O (l) + CO~2~ (g)

- 50.0 cm^3^ of hydrochloric acid was added to 10 g of small pieces of calcium carbonate (an excess) in a conical flask placed on an electronic balance.
- The loss in mass of the flask and its contents was recorded every 30 seconds for 10 minutes.
- The experiment was repeated using a different concentration of hydrochloric acid or a different temperature.

The student repeated each experiment but used 10.0 g of larger sized pieces of calcium carbonate.

Suggest what effect this would have on the rate of reaction. Give your reasoning.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The effect of using larger pieces of calcium carbonate on the rate of reaction is:
> 
> - The rate would decrease; **[1 mark]**
> - Larger pieces have a smaller (total) surface area, so fewer (effective) collisions occur between the solid and acid per unit time; **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Surface area affects the rate because the reaction can only occur at the surface of the solid CaCO<sub>3</sub>, where it is in contact with the HCl (aq). Larger pieces have less surface area exposed per unit mass, so fewer collisions occur per second.
> 
> The total mass of calcium carbonate is unchanged (10.0 g), so the total amount of CO<sub>2</sub> produced (and the final mass loss) would be the same. Only the rate changes, not the total amount of product.

parts.problemMd:
A student is asked to investigate how the rate of reaction between sodium thiosulfate and hydrochloric acid depends on the concentration of sodium thiosulfate.

The reaction produces a precipitate of sulfur.

Na<sub>2</sub>S<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> (aq) + 2HCl (aq) → 2NaCl (aq) + SO<sub>2</sub> (g) + S (s) + H<sub>2</sub>O (l)

The student is provided with:

- 0.10 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> sodium thiosulfate solution
- 1.0 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> hydrochloric acid
- distilled water
- standard laboratory apparatus

The reaction mixture must be maintained at 30.0 °C throughout the investigation.

i) Predict the relationship between the rate of reaction and the concentration of sodium thiosulfate.

[1]

ii) Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable in this investigation.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The relationship between the rate of reaction and the concentration of sodium thiosulfate:
> 
> - The rate increases as concentration of sodium thiosulfate increases
> **OR**
> The rate is proportional to concentration **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The variables are:
> 
> - Independent variable: concentration of sodium thiosulfate
> **AND**
> Dependent variable: time for cross to disappear **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> When asked to predict a relationship, don't just say "they are related." Be specific: "Rate increases as concentration increases." If you can, state whether it is directly proportional.
> 
> For the variables, remember:
> 
> **I**ndependent is what **I** change (Concentration).
> 
> **D**ependent is the **D**ata I collect (Time).
> 
> Rate is not an accepted answer for the dependent variable because it is calculated from time.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A student is asked to investigate how the rate of reaction between sodium thiosulfate and hydrochloric acid depends on the concentration of sodium thiosulfate.

The reaction produces a precipitate of sulfur.

Na~2~S~2~O~3~ (aq) + 2HCl (aq) → 2NaCl (aq) + SO~2~ (g) + S (s) + H~2~O (l)

The student is provided with:

- 0.10 mol dm^-3^ sodium thiosulfate solution
- 1.0 mol dm^-3^ hydrochloric acid
- distilled water
- standard laboratory apparatus

The reaction mixture must be maintained at 30.0 °C throughout the investigation.

Describe a method the student could use to investigate this relationship.

Your method should include:

- how to prepare at least five solutions of sodium thiosulfate with different concentrations
- how the reaction is carried out
- how the rate of reaction is determined
- how reliability of results is ensured
- appropriate safety precautions
parts.solutionMd:
To investigate how the rate depends on sodium thiosulfate concentration, prepare several dilutions of the sodium thiosulfate solution and measure the time taken for a sulfur precipitate to obscure a cross.

**Preparing at least five different concentrations**

- Keep the total volume of sodium thiosulfate + water the same each time (e.g. 50.0 cm<sup>3</sup>)
- Use a volumetric pipette or burette to measure the sodium thiosulfate accurately, then add distilled water to make the total up to 50.0 cm<sup>3</sup>
- Example set of five mixtures (all total 50.0 cm<sup>3</sup>):

- 10.0 cm<sup>3</sup> Na<sub>2</sub>S<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> + 40.0 cm<sup>3</sup> water
- 20.0 cm<sup>3</sup> Na<sub>2</sub>S<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> + 30.0 cm<sup>3</sup> water
- 30.0 cm<sup>3</sup> Na<sub>2</sub>S<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> + 20.0 cm<sup>3</sup> water
- 40.0 cm<sup>3</sup> Na<sub>2</sub>S<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> + 10.0 cm<sup>3</sup> water
- 50.0 cm<sup>3</sup> Na<sub>2</sub>S<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> + 0.0 cm<sup>3</sup> water

**How the reaction is carried out**

- Place a conical flask over a paper cross
- Add one sodium thiosulfate dilution to the flask
- Measure a fixed volume of 1.0 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> HCl (same volume every time, so the acid is in excess)
- Add the acid to the flask, start the stopwatch immediately, swirl once to mix, then leave the flask on the cross

**Temperature control**

- Use a water bath to keep the reaction mixture at **30.0 °C**
- Check with a thermometer and allow solutions to reach **30.0 °C** before mixing

**How the rate is determined**

- Stop the stopwatch when the cross is no longer visible
- Record the time, *t*
- Compare rates using **1/*t*** (rate is proportional to 1/*t*)

**How reliability is ensured**

- Repeat each concentration at least three times
- Calculate a mean time (and then a mean 1/*t* if used)

**Safety precautions**

- Wear eye protection when handling acid
- Work in a well-ventilated area / fume cupboard
- Avoid inhaling sulfur dioxide

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - Preparation of different concentrations by mixing sodium thiosulfate solution with distilled water **[1 mark]**
> - Total volume of reaction mixture kept constant **[1 mark]**
> - Volume and/or concentration of hydrochloric acid kept constant and in excess **[1 mark]**
> - Temperature kept constant at 30.0 °C (e.g. water bath; solutions equilibrated before mixing) **[1 mark]**
> - Disappearing cross method described (flask over cross, timing until cross is obscured) **[1 mark]**
> - Repeats carried out and mean time calculated
> **OR**
> Results processed to rate using 1/*t* **[1 mark]**
> - Suitable precaution stated (e.g. work in a well-ventilated area / avoid inhaling SO<sub>2</sub> / eye protection) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Students often lose credit by changing concentration without keeping the total volume of sodium thiosulfate plus water constant.
> 
> It is also easy to forget reliability. Stating repeats and a mean is usually enough, but adding that you will compare rates using 1/*t* makes the processing step explicit.
> 
> Using volumetric apparatus helps because small volume errors change the concentration and make the comparison unfair.
> 
> If a temperature is specified (like 30.0 °C), you must say how you will keep it constant (water bath + thermometer), otherwise it looks like you ignored the constraint.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

i) Predict the relationship between the rate of reaction and the concentration of sodium thiosulfate.

The student processes the results and plots a graph.

i) State the quantities that should be plotted on the x-axis and y-axis.

[1]

ii) Sketch the line you would expect if the rate is directly proportional to the concentration of sodium thiosulfate.

Label both axes.

[2]

iii) Explain how the graph supports the prediction made in (a)(i).

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The quantities that should be plotted on the x-axis and y-axis are:
> 
> - x-axis: concentration of sodium thiosulfate
> **AND**
> y-axis: rate of reaction **OR** 1/*t* **[1 mark]**

ii) The line you would expect if the rate is directly proportional to the concentration of sodium thiosulfate is:

![Graph with a linear upward trend showing the relationship between the rate of reaction on the y-axis and the concentration of sodium thiosulfate on the x-axis](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/8-reaction-kinetics/8-1-rate-of-reaction/assets/003-graph-with-a-linear-upward-trend-showing-the-rel.png)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for axes labelled correctly with appropriate quantities
> 
> 1 mark for straight line with positive gradient passing through or close to the origin

> **[mark-scheme]**
> iii) The graph supports the prediction made in (a)(i) because:
> 
> - The straight line relationship shows rate increases in direct proportion to concentration **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For a straight line through the origin, you must plot rate, not time. Plotting time gives a curve because time decreases as concentration increases. Using 1/*t* makes the relationship clear and matches the prediction of direct proportionality.
>

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A student is asked to investigate how the rate of reaction between sodium thiosulfate and hydrochloric acid depends on the concentration of sodium thiosulfate.

The reaction produces a precipitate of sulfur.

Na~2~S~2~O~3~ (aq) + 2HCl (aq) → 2NaCl (aq) + SO~2~ (g) + S (s) + H~2~O (l)

Disappearing cross method described (flask over cross, timing until cross is obscured)

A second student performs the same investigation but measures the volume of sulfur dioxide gas produced over time instead of using the precipitation method.

State one advantage and one disadvantage of this alternative method compared with the disappearing cross method.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> **One** advantage of this alternative method is:
> 
> Any **one** from:
> 
> - There is a more objective endpoint than judging when a cross "disappears"
> - It is continuous data collection (volume vs time) rather than a single endpoint
> - It is possible to obtain an initial rate from the early gradient / a more detailed rate profile
> 
> **[1 mark]**
> 
> **One** disadvantage of this alternative method is:
> 
> Any **one** from:
> 
> - Sulfur dioxide is soluble in water so the measured volume is lower than the actual volume produced
> - It needs sealed apparatus (gas syringe) so leaks reduce the measured volume
> - There is a greater safety risk (handling toxic gas, pressure build-up)
> 
> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> When evaluating gas collection methods involving SO<sub>2</sub> or CO<sub>2</sub>, remember that these gases are **soluble in water**. This is a classic disadvantage because the volume collected will be less than the actual volume produced.
> 
> While "toxic gas" is a valid disadvantage, examiners usually prefer points that affect the accuracy or reliability of the data (like solubility or leaks) rather than general lab safety, unless the question specifically asks about hazards.

parts.problemMd:
0.5 g of magnesium reacts with 50 cm<sup>3</sup> of 0.1 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> nitric acid. Magnesium is in excess.

A graph monitoring the volume of hydrogen gas produced is shown below:

![Graph showing volume of hydrogen gas produced over time as magnesium reacts with nitric acid, with volume rising steeply then levelling off](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/8-reaction-kinetics/8-1-rate-of-reaction/assets/008-graph-showing-volume-of-hydrogen-gas-produced-ov.png)

i) Calculate the average rate of reaction over the first 15 seconds of the reaction.

[1]

ii) Calculate the actual rate of reaction at 15 seconds.

[3]

iii) Explain the difference in values for rate.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
i) To calculate the mean rate of reaction over the first 15 seconds:

average rate = change in volume ÷ change in time

average rate = 50 ÷ 15

average rate = **3.3 cm**<sup>**3**</sup>** s**<sup>**-1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii) To calculate the actual rate of reaction at t = 15 s:
> 
> - Tangent drawn to the curve at t = 15 s with coordinates recorded correctly **[1 mark]**
> - Gradient of tangent calculated: gradient = Δ*V* ÷ Δ*t* **[1 mark]**
> - Rate in the range 1.5–2.0 cm<sup>3</sup> s<sup>-1</sup> **[1 mark]**
> 
> iii) The actual rate at t = 15 s is lower than the mean rate because:
> 
> - The rate is fastest at the very start of the reaction and has already decreased by t = 15 s
> **OR**
> The gradient of the curve is shallower at t = 15 s than at t = 0 / the curve has already started to level off **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The mean rate (part i) is calculated by dividing total volume produced by total time. It gives an average across the whole 15-second period. Since the rate is highest at t = 0 and decreases as reactants are consumed, the mean rate is higher than the actual rate at t = 15 s.
> 
> The actual rate at t = 15 s (part ii) is the gradient of the tangent drawn at that specific point. Extend the tangent as far as possible across the graph to minimise reading errors. Any rate in the range 1.5–2.0 cm<sup>3</sup> s<sup>-1</sup> is accepted.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

0.5 g of magnesium reacts with 50 cm^3^ of 0.1 mol dm^-3^ nitric acid. Magnesium is in excess.

A graph monitoring the volume of hydrogen gas produced is shown below:

Compare the expected rate and progress of the reaction if 25 cm<sup>3</sup> of 0.2 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> nitric acid was used instead of 50 cm<sup>3</sup> of 0.1 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> nitric acid.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Using 25 cm<sup>3</sup> of 0.2 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> nitric acid instead of 50 cm<sup>3</sup> of 0.1 mol dm<sup>-3</sup>:
> 
> - The initial rate of reaction would be higher / the initial gradient of the graph would be steeper; **[1 mark]**
> - The reaction would finish in less time; **[1 mark]**
> - The total / final volume of gas produced would remain the same (at 60 cm<sup>3</sup>); **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Both solutions contain the same number of moles of nitric acid:
> 
> 25 cm<sup>3</sup> x 0.2 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> = 0.005 mol HNO<sub>3</sub>
> 
> 50 cm<sup>3</sup> x 0.1 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> = 0.005 mol HNO<sub>3</sub>
> 
> Since the magnesium is in excess, the acid is the limiting reagent. The same moles of acid produce the same total volume of hydrogen gas in both cases, so the final volume is unchanged.
> 
> The more concentrated acid (0.2 mol dm<sup>-3</sup>) has more particles per unit volume, leading to more frequent effective collisions and a faster initial rate.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

0.5 g of magnesium reacts with 50 cm^3^ of 0.1 mol dm^-3^ nitric acid. Magnesium is in excess.

Suggest one change to the reaction that could be made to produce more hydrogen gas in total and explain your choice.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> One change that would produce more hydrogen gas in total is:
> 
> Any **one** from:
> 
> - Increase the concentration of the acid without decreasing the volume
> - Increase the volume of the acid without decreasing the concentration
> - Use more moles of acid
> 
> **[1 mark]**
> 
> The reasoning is:
> 
> - Increasing the moles of the limiting reagent (acid) increases the moles / volume of hydrogen gas produced; **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The magnesium is in excess, so the acid is the limiting reagent. The total volume of hydrogen produced is determined only by the moles of the limiting reagent. Changing the temperature, surface area of the magnesium, or adding a catalyst would affect the rate but not the total volume of gas.

parts.problemMd: Suggest why it is often better to study a slower reaction instead of a faster one.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Reasons why it is often better to study a slower reaction are:
> 
> Any **two** from (1 mark for each point):
> 
> - Shorter reaction times give a larger (percentage) error in timing
> - More readings can be taken in the initial part of the reaction, reducing the chance of anomalies being missed
> - The initial rate can be compared between reactions without the reaction needing to go to completion
> 
> **[2 marks]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For very fast reactions, the time interval is so short that even a small absolute error (e.g. ±0.5 s) represents a much larger percentage of the total time. This makes the calculated rate less accurate.
> 
> Slower reactions also allow more data points to be collected during the initial part of the reaction, making it easier to spot trends and anomalous results before the rate has changed significantly.

name: Effect of Temperature on Reaction Rates & the Concept of Activation Energy

parts.problemMd:
A reversible reaction is shown.

A + B ⇌ C + D

The reaction pathway diagram for this reaction is shown in Fig. 1.1.

![Reaction pathway diagram for A + B ⇌ C + D, with products C + D at a higher energy level than reactants A + B; activation energy Ea and enthalpy change ΔH are labelled](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/8-reaction-kinetics/8-2-effect-of-temperature-on-reaction-rates-and-the-concept-of-activation-energy/assets/025-reaction-pathway-diagram-for-a-b-c-d-with-produc.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

Use Fig. 1.1 to deduce whether the forward reaction is exothermic or endothermic. Explain your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The forward reaction is endothermic:
> 
> - Endothermic **[1 mark]**
> - The energy level of the products is higher than / greater than / above the energy level of the reactants **[1 mark]**
> 
> 'Exothermic' is not accepted.

> **[exam-tip]**
> In an endothermic reaction, energy is taken in from the surroundings, so the products end up at a higher energy level than the reactants. In Fig. 1.1, C + D are at a higher energy level than A + B, confirming the forward reaction is endothermic.
> 
> Do not confuse the direction of Δ*H* with the direction of activation energy. The activation energy arrow always points upward from the reactants to the peak of the curve. The Δ*H* arrow shows the overall energy change between reactants and products.

parts.problemMd: Define the term activation energy, *E*<sub>a</sub>.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The activation energy, *E*<sub>a</sub>, is:
> 
> - The minimum energy required **[1 mark]**
> - For a collision to be effective / for a reaction to take place **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The syllabus defines activation energy as the minimum energy required for a collision to be effective. Both parts of the definition are required for full marks:
> 
> - The minimum energy threshold
> - The requirement that the collision is effective (not just any collision).
> 
> The activation energy of a reaction is not changed by temperature. It is only lowered by a catalyst, which provides an alternative reaction pathway of lower activation energy.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A reversible reaction is shown.

A + B ⇌ C + D

The reaction pathway diagram for this reaction is shown in Fig. 1.1.

Fig. 1.1

Use Fig. 1.1 to determine the activation energy for the forward reaction and for the reverse reaction.

activation energy of the forward reaction = .............................. kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>

activation energy of the reverse reaction = .............................. kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>
parts.solutionMd:
To determine the activation energies from Fig. 1.1:

- Forward reaction:

activation energy = 150 + 180

activation energy = 330 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> **[1 mark]**

- Reverse reaction:

activation energy = 180 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The activation energy of the forward reaction is the energy difference between the reactants (A + B) and the peak of the curve. Since the reaction is endothermic, the forward activation energy equals the enthalpy change Δ*H* plus the activation energy of the reverse reaction: 150 + 180 = 330 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>.
> 
> The activation energy of the reverse reaction is the energy difference between the products (C + D) and the peak of the curve: 180 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>. For an endothermic forward reaction, the reverse activation energy is always less than the forward activation energy.

parts.problemMd:
Fig. 1.2 shows the reaction pathway diagram for the same reaction in the presence of a catalyst.

![Reaction pathway diagram showing the original reaction profile and a second catalysed reaction pathway with a lower activation energy peak, both curves sharing the same reactant and product energy levels](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/8-reaction-kinetics/8-2-effect-of-temperature-on-reaction-rates-and-the-concept-of-activation-energy/assets/026-reaction-pathway-diagram-showing-the-original-re.png)

**Fig. 1.2**

Use Fig. 1.2 to explain how the addition of a catalyst increases the rate of reaction.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The addition of a catalyst increases the rate of reaction because:
> 
> - It provides an alternative pathway / route for the reaction **[1 mark]**
> - The alternative pathway has a lower activation energy / *E*<sub>a</sub> **[1 mark]**
> - A greater proportion of molecules have energy greater than or equal to *E*<sub>a</sub>, so there are more frequent effective collisions **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> A catalyst does not change the energy levels of the reactants or products, or the shape of the Boltzmann distribution. It only provides an alternative reaction mechanism with a lower activation energy, as shown by the lower peak in Fig. 1.2.
> 
> The answer is:
> 
> - alternative pathway
> - → lower *E*<sub>a</sub>
> - → greater proportion of molecules with energy ≥ *E*<sub>a</sub>
> - → more frequent effective collisions
> - → faster rate.

parts.problemMd:
This question is about Boltzmann distribution curves.

The Boltzmann distribution curve of molecular energies for a general reaction at a given temperature is shown in **Fig. 2.1**.

![Boltzmann distribution curve showing number of molecules on the y-axis and energy on the x-axis, with the activation energy Ea marked as a vertical dashed line](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/8-reaction-kinetics/8-2-effect-of-temperature-on-reaction-rates-and-the-concept-of-activation-energy/assets/034-boltzmann-distribution-curve-showing-number-of-m.png)

**Fig. 2.1**

State what will happen to the curve when the temperature of the reaction is decreased.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> When the temperature is decreased:
> 
> - The curve shifts to the left
> **AND**
> The peak of the curve is higher / the maximum moves up **[1 mark]**
> - The curve finishes below the level of the original curve **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> At a lower temperature, molecules have less energy on average. The peak of the distribution shifts to the left (towards lower energy) and becomes higher because more molecules cluster around the lower most probable energy value.
> 
> The curve must also finish below the original at high energies, since fewer molecules have very high kinetic energies at a lower temperature.
> 
> ![Boltzmann distribution curves at two temperatures, showing that the lower temperature curve has a higher peak shifted to the left and finishes below the original curve at high energies](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/8-reaction-kinetics/8-2-effect-of-temperature-on-reaction-rates-and-the-concept-of-activation-energy/assets/035-boltzmann-distribution-curves-at-two-temperature.png)
> 
> Make sure you read the question carefully. Many students incorrectly describe the changes for an increase in temperature when the question asks about a decrease.

parts.problemMd: State how, if at all, the total area under a Boltzmann distribution curve changes with temperature.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> With changing temperature, the total area under the Boltzmann distribution:
> 
> - Does not change / remains the same **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The total area under the Boltzmann distribution curve represents the total number of molecules in the sample.
> 
> This number does not change with temperature, so the area under the curve remains constant regardless of the temperature.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

This question is about Boltzmann distribution curves.

The Boltzmann distribution curve of molecular energies for a general reaction at a given temperature is shown in **Fig. 2.1**.

{align=center} **Fig. 2.1**

State the effect of adding a catalyst on the activation energy, *E*<sub>a</sub>, of the reaction.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> When a catalyst is added:
> 
> - The activation energy / *E*<sub>a</sub> decreases / is lower 
> **OR**
> The line for *E*<sub>a</sub> shifts to the left **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Adding a catalyst does not change the distribution of molecular energies or the Boltzmann distribution curve. It only provides an alternative reaction mechanism with a lower activation energy.
> 
> Since *E*<sub>a</sub> is lower, a greater proportion of molecules in the existing distribution now have sufficient energy to react, which increases the rate of reaction.

parts.problemMd:
The Boltzmann distribution of energies for a gas is shown in Fig. 2.2.

![Boltzmann distribution curve with a shaded region to the left of the activation energy Ea, representing molecules with energy less than or equal to Ea](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/8-reaction-kinetics/8-2-effect-of-temperature-on-reaction-rates-and-the-concept-of-activation-energy/assets/036-boltzmann-distribution-curve-with-a-shaded-regio.png)

**Fig. 2.2**

State what the shaded area of Fig. 2.2 represents.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The shaded area of Fig. 2.2 represents:
> 
> - The number of molecules that do not have enough energy to react
> **OR**
> The number of molecules with energy less than or equal to *E*<sub>a</sub>; **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Boltzmann distribution questions often focus on the unshaded area to the right of *E*<sub>a</sub>, which represents the molecules with sufficient energy to react. The shaded area is the complement: molecules with energy less than *E*<sub>a</sub> that cannot react.
> 
> Mark schemes often express the shaded region as *E* ≤ *E*<sub>a</sub>. If you are unsure about inequality symbols, describe them in words instead. For example, 'molecules with energy less than or equal to the activation energy'.

parts.problemMd:

i) The sketch of the Boltzmann distribution at lower temperature *T*<sub>2</sub> is:

parts.problemMd: Define the term *activation energy*, *E*<sub>a</sub>.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The activation energy, *E*<sub>a</sub>, is:
> 
> - The minimum energy required; **[1 mark]**
> - For a collision to be effective / for a reaction to take place; **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The syllabus defines activation energy as the minimum energy required for a collision to be effective. Both parts of the definition are required for full marks: the minimum energy threshold, and the requirement that the collision is effective.

parts.problemMd:
Two reactions involving aqueous sodium hydroxide, NaOH (aq), are given below.

CH<sub>3</sub>CHBrCH<sub>3</sub> + NaOH → CH<sub>3</sub>CH(OH)CH<sub>3</sub> + NaBr     **Reaction 1**

H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> + 2NaOH → Na<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O     **Reaction 2**

The reagents in Reaction 1 must be heated together for some time for the reaction to occur. Reaction 2 is almost instantaneous at room temperature.

Suggest why these reactions occur at different rates.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Reactions 1 and 2 occur at different rates because:
> 
> - Reaction 1 requires energy to break covalent C–Br bonds / has a higher activation energy / greater *E*<sub>a</sub>; **[1 mark]**
> - Reaction 2 involves the reaction between oppositely charged ions (H<sup>+</sup> + OH<sup>-</sup> → H<sub>2</sub>O) / has a lower activation energy / *E*<sub>a</sub>; **[1 mark]**
> - At room temperature, a greater proportion of molecules have energy ≥ *E*<sub>a</sub> for Reaction 2, leading to more frequent effective collisions; **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The rate of a reaction depends on the activation energy.
> 
> Reaction 1 has a high activation energy because covalent C–Br bonds must be broken.
> 
> Reaction 2 is effectively H<sup>+</sup> (aq) + OH<sup>-</sup> (aq) → H<sub>2</sub>O (l), which has a very low activation energy because no strong bonds need to be broken and the ions are attracted to each other.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Ammonia can be produced by the reaction of nitrogen and hydrogen in the presence of an iron catalyst.

N~2~ (g) + 3H~2~ (g) ⇌ 2NH~3~ (g)          Δ*H* = −92 kJ mol^-1^

The activation energy for the forward catalysed reaction, *E*~a,cat~, is +109 kJ mol^-1^.

Calculate the activation energy of the catalysed decomposition of ammonia into nitrogen and hydrogen. Show your working.

activation energy = ......................................................... kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the activation energy of the catalysed decomposition of ammonia:

- The decomposition of NH<sub>3</sub> is the reverse of the synthesis, so:

activation energy = *E*<sub>a,cat</sub> + Δ*H*(decomposition):

activation energy = 109 + 92 **[1 mark]**

activation energy = **201 kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> The final mark is awarded for a correct value with correct units

> **[exam-tip]**
> The decomposition of ammonia (N<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub> → NH<sub>3</sub>) is the reverse of the synthesis reaction. On the reaction pathway diagram, the activation energy of the reverse catalysed reaction is measured from the energy level of the products (2NH<sub>3</sub>) to the peak of the catalysed curve.
> 
> Since the synthesis is exothermic (Δ*H* = −92 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>), the products are 92 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> lower in energy than the reactants. The activation energy of the reverse catalysed reaction is therefore: 109 + 92 = 201 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>.
> 
> ![Enthalpy profile for N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g), showing lower-energy products, −92 kJ mol⁻¹ enthalpy change and 201 kJ mol⁻¹ activation energy.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/8-reaction-kinetics/8-2-effect-of-temperature-on-reaction-rates-and-the-concept-of-activation-energy/assets/032-enthalpy-profile-for-n-g-3h-g-2nh-g-showing-lowe.png)

parts.problemMd:
Catalysts, such as iron used in the production of ammonia, increase the rate of reaction.

Use the Boltzmann distribution to explain how an iron catalyst increases the rate of this reaction.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> An iron catalyst increases the rate of reaction because:
> 
> - It provides an alternative reaction mechanism / pathway with a lower activation energy / *E*<sub>a,cat</sub>; **[1 mark]**
> - A greater proportion of molecules have energy greater than or equal to *E*<sub>a,cat</sub>; **[1 mark]**
> - So there are more frequent effective collisions; **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The answer is:
> 
> - lower *E*<sub>a,cat</sub>
> - → greater proportion of molecules with energy ≥ *E*<sub>a,cat</sub>
> - → more frequent effective collisions

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

In any chemical reaction, the particles will all be moving in different directions, at different speeds and with different amounts of energy. Boltzmann distributions show the distribution of energy amongst particles in a chemical reaction.

State why a Boltzmann distribution curve always starts at the origin, and what the area under the curve represents.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> A Boltzmann distribution curve always starts at the origin because:
> 
> - There are no molecules with zero energy / all molecules have some energy / all molecules are moving **[1 mark]**
> 
> The area under the curve represents:
> 
> - The total number of molecules / particles in the sample **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The curve starts at (0, 0) because at zero energy there are zero molecules. All particles are in motion and therefore possess some kinetic energy.
> 
> The total area under the curve represents the total number of molecules. This does not change with temperature, which is why Boltzmann curves at different temperatures always enclose the same total area.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

In any chemical reaction, the particles will all be moving in different directions, at different speeds and with different amounts of energy. Boltzmann distributions show the distribution of energy amongst particles in a chemical reaction.

Fig. 3.1 below shows the Boltzmann distribution in a sample of a gas at a fixed temperature, *T*~1~.

x (horizontal) axis: Energy / Molecular energy / Kinetic energy
y (vertical) axis: Number / proportion of molecules

A Boltzmann distribution curve always starts at the origin because there are no molecules with zero energy / all molecules have some energy.

The area under the curve represents the total number of molecules / particles in the sample.

Some changes were made individually to the reaction in part **(a)**.

Consider the Boltzmann distribution from Fig. 3.1. For each of the changes in parts (i), (ii) and (iii) below, state and explain the effect that the change would have on:

- The area under the curve
- The value at which the peak of the curve occurs (the most probable energy of the molecules)
- The proportion of molecules with energy greater than or equal to *E*<sub>a</sub>

i) The temperature of the original reaction is increased, but no other changes are made.

[2]

ii) The number of molecules in the original reaction mixture is increased, but no other changes are made.

[2]

iii) A catalyst is added to the original reaction mixture, but no other changes are made.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> For each of the following changes, the effects on the Boltzmann distribution are:
> 
> i) The temperature of the original reaction is increased:
> 
> - The area under the curve is unchanged, as the number of molecules is unchanged; **[1 mark]**
> - The most probable energy of the molecules / the position of the peak shifts to the right / increases
> **AND**
> The proportion of molecules with energy greater than or equal to *E*<sub>a</sub> increases; **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The number of molecules in the original reaction mixture is increased:
> 
> - The area under the curve increases, as the number of molecules increases; **[1 mark]**
> - The most probable energy of the molecules / the position of the peak does not change
> **AND**
> The proportion of molecules with energy ≥ *E*<sub>a</sub> remains the same / is unchanged (though the total number of molecules with energy ≥ *E*<sub>a</sub> increases); **[1 mark]**
> 
> iii) A catalyst is added to the original reaction mixture:
> 
> - The area under the curve is unchanged, as the number of molecules is unchanged; **[1 mark]**
> - The most probable energy of the molecules / the position of the peak does not change
> **AND**
> The proportion of molecules with energy greater than or equal to *E*<sub>a</sub> increases, as the addition of a catalyst lowers the activation energy; **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> A catalyst lowers the activation energy by providing an alternative reaction pathway. This increases the proportion of molecules with energy ≥ *E*<sub>a</sub>, even though the shape of the Boltzmann distribution itself does not change.
> 
> When the number of molecules increases at constant temperature, the curve scales upward (greater total area) but its shape and peak position are unchanged. The proportion of molecules with energy ≥ *E*<sub>a</sub> therefore stays the same, even though the total number of such molecules increases.
> 
> Increasing the temperature shifts the peak to the right and lowers it. The area under the curve remains constant because the total number of molecules is unchanged.

parts.problemMd:
Hydrogen iodide can be used in the manufacturing of pharmaceuticals and can be broken down back into its elements in standard form, iodine and hydrogen.

2HI (g) → H<sub>2</sub> (g) + I<sub>2</sub> (g)  Δ*H* = −52 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>

The activation energy when uncatalysed is +183 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> and when catalysed with gold it is +105 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>.

i) Sketch a reaction profile for the reaction, including the curves for the activation energies for both the catalysed and uncatalysed reactions.

[2]

ii) Calculate the activation energy for the *reverse reaction* in both the uncatalysed and catalysed reactions. Show your working.

[2]

iii) Explain why increasing the concentration of hydrogen iodide gas results in a faster reaction rate.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
i) The reaction profile for the decomposition of hydrogen iodide is:

![Reaction energy profile diagram showing an exothermic reaction with reactants 2HI(g) at higher energy and products H₂(g) + I₂(g) at lower energy, with two activation energy humps where the uncatalysed hump is higher than the catalysed hump](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/8-reaction-kinetics/8-3-homogeneous-and-heterogeneous-catalysts/assets/013-reaction-energy-profile-diagram-showing-an-exoth.png)

> 
> 1 mark for the uncatalysed curve drawn higher (larger hump) than the catalysed curve

ii) The activation energy for the reverse reaction is calculated by adding |Δ*H*| to *E*<sub>a</sub> of the forward reaction:

- Calculate *E*<sub>a</sub> for the uncatalysed reverse reaction:

*E*<sub>a</sub> (reverse, uncatalysed) = 183 + 52

*E*<sub>a</sub> (reverse, uncatalysed) = **(+) 235 kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

- Calculate *E*<sub>a</sub> for the catalysed reverse reaction:

*E*<sub>a</sub> (reverse, catalysed) = 105 + 52

*E*<sub>a</sub> (reverse, catalysed) = **(+) 157 kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for *E*<sub>a</sub> uncatalysed (reverse) = 235 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for *E*<sub>a</sub> catalysed (reverse) = 157 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>

> **[mark-scheme]**
> iii) Increasing the concentration of hydrogen iodide gas increases the rate of reaction because:
> 
> - More molecules are present in the same volume / molecules are closer together **[1 mark]**
> - The frequency of successful collisions increases **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For part (i), make sure the catalysed and uncatalysed curves do not merge before reaching the products; each should have a distinct, separate peak.
> 
> For part (ii), to find the activation energy of the reverse reaction, add the magnitude of Δ*H* to the forward *E*<sub>a</sub>. The forward reaction is exothermic (Δ*H* = −52 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>), so the products are at a lower energy level than the reactants. Reversing the direction means starting from the products and climbing up to the transition state, so the reverse *E*<sub>a</sub> = forward *E*<sub>a</sub> + |Δ*H*|.
> 
> For part (iii), increasing the concentration places more molecules in the same volume, so collisions between reactant molecules are more frequent. More total collisions per unit time means more successful collisions (those with sufficient energy and the correct orientation), increasing the rate of reaction.

Catalysts are often used in industrial processes and can be used in a variety of forms.

i) Explain why it is likely that the solid gold catalyst was used in powder form to catalyse the reaction mentioned in part **(b)**.

[1]

ii) Gold is a heterogeneous catalyst used in the formation of hydrogen iodide. State the difference between a homogeneous and heterogeneous catalyst.

[1]

iii) State how, if at all, the area under the curve of a Boltzmann distribution changes as a catalyst is introduced, without changing the temperature or the total number of molecules.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) Gold was used in powdered form because:
> 
> - (Powder form) increases the surface area (available for the reaction to occur on) **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii) The difference between a homogeneous and heterogeneous catalyst is:
> 
> - A homogeneous catalyst is in the same physical state / phase as the reactants
> **AND**
> A heterogeneous catalyst is in a different physical state / phase from the reactants **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> iii) When a catalyst is introduced, the area under the Boltzmann distribution curve:
> 
> - Stays the same / is unchanged **[1 mark]**

Reactant molecules are adsorbed onto the catalyst surface, react, and then the products are desorbed. Increasing the surface area allows more reactant molecules to interact with the catalyst at the same time.

parts.problemMd:
The Contact process is an important industrial process, contributing to the production of sulfuric acid. In the Contact process, solid vanadium(V) oxide, a heterogeneous catalyst, is used to make sulfur trioxide from sulfur dioxide and oxygen. This process is reversible.

i) Construct a balanced symbol equation for this reaction. Include state symbols in your answer.

[1]

ii) Explain the mode of action of the vanadium(V) oxide catalyst in the Contact process.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The balanced equation for the Contact process is:
> 
> - 2SO<sub>2</sub> (g) + O<sub>2</sub> (g) ⇌ 2SO<sub>3</sub> (g) **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii) The mode of action of the vanadium(V) oxide catalyst is:
> 
> - Reactant molecules (SO<sub>2</sub> and/or O<sub>2</sub>) are adsorbed onto the surface of the catalyst **[1 mark]**
> - Product molecules (SO<sub>3</sub>) are desorbed from the surface of the catalyst **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For part (i), all the information needed to construct the equation is in the question:
> 
> - Sulfur dioxide + oxygen → sulfur trioxide: SO<sub>2</sub> + O<sub>2</sub> → SO<sub>3</sub>
> - Balance by inspection: 2SO<sub>2</sub> + O<sub>2</sub> → 2SO<sub>3</sub>
> - The reaction is reversible: use ⇌
> - All species are gases (g)
> 
> For part (ii), heterogeneous catalysts work by adsorption and desorption. Reactant molecules (SO<sub>2</sub> and O<sub>2</sub>) bind to the solid surface of the catalyst (adsorption). After the reaction takes place on the surface, the product molecules (SO<sub>3</sub>) leave the surface (desorption), freeing up the catalyst surface for further reactions.

name: Periodicity of Physical Properties of the Elements in Period 3

parts.problemMd: State the trend in atomic radius across Period 3.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The trend in atomic radius across Period 3:
> 
> - Decreases (across the period) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> This trend can seem counter-intuitive as more electrons are added going across Period 3. However, each successive element also has one more proton, increasing the nuclear charge. The greater nuclear attraction pulls the outer electrons closer to the nucleus, so the atomic radius decreases. The number of electron shells stays constant across the period, so shielding does not change significantly.

parts.problemMd:
The electrical conductivity of the elements in Period 3 varies across the period as shown in Fig. 1.1.

![Bar graph showing electrical conductivity of Period 3 elements from Na to Cl](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/9-the-periodic-table-chemical-periodicity/9-1-periodicity-of-physical-properties-of-the-elements-in-period-3/assets/006-bar-graph-showing-electrical-conductivity-of-per.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

i) Explain why aluminium has a much higher electrical conductivity than sulfur. You should refer to the structure of both elements.

[2]

ii) Explain why aluminium has a higher electrical conductivity than magnesium.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) Aluminium has much higher electrical conductivity than sulfur because:
> 
> - Aluminium has a giant metallic structure
> **AND**
> (Has) free / delocalised electrons (to carry the charge) **[1 mark]**
> - Sulfur has a simple molecular structure
> **AND**
> (Has) no free / delocalised electrons **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) Aluminium has higher electrical conductivity than magnesium because:
> 
> - Aluminium has more delocalised / outer electrons (per atom) than magnesium
> **OR**
> Aluminium has 3 outer electrons and magnesium has 2 outer electrons **[1 mark]**
> - (So) there are more delocalised electrons to carry the charge **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> When explaining electrical conductivity of elements, always identify the structure type first. Metallic structures contain free/delocalised electrons that move under an applied potential difference to carry charge. Simple molecular structures have no such mobile electrons.
> 
> For the Al vs Mg comparison, the difference lies in how many electrons each atom contributes to the delocalised sea. Aluminium is in Group 13, contributing 3 electrons per atom, while magnesium is in Group 2 and contributes 2. More delocalised electrons means greater conductivity.

parts.problemMd:
The melting points of three successive elements in Period 3 are shown in Table 1.1.

**Table 1.1**

| **Element** | **Melting point / °C** |
|---|---|
| Aluminium | 660 |
| Silicon | 1410 |
| Phosphorus | 44 |

i) Explain, referring to its structure and bonding, why the melting point of silicon is high.

[3]

ii) Explain, referring to its structure and bonding, why the melting point of phosphorus is low.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The melting point of silicon is high because:
> 
> - Silicon has a giant molecular / covalent structure **[1 mark]**
> - (With) strong covalent bonds (between silicon atoms) **[1 mark]**
> - (Which) require a large amount of energy to break / overcome **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The melting point of phosphorus is low because:
> 
> - Phosphorus has a simple molecular structure **[1 mark]**
> - (With) weak instantaneous dipole-induced dipole (id-id) forces (between molecules), which require little energy to overcome **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For melting point explanations, always address three things: the type of structure, the type and relative strength of the bonds or forces holding the structure together, and the energy required to overcome them.
> 
> Silicon has a giant covalent/molecular structure in which every silicon atom is bonded to four others by strong covalent bonds throughout the entire lattice. A very large amount of energy is needed to break these bonds, giving silicon a high melting point.
> 
> Phosphorus exists as P<sub>4</sub> molecules, which is a simple molecular structure. The only forces between P<sub>4</sub> molecules are weak instantaneous dipole-induced dipole (id-id) forces. Only a small amount of energy is needed to overcome these, giving phosphorus a low melting point.

parts.problemMd:
The elements in Period 3 of the Periodic Table show variations in their behaviour across the period.

Fig. 3.1 shows the variation of melting points of the elements across Period 3.

![Graph showing melting points of Period 3 elements from Na to Cl, with a peak at Si](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/9-the-periodic-table-chemical-periodicity/9-1-periodicity-of-physical-properties-of-the-elements-in-period-3/assets/003-graph-showing-melting-points-of-period-3-element.png)

**Fig. 3.1**

Explain the general increase in melting point from Na to Al.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The general increase in melting point from Na to Al is because:
> 
> - (Na, Mg and Al all have) metallic bonding **[1 mark]**
> - The strength of the attraction between the positive metal ions and delocalised electrons increases
> **OR**
> More energy is needed to break the metallic bonds **[1 mark]**
> - Due to an increasing number of delocalised electrons / increasing cation charge / increasing charge density **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Na, Mg, and Al are all metals with giant metallic structures. The key is how the strength of metallic bonding changes across these three elements.
> 
> Think about which Group each element is in: Na is in Group 1 (Na<sup>+</sup> ions, 1 delocalised electron per atom), Mg is in Group 2 (Mg<sup>2+</sup> ions, 2 delocalised electrons), and Al is in Group 13 (Al<sup>3+</sup> ions, 3 delocalised electrons). As the ion charge and the number of delocalised electrons both increase, the electrostatic attraction between the positive ions and the electron sea becomes stronger, requiring more energy to overcome and giving a higher melting point.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The elements in Period 3 of the Periodic Table show variations in their behaviour across the period.

Fig. 3.1 shows the variation of melting points of the elements across Period 3.

Explain the variation of melting points from P to Ar.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The variation of melting points from P to Ar:
> 
> - (P, S, Cl and Ar) all have / contain instantaneous dipole-induced dipole (id-id) forces (between molecules / atoms) **[1 mark]**
> - These forces are greatest in sulfur
> **OR**
> The relative magnitude is S > P > Cl > Ar **[1 mark]**
> - (Because) sulfur has the greatest number of electrons / the number of electrons decreases (from S to Ar) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Although P, S, and Cl have strong covalent bonds within their molecules, it is the instantaneous dipole-induced dipole (id-id) forces between molecules (or atoms, for Ar) that are broken at the melting point.
> 
> The strength of id-id forces depends on the number of electrons. Consider the size of the molecules: P<sub>4</sub>, S<sub>8</sub>, Cl<sub>2</sub>, Ar.
> 
> - Sulfur molecules are the largest with the most electrons, so the id-id forces between S<sub>8</sub> molecules are the strongest and sulfur has the highest melting point in this section.
> - Argon exists as single atoms and has very few electrons, so its id-id forces are very weak.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The elements in Period 3 of the Periodic Table show variations in their behaviour across the period.

Fig. 3.1 shows the variation of melting points of the elements across Period 3.

Explain why Si has a much higher melting point than any of the other elements in the period.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Si has a much higher melting point than any other element in Period 3 because:
> 
> - Silicon has a giant molecular / covalent structure **[1 mark]**
> - (With) strong covalent bonds (between silicon atoms) (throughout the lattice) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> All other elements in Period 3 are either simple molecular structures (P, S, Cl, Ar) or giant metallic structures (Na, Mg, Al). Simple molecular structures have only weak id-id forces between molecules; metallic structures have metallic bonding of moderate strength.
> 
> Silicon, however, has a giant covalent/molecular structure in which every Si atom is covalently bonded to four others in a tetrahedral arrangement throughout the entire lattice. Breaking these many strong covalent bonds requires far more energy than overcoming weak intermolecular forces or breaking metallic bonds, giving silicon a much higher melting point than all other Period 3 elements.

ii) The completed electronegativity trend across Period 3:

parts.problemMd:
The properties of elements and their compounds show similarities, differences and trends depending on the positions of the elements in the Periodic Table.

i) State what is meant by the term *ionic radius*.

[1]

ii) Explain why a cation is smaller than its parent atom, whereas an anion is larger than its parent atom.

[3]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The ionic radius is:
> 
> - The size / radius of an ion
> **AND**
> (Measured as the distance) from the nucleus to the outermost electron shell **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) A cation is smaller and an anion is larger than their parent atoms because:
> 
> Cations:
> 
> - (Cations are smaller because they) lose outer shell electrons **[1 mark]**
> - (So the) nuclear charge (now) acts on fewer electrons, increasing the nuclear attraction and pulling the remaining electrons closer (to the nucleus) **[1 mark]**
> 
> Anions:
> 
> - (Anions are larger because they) gain electrons, increasing electron-electron repulsion (which expands the electron cloud) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Ionic radius is defined as the size of an ion, measured from the nucleus to the outermost electron shell. You are expected to know what ionic and atomic radii are.
> 
> For cations (positive ions), electrons are removed. The same nuclear charge then acts on fewer electrons, so the attraction per electron is greater and the remaining electrons are pulled closer to the nucleus. Cations are therefore smaller than their parent atoms.
> 
> For anions (negative ions), electrons are gained. The extra electrons increase electron-electron repulsion within the outer shell, which pushes the electrons further from the nucleus. Anions are therefore larger than their parent atoms.

parts.problemMd:

![Blank graph with Period 3 elements on the x-axis and ionic radius on the y-axis](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/9-the-periodic-table-chemical-periodicity/9-1-periodicity-of-physical-properties-of-the-elements-in-period-3/assets/007-blank-graph-with-period-3-elements-on-the-x-axis.png)

**Fig. 2.1**
parts.solutionMd:
The trend in ionic radius across Period 3:

![Graph showing ionic radius of Period 3 elements: decreasing from Na to Si, sharp increase from Si to P, then decreasing from P to Cl](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/9-the-periodic-table-chemical-periodicity/9-1-periodicity-of-physical-properties-of-the-elements-in-period-3/assets/008-graph-showing-ionic-radius-of-period-3-elements-.png)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for a decreasing trend from Na to Si (atomic numbers 11–14)
> 
> 1 mark for a sharp increase from Si to P (atomic numbers 14–15) followed by a decreasing trend from P to Cl (atomic numbers 15–17)

> **[exam-tip]**
> The graph of ionic radius across Period 3 has a distinctive shape: two separate decreasing sections connected by a sharp upward jump.
> 
> From Na to Si, the ions are cations (Na<sup>+</sup>, Mg<sup>2+</sup>, Al<sup>3+</sup>, Si<sup>4+</sup>) formed by losing electrons. As nuclear charge increases across this section with the same outer electron shell, ionic radius decreases.
> 
> At phosphorus, the trend reverses sharply. P, S, and Cl form anions (P<sup>3-</sup>, S<sup>2-</sup>, Cl<sup>-</sup>), which are much larger than the cation series because electrons are now added to the outer shell rather than removed. This sharp jump is the key feature to reproduce correctly.
> 
> Within the anion section (P to Cl), ionic radius decreases again as nuclear charge increases while shielding remains roughly constant.

The trend in ionic radius across Period 3:
1 mark for a decreasing trend from Na to Si (atomic numbers 11–14)
1 mark for a sharp increase from Si to P (atomic numbers 14–15) followed by a decreasing trend from P to Cl (atomic numbers 15–17)

Explain the trend shown in part **(b)**.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The trend in ionic radius shown in part (b):
> 
> Na to Si (cations):
> 
> - (Ionic radius decreases because) nuclear charge increases across the period
> **AND**
> Shielding remains (roughly) constant **[1 mark]**
> 
> Si to P (sharp jump):
> 
> - Electrons are now added to the outer shell to form anions (rather than removed)
> **AND**
> (So) the force of attraction between the nucleus and outermost electrons is weaker **[1 mark]**
> 
> P to Cl (anions):
> 
> - (Ionic radius decreases because) nuclear charge increases across the period
> **AND**
> Shielding remains (roughly) constant **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The explanation has three distinct sections matching the three features of the graph:
> 
> 1. Na to Si (cations):
> 
>   - Increasing nuclear charge with constant shielding means each successive cation experiences a stronger nuclear attraction on the same outer electron shell, so ionic radius decreases.
> 2. Si to P (the sharp jump):
> 
>   - Si<sup>4+</sup> has lost all outer-shell electrons. P forms P<sup>3-</sup> by gaining electrons into the same (third) shell.
>   - Adding electrons to an outer shell reduces the average nuclear attraction per electron and increases electron-electron repulsion, so P<sup>3-</sup> is much larger than Si<sup>4+</sup>.
> 3. P to Cl (anions):
> 
>   - The same logic as the cation section applies.
>   - Nuclear charge increases while shielding stays roughly constant, so ionic radius decreases across the anion series.

Explain why magnesium has a higher melting point than sodium.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Magnesium has a higher melting point than sodium because:
> 
> - Magnesium ions have a greater (positive) charge / higher charge density (than sodium ions) **[1 mark]**
> - Magnesium has more delocalised electrons (per atom) (than sodium) **[1 mark]**
> - (So) there is a stronger / greater (electrostatic) attraction between ions and delocalised electrons
> **OR**
> Magnesium has stronger metallic bonds **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Both sodium and magnesium have giant metallic structures. The strength of metallic bonding depends on two factors: the charge of the positive metal ions and the number of delocalised electrons.
> 
> Sodium is in Group 1 (Na<sup>+</sup> ions, 1 delocalised electron per atom), while magnesium is in Group 2 (Mg<sup>2+</sup> ions, 2 delocalised electrons per atom). The higher ion charge and greater number of delocalised electrons in magnesium result in stronger metallic bonds, requiring more energy to break and giving a higher melting point.

parts.solutionMd:

> **AND**
> Sulfur exists as S<sub>8</sub> molecules **[1 mark]**

> - (So) phosphorus has weaker instantaneous dipole-induced dipole (id-id) forces between molecules (than sulfur) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Both phosphorus and sulfur have simple molecular structures. The forces between molecules are instantaneous dipole-induced dipole (id-id) forces, and their strength depends on the number of electrons in the molecule.
> 
> Phosphorus forms P<sub>4</sub> molecules (4 atoms) while sulfur forms S<sub>8</sub> molecules (8 atoms). S<sub>8</sub> molecules are larger and have more electrons, so the id-id forces between S<sub>8</sub> molecules are stronger. More energy is needed to overcome these forces, giving sulfur a higher melting point.

Name the type of bond or force overcome when each of the following oxides melts.

Na<sub>2</sub>O

SiO<sub>2</sub>

P<sub>4</sub>O<sub>10</sub>
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The type of bond or force overcome when each of the following oxides melts:
> 
> - Na<sub>2</sub>O: ionic bonds **[1 mark]**
> - SiO<sub>2</sub>: covalent bonds **[1 mark]**
> - P<sub>4</sub>O<sub>10</sub>: van der Waals' forces / instantaneous dipole-induced dipole (id-id) forces **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> - Na<sub>2</sub>O has a giant ionic structure. When it melts, the strong forces of attraction between oppositely charged ions (ionic bonds) are overcome.
> - SiO<sub>2</sub> has a giant covalent structure. When it melts, the strong covalent bonds between Si and O atoms are overcome.
> - P<sub>4</sub>O<sub>10</sub> has a simple molecular structure with strong covalent bonds within molecules but weak id-id forces between molecules. When it melts, only the weak id-id forces are overcome, while the covalent bonds within the molecule remain intact.
