parts.solutionMd:
The completed graph showing variation in ionic radius across Period 3 is:

![Graph showing ionic radius plotted against Period 3 elements: values decrease from Na+ to Si4+, sharp increase at P3-, then decrease from P3- to Cl-](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/9-the-periodic-table-chemical-periodicity/9-2-periodicity-of-chemical-properties-of-the-elements-in-period-3/assets/006-graph-showing-ionic-radius-plotted-against-perio.png)

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for a correct decreasing trend from Na<sup>+</sup> to Si<sup>4+</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for a sharp increase at P<sup>3-</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for a decreasing trend from P<sup>3-</sup> to Cl<sup>-</sup>

> **[exam-tip]**
> Ionic radius is the distance from the nucleus to the outermost electron of an ion.
> 
> For cations (Na<sup>+</sup> to Si<sup>4+</sup>): nuclear charge increases across the period but shielding remains roughly constant. The stronger nuclear attraction pulls the electron shells closer to the nucleus, so ionic radius decreases.
> 
> For anions (P<sup>3-</sup> to Cl<sup>-</sup>): these ions have gained electrons, making them considerably larger than the cations. The sharp increase at P<sup>3-</sup> reflects this. From P<sup>3-</sup> to Cl<sup>-</sup>, nuclear charge increases while the electron shell count remains the same, so ionic radius decreases.

parts.problemMd:
i) On Fig. 5.2, sketch a graph to show the variation in electrical conductivity across Period 3.

![A blank graph for plotting electrical conductivity against Period 3 elements](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/9-the-periodic-table-chemical-periodicity/9-2-periodicity-of-chemical-properties-of-the-elements-in-period-3/assets/007-a-blank-graph-for-plotting-electrical-conductivi.png)

**Fig. 5.2**

[2]

ii) Explain the variation in electrical conductivity of the elements across Period 3.

[3]
parts.solutionMd:
i) The completed graph showing variation in electrical conductivity across Period 3 is:

![Graph showing electrical conductivity plotted against Period 3 elements: values increase from Na to Al, drop at Si, then remain low from P to Ar](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/9-the-periodic-table-chemical-periodicity/9-2-periodicity-of-chemical-properties-of-the-elements-in-period-3/assets/008-graph-showing-electrical-conductivity-plotted-ag.png)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for an increasing trend from Na to Al
> 
> 1 mark for Si below Al, with P to Ar at low conductivity (below Na)

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii) Explaining the variation in electrical conductivity across Period 3:
> 
> - Na, Mg and Al have metallic bonding with increasing numbers of delocalised electrons from Na to Al **[1 mark]**
> - Si is a metalloid / semi-conductor **[1 mark]**
> - P, S, Cl and Ar have simple molecular / covalent structures with no delocalised electrons **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For part i), no data is provided. This graph requires you to apply your knowledge of structure and bonding.
> 
> For Na, Mg and Al: these are metals with a metallic lattice and delocalised electrons. Conductivity increases from Na to Al because each successive metal contributes more electrons to the delocalised sea (Na: 1, Mg: 2, Al: 3).
> 
> Silicon is a metalloid (semi-conductor) with a giant covalent structure. It has some ability to conduct electricity, but far less than a metal.
> 
> Phosphorus, sulfur, chlorine and argon all have simple molecular or covalent structures with no freely delocalised electrons, so they do not conduct electricity.
> 
> Note: the term "metalloid" or "semi-conductor" does not appear on the specification but does appear in mark schemes. Learn it for this context.

parts.problemMd:
Period 3 elements can react with oxygen to form oxides.

Complete the table to give the formula of one oxide of each of these elements.

| sodium | magnesium | aluminium | phosphorus | sulfur |
|---|---|---|---|---|
|   |   |   |   |   |
parts.solutionMd:
The completed table is:

| sodium | magnesium | aluminium | phosphorus | sulfur |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Final answer:** **Na**<sub>**2**</sub>**O** | **Final answer:** **MgO** | **Final answer:** **Al**<sub>**2**</sub>**O**<sub>**3**</sub> | **Final answer:** **P**<sub>**2**</sub>**O**<sub>**5**</sub> | **Final answer:** **SO**<sub>**2**</sub> |

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 2 marks for all five formulae correct
> 
> 1 mark for three or four formulae correct
> 
> Alternative correct formulae:
> 
> - Phosphorus: P<sub>4</sub>O<sub>10</sub> or P<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> are also accepted
> - Sulfur: SO<sub>3</sub> is also accepted

> **[exam-tip]**
> You need to know the common oxides of Period 3 elements from sodium to chlorine.
> 
> The most commonly tested formulae are Na<sub>2</sub>O, MgO, Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>, and SO<sub>2</sub>/SO<sub>3</sub>. For phosphorus, P<sub>2</sub>O<sub>5</sub> (also written as P<sub>4</sub>O<sub>10</sub>) is the most common, but P<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> is also accepted.

parts.problemMd: Aluminium oxide is amphoteric. Explain what is meant by the term amphoteric and include equations for its reactions to illustrate your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The term amphoteric and equations for aluminium oxide:
> 
> - Amphoteric means the substance reacts with both acids and bases / can act as both an acid and a base **[1 mark]**
> - Reaction with acid: Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> + 3H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> → Al<sub>2</sub>(SO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>3</sub> + 3H<sub>2</sub>O
> **OR**
> Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> + 6HCl → 2AlCl<sub>3</sub> + 3H<sub>2</sub>O **[1 mark]**
> - Reaction with base: Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> + 2NaOH + 3H<sub>2</sub>O → 2NaAl(OH)<sub>4</sub> **[1 mark]**
> 
> The sodium hydroxide equation is the only base reaction required by the specification.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Amphoteric means the substance can act as both an acid and a base. Aluminium oxide reacts with acids to produce a salt and water, and also reacts with bases.
> 
> The sodium hydroxide equation requires care. The product is NaAl(OH)<sub>4</sub> (sodium aluminate), which contains four hydroxide groups. Balance carefully: 2NaOH and 3H<sub>2</sub>O are required on the left-hand side.
> 
> For the acid reaction, either H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> or HCl is accepted.

parts.problemMd:
Sodium oxide, Na<sub>2</sub>O, and sulfur dioxide, SO<sub>2</sub>, are added separately to water.

For each oxide, construct an equation for its reaction with water, describe what is observed and state the pH of the resulting solution.

**Reaction of Na**<sub>**2**</sub>**O with water**

equation

observation

pH

**Reaction of SO**<sub>**2**</sub>** with water**

equation

observation

pH
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The reaction of Na<sub>2</sub>O with water:
> 
> - Na<sub>2</sub>O (s) + H<sub>2</sub>O (l) → 2NaOH (aq) **[1 mark]**
> - Vigorous / exothermic reaction
> **AND**
> Colourless solution produced **[1 mark]**
> - pH 13 to 14 **[1 mark]**
> 
> The reaction of SO<sub>2</sub> with water:
> 
> - SO<sub>2</sub> (g) + H<sub>2</sub>O (l) → H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>3</sub> (aq) **[1 mark]**
> - Colourless solution produced **[1 mark]**
> - pH 1 to 4 **[1 mark]**
> 
> State symbols are not required for the equations

> **[exam-tip]**
> - Na<sub>2</sub>O is a basic oxide: it reacts vigorously with water to form a strongly alkaline solution of NaOH (pH 13–14).
> - SO<sub>2</sub> is an acidic oxide: it dissolves in water to form sulfurous acid, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>3</sub>, giving an acidic solution (pH 1–4).
> - The acid-base character of Period 3 oxides changes across the period:
> 
>   - Na<sub>2</sub>O and MgO are basic
>   - Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> is amphoteric
>   - SiO<sub>2</sub>, P<sub>4</sub>O<sub>10</sub>, SO<sub>2</sub> and SO<sub>3</sub> are acidic

parts.problemMd:
Silicon dioxide, SiO<sub>2</sub>, is heated with concentrated aqueous sodium hydroxide.

Construct an ionic equation for this reaction.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The ionic equation for this reaction is:
> 
> - SiO<sub>2</sub> + 2OH<sup>–</sup> → SiO<sub>3</sub><sup>2–</sup> + H<sub>2</sub>O **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> - The full equation is: SiO<sub>2</sub> + 2NaOH → Na<sub>2</sub>SiO<sub>3</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O
> - To write the ionic equation: split ionic compounds into their ions, then cancel the spectator ion (Na<sup>+</sup>).
> - This reaction requires hot, concentrated NaOH. SiO<sub>2</sub> is an acidic oxide so it reacts with concentrated alkali.

parts.problemMd:
Compound **A** is an oxide of a Period 3 element. It dissolves in hot, concentrated potassium hydroxide and in nitric acid, but it is insoluble in water.

i) State the term used to describe this behaviour of compound **A**.

[1]

ii) Write equations for the reactions of compound **A** with potassium hydroxide and with nitric acid.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The term used to describe the behaviour of compound **A**:
> 
> - Amphoteric **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The equations for the reactions of compound **A** (Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>) are:
> 
> - Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> (s) + 2KOH (aq) + 3H<sub>2</sub>O (l) → 2KAl(OH)<sub>4</sub> (aq) **[1 mark]**
> - Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> (s) + 6HNO<sub>3</sub> (aq) → 2Al(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub> (aq) + 3H<sub>2</sub>O (l) **[1 mark]**
> 
> NaOH is accepted in place of KOH for the alkali equation

> **[exam-tip]**
> - Compound A is aluminium oxide, Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>, which is the only Period 3 oxide that is amphoteric.
> - It is insoluble in water but reacts with both concentrated acids and concentrated alkalis.
> - The other insoluble Period 3 oxide is SiO<sub>2</sub>, but SiO<sub>2</sub> only reacts with alkalis (it is acidic, not amphoteric).

parts.problemMd: Explain the variation in the acid-base character of the Period 3 oxides from sodium to sulfur. In your explanation, refer to electronegativity and bonding.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The variation in acid-base character of the Period 3 oxides:
> 
> - The acid-base character is related to the difference in electronegativity between the Period 3 element and the oxide ion **[1 mark]**
> - Low electronegativity of Period 3 element means that the element forms X<sup>+</sup> and OH<sup>–</sup>
> **AND**
> Therefore the oxide is basic **[1 mark]**
> - High electronegativity of Period 3 element means that the element forms X–O<sup>–</sup> and H<sup>+</sup>
> **AND**
> Therefore the oxide is acidic **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> - Na has a much lower electronegativity than oxygen, so the large electronegativity difference leads to ionic bonding
> 
>   - Na<sub>2</sub>O and MgO are basic oxides.
> - S and P have electronegativities closer to oxygen
> 
>   - → small electronegativity difference
>   - → covalent bonding
>   - → SO<sub>2</sub> and P<sub>4</sub>O<sub>10</sub> are acidic oxides.
> - Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> sits at the borderline and is amphoteric.

parts.problemMd:
Phosphorus(V) oxide, P<sub>4</sub>O<sub>10</sub>, reacts with water.

i) Construct an equation for this reaction and state the expected pH of the resulting solution.

[2]

ii) Explain why phosphorus(V) oxide has a low melting point.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The equation for the reaction of phosphorus(V) oxide with water and the expected pH:
> 
> - P<sub>4</sub>O<sub>10</sub> (s) + 6H<sub>2</sub>O (l) → 4H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>4</sub> (aq) **[1 mark]**
> - pH in the range 1 to 2 **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) Phosphorus(V) oxide has a low melting point because:
> 
> - P<sub>4</sub>O<sub>10</sub> has a simple molecular structure **[1 mark]**
> - Only weak instantaneous dipole-induced dipole (id-id) forces act between molecules, which require little energy to overcome **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> - The equation P<sub>4</sub>O<sub>10</sub> + 6H<sub>2</sub>O → 4H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>4</sub> is a key equation to learn. The product is phosphoric acid, which forms a strongly acidic solution (pH 1–2).
> - For melting point questions, always address both the structure type (simple molecular) and the type of intermolecular force (id-id forces). Both points are needed for full marks.

parts.problemMd:
Phosphorus(V) oxide reacts with aqueous sodium hydroxide to form a phosphate salt.

i) Construct an equation for this reaction.

[1]

ii) Use oxidation numbers to explain whether or not this reaction is a redox reaction.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The equation for the reaction of phosphorus(V) oxide with aqueous sodium hydroxide:
> 
> - P<sub>4</sub>O<sub>10</sub> (s) + 12NaOH (aq) → 4Na<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>4</sub> (aq) + 6H<sub>2</sub>O (l)
> **OR**
> 3NaOH (aq) + H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>4</sub> (aq) → Na<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>4</sub> (aq) + 3H<sub>2</sub>O (l) **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) Using oxidation numbers to determine whether this is a redox reaction:
> 
> - Sodium remains +1 in NaOH and Na<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>4</sub>, and phosphorus remains +5 in both P<sub>4</sub>O<sub>10</sub> and Na<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>4</sub> **[1 mark]**
> - There is no change in oxidation numbers, therefore this reaction is not a redox reaction **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> - When P<sub>4</sub>O<sub>10</sub> is in aqueous conditions it first reacts with water to form H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>4</sub>, so the alternative equation via H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>4</sub> is also valid.
> - A redox reaction requires a change in oxidation number. Since neither P nor Na changes oxidation state, this is an acid-base reaction only.

parts.problemMd:
Silicon(IV) chloride, SiCl<sub>4</sub>, is formed by the reaction of silicon with chlorine.

i) Construct an equation for this reaction.

[1]

ii) State the shape of a molecule of silicon(IV) chloride.

[1]

iii) Explain why silicon(IV) chloride is a liquid at room temperature.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The equation for the reaction of silicon with chlorine to form silicon(IV) chloride:
> 
> - Si + 2Cl<sub>2</sub> → SiCl<sub>4</sub> **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The shape of a molecule of silicon(IV) chloride:
> 
> - Tetrahedral **[1 mark]**
> 
> iii) Silicon(IV) chloride is a liquid at room temperature because:
> 
> - It has a simple molecular structure **[1 mark]**
> - Only weak instantaneous dipole-induced dipole (id-id) forces exist between molecules, which require little energy to overcome **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> - Silicon(IV) chloride is a simple molecular compound. Its four Si–Cl bonds are polar, but the symmetrical tetrahedral arrangement means the overall molecule is non-polar.
> - As a non-polar simple molecule, the only intermolecular forces are id-id forces, which are weak and easily overcome at room temperature.
> - All four bond pairs and no lone pairs around Si give a tetrahedral shape (bond angle 109.5°).

parts.problemMd:
Silicon(IV) chloride reacts vigorously with water, whereas tetrachloromethane, CCl<sub>4</sub>, does not react with water.

Explain this difference in reactivity.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The difference in reactivity is due to:
> 
> - Si has vacant 3d orbitals available for bonding
> **OR**
> C has no vacant 3d orbitals / d orbitals are not energetically accessible in carbon **[1 mark]**
> - A lone pair from the oxygen of water can bond to Si before breaking Si–Cl bonds **[1 mark]**
> - A large amount of energy is released in the Si–O bond formation, making the reaction thermodynamically feasible
> **OR**
> CCl<sub>4</sub> has a high activation energy for reaction with water because no intermediate can form **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> - The key is the presence of vacant 3d orbitals on Si. These allow an oxygen lone pair to coordinate to Si, lowering the activation energy for the reaction.
> - Carbon is in the second period and has no available 3d orbitals. Without an accessible intermediate, the water molecule cannot react with CCl<sub>4</sub>.

parts.problemMd:
i) Construct an equation for the reaction of silicon(IV) oxide with hot concentrated aqueous sodium hydroxide.

[1]

ii) Suggest why silicon(IV) oxide does not react with acids.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The equation for the reaction of silicon(IV) oxide with hot concentrated aqueous sodium hydroxide:
> 
> - SiO<sub>2</sub> + 2NaOH → Na<sub>2</sub>SiO<sub>3</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) Why silicon(IV) oxide does not react with acids:
> 
> - SiO<sub>2</sub> does not contain oxide / O<sup>2–</sup> ions, so it cannot accept protons / H<sup>+</sup> from an acid **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> - SiO<sub>2</sub> is a giant covalent structure and an acidic oxide. It reacts with hot concentrated alkalis but not with acids.
> - Basic oxides react with acids because they contain O<sup>2–</sup> ions that accept protons. In SiO<sub>2</sub>, all oxygen atoms are covalently bonded and there are no O<sup>2–</sup> ions , which means that it cannot act as a base.

parts.problemMd:
The positions of some elements are shown.

![Periodic Table diagram showing the positions of selected elements including Group 1, 2, and 17 elements](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/9-the-periodic-table-chemical-periodicity/9-3-chemical-periodicity-of-other-elements/assets/001-periodic-table-diagram-showing-the-positions-of-.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

i) Using Fig. 1.1 identify the element that forms a soluble hydroxide and an insoluble sulfate.

[1]

ii) Using Fig. 1.1 identify the most volatile element in a group that contains elements in all three states of matter at room temperature and pressure.

[1]

iii) Using Fig. 1.1 identify the element that forms the largest cation.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The element that forms a soluble hydroxide and an insoluble sulfate:
> 
> - Ba **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The most volatile element in a group that contains elements in all three states of matter at room temperature and pressure:
> 
> - F **[1 mark]**
> 
> iii) The element that forms the largest cation:
> 
> - Cs **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The trend in solubility for Group 2 hydroxides and sulfates:
> 
> - Going down Group 2, the solubility of the hydroxides increases
> - Going down Group 2, the solubility of the sulfates decreases
> 
> Barium hydroxide is soluble and barium sulfate is insoluble. Barium is therefore the only Group 2 element that satisfies both conditions in part i).
> 
> Group 17 is the only group that contains elements in all three states of matter at room temperature and pressure:
> 
> - Fluorine = gas
> - Chlorine = gas
> - Bromine = liquid
> - Iodine = solid
> - Astatine = solid
> 
> Volatility refers to how easily a substance can evaporate. The lower the boiling point, the more volatile a substance is. Fluorine has the lowest boiling point in Group 17 and is therefore the most volatile.
> 
> Metals form cations (positively charged ions). For part iii), this eliminates the non-metal elements on the right-hand side of the Periodic Table. Caesium and barium are in the same period but caesium has a lower nuclear charge, so its outer electrons are held less strongly. Therefore, caesium forms the largest cation.

parts.problemMd:
Fig. 1.2 shows the relative first ionisation energies of six successive elements in the Periodic Table.

The letters are **not** the symbols of the elements.

![Bar graph showing relative first ionisation energies of six successive elements labelled A to F, with element B having a notably lower value than element A](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/9-the-periodic-table-chemical-periodicity/9-3-chemical-periodicity-of-other-elements/assets/002-bar-graph-showing-relative-first-ionisation-ener.png)

**Fig. 1.2**

i) Define first ionisation energy.

[2]

ii) Suggest why the first ionisation energy of **B** is much less than that of **A** in Fig 1.2.

[3]
parts.solutionMd:
i) The first ionisation energy is:

- Energy required / energy change
- when one electron is removed
- from each atom in one mole of
- gaseous atoms

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 2 marks for all four points
> 
> 1 mark for any two or three points.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii) The first ionisation energy of **B** is much less than that of **A** because:
> 
> - (For element **B**) the outer electron is removed from a higher energy level **[1 mark]**
> - There is more shielding (by inner electrons) **[1 mark]**
> - So there is less attraction to the nucleus **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The four factors that affect the first ionisation energy are:
> 
> - Nuclear charge
> - Distance of outer electrons from nucleus
> - Shielding by inner electrons
> - Spin-pair repulsion
> 
> The question states that the ionisation energies are for six successive elements. Generally, across a period, ionisation energy increases due to increasing nuclear charge and reasonably constant shielding. Element **B** is an exception as its outer electron is in a new, higher energy level with more inner shells providing additional shielding, making the electron easier to remove despite the higher nuclear charge.

parts.problemMd:
i) On Fig. 1.3, sketch a graph to show the trend in the atomic radius of successive elements in Period 3.

![Blank graph with Period 3 elements Na to Ar on the x-axis and atomic radius on the y-axis, for sketching the trend](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/9-the-periodic-table-chemical-periodicity/9-3-chemical-periodicity-of-other-elements/assets/003-blank-graph-with-period-3-elements-na-to-ar-on-t.png)

**Fig. 1.3**

[1]

ii) Explain your answer to **(c)(i).**

[3]
parts.solutionMd:
i) A graph showing the trend in atomic radius across Period 3 is:

![Graph showing atomic radius decreasing smoothly from Na to Ar across Period 3, with a general downward trend from left to right](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/9-the-periodic-table-chemical-periodicity/9-3-chemical-periodicity-of-other-elements/assets/004-graph-showing-atomic-radius-decreasing-smoothly-.png)

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for a line that decreases from left to right across Period 3 (Na to Ar)

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii) The trend occurs because:
> 
> - Increasing nuclear charge (across Period 3) **[1 mark]**
> - Electrons remain in the same electron shell / number of shells does not change **[1 mark]**
> - Greater attraction between the nucleus and outer electrons / increased effective nuclear charge **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Atomic radius is the distance between the nucleus and the outermost electron.
> 
> Going across Period 3, each successive element has one more proton in the nucleus (greater nuclear charge), but all electrons are still added to the third shell. The shielding remains approximately constant, so the effective nuclear charge experienced by the outer electrons increases across the period. The nucleus pulls the outer electrons closer, reducing the atomic radius.

parts.problemMd:
Table 2.1 shows successive ionisation energies of an element **A**, found in Period 3 of the Periodic Table.

**Table 2.1**

| **Number of electrons** | **1** | **2** | **3** | **4** | **5** | **6** | **7** | **8** |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Ionisation Energy (kJ mol**<sup>-1</sup>**)** | 1012 | 1907 | 2914 | 4964 | 6274 | 21268 | 25431 | 29872 |

Identify element **A**.

Explain your answer using data from Table 2.1.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Element **A** is:
> 
> - Phosphorus / P **[1 mark]**
> - There is a (very) large jump between the 5th and 6th ionisation energies
> **OR**
> There is a (very) large jump in ionisation energy after the 5th ionisation energy **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Successive ionisation energies increase because once an electron has been removed from an atom, you are left with a positive ion. Removing an electron from an increasingly positive ion requires progressively more energy.
> 
> The key to identifying an element from its successive ionisation energies is to look for the large jump in ionisation energy. In this question, the jump from the 5th to the 6th ionisation energy is almost 15,000 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>, far greater than any earlier increase.
> 
> A common mistake is to correctly identify the large jump between the 5th and 6th ionisation energies, then incorrectly identify the element as being in Group 6. If the large jump occurs after the 5th ionisation energy, the element has 5 electrons in its outer shell and must be in Group 5.

parts.problemMd:
The graph below in Fig. 2.1 shows some information on the elements of Period 3 of the Periodic Table.

![Graph showing first ionisation energy against atomic number for Period 3 elements Na to Ar, with a general increasing trend and lower values at Al and S deviating from the trend](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/9-the-periodic-table-chemical-periodicity/9-3-chemical-periodicity-of-other-elements/assets/005-graph-showing-first-ionisation-energy-against-at.png)

**Fig. 2.1**

State and explain the trend that this graph shows, including why there are values that deviate from the trend.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The trend shown in the graph:
> 
> - A general increase in first ionisation energy across Period 3 **[1 mark]**
> - (Across a period) nuclear charge increases / a proton is added to the nucleus **[1 mark]**
> - Aluminium deviates from the general trend because its outermost / valence electron is in a 3p orbital **[1 mark]**
> - The 3p orbital is further from the nucleus
> **OR**
> The 3p orbital has a slightly higher energy than the 3s orbital **[1 mark]**
> - Sulfur deviates because its outermost / valence electron is paired / shares a 3p orbital with another electron
> **AND**
> There is repulsion between the paired electrons (in the 3p orbital) **[1 mark]**

parts.problemMd: Explain why the second ionisation energy of aluminium is a larger value than the first ionisation energy.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The second ionisation energy of aluminium is larger than the first because:
> 
> - Electrons are now being removed from a positive ion
> **OR**
> The electrons being removed are closer to the nucleus
> **OR**
> Al<sup>+</sup> ions are smaller than Al atoms
> **OR**
> The electron is being removed from a 3s orbital rather than a 3p orbital **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Successive ionisation energies increase because the more positive an ion becomes, the more energy is needed to remove the next electron. You are removing a negatively charged electron from an increasingly positive ion.
> 
> In the case of aluminium, the 1st ionisation energy removes an electron from a 3p orbital, and the 2nd removes an electron from a 3s orbital. The 3s orbital is closer to the nucleus and at a lower energy than the 3p, so more energy is required to remove a 3s electron than a 3p electron.

parts.problemMd:
The successive ionisation energies of an element, **X**, are shown in Fig. 3.1. The vertical axis plots log (ionisation energy) instead of ionisation energy to represent the data without an unreasonably long vertical axis.

![Graph of log(ionisation energy) against electron number for element X, showing large increases between the 1st and 2nd, and between the 9th and 10th electrons, indicating three electron shells](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/9-the-periodic-table-chemical-periodicity/9-3-chemical-periodicity-of-other-elements/assets/006-graph-of-log-ionisation-energy-against-electron-.png)

**Fig. 3.1**

Identify element **X** and give its full electron configuration.

**X**:

Electronic configuration:
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Element **X** is:
> 
> - Sodium / Na **[1 mark]**
> 
> Its full electron configuration is:
> 
> - 1s<sup>2</sup> 2s<sup>2</sup> 2p<sup>6</sup> 3s<sup>1</sup> **[1 mark]**
> 
> [Ne] 3s<sup>1</sup> is not accepted as a full electron configuration.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The graph shows that a total of 11 electrons are removed from element X. The number of electrons equals the number of protons, so element X has 11 protons and is sodium.
> 
> The number of electron shells can be determined from the large jumps in ionisation energy. A large jump indicates the next electron is being removed from a shell closer to the nucleus:
> 
> - Large jump between the 1st and 2nd ionisation energies: only 1 electron in the outermost shell (n = 3)
> - Large jump between the 9th and 10th ionisation energies: the 10th electron is in the innermost shell (n = 1), so there are 2 electrons in that shell
> - Electrons 2 to 9 (8 electrons) are in the second shell (n = 2)
> 
> The question asks for the full electron configuration. The condensed noble gas configuration [Ne] 3s<sup>1</sup> is not accepted for the second mark.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The successive ionisation energies of an element, **X**, are shown in Fig. 3.1. The vertical axis plots log (ionisation energy) instead of ionisation energy to represent the data without an unreasonably long vertical axis.

![Graph of log(ionisation energy) against electron number for element X, showing large increases between the 1st and 2nd, and between the 9th and 10th electrons, indicating three electron shells](https://cdn.savemyexams.com/uploads/2022/03/q1_12-1_electrons-in-atoms-sq-medium_ib_hl.png)

{align=center} **Fig. 3.1**

Explain how the successive ionisation energy data for element **X** are related to its electron configuration.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The successive ionisation energy data relates to the electron configuration of element **X** as follows:
> 
> - The first electron is the easiest to remove
> **OR**
> There is 1 electron in the outermost energy level (n = 3) **[1 mark]**
> - Large increase between the 1st and 2nd ionisation energies as the electron is now removed from n = 2
> **AND**
> The next 8 electrons show a relatively small increase as these electrons are all in the same energy level (n = 2) **[1 mark]**
> - Large increase between the 9th and 10th ionisation energies as the electron is now removed from n = 1
> **AND**
> The final two electrons are the most difficult to remove / are in the innermost energy level (n = 1) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> As successive electrons are removed, it becomes increasingly difficult to remove the next electron. This is because the effective nuclear charge experienced by the remaining electrons increases as the ion becomes more positive, strengthening the attraction to the nucleus.

name: Similarities & Trends in the Properties of the Group 2 Metals, Magnesium to Barium, & Their Compounds

parts.problemMd:
i) State the name of a Group 2 element that burns in air to give a bright white flame.

[1]

ii) Construct an equation for the reaction of this element with oxygen.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The Group 2 element that burns in air with a bright white flame is:
> 
> - Magnesium / Mg **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The equation for the combustion of magnesium with oxygen is:
> 
> - 2Mg + O<sub>2</sub> → 2MgO **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Of the Group 2 metals from magnesium to barium, only magnesium burns with a characteristic bright white flame. The other Group 2 metals produce coloured flames when burned in air.
> 
> The combustion equation 2Mg + O<sub>2</sub> → 2MgO must be balanced so that the number of atoms of each element is equal on both sides.

parts.problemMd:
i) State the reagent and conditions required for magnesium to react to form magnesium hydroxide.

[2]

ii) Construct an equation for this reaction. Include state symbols.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The reagent and conditions required for magnesium to react to form magnesium hydroxide are:
> 
> - Reagent: water **[1 mark]**
> - Condition: cold / the water must be cold **[1 mark]**

ii) The equation for the reaction of magnesium with cold water is:

Mg (s) + 2H<sub>2</sub>O (l) → Mg(OH)<sub>2</sub> (s) + H<sub>2</sub> (g)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct equation: Mg + 2H<sub>2</sub>O → Mg(OH)<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>
> 
> 1 mark for all four state symbols correct: (s), (l), (s), (g)

> **[exam-tip]**
> The reaction of magnesium with cold water is slow. Magnesium hydroxide is almost insoluble, forming a solid precipitate (s) on the surface of the magnesium, which slows the reaction further.
> 
> Note that magnesium reacts with steam to form magnesium oxide (MgO), not magnesium hydroxide. The conditions (cold water versus steam) determine which product forms.

parts.problemMd:
Calcium is added to dilute hydrochloric acid.

i) State one observation for this reaction.

[1]

ii) Construct an equation for this reaction. Include state symbols.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) One observation for the reaction of calcium with dilute hydrochloric acid:
> 
> Any **one** from:
> 
> - Effervescence / fizzing / bubbles (of hydrogen gas)
> - The solid calcium dissolves / decreases in size
> - The solution warms up / (the reaction is exothermic)
> 
> **[1 mark]**

ii) The equation for the reaction of calcium with dilute hydrochloric acid is:

Ca (s) + 2HCl (aq) → CaCl<sub>2</sub> (aq) + H<sub>2</sub> (g)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct equation: Ca + 2HCl → CaCl<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>
> 
> 1 mark for all four state symbols correct: (s), (aq), (aq), (g)

> **[exam-tip]**
> Calcium reacts vigorously with dilute hydrochloric acid. The product calcium chloride (CaCl<sub>2</sub>) is soluble in water, so the aqueous solution remains clear.
> 
> When assigning state symbols:
> 
> - Calcium is a solid (s)
> - Hydrochloric acid is aqueous (aq)
> - Calcium chloride is soluble so remains aqueous (aq)
> - Hydrogen is a gas (g)

parts.problemMd:
i) Barium reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid. Construct an equation for this reaction. Include state symbols.

[2]

ii) Barium reacts with dilute sulfuric acid. Construct an equation for this reaction. Include state symbols.

[2]

iii) Explain why the reaction of barium with dilute sulfuric acid soon slows down and stops.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
i) The equation for the reaction of barium with dilute hydrochloric acid is:

Ba (s) + 2HCl (aq) → BaCl<sub>2</sub> (aq) + H<sub>2</sub> (g)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct equation: Ba + 2HCl → BaCl<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>
> 
> 1 mark for all four state symbols correct: (s), (aq), (aq), (g)

ii) The equation for the reaction of barium with dilute sulfuric acid is:

Ba (s) + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (aq) → BaSO<sub>4</sub> (s) + H<sub>2</sub> (g)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct equation: Ba + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> → BaSO<sub>4</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>
> 
> 1 mark for all four state symbols correct: (s), (aq), (s), (g)

> **[mark-scheme]**
> iii) The reaction of barium with dilute sulfuric acid slows down and stops because:
> 
> - Barium sulfate (BaSO<sub>4</sub>) is insoluble / forms an insoluble solid layer on the surface of the barium **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The key difference between the two reactions is the solubility of the product salt. Barium chloride (BaCl<sub>2</sub>) is soluble (aq), so the reaction with hydrochloric acid continues until the barium dissolves. Barium sulfate (BaSO<sub>4</sub>) is insoluble (s), so it forms a solid coating on the barium surface that prevents further reaction.
> 
> Both reactions produce hydrogen gas, so both show initial effervescence. The reaction with sulfuric acid stops quickly, while the reaction with hydrochloric acid continues to completion.

parts.problemMd:
Group 2 oxides react with water to form Group 2 hydroxides.

Describe the general trends in solubility and pH of the Group 2 hydroxides as you move down Group 2.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The general trends in solubility and pH of the Group 2 hydroxides as you move down Group 2 are:
> 
> - The solubility increases
> **OR**
> The hydroxides become more soluble / the Group 2 hydroxides become more soluble **[1 mark]**
> - The pH increases
> **OR**
> The solutions become more alkaline **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Moving down Group 2, the hydroxides become more soluble in water, so more OH<sup>-</sup> ions are present in solution. This raises the pH of the solution.
> 
> Be precise about the direction of both trends, as you move from magnesium to barium:
> 
> 1. Solubility increases
> 2. pH increases

parts.problemMd:
3.71 g of calcium hydroxide, Ca(OH)<sub>2</sub>, is added to hydrochloric acid.

i) Construct an equation for this reaction.

[2]

ii) Calculate the mass of calcium chloride produced in this reaction. Show your working.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
i) The equation for the reaction of calcium hydroxide with hydrochloric acid is:

Ca(OH)<sub>2</sub> + 2HCl → CaCl<sub>2</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct formulae: Ca(OH)<sub>2</sub>, HCl, CaCl<sub>2</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>O
> 
> 1 mark for correct balancing: Ca(OH)<sub>2</sub> + 2HCl → CaCl<sub>2</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O

ii) To calculate the mass of calcium chloride produced:

- Determine the moles of calcium hydroxide, Ca(OH)<sub>2</sub>:

*M*<sub>r</sub> of Ca(OH)<sub>2</sub> = 40.1 + 2(16.0 + 1.0) = 74.1 g mol<sup>-1</sup>

moles of Ca(OH)<sub>2</sub> = $\frac{3.71}{74.1}$ = 0.0501 mol

**[1 mark]**

- Calculate the mass of calcium chloride, CaCl<sub>2</sub>:

*M*<sub>r</sub> of CaCl<sub>2</sub> = 40.1 + 2(35.5) = 111.1 g mol<sup>-1</sup>

moles of CaCl<sub>2</sub> = 0.0501 mol (1:1 molar ratio with Ca(OH)<sub>2</sub>)

mass of CaCl<sub>2</sub> = 0.0501 x 111.1 = **5.56 g**

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for *M*<sub>r</sub> (Ca(OH)<sub>2</sub>) = 74.1 **AND** moles = 0.0500–0.0501 mol
> 
> 1 mark for *M*<sub>r</sub> (CaCl<sub>2</sub>) = 111.1 **AND** mass = 5.55–5.56 g

> **[exam-tip]**
> The reaction follows the general pattern:
> 
> metal hydroxide + acid → metal salt + water.
> 
> The coefficient of HCl must be 2 to balance the two OH groups in Ca(OH)<sub>2</sub>.
> 
> For the calculation:
> 
> - *M*<sub>r</sub> (Ca(OH)<sub>2</sub>) = 40.1 + 2(17.0) = 74.1 and *M*<sub>r</sub> (CaCl<sub>2</sub>) = 40.1 + 2(35.5) = 111.1
> - The 1:1 molar ratio means the moles of CaCl<sub>2</sub> equals the moles of Ca(OH)<sub>2</sub> used.

parts.problemMd:
Strontium carbonate reacts with hydrochloric acid to form strontium chloride, water and carbon dioxide.

i) Describe a test to identify the gas produced as carbon dioxide.

[2]

ii) Carbon dioxide is also produced when strontium carbonate reacts with sulfuric acid. The effervescence observed in this reaction stops after a short period of time.

Suggest why the reaction stops even though the reactants have not been used up.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) To test that the gas produced is carbon dioxide:
> 
> - Pass / bubble the gas through limewater (calcium hydroxide solution) **[1 mark]**
> - The limewater turns cloudy / milky
> **OR**
> A white precipitate forms **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The reason the reaction stops even though the reactants have not been used up:
> 
> - Insoluble strontium sulfate (SrSO<sub>4</sub>) is formed **[1 mark]**
> - (Which) coats the surface of the strontium carbonate / forms a barrier between the acid and the strontium carbonate **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The test for carbon dioxide uses limewater (calcium hydroxide solution). Carbon dioxide reacts with calcium hydroxide to form insoluble calcium carbonate, which turns the solution cloudy or milky.
> 
> The same principle applies whenever a Group 2 carbonate reacts with sulfuric acid. The Group 2 sulfate salts are insoluble, so the sulfate product coats the carbonate surface and prevents further reaction.

parts.problemMd:
State the type of reaction that occurs when strontium carbonate is heated to form strontium oxide and carbon dioxide.

SrCO<sub>3</sub> (s) → SrO (s) + CO<sub>2</sub> (g)
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The type of reaction is:
> 
> - Thermal decomposition **[1 mark]**
> 
> Both 'thermal' and 'decomposition' are required for the mark.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The word 'thermal' indicates that heat is required to drive the reaction.
> 
> The word 'decomposition' indicates that a compound breaks down into simpler substances.
> 
> Together, thermal decomposition describes a reaction where a compound breaks down due to heating.

parts.problemMd:
When heated, strontium nitrate breaks down to form strontium oxide, nitrogen dioxide and oxygen.

Complete the balanced chemical equation for this reaction.

2Sr(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> (s) → .......... (.....) + .......... (.....) + .......... (.....)
parts.solutionMd:
The completed equation is:

2Sr(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> (s) → 2SrO (s) + 4NO<sub>2</sub> (g) + O<sub>2</sub> (g)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct formulae of all products **AND** all three state symbols correct: (s), (g), (g)
> 
> 1 mark for correct balancing: 2SrO, 4NO<sub>2</sub>, O<sub>2</sub>

> **[exam-tip]**
> Strontium nitrate decomposes in a similar way to other Group 2 nitrates. The products are the metal oxide, nitrogen dioxide and oxygen.
> 
> To balance, start with strontium:
> 
> - 2 Sr on the left means two SrO on the right
> - Then count nitrogen:
> 
>   - 4N (from two Sr(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>) gives 4NO<sub>2</sub>.
> - Finally, count oxygen:
> 
>   - 12O on the left (4 x 3) versus 5O in 2SrO and 4NO<sub>2</sub> (2 + 4), leaving one O<sub>2</sub> to balance.

parts.problemMd:
5.00 g of magnesium carbonate breaks down to form 1.75 g of magnesium oxide and carbon dioxide when heated.

MgCO<sub>3</sub> (s) → MgO (s) + CO<sub>2</sub> (g)

Calculate the percentage yield of magnesium oxide. Show your working.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the percentage yield of magnesium oxide:

- Determine the moles of magnesium carbonate, MgCO<sub>3</sub>:

*M*<sub>r</sub> of MgCO<sub>3</sub> = 24.3 + 12.0 + 3(16.0) = 84.3 g mol<sup>-1</sup>

moles of MgCO<sub>3</sub> = $\frac{5.00}{84.3}$ = 0.0593 mol

**[1 mark]**

- Calculate the theoretical mass of magnesium oxide, MgO:

*M*<sub>r</sub> of MgO = 24.3 + 16.0 = 40.3 g mol<sup>-1</sup>

moles of MgO = 0.0593 mol (1:1 molar ratio with MgCO<sub>3</sub>)

theoretical mass of MgO = 0.0593 x 40.3 = 2.39 g

**[1 mark]**

- Calculate the percentage yield:

% yield = $\frac{\text{actual yield}}{\text{theoretical yield}}$ x 100

% yield = $\frac{1.75}{2.39}$ x 100 = **73.2%**

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for *M*<sub>r</sub> (MgCO<sub>3</sub>) = 84.3 **AND** moles = 0.0593 mol
> 
> 1 mark for *M*<sub>r</sub> (MgO) = 40.3 **AND** theoretical mass = 2.38–2.39 g
> 
> 1 mark for % yield = 73.2% (allow 73.2–73.3%)

> **[exam-tip]**
> Percentage yield compares the actual mass of product obtained with the maximum theoretical mass assuming complete conversion of the limiting reagent. It is always ≤100%.
> 
> In this reaction the molar ratio of MgCO<sub>3</sub> to MgO is 1:1, so the moles of MgO that could theoretically form equals the moles of MgCO<sub>3</sub> that decomposes.
> 
> A percentage yield below 100% indicates that not all the MgCO<sub>3</sub> decomposed, or that some product was lost during collection.

parts.problemMd: Describe the trend in the thermal stability of the Group 2 carbonates and nitrates as you move down Group 2.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The trend in thermal stability of the Group 2 carbonates and nitrates as you move down Group 2 is:
> 
> - The thermal stability increases (as you move down Group 2) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Moving down Group 2 from magnesium to barium, the carbonates and nitrates become increasingly difficult to decompose by heat, meaning higher temperatures are required to break them down.
> 
> For example, magnesium carbonate decomposes at a much lower temperature than barium carbonate. This trend also applies to the Group 2 nitrates.

Complete Table 4.1 to describe the general trends as you move down Group 2.

**Table 4.1**

| **Property** | **Trend** |
|---|---|
| Melting point |   |
| Atomic radius |   |
| First ionisation energy |   |
parts.solutionMd:
The completed table is:

| **Property** | **Trend** |
|---|---|
| Melting point | **Final answer:** **Decreases** |
| Atomic radius | **Final answer:** **Increases** |
| First ionisation energy | **Final answer:** **Decreases** |

**[3 marks]**

>

>
