parts.problemMd:
Sodium iodide reacts with concentrated sulfuric acid via the following equation.

H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (l) + NaI (s) → HI (g) + NaHSO<sub>4</sub> (s)

Hydrogen iodide reacts further with concentrated H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> to produce a yellow solid, a purple vapour, and a gas with a smell of rotten eggs.

i) Identify the three products responsible for these observations.

yellow solid ........................................

smell of rotten eggs ........................................

purple vapour ........................................

[3]

ii) Construct an equation for the reaction of HI with H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> to form the yellow solid and the purple vapour. Include state symbols in your answer.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The three products responsible for the observations are:
> 
> - Yellow solid: sulfur / S **[1 mark]**
> - Smell of rotten eggs: hydrogen sulfide / H<sub>2</sub>S **[1 mark]**
> - Purple vapour: iodine / I<sub>2</sub> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For part i), the concentrated sulfuric acid oxidises hydrogen iodide. The sulfur in H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> starts at oxidation state +6. It can be reduced to S (yellow solid, oxidation state 0) or further to H<sub>2</sub>S (rotten egg smell, oxidation state -2). Iodine is produced as a purple vapour.
> 
> There is a further product in this reaction: sulfur dioxide gas.

ii) The equation for the reaction of HI with concentrated H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> to form the yellow solid and the purple vapour is:

6HI (g) + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (l) → 3I<sub>2</sub> (g) + S (s) + 4H<sub>2</sub>O (l)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct reactants and products
> 
> 1 mark for correct balancing and state symbols

> **[exam-tip]**
> To balance this equation, start with S (already balanced), then balance O using H<sub>2</sub>O, then work back to balance H and finally I:
> 
> - H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (l) → S (s) + 4H<sub>2</sub>O (l)
> - 6HI (g) + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (l) → 3I<sub>2</sub> (g) + S (s) + 4H<sub>2</sub>O (l)

parts.problemMd:
When sodium bromide reacts with concentrated sulfuric acid, bromine and sulfur dioxide are formed.

Construct an ionic half-equation for the oxidation of bromide ions to bromine.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The ionic half-equation for the oxidation of bromide ions to bromine is:
> 
> - 2Br<sup>-</sup> → Br<sub>2</sub> + 2e<sup>-</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> When sodium bromide reacts with concentrated sulfuric acid, hydrogen bromide is produced initially:
> 
> NaBr (s) + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (l) → NaHSO<sub>4</sub> (s) + HBr (g)
> 
> This is followed by the oxidation of HBr, with sulfuric acid acting as the oxidising agent and being reduced to sulfur dioxide:
> 
> 2HBr (g) + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (l) → Br<sub>2</sub> (g) + SO<sub>2</sub> (g) + 2H<sub>2</sub>O (l)
> 
> Iodide ions are stronger reducing agents than bromide ions and can reduce the sulfur in sulfuric acid further, all the way to H<sub>2</sub>S. This is because the larger iodide ion has more electron shells, so its outermost electrons are further from the nucleus and held less tightly, making them easier to donate.

parts.problemMd:
This question is about the redox reactions of halide ions.

Chlorine can displace iodine from potassium iodide.

i) Construct the balanced equation for this reaction.

[1]

ii) Construct the ionic equation for this reaction.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The balanced equation for the displacement of iodine by chlorine is:
> 
> - Cl<sub>2</sub> + 2KI → 2KCl + I<sub>2</sub> **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The ionic equation for this reaction is:
> 
> - Cl<sub>2</sub> + 2I<sup>-</sup> → 2Cl<sup>-</sup> + I<sub>2</sub> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> When constructing the ionic equation, the spectator ion K<sup>+</sup> cancels out. Remember to include the balancing numbers for the halide ions.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

This question is about the redox reactions of halide ions.

Chlorine can displace iodine from potassium iodide.

i) Construct the balanced equation for this reaction.

ii) Construct the ionic equation for this reaction.

i) The balanced equation for the displacement of iodine by chlorine is:

- Cl~2~ + 2KI → 2KCl + I~2~

ii) The ionic equation for this reaction is:

- Cl~2~ + 2I^-^ → 2Cl^-^ + I~2~

Using oxidation numbers, explain how iodide ions act as a reducing agent in this reaction.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Iodide ions act as a reducing agent in this reaction:
> 
> - Reducing agents decrease the oxidation number of another atom
> - Iodide ions / I<sup>-</sup> cause the oxidation number of Cl to decrease from 0 (in Cl<sub>2</sub>) to −1 (in Cl<sup>-</sup>)
> 
> **OR**
> 
> - The reducing agent is the substance that gets oxidised
> - The oxidation number of I increases from −1 (in I<sup>-</sup>) to 0 (in I<sub>2</sub>), so I is oxidised
> 
> **[2 marks]**
> 
> References to electrons instead of oxidation numbers are not accepted

> **[exam-tip]**
> This question asks for an explanation in terms of oxidation numbers. Any reference to electron transfer instead of oxidation number changes will not be credited.
> 
> A reducing agent can be identified in two ways: by identifying which species causes a decrease in another’s oxidation number (Cl in Cl<sub>2</sub> goes from 0 to −1), or by identifying which species is itself oxidised (I goes from −1 to 0 in I<sub>2</sub>).

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

This question is about the redox reactions of halide ions.

Chlorine can displace iodine from potassium iodide.

i) Construct the balanced equation for this reaction.

The balanced equation for the displacement of iodine by chlorine is:
- Cl~2~ + 2KI → 2KCl + I~2~

The ionic equation for this reaction is:
- Cl~2~ + 2I^-^ → 2Cl^-^ + I~2~

i) Chlorine also displaces bromine from potassium bromide but not as readily as it can displace iodine from potassium iodide.

Explain how you can use these results to determine which is the stronger reducing agent, bromide ions or iodide ions.

[2]

ii) Explain why the halide ions show this trend in reducing power.

[4]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) To determine which is the stronger reducing agent:
> 
> - A stronger reducing agent will donate electrons more readily **[1 mark]**
> - Iodide ions donate electrons more readily than bromide ions to chlorine, so iodide ions are the stronger reducing agent **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The trend in reducing power down Group 17 is explained by:
> 
> - Going down the group, the halide ions become larger / ionic radius increases **[1 mark]**
> - The outermost electrons are further from the nucleus
> **OR**
> The outer electrons experience greater shielding from inner electrons **[1 mark]**
> - There is less attraction between the outer electrons and the nucleus **[1 mark]**
> - The halide ions lose electrons more readily going down the group, so reducing power increases **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For part i), link the experimental observation directly to reducing ability, i.e. the halide ion that is displaced more readily by chlorine is the stronger reducing agent.
> 
> For part ii), the trend in reducing power down Group 17 is due to increasing ionic radius. More electron shells means more shielding, which weakens the attraction between the nucleus and the outermost electrons, making them more easily donated.

parts.problemMd:
Iodide ions can also act as a reducing agent to reduce Fe<sup>3+</sup> ions to Fe<sup>2+</sup>.

i) Construct the ionic equation for this reaction.

[2]

ii) Explain, in terms of electrons, how Fe<sup>3+</sup> ions act as an oxidising agent.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
i) The ionic equation for the reaction between iodide ions and Fe<sup>3+</sup> ions is:

2I<sup>-</sup> + 2Fe<sup>3+</sup> → I<sub>2</sub> + 2Fe<sup>2+</sup>

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct reactants and products
> 
> 1 mark for correct balancing

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii) Fe<sup>3+</sup> ions act as an oxidising agent because:
> 
> - Oxidising agents accept electrons from another species **[1 mark]**
> - Fe<sup>3+</sup> accepts an electron from I<sup>-</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> To construct the ionic equation, write the two half-equations:
> 
> - Oxidation: 2I<sup>-</sup> → I<sub>2</sub> + 2e<sup>-</sup>
> - Reduction: Fe<sup>3+</sup> + e<sup>-</sup> → Fe<sup>2+</sup>
> 
> Multiply the iron half-equation by 2 so both contain 2e<sup>-</sup>, then cancel the electrons:
> 
> - 2Fe<sup>3+</sup> + 2e<sup>-</sup> → 2Fe<sup>2+</sup>
> - 2I<sup>-</sup> + 2Fe<sup>3+</sup> → I<sub>2</sub> + 2Fe<sup>2+</sup>
> 
> For part ii), the question asks for an explanation in terms of electrons only. References to oxidation numbers will not be credited.

parts.problemMd:
Three solutions of sodium salts are labelled **X**, **Y** and **Z**. The results of tests carried out on each solution are shown in Table 1.1.

**Table 1.1**

| **Unknown** | **Test** | **Result** |
|---|---|---|
| **X** | Added acidified silver nitrate solution. Then added concentrated ammonia solution. | Yellow precipitate formed. Precipitate remained. |
| **Y** | Added acidified barium chloride solution. | White precipitate formed. |
| **Z** | Added acidified silver nitrate solution. Then added concentrated ammonia solution. | Cream precipitate formed. Precipitate dissolved. |

Identify **X**, **Y** and **Z** and construct ionic equations, including state symbols, to demonstrate the key reaction in each test.

- **X**:
- ionic equation:

[2]

- **Y**:
- ionic equation:

[2]

- **Z**:
- ionic equation:

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The identity of **X** and its ionic equation are:
> 
> - X = sodium iodide / NaI **[1 mark]**
> - Ag<sup>+</sup> (aq) + I<sup>-</sup> (aq) → AgI (s) **[1 mark]**
> 
> The identity of **Y** and its ionic equation are:
> 
> - Y = sodium sulfate / Na<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> **[1 mark]**
> - Ba<sup>2+</sup> (aq) + SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2-</sup> (aq) → BaSO<sub>4</sub> (s) **[1 mark]**
> 
> The identity of **Z** and its ionic equation are:
> 
> - Z = sodium bromide / NaBr **[1 mark]**
> - Ag<sup>+</sup> (aq) + Br<sup>-</sup> (aq) → AgBr (s) **[1 mark]**
> 
> If chemical formulae are given, they must be correct

> **[exam-tip]**
> All ionic precipitation equations require state symbols: (aq) for dissolved ions and (s) for the precipitate.
> 
> For the silver nitrate test, the colour of the precipitate identifies the halide:
> 
> - Yellow precipitate = iodide (I<sup>-</sup>)
> - Cream precipitate = bromide (Br<sup>-</sup>)
> - White precipitate = chloride (Cl<sup>-</sup>)
> 
> The barium chloride test must be acidified (with dilute HCl) to be specific for sulfate ions. Acidification removes interfering anions such as sulfite and carbonate.

parts.problemMd:
The following statements are about oxidising ability in Group 17.

Statement **A**: The oxidising ability of the halide ions increases down the group.

Statement **B**: The oxidising ability of the halogen molecules increases down the group.

State whether Statement **A**, Statement **B** or neither is correct. Justify your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Assessing the two statements:
> 
> - Neither statement is correct **[1 mark]**
> - Oxidising ability involves the gain of electrons, and halide ions do not gain electrons
> **OR**
> Halide ions lose / donate electrons (so have reducing ability, not oxidising ability)
> **OR**
> Reducing ability of halide ions increases down the group
> **OR**
> It is the halogens (not halide ions) that gain electrons **[1 mark]**
> - Oxidising ability of the halogens decreases down the group
> **OR**
> Oxidising ability of the halogens increases up the group **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> It is important to distinguish between halogens (X<sub>2</sub>, diatomic molecules) and halide ions (X<sup>-</sup>, anions).
> 
> - Halogens gain electrons and act as oxidising agents. Oxidising ability decreases down Group 17.
> - Halide ions lose electrons and act as reducing agents. Reducing ability increases down Group 17.

parts.problemMd:
On gently heating, the compound KClO<sub>3</sub> reacts as shown in the equation.

4KClO<sub>3</sub> (s) → KCl (s) + 3KClO<sub>4</sub> (s)

This reaction is an example of disproportionation.

State what is meant by disproportionation and use oxidation numbers to show that disproportionation has taken place.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The meaning of disproportionation and evidence from oxidation numbers:
> 
> - Disproportionation is the simultaneous oxidation and reduction of the **same element** (in a single reaction) **[1 mark]**
> - Cl is oxidised from +5 (in KClO<sub>3</sub>) to +7 (in KClO<sub>4</sub>) **[1 mark]**
> - Cl is reduced from +5 (in KClO<sub>3</sub>) to −1 (in KCl) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Disproportionation must involve the same element, not just the same compound. In this example, it is the chlorine atom that undergoes both oxidation (+5 to +7) and reduction (+5 to −1) simultaneously.

parts.problemMd:
Bromine is used to extract iodine from a solution containing iodide ions.

Explain why iodine is a weaker oxidising agent than bromine.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Iodine is a weaker oxidising agent than bromine because:
> 
> - Iodine has a larger atomic radius than bromine **[1 mark]**
> - Iodine has more electron shells, so there is greater shielding of the nucleus **[1 mark]**
> - There is weaker nuclear attraction on a gained electron (than in bromine) / iodine gains electrons less readily than bromine **[1 mark]**
> 
> The reverse argument (explaining why bromine is the stronger oxidising agent) is also accepted

> **[exam-tip]**
> Oxidising ability decreases down Group 17 because each successive element has a larger atomic radius and more electron shielding. This reduces the nuclear attraction on incoming electrons, making it harder to gain an electron.
> 
> Bromine is above iodine in Group 17, so it has a smaller radius, less shielding, and stronger nuclear attraction. This makes it a better oxidising agent.

parts.problemMd:
When solid NaCl reacts with concentrated sulfuric acid the only gas produced is HCl (g) and when solid NaBr reacts with concentrated sulfuric acid the gases produced are brown fumes of Br<sub>2</sub> (g) as well as HBr (g).

Explain the difference in the reactions of concentrated sulfuric acid with NaBr and with NaCl. Your answer should refer to the role of the sulfuric acid in each reaction.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The difference in the reactions of concentrated sulfuric acid with NaBr and with NaCl is:
> 
> - H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> acts only as an acid with NaCl, producing HCl
> **OR**
> NaCl + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> → NaHSO<sub>4</sub> + HCl
> **OR**
> 2NaCl + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> → Na<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> + 2HCl **[1 mark]**
> - H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> also acts as an oxidising agent with NaBr, producing Br<sub>2</sub>
> **OR**
> Br<sup>-</sup> / NaBr acts as a reducing agent **[1 mark]**
> - Br<sup>-</sup> is a stronger reducing agent than Cl<sup>-</sup> / Br<sup>-</sup> is more easily oxidised than Cl<sup>-</sup>
> **OR**
> H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> can oxidise Br<sup>-</sup> but not Cl<sup>-</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> With NaCl, the reaction is acid-base only: H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> donates H<sup>+</sup> to Cl<sup>-</sup>, forming HCl. No oxidation or reduction occurs.
> 
> With NaBr, there is both an acid-base reaction (forming HBr) and a redox reaction: H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> acts as an oxidising agent, accepting electrons from Br<sup>-</sup>. This occurs because Br<sup>-</sup> is a stronger reducing agent than Cl<sup>-</sup> and is more readily oxidised.
> 
> Reducing power of halide ions increases down Group 17: the larger the ion, the more easily it donates electrons.

parts.problemMd:
Solid sodium iodide, NaI (s), reacts with concentrated sulfuric acid to form purple fumes of I<sub>2</sub> (g), a yellow solid and hydrogen sulfide gas, H<sub>2</sub>S (g).

i) Construct the half-equation for the formation of the yellow solid.

[1]

ii) Construct the half-equation for the formation of iodine gas.

[1]

iii) Hence construct the full equation using your answers to parts **(b)(i)** and **(b)(ii)**.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The half-equation for the formation of the yellow solid (S) is:
> 
> - H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> + 6H<sup>+</sup> + 6e<sup>-</sup> → S + 4H<sub>2</sub>O **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The half-equation for the formation of iodine is:
> 
> - 2I<sup>-</sup> → I<sub>2</sub> + 2e<sup>-</sup> **[1 mark]**
> 
> iii) The full equation is:
> 
> - 6I<sup>-</sup> + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> + 6H<sup>+</sup> → 3I<sub>2</sub> + S + 4H<sub>2</sub>O **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> To balance the half-equation for sulfur formation:
> 
> 1. Balance S atoms (already balanced)
> 2. Balance O atoms by adding H<sub>2</sub>O: H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> → S + 4H<sub>2</sub>O
> 3. Balance H atoms by adding H<sup>+</sup>: H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> + 6H<sup>+</sup> → S + 4H<sub>2</sub>O
> 4. Balance charge by adding e<sup>-</sup>: H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> + 6H<sup>+</sup> + 6e<sup>-</sup> → S + 4H<sub>2</sub>O
> 
> To construct the full equation, multiply the iodide half-equation by 3 so both contain 6e<sup>-</sup>:
> 
> - 6I<sup>-</sup> → 3I<sub>2</sub> + 6e<sup>-</sup>
> 
> Cancel the electrons: 6I<sup>-</sup> + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> + 6H<sup>+</sup> → 3I<sub>2</sub> + S + 4H<sub>2</sub>O

parts.problemMd:
Chlorine reacts with hot concentrated sodium hydroxide solution.

i) Construct the equation for this reaction.

[1]

ii) Use oxidation numbers to explain why this is a disproportionation reaction.

[2]

iii) In terms of electrons, state the meaning of the term oxidising agent.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The equation for the reaction of chlorine with hot concentrated sodium hydroxide is:
> 
> - 3Cl<sub>2</sub> (g) + 6NaOH (aq) → 5NaCl (aq) + NaClO<sub>3</sub> (aq) + 3H<sub>2</sub>O (l) **[1 mark]**
> 
> State symbols are not required
> 
> ii) This is a disproportionation reaction because:
> 
> - Chlorine is simultaneously oxidised and reduced / the same element is both oxidised and reduced **[1 mark]**
> - Cl oxidation state changes from 0 (in Cl<sub>2</sub>) to +5 (in NaClO<sub>3</sub>)
> **AND**
> Cl oxidation state changes from 0 (in Cl<sub>2</sub>) to −1 (in NaCl) **[1 mark]**
> 
> iii) The meaning of the term oxidising agent is:
> 
> - (A species that) gains electrons
> **OR**
> An electron acceptor **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> You need to know the equations for the reaction of chlorine with both hot and cold sodium hydroxide:
> 
> - Cold NaOH  (forming sodium chlorate(I)):
> 
> Cl<sub>2</sub> (g) + 2NaOH (aq) → NaCl (aq) + NaOCl (aq) + H<sub>2</sub>O (l)
> 
> - Hot NaOH (forming sodium chlorate(V)):
> 
> 3Cl<sub>2</sub> (g) + 6NaOH (aq) → 5NaCl (aq) + NaClO<sub>3</sub> (aq) + 3H<sub>2</sub>O (l)
> 
> For part ii), the oxidation state of Cl in NaClO<sub>3</sub>: Na (+1) and 3 × O (−2) = −6, so Cl = +5.
> 
> For part iii), oxidising agents gain electrons (they are reduced). Do not confuse with reducing agents, which lose electrons (they are oxidised).

parts.problemMd:
Chlorine is added to drinking water to ensure that it is safe to drink.

State a concern with adding chlorine to drinking water.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> A valid concern with adding chlorine to drinking water is:
> 
> Any **one** from:
> 
> - Chlorine is potentially toxic if too concentrated
> - Some people find the taste unpleasant
> - Can react with organic compounds to produce harmful / toxic substances
> 
> **[1 mark]**

parts.problemMd:
Aqueous silver nitrate, AgNO<sub>3</sub> (aq), is added to separate solutions of NaI and NaCl and precipitates form. An excess of aqueous ammonia is then added to both precipitates.

i) Complete Table 1.1 to state the colour and name of the precipitate formed in each reaction and the effect of the addition of an excess of aqueous ammonia to each of the precipitates formed.

**Table 1.1**

|   | **NaI (aq) + AgNO**<sub>3</sub>** (aq)** | **NaCl (aq) + AgNO**<sub>3</sub>** (aq)** |
|---|---|---|
| **Colour of precipitate** |   |   |
| **Name of precipitate** |   |   |
| **Effect of addition of an excess of aqueous ammonia to the precipitate** |   |   |

[3]

ii) Construct an ionic equation to show the reaction occurring when AgNO<sub>3</sub> (aq) is added to NaI (aq).

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
i) The completed Table 1.1 is:

|   | **NaI (aq) + AgNO**<sub>3</sub>** (aq)** | **NaCl (aq) + AgNO**<sub>3</sub>** (aq)** |
|---|---|---|
| **Colour of precipitate** | **Final answer:** **yellow** | **Final answer:** **white** |
| **Name of precipitate** | **Final answer:** **silver iodide** | **Final answer:** **silver chloride** |
| **Effect of addition of an excess of aqueous ammonia to the precipitate** | **Final answer:** **no (visible) change** | **Final answer:** **dissolves / soluble** |

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct colour and name of precipitate from NaI: yellow, silver iodide
> 
> 1 mark for correct colour and name of precipitate from NaCl: white, silver chloride
> 
> 1 mark for correct effects of aqueous ammonia: no change (AgI); dissolves to form a colourless solution (AgCl)

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii) The ionic equation for the reaction when AgNO<sub>3</sub> (aq) is added to NaI (aq) is:
> 
> - Ag<sup>+</sup> (aq) + I<sup>-</sup> (aq) → AgI (s) **[1 mark]**
> 
> State symbols are required for this precipitation reaction.

> **[exam-tip]**
> You must learn the tests for halide ions thoroughly. The colour of the silver halide precipitate and its solubility in aqueous ammonia are the key distinguishing observations:
> 
> - AgCl (white) dissolves in dilute aqueous ammonia
> - AgBr (cream) dissolves only in concentrated aqueous ammonia
> - AgI (yellow) is insoluble in aqueous ammonia at any concentration
> 
> Include state symbols when writing ionic equations for precipitation reactions, even if not explicitly asked, as these may be required for the mark.

parts.problemMd:
Solid NaI reacts with concentrated sulfuric acid to form purple fumes of I<sub>2</sub> (g) and hydrogen sulfide gas, H<sub>2</sub>S (g). However, when solid NaCl reacts with concentrated sulfuric acid, the only gas produced is HCl (g).

Explain this difference in the reactions. Your answer should state the role of the sulfuric acid in each reaction.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The difference in the reactions is:
> 
> - Sulfuric acid acts as an acid / proton donor with NaCl
> **OR**
> NaCl + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> → NaHSO<sub>4</sub> + HCl
> **OR**
> 2NaCl + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> → Na<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> + 2HCl **[1 mark]**
> - Sulfuric acid acts as an oxidising agent with NaI / I<sup>-</sup>
> **OR**
> NaI is a reducing agent **[1 mark]**
> - I<sup>-</sup> is a more powerful reducing agent than Cl<sup>-</sup>
> **OR**
> Sulfuric acid can oxidise I<sup>-</sup> but not Cl<sup>-</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The only reaction between NaCl and concentrated sulfuric acid is acid-base: sulfuric acid donates a proton to produce HCl gas. Chloride ions are not strong enough reducing agents to reduce the sulfur in sulfuric acid.
> 
> As you go down Group 17, the halide ions become stronger reducing agents. Iodide ions can reduce the sulfur in sulfuric acid all the way from +6 to -2, producing H<sub>2</sub>S gas along with I<sub>2</sub> and S.

parts.problemMd:
Chlorine is used in water purification. It reacts with water to produce a mixture of acids, one of which is chloric(I) acid, HClO.

i) Explain what is meant by the term oxidising agent in terms of electron transfer.

[1]

ii) Construct an equation for this reaction of chlorine with water.

[1]

iii) Construct an equation for the reaction of chlorine with hot aqueous sodium hydroxide.

Use oxidation numbers to explain why this is a disproportionation reaction.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) An oxidising agent is a species that:
> 
> - Gains electrons / accepts electrons / is an electron acceptor **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The equation for the reaction of chlorine with water is:
> 
> - Cl<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O → HCl + HClO **[1 mark]**
> 
> iii) The equation for the reaction of chlorine with hot aqueous sodium hydroxide is:
> 
> - 3Cl<sub>2</sub> + 6NaOH → 5NaCl + NaClO<sub>3</sub> + 3H<sub>2</sub>O **[1 mark]**
> 
> This is a disproportionation reaction because:
> 
> - The oxidation number of chlorine changes from 0 (in Cl<sub>2</sub>) to -1 (in NaCl) AND to +5 (in NaClO<sub>3</sub>), showing chlorine is simultaneously oxidised and reduced **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Make sure you know the definitions for both oxidising agent (gains electrons / electron acceptor) and reducing agent (loses electrons / electron donor) in terms of electron transfer.
> 
> You should know the equations for the reaction of chlorine with both hot and cold sodium hydroxide:
> 
> - Hot: 3Cl<sub>2</sub> + 6NaOH → 5NaCl + NaClO<sub>3</sub> + 3H<sub>2</sub>O
> - Cold: Cl<sub>2</sub> + 2NaOH → NaCl + NaClO + H<sub>2</sub>O
> 
> Both are disproportionation reactions because chlorine is simultaneously oxidised and reduced. If the oxidation number increases, oxidation has occurred; if it decreases, reduction has occurred.
> 
> To verify the oxidation state of Cl in NaClO<sub>3</sub>: Na = +1, each O = -2 (three O atoms = -6), the compound is neutral overall, so Cl must be +5.

parts.problemMd:
The equation for the reaction between solid potassium bromide and concentrated sulfuric acid is:

2H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (l) + 2KBr (s) → K<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (aq) + SO<sub>2</sub> (g) + Br<sub>2</sub> (g) + 2H<sub>2</sub>O (l)

Identify the **two** redox products and one possible observation for each.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The two redox products and a possible observation for each are:
> 
> - SO<sub>2</sub> / sulfur dioxide **[1 mark]**
> - Colourless gas evolved / colourless fumes **[1 mark]**
> - Br<sub>2</sub> / bromine **[1 mark]**
> - Brown / orange gas / vapour evolved **[1 mark]**
> 
> K<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>O are not accepted because they are not redox products

> **[exam-tip]**
> Only products that have undergone a change in oxidation state count as redox products. K<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>O are not redox products.
> 
> The redox products are SO<sub>2</sub> (sulfur is reduced from +6 to +4) and Br<sub>2</sub> (bromine is oxidised from −1 to 0).
> 
> SO<sub>2</sub> is colourless but has a pungent smell. It can be confirmed by holding it near filter paper soaked in acidified potassium dichromate(VI) solution nearby, which changes colour from orange to green.

parts.problemMd: Explain why the reaction between solid potassium iodide and concentrated sulfuric acid produces hydrogen sulfide whereas the reaction between solid potassium bromide and concentrated sulfuric acid does not.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The iodide ion reduces H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> to H<sub>2</sub>S, but the bromide ion cannot, because:
> 
> - I<sup>–</sup> / iodide ion is a stronger reducing agent than Br<sup>–</sup> / bromide ion **[1 mark]**
> - I<sup>–</sup> / iodide ion has a larger ionic radius / more electron shells / greater shielding than Br<sup>–</sup> / bromide ion **[1 mark]**
> - Outer electron(s) more easily removed / donated from I<sup>–</sup> than Br<sup>–</sup> / I<sup>–</sup> more readily donates electrons **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Reducing power increases down Group 17. Iodide ions are stronger reducing agents than bromide ions because they have more electron shells, which increases shielding and means the outermost electrons are further from the nucleus.
> 
> This makes the outermost electrons more easily donated. Iodide is therefore strong enough to reduce the sulfur in H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> from an oxidation state of +6 to −2 in H<sub>2</sub>S. Bromide is not.

parts.problemMd: In aqueous solution, hydrogen fluoride is classified as a weak acid, whereas hydrogen chloride is classified as a strong acid. Explain this difference.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The difference in acid strength is due to the relative H–X bond strengths:
> 
> - The H–F bond is stronger / shorter than the H–Cl bond **[1 mark]**
> - H–Cl bond breaks more readily / dissociates more fully, releasing more H<sup>+</sup> ions
> **OR**
> H–F bond does not break as easily, so fewer H<sup>+</sup> ions are released **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> A strong acid fully dissociates in solution, releasing a high concentration of H<sup>+</sup> ions. A weak acid only partially dissociates, releasing far fewer H<sup>+</sup> ions.
> 
> HCl → H<sup>+</sup> (aq) + Cl<sup>–</sup> (aq) (complete dissociation)
> 
> HF ⇌ H<sup>+</sup> (aq) + F<sup>–</sup> (aq) (partial dissociation)
> 
> Fluorine is the smallest halogen, so the H–F bond is the shortest and strongest of the hydrogen halides. This makes HF much less likely to dissociate completely, so it is classified as a weak acid.

parts.problemMd: Explain why fluorine has a lower boiling point than chlorine.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Fluorine has a lower boiling point than chlorine as:
> 
> - Fluorine is smaller than chlorine **[1 mark]**
> - The forces between F<sub>2</sub> molecules are weaker than the forces between Cl<sub>2</sub> molecules **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Make sure you use comparative words when comparing two substances, for example "smaller" or "larger."
> 
> The forces here are between fluorine and chlorine molecules, not atoms.
> 
> Be specific with your language, as examiners will deduct marks for vague answers.

parts.problemMd: Construct an ionic equation for the reaction between chlorine and cold aqueous sodium hydroxide.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The ionic equation for the reaction between chlorine and cold aqueous sodium hydroxide is:
> 
> - Cl<sub>2</sub> + 2OH<sup>–</sup> → OCl<sup>–</sup> + Cl<sup>–</sup> + H<sub>2</sub>O **[1 mark]**
> 
> State symbols are not required.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The full equation for this reaction is:
> 
> Cl<sub>2</sub> (aq) + 2NaOH (aq) → NaClO (aq) + NaCl (aq) + H<sub>2</sub>O (l)
> 
> To find the ionic equation, split ionic substances into ions and remove spectator ions (Na<sup>+</sup>). Cl<sub>2</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>O are covalent so they cannot be split into ions.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Construct an ionic equation for the reaction between chlorine and cold aqueous sodium hydroxide.

The ionic equation for the reaction between chlorine and cold aqueous sodium hydroxide is:

Cl~2~ + 2OH^–^ → OCl^–^ + Cl^–^ + H~2~O

State the oxidation numbers of chlorine in each of the chlorine-containing ions formed in this reaction.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The oxidation numbers of chlorine in the chlorine-containing ions are:
> 
> - OCl<sup>–</sup> = +1
> **AND**
> Cl<sup>–</sup> = –1 **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> To find the oxidation number of Cl in OCl<sup>–</sup>:
> 
> - Oxygen has an oxidation state of –2
> - (–2) + Cl = –1
> - Cl = +1
> 
> The oxidation number of Cl in Cl<sup>–</sup> is simply –1, determined by the charge on the ion.

parts.problemMd:

i) Construct an equation for this reaction.

[1]

ii) State the name of the product containing both oxygen and chlorine.

[1]

iii) Explain, in terms of changes in oxidation number, why this reaction is an example of a disproportionation reaction.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The equation for this reaction is:
> 
> - Cl<sub>2</sub> + 2NaOH → NaClO + NaCl + H<sub>2</sub>O **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The name of the product containing both oxygen and chlorine is:
> 
> - Sodium chlorate(I) **[1 mark]**
> 
> iii) This is a disproportionation reaction because:

> **[exam-tip]**
> The product in this reaction is sodium chlorate(I). Make sure you give the correct name including the Roman numeral (I).
> 
> Sodium chlorate(V), NaClO<sub>3</sub>, is a different product formed when chlorine reacts with hot aqueous sodium hydroxide.
> 
> When explaining why a reaction is a disproportionation reaction, state the starting and finishing oxidation numbers for chlorine. Simply stating that chlorine is simultaneously oxidised and reduced earns only one of the two marks.

parts.problemMd:
Chlorine is added to drinking water to ensure that it is safe to drink.

i) Construct an equation for the reaction of chlorine with cold water.

ii) Identify the two active species produced in this reaction that are responsible for killing bacteria.

parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The equation for the reaction of chlorine with cold water is:
> 
> - Cl<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O → HClO + HCl
> **OR**
> Cl<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O → 2H<sup>+</sup> + ClO<sup>–</sup> + Cl<sup>–</sup> **[1 mark]**
> 
> A reversible arrow (⇌) is also accepted.
> 
> ii) The two active species responsible for killing bacteria are:
> 
> - HClO / HOCl
> **AND**
> ClO<sup>–</sup> / OCl<sup>–</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> You must know all the reactions of chlorine, as they are asked about frequently. Chlorine also reacts with both cold and hot aqueous sodium hydroxide to form different products.
> 
> HClO (hypochlorous acid) and ClO<sup>–</sup> (chlorate(I) ion / hypochlorite ion) are the active species that kill bacteria by acting as oxidising agents.

parts.problemMd:

parts.problemMd: Suggest one disadvantage of treating drinking water with chlorine.
parts.solutionMd:

> Any **one** from:

> **[1 mark]**

parts.problemMd: Explain, in terms of electron transfer, what is meant by the term *oxidising agent*.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> An oxidising agent is a substance that:
> 
> - Accepts electrons (from another substance) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> An oxidising agent is itself reduced, so it accepts electrons. A reducing agent is itself oxidised, so it donates electrons.

parts.problemMd:
Chlorine is added to drinking water to kill harmful bacteria and make it safe to drink. During this process, chlorine undergoes a disproportionation reaction.

i) Construct an equation for this reaction.

parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**

> 
> - Cl<sub>2</sub> (aq) + H<sub>2</sub>O (l) → HCl (aq) + HClO (aq) **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The oxidation numbers of chlorine in the products are:
> 
> - Cl in HCl = –1
> **AND**
> Cl in HClO = +1 **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> This is an equation you need to know. Make sure you learn all the reactions of chlorine with water and with aqueous sodium hydroxide.

parts.problemMd:
The reaction of chlorine with water can be described as a disproportionation reaction. Chlorine also undergoes a disproportionation reaction when it reacts with hot aqueous sodium hydroxide.

i) Construct an equation for the reaction of chlorine with hot aqueous sodium hydroxide.

[1]

ii) Explain, in terms of changes in oxidation number, why this is also an example of a disproportionation reaction.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The equation for this reaction is:
> 
> - 3Cl<sub>2</sub> (aq) + 6NaOH (aq) → 5NaCl (aq) + NaClO<sub>3</sub> (aq) + 3H<sub>2</sub>O (l) **[1 mark]**

> ii) This is a disproportionation reaction because:
> 
> - Cl<sub>2</sub> is both oxidised and reduced at the same time **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Chlorine can react with both cold and hot aqueous sodium hydroxide and you need to know both equations:
> 
> - When hot aqueous sodium hydroxide is used, NaClO<sub>3</sub> is produced
> - When cold aqueous sodium hydroxide is used, NaClO is produced
> 
> When describing oxidation and reduction in a disproportionation reaction, state the oxidation states of the relevant species to gain the marks.

parts.problemMd:
The halogens can react with iron wool to produce various iron compounds including iron(III) chloride, iron(III) bromide and iron(II) iodide.

The Fe<sup>2+</sup> ion can also react with chlorine, Cl<sub>2</sub>, and bromine, Br<sub>2</sub>.

i) Construct an ionic half-equation for the reduction of bromine.

[1]

ii) Construct an ionic half-equation for the oxidation of Fe<sup>2+</sup> to Fe<sup>3+</sup>.

[1]

iii) Hence, construct an overall equation for the reaction of Br<sub>2</sub> with Fe<sup>2+</sup>.

[1]

iv) Explain why iodine does not oxidise Fe<sup>2+</sup> ions.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The ionic half-equation for the reduction of bromine is:
> 
> - Br<sub>2</sub> + 2e<sup>–</sup> → 2Br<sup>–</sup> **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The ionic half-equation for the oxidation of Fe<sup>2+</sup> is:
> 
> - Fe<sup>2+</sup> → Fe<sup>3+</sup> + e<sup>–</sup> **[1 mark]**
> 
> iii) The overall equation for the reaction of Br<sub>2</sub> with Fe<sup>2+</sup> is:
> 
> - Br<sub>2</sub> + 2Fe<sup>2+</sup> → 2Br<sup>–</sup> + 2Fe<sup>3+</sup> **[1 mark]**
> 
> iv) Iodine does not oxidise Fe<sup>2+</sup> ions because:
> 
> - Iodine / I<sub>2</sub> is not a strong enough oxidising agent **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The oxidising power of the halogens decreases down the group. Halogen molecules become larger with more electron shells and greater shielding. The increased distance between the nucleus and outer shell weakens nuclear attraction, making it harder to gain electrons.
> 
> The reducing power of the halogens increases down the group. The further the outer shell is from the nucleus, the weaker the attraction and the easier it is to donate an electron.
> 
> Halide ions are good reducing agents as they can donate the electron responsible for their 1– charge. The reducing ability of halide ions increases down the group.

parts.problemMd:

Deduce the oxidation number of chlorine in HClO and in Cl<sup>–</sup>.

oxidation number of Cl in HClO:

> To find the oxidation number of Cl in HClO: H = +1 and O = –2. For the molecule to be neutral: +1 + Cl + (–2) = 0, so Cl = +1.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The bromate(V) ion, BrO₃⁻, is formed when bromide ions react with hypochlorous acid, HClO, in aqueous alkali, as shown in the equation.

Br⁻ + 3HClO + 3OH⁻ → BrO₃⁻ + 3Cl⁻ + 3H₂O

Identify the oxidising agent in the reaction in part **(b)**. Explain your answer.
parts.solutionMd:

> 
> - HClO **[1 mark]**
> - HClO oxidises Br<sup>–</sup> from –1 to +5 in BrO<sub>3</sub><sup>–</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Writing all the oxidation numbers on the equation helps identify changes:
> 
> ![Redox equation Br⁻ + 3HClO + 3OH⁻ → BrO₃⁻ + 3Cl⁻ + 3H₂O, with arrows showing Br oxidised −1 to +5 and Cl reduced +1 to −1.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/11-group-17/11-4-the-reactions-of-chlorine/assets/001-redox-equation-br-3hclo-3oh-bro-3cl-3h-o-with-ar.jpeg)
> 
> An increase in oxidation number indicates oxidation. A decrease indicates reduction.

parts.problemMd:
Nitrogen gas, N<sub>2</sub>, is very unreactive.

Give **two** reasons for the lack of reactivity of the nitrogen molecule.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Two reasons for the lack of reactivity of the nitrogen molecule are:
> 
> - (Due to the) strong N≡N / triple bond **[1 mark]**
> - N<sub>2</sub> is a non-polar molecule **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The N≡N triple bond has a high bond enthalpy, meaning a large amount of energy is required to break the bond. As it is so difficult to break, the N<sub>2</sub> molecule is very unreactive and requires extreme conditions.
> 
> Electrons are shared equally between the two nitrogen atoms, so nitrogen molecules are non-polar. This lack of polarity means that nitrogen molecules are not likely to attract or react with other molecules.

parts.problemMd:
Under conditions of high temperature, nitrogen and oxygen react together to give oxides of nitrogen.

i) Construct an equation for a possible reaction between nitrogen and oxygen.

[1]

ii) Identify one natural process and one man-made process in which nitrogen and oxygen react together to form oxides of nitrogen.

[2]

iii) State the **two** main environmental effects of the presence of nitrogen oxides in the atmosphere.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) A possible equation for a reaction between nitrogen and oxygen is:
> 
> - N<sub>2</sub> + O<sub>2</sub> → 2NO
> **OR**
> N<sub>2</sub> + 2O<sub>2</sub> → 2NO<sub>2</sub> **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) Two processes in which nitrogen and oxygen react together are:
> 
> - Natural process: Lightning **[1 mark]**
> - Man-made process: In an engine / combustion of fuels (or a specific example) **[1 mark]**
> 
> iii) Two main environmental effects of the presence of nitrogen oxides in the atmosphere are:
> 
> - Formation of photochemical smog **[1 mark]**
> - Production of acid rain **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Any balanced equation that forms a stable nitrogen oxide is acceptable for part (i). For example, the formation of nitrous oxide:
> 
> 2N<sub>2</sub> + O<sub>2</sub> → 2N<sub>2</sub>O
> 
> You should know the equations for the formation of nitrogen monoxide, NO, and nitrogen dioxide, NO<sub>2</sub>.
> 
> Lightning is a natural situation that causes nitrogen and oxygen to react. The high temperatures inside car engines and aeroplane engines are also extreme enough to cause this reaction.
> 
> Other man-made sources that would be credited include combustion of coal or oil at power stations, manufacture of fertilisers, and biological decay.

parts.problemMd:
i) State how nitrogen monoxide is removed from the exhaust gases of motor vehicles.

[1]

ii) Construct an equation for this process.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) Nitrogen monoxide is removed from the exhaust gases of motor vehicles by:
> 
> - A catalytic converter
> **OR**
> Passing the exhaust gases over a (hot) catalyst / Pt / Rh **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The equation for this process is:
> 
> - 2NO + 2CO → N<sub>2</sub> + 2CO<sub>2</sub> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Catalytic converters remove carbon monoxide and nitrogen oxides from exhaust gases by passing them over a hot metal catalyst (platinum, palladium, or rhodium) with a honeycombed structure to maximise surface area.
> 
> For nitrogen dioxide, the equation is:
> 
> NO<sub>2</sub> + 2CO → ½N<sub>2</sub> + 2CO<sub>2</sub>
> 
> Both nitrogen monoxide and nitrogen dioxide are reduced in the catalytic converter.

parts.problemMd:
Atmospheric oxides of nitrogen react with unburned hydrocarbons to form peroxyacetyl nitrate (PAN), which is a component of photochemical smog.

i) Identify the type of organic compound that reacts with nitrogen oxides to form PAN.

[1]

ii) Explain why the term *photochemical* is used to describe this type of smog.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The type of organic compound that reacts with nitrogen oxides to form PAN is:
> 
> - Unburned hydrocarbons (from fuel)
> **OR**
> VOCs / volatile organic compounds **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The term *photochemical* is used because:
> 
> - Sunlight provides the energy to start the reaction between nitrogen oxides and unburned hydrocarbons / VOCs **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Nitrogen oxides and unburned hydrocarbons are both primary pollutants as they are given off directly into the air from the source of pollution. Volatile organic compounds (VOCs) are mainly unburned hydrocarbons and their oxidation products.
> 
> PAN (formula CH<sub>3</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>NO<sub>2</sub>) is a secondary pollutant as it forms through atmospheric reactions rather than being released directly from human activity.
> 
> Photochemical smog tends to be worst in cities on sunny afternoons, when concentrations of NOx and VOCs have built up during the day and sunlight drives the reaction.

parts.problemMd:
Nitrogen dioxide, NO<sub>2</sub>, contributes to the formation of acid rain.

i) Construct an equation for the formation of nitric acid from nitrogen dioxide, NO<sub>2</sub>, in the atmosphere.

[2]

ii) State the role that nitrogen dioxide, NO<sub>2</sub>, plays in the oxidation of atmospheric sulfur dioxide, SO<sub>2</sub>, to form acid rain.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
i) The equation for the formation of nitric acid from NO<sub>2</sub> in the atmosphere is:

4NO<sub>2</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O + O<sub>2</sub> → 4HNO<sub>3</sub>

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct formulae
> 
> 1 mark for correct balancing
> 
> ii) The role of NO<sub>2</sub> in the oxidation of atmospheric SO<sub>2</sub> to form acid rain is:
> 
> - Catalyst **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> When SO<sub>2</sub> is oxidised, it forms SO<sub>3</sub> which reacts with rainwater to form dilute sulfuric acid:
> 
> SO<sub>3</sub> (g) + H<sub>2</sub>O (l) → H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (aq)
> 
> NO<sub>2</sub> catalyses the oxidation of SO<sub>2</sub> to SO<sub>3</sub>:
> 
> NO<sub>2</sub> (g) + SO<sub>2</sub> (g) → SO<sub>3</sub> (g) + NO (g)
> 
> The NO formed is then oxidised to regenerate NO<sub>2</sub>:
> 
> NO (g) + ½O<sub>2</sub> (g) → NO<sub>2</sub> (g)

parts.problemMd:
Deduce the oxidation number of nitrogen in nitrogen monoxide, NO, and nitrogen dioxide, NO<sub>2</sub>.

| oxidation number in NO |   |
|---|---|
| oxidation number in NO<sub>2</sub> |   |
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The oxidation numbers of nitrogen in nitrogen monoxide and nitrogen dioxide are:
> 
> - +2 in NO **AND** +4 in NO<sub>2</sub> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Oxygen has an oxidation number of −2. Since the overall charge on each compound is 0:
> 
> - In NO: nitrogen must be +2 (since −2 + 2 = 0)
> - In NO<sub>2</sub>: two oxygen atoms give −4, so nitrogen must be +4 (since −4 + 4 = 0)

parts.problemMd:
Ammonia, NH<sub>3</sub>, acts as a weak Brønsted–Lowry base in aqueous solution.

Explain why, and include an equation in your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Ammonia can be described as a weak Brønsted–Lowry base because:
> 
> - It is a proton acceptor **[1 mark]**
> - It only partially dissociates / ionises in aqueous solution **[1 mark]**
> - NH<sub>3</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O ⇌ NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> + OH<sup>–</sup> **[1 mark]**
> 
> The reversible arrow ⇌ must be used in the equation

> **[exam-tip]**
> Acids are proton donors and bases are proton acceptors.
> 
> When dissolved in water, ammonia reacts with water to produce ammonium ions and hydroxide ions. The ⇌ symbol shows the reaction is reversible, so not all of the ammonia has reacted. In fact, only about 1% of ammonia reacts to form ammonium ions, so the equilibrium lies well to the left.

parts.problemMd:
i) Construct an equation for the neutralisation of aqueous ammonia by dilute sulfuric acid.

[1]

ii) State the H-N-H bond angle in ammonia and in the ammonium ion. Explain any difference.

[3]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The equation for the neutralisation of aqueous ammonia by dilute sulfuric acid is:
> 
> - 2NH<sub>3</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> → (NH<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The H-N-H bond angles are:
> 
> - NH<sub>3</sub> = 107°
> **AND**
> NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> = 109.5° **[1 mark]**
> 
> The difference is because:
> 
> - NH<sub>3</sub> has 3 bonded pairs of electrons and 1 lone pair
> **AND**
> NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> has 4 bonded pairs of electrons and no lone pairs **[1 mark]**
> - The lone pair in NH<sub>3</sub> repels the bonded pairs more strongly, pushing them closer together **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> When neutralising ammonia with acid, an ammonium salt is formed but no water is produced, unlike typical acid-base reactions.
> 
> When explaining bond angles, always state the number of bonded pairs and lone pairs on the central atom. Four bonded pairs repel each other equally, giving a tetrahedral shape with a bond angle of 109.5°. The presence of a lone pair reduces this angle by approximately 2.5°.

parts.problemMd:
Ammonia can be displaced from an ammonium salt by an acid–base reaction. One such reaction is between ammonium chloride and calcium hydroxide.

i) Construct an equation for the reaction between ammonium chloride and calcium hydroxide.

[2]

ii) Describe a test and the expected observation to confirm the presence of ammonia gas.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
i) The equation for the reaction between ammonium chloride and calcium hydroxide is:

2NH<sub>4</sub>Cl + Ca(OH)<sub>2</sub> → CaCl<sub>2</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O + 2NH<sub>3</sub>

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct formulae
> 
> 1 mark for correct balancing
> 
> ii) A test and expected observation to confirm the presence of ammonia gas:
> 
> - Hold damp red litmus paper near the gas; the paper turns blue **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> In this acid-base reaction, NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> acts as a proton donor (acid) and OH<sup>–</sup> acts as a proton acceptor (base).
> 
> As with any acid-base reaction, a salt and water are produced, along with ammonia gas.

parts.problemMd:
Nitrogen and oxygen react together under conditions of high temperature to give oxides of nitrogen.

i) Draw a dot-and-cross diagram to show the arrangement of outer-shell electrons in a molecule of nitrogen.

[2]

ii) Explain why high temperatures are required for oxides of nitrogen to form.

[3]
parts.solutionMd:
i) The dot-and-cross diagram of a nitrogen molecule:

![Venn diagram with two overlapping sets labelled N, showing shaded circles and crosses in the overlap and on the outer edges to represent shared and unique elements](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/12-nitrogen-and-sulfur/12-1-nitrogen-and-sulfur/assets/002-venn-diagram-with-two-overlapping-sets-labelled-.png)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for 3 shared pairs of electrons between the two nitrogen atoms
> 
> 1 mark for 2 non-bonded electrons on each nitrogen atom
> 
> ii) High temperatures are required because:
> 
> - Nitrogen is very unreactive **[1 mark]**
> - It requires a lot of energy to break the N≡N triple bond (high bond enthalpy) **[1 mark]**
> - N<sub>2</sub> is a non-polar molecule, so it is not attracted to other molecules **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Each nitrogen atom has 5 outer electrons. To achieve a full outer shell, each atom shares 3 electrons, forming a triple bond. After drawing the diagram, check that each nitrogen atom has 8 electrons in total.
> 
> High temperatures are needed because nitrogen is so unreactive. Part (ii) is essentially asking you to state and explain the reasons for nitrogen's lack of reactivity.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Nitrogen and oxygen react together under conditions of high temperature to give oxides of nitrogen.

i) Construct an equation for a possible reaction between nitrogen and oxygen.

[1]

ii) The bond enthalpy of the N≡N triple bond in N<sub>2</sub> is +944 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>.

Suggest the bond enthalpy of the O=O bond in oxygen. Give a reason for your answer.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) A possible equation for a reaction between nitrogen and oxygen is:
> 
> - N<sub>2</sub> + O<sub>2</sub> → 2NO
> **OR**
> N<sub>2</sub> + 2O<sub>2</sub> → 2NO<sub>2</sub> **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The bond enthalpy of O=O:
> 
> - A value below +944 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup> **AND** O=O is a double bond, which requires less energy to break than the triple bond in N≡N **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Any reasonable positive value below +944 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup> is accepted. Bond enthalpies are always positive (endothermic process).
> 
> The actual bond enthalpy of O=O is +496 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup> (given in the Data Booklet).

parts.problemMd:
i) Identify one natural process and one man-made process in which nitrogen and oxygen react together to form oxides of nitrogen.

[2]

ii) State **two** environmental effects of the presence of nitrogen oxides in the atmosphere.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) Two processes in which nitrogen and oxygen react together:
> 
> - Natural process: Lightning **[1 mark]**
> - Man-made process: In an engine / combustion of fuels **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) Two environmental effects of the presence of nitrogen oxides in the atmosphere:
> 
> - (NOx produces) acid rain **[1 mark]**
> - (NOx) forms (photochemical) smog **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> A specific example of a man-made process, such as in a car engine or an aeroplane engine, is also accepted.

parts.problemMd: State the systematic name of N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>5</sub>.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The systematic name of N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>5</sub> is:
> 
> - Nitrogen(V) oxide **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> To find the systematic name, determine the oxidation number of nitrogen: 5 oxygen atoms × (−2) = −10; overall charge = 0; so nitrogen = +10 ÷ 2 = +5.
> 
> The Roman numeral (V) in the name shows the oxidation number of nitrogen in this compound.

parts.problemMd:
Nitrogen oxides in the atmosphere act as homogeneous catalysts in the formation of acid rain.

Explain what is meant by the term *homogeneous catalyst*.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> A homogeneous catalyst:
> 
> - Is in the same phase / state as the reactants **[1 mark]**
> - Increases the rate of a reaction by providing an alternative reaction pathway of lower activation energy **[1 mark]**
> - Is not used up / remains chemically unchanged at the end of the reaction **[1 mark]**
> 
> 'Alters' or 'changes' the rate of reaction is not accepted as the catalyst must be described as increasing the rate

> **[exam-tip]**
> These definitions are frequently tested. Always state that a catalyst increases (not just 'affects') the rate of reaction.

parts.problemMd: Identify one man-made source of oxides of nitrogen in the atmosphere. Explain how they are formed.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> One man-made source of nitrogen oxides in the atmosphere:
> 
> Any **one** from:
> 
> - Car exhausts / internal combustion engines
> - Aeroplanes
> - Power stations
> - Burning fuels
> 
> **[1 mark]**
> 
> How they are formed:
> 
> - Nitrogen (N<sub>2</sub>) reacts with oxygen (O<sub>2</sub>) at the high temperatures reached during combustion **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> This is a common question about knowing how nitrogen oxides are formed both naturally (lightning) and through human activities (combustion engines, power stations).

parts.problemMd: Construct equations to show the role played by nitrogen oxides in the formation of acid rain.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The role of nitrogen oxides in the formation of acid rain:
> 
> Any **three** from the following (1 mark for each):
> 
> - NO<sub>2</sub> + SO<sub>2</sub> → NO + SO<sub>3</sub>
> - NO + ½O<sub>2</sub> → NO<sub>2</sub>
> - SO<sub>3</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O → H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>
> - 4NO<sub>2</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O + O<sub>2</sub> → 4HNO<sub>3</sub>
> **OR**
> 3NO<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O → 2HNO<sub>3</sub> + NO
> 
> **[3 marks]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Nitrogen oxides contribute to acid rain in two ways:
> 
> 1. Directly, by reacting with water and oxygen to form nitric acid:
> 
> 4NO<sub>2</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O + O<sub>2</sub> → 4HNO<sub>3</sub>
> 
> 2. As a catalyst in the oxidation of SO<sub>2</sub> to SO<sub>3</sub>, which dissolves in rainwater to form sulfuric acid:
> 
> NO<sub>2</sub> + SO<sub>2</sub> → SO<sub>3</sub> + NO
> 
> NO + ½O<sub>2</sub> → NO<sub>2</sub> (catalyst regenerated)
> 
> SO<sub>3</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O → H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>

parts.problemMd:

Label the enthalpy change of reaction, Δ*H*, and the activation energy, *E*<sub>a</sub>, for both pathways.

The fully labelled reaction pathway diagram is:
