parts.problemMd:
Ammonia, NH<sub>3</sub>, is synthesised from its elements in the Haber process.

i) Construct an equation for this process.

[1]

ii) State the three usual operating conditions of the Haber process.

[3]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) An equation for the Haber process:
> 
> - N<sub>2</sub> (g) + 3H<sub>2</sub> (g) ⇌ 2NH<sub>3</sub> (g) **[1 mark]**
> 
> State symbols are not required
> 
> ii) Three usual operating conditions of the Haber process:
> 
> - Temperature: approximately 450 °C (accept 400–500 °C) **[1 mark]**
> - Pressure: approximately 200 atm (accept 150–300 atm) **[1 mark]**
> - Catalyst: iron **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The conditions for the Haber process represent a compromise between equilibrium yield, rate of reaction, and economic cost. A lower temperature gives a higher yield but a slower rate; very high pressure improves yield but is expensive and technically demanding. Both must be balanced for the process to be industrially viable.

parts.problemMd:
Ammonia can act as a Brønsted–Lowry base.

Explain why.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Ammonia acts as a Brønsted–Lowry base because:
> 
> - It accepts a proton / H<sup>+</sup> ion **[1 mark]**
> - To form the ammonium ion / NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Acids are proton donors and bases are proton acceptors. When ammonia accepts a proton, the ammonium ion is formed:
> 
> NH<sub>3</sub> (aq) + H<sup>+</sup> (aq) → NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> (aq)

parts.problemMd:
1.50 dm<sup>3</sup> of ammonia gas were dissolved in water to form 300 cm<sup>3</sup> of aqueous alkali at room conditions.

i) Calculate the amount, in mol, of NH<sub>3</sub>(g) dissolved.

Show your working.

[1]

ii) Construct an equation for the neutralisation of aqueous ammonia by dilute sulfuric acid.

[1]

iii) Calculate the volume of 0.80 mol dm<sup>–3</sup> sulfuric acid that is required to neutralise the 300 cm<sup>3</sup> of aqueous ammonia.

Show your working.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
i) To calculate the amount, in mol, of NH<sub>3</sub>(g) dissolved:

- List the known values:

  - Volume of NH<sub>3</sub> = 1.50 dm<sup>3</sup>
  - Molar gas volume at room conditions = 24.0 dm<sup>3</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>
- Calculate the amount of NH<sub>3</sub>:

n(NH<sub>3</sub>) = $\frac{\text{volume}}{\text{molar gas volume}}$

n(NH<sub>3</sub>) = $\frac{1.50}{24.0}$

n(NH<sub>3</sub>) = **0.0625 mol** **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii) An equation for the neutralisation of aqueous ammonia by dilute sulfuric acid:
> 
> - 2NH<sub>3</sub> (aq) + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (aq) → (NH<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (aq) **[1 mark]**
> 
> State symbols are not required

iii) To calculate the volume of 0.80 mol dm<sup>–3</sup> sulfuric acid required:

- From the equation in (ii), n(H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>) = n(NH<sub>3</sub>) ÷ 2:

n(H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>) = $\frac{0.0625}{2}$ = 0.03125 mol **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the volume:

V(H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>) = $\frac{n}{c}$ = $\frac{0.03125}{0.80}$

V(H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>) = 0.0391 dm<sup>3</sup> = **39.1 cm**<sup>**3**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Allow error carried forward from (i) for the volume calculation in (iii)

> **[exam-tip]**
> The molar gas volume at room conditions is 24.0 dm<sup>3</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup> and is provided in the data booklet. Note that the neutralisation of ammonia with sulfuric acid produces the ammonium salt (NH<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>, but no water is produced as a product.

parts.problemMd:
i) Draw a three-dimensional diagram of each species below to show its shape. Clearly show the bond angles.

[4]

| **Ammonia** | **Ammonium ion** |
|---|---|
|   |   |

ii) State the name of the shape of an ammonia molecule and an ammonium ion.

Ammonia molecule ................................................................................

Ammonium ion .........................................................................................

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
i) Three-dimensional diagrams showing the shape and bond angles:

| **Ammonia** | **Ammonium ion** |
|---|---|
| ![Diagram of an ammonia molecule showing nitrogen with a lone pair and three hydrogens, with a marked H–N–H bond angle of 107 degrees](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/12-nitrogen-and-sulfur/12-1-nitrogen-and-sulfur/assets/003-diagram-of-an-ammonia-molecule-showing-nitrogen-.png) | ![Diagram of ammonium ion showing tetrahedral N–H bonds, 109.5° bond angle marked, wedge and dash notation, in square brackets with positive charge](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/12-nitrogen-and-sulfur/12-1-nitrogen-and-sulfur/assets/004-diagram-of-ammonium-ion-showing-tetrahedral-n-h-.png) |

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for a correct three-dimensional diagram of an ammonia molecule
> 
> 1 mark for a H–N–H bond angle of 107° shown on the ammonia diagram
> 
> 1 mark for a correct three-dimensional diagram of an ammonium ion
> 
> 1 mark for a H–N–H bond angle of 109.5° shown on the ammonium ion diagram
> 
> ii) Names of the shapes:
> 
> - Ammonia molecule: (trigonal) pyramidal **[1 mark]**
> - Ammonium ion: tetrahedral **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> In ammonia, the lone pair on nitrogen repels the three N–H bonding pairs more strongly than bonding pairs repel each other, compressing the bond angle to 107° and giving a trigonal pyramidal shape.
> 
> In the ammonium ion, the lone pair is used to form a dative covalent bond with a proton, leaving four equivalent bonding pairs arranged tetrahedrally with a bond angle of 109.5°.

parts.problemMd:
Ammonia gas can also be prepared by heating a mixture of ammonium chloride and calcium hydroxide.

Construct an equation for this reaction.
parts.solutionMd:
An equation for the reaction of ammonium chloride with calcium hydroxide is:

- 2NH<sub>4</sub>Cl (s) + Ca(OH)<sub>2</sub> (s) → CaCl<sub>2</sub> (s) + 2H<sub>2</sub>O (g) + 2NH<sub>3</sub> (g) **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> State symbols are not required

> **[exam-tip]**
> Ammonia is prepared in the laboratory by heating an ammonium salt with a base. The ammonium ion (NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>) acts as an acid (proton donor) and the hydroxide ion (OH<sup>−</sup>) acts as a base (proton acceptor).

parts.problemMd:
The high temperatures reached in an internal combustion engine cause nitrogen and oxygen from the air to react, forming nitrogen monoxide.

i) Construct an equation for this reaction.

[1]

ii) Deduce the oxidation number of nitrogen in N<sub>2</sub> and NO to show that nitrogen is oxidised in this reaction.

[1]

iii) Nitrogen monoxide reacts further with oxygen to form nitrogen dioxide.

Construct an equation for this reaction.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) An equation for the formation of nitrogen monoxide:
> 
> - N<sub>2</sub> (g) + O<sub>2</sub> (g) → 2NO (g) **[1 mark]**
> 
> State symbols are not required
> 
> ii) Oxidation numbers of nitrogen:
> 
> - Oxidation number of N in N<sub>2</sub> = 0
> **AND**
> Oxidation number of N in NO = +2
> **AND**
> An increase in oxidation number shows nitrogen has been oxidised **[1 mark]**
> 
> iii) An equation for the further oxidation of nitrogen monoxide:
> 
> - 2NO (g) + O<sub>2</sub> (g) → 2NO<sub>2</sub> (g) **[1 mark]**
> 
> State symbols are not required

> **[exam-tip]**
> When explaining oxidation or reduction using oxidation numbers, always state the oxidation number of the element in both the reactant and product and note whether it has increased (oxidation) or decreased (reduction). You must know the equations for the formation of NO and NO<sub>2</sub> from their elements.

parts.problemMd: Nitrogen oxides play a role in the formation of photochemical smog. Explain how.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Nitrogen oxides contribute to the formation of photochemical smog by:
> 
> - Reacting with unburnt hydrocarbons / VOCs in the presence of sunlight **[1 mark]**
> - To form photochemical oxidants / pollutants such as PAN (peroxyacetyl nitrate, CH<sub>3</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>NO<sub>2</sub>) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Photochemical smog forms when nitrogen oxides react with unburnt hydrocarbons in the presence of sunlight, hence the term photochemical. You are not required to know the equations for these reactions; knowing that PAN is one pollutant produced is sufficient.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Nitrogen oxides contribute to the formation of photochemical smog by:
- Reacting with unburnt hydrocarbons / VOCs in the presence of sunlight
- To form photochemical oxidants / pollutants such as PAN (peroxyacetyl nitrate, CH~3~CO~3~NO~2~)

The brown haze associated with photochemical smog is typically worse in cities in the afternoons of hot sunny days.

Suggest why.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Any **two** from (1 mark for each point):
> 
> - In cities: higher traffic density / more cars means greater concentrations of nitrogen oxides and unburnt hydrocarbons
> - In afternoons: pollutants accumulate throughout the day as traffic builds up
> - On hot sunny days: greater light intensity drives the photochemical reactions more rapidly
> 
> **[2 marks]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The 'suggest' command word means you should apply your knowledge to a novel context. Consider the three aspects separately: cities (sources of emissions), afternoons (time for accumulation), and hot sunny days (energy for photochemical reactions). Two marks means two distinct points.

parts.problemMd:
Catalytic converters are fitted to exhaust systems to reduce the pollutants emitted by car engines. Nitrogen monoxide, NO, and carbon monoxide, CO, are removed in a catalytic converter, forming nitrogen and carbon dioxide.

i) Construct an equation for the removal of NO and CO.

[1]

ii) Identify the reducing agent in this reaction. Explain your answer using changes in oxidation numbers.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) An equation for the removal of NO and CO in a catalytic converter:
> 
> - 2CO (g) + 2NO (g) → 2CO<sub>2</sub> (g) + N<sub>2</sub> (g) **[1 mark]**
> 
> State symbols are not required
> 
> ii) The reducing agent:
> 
> - Carbon monoxide / CO **[1 mark]**
> - Oxidation number of C increases from +2 (in CO) to +4 (in CO<sub>2</sub>), showing CO is oxidised and therefore the reducing agent
> **OR**
> Oxidation number of N decreases from +2 (in NO) to 0 (in N<sub>2</sub>), showing NO is reduced by CO **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> A reducing agent reduces another species and is itself oxidised in the process.
> 
> To identify the reducing agent, track oxidation number changes:
> 
> - Carbon in CO increases from +2 to +4 (oxidised), so CO is the reducing agent.
> - Alternatively, nitrogen in NO decreases from +2 to 0 (reduced), confirming that CO causes the reduction.

parts.problemMd:
Nitrogen dioxide, NO<sub>2</sub>, is a pollutant gas produced in the combustion of fuels in motor vehicles and power stations.

Construct an equation for the formation of NO<sub>2</sub> from its elements.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The equation for the formation of NO<sub>2</sub> from its elements is:
> 
> - N<sub>2</sub> + 2O<sub>2</sub> → 2NO<sub>2</sub>
> **OR**
> 2NO + O<sub>2</sub> → 2NO<sub>2</sub> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> You can either give the equation for the direct formation of nitrogen dioxide from nitrogen and oxygen in the air, or show the oxidation of nitrogen monoxide to nitrogen dioxide.

parts.problemMd:
i) State how NO<sub>2</sub> is removed from the exhaust gases of motor vehicles.

[1]

ii) Construct an equation for this process.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) NO<sub>2</sub> is removed from the exhaust gases of motor vehicles by:
> 
> - A catalytic converter
> **AND**
> Passing the exhaust gases over a (hot) catalyst / Pt / Rh **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The equation for this process is:
> 
> - NO<sub>2</sub> + 2CO → ½N<sub>2</sub> + 2CO<sub>2</sub>
> **OR**
> 2NO<sub>2</sub> + CH<sub>4</sub> → CO<sub>2</sub> + N<sub>2</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Sometimes a question asks only that a catalytic converter removes NO<sub>2</sub>; other times it also asks for the catalyst type or reaction equation. Give all available information to maximise your marks.
> 
> The most commonly expected equation uses carbon monoxide as the reductant.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Nitrogen dioxide, NO~2~, is a pollutant gas produced in the combustion of fuels in motor vehicles and power stations.

The equation for the formation of NO~2~ from its elements is:
N~2~ + 2O~2~ → 2NO~2~

Suggest whether the production of the pollutant NO<sub>2</sub> in motor vehicles would be reduced if fossil fuels were replaced by hydrogen as a fuel for combustion. Explain your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Whether the production of NO<sub>2</sub> would be reduced:
> 
> - No, it would not be reduced
> **AND**
> NO<sub>2</sub> is formed from N<sub>2</sub> and O<sub>2</sub> in the air at high temperature, not from the fuel itself **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The fuel used for combustion has no impact on the formation of nitrogen dioxide. Both nitrogen and oxygen come from the air, not the fuel. It is the high temperatures in the combustion engine that cause them to react, regardless of the fuel type.

parts.problemMd:
In the atmosphere, NO<sub>2</sub> acts as a homogeneous catalyst for the oxidation of SO<sub>2</sub> to SO<sub>3</sub>.

SO<sub>2</sub> (g) + ½ O<sub>2</sub> (g) $\overset{NO_{2}}{\rightarrow}$ SO<sub>3</sub> (g)

i) State one environmental consequence of the formation of SO<sub>3</sub> in the atmosphere.

[1]

The oxidation takes place in two steps. The initial reaction is between NO<sub>2</sub> and SO<sub>2</sub>.

reaction **1**     NO<sub>2</sub> (g) + SO<sub>2</sub> (g) $\rightleftharpoons$ NO (g) + SO<sub>3</sub> (g)     Δ*H* = −42 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>

ii) Construct an equation to show how the NO<sub>2</sub> catalyst is regenerated in the second step.

[1]

iii) The temperature of the atmosphere decreases with height from the ground.

Suggest how the position of the equilibrium in reaction **1** changes as height increases. Explain your answer.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) One environmental consequence of the formation of SO<sub>3</sub> in the atmosphere is:
> 
> - SO<sub>3</sub> dissolves in rainwater to form sulfuric acid / SO<sub>3</sub> contributes to acid rain **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The equation for regeneration of the NO<sub>2</sub> catalyst is:
> 
> - NO + ½O<sub>2</sub> → NO<sub>2</sub> **[1 mark]**
> 
> iii) The position of the equilibrium in reaction 1 as height increases:
> 
> - The equilibrium shifts to the right (towards products) **[1 mark]**
> - Because the reaction is exothermic (ΔH = −42 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>), a decrease in temperature favours the forward reaction **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> When SO<sub>3</sub> dissolves in rainwater, dilute sulfuric acid is formed:
> 
> SO<sub>3</sub> (g) + H<sub>2</sub>O (l) → H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (aq)
> 
> When explaining how equilibrium is affected by changing conditions, always state the direction the equilibrium shifts **AND** give a reason.
> 
> As height increases, temperature decreases. A decrease in temperature always favours the exothermic direction.
> 
> In this reaction, the forward reaction has a negative Δ*H*. So, a decrease in temperature increases the yield of NO and SO<sub>3</sub>.

parts.problemMd:
Ammonia gas can be prepared from ammonium chloride and calcium hydroxide.

i) Explain how ammonia can be prepared from these reagents.

[2]

ii) Describe a test and the expected observation to confirm the presence of ammonia gas.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) Ammonia can be prepared from ammonium chloride and calcium hydroxide by:
> 
> - Mixing and heating (ammonium chloride and calcium hydroxide) **[1 mark]**
> - Drying (the ammonia) with calcium oxide **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) A test and expected observation to confirm the presence of ammonia gas:
> 
> - Hold damp red litmus paper near the gas; the paper turns blue **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Ammonium chloride and calcium hydroxide are both solids. The ammonia gas produced is typically passed through a U-tube containing calcium oxide, which acts as a drying agent to absorb any water.

parts.problemMd: Explain, using the Brønsted–Lowry theory, why the reaction between ammonium chloride and calcium hydroxide is an example of an acid-base reaction.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Using the Brønsted–Lowry theory, this is an acid-base reaction because:
> 
> - NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> acts as a Brønsted–Lowry acid as it is a proton donor **[1 mark]**
> - OH<sup>–</sup> acts as a Brønsted–Lowry base as it is a proton acceptor **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> You must identify which species is acting as an acid and which as a base, and explain why in terms of proton donation and acceptance.

parts.problemMd:
i) Draw a dot-and-cross diagram to show the bonding in an ammonium ion.

Show outer-shell electrons only.

[2]

ii) All four N-H bonds in the ammonium ion are equal in length. Explain why.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
i) The dot-and-cross diagram of the ammonium ion is:

![Diagram of the ammonium ion: nitrogen bonded to four hydrogens, with one N–H shown as a dative bond using an arrow, enclosed in brackets with a plus sign](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/12-nitrogen-and-sulfur/12-1-nitrogen-and-sulfur/assets/005-diagram-of-the-ammonium-ion-nitrogen-bonded-to-f.png)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for an arrow pointing from N to an H atom (showing the dative covalent bond)
> 
> 1 mark for the rest of the structure including square brackets and + charge
> 
> ii) All four N-H bonds in the ammonium ion are equal in length because:
> 
> - All four covalent bonds are equivalent (the dative bond is indistinguishable from the other bonds once formed)
> **OR**
> The positive charge is spread evenly around the ion **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The ammonium ion has a coordinate (dative covalent) bond shown by an arrow pointing from N (which donates the lone pair) to the H<sup>+</sup> ion. Once formed, this bond is completely indistinguishable from the other three N-H bonds in terms of length and strength.

parts.problemMd:
Nitrogen gas, N<sub>2</sub>, is very unreactive.

i) Explain the lack of reactivity of the nitrogen molecule.

[2]

ii) State the number of σ (sigma) and π (pi) bonds in a nitrogen molecule.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The nitrogen molecule is unreactive because:
> 
> - It has a strong N≡N triple bond / high bond enthalpy **[1 mark]**
> - N<sub>2</sub> is a non-polar molecule **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The nitrogen molecule contains:
> 
> - 1 σ bond **AND** 2 π bonds **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> As nitrogen is made from two identical nitrogen atoms, electrons are shared equally and the molecule is non-polar. This means it is not attracted to or likely to react with other molecules.
> 
> The triple bond consists of one sigma bond (end-on overlap of sp hybrid orbitals) and two pi bonds (sideways overlap of p orbitals at right angles to each other).

parts.problemMd:
In an internal combustion engine, nitrogen reacts with oxygen to form nitrogen monoxide, NO. In the atmosphere, NO is further oxidised to nitrogen dioxide, NO<sub>2</sub>. Nitrogen dioxide then reacts with oxygen and water in the atmosphere to form dilute nitric acid, HNO<sub>3</sub>.

i) Construct equations for these three reactions. Include state symbols.

[3]

ii) Identify the change in oxidation number of nitrogen in each reaction, and state whether nitrogen is oxidised or reduced.

[3]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The three equations are:
> 
> - Step 1: N<sub>2</sub> (g) + O<sub>2</sub> (g) → 2NO (g) **[1 mark]**
> - Step 2: 2NO (g) + O<sub>2</sub> (g) → 2NO<sub>2</sub> (g) **[1 mark]**
> - Step 3: 4NO<sub>2</sub> (g) + 2H<sub>2</sub>O (l) + O<sub>2</sub> (g) → 4HNO<sub>3</sub> (aq) **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The changes in oxidation number of nitrogen and whether it is oxidised or reduced:
> 
> - Step 1: 0 to +2 **AND** oxidised **[1 mark]**
> - Step 2: +2 to +4 **AND** oxidised **[1 mark]**
> - Step 3: +4 to +5 **AND** oxidised **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Nitrogen in NO has oxidation number +2, and in NO<sub>2</sub> has oxidation number +4 (oxygen is always −2, overall compound is 0).
> 
> In nitric acid, HNO<sub>3</sub>: H = +1, three O atoms = −6 total, so N = +5.
> 
> In each reaction the oxidation number of nitrogen increases, so nitrogen is oxidised in all three steps.

parts.problemMd:
A car travelled one kilometre and released 0.23 g of an oxide of nitrogen, N~*x*<sub>O</sub>*y*~, which occupies 120 cm<sup>3</sup> at room conditions.

Calculate the values of *x* and *y*. Show your working.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the values of *x* and *y*:

- Calculate the moles of N<sub>x</sub>O<sub>y</sub>:

n = $\frac{120}{24000}$

n = 0.005 mol **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the relative molecular mass, *M*<sub>r</sub>:

*M*<sub>r</sub> = $\frac{0.23}{0.005}$

*M*<sub>r</sub> = 46 g mol<sup>−1</sup> **[1 mark]**

- Deduce *x* and *y* from the *M*<sub>r</sub>:

*x* = **1**
**AND**
*y* = **2** **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Allow error carried forward throughout.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Make sure the volume and the molar gas volume are in the same units before dividing: 120 ÷ 24 000 (both in cm<sup>3</sup>) or 0.120 ÷ 24 (both in dm<sup>3</sup>). The molar gas volume (24.0 dm<sup>3</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup> at room conditions) is given in the Data Booklet.
> 
> Once you have the *M*<sub>r</sub>, find the formula by trial and error: 14 + 32 = 46, so *x* = 1 (one nitrogen atom) and *y* = 2 (two oxygen atoms).

name: Formulas, Functional Groups & the Naming of Organic Compounds
section: 13. An Introduction to AS Level Organic Chemistry

parts.problemMd:
**X**, **Y** and **Z** are all organic compounds.

**X** can be manufactured by the oxidation of propene.

CH<sub>3</sub>CH=CH<sub>2</sub> + O<sub>2</sub> → CH<sub>2</sub>=CHCHO + H<sub>2</sub>O

Name **X** and name all the functional groups present in **X**.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The name and functional groups of **X** are:
> 
> - Name: propenal **[1 mark]**
> - Functional groups: alkene
> **AND**
> aldehyde / carbonyl **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> To name **X** (CH<sub>2</sub>=CHCHO), identify the longest carbon chain and the principal functional group:
> 
> - Three carbons = prop-
> - The aldehyde group (-CHO) has the highest priority and gives the suffix -al
> - The double bond gives the infix -en-
> - Combining these: prop + en + al = propenal
> 
> The compound contains two functional groups: an aldehyde (the -CHO group) and an alkene (the C=C bond).

parts.problemMd:
Fig. 1.1 shows the skeletal formula of **Y**.

![Skeletal formula of isobutyric acid (2-methylpropanoic acid) showing a branched 4-carbon chain with a carboxylic acid group](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/13-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistry/13-1-formulas-functional-groups-and-the-naming-of-organic-compounds/assets/026-skeletal-formula-of-isobutyric-acid-2-methylprop.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

Deduce the empirical and molecular formulae of **Y**.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The empirical and molecular formulae of **Y** are:
> 
> - Empirical formula = C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>O **[1 mark]**
> - Molecular formula = C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O<sub>2</sub> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> To find the formulae of **Y**, it helps to draw the fully displayed formula first so that all carbon and hydrogen atoms are shown explicitly and none are missed when counting.
> 
> ![Structural formula of 2-methyl propanoic acid](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/13-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistry/13-1-formulas-functional-groups-and-the-naming-of-organic-compounds/assets/027-structural-formula-of-2-methyl-propanoic-acid.png)
> 
> **Y** has the molecular formula C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O<sub>2</sub>.
> 
> To find the empirical formula, divide all subscripts by their highest common factor: HCF of 4, 8, and 2 is 2, giving C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>O.

parts.problemMd:
**Z** is a saturated hydrocarbon that is a structural isomer of pentene.

Draw the skeletal formula of **Z**.
parts.solutionMd:
The skeletal formula of **Z** is:

![Skeletal formula of cyclopentane showing a regular five-membered ring](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/13-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistry/13-1-formulas-functional-groups-and-the-naming-of-organic-compounds/assets/028-skeletal-formula-of-cyclopentane-showing-a-regul.png)

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct skeletal formula of cyclopentane (a five-membered ring with no substituents or double bonds)

> **[exam-tip]**
> Pentene has the molecular formula C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub>. A saturated hydrocarbon with this molecular formula cannot be a straight-chain alkane (alkanes have the general formula C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n+2</sub>, which would give C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub> for five carbons). The formula C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub> fits the general formula C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n</sub>, which cycloalkanes also satisfy. The only saturated cyclic hydrocarbon with five carbons is cyclopentane, drawn as a regular pentagon in skeletal form.

parts.problemMd: Crotonic acid has the molecular formula C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>6</sub>O<sub>2</sub>. Deduce the empirical formula of crotonic acid.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The empirical formula of crotonic acid is:
> 
> - C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>3</sub>O **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> To find the empirical formula, divide all the subscripts in the molecular formula by their highest common factor (HCF). For C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>6</sub>O<sub>2</sub>, the HCF of 4, 6 and 2 is 2, giving C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>3</sub>O.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Crotonic acid has the molecular formula C4H6O2.

The systematic name of crotonic acid is but-2-enoic acid.

Draw the displayed formulae of **two** structural isomers of crotonic acid that also contain the carboxylic acid functional group.
parts.solutionMd:
Any **two** of the following displayed formulae are:

But-3-enoic acid:

![Displayed formula of but-3-enoic acid, a structural isomer of but-2-enoic acid with the C=C double bond between C3 and C4](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/13-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistry/13-1-formulas-functional-groups-and-the-naming-of-organic-compounds/assets/033-displayed-formula-of-but-3-enoic-acid-a-structur.png)

**OR**

2-methylprop-2-enoic acid:

![Displayed formula of 2-methylprop-2-enoic acid, a branched structural isomer with a methyl group on C2 and the C=C double bond between C2 and C3](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/13-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistry/13-1-formulas-functional-groups-and-the-naming-of-organic-compounds/assets/034-displayed-formula-of-2-methylprop-2-enoic-acid-a.png)

**OR**

Cyclopropanecarboxylic acid

![Displayed formula of cyclopropanecarboxylic acid, a cyclic structural isomer with a cyclopropane ring and a carboxylic acid group](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/13-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistry/13-1-formulas-functional-groups-and-the-naming-of-organic-compounds/assets/035-displayed-formula-of-cyclopropanecarboxylic-acid.png)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for each correct displayed formula of a structural isomer of but-2-enoic acid that retains the carboxylic acid functional group, up to a maximum of 2 marks
> 
> Correct structural isomers include but-3-enoic acid, 2-methylprop-2-enoic acid, and cyclopropanecarboxylic acid

> **[exam-tip]**
> But-3-enoic acid is a position isomer of but-2-enoic acid. The C=C double bond moves from between C2 and C3 to between C3 and C4.

> 
> Cyclopropanecarboxylic acid is formed by incorporating the double bond into a cyclic structure. The carboxylic acid group remains outside the ring.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Crotonic acid has the molecular formula C4H6O2.
The systematic name of crotonic acid is but-2-enoic acid.

The structure of oleic acid is shown in Fig. 2.1.

![Skeletal formula of oleic acid (C18H34O2), showing a long hydrocarbon chain with one cis C=C double bond and a carboxylic acid group](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/13-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistry/13-1-formulas-functional-groups-and-the-naming-of-organic-compounds/assets/036-skeletal-formula-of-oleic-acid-c18h34o2-showing-.png)

**Fig. 2.1**

i) State the type of formula shown in Fig. 2.1.

[1]

ii) Deduce the molecular formula of oleic acid.

[1]

iii) Explain whether oleic acid belongs to the same homologous series as crotonic acid.

[3]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The type of formula shown in Fig. 2.1 is:
> 
> - A skeletal formula **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The molecular formula of oleic acid is:
> 
> - C<sub>18</sub>H<sub>34</sub>O<sub>2</sub> **[1 mark]**
> 
> iii) Whether oleic acid belongs to the same homologous series as crotonic acid:

> **[exam-tip]**
> In a skeletal formula, hydrogen atoms bonded to carbon atoms are omitted. Line ends and vertices represent carbon atoms, and functional groups and non-C/H atoms are still shown.
> 
> To find the molecular formula from a skeletal formula, count each type of atom, including hydrogen atoms on functional groups.

parts.problemMd:
Terpenes are a class of organic compounds widely used as fragrances in products such as perfumes. Nerol is a terpene found in many essential oils such as lemongrass and hops. The structure of nerol is shown in Fig. 1.1.

![Skeletal formula of nerol, a 10-carbon unsaturated alcohol with a hydroxyl group](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/13-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistry/13-1-formulas-functional-groups-and-the-naming-of-organic-compounds/assets/023-skeletal-formula-of-nerol-a-10-carbon-unsaturate.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

i) Deduce the molecular formula of nerol.

[1]

ii) Calculate the relative molecular mass, *M*<sub>r</sub>, of nerol. Show your working.

[1]

iii) Deduce the empirical formula of nerol.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The molecular formula of nerol is:
> 
> - C<sub>10</sub>H<sub>18</sub>O **[1 mark]**

ii) To calculate the relative molecular mass of nerol:

*M*<sub>r</sub> = (10 x 12.0) + (18 x 1.0) + 16.0

*M*<sub>r</sub> = 154.0 **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> iii) The empirical formula of nerol is:
> 
> - C<sub>10</sub>H<sub>18</sub>O **[1 mark]**
> 
> The empirical formula is the same as the molecular formula for nerol.

> **[exam-tip]**
> When counting atoms in a skeletal formula, trace each line end and vertex systematically to avoid missing any carbon or hydrogen atoms.
> 
> To find the empirical formula, find the highest common factor (HCF) of all subscripts in the molecular formula. For C<sub>10</sub>H<sub>18</sub>O, the HCF of 10, 18, and 1 is 1, so the empirical formula is the same as the molecular formula: C<sub>10</sub>H<sub>18</sub>O.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Terpenes are a class of organic compounds widely used as fragrances in products such as perfumes. Nerol is a terpene found in many essential oils such as lemongrass and hops. The structure of nerol is shown in Fig. 1.1.

Deduce whether molecules of nerol show geometrical (cis-trans) isomerism and whether they show optical isomerism. Explain your answers.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Geometrical (cis-trans) isomerism:
> 
> - Nerol does show geometrical (cis-trans) isomerism
> **AND**
> there are two different groups attached to each carbon of one of the C=C bonds **[1 mark]**
> - The C=C adjacent to the CH<sub>2</sub>OH group shows geometrical isomerism; the terminal C=C does not (one carbon of the terminal C=C has two identical methyl groups attached) **[1 mark]**
> 
> Optical isomerism:
> 
> - Nerol does not show optical isomerism
> **AND**
> there are no chiral centres / no carbon atom with four different groups attached **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Geometrical (cis-trans) isomerism requires restricted rotation around a C=C bond AND two different groups on each of the two carbons forming that bond.
> 
> Nerol has two C=C bonds. The terminal C=C has two methyl groups on one carbon; having identical groups on one carbon means this bond cannot show geometrical isomerism. The other C=C, adjacent to the CH<sub>2</sub>OH group, has two different groups on each carbon and does show geometrical isomerism. Nerol and geraniol are geometrical isomers of each other.
> 
> Optical isomerism requires a chiral centre: a carbon atom bonded to four different groups. There is no such carbon in nerol, so it does not show optical isomerism.

**[1 mark]**

Geraniol (3,7-dimethylocta-2,6-dien-1-ol):

> **[exam-tip]**
> To draw skeletal formulae from IUPAC names, work through the name systematically:
>

>

> 2. Identify the principal functional group:

> 3. Locate the double bonds:

>   - "2,6-dien" (geraniol) means double bonds between C2 and C3, and between C6 and C7.
> 4. Add the substituents:
> 
>   - "3,7-dimethyl" means methyl groups at C3 and C7 for both isomers.

parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**

> 
> Any **two** from (1 mark for each point):

> **[2 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
Complete Table 1.1 to state the number of σ and π bonds in each type of hybridised bond.

**Table 1.1**

| hybridisation | number of σ bonds | number of π bonds |
|---|---|---|
| sp<sup>3</sup> |   |   |
| sp<sup>2</sup> |   |   |
| sp |   |   |
parts.solutionMd:
The completed Table 1.1 is:

| hybridisation | number of σ bonds | number of π bonds |
|---|---|---|
| sp<sup>3</sup> | **Final answer:** **4** | **Final answer:** **0** |
| sp<sup>2</sup> | **Final answer:** **3** | **Final answer:** **1** |
| sp | **Final answer:** **2** | **Final answer:** **2** |

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for sp<sup>3</sup>: 4 σ bonds and 0 π bonds
> 
> 1 mark for sp<sup>2</sup>: 3 σ bonds and 1 π bond
> 
> 1 mark for sp: 2 σ bonds and 2 π bonds

> **[exam-tip]**
> Each sp<sup>3</sup> hybridised carbon forms 4 sigma bonds (from the 4 sp<sup>3</sup> orbitals overlapping head-on) and no pi bonds, because all valence orbitals are involved in hybridisation.
> 
> An sp<sup>2</sup> hybridised carbon forms 3 sigma bonds and 1 pi bond: the 3 sp<sup>2</sup> orbitals each form a sigma bond, and the remaining unhybridised p orbital overlaps sideways with an adjacent p orbital to form 1 pi bond.
> 
> An sp hybridised carbon forms 2 sigma bonds and 2 pi bonds: the 2 sp orbitals each form a sigma bond, and the 2 unhybridised p orbitals each overlap sideways to form 2 pi bonds.

parts.problemMd: By reference to the hybridisation of the carbon atoms and orbital overlap, describe how the σ and π bonds are formed in the triple bond of propyne.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The σ and π bonds in the triple bond of propyne are formed as follows:
> 
> - The carbon atoms forming the triple bond are sp hybridised **[1 mark]**
> - The σ bond is formed from the head-on overlap of sp orbitals (from each carbon atom) **[1 mark]**
> - Two π bonds are formed from the sideways overlap of unhybridised p orbitals (on each carbon atom) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> A triple bond consists of one σ bond and two π bonds. To form a triple bond, the two carbon atoms must be sp hybridised.
> 
> The σ bond forms from the head-on (direct) overlap of one sp orbital from each carbon atom. The two π bonds are formed from the sideways overlap of the two unhybridised p orbitals on each carbon.

parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) By reference to hybridisation and orbital overlap, the carbonyl carbon in pentanal is trigonal planar because:
> 
> - The carbonyl carbon is sp<sup>2</sup> hybridised / the carbonyl bond contains one σ bond **[1 mark]**
> - The unhybridised p orbitals overlap sideways to form a π bond **[1 mark]**
> - The bonding pairs of electrons are in the same plane
> **AND**
> This causes repulsion, giving a trigonal planar shape **[1 mark]**

A common error is to give the answer as linear and 180°, which describes the nitrile carbon at the end of the chain (from the HCN), not carbon-2.

parts.problemMd: Explain why the ring of carbon atoms in cyclohexane, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>, is non-planar. In your answer, refer to the hybridisation of the carbon atoms and the C–C–C bond angles.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Cyclohexane has a non-planar ring of carbon atoms because:
> 
> - The carbon atoms are sp<sup>3</sup> hybridised **[1 mark]**
> - Each carbon has a tetrahedral arrangement of bonds
> **AND**
> The C–C–C bond angles are 109.5° **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Hybridisation determines the geometry around each atom:
> 
> - sp<sup>3</sup> hybridised carbon ↔ tetrahedral geometry ↔ bond angles of 109.5°
> - sp<sup>2</sup> hybridised carbon ↔ trigonal planar geometry ↔ bond angles of 120°
> - sp hybridised carbon ↔ linear geometry ↔ bond angles of 180°
> 
> In cyclohexane, the 109.5° tetrahedral bond angles prevent the ring from being flat:
> 
> ![Skeletal formula of cyclohexane showing six linked carbon atoms, each bonded to hydrogen atoms, illustrating a non-planar branched hydrocarbon structure](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/13-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistry/13-3-shapes-of-organic-molecules--and--bonds/assets/020-skeletal-formula-of-cyclohexane-showing-six-link.png)
> 
> A flat ring would require 120° bond angles, which would require sp<sup>2</sup> hybridisation and double bonds. The puckered shape allows each carbon to maintain its preferred tetrahedral geometry.

parts.problemMd:
State the hybridisation of the carbon atom in methane, CH<sub>4</sub>. Name the shape of the molecule and explain why it has this shape.

hybridisation:

shape:

explanation:
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The hybridisation and shape of the carbon atom in methane are:
> 
> - Hybridisation: sp<sup>3</sup> **[1 mark]**
> - Shape: tetrahedral **[1 mark]**
> 
> Explanation:
> 
> - 4 bonding pairs of electrons (4 electron domains) around the central carbon **[1 mark]**
> - The electron pairs repel equally to maximise separation, giving bond angles of 109.5° **[1 mark]**

> 
> The bond angle in methane is 109.5°, the ideal tetrahedral angle.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The structure of ibuprofen is shown in Fig. 1.1.

Describe and explain the shape of the benzene ring in ibuprofen.

In your answer, include:

- the bond angle between carbon atoms
- the hybridisation of the carbon atoms
- how orbital overlap forms σ and π bonds between the carbon atoms
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The shape of the benzene ring in ibuprofen is:
> 
> - Bond angle between carbon atoms is 120° **[1 mark]**
> - All carbon atoms in the ring are sp<sup>2</sup> hybridised **[1 mark]**
> - The sp<sup>2</sup> orbitals overlap head-on to form σ bonds between adjacent carbons; the unhybridised p orbitals overlap sideways to form a delocalised π system above and below the ring **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> All carbons in the benzene ring are sp<sup>2</sup> hybridised, giving a trigonal planar arrangement around each carbon with bond angles of 120°. This forces all six carbons into the same plane, making the ring planar.
> 
> The sp<sup>2</sup> hybrid orbitals form sigma bonds between adjacent carbon atoms (head-on overlap). Each carbon also has one unhybridised p orbital perpendicular to the ring; these overlap sideways with neighbouring p orbitals to form a delocalised π system above and below the plane of the ring.

name: Isomerism: Structural Isomerism & Stereoisomerism
section: 13. An Introduction to AS Level Organic Chemistry

parts.problemMd: State the **three** different types of structural isomerism.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The three types of structural isomerism are:
> 
> - Chain (isomerism) **[1 mark]**
> - Positional (isomerism) **[1 mark]**
> - Functional group (isomerism) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Structural isomers are compounds that have the same molecular formula but different structural formulae.
> 
> You should know the three different types and be prepared to determine the possible structural formulae of an organic molecule given its molecular formula.

parts.problemMd:
State the type of **structural** isomerism that occurs between the following pairs of compounds.

i) 2-methylpentane and 2,3-dimethylbutane.

[1]

ii) butan-1-ol and butan-2-ol

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The type of structural isomerism shown by 2-methylpentane and 2,3-dimethylbutane is:
> 
> - Chain (isomerism) **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The type of structural isomerism shown by butan-1-ol and butan-2-ol is:
> 
> - Positional (isomerism) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Chain isomers have the same molecular formula but different longest carbon chain lengths because a section of the chain has been branched off.
> 
> Positional isomers arise from differences in the position of a functional group along the carbon chain. Both butan-1-ol and butan-2-ol are C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O alcohols but the –OH group is on a different carbon.

parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The systematic name of compound **B** is:
> 
> - Butanoic acid **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The type of structural isomerism shown by compounds **A** and **D** is:
> 
> - Functional group isomerism **[1 mark]**
> 
> iii) The type of structural isomerism shown by compounds **C** and **E** is:
>

parts.problemMd: State the two types of stereoisomerism.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The two types of stereoisomerism are:
> 
> - Geometrical (cis/trans)
> **AND**
> Optical **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Stereoisomers are molecules with the same structural formula but a different arrangement of atoms in 3D space.

parts.problemMd: Explain what is meant by the term *chiral centre*.
parts.solutionMd:

> A chiral centre is:

> **[exam-tip]**
> Defining a chiral centre is not a common question as the focus is usually on identifying and drawing them. However, you cannot identify or draw chiral centres without knowing this definition.

> - There is a methyl group on carbon-3: 3-methylbut-2-enoic acid

> - The C=C of compound **4** has two identical groups / methyl groups on one carbon **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For an alkene to show geometrical (cis/trans) isomerism, each carbon of the C=C double bond must have two different atoms or groups attached.

[3]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The mechanism for this reaction is:
> 
> - Electrophilic addition **[1 mark]**

ii) The three-dimensional structures of this pair of stereoisomers are:

| ![Chemical structure of a chloromethyl cyclohexanone with a marked chiral centre inside the ring and wedge bonds showing chlorine and CH₃ orientation](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/13-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistry/13-4-isomerism-structural-isomerism-and-stereoisomerism/assets/026-chemical-structure-of-a-chloromethyl-cyclohexano.png) | ![Cyclohexanone ring with a marked chiral carbon bearing a wedge methyl group and a dashed wedge chlorine substituent shown in skeletal formula style](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/13-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistry/13-4-isomerism-structural-isomerism-and-stereoisomerism/assets/027-cyclohexanone-ring-with-a-marked-chiral-carbon-b.png) |
|---|---|

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for one correct three-dimensional structure of the product
> 
> 1 mark for the second structure drawn as a mirror image of the first
> 
> 1 mark for an asterisk (*) correctly placed on the chiral carbon in one of the structures

> **[exam-tip]**
> Compound **D** is a cyclic alkene. When HCl adds across the C=C bond, the major product (Markovnikov's rule) is 3-chloro-3-methylcyclohexan-1-one, which has a chiral centre at C3.
> 
> The four different groups on C3 are: Cl, CH<sub>3</sub>, and the two non-equivalent portions of the ring (one side leads to the C=O group; the other does not).

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The organic compounds in **Fig. 1.1** are shown below.

![Five organic compounds A to E: an alcohol with two chiral centres, two acyclic alkenes with geometric isomers, a cyclic alkene and a methyl ester of a polyunsaturated acid](https://cdn.savemyexams.com/uploads/2023/03/s55z~ain_10.png)

{align=center} **Fig. 1.1**

Name the type of reaction that occurs when compound **E** reacts to form methanol and deca-2,4-dienoic acid.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The type of reaction is:
> 
> - Hydrolysis **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Compound **E** is a methyl ester. Hydrolysis is the reaction in which the ester bond is broken by water, producing the parent alcohol (methanol) and the carboxylic acid (deca-2,4-dienoic acid). This can occur under acid or alkaline conditions.

parts.problemMd: Explain why alkanes are generally unreactive.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Alkanes are generally unreactive because:
> 
> - The C–H and C–C bonds have high bond enthalpies / bond strengths **[1 mark]**
> - The C–H bonds are non-polar / have very low polarity **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The two marking points are the strength of the bonds and their lack of polarity.
> 
> The C–H bond has a bond enthalpy of 411 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> and the C–C bond has a bond enthalpy of 346 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>. These high values mean a large amount of energy is needed to break them.
> 
> Carbon and hydrogen have very similar electronegativities, so C–H bonds have very low polarity. There is no significant dipole to attract ionic reagents or nucleophiles.

parts.problemMd:
Methane reacts with chlorine to produce chloromethane, CH<sub>3</sub>Cl. The reaction is initiated by the formation of chlorine free radicals.

i) Explain what is meant by the term *free radical*.

[1]

ii) State the condition required to form chlorine free radicals from Cl<sub>2</sub>.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) A free radical is:
> 
> - A species with an unpaired electron **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The condition required to form chlorine free radicals from Cl<sub>2</sub> is:
> 
> - Ultraviolet / UV light **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> A free radical is represented as X<sup>•</sup>, where the dot indicates the unpaired electron.
> 
> In CIE A Level Chemistry, always use the full term "free radical" rather than just "radical".

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Methane reacts with chlorine to produce chloromethane, CH~3~Cl. The reaction is initiated by the formation of chlorine free radicals.

Name the type of bond fission that occurs in the initiation step.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The type of bond fission in the initiation step is:
> 
> - Homolytic fission **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> In homolytic fission, the covalent bond breaks symmetrically: each atom receives one electron from the shared pair, forming two radicals. This is shown by single-headed (fish-hook) curly arrows in mechanism diagrams.
> 
> ![Diagram showing homolytic fission of Cl2 producing two chlorine radicals](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/14-hydrocarbons/14-1-alkanes/assets/005-diagram-showing-homolytic-fission-of-cl2-produci.png)
> 
> Compare with heterolytic fission, where both electrons go to one atom, forming a positive ion and a negative ion. Alkanes undergo homolytic fission with halogens because the Cl–Cl bond breaks equally due to the identical electronegativities of the two atoms.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Methane reacts with chlorine to produce chloromethane, CH~3~Cl. The reaction is initiated by the formation of chlorine free radicals.

i) Construct two equations to show the propagation steps in this mechanism.

[2]

ii) Ethane is produced as a by-product in this reaction.

Construct an equation for the termination step that forms ethane.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The two propagation steps are:
> 
> - Cl<sup>•</sup> + CH<sub>4</sub> → CH<sub>3</sub><sup>•</sup> + HCl **[1 mark]**
> - CH<sub>3</sub><sup>•</sup> + Cl<sub>2</sub> → CH<sub>3</sub>Cl + Cl<sup>•</sup> **[1 mark]**
> 
> State symbols are not required.
> 
> ii) The termination step that forms ethane is:
> 
> - CH<sub>3</sub><sup>•</sup> + CH<sub>3</sub><sup>•</sup> → C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub> / CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> **[1 mark]**
> 
> State symbols are not required.

> **[exam-tip]**
> In each propagation step, a free radical reacts with a molecule to generate a new free radical. The chlorine radical consumed in step 1 is regenerated in step 2, keeping the chain reaction going.
> 
> Ethane forms in a termination step, where two methyl radicals combine. This illustrates a key limitation of free radical substitution: unwanted by-products are produced alongside the desired product.
> 
> Other valid termination steps are:
> 
> Cl<sup>•</sup> + Cl<sup>•</sup> → Cl<sub>2</sub>
> 
> Cl<sup>•</sup> + CH<sub>3</sub><sup>•</sup> → CH<sub>3</sub>Cl.

parts.problemMd:
Describe the difference in conditions between the complete and incomplete combustion of octane.

Construct one equation for the complete combustion and one equation for the incomplete combustion of octane.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The difference in conditions and equations are:
> 
> - Complete combustion occurs with an excess / plentiful supply of oxygen
> **AND**
> Incomplete combustion occurs with a limited / insufficient supply of oxygen **[1 mark]**
> - C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>18</sub> + 12.5O<sub>2</sub> → 8CO<sub>2</sub> + 9H<sub>2</sub>O **[1 mark]**
> - C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>18</sub> + 8.5O<sub>2</sub> → 8CO + 9H<sub>2</sub>O
> **OR**
> C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>18</sub> + 4.5O<sub>2</sub> → 8C + 9H<sub>2</sub>O **[1 mark]**
> 
> Fractional coefficients are accepted.
> 
> Allow doubled coefficients (e.g. 2C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>18</sub> + 25O<sub>2</sub> → 16CO<sub>2</sub> + 18H<sub>2</sub>O for complete combustion).

> **[exam-tip]**
> The key difference between complete and incomplete combustion is the oxygen supply. Complete combustion requires excess oxygen and produces only carbon dioxide and water. Incomplete combustion occurs when oxygen is limited and produces carbon monoxide (and/or carbon) and water.
> 
> To balance the complete combustion equation for octane (C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>18</sub>): balance C first (8CO<sub>2</sub>), then H (9H<sub>2</sub>O), then O (12.5O<sub>2</sub>). Fractional coefficients are acceptable in CIE exams, or you can double all coefficients to give whole numbers.

parts.problemMd:
Carbon monoxide is an atmospheric pollutant produced in the internal combustion engines of motor vehicles.

i) State one adverse effect of carbon monoxide on human health.

[1]

ii) Identify one other pollutant produced in internal combustion engines. State the environmental consequence of this pollutant.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) One adverse effect of carbon monoxide on human health is:
> 
> Any **one** from:
> 
> - It is toxic / poisonous
> - It binds irreversibly to haemoglobin, reducing the blood's ability to carry oxygen
> - It prevents oxygen being delivered to cells / organs
> - It forms carboxyhaemoglobin instead of oxyhaemoglobin
> 
> **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) A pollutant and its environmental consequence:
> 
> Any **one** of the following (1 mark for each point):
> 
> Set 1
> 
> - Pollutant: oxides of nitrogen / NO<sub>x</sub> / nitrogen monoxide / nitrogen dioxide
> - Consequence: reacts with water to form nitric acid / causes acid rain
> **OR**
> Reacts with unburnt hydrocarbons to form photochemical smog / peroxyacetyl nitrate (PAN)
> 
> **OR**
> 
> Set 2
> 
> - Pollutant: unburnt hydrocarbons / volatile organic compounds / VOCs
> - Consequence: reacts with oxides of nitrogen to form photochemical smog / peroxyacetyl nitrate (PAN)
> 
> **[2 marks]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Carbon monoxide is toxic because it binds to haemoglobin more strongly than oxygen. This prevents oxygen from being transported to cells.
> 
> For part ii), you need to name a specific pollutant AND give its environmental consequence. The two main pollutants tested at CIE A Level are oxides of nitrogen and unburnt hydrocarbons. One mark is for correctly identifying the pollutant, one mark is for stating its environmental consequence.

parts.problemMd:
Octane can be cracked to form pentane and one other product.

i) Construct an equation for this reaction.

[1]

ii) State the reagent and conditions required for this cracking reaction.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The equation for the reaction is:
> 
> - C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>18</sub> → C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub> + C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>6</sub> **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The reagent and conditions required are:
> 
> - Reagent: aluminium oxide / Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> / zeolite / aluminosilicate **[1 mark]**
> - Conditions: high temperature **[1 mark]**
> 
> State symbols are not required.

> **[exam-tip]**
> For the cracking equation, balance carbon and hydrogen atoms on both sides.
> 
> - Octane (C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>18</sub>) → pentane (C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub>) + propene (C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>6</sub>).
> - Check:
> 
>   - 8C = 5 + 3 ✓
>   - 18H = 12 + 6 ✓
> 
> For the conditions, "heat" alone is not sufficient, you must specify "high temperature".

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Octane can be cracked to form pentane and one other product.

i) Construct an equation for this reaction.

The equation for the reaction is:

- C~8~H~18~ → C~5~H~12~ + C~3~H~6~

Describe a chemical test and the expected observations to distinguish between the two organic products formed in (c).
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> A chemical test to distinguish between pentane and propene:
> 
> - Add aqueous bromine / bromine water / Br<sub>2</sub> (aq) **[1 mark]**
> - Pentane / C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub>: the bromine water remains orange / no change **[1 mark]**
> - Propene / C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>6</sub>: the bromine water turns colourless / decolourises **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> This test works because propene (an alkene) contains a C=C double bond, which reacts with bromine by electrophilic addition. Bromine is used up, so the orange colour disappears.
> 
> Pentane (an alkane) does not react with bromine water under these conditions, so the orange colour remains.
> 
> You need to state the reagent clearly (bromine water, not just "bromine") and give distinct observations for both products to score all three marks.

parts.problemMd:
A reaction scheme involving cyclohexane is shown in Fig. 1.1.

![Reaction scheme: cyclohexane converted by reaction 1 to chlorocyclohexane, then by reaction 2 to cyclohexene with a double bond in the ring](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/14-hydrocarbons/14-1-alkanes/assets/002-reaction-scheme-cyclohexane-converted-by-reactio.png)

**Fig. 1.1.**

Reaction **1** involves a free radical substitution mechanism.

State the essential condition required for reaction **1** to occur.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The essential condition required for reaction **1** to occur is:
> 
> - Ultraviolet / UV light **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Reaction **1** is a free-radical substitution. UV light provides the energy needed to break the Cl–Cl bond homolytically, generating two chlorine radicals that initiate the chain reaction.
> 
> Without UV light, the Cl–Cl bond cannot break, so no free radicals form and the reaction does not proceed. Alkanes are too unreactive to react with Cl<sub>2</sub> in the dark.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A reaction scheme involving cyclohexane is shown in Fig. 1.1.

Reaction 1 involves a free radical substitution mechanism.

Complete Table 1.1 to give details of the mechanism in reaction **1**. Include curly arrows to show the movement of electrons occurring in the termination step.

**Table 1.1**

![Incomplete table showing free radical chlorination of cyclohexane, with initiation, propagation and termination steps containing incomplete equations](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/14-hydrocarbons/14-1-alkanes/assets/003-incomplete-table-showing-free-radical-chlorinati.png)
parts.solutionMd:
The completed Table 1.1 is:

![Completed table showing initiation, propagation, and termination steps for the free-radical substitution of cyclohexane with chlorine](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/14-hydrocarbons/14-1-alkanes/assets/004-completed-table-showing-initiation-propagation-a.png)

**[5 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for naming the initiation step
> 
> 1 mark for HCl as a product in the first propagation step
> 
> 1 mark for naming the propagation step
> 
> 1 mark for correct species in the termination step
> 
> 1 mark for correct single-headed (fish-hook) curly arrows in the termination step

> **[exam-tip]**
> Free-radical substitution has three stages. Make sure you know the names and equations for each:
> 
> - Initiation: Cl<sub>2</sub> → 2Cl<sup>•</sup> (one molecule gives two radicals)
> - Propagation (two steps): radicals react with molecules to produce new radicals, keeping the chain going
> - Termination: two radicals combine to give a molecule (the chain ends)
> 
> For the curly arrows in the termination step, use single-headed (fish-hook) arrows to show movement of single electrons. These are different from the double-headed arrows used in ionic mechanisms.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A reaction scheme involving cyclohexane is shown in Fig. 1.1.

Reaction scheme: cyclohexane converted by reaction 1 to chlorocyclohexane, then by reaction 2 to cyclohexene with a double bond in the ring

Fig. 1.1.

Deduce the type of reaction that occurs in reaction **2.**
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The type of reaction that occurs in reaction **2** is:
> 
> - Elimination **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> In reaction **2**, chlorocyclohexane loses HCl to form cyclohexene. The removal of a small molecule (HCl) from adjacent carbon atoms to form a C=C double bond is called elimination.
> 
> The conditions for this reaction are heat with ethanolic sodium hydroxide (NaOH in ethanol). Compare this with aqueous NaOH, which gives nucleophilic substitution to form cyclohexanol instead.

parts.problemMd:
Hex-3-ene is an isomer of cyclohexane. Hex-3-ene can be converted into propanoic acid.

hex-3-ene $\overset{\mathrm{reaction}3}{\rightarrow}$ propanoic acid

Deduce the reagents and conditions for reaction **3.**
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The reagents and conditions for reaction **3** are:
> 
> - Reagent: potassium manganate(VII) / KMnO<sub>4</sub>
> **AND**
> Acid / acidified / acidic conditions **[1 mark]**
> - Conditions: hot
> **AND**
> Concentrated **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Reaction **3** is an oxidative cleavage of the C=C double bond in hex-3-ene to form propanoic acid. This requires hot, concentrated acidified KMnO<sub>4</sub>.
> 
> Be careful with the conditions. Cold, dilute KMnO<sub>4</sub> opens the double bond to form a diol rather than cleaving it to form carboxylic acids.
> 
> Hex-3-ene is a symmetrical internal alkene, so oxidative cleavage produces two identical molecules of propanoic acid.

parts.problemMd:
i) Explain what is meant by the term *cracking*.

[1]

ii) Suggest why cracking is a useful process in the petroleum industry.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) Cracking is:
> 
> - The breaking down of large hydrocarbon molecules into smaller, more useful ones **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) Cracking is useful in the petroleum industry because:
> 
> - Smaller hydrocarbons are more useful / in greater demand (as fuels and chemical feedstocks)
> **OR**
> Alkenes produced can be used to make polymers / other useful chemicals **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Crude oil contains a large proportion of long-chain hydrocarbons, which are less in demand. Cracking breaks these down into shorter-chain alkanes (useful as fuels) and alkenes (useful for making plastics and other chemicals).
> 
> "Cracking" specifically means the decomposition of long-chain hydrocarbons into shorter chains. Do not describe it simply as "breaking bonds". The answer must make clear that large molecules are converted into smaller, more useful ones.

parts.problemMd:
i) State the reagent and conditions required for the cracking of alkanes.

[2]

ii) Construct an equation for the cracking of tetradecane, C<sub>14</sub>H<sub>30</sub>, to form heptane, C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>16</sub>, and two other organic products.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The reagent and conditions required are:
> 
> - Reagent: aluminium oxide / Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> / zeolite / aluminosilicate **[1 mark]**
> - Conditions: high temperature **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) An equation for the cracking of tetradecane to form heptane and two other products:
> 
> - C<sub>14</sub>H<sub>30</sub> → C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>16</sub> + C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub> + C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub>
> **OR**
> C<sub>14</sub>H<sub>30</sub> → C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>16</sub> + C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>6</sub> + C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub>
> **OR**
> C<sub>14</sub>H<sub>30</sub> → C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>16</sub> + 2C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub> + C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>6</sub> **[1 mark]**
> 
> State symbols are not required.
> 
> The equation must show exactly two other organic products in addition to heptane.
> 
> The equation C<sub>14</sub>H<sub>30</sub> → C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>16</sub> + C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>14</sub> is not accepted because it gives only one other product.

> **[exam-tip]**

> 
> For part ii), balance the carbon and hydrogen atoms on both sides. Heptane uses 7 of the 14 carbons, so the remaining 7 carbons must be distributed across two other products. Remember that cracking produces a mixture of alkanes and alkenes.

parts.problemMd:
The combustion of octane, C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>18</sub>, in internal combustion engines produces a mixture of pollutants, including carbon monoxide, nitrogen monoxide and unburnt hydrocarbons.

i) State one adverse effect of carbon monoxide on human health.

[1]

ii) State one environmental consequence of releasing nitrogen monoxide / oxides of nitrogen into the atmosphere.

[1]

iii) State one environmental consequence of releasing unburnt hydrocarbons into the atmosphere.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) One adverse effect of carbon monoxide on human health is:
> 
> Any **one** from:
> 
> - It is toxic / poisonous
> - It binds irreversibly to haemoglobin, preventing oxygen from being carried in the blood
> - It prevents oxygen being delivered to cells / organs
> 
> **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) One environmental consequence of nitrogen monoxide / oxides of nitrogen is:
> 
> Any **one** from:
> 
> - It causes acid rain (by reacting with water to form nitric acid)
> - It damages / kills aquatic life
> - It causes respiratory problems
> 
> **[1 mark]**
> 
> iii) One environmental consequence of unburnt hydrocarbons is:
> 
> Any **one** from:
> 
> - They react with nitrogen oxides in sunlight to form photochemical smog / peroxyacetyl nitrate (PAN)
> - They contribute to global dimming
> 
> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Carbon monoxide is toxic because it binds to haemoglobin more strongly than oxygen, preventing oxygen transport to cells.
> 
> Oxides of nitrogen react with water in the atmosphere to form nitric acid, which contributes to acid rain. This damages ecosystems, particularly lakes and rivers.
> 
> Unburnt hydrocarbons react with nitrogen oxides in sunlight to produce photochemical smog, a complex mixture of pollutants including peroxyacetyl nitrate (PAN), which is harmful to human health and vegetation.

parts.problemMd: Construct an equation to demonstrate how a catalytic converter removes carbon monoxide and nitrogen monoxide from exhaust gases.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The equation for the catalytic converter reaction is:
> 
> - 2CO + 2NO → 2CO<sub>2</sub> + N<sub>2</sub> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> In a catalytic converter, carbon monoxide is oxidised to carbon dioxide and nitrogen monoxide is reduced to nitrogen. This single reaction removes both pollutants simultaneously.
> 
> The catalyst (typically platinum, palladium, or rhodium) lowers the activation energy for this reaction, allowing it to occur at the relatively low temperatures found in exhaust gases.

parts.problemMd:
Methane reacts with chlorine gas under suitable conditions to form chloromethane.

i) Name the mechanism that occurs in this reaction.

[1]

ii) Two test tubes are set up, each containing a small amount of methane and pale green chlorine gas. One test tube is left in the dark, whereas the other is placed in direct sunlight.

State and explain the observations in each test tube.

[3]

iii) Construct an equation for the overall reaction that occurs in the sunlight.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The mechanism is:
> 
> - Free-radical substitution **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The observations in each test tube are:
> 
> In the dark:
> 
> - No change / the mixture remains pale green **[1 mark]**
> 
> In sunlight:
> 
> - The pale green colour disappears / the mixture becomes colourless
> **OR**
> Misty / steamy fumes of hydrogen chloride (HCl) are produced **[1 mark]**
> 
> Explanation:
> 
> - UV light is required to initiate the reaction / to cause homolytic fission of the Cl–Cl bond **[1 mark]**
> 
> iii) The equation for the overall reaction in sunlight is:
> 
> - CH<sub>4</sub> + Cl<sub>2</sub> → CH<sub>3</sub>Cl + HCl **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Free-radical substitution is a three-stage chain reaction: initiation, propagation, and termination. Only the initiation step requires UV light.
> 
> The pale green colour of the reaction mixture is due to chlorine gas. When UV light causes homolytic fission of the Cl–Cl bond, the reaction proceeds and the chlorine is consumed, so the pale green colour disappears.
> 
> Misty or steamy fumes in the test tube placed in sunlight are hydrogen chloride (HCl) gas produced during the reaction.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Methane reacts with chlorine gas under suitable conditions to form chloromethane.

The mechanism for this reaction involves an initiation step.

i) Name the type of bond breaking that occurs in the initiation step. Explain what happens to the electrons in the bond.

[2]

ii) Explain what is meant by the term *free radical*.

[1]

iii) Suggest why the Cl–Cl bond is broken in the initiation step rather than the C–H bond.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The type of bond breaking is:
> 
> - Homolytic fission **[1 mark]**
> - Each atom in the covalent bond receives one electron when the bond breaks **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) A free radical is:
> 
> - A species with an unpaired electron **[1 mark]**
> 
> iii) The Cl–Cl bond is broken in preference to the C–H bond because:
> 
> - The C–H bond requires more energy to break than is available from UV light
> **OR**
> UV light does not provide enough energy to break the C–H bond **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Bonds can break in two ways.
> 
> 1. In homolytic fission, the covalent bond splits equally and each atom receives one electron, forming two free radicals.
> 2. In heterolytic fission, the bond splits unequally and one atom receives both electrons, forming a positive ion and a negative ion.
> 
> Free radicals are highly reactive because of their unpaired electron. They can also be called radicals, without the word "free".
> 
> The bond enthalpy of C–H is higher than that of Cl–Cl, so UV light provides sufficient energy to break the Cl–Cl bond but not the C–H bond.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Methane reacts with chlorine gas under suitable conditions to form chloromethane.

i) Name the mechanism that occurs in this reaction.

The mechanism is:
- Free-radical substitution

The mechanism also involves propagation and termination steps.

i) Construct two equations to show the propagation steps in this mechanism.

[2]

ii) Construct an equation to show one possible termination step.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
i) The two propagation steps are:

CH<sub>4</sub> + Cl<sup>•</sup> → CH<sub>3</sub><sup>•</sup> + HCl

CH<sub>3</sub><sup>•</sup> + Cl<sub>2</sub> → CH<sub>3</sub>Cl + Cl<sup>•</sup>

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for each correct propagation equation (in any order)

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii) One possible termination step is:
> 
> - CH<sub>3</sub><sup>•</sup> + CH<sub>3</sub><sup>•</sup> → C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub>
> **OR**
> Cl<sup>•</sup> + Cl<sup>•</sup> → Cl<sub>2</sub>
> **OR**
> Cl<sup>•</sup> + CH<sub>3</sub><sup>•</sup> → CH<sub>3</sub>Cl **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> In each propagation step, one free radical is consumed and another is produced. This keeps the chain reaction going. The two propagation steps must be given in the correct stoichiometric form.
> 
> In termination steps, two free radicals combine to form a stable, non-radical molecule. Any one of the three possible termination steps is acceptable unless the question specifies otherwise.

parts.problemMd:
1,2-dibromoethane reacts with bromine in the presence of ultraviolet light to produce a mixture of further substituted halogenoalkanes.

i) Construct an equation for the initiation step of this reaction.

[1]

ii) Explain why the bond breaking in the initiation step is described as homolytic fission.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The initiation step is:
> 
> - Br<sub>2</sub> → 2Br<sup>•</sup> **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The bond breaking is described as homolytic fission because:
> 
> - Each bromine atom receives one electron from the Br–Br covalent bond / shared pair of electrons **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> In homolytic fission, the bond breaks symmetrically: each atom takes one electron from the shared pair. This produces two radicals (species with unpaired electrons) rather than ions.
> 
> This is different from heterolytic fission, where both electrons go to one atom, forming a positive ion and a negative ion.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

1,2-dibromoethane reacts with bromine in the presence of ultraviolet light to produce a mixture of further substituted halogenoalkanes.

Construct two equations to show the propagation steps in this mechanism that produce 1,1,2-tribromoethane.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The two propagation steps are:
> 
> - CH<sub>2</sub>BrCH<sub>2</sub>Br + Br<sup>•</sup> → CH<sub>2</sub>BrCHBr<sup>•</sup> + HBr **[1 mark]**
> - CH<sub>2</sub>BrCHBr<sup>•</sup> + Br<sub>2</sub> → CH<sub>2</sub>BrCHBr<sub>2</sub> + Br<sup>•</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> In each propagation step, a free radical reacts with a molecule to produce a new free radical. The bromine radical consumed in step 1 is regenerated in step 2, allowing the chain to continue.
> 
> In step 1, the bromine radical removes a hydrogen atom from 1,2-dibromoethane to form HBr, leaving a carbon radical on C-2. In step 2, this carbon radical reacts with Br<sub>2</sub> to form 1,1,2-tribromoethane and regenerate a Br<sup>•</sup>.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

1,2-dibromoethane reacts with bromine in the presence of ultraviolet light to produce a mixture of further substituted halogenoalkanes.

The two propagation steps are:
- CH₂BrCH₂Br + Br• → CH₂BrCHBr• + HBr
- CH₂BrCHBr• + Br₂ → CH₂BrCHBr₂ + Br•

Traces of 1,2,3,4-tetrabromobutane are found in the reaction mixture.

i) Construct an equation for the termination step that forms 1,2,3,4-tetrabromobutane.

[1]

ii) Construct an equation to show the overall reaction for the formation of hexabromoethane from 1,1,2-tribromoethane.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The termination step that forms 1,2,3,4-tetrabromobutane is:
> 
> - CH<sub>2</sub>BrCHBr<sup>•</sup> + CH<sub>2</sub>BrCHBr<sup>•</sup> → CH<sub>2</sub>BrCHBrCHBrCH<sub>2</sub>Br **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The overall equation for the formation of hexabromoethane is:
> 
> - CHBr<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Br + 3Br<sub>2</sub> → CBr<sub>3</sub>CBr<sub>3</sub> + 3HBr **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> 1,2,3,4-Tetrabromobutane forms when two CH<sub>2</sub>BrCHBr<sup>•</sup> radicals combine in a termination step. Two free radicals combine to form one molecule with no unpaired electrons, ending the chain reaction.
> 
> For the overall equation, count the hydrogen atoms on 1,1,2-tribromoethane (3 H atoms). Each H removed requires one Br<sub>2</sub>, so 3Br<sub>2</sub> are needed and 3HBr are produced.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

1,2-dibromoethane reacts with bromine in the presence of ultraviolet light to produce a mixture of further substituted halogenoalkanes.

Suggest two reasons why free-radical substitution is not a good method for producing a single, pure halogenoalkane.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Free-radical substitution is not a good method for producing a single, pure halogenoalkane because:
> 
> Any **two** from (1 mark for each point):
> 
> - Further substitution can occur, producing a mixture of mono-, di-, and tri-substituted products
> - The halogen can be substituted at different positions in the carbon chain, forming structural isomers
> - Termination steps produce unexpected by-products (e.g. longer-chain hydrocarbons)
> - The reaction is difficult to control
> 
> **[2 marks]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The main limitations are:
> 
> - Further substitution (once one H is replaced, the product can react again)
> - Positional isomers (for chains with more than one type of H atom, different structural isomers form)
> - Unexpected by-products from termination steps.
> 
> These limitations mean free-radical substitution produces a mixture of products rather than a single pure compound.

parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> A major and a minor product are produced because:
> 
> - The intermediate can be a primary or secondary carbocation **[1 mark]**
> - The secondary carbocation is more stable than the primary carbocation **[1 mark]**
> - The major product is formed from the more stable secondary carbocation **[1 mark]**
> 
> The reverse argument (primary carbocation is less stable → forms the minor product) is also accepted.

parts.problemMd:
A sample of pent-1-ene, with a mass of 1.33 g, is warmed to 60°C in a sealed container. The volume of the container is 500 cm<sup>3</sup>.

Calculate the pressure inside the container.

Include units and give your answer to an appropriate number of significant figures. [molar gas constant (*R*) = 8.31 J mol<sup>−1</sup> K<sup>−1</sup>]
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the pressure inside the container:

- Calculate the moles of pent-1-ene:

moles = $\frac{1.33}{70.0}$

moles = 0.0190 mol

**[1 mark]**

- Convert the volume and temperature to SI units:

volume = 500 x 10<sup>-6</sup> m<sup>3</sup>

temperature = 60 + 273 = 333 K

**[1 mark]**

- Rearrange the ideal gas equation and substitute:

*p* = $\frac{nRT}{V}$

*p* = $\frac{0.0190\times8.31\times333}{500\times10^{-6}}$

*p* = 105 154 Pa

**[1 mark]**

- Round to an appropriate number of significant figures and state units:

*p* = **105 000 Pa**

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for moles of pent-1-ene = 0.019 mol (M<sub>r</sub> of C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub> = 70.0)
> 
> 1 mark for volume = 500 x 10<sup>-6</sup> m<sup>3</sup> **AND** temperature = 333 K (both required)
> 
> 1 mark for correct substitution into *pV* = *nRT*
> 
> 1 mark for final answer to 2 or 3 sf with correct units
> 
> Allow 1.05 x 10<sup>5</sup> Pa or 1.1 x 10<sup>5</sup> Pa. Allow N m<sup>-2</sup> in place of Pa or answer expressed in kPa (105 kPa).

> **[exam-tip]**
> The molar mass of pent-1-ene (C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub>) = (5 x 12.0) + (10 x 1.0) = 70.0 g mol<sup>-1</sup>.
> 
> The ideal gas equation *pV* = *nRT* requires SI units throughout: pressure in Pa, volume in m<sup>3</sup>, temperature in K, and amount in mol. Divide the volume in cm<sup>3</sup> by 10<sup>6</sup> to convert to m<sup>3</sup>, and add 273 to convert °C to K.
> 
> A correct final answer with units and no working shown still scores 4 marks, but showing your working allows error-carried-forward credit if an earlier step is wrong.

parts.solutionMd:

> Propane is relatively unreactive because:
> 
> - C–C and C–H bonds are strong / have high bond enthalpies **[1 mark]**
> - Propane is non-polar / there is very little difference in electronegativity between C and H **[1 mark]**

The very small difference in electronegativity between carbon and hydrogen means there are no partial charges, so propane does not react with polar reagents such as acids, bases, or nucleophiles.
