parts.problemMd:
This question is about carboxylic acids.

State the general formula of a carboxylic acid
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The general formula of a carboxylic acid is:
> 
> - C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n+1</sub>COOH **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The general formula can be understood by thinking about the carbon chain:
> 
> ![Hand-drawn structural formula of a carboxylic acid with a carbon chain and labelled hydrogens, showing an attached COOH group and notes “Above” and “Below”](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/18-carboxylic-acids-and-derivatives/18-1-carboxylic-acids/assets/016-hand-drawn-structural-formula-of-a-carboxylic-ac.png)
> 
> - For every carbon in the hydrocarbon chain, there is a hydrogen above and a hydrogen below, giving 2n hydrogens for n carbons
> - There is also one extra hydrogen at the end of the chain, giving 2n + 1 hydrogens in total
> - This gives the C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n+1</sub> portion of the formula, with the carboxylic acid group (–COOH) added at the end

parts.problemMd:
State the systematic name of the carboxylic acid shown in Fig. 1.1.

![Displayed formula of a carboxylic acid, CH3CH(CH3)CH2COOH](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/18-carboxylic-acids-and-derivatives/18-1-carboxylic-acids/assets/017-displayed-formula-of-a-carboxylic-acid-ch3ch-ch3.png)

**Fig. 1.1**
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The systematic name of the carboxylic acid in Fig. 1.1 is:
> 
> - 3-methylbutanoic acid **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> To name a carboxylic acid systematically:
> 
> - Identify the longest carbon chain that includes the –COOH group — four carbons gives the stem "butan-"
> - The –COOH carbon is always carbon-1, so it does not need to be numbered in the name
> - Identify any substituents: there is a methyl group attached to carbon-3
> - Combine to give: 3-methylbutanoic acid

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

State the systematic name of the carboxylic acid shown in Fig. 1.1.

Displayed formula of a carboxylic acid, CH3CH(CH3)CH2COOH

Fig. 1.1

The systematic name of the carboxylic acid in Fig. 1.1 is:

- 3-methylbutanoic acid

i) Construct a balanced symbol equation to show the dissociation of the acid from part (b).

[1]

ii) State where the position of the equilibrium lies and what this says about the strength of the acid.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The balanced equation for the dissociation of 3-methylbutanoic acid is:
> 
> - CH<sub>3</sub>CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)CH<sub>2</sub>COOH ⇋ CH<sub>3</sub>CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)CH<sub>2</sub>COO<sup>-</sup> + H<sup>+</sup>
> **OR**
> C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>9</sub>COOH ⇋ C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>9</sub>COO<sup>-</sup> + H<sup>+</sup> **[1 mark]**
> 
> The equation must have a reversible arrow
> 
> ii) The position of the equilibrium and what this indicates:
> 
> - To the left **[1 mark]**
> - (This indicates it is a) weak acid **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Carboxylic acids are weak acids because they only partially dissociate in aqueous solution. The equilibrium lies to the left, meaning most molecules remain in the undissociated acid form.
> 
> Compare this with strong acids such as HCl, which fully dissociate and their equilibria lie completely to the right.
> 
> Always use the equilibrium symbol (⇋) rather than a forward arrow (→) when showing the dissociation of a weak acid, to reflect the reversible nature of the reaction.

parts.problemMd: Construct a balanced symbol equation, including state symbols, for the reaction of propanoic acid with sodium hydrogen carbonate powder.
parts.solutionMd:
The balanced symbol equation for the reaction of propanoic acid with sodium hydrogen carbonate is:

CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COOH (aq) + NaHCO<sub>3</sub> (s) → CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COONa (aq) + H<sub>2</sub>O (l) + CO<sub>2</sub> (g)

**OR**

C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>COOH (aq) + NaHCO<sub>3</sub> (s) → C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>COONa (aq) + H<sub>2</sub>O (l) + CO<sub>2</sub> (g)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for a correct balanced equation with correct formulae for all species
> 
> Allow CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COOH or C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>COOH for propanoic acid
> 
> 1 mark for correct state symbols: (aq) for propanoic acid and sodium propanoate, (s) for sodium hydrogen carbonate, (l) for water, and (g) for carbon dioxide

> **[exam-tip]**
> The reaction of a carboxylic acid with a hydrogen carbonate follows the pattern:
> 
> acid + hydrogen carbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide
> 
> The salt formed is sodium propanoate (CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COONa), which is soluble and has the state symbol (aq). The sodium hydrogen carbonate is a solid powder (s), the water produced is a liquid (l), and the carbon dioxide produced is a gas (g).

parts.problemMd:
A series of reactions based on propanoic acid is shown.

![Flow chart of a series of reactions based on propanoic acid, showing reactions 1, 2, and 3 as arrows between structures](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/18-carboxylic-acids-and-derivatives/18-1-carboxylic-acids/assets/018-flow-chart-of-a-series-of-reactions-based-on-pro.png)

Construct an equation for reaction **1**, using [H] to represent one atom of hydrogen from the reducing agent.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> An equation for reaction 1, using [H] to represent one atom of hydrogen from the reducing agent:
> 
> - CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>H + 4[H] → CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH + H<sub>2</sub>O **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Reaction 1 shows the reduction of propanoic acid to propan-1-ol. The [H] notation represents one atom of hydrogen from the reducing agent, so four [H] atoms are needed overall.
> 
> The reduction of a carboxylic acid follows the pattern:
> 
> R–COOH + 4[H] → R–CH<sub>2</sub>OH + H<sub>2</sub>O

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A series of reactions based on propanoic acid is shown.

![Flow chart of a series of reactions based on propanoic acid, showing reactions 1, 2, and 3 as arrows between structures](https://cdn.savemyexams.com/uploads/2023/04/3-6-1a-m-3-6-reaction-of-carboxylic-acid-flow-chart.png)

i) Name the type of reaction for reaction **2**.

[1]

ii) State a suitable reagent and conditions for reaction **2**.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The type of reaction for reaction 2 is:
> 
> - Oxidation **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) A suitable reagent and conditions for reaction 2:
> 
> - Acidified potassium dichromate(VI) / acidified potassium manganate(VII) **[1 mark]**
> - Reflux **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Reaction 2 converts propan-1-ol to propanoic acid. Since the organic product gains oxygen compared to the reactant, this is oxidation.
> 
> The two standard oxidising agents for oxidising primary alcohols to carboxylic acids are:
> 
> - Acidified potassium dichromate(VI) (K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub>): orange solution turns green as Cr(VI) is reduced to Cr(III)
> - Acidified potassium manganate(VII) (KMnO<sub>4</sub>): purple solution turns colourless as Mn(VII) is reduced
> 
> Reflux conditions are required to ensure complete oxidation to the carboxylic acid and to prevent any aldehyde intermediate from escaping as vapour.

parts.problemMd: Construct an equation for the reaction of propanoic acid with calcium carbonate, CaCO<sub>3</sub>.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> An equation for the reaction of propanoic acid with calcium carbonate:
> 
> - 2CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>H + CaCO<sub>3</sub> → (CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>)<sub>2</sub>Ca + H<sub>2</sub>O + CO<sub>2</sub> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Propanoic acid reacts with calcium carbonate in the same way as any acid reacts with a metal carbonate:
> 
> acid + metal carbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide
> 
> The salt formed is calcium propanoate, (CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>)<sub>2</sub>Ca. Two molecules of propanoic acid are needed to react with one molecule of CaCO<sub>3</sub> because calcium forms a 2+ ion, so two propanoate anions are required to balance the charge.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A series of reactions based on propanoic acid is shown.

![Flow chart of a series of reactions based on propanoic acid, showing reactions 1, 2, and 3 as arrows between structures](https://cdn.savemyexams.com/uploads/2023/04/3-6-1a-m-3-6-reaction-of-carboxylic-acid-flow-chart.png)

i) State a suitable reagent and conditions for reaction **3**.

[2]

ii) Identify the other product of reaction **3**.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) A suitable reagent and conditions for reaction 3:
> 
> - CH<sub>3</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>H / ethanoic acid **[1 mark]**
> - Warm / heat / reflux
> **AND**
> Concentrated sulfuric acid **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The other product of reaction 3:
> 
> - Water **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Reaction 3 shows propan-1-ol reacting with ethanoic acid to form propyl ethanoate, which is an esterification reaction.
> 
> The name of the ester tells you the reagents: the first part of the name (propyl) comes from the alcohol (propan-1-ol), and the second part (ethanoate) comes from the carboxylic acid (ethanoic acid, CH<sub>3</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>H).
> 
> Esterification is a condensation reaction, where the two reactants join together and a small molecule (water) is eliminated. Concentrated sulfuric acid acts as a catalyst, and heating is required to achieve a reasonable rate of reaction.

parts.problemMd:
2-ethyl-3-methylbutanoic acid is present in fermented products such as rum.

i) Deduce the molecular formula of 2-ethyl-3-methylbutanoic acid.

[1]

ii) State the number of chiral carbon atoms in a molecule of 2-ethyl-3-methylbutanoic acid.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The molecular formula of 2-ethyl-3-methylbutanoic acid is:
> 
> - C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>14</sub>O<sub>2</sub> **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The number of chiral carbon atoms:
> 
> - 1 / one **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> To deduce the molecular formula, count the atoms in the structural formula:
> 
> ![Structure of 2-ethyl-3-methylbutanoic acid](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/18-carboxylic-acids-and-derivatives/18-1-carboxylic-acids/assets/019-structure-of-2-ethyl-3-methylbutanoic-acid.png)
> 
> - Count carbons:
> 
>   - Main chain (4) + ethyl substituent (2) + methyl substituent (1) = 7 carbons
> - Saturated monocarboxylic acids follow C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n</sub>O<sub>2</sub>
> 
>   - For n = 7 this gives C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>14</sub>O<sub>2</sub>
> 
> To identify chiral carbons, use the displayed formula shown above and look for carbons bonded to four different groups:
> 
> - Carbon-2 is bonded to H, the ethyl group (–C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>), the carboxylic acid group (–CO<sub>2</sub>H), and the C3–C4 chain (–CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)CH<sub>3</sub>)
> 
>   - All four are different, so carbon-2 is chiral
> - Carbon-3 is bonded to H, the methyl substituent (–CH<sub>3</sub>), the terminal methyl (C4, also –CH<sub>3</sub>), and the C2 chain
> 
>   - It has two identical methyl groups, so it is not chiral

parts.problemMd:
A sample of 2-ethyl-3-methylbutanoic acid may be prepared in a school or college laboratory by the oxidation of:

**2-ethyl-3-methylbutan-1-ol** (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CHCH(C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>)CH<sub>2</sub>OH

i) State the reagent(s) that would be used for this oxidation.

reagent(s) .................................................................................................

colour change from .............................. to ..............................

[2]

ii) This reaction is carried out by heating the reacting chemicals together. What could be the main organic impurity present in the sample of the acid? Explain your answer.

[2]

iii) State whether a distillation apparatus or a reflux apparatus should be used.

Explain your answer.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The reagent and colour change for this oxidation:
> 
> - Acidified potassium dichromate(VI) / acidified K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub>
> **OR**
> Acidified potassium manganate(VII) / acidified KMnO<sub>4</sub> **[1 mark]**
> - Orange to green (for K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub>)
> **OR**
> Purple to colourless (for KMnO<sub>4</sub>) **[1 mark]**
> 
> The colour change must match the reagent chosen.
> 
> ii) The main organic impurity and reason:
> 
> - 2-ethyl-3-methylbutanal / (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CHCH(C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>)CHO **[1 mark]**
> - (Because) partial oxidation of the primary alcohol produces an aldehyde / the primary alcohol is not fully oxidised **[1 mark]**
> 
> iii) The apparatus and reason:
> 
> - Reflux **[1 mark]**
> - To ensure complete oxidation of the primary alcohol to the carboxylic acid / to prevent the intermediate aldehyde from escaping as vapour **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The two common oxidising agents both change colour as they are reduced:
> 
> - Acidified potassium dichromate(VI): orange turns green (Cr(VI) reduced to Cr(III))
> - Acidified potassium manganate(VII): purple turns colourless (Mn(VII) reduced to Mn(II))
> 
> Distillation is used when you want to collect the product as it forms and prevent further oxidation. For example, when stopping at the aldehyde stage. Reflux keeps the mixture in the flask to ensure complete oxidation all the way to the carboxylic acid.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

i) State the reagent(s) that would be used for this oxidation.

reagent(s) .................................................................................................

colour change from .............................. to ..............................

A structural isomer of 2-ethyl-3-methylbutan-1-ol is 2-ethyl-3-methylbutan-2-ol, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CHC(OH)(C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>)CH<sub>3</sub>.

What colour change would be seen if this were heated with the reagents you have given in part **(b)(i)**?

Explain your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The colour change observed when 2-ethyl-3-methylbutan-2-ol is heated with the oxidising agent from part (b)(i):
> 
> - No colour change **[1 mark]**
> - (Because) 2-ethyl-3-methylbutan-2-ol is a tertiary alcohol / the –OH group is bonded to a carbon bearing three alkyl groups **[1 mark]**
> 
> Tertiary alcohols cannot be oxidised by acidified dichromate(VI) or manganate(VII).

> **[exam-tip]**
> Classify the alcohol before predicting the outcome of oxidation:
> 
> - Primary alcohols (–OH on a carbon bonded to one alkyl group) can be oxidised to aldehydes, then to carboxylic acids
> - Secondary alcohols (–OH on a carbon bonded to two alkyl groups) can be oxidised to ketones only
> - Tertiary alcohols (–OH on a carbon bonded to three alkyl groups) cannot be oxidised
> 
> 2-ethyl-3-methylbutan-2-ol has the –OH group on a carbon bonded to three alkyl groups, making it a tertiary alcohol. No oxidation occurs and no colour change is observed.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

2-ethyl-3-methylbutanoic acid is present in fermented products such as rum.

The molecular formula of 2-ethyl-3-methylbutanoic acid is: C7H14O2

An isomer of 2-ethyl-3-methylbutanoic acid which is an ethyl ester is a very strong smelling compound which is found in some wines. This ethyl ester contains a branched hydrocarbon chain and is chiral.

Draw the displayed formula of this ethyl ester.

Identify the chiral carbon atom with an asterisk (*).
parts.solutionMd:
The displayed formula of the ethyl ester with the chiral carbon atom marked is:

![Displayed formula of the ethyl ester of 3-methylbutanoic acid with the chiral carbon atom identified using an asterisk](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/18-carboxylic-acids-and-derivatives/18-1-carboxylic-acids/assets/020-displayed-formula-of-the-ethyl-ester-of-3-methyl.png)

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for a correct displayed formula of the ethyl ester
> 
> 1 mark for all bonds between atoms shown explicitly in the displayed formula
> 
> 1 mark for the correct chiral carbon atom identified with an asterisk (*)
> 
> If the overall structure is incorrect, 1 mark may still be awarded for correctly identifying a chiral carbon in the drawn structure.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The compound is an ethyl ester and an isomer of 2-ethyl-3-methylbutanoic acid (C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>14</sub>O<sub>2</sub>). Replacing the –OH of the carboxylic acid with –OC<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub> gives the ester group; the remaining acid fragment must be rearranged to give a branched chain with a chiral centre.
> 
> In a displayed formula, all bonds including C–H bonds must be drawn explicitly as this distinguishes it from a structural formula where C–H bonds are implied.

parts.problemMd:
Propan-1-ol can be oxidised to propanoic acid using acidified potassium dichromate(VI).

State the systematic name of the intermediate formed during this oxidation.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The systematic name of the intermediate is:
> 
> - Propanal **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> When a primary alcohol is oxidised, the reaction proceeds in two stages:
> 
> 1. Partial oxidation: primary alcohol → aldehyde (using distillation conditions to remove the aldehyde as it forms)
> 2. Full oxidation: primary alcohol → carboxylic acid (using excess oxidising agent under reflux)
> 
> Propan-1-ol oxidises to propanal as the intermediate, which then further oxidises to propanoic acid.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Propan-1-ol can be oxidised to propanoic acid using acidified potassium dichromate(VI).

i) State the final colour of the reaction mixture after the potassium dichromate(VI) has reacted.

[1]

ii) State the conditions to ensure that propanoic acid is obtained in a high yield.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The final colour of the reaction mixture after the potassium dichromate(VI) has reacted:
> 
> - Green **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The conditions to obtain propanoic acid in a high yield:
> 
> - Excess acidified potassium dichromate(VI) **[1 mark]**
> - Reflux **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> When propan-1-ol is fully oxidised to propanoic acid:
> 
> - The potassium dichromate(VI) is reduced: the orange Cr(VI) solution turns green as it is converted to Cr(III)
> - Excess oxidising agent is needed to ensure all the aldehyde intermediate (propanal) is further oxidised to propanoic acid
> - Reflux prevents the volatile propanal from escaping as vapour and keeps it in contact with the oxidising agent until fully converted

parts.problemMd: Describe a chemical test and observation which confirms the presence of a carboxyl functional group.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> A chemical test and observation to confirm the presence of a carboxyl group:
> 
> - Add sodium carbonate (Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>) / potassium carbonate (K<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>)
> **OR**
> Add sodium hydrogen carbonate (NaHCO<sub>3</sub>) / potassium hydrogen carbonate (KHCO<sub>3</sub>) **[1 mark]**
> - Effervescence / fizzing / bubbling observed **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Carboxylic acids react with carbonates and hydrogen carbonates to produce carbon dioxide gas, which is observed as effervescence. This is a classic test for the carboxyl (–COOH) functional group.
> 
> Note that phenols do not react with sodium hydrogen carbonate, so NaHCO<sub>3</sub> in particular is useful for distinguishing carboxylic acids from other weakly acidic compounds.

parts.problemMd:
LiAlH<sub>4</sub> is a reducing agent.

LiAlH<sub>4</sub> cannot be used in aqueous solution because it reacts with water to produce LiOH(aq), H<sub>2</sub> (g) and a white precipitate which is soluble in excess sodium hydroxide. Identify the white precipitate.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The white precipitate is:
> 
> - Aluminium hydroxide / Al(OH)<sub>3</sub> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> LiAlH<sub>4</sub> contains both lithium and aluminium. When it reacts with water:
> 
> - Lithium forms LiOH (given in the question)
> - Aluminium forms Al(OH)<sub>3</sub>, a white precipitate
> 
> Al(OH)<sub>3</sub> is amphoteric and it dissolves in excess NaOH to form the aluminate ion [Al(OH)<sub>4</sub>]<sup>-</sup>. This behaviour is a useful identifier: if a white precipitate dissolves in excess sodium hydroxide solution, aluminium ions are present.

parts.problemMd:
Butane-1,2-diol is oxidised to form compound **P** in reaction 1. Compound **P** is then reduced using LiAlH<sub>4</sub> in reaction 2 to give **Q**, and using NaBH<sub>4</sub> in reaction 3 to give **R**, as shown in Fig. 1.1.

![Reaction pathway diagram showing butane-1,2-diol oxidised to compound P, then P reduced by LiAlH4 to give Q and by NaBH4 to give R](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/18-carboxylic-acids-and-derivatives/18-1-carboxylic-acids/assets/011-reaction-pathway-diagram-showing-butane-1-2-diol.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

i) State the reagents and conditions required for reaction 1.

[2]

ii) Deduce whether **Q** or **R** is 2-hydroxybutanoic acid and explain the difference between reactions 2 and 3.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The reagents and conditions for reaction 1:
> 
> - Potassium dichromate(VI) (K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub>) / potassium manganate(VII) (KMnO<sub>4</sub>) **[1 mark]**
> - Acidified (with dilute sulfuric acid)
> **AND**
> Heat under reflux **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) Which compound is 2-hydroxybutanoic acid and the difference between reactions 2 and 3:
> 
> - **R** is 2-hydroxybutanoic acid **[1 mark]**
> - NaBH<sub>4</sub> reduces only carbonyl (C=O) groups and cannot reduce carboxyl (–COOH) groups; LiAlH<sub>4</sub> reduces both **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Compound P contains both a ketone (C=O) and a carboxylic acid (–COOH) group, formed by oxidising both alcohol groups in butane-1,2-diol.
> 
> NaBH<sub>4</sub> is a mild reducing agent that selectively reduces aldehydes and ketones but cannot reduce the more stable carboxylic acid group. This gives R, which retains the –COOH group and is therefore 2-hydroxybutanoic acid.
> 
> LiAlH<sub>4</sub> is a stronger reducing agent that reduces both C=O and –COOH groups, converting the carboxylic acid to a primary alcohol. Q therefore has two alcohol groups rather than the required carboxylic acid.

parts.problemMd:
A third student prepares 2-hydroxybutanoic acid using propanal as the starting material as shown in Fig. 1.2. In step 1, propanal reacts with a mixture of NaCN and HCN.

![Reaction pathway diagram showing propanal reacting with NaCN and HCN to form S in step 1, then S reacting with HCl under reflux in step 2 to give 2-hydroxybutanoic acid](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/18-carboxylic-acids-and-derivatives/18-1-carboxylic-acids/assets/012-reaction-pathway-diagram-showing-propanal-reacti.png)

**Fig. 1.2**

Draw the mechanism for the reaction of propanal with the mixture of NaCN and HCN to form **S**.

In your mechanism, include:

- the identity of the ion that reacts with propanal
- the structure of the intermediate
- all charges, partial charges, lone pairs and curly arrows
parts.solutionMd:
The mechanism for the reaction of propanal with HCN / NaCN to form S is:

![Nucleophilic addition mechanism showing CN- attacking the carbonyl carbon of propanal, with curly arrows and the tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/18-carboxylic-acids-and-derivatives/18-1-carboxylic-acids/assets/013-nucleophilic-addition-mechanism-showing-cn-attac.png)

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for :CN<sup>-</sup> identified as the ion that reacts with propanal
> 
> 1 mark for a curly arrow from the lone pair on :CN<sup>-</sup> to the carbonyl carbon
> 
> 1 mark for correct partial charges (δ+ on carbonyl carbon, δ− on oxygen) AND a curly arrow from the C=O bond to the oxygen
> 
> 1 mark for a correct tetrahedral intermediate drawn

> **[exam-tip]**
> This is a nucleophilic addition mechanism. The cyanide ion (:CN<sup>-</sup>) is the nucleophile as it carries a lone pair on the carbon atom and attacks the δ+ carbonyl carbon.
> 
> In the NaCN / HCN mixture, NaCN provides the CN<sup>-</sup> ions and HCN provides the proton that converts the alkoxide intermediate to the hydroxyl group in product S.
> 
> When drawing the mechanism:
> 
> - The curly arrow from :CN<sup>-</sup> must originate from the lone pair on the cyanide carbon (not from the nitrogen end)
> - The curly arrow from C=O must come from the double bond, pushing electrons onto the oxygen to form O<sup>-</sup>
> - The intermediate must show a tetrahedral carbon with an O<sup>-</sup> charge

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A third student prepares 2-hydroxybutanoic acid using propanal as the starting material as shown in Fig. 1.2. In step 1, propanal reacts with a mixture of NaCN and HCN.

Fig. 1.2

In step 1, propanal reacts with NaCN and HCN to form S. In step 2, S reacts with HCl under reflux to give 2-hydroxybutanoic acid.

Construct a balanced equation for step 2, in which **S** is heated under reflux with dilute hydrochloric acid.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> A balanced equation for the acid hydrolysis of S in step 2:
> 
> - C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CH(OH)CN + HCl + 2H<sub>2</sub>O → C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CH(OH)COOH + NH<sub>4</sub>Cl **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The nitrile group (–C≡N) is hydrolysed to a carboxylic acid (–COOH) by heating under reflux with dilute acid. Both HCl and water are required as reactants, but the question may not make this obvious.
> 
> The same hydrolysis can also be carried out using an alkali, but this produces a carboxylate salt and ammonia rather than the free carboxylic acid and ammonium chloride.

parts.problemMd:
Lactic acid, 2-hydroxypropanoic acid, CH<sub>3</sub>CH(OH)COOH, occurs naturally in sour milk.

Lactic acid is chiral and shows stereoisomerism.

Draw the three-dimensional structures of the two optical isomers of lactic acid.

Use an asterisk (*) to identify the chiral carbon atom in one of the structures.
parts.solutionMd:
The three-dimensional structures of the two optical isomers of lactic acid are:

![Three-dimensional structures of the two optical isomers of lactic acid shown with wedge-and-dash bonds, with the chiral carbon atom marked with an asterisk](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/18-carboxylic-acids-and-derivatives/18-1-carboxylic-acids/assets/014-three-dimensional-structures-of-the-two-optical-.png)

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 marks for one correct three-dimensional structures with wedge-and-dash bonds shown
> 
> 1 mark for the non-superimposable mirror image
> 
> Allow 1 mark if the structures are drawn as displayed formulae without 3D representation but are otherwise correct
> 
> 1 mark for the chiral carbon atom correctly identified with an asterisk (*) in one of the structures

> **[exam-tip]**
> Optical isomers are non-superimposable mirror images of each other. To draw them correctly for lactic acid:
> 
> - Draw all bonds to the chiral carbon (the one bearing four different groups: H, OH, CH<sub>3</sub>, and COOH)
> - Use wedge bonds (solid triangle) for bonds coming towards you and dashed bonds for bonds going away
> - The second isomer is the mirror image of the first, with the arrangement of groups reversed
> 
> Note that the carbon atom in the COOH group is not chiral as it is bonded to only three different groups (=O, –OH, and the carbon chain), not four.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Step 1:
> 
> - Acidified potassium dichromate(VI) / acidified potassium manganate(VII) **[1 mark]**
> - Distillation **[1 mark]**
> 
> Step 2:
> 
> - HCN / mixture of HCN and NaCN
> **OR**
> KCN with dilute acid **[1 mark]**
> - Room temperature **[1 mark]**
> 
> Step 3:
> 
> - Dilute acid (e.g. HCl / H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>)
> **OR**
> Dilute alkali / NaOH **[1 mark]**
> - Heat under reflux **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The reaction pathway converts ethanol to lactic acid through three steps:
> 
> - Step 1: Ethanol (primary alcohol) → ethanal (aldehyde) by partial oxidation
> - Step 2: Ethanal → 2-hydroxypropanenitrile (hydroxynitrile) by nucleophilic addition of HCN
> - Step 3: 2-hydroxypropanenitrile → 2-hydroxypropanoic acid by hydrolysis of the nitrile group
> 
> In step 1, distillation is essential to remove ethanal as it forms and prevent further oxidation to ethanoic acid.
> 
> In step 3, acid hydrolysis gives the free carboxylic acid; alkali hydrolysis gives a carboxylate salt and ammonia. Both are accepted.

parts.problemMd:
Lactic acid, CH<sub>3</sub>CH(OH)COOH can be reduced by LiAlH<sub>4</sub>.

i) Construct an equation to show this reaction, using [H] to represent one atom of hydrogen from the reducing agent.

[1]

ii) State the systematic name of the organic product formed in this reaction.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) An equation for the reduction of lactic acid by LiAlH<sub>4</sub>:
> 
> - CH<sub>3</sub>CH(OH)COOH + 4[H] → CH<sub>3</sub>CH(OH)CH<sub>2</sub>OH + H<sub>2</sub>O **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The systematic name of the organic product:
> 
> - Propane-1,2-diol **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> LiAlH<sub>4</sub> reduces the carboxylic acid group (–COOH) to a primary alcohol (–CH<sub>2</sub>OH). Four [H] atoms are needed overall: two to add across the C=O, one to protonate the O<sup>-</sup> to give –OH, and one is lost as part of the water molecule produced.
> 
> The product (propane-1,2-diol) has two alcohol groups:
> 
> ![Displayed formula of propane-1,2-diol showing two hydroxyl groups attached to carbons 1 and 2 of a three-carbon chain](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/18-carboxylic-acids-and-derivatives/18-1-carboxylic-acids/assets/015-displayed-formula-of-propane-1-2-diol-showing-tw.png)
> 
> - The secondary alcohol on carbon-2 was already present in the lactic acid molecule
> - The primary alcohol on carbon-1 is newly formed from reduction of the –COOH group

parts.problemMd:
Glycolic acid is commonly used in skin care products.

The structure is shown in Fig. 3.1.

![Structural formula of glyolic acid, showing two carbon atoms with attached hydrogen, hydroxyl and carboxyl groups in a simple line diagram](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/18-carboxylic-acids-and-derivatives/18-1-carboxylic-acids/assets/021-structural-formula-of-glyolic-acid-showing-two-c.png)

**Fig. 3.1**

Glycolic acid is added separately to each of the three reagents below.

Complete the table to show what you would observe. If a reaction occurs, state the functional group of glycolic acid responsible for the reaction.

| reagent | observation with glycolic acid | functional group |
|---|---|---|
| Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> |   |   |
| 2,4-DNPH |   |   |
| acidified K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> (aq) and heat |   |   |
parts.solutionMd:
The completed table is:

| reagent | observation with glycolic acid | functional group |
|---|---|---|
| Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> | **Final answer:** **Effervescence / fizzing / bubbling** | **Final answer:** **–COOH / carboxylic acid** |
| 2,4-DNPH | **Final answer:** **No visible reaction** | **Final answer:** **–** |
| acidified K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> (aq) and heat | **Final answer:** **Orange to green** | **Final answer:** **–OH / alcohol** |

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for effervescence / fizzing **AND** –COOH / carboxylic acid for Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>
> 
> 1 mark for no visible reaction for 2,4-DNPH (no functional group required)
> 
> 1 mark for orange to green **AND** –OH / alcohol for acidified K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub>(aq) and heat

> **[exam-tip]**
> Glycolic acid (HOCH<sub>2</sub>COOH) contains two functional groups: a primary alcohol (–OH) and a carboxylic acid (–COOH).
> 
> - Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>: reacts with the –COOH group, producing CO<sub>2</sub> (seen as effervescence), water, and sodium glycolate
> - 2,4-DNPH: tests specifically for aldehydes and ketones (C=O groups); glycolic acid has no aldehyde or ketone group, so no reaction occurs
> - Acidified K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub>(aq) and heat: the primary alcohol (–OH) is oxidised; Cr(VI) (orange) is reduced to Cr(III) (green)

parts.problemMd:
Two reaction sequences to produce glycolic acid are shown.

**Sequence A**:

> **OR**

parts.problemMd:
i) Compound **B**, CH<sub>3</sub>CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)CH(OH)COOH, can be oxidised into compound **C**.

Construct an equation for this oxidation, using [O] to represent the oxidising agent.

[1]

ii) The half-equation for the reduction of acidified potassium dichromate(VI) is:

Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub><sup>2-</sup> (aq) + 14H<sup>+</sup> (aq) + 6e<sup>–</sup> → 2Cr<sup>3+</sup> (aq) + 7H<sub>2</sub>O (l)

Deduce the overall ionic equation for the oxidation of compound **B** to compound **C** using acidified dichromate(VI).

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The equation for this oxidation, using [O] to represent the oxidising agent is:
> 
> - CH<sub>3</sub>CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)CH(OH)COOH + [O] → CH<sub>3</sub>CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)COCOOH + H<sub>2</sub>O **[1 mark]**
> 
> State symbols are not required

ii) The overall ionic equation for the oxidation of B to C is:

3CH<sub>3</sub>CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)CH(OH)COOH (aq) + Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub><sup>2-</sup> (aq) + 8H<sup>+</sup> (aq) → 3CH<sub>3</sub>CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)COCOOH (aq) + 2Cr<sup>3+</sup> (aq) + 7H<sub>2</sub>O (l)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct reactants and products in the overall equation
> 
> 1 mark for correct balancing
> 
> State symbols are not required

> **[exam-tip]**
> For part (i):
> 
> - [O] represents one oxygen atom from the oxidising agent.
> - In the oxidation of a secondary alcohol –CHOH– to a ketone –C=O–, two hydrogen atoms are removed as H<sub>2</sub>O, so one [O] is needed.
> 
> For part (ii):
> 
> - The B→C half-equation shows 2 electrons transferred.
> - The dichromate half-equation shows 6 electrons.
> - Multiply the B→C half-equation by 3 (to give 6e<sup>–</sup>), add the two half-equations, then cancel the 6H<sup>+</sup> that appear on both sides:
> 
>   - 14H<sup>+</sup> − 6H<sup>+</sup> = 8H<sup>+</sup> on the left.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

An organic ester, **B**, has the empirical formula C~2~H~4~O. The relative molecular mass, *M*~r~, of **B** is 88.0.

The student hydrolysed his sample of **B** by heating with aqueous mineral acid and then separating the alcohol, **C**, that was formed. He heated the alcohol **C** under reflux with acidified dichromate(VI) ions and collected the product **D**.

A sample of **D** gave a yellow/orange precipitate with 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine (2,4-DNP) reagent. A second sample of **D** gave no reaction with Tollens' reagent.

i) State the functional group shown to be present in **D** by the reaction with 2,4-DNP reagent.

[1]

ii) State what the result of the test with Tollens' reagent shows about **D**.

[1]

iii) Deduce the structural formula of the alcohol **C**.

[1]

iv) Which ester has the same structure as that of the ester **B**?

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The functional group shown to be present in D:
> 
> - C=O / carbonyl group **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The result of the Tollens' reagent test shows:
> 
> - No aldehyde / –CHO group is present
> **OR**
> D is a ketone **[1 mark]**
> 
> iii) The structural formula of alcohol C:
> 
> - (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CHOH **[1 mark]**
> 
> iv) The ester with the same structure as B:
> 
> - 1-methylethyl methanoate / HCO<sub>2</sub>CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> 2,4-DNP reacts with all carbonyl compounds (aldehydes and ketones) to form a yellow/orange precipitate. Tollens' reagent gives a silver mirror only with aldehydes. A positive 2,4-DNP result combined with a negative Tollens' result confirms D is a ketone, not an aldehyde.
> 
> The ketone D must be propanone (3 carbons), so the original alcohol C was a secondary alcohol: propan-2-ol, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CHOH. The –OR side of the ester –COO– comes from the alcohol. Propan-2-ol gives the –OCH(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> group, which matches 1-methylethyl methanoate / HCO<sub>2</sub>CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>.

parts.problemMd:
Propylamine can be produced from 1-bromopropane.

Construct an equation for this reaction.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The equation for this reaction is:
> 
> - CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Br + NH<sub>3</sub> → CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> + HBr **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Propylamine has the formula CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>. The propyl- prefix tells you there is a three-carbon chain (CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>–) and the -amine suffix tells you an NH<sub>2</sub> group is attached to it.
> 
> If you cannot recall the product, work backwards from the name. You know the product is an amine (contains N) and the three-carbon chain comes from 1-bromopropane. So the product is CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>.
> 
> Once you know both organic species, balance by counting atoms: you need NH<sub>3</sub> on the left to provide the N and two extra H atoms, and HBr forms as the bromide leaves.

parts.problemMd: State the reagents and conditions required to produce propylamine from 1-bromopropane.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The reagents and conditions required are:
> 
> - Excess ammonia / NH<sub>3</sub> in ethanol / ethanolic solution of ammonia **[1 mark]**
> - Heated under pressure / in a sealed tube **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Excess ammonia is used to prevent the newly formed propylamine from acting as a nucleophile and attacking another molecule of 1-bromopropane. If the ammonia is not in excess, a secondary amine (dipropylamine) would form as a by-product.
> 
> The reaction must be carried out under pressure because ammonia is a gas at room temperature. A sealed tube or pressurised vessel keeps the ammonia in contact with 1-bromopropane long enough to react.

parts.problemMd: Name the mechanism for the reaction of 1-bromopropane with ammonia.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The mechanism for this reaction is:
> 
> - Nucleophilic substitution **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The bromine atom in 1-bromopropane is more electronegative than carbon, so the C–Br bond is polarised (δ+C–δ–Br). The lone pair on the nitrogen atom of ammonia is attracted to this δ+C, making ammonia the nucleophile. The C–Br bond breaks and the bromide ion (Br<sup>–</sup>) leaves, so the overall process is nucleophilic substitution.

parts.problemMd:

CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Cl $\overset{\mathrm{NH}_{3}}{\rightarrow}$ CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>

i) State the role of ammonia in this reaction.

[1]

ii) Name the mechanism of this reaction.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The role of ammonia in this reaction is:
> 
> - Nucleophile **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The mechanism of this reaction is:
> 
> - Nucleophilic substitution **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The nitrogen atom in ammonia has a lone pair of electrons. The carbon of the C–Cl bond carries a partial positive charge (δ+C) because chlorine is more electronegative. The lone pair on N attacks this δ+C, making ammonia the nucleophile.
> 
> Since the Cl atom is replaced by the NH<sub>2</sub> group and a nucleophile performs the replacement, the mechanism is nucleophilic substitution.

parts.problemMd: Use a chemical equation to explain why propylamine acts as a Brønsted-Lowry base when it dissolves in water.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Propylamine acts as a Brønsted-Lowry base because:
> 
> - It accepts a proton / H<sup>+</sup> from water / it has a lone pair of electrons that accepts a proton **[1 mark]**
> 
> The equation is:
> 
> - CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O ⇌ CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup> + OH<sup>-</sup> 
> **OR**
> C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>7</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O ⇌ C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>7</sub>NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup> + OH<sup>-</sup>**[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> A Brønsted-Lowry base is a species that accepts a proton (H<sup>+</sup>). Propylamine has a lone pair on its nitrogen atom. When dissolved in water, this lone pair accepts a proton from H<sub>2</sub>O, forming the propylammonium ion (CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup>) and releasing a hydroxide ion (OH<sup>-</sup>).
> 
> The question asks you to explain, not just state. You must link the lone pair on nitrogen to the ability to accept a proton. Stating 'it accepts a proton' without reference to the lone pair will not score the first mark.
> 
> The equilibrium arrow (⇌) is required because propylamine is a weak base. Weak bases only partially ionise in water.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Propylamine can be produced by the reaction of 1-chloropropane with ammonia.

CH~3~CH~2~CH~2~Cl → CH~3~CH~2~CH~2~NH~2~

The reaction between 1-chloropropane and ammonia proceeds in two steps. Step 1 involves the formation of an intermediate. Step 2 forms the final propylamine product.

As the reaction proceeds, the bond angles around the nitrogen atom change. Explain these changes in the bond angles around the nitrogen atom.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> As the reaction proceeds, the bond angles around nitrogen change:
> 
> - Bond angle in ammonia **AND** propylamine = 107°
> **AND**
> Bond angle in the intermediate = 109.5° **[1 mark]**
> - Lone pair(s) on nitrogen in ammonia **AND** propylamine cause greater repulsion than bonding pairs
> **AND**
> The molecules have a pyramidal shape **[1 mark]**
> - All four bonds / bonding pairs around nitrogen in the intermediate
> **AND**
> The intermediate has a tetrahedral shape **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> In step 1, the lone pair on ammonia attacks the C–Cl bond. This forms an intermediate where nitrogen is bonded to four groups (no lone pairs remaining on N). Four bonding pairs with no lone pairs gives a tetrahedral shape with a bond angle of 109.5°.
> 
> In step 2, a proton is lost from the intermediate and the lone pair is restored on nitrogen in propylamine. One lone pair with three bonding pairs gives a pyramidal shape. The lone pair repels bonding pairs more strongly than bonding pairs repel each other, compressing the angle below the tetrahedral value to 107°.
> 
> Note that ammonia and propylamine have the same bond angle (107°) because both have one lone pair and three bonding pairs around nitrogen.

> **[exam-tip]**

> To find the isomers:

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

**Fig. 3.1**

Draw the mechanism for reaction **1** and label compound **X** in your answer. Include charges, dipoles, lone pairs of electrons and curly arrows, as appropriate.
parts.solutionMd:
The mechanism for reaction **1** is:

![Nucleophilic substitution mechanism showing an ammonia molecule attacking the electron-deficient carbon in 1-chlorobutane, with curly arrows indicating electron movement, partial charges on C and Cl, and the intermediate compound X with a positive charge on nitrogen](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/19-nitrogen-compounds/19-1-primary-amines/assets/014-nucleophilic-substitution-mechanism-showing-an-a.jpg)

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for a curly arrow from the lone pair on N of NH<sub>3</sub> to the C of C–Cl
> 
> 1 mark for a curly arrow from the C–Cl bond to the Cl
> 
> 1 mark for all correct partial charges (δ+ on C and δ– on Cl)
> 
> 1 mark for compound **X** correctly drawn with a positive charge on N and :Cl<sup>-</sup> shown as a byproduct

> **[exam-tip]**
> An ammonia molecule (NH<sub>3</sub>) acts as a nucleophile as the nitrogen atom has a lone pair of electrons that it donates to the electron-deficient carbon atom.
> 
> Since the carbon atom in C–Cl cannot have five bonds, the C–Cl bond breaks and the chlorine is displaced by NH<sub>3</sub>.
> 
> The product formed (compound X) has a nitrogen atom bonded to four atoms and therefore carries a positive charge.
> 
> Read the question carefully as compound X is the intermediate formed before the mechanism is complete, not butylamine itself.
> 
> Curly arrows must start from a lone pair or a bond (not the atom itself):
>

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

One possible method of making butylamine from 1-chlorobutane is shown in Fig. 3.1.

![Reaction scheme showing the two-step synthesis of butylamine from 1-chlorobutane, via intermediate compound X, with compound Y as a byproduct](https://cdn.savemyexams.com/uploads/2024/03/butylamine-synthesis.png)

**Fig. 3.1**

Compound **X** undergoes another reaction in reaction **2** before butylamine is formed.

i) State the role of ammonia in reaction **2**.

[1]

ii) State the formula of compound **Y**.

[1]

iii) The by-products Cl<sup>-</sup> and compound **Y** can combine together to form compound **Z**. State the name of compound **Z**.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The role of ammonia in reaction **2** is:
> 
> - (Brønsted-Lowry) base / proton acceptor **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The formula of compound **Y** is:
> 
> - NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> **[1 mark]**
> 
> iii) The name of compound **Z** is:
> 
> - Ammonium chloride **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Compound X is an organic molecule with an –NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup> group, where the nitrogen atom is bonded to four atoms and carries a positive charge.
> 
> Since ammonia is a neutral nucleophile, a proton (H<sup>+</sup>) must be lost from compound X to form the neutral amine product. Ammonia acts as a Brønsted-Lowry base in reaction 2 by accepting this proton to form NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> (compound Y). This is why excess ammonia is used.
> 
> The ammonium ion (NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>) combines with the chloride ion (Cl<sup>-</sup>) displaced in reaction 1 to form ammonium chloride (NH<sub>4</sub>Cl).
> 
> If a different halogenoalkane were used (for example 1-bromobutane), a Br<sup>-</sup> ion would be formed instead, combining with the ammonium ion to give ammonium bromide (NH<sub>4</sub>Br).

parts.problemMd:
Compound **X** is produced from cyclohexene by reaction with a hydrogen halide.

An amine which is a relatively weak base containing one nitrogen atom can be produced from compound **X** in one step.

Draw the mechanism for the formation of compound **X** from cyclohexene. Include charges, dipoles, lone pairs of electrons and curly arrows, as appropriate. State the hydrogen halide used in your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
The mechanism for the formation of compound **X** from cyclohexene using HBr is:

![Electrophilic addition mechanism showing HBr reacting with cyclohexene: curly arrow from C=C to H of HBr, dipoles on HBr, carbocation intermediate formed, then Br– attacks C+ to form bromocyclohexane](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/19-nitrogen-compounds/19-1-primary-amines/assets/012-electrophilic-addition-mechanism-showing-hbr-rea.png)

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for a curly arrow from the C=C π bond to the H atom of H–Br / H–Cl / H–I
> 
> 1 mark for correct partial charges on the H–X bond (δ+H, δ–X) **AND** a curly arrow from the H–X bond to the X atom
> 
> 1 mark for the correct carbocation intermediate drawn
> 
> 1 mark for a curly arrow from the lone pair on X<sup>–</sup> to the positively charged carbon of the carbocation
> 
> Allow HBr, HCl, or HI as the hydrogen halide; compound **X** is then the corresponding halocyclohexane

> **[exam-tip]**
> This is an electrophilic addition mechanism. The π electrons of the C=C bond act as a nucleophile and are attracted to the δ+ hydrogen of H–Br. Two curly arrows are needed in the first step: one from the C=C to H, and one from the H–Br bond to Br. Both bonds must be shown breaking and forming simultaneously.
> 
> The carbocation intermediate has a positive charge on the carbon that did not bond to H. In the second step, Br<sup>–</sup> attacks this C<sup>+</sup> using its lone pair. The curly arrow must start from the lone pair on Br<sup>–</sup>, not from the Br<sup>–</sup> ion itself.
> 
> You can use HBr, HCl, or HI. The mechanism is the same for all three; compound **X** is the corresponding halocyclohexane (e.g. bromocyclohexane if HBr is used). Compound **X** is a halogenoalkane that can then undergo nucleophilic substitution with excess ethanolic ammonia to form cyclohexylamine.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Compound **X** is produced from cyclohexene by reaction with a hydrogen halide.

An amine which is a relatively weak base containing one nitrogen atom can be produced from compound **X** in one step.

Allow HBr, HCl, or HI as the hydrogen halide; compound **X** is then the corresponding halocyclohexane

Compound **X** reacts with ammonia to form cyclohexylamine.

i) State the reagents and conditions required for this reaction.

[2]

ii) Suggest why an excess of ammonia is used.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The reagents and conditions required are:
> 
> - Excess ammonia / NH<sub>3</sub> in ethanol / ethanolic solution of ammonia **[1 mark]**
> - Heated under pressure / in a sealed tube **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) An excess of ammonia is used to:
> 
> - Prevent the amine / cyclohexylamine from acting as a nucleophile and reacting with (another molecule of) compound **X** / the halogenoalkane
> **OR**
> Prevent the formation of secondary / tertiary amines **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The reaction must be carried out under pressure because ammonia is a gas at room temperature. A sealed tube or pressurised vessel keeps the ammonia in contact with compound **X** long enough to react.
> 
> If ammonia is not in excess, the newly formed cyclohexylamine can act as a nucleophile (it also has a lone pair on nitrogen) and attack another molecule of compound **X**. This produces a secondary amine as a by-product. Excess ammonia ensures the ammonia outcompetes the amine for the available halogenoalkane.

parts.problemMd:
Propylamine acts as a Brønsted-Lowry base when it dissolves in water.

Construct an equation to show this behaviour.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The equation is:
> 
> - CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O ⇌ CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup> + OH<sup>-</sup> 
> **OR**
> C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>7</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O ⇌ C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>7</sub>NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup> + OH<sup>-</sup>**[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> A Brønsted-Lowry base is a species that accepts a proton (H<sup>+</sup>). Propylamine has a lone pair on its nitrogen atom. When dissolved in water, the lone pair accepts a proton from H<sub>2</sub>O, forming the propylammonium ion (CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup>) and releasing a hydroxide ion (OH<sup>-</sup>).
> 
> The equilibrium arrow (⇌) is required because propylamine is a weak base. Weak bases only partially ionise in water, so the forward and reverse reactions both occur simultaneously.

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii) The systematic name of this organic product is:
> 
> - Butanenitrile **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> When halogenoalkanes react with KCN, or NaCN, in ethanol, a nitrile is formed.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

When 1-chloropropane is heated under reflux with ethanolic potassium cyanide, KCN, the following reaction occurs.

CH~3~CH~2~CH~2~Cl + KCN → CH~3~CH~2~CH~2~CN + KCl

Suggest why this reaction is useful to chemists during the synthesis of other organic compounds.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> This reaction is useful to chemists during the synthesis of other organic compounds because:
> 
> - It lengthens the carbon chain / forms a C–C bond **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> This reaction is of particular importance as it forms a carbon-carbon bond which can lengthen the carbon chain.
> 
> This is useful as new compounds can be synthesised which have more carbon atoms.
> 
> Sometimes, an organic compound may not be easily available as a raw material, but another organic compound with one less carbon atom may be readily available.
> 
> If this compound with one less carbon atom is made into a halogenoalkane and then refluxed with ethanolic KCN, a nitrile can be made with the desired number of carbon atoms which can undergo further synthesis.

parts.problemMd:
The CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CN can undergo hydrolysis.

i) Construct an equation for the acid hydrolysis of CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CN.

[1]

ii) Draw the displayed formula of the intermediate formed when CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CN is hydrolysed by sodium hydroxide.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The equation for the acid hydrolysis of CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CN is:
> 
> - CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CN + HCl + 2H<sub>2</sub>O → CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COOH + NH<sub>4</sub>Cl **[1 mark]**

ii) The displayed formula of the intermediate formed when CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CN is hydrolysed by sodium hydroxide is:

![Displayed formula of sodium butanoate](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/19-nitrogen-compounds/19-2-nitriles-and-hydroxynitriles/assets/014-displayed-formula-of-sodium-butanoate.png)

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct displayed formula of sodium butanoate

> **[exam-tip]**
> Hydrolysis of nitriles can occur either by dilute acid or dilute alkali followed by acidification.
> 
> A carboxylic acid is the product in both cases, but when hydrolysed by dilute alkali, a carboxylate salt is the intermediate which requires acidification to form the carboxylic acid.
> 
> Alkali hydrolysis:
> 
> CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CN + NaOH + 2H<sub>2</sub>O → CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COO<sup>–</sup>Na<sup>+</sup> + NH<sub>3</sub>
> 
> Acidification of sodium butanoate produces the carboxylic acid CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COOH.
> 
> Unlike the formation of nitriles (which adds a carbon atom to the carbon chain), hydrolysis does not change the number of carbon atoms.

[2]

**Extract:**

Butene, C~4~H~8~, can exist as three isomers.

Isomer **A** is a position isomer of isomers **B** and **C** and does not show geometric isomerism.

Isomer **B** is the *cis* isomer.

Isomer **C** is the *trans* isomer.

A student was asked to draw the displayed formula of the addition polymer of isomers **B** and **C**. They suggested that there were two structures as shown in Fig. 2.1.

![Two displayed formulae of the addition polymer from but-2-ene isomers, showing apparently different arrangements of methyl groups along the backbone](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/20-polymerisation/20-1-addition-polymerisation/assets/054-two-displayed-formulae-of-the-addition-polymer-f.png)

State why the student's two suggested structures are the same addition polymer.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The two structures are the same addition polymer because:
> 
> - There is free rotation around the C–C single bond
> **OR**
> The C–C bond can freely rotate
> **OR**
> There is no longer a C=C double bond to restrict rotation **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Single C–C bonds allow free rotation, unlike C=C double bonds which are restricted and planar. This means that the geometric isomers **B** and **C** produce identical addition polymers. Once the C=C becomes C–C, the arrangement of groups around that bond no longer matters.

parts.problemMd:

> **[exam-tip]**
> When explaining differences in state for covalent molecules, refer to the type and strength of intermolecular forces. Poly(hept-2-ene) is a much larger molecule with far more electrons than the monomer, so its London (id–id) forces are much stronger. 'Van der Waals forces' is accepted but being specific about London forces is better practice.

parts.problemMd:
The table shows the melting points of two polymers.

| **Polymer** | **Melting point / °C** |
|---|---|
| Poly(ethene) | 137 |
| Poly(chloroethene) (PVC) | 212 |

Explain the differences in melting point of these two polymers in terms of the intermolecular forces between the chains.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explaining the differences in melting point in terms of intermolecular forces:
> 
> - Both polymers have instantaneous dipole–induced dipole / London dispersion forces **[1 mark]**
> - Poly(chloroethene) / PVC also has permanent dipole–permanent dipole forces (due to the polar C–Cl bond) **[1 mark]**
> - Poly(chloroethene) / PVC therefore requires more energy to separate its chains and has a higher melting point **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> PVC is similar to poly(ethene) but has one H atom per repeat unit replaced by Cl. Because Cl is more electronegative than C, the C–Cl bond is polar, giving PVC a permanent dipole. This means PVC has both id–id and pd–pd forces, while poly(ethene) has only id–id forces. The additional pd–pd forces make PVC harder to melt. Note: van der Waals forces is accepted for id–id, but being specific scores better in CIE mark schemes.

parts.problemMd: State **one **advantage and **one **disadvantage of the unreactivity of addition polymers.
parts.solutionMd:

> **[1 mark]**
> 
> Disadvantage:
> 
> Any **one **from:

> **[1 mark]**

parts.problemMd:
Describe one simple test-tube reaction that allows you to distinguish between compounds **I** and **J**, shown in Fig. 2.2.

![methylcyclopentane (I) and (chloromethyl)cyclopentane (J) — skeletal formulae](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/21-organic-synthesis/21-1-organic-synthesis/assets/031-methylcyclopentane-i-and-chloromethyl-cyclopenta.png)

**Fig. 2.2**
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> A test-tube reaction to distinguish between compounds **I** and **J** is:
> 
> - Reagent: warm with aqueous silver nitrate / AgNO<sub>3</sub> (aq) **[1 mark]**
> - Compound **J** (halogenoalkane) produces a white precipitate (silver chloride / AgCl)
> **AND**
> Compound **I** (saturated hydrocarbon) produces no precipitate **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Compound **I** is methylcyclopentane, a saturated hydrocarbon. Compound **J** is (chloromethyl)cyclopentane, a halogenoalkane.
> 
> When warmed with aqueous silver nitrate, the C–Cl bond in **J** undergoes hydrolysis, releasing Cl<sup>-</sup> ions that precipitate as white silver chloride (AgCl). The saturated hydrocarbon **I** has no halogen and produces no precipitate.
> 
> Warming is needed to provide sufficient energy for hydrolysis of the C–Cl bond. State the colour and composition of the precipitate clearly: white AgCl.

parts.problemMd:
Describe one simple test-tube reaction that allows you to distinguish between compounds **K** and **L**, shown in Fig. 2.3.

![propanal (K) and propanoic acid (L) — skeletal formulae](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/21-organic-synthesis/21-1-organic-synthesis/assets/032-propanal-k-and-propanoic-acid-l-skeletal-formula.png)

**Fig. 2.3**
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> A test-tube reaction to distinguish between compounds **K** and **L** is:
> 
> Any **one** of the following pairs (1 mark for the reagent and 1 mark for the associated observation):
> 
> Pair 1
> 
> - Reagent: Tollens' reagent / ammoniacal silver nitrate
> - Observations: Compound **K** (aldehyde / propanal) produces a silver mirror
> **AND**
> Compound **L** (carboxylic acid / propanoic acid) produces no reaction
> 
> Pair 2
> 
> - Reagent: Benedict's / Fehling's solution
> - Observations: Compound **K** (aldehyde / propanal) produces a red / brick-red precipitate
> **AND**
> Compound **L** (carboxylic acid / propanoic acid) produces no reaction
> 
> Pair 3
> 
> - Reagent: Sodium carbonate / Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> / sodium hydrogencarbonate / NaHCO<sub>3</sub>
> - Observations: Compound **K** (aldehyde / propanal) produces no reaction
> **AND**
> Compound **L** (carboxylic acid / propanoic acid) produces effervescence / CO<sub>2</sub> / bubbles
> 
> **[2 marks]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Compound **K** is propanal, an aldehyde. Compound **L** is propanoic acid, a carboxylic acid.
> 
> Aldehydes are reducing agents:
> 
> - Tollens' reagent is reduced to give a silver mirror
> - Fehling's solution is reduced to give a red/brick-red precipitate.
> - Carboxylic acids do not reduce these reagents.
> 
> Alternatively, sodium carbonate or sodium hydrogencarbonate reacts with the carboxylic acid (**L**) to produce CO<sub>2</sub> effervescence; the aldehyde (**K**) does not react. If using this reagent, the positive observation is for compound **L**, not compound **K**.

parts.problemMd:
A reaction pathway is shown in Fig. 3.1.

![Reaction pathway showing 1-bromopropane (compound A) converting to propene (compound B) via elimination, and to butanenitrile (compound C) via nucleophilic substitution](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/21-organic-synthesis/21-1-organic-synthesis/assets/034-reaction-pathway-showing-1-bromopropane-compound.png)

**Fig. 3.1**

State the reagents and conditions required for the conversion of:

i) compound **A** to compound **B**

[3]

ii) compound **A** to compound **C**

[3]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The reagents and conditions required are:
> 
> i) Conversion of compound **A** to compound **B** (elimination):
> 
> - Potassium hydroxide / KOH / sodium hydroxide / NaOH **[1 mark]**
> - Ethanol / ethanolic / alcoholic **[1 mark]**
> - Heat / heat under reflux **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) Conversion of compound **A** to compound **C** (nucleophilic substitution):
> 
> - Potassium cyanide / KCN **[1 mark]**
> - Ethanol / ethanolic / alcoholic **[1 mark]**
> - Heat / heat under reflux **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The conversion of a halogenoalkane to an alkene (**A** to **B**) is an elimination reaction. It requires an alkoxide/hydroxide base dissolved in ethanol as the solvent, heated under reflux. Using aqueous conditions instead would give nucleophilic substitution to produce an alcohol, not the alkene.
> 
> The conversion of a halogenoalkane to a nitrile (**A** to **C**) is a nucleophilic substitution. The cyanide ion (CN<sup>-</sup>) from KCN acts as the nucleophile, displacing the halide. Ethanol is used as solvent and heat is applied.

**Fig. 3.1**

State the systematic name of compound **C** shown in Fig. 3.1 in part **(a)**.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The systematic name of compound **C** is:
> 
> - Butanenitrile **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> When a cyanide ion (CN<sup>-</sup>) reacts with a halogenoalkane by nucleophilic substitution, the CN group adds one carbon to the chain. Compound **A** has three carbon atoms, so compound **C** has four carbons in total.
> 
> When naming a nitrile, count the CN carbon as part of the main chain. Butanenitrile has four carbons: CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CN.

parts.problemMd:
But-2-ene can be converted into butan-2-ol by two different synthetic routes. One route is a one-step process and the other is a two-step process.

State the reagents and conditions required for the one-step process. Construct an equation for this reaction using structural formulae.

reagents and conditions

......................................................................................................................

equation

......................................................................................................................
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The reagents, conditions and equation for the one-step process (hydration) are:
> 
> - Steam / water vapour / H<sub>2</sub>O (g) **[1 mark]**
> - Concentrated phosphoric acid / H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>4</sub> catalyst
> **OR**
> Concentrated sulfuric acid / H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> catalyst **[1 mark]**
> - CH<sub>3</sub>CH=CHCH<sub>3</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O → CH<sub>3</sub>CH(OH)CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The one-step conversion of an alkene directly to an alcohol is hydration. It requires steam (not liquid water) and a strong acid catalyst such as phosphoric acid or sulfuric acid.
> 
> This reaction is also an example of electrophilic addition.

parts.problemMd:

But-2-ene can be converted into butan-2-ol by two different synthetic routes. One route is a one-step process and the other is a two-step process.

For the two-step process, identify the intermediate organic compound and state the reagents and conditions required for each step.

intermediate

......................................................................................................................

step 1 reagents and conditions

......................................................................................................................

step 2 reagents and conditions

......................................................................................................................
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The intermediate and reagents/conditions are:
> 
> - Intermediate: 2-bromobutane **[1 mark]**
> - Step 1 reagent: hydrogen bromide / HBr **[1 mark]**
> - Step 2 reagent: aqueous sodium hydroxide / NaOH (aq) **AND **heat under reflux
> **OR**
> Aqueous potassium hydroxide / KOH (aq) **AND **heat under reflux **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Step 1 is electrophilic addition of HBr to but-2-ene. Because but-2-ene is a symmetrical alkene, there is only one possible product: 2-bromobutane.
> 
> Step 2 is nucleophilic substitution: aqueous NaOH (or KOH) replaces the Br with OH, giving butan-2-ol.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

But-2-ene can be converted into butan-2-ol by two different synthetic routes. One route is a one-step process and the other is a two-step process.

One-step process (hydration):
- Reagents: Steam / water vapour / H₂O (g)
- Conditions: Concentrated phosphoric acid / H₃PO₄ catalyst OR Concentrated sulfuric acid / H₂SO₄ catalyst

Two-step process:
- Intermediate: 2-bromobutane
- Step 1 reagent: hydrogen bromide / HBr
- Step 2 reagent: aqueous sodium hydroxide / NaOH (aq) AND heat under reflux OR Aqueous potassium hydroxide / KOH (aq) AND heat under reflux

But-1-ene can also be used to form butan-2-ol by both the one-step and two-step reaction routes.

Explain why using but-1-ene gives a lower yield of butan-2-ol compared to using but-2-ene.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Using but-1-ene gives a lower yield of butan-2-ol because:
> 
> - But-1-ene is an unsymmetrical alkene, so when the C=C breaks it can form a primary or a secondary carbocation intermediate **[1 mark]**
> - This results in the formation of both butan-1-ol and butan-2-ol, reducing the yield of butan-2-ol **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> But-2-ene is a symmetrical alkene where the two carbons of the C=C are equivalent, so only one product is possible: butan-2-ol.
> 
> But-1-ene is unsymmetrical, so two different carbocation intermediates can form, giving a mixture of products. The yield of butan-2-ol is lower because some of the but-1-ene converts to butan-1-ol instead.

Reaction with cold dilute acidified KMnO<sub>4</sub>:

![Fully displayed formula of butane-2,3-diol, the product of cold dilute acidified KMnO4 with but-2-ene](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/21-organic-synthesis/21-1-organic-synthesis/assets/028-fully-displayed-formula-of-butane-2-3-diol-the-p.jpeg)

**[1 mark]**

Reaction with hot concentrated acidified KMnO<sub>4</sub>:

![Fully displayed formula of ethanoic acid, two molecules formed from hot concentrated acidified KMnO4 with but-2-ene](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/21-organic-synthesis/21-1-organic-synthesis/assets/029-fully-displayed-formula-of-ethanoic-acid-two-mol.jpeg)

> - Colour change: purple to colourless.

> Hot concentrated acidified KMnO<sub>4</sub>:

Draw the structural formulae of compounds **U** and **V**.

**U** ......................................................................................................................

**V** ......................................................................................................................
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The structural formulae of **U** and **V** are:
> 
> Any **one** of the following pairs (1 mark for **U** and 1 mark for **V**):
> 
> Pair 1
> 
> - **U** = CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH(OH)CH<sub>3</sub>
> - **V** = CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CHBrCH<sub>3</sub>
> 
> Pair 2
> 
> - **U** = CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH
> - **V** = CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Br
> 
> **[2 marks]**
> 
> **U** and **V** must be consistent with each other (i.e. if **U** is the secondary alcohol, **V** must be the secondary bromoalkane).

> **[exam-tip]**
> But-1-ene is an unsymmetrical alkene. When it reacts with steam (electrophilic addition / hydration), two alcohols can form:
> 
> - Butan-2-ol: major product (via more stable secondary carbocation)
> - Butan-1-ol: minor product (via less stable primary carbocation)
> 
> Whichever alcohol you choose for **U**, compound **V** is the corresponding bromoalkane formed by reaction of that alcohol with HBr.

parts.problemMd: Explain why 2-hydroxy-2-methylpropanenitrile does not exhibit optical isomerism.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> 2-hydroxy-2-methylpropanenitrile does not exhibit optical isomerism because:
>

> - The central carbon bears two identical methyl groups (two of the four substituents are the same), so it does not have four different groups attached; **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For optical isomerism to occur, a molecule must contain a chiral carbon (a carbon with four different atoms or groups attached).
> 
> It can help to draw out the structure and identify the main carbon chain. In nitriles, the CN carbon is the first carbon.
> 
> ![Structure showing a three‑carbon chain with OH, CH₃ and CN substituents labelled on carbons 1–3 in a stylised organic chemistry diagram](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/21-organic-synthesis/21-1-organic-synthesis/assets/039-structure-showing-a-three-carbon-chain-with-oh-c.jpeg)
> 
> In 2-hydroxy-2-methylpropanenitrile, the central carbon is bonded to: –OH, –CN, –CH<sub>3</sub>, and –CH<sub>3</sub>. Since two of the groups are identical (–CH<sub>3</sub>), this carbon is not chiral and optical isomers cannot form.

parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> A major and a minor product are produced because:
> 
> - The reaction proceeds via a tertiary carbocation intermediate (giving the major product)
> **OR**
> A secondary carbocation intermediate (giving the minor product) **[1 mark]**
> - The tertiary carbocation is more stable than the secondary carbocation, due to the greater electron-donating effect of three alkyl groups delocalising the positive charge **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**

> 
> Tertiary carbocations are more stable because three alkyl groups donate electron density towards the positive charge. The more stable intermediate forms more readily, so the tertiary carbocation pathway is favoured and 1-bromo-1-methylcyclohexane is the major product.

*M*<sub>r</sub> = $\frac{2.754}{0.0270}$

*M*<sub>r</sub> = 102.0 g mol<sup>-1</sup> **[1 mark]**

- Compound **Y** has 5 carbons
- It is a carboxylic acid (oxidation product of a primary alcohol)
- So, compound **Y** is:

**pentanoic acid** **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Start by calculating *M*<sub>r</sub>.
> 
> - With 5 carbons (60 g mol<sup>-1</sup>) accounted for, the remaining mass is 42 g mol<sup>-1</sup>.
> - Testing with 2 oxygen atoms: 42 − 32 = 10 g mol<sup>-1</sup> of hydrogen, giving C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O<sub>2</sub>
> - This is consistent with a carboxylic acid.
> 
> Compound **X** is a primary alcohol (pentan-1-ol), which oxidises fully to the carboxylic acid (compound **Y**). A carboxylic acid has two oxygen atoms in the formula.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Compounds **W**, **X**, **Y** and **Z** contain carbon, hydrogen and oxygen only. Compounds **X** and **Y** are unbranched molecules, each containing five carbon atoms. **X** reacts with **Y** in the presence of an acid catalyst to form **W** and a by-product, **Z**. **X** can be oxidised by heating with acidified potassium dichromate(VI) to give **Y**.

Draw the structural formula of compound **W** and identify by-product **Z**.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The structural formula of compound **W** and identity of **Z** are:
> 
> - **W** = CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COOCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> **[1 mark]**
> - Compound **Z** = H<sub>2</sub>O, formed by condensation reaction between compound **X** (pentan-1-ol) and compound **Y** (pentanoic acid); **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Compound **W** is an ester formed from pentanoic acid (**Y**) and pentan-1-ol (**X**). Its systematic name is pentyl pentanoate.
> 
> The condensation reaction between an alcohol and a carboxylic acid always produces an ester and water. The water molecule is lost from the −OH of the acid and the H of the alcohol's −OH group.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Compounds **W**, **X**, **Y** and **Z** contain carbon, hydrogen and oxygen only. Compounds **X** and **Y** are unbranched molecules, each containing five carbon atoms. **X** reacts with **Y** in the presence of an acid catalyst to form **W** and a by-product, **Z**. **X** can be oxidised by heating with acidified potassium dichromate(VI) to give **Y**.

By altering the reaction conditions, the oxidation of compound **X** can be stopped before compound **Y** is produced.

Identify the homologous series of the organic compound produced at this intermediate stage and state the conditions required to favour its formation.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The homologous series and conditions are:
> 
> - Aldehyde / pentanal **[1 mark]**
> - Distil the product immediately as it forms / use distillation conditions so it is removed from the reaction mixture before further oxidation can occur **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> A primary alcohol oxidises in two stages: first to an aldehyde, then to a carboxylic acid. To stop at the aldehyde stage, the aldehyde must be removed from the reaction mixture as soon as it forms. This is achieved by distilling it off immediately.
> 
> Under reflux conditions, the aldehyde stays in the flask and is further oxidised to the carboxylic acid. Using distillation instead of reflux prevents this.

Compound **X** is a primary alcohol (pentan-1-ol), which oxidises fully to the carboxylic acid (compound **Y**).

Draw the skeletal formula of a structural isomer of compound **X** that does not react with acidified potassium dichromate(VI), H<sup>+</sup>/K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub>, and state its systematic name.

> **[exam-tip]**
> For a C<sub>5</sub> alcohol to not react with acidified K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub>, it must be a tertiary alcohol. Only 2-methylbutan-2-ol fits: the central carbon has an OH group and is bonded to three other carbon atoms (no H on the OH-bearing carbon).

parts.problemMd:
There are three possible isomers, **A**, **B** and **C**, with the molecular formula C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O.

Isomers **A** and **B** are positional isomers of each other.

Isomer **C** is a functional group isomer of **A** and **B**.

The percentage by mass of carbon in all three isomers is 60.0%.

Calculate the percentage by mass of hydrogen and oxygen in all three isomers.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the percentage by mass of hydrogen and oxygen in C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O:

- Calculate the *M*<sub>r</sub> of C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O:

*M*<sub>r</sub> = (3 x 12.0) + (8 x 1.0) + 16.0

*M*<sub>r</sub> = 60.0

**[1 mark]**

- Calculate the percentage by mass of each element:

% by mass = $\frac{\mathrm{total} \mathrm{mass} \mathrm{of} \mathrm{element}}{\mathrm{overall} \mathrm{mass} \mathrm{of} \mathrm{compound}}$ x 100

% by mass of H = $\frac{8.0}{60.0}$ x 100 = 13.3%

% by mass of O = $\frac{16.0}{60.0}$ x 100 = 26.7%

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for *M*<sub>r</sub> = 60.0
> 
> 1 mark for % H = 13.3% **AND** % O = 26.7%
> 
> Percentages given to 2 significant figures are accepted

> **[exam-tip]**
> All three isomers have the same molecular formula, so they all have the same percentage by mass for each element.
> 
> To find percentage by mass: divide the total mass of the element in one molecule by *M*<sub>r</sub>, then multiply by 100.
> 
> Check your answer:
> 
> 60.0 + 13.3 + 26.7 = 100.0
